000f67a6-4594-47b4-b88b-3341a6bf9255.title: ASP - ARK SERVICE PROVIDER
000f67a6-4594-47b4-b88b-3341a6bf9255.body:
An operator of the Ark protocol, responsible for managing VTXOs and for periodically anchoring transactions on the Bitcoin blockchain. The ASP organizes “rounds” (every 15 to 60 minutes depending on configuration) during which users' VTXO transactions are consolidated and recorded *on-chain*, preventing any fractional reserve.

The ASP is *non-custodial*: it does not directly hold users' funds and therefore cannot steal them. However, if a user does not connect during the expiry period of their VTXOs (typically 4 weeks), the ASP can recover the associated liquidity. This model orients Ark toward everyday payments rather than long-term storage. The ASP also ensures interoperability with the Lightning Network via gateways, allowing Ark users to send and receive Lightning payments.

ASPs are by nature larger than *Lightning Service Providers* (LSPs), which could encourage a certain centralization of the system. To mitigate this risk, ASPs can be federated or operate peer-to-peer. For institutions or large bitcoin holders, operating an ASP is a yield opportunity with a minimum of required trust, by providing the liquidity needed by the protocol.

001a4e7a-069b-495b-b579-0e478248b1d2.title: DEFLATION
001a4e7a-069b-495b-b579-0e478248b1d2.body:
An economic phenomenon characterized by a general and lasting decline in the price level of goods and services. Unlike inflation, deflation means that the purchasing power of money increases over time: with the same amount of money, one can acquire more goods.

Deflation can result from a contraction of the money supply, an increase in productivity or a drop in demand. Keynesian economists generally consider it harmful, because it would encourage agents to postpone their purchases, thereby slowing economic activity. Economists of the Austrian school, however, distinguish monetary deflation (an artificial contraction of credit) from the fall in prices linked to productivity gains, the latter being seen as beneficial.

Bitcoin is often described as "deflationary" because of its supply capped at 21 million units and the gradual reduction of its issuance through *halvings*. More precisely, it is disinflationary: its issuance rate decreases over time and will converge toward zero.

004843a3-f352-4f82-a505-32e9c522edb1.title: CGMINER
004843a3-f352-4f82-a505-32e9c522edb1.body: *Open-source* mining software initially developed for CPU and GPU. CGminer allows users to manage and optimize their mining operations, with features such as *multi-threading*, management of multiple pools and real-time performance monitoring. The software is no longer really maintained these days, but it has been replaced by Braiins' *open-source* BOSminer project, which was rewritten from scratch in Rust.

0078e884-b7a8-4727-83cd-7f1945cca8a0.title: ROUTING NODE
0078e884-b7a8-4727-83cd-7f1945cca8a0.body:
A Lightning Network node that forwards payments between other nodes by acting as an intermediary in the routing of transactions. When a payment is sent between two users who do not share a direct channel, the Lightning network identifies a path made up of one or more routing nodes to relay the funds step by step via HTLCs. Each routing node temporarily locks funds in a channel, then passes them on to the next node, possibly collecting small routing fees in return for this service. Routing nodes play an essential role in the connectivity of the Lightning network, because they make it possible to reach any recipient without needing a direct channel with each counterparty. A good routing node maintains sufficient liquidity and good connectivity with the other nodes of the network.

By extension, operating a routing node can be a strategy for a node operator wishing to generate income from routing fees.

007c2d5c-ab8d-43d0-9816-049921308ceb.title: BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY
007c2d5c-ab8d-43d0-9816-049921308ceb.body:
Refers to the ability of a protocol rule update to maintain compatibility with earlier versions. This means the changes are designed so that old nodes (nodes running versions prior to the rule change) can still interact with the network and follow the chain with the most accumulated work. Old nodes must therefore reject neither the new blocks nor the new transactions.

Backward compatibility greatly reduces the probability that an update fragments the network, thus avoiding the division of nodes into subgroups on different chains. To ensure compatibility with earlier versions of the protocol, an update must make the existing rules stricter or introduce new ones. This principle is what defines a “soft fork”. Conversely, if an update loosens existing rules or removes some of them, it will not be backward compatible. It will then be a “hard fork”.

00b5e757-9db2-4dc5-814c-3f5b5054ac19.title: OP_2ROT - 0X71
00b5e757-9db2-4dc5-814c-3f5b5054ac19.body:
Moves the two items that are at the sixth and fifth places from the top of the stack to the top. For example, if the stack is:

```text
A
B
C
D
E
F
```

`OP_2ROT` will produce:

```text
E
F
A
B
C
D
```

0122057f-422b-4468-9b94-514d0cd9897a.title: XMR - MONERO
0122057f-422b-4468-9b94-514d0cd9897a.body: Alternative cryptocurrency (altcoin) launched in April 2014, focused on transaction privacy. Monero (XMR) uses several cryptographic techniques to conceal by default the identity of senders, recipients and the amounts exchanged: ring signatures (*ring signatures*), stealth addresses (*stealth addresses*) and the RingCT protocol (*Ring Confidential Transactions*). Unlike Bitcoin, where transactions are pseudonymous and traceable on a public blockchain, Monero makes chain analysis significantly more difficult. Its mining algorithm, RandomX, is designed to resist ASICs and to favor mining with processors (CPUs).

012a6fa2-e437-4f13-82ac-002bc44bf738.title: STUCKLESS PAYMENT
012a6fa2-e437-4f13-82ac-002bc44bf738.body:
A proposal to solve the problem of stuck payments on the Lightning Network. With current HTLCs, a payment can remain stuck without being either completed or canceled, for example if an intermediate node goes offline or deliberately holds the HTLC. The sender must then wait for the *timelock* to expire to recover their funds, and cannot retry the same payment without risking paying the recipient twice.

*Stuckless payments*, proposed by Hiroki Gondo, are based on PTLCs and add an extra round of communication between the sender and the recipient when the payment is set up and settled. This mechanism introduces a confirmation key (*acknowledgment key*) that the sender controls: the recipient can only finalize the payment after receiving this key. The sender can thus launch several attempts in parallel over different routes, with the guarantee that if one succeeds, all the others will automatically fail. This eliminates the risk of double payment and improves routing reliability on Lightning.

013c96c4-6b48-46d0-bfa8-0fc0d0b31959.title: POOL HOPPING
013c96c4-6b48-46d0-bfa8-0fc0d0b31959.body: Refers to the practice of some miners who frequently switch mining pools in order to maximize their earnings. These miners move from one pool to another depending on variations in profitability. This strategy exploits the differences in the pools' reward calculation methods. *Pool hopping* can unbalance the distribution of rewards within pools and is generally considered an unfair practice in the community.

01676c23-17d9-48c4-8817-bf7be488b5e0.title: NONCE
01676c23-17d9-48c4-8817-bf7be488b5e0.body:
In the context of computing, the term "nonce" designates a number used only once, then replaced. It is often random or pseudo-random. It is used in various cryptographic protocols to guarantee the security of the process. For example, the ECDSA signatures used within the Bitcoin protocol involve the use of a nonce. This means that this number must be new for each signature. If it is not, it is possible to calculate the private key used by comparing two signatures that use the same nonce.

Nonces are also used in the mining process on Bitcoin. Miners increment these modifiable values within their candidate blocks. They change the value of the nonce in order to find a cryptographic fingerprint less than or equal to the difficulty target. This process requires a great deal of computing power, because it is an exhaustive search among a large number of possible nonces. When a miner finds a nonce which, when included in its block, produces a hash meeting the difficulty criteria, the block is broadcast to the network, and the miner wins the reward.

*In 2010, researchers discovered that Sony's PlayStation 3 used the same nonce when signing different packets of code. This reuse of the nonce allowed attackers to calculate the private key used to sign the software. With the private key in hand, the attackers could create valid signatures for any code, which allowed them to run unauthorized software, including pirated games or custom operating systems, directly on the PS3.*

*There is a common misconception about the origin of the term "nonce". Some claim that it stands for the abbreviation of "number only used once". In reality, the origin of the word goes back to the 12th century and comes from the semantic evolution of the Middle English expression "for then anes", which meant "for this occasion".*

0192b056-c5ab-4396-b1e2-18cffaa1ea8d.title: BRANCH - BITCOIN
0192b056-c5ab-4396-b1e2-18cffaa1ea8d.body: In the context of Bitcoin, a branch is a sequence of valid blocks in which each new block is linked to the previous one. The blockchain represents the branch that contains the most accumulated work, but competing branches may exist as a result of forks. Each branch shares at least one block in common with the main branch, namely the Genesis block. The part of the blocks specific to the branch is sometimes called the “segment”. When two competing branches are present, honest nodes synchronize on the one with the most accumulated work. A branch is sometimes described as “strong” if it has more accumulated work than another, and as “weak” otherwise.

01af2432-df27-4716-bd5d-5d6ab1239ce2.title: OP_ROLL - 0X7A
01af2432-df27-4716-bd5d-5d6ab1239ce2.body: Moves an element of the stack to the top of the stack, based on the depth specified by the value at the top of the stack before the operation. For example, if the value at the top of the stack is `4`, `OP_ROLL` will select the fifth element of the stack from the top (indexing starts at `0`), and it will move this value to the top. `OP_ROLL` plays the same role as `OP_PICK`, except that it removes the element from its original position.

01b2a7ec-2c60-4ba1-bd45-468f64757cdb.title: CODEX32
01b2a7ec-2c60-4ba1-bd45-468f64757cdb.body:
Scheme for encoding and backing up BIP-0032 seeds on paper, specified in BIP-0093. Codex32 stands out from existing alternatives through the ability to manually verify the integrity of a backup, without using any electronic device.

The system relies on Shamir's secret sharing: the seed can be split into several shares (*shares*), of which only a configurable subset (quorum) is needed to reconstruct the secret. Each share is encoded as a Bech32 character string that includes a checksum (*checksum*). It is this checksum that makes Codex32 unique: it can be computed and verified entirely by hand using lookup tables or rotating paper templates called “volvelles”. The operation remains laborious, but it guarantees that a user can audit their backups in a completely offline environment and without any digital component.

Codex32 supports 128-bit and 256-bit seeds. It is an alternative to SatoshiLabs' SLIP39 scheme, which also offers Shamir sharing but requires an electronic device for verification. Core Lightning integrated support for Codex32 for seed backup and restoration in 2023.

0234d21f-7018-4225-a34b-5906a7754219.title: ASSIGNMENT
0234d21f-7018-4225-a34b-5906a7754219.body:
In the logic of the RGB protocol, an Assignment is the equivalent of a transaction output that modifies, updates or creates certain properties within the state of a contract. An Assignment has two elements:
* A Seal Definition (the reference to a specific UTXO);
* An Owned State (the data describing the state associated with this new holder).

An Assignment therefore indicates that a portion of the state (for example, an asset) is now allocated to a particular holder, identified via a Single-use Seal linked to a UTXO.

027690a7-0005-4df0-ab40-0524604a91e5.title: NEUTRINO
027690a7-0005-4df0-ab40-0524604a91e5.body:
A lightweight Bitcoin client written in Go and developed by Lightning Labs. Designed for mobile applications using the Lightning Network, Neutrino implements the *compact block filters* protocol defined in BIP-0157 and BIP-0158 to synchronize the blockchain while minimizing bandwidth and storage.

Neutrino downloads only block headers and compact filter headers. Filters and full blocks are loaded on demand when a match is detected with the watched scripts. It offers *rescan* features to scan the blockchain for relevant transactions, as well as a `GetUtxo` function to verify the existence and spent status of an output.

Neutrino is notably used as a *backend* by LND for lightweight setups that do not require a full Bitcoin Core node. The term "Neutrino" is sometimes used loosely to refer to the BIP-0157/0158 protocol itself, whereas it designates only this specific client library.

0276bbc2-a706-44ab-8b9a-706d5ae949a7.title: COINS/
0276bbc2-a706-44ab-8b9a-706d5ae949a7.body: Name of the old folder used in Bitcoin Core to store the UTXO set, replaced by the `chainstate/` folder in version 0.8.0.

028ffb5d-98f6-46c0-9d3e-317e7f06e03a.title: REGTEST
028ffb5d-98f6-46c0-9d3e-317e7f06e03a.body: A private testing environment for Bitcoin that allows developers to create a local Bitcoin network with the same basic rules as the *testnet*. Unlike the *testnet*, a *regtest* is private, meaning it is not possible to connect to it freely. Also, it offers total control over the network parameters. It notably allows rapid mining of blocks and the testing of specific scenarios. It is used for development, debugging and experimentation before implementation on the *testnet* or the *mainnet*. The bitcoins in circulation on a *regtest* have no value.

02b92c71-1e90-4093-bb95-e26cba03d2e6.title: NOSTR
02b92c71-1e90-4093-bb95-e26cba03d2e6.body: An open and decentralized communication protocol, whose acronym stands for *Notes and Other Stuff Transmitted by Relays*. Created by fiatjaf in 2020, Nostr relies on a simple architecture: clients cryptographically sign events (the protocol's unique data structure) and publish them to relays, servers that store and redistribute these events. A user's identity is a pair of cryptographic keys on the secp256k1 curve, the same one used by Bitcoin. No central server controls access or content: if a relay censors a user, that user can migrate to other relays without losing their identity or their audience. Nostr is closely linked to the Bitcoin ecosystem, notably through the native integration of *zaps* (Lightning micropayments) and the use of the same cryptographic infrastructure. The protocol is extensible thanks to NIPs (*Nostr Implementation Possibilities*), community specifications that define event formats and features. Beyond *micro-blogging*, Nostr serves as a foundation for a variety of applications: encrypted messaging, long-form articles, *marketplaces*, closed groups or even code collaboration via Git.

02b9a69f-7212-4e1f-b32a-6692a27977a8.title: COVERT ASICBOOST
02b9a69f-7212-4e1f-b32a-6692a27977a8.body: Secret version of AsicBoost. AsicBoost is an algorithmic optimization method for Bitcoin mining. In its Covert version, miners manipulate the Merkle tree rather than the Nonce, which thus reduces the calculations needed for each SHA256 hash by keeping certain data unchanged between hashing attempts. Unlike the Overt version of AsicBoost, the Covert version conceals the use of AsicBoost during the mining process. However, since the introduction of SegWit and its second Merkle tree, this method is no longer effective, because the number of calculations required to use it has become too large compared to a classic mining process.

02ea6b8a-aa60-4bd0-aa13-b9e8b07323b1.title: APO - ANYPREVOUT
02ea6b8a-aa60-4bd0-aa13-b9e8b07323b1.body: Name given to BIP-0118, which proposes adding two new modifier SigHash Flags, named `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` and `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUTANYSCRIPT`. The term "*AnyPrevOut*" comes from the contraction of "*Any Previous Output*", which could be translated into French as "toute sortie précédente".

03141aa4-ec98-4507-96c8-c786a84c35b9.title: BIP-0345
03141aa4-ec98-4507-96c8-c786a84c35b9.body: Proposal to add two opcodes, `OP_VAULT` and `OP_VAULT_RECOVER`, making it possible to create native “*vaults*” on Bitcoin. A vault is a security mechanism that imposes a waiting period when withdrawing funds: during this period, the owner can cancel the transaction and redirect the funds to a predefined recovery address. This system protects against theft by offering a window to react even if the main keys are compromised. Proposed by James O'Beirne, BIP-0345 was closed in favor of `OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY` (BIP-0443).

03547138-8047-405c-bb69-8dbe02bb2c86.title: ANTI-EXFIL SIGNING
03547138-8047-405c-bb69-8dbe02bb2c86.body:
A signing protocol that prevents a compromised hardware wallet from leaking the user's private key through the signatures it produces. In the ECDSA or Schnorr signature scheme, each signature requires a random nonce. A malicious device can manipulate this nonce to discreetly encode information about the private key in it, an attack known as a "covert channel" (*covert channel*) attack. The Dark Skippy attack notably showed that it is possible to extract an entire HD seed with only two signatures.

The anti-exfiltration protocol (also called "anti-kleptography") relies on an exchange of nonce contributions between the host (the wallet software) and the hardware wallet. The host first provides a random value to the hardware signer, which must incorporate it into the computation of its nonce. The final nonce therefore results from the combination of the two contributions, which prevents either party from controlling it alone. Thanks to a cryptographic commitment, the host can verify that its contribution was indeed taken into account in the signature produced.

This mechanism is implemented in hardware wallets such as the BitBox02 and Blockstream's Jade. It is an essential defense against supply chain attacks, where a device's firmware could have been modified before delivery.

03736df6-22a9-4fa3-8e9b-5806c5ab2c3c.title: STONEWALL X2
03736df6-22a9-4fa3-8e9b-5806c5ab2c3c.body:
A specific form of Bitcoin transaction aimed at increasing users' privacy when spending, through collaboration with a third party not involved in that spend. This method simulates a mini-coinjoin between two participants, while making a payment to a third party. Stonewall x2 transactions are available on both the Samourai Wallet application and the Sparrow Wallet software (the two are interoperable).

Its operation is relatively simple: one uses a UTXO in one's possession to make the payment and asks for the help of a third person who also contributes a UTXO belonging to them. The transaction ends up with four outputs: two of them of equal amounts, one destined for the payment recipient's address, the other for an address belonging to the collaborator. A third UTXO is sent back to another address of the collaborator, allowing them to recover the initial amount (a neutral action for them, modulo mining fees), and a last UTXO returns to an address belonging to us, which constitutes the change of the payment. Three different roles are thus defined in Stonewall x2 transactions:
* The sender, who makes the actual payment;
* The collaborator, who makes bitcoins available in order to improve the transaction's anonymity set, while recovering their funds in full at the end;
* The recipient, who may be unaware of the specific nature of the transaction and simply expects a payment from the sender.

![Stonewall x2: 2 inputs from the sender and a collaborator, 4 outputs including two of identical amounts to blur the analysis.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/s/stonewall-x2/assets/image-1.png)

The Stonewall x2 structure adds a great deal of entropy to the transaction and muddies the trail for chain analysis. Seen from the outside, such a transaction can be interpreted as a small coinjoin between two people. But in reality, it is a payment. This method therefore generates uncertainty in chain analysis, and even points toward false leads. Even if the outside observer manages to identify the pattern of the Stonewall x2 transaction, they will not have all the information. They will not be able to determine which of the two UTXOs of the same amounts corresponds to the payment. Moreover, they will not be able to know who made the payment. Finally, they will not be able to determine whether the two input UTXOs come from two different people or belong to a single person who merged them. This last point is due to the fact that classic Stonewall transactions follow exactly the same pattern as Stonewall x2 transactions. Seen from the outside and without additional information about the context, it is impossible to differentiate a Stonewall transaction from a Stonewall x2 transaction. Yet the former are not collaborative transactions, whereas the latter are. This adds even more doubt about the spend.

03bffb41-760c-40ef-b60c-3f66d2f13679.title: LITD
03bffb41-760c-40ef-b60c-3f66d2f13679.body: Daemon (*daemon*) that bundles several Lightning Labs tools into a single process: LND, Loop, Pool, Faraday and Taproot Assets. By running *litd*, a node operator gains access to all of these services without having to install and configure them separately. The daemon also provides the Lightning Terminal web interface for administering the node, and exposes the *Lightning Node Connect* (LNC) protocol, allowing secure remote access from a web browser, without requiring complex network configuration such as a VPN or port forwarding.

03e70701-8eaf-4384-916b-f5039cba82f5.title: ASSET ID
03e70701-8eaf-4384-916b-f5039cba82f5.body:
A unique 32-byte identifier assigned to each asset issued via the Taproot Assets protocol. The *asset ID* is produced by hashing with SHA-256 five concatenated elements: the outpoint of the genesis transaction (the one that creates the asset), a tag chosen by the issuer (for example the hash of a brand name), the hash of the metadata associated with the asset (links, images, documents), the index of the output containing the Taproot Assets *commitment* in the genesis transaction, and the type of the asset (normal or *collectible*).

```
asset_id=sha256(genesis_outpoint‖asset_tag‖asset_meta_hash‖output_index‖asset_type)
```

Since it depends on the genesis outpoint, the *asset ID* is globally unique: two distinct issuances will always produce different identifiers. It serves as a key to find an asset in a *Universe*, verify its provenance and distinguish the different types of assets committed in the same *Sparse Merkle Sum Tree*.

03e9c931-5f07-4a41-a9f7-fd2bc113c2ac.title: BIP-0144
03e9c931-5f07-4a41-a9f7-fd2bc113c2ac.body: Defines new network message formats and serializations for the broadcast of transactions and blocks that integrate segregated witness structures (SegWit). BIP-0144 notably establishes mechanisms allowing peers to signal their support for SegWit and to relay witness structures without compromising compatibility with nodes that are not up to date.

03ef9767-90b8-4dfc-b1e5-08cc19b2fc0a.title: MAGMA
03ef9767-90b8-4dfc-b1e5-08cc19b2fc0a.body:
Liquidity marketplace for the Lightning Network developed by Amboss Technologies. Magma allows node operators to buy or sell inbound capacity in the form of payment channels, regardless of the implementation used (LND, CLN, Eclair).

The mechanism relies on *HODL invoices* to create conditional contracts: the seller only receives payment if they actually open the agreed channel within a short time frame. This system allows Magma to facilitate exchanges without ever taking custody of users' funds.

Magma addresses a recurring need on the Lightning Network: obtaining inbound liquidity. A node that has just opened a channel only has outbound capacity; to receive payments, it must convince a peer to allocate funds on their side of the channel. Magma turns this process into an open market where liquidity is exchanged for fees negotiated between the parties.

044e7b8c-b87f-4116-9ee9-f0cb8c67d386.title: BECH32 AND BECH32M
044e7b8c-b87f-4116-9ee9-f0cb8c67d386.body:
`Bech32` and `Bech32m` are two address encoding formats for receiving bitcoins. They are based on a slightly modified base 32. They embed a checksum based on an error-correcting algorithm called BCH (*Bose-Chaudhuri-Hocquenghem*). Compared with Legacy addresses, encoded in `Base58check`, `Bech32` and `Bech32m` addresses have a more powerful checksum, making it possible to detect and potentially locate typing errors. Their format also has better readability, with only lowercase characters. Here is the addition matrix of this format from base 10: 

| +   | 0   | 1   | 2   | 3   | 4   | 5   | 6   | 7   |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0   | q   | p   | z   | r   | y   | 9   | x   | 8   |
| 8   | g   | f   | 2   | t   | v   | d   | w   | 0   |
| 16  | s   | 3   | j   | n   | 5   | 4   | k   | h   |
| 24  | c   | e   | 6   | m   | u   | a   | 7   | l   |

`Bech32` and `Bech32m` are encoding formats used to represent SegWit addresses. `Bech32` is an address encoding format introduced by BIP-0173 in 2017. It uses a specific set of characters, made up of digits and lowercase letters, to minimize typing errors and make reading easier. `Bech32` addresses generally start with `bc1` to indicate that they are native SegWit. This format is used only on SegWit V0 addresses, with the P2WPKH (*Pay to Witness Public Key Hash*) and P2WSH (*Pay to Witness Script Hash*) scripts. However, there is a small unexpected flaw specific to the `Bech32` format. Whenever the last character of the address is a `p`, inserting or deleting any number of `q` characters immediately before it does not invalidate the checksum. This does not affect existing uses of SegWit V0 addresses (BIP-0173) because of their restriction to two defined lengths. However, it could affect future uses of the `Bech32` encoding. The `Bech32m` format is simply a `Bech32` format with this error corrected. It was introduced with BIP-0350 in 2020. `Bech32m` addresses also start with `bc1`, but they are specifically designed to be compatible with SegWit version V1 (Taproot) and later versions, with the P2TR (*Pay to TapRoot*) script.

046d1944-64cf-44f0-bc47-8bb791401e51.title: SHAREDCOIN
046d1944-64cf-44f0-bc47-8bb791401e51.body: Bitcoin coin mixing service launched in 2013 by Blockchain.info, but no longer in operation today. This service offered users the ability to improve their privacy on Bitcoin by combining their transactions with those of other people, using a mixing technique similar to coinjoins. SharedCoin provided a form of privacy without requiring trust in the coordinator, because users' coins remained under their control throughout the process. Unlike the centralized mixing services of the time, the bitcoins could not be stolen by the intermediary. SharedCoin subsequently faced problems leading to the deanonymization of some of its mixes in early summer 2014.

046f1460-1594-43bf-805c-7e6c33360c61.title: PAY-TO-CONTRACT
046f1460-1594-43bf-805c-7e6c33360c61.body:
Cryptographic protocol that makes it possible to commit arbitrary data into a Bitcoin public key, so that a payment made to this key simultaneously constitutes proof of commitment to that data.

The principle relies on “tweaking” a public key: from an original public key `P` and a contract `c`, a new key `P' = P + H(P \| c) \cdot G` is computed, where `H` is a hash function and `G` the generator point of the curve. The resulting key `P'` appears to be an ordinary public key, but it encodes a verifiable commitment to the contract `c`. The payer can then prove to a third party what they paid for, by revealing the original key `P` and the contract `c`, without this proof being visible on the blockchain.

04733e12-e0e3-4e86-bddb-ededd4f992ba.title: BIG BLOCKERS
04733e12-e0e3-4e86-bddb-ededd4f992ba.body: Name given to the supporters of increasing the block size during the Blocksize War between 2015 and 2017. Big blockers believe that it is necessary to increase this limit to allow Bitcoin to scale. They support proposals such as Bitcoin XT, Bitcoin Classic and Bitcoin Unlimited. They have no problem with implementing changes via hard forks, unlike small blockers, who prefer soft forks.

0489415f-d009-441f-9a7b-248541cc24a4.title: STALE - BLOCK
0489415f-d009-441f-9a7b-248541cc24a4.body: Refers to a block with no child: a valid block, but one excluded from the main Bitcoin chain. It occurs when two miners find a valid block at the same chain height within a short span of time and broadcast it on the network. The nodes eventually choose a single block to include in the chain, according to the principle of the chain with the most accumulated work, making the other one "orphaned," "obsolete," or "stale."

04aa6bd9-dc60-461d-81be-5733c85b7af3.title: QE - QUANTITATIVE EASING
04aa6bd9-dc60-461d-81be-5733c85b7af3.body:
An unconventional monetary policy in which a central bank buys financial assets on a large scale, mainly government bonds and asset-backed securities, in order to inject liquidity into the financial system. The goal is to lower long-term interest rates, stimulate credit and, ultimately, support economic activity when conventional tools (such as lowering the policy rate) have reached their limits, particularly when the rate is close to zero (*zero lower bound*).

QE was widely deployed by the major central banks starting with the financial crisis of 2008. The US Federal Reserve (Fed), the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan (BoJ) carried out successive programs that considerably inflated the size of their balance sheets. This monetary expansion is criticized for its redistributive effects: by driving up the price of financial assets (stocks, bonds, real estate), QE benefits the holders of these assets more than the real economy, which illustrates the Cantillon effect.

In the Bitcoin community, quantitative easing is often cited as one of the fundamental motivations for adopting BTC. Faced with a money creation perceived as unlimited and discretionary, Bitcoin offers a transparent and immutable monetary policy, with issuance capped at 21 million units.

04fc27ec-693a-4e17-aea6-5c3a1f732c8b.title: OMNI
04fc27ec-693a-4e17-aea6-5c3a1f732c8b.body: Omni Layer (formerly Mastercoin) is an *open-source*, decentralized platform for creating and managing assets on the Bitcoin blockchain. Assets on Omni include Tether (USDT) and MaidSafeCoin (MAID).

0501ad72-bdda-4cd6-b558-2b8d09f509af.title: UMBREL
0501ad72-bdda-4cd6-b558-2b8d09f509af.body:
Operating system for personal servers that allows self-hosting applications, including a Bitcoin node and a Lightning node. Umbrel offers a "*plug-and-play*" style web interface that simplifies the installation and management of a full node, without requiring advanced technical skills.

Umbrel runs on dedicated hardware (Umbrel Home, Umbrel Pro) or on any compatible computer via umbrelOS. Its app store includes dozens of self-hosted applications: Bitcoin Core, LND, Core Lightning, Nextcloud, Tailscale, Nostr relays, and others.

05440831-a6a6-4676-b135-5468b60886df.title: PROP - PROPORTIONAL
05440831-a6a6-4676-b135-5468b60886df.body: A method of calculating miner payouts in the context of mining pools. PROP simply distributes the block reward among miners in proportion to their contribution in *shares*. The counting of *shares* begins at the last block found by the pool and ends when a new block is found. Each new block resets the *share* counter to zero. This payout method directly reflects each miner's work.

0579af44-0bfc-4d18-9cc7-86b0421aa56d.title: GOLDFINGER
0579af44-0bfc-4d18-9cc7-86b0421aa56d.body:
Hypothetical scenario on the Bitcoin system where a malicious actor controls more than 50% of the total mining computing power (*hashrate*). With such dominance, the attacker can manipulate the consensus process, enabling malicious actions such as double spending, where the same bitcoins are spent a first time on a chain that is ultimately made obsolete, then a second time on the valid chain. Another purpose of a Goldfinger attack is transaction censorship. However, carrying out an attack of this type requires considerable financial, human, energy and technical resources, and makes the malicious actor liable to be discovered before the attack takes place. Although theoretically possible, a Goldfinger attack on Bitcoin is considered highly unlikely because of the decentralization of mining and the large amount of computing power currently deployed.

*This attack is also called the “51% Attack”.*

05b099c7-97e6-4478-b169-00e34e9477cf.title: PEER DISCOVERY

05d7c716-626f-4382-8b0f-47e21b151447.title: INTERNAL ADDRESS REUSE
05d7c716-626f-4382-8b0f-47e21b151447.body:
Address reuse is said to be “internal” when it occurs within a single transaction, in both input and output. In this configuration, internal address reuse is a chain analysis heuristic that makes it possible to put forward a plausible hypothesis about the change of the transaction. Indeed, if there are two outputs and one of them uses the same receiving address as in the input, then it is likely that the second output leaves the possession of the initial user. The output with the reused address likely represents the change.

![Internal reuse: the address bc1q...xyz appears as both an input and an output, which reveals the change output.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/r/reutilisation-d-adresse-int/assets/image-1.png)

06291be2-781b-4791-b083-ffbc564ec394.title: LABEL
06291be2-781b-4791-b083-ffbc564ec394.body: A tag or annotation assigned to a UTXO in a Bitcoin wallet to remember where it came from. For example, if I own a UTXO coming from a P2P purchase on Bisq with Charles, I could give it the label “`Non-KYC Bisq Charles`”. This is a good practice that helps remember the origin or intended destination of that UTXO, which makes managing funds and optimizing privacy easier. *Labelling* is all the more important when it is used with *coin control*. Indeed, by allowing users to differentiate and precisely select UTXOs for their transactions, this practice helps avoid merging UTXOs coming from different sources. This limits the risks associated with the CIOH (*Common Input Ownership Heuristic*) chain analysis heuristic, which can reveal the common ownership of a transaction's inputs.

06cedacf-d0da-430d-aecc-0c24142f066c.title: BIP-0053
06cedacf-d0da-430d-aecc-0c24142f066c.body: Proposal to prohibit 64-byte transactions in order to fix a vulnerability in the verification of Merkle trees. A serialized 64-byte transaction can be confused with an internal node of the Merkle tree, because both share the same size. This ambiguity would potentially make it possible to build fraudulent SPV proofs that deceive light nodes. BIP-0053 is part of the "consensus cleanup" proposed in BIP-0054, a set of minor fixes to the consensus rules.

06f855c0-b100-46f5-a5d1-fe43617968e1.title: COINMUX
06f855c0-b100-46f5-a5d1-fe43617968e1.body: Coinjoin implementation developed in 2014. Coinmux is a decentralized and trustless bitcoin mixing protocol, which requires neither trust between participants nor the intervention of a central actor. The software pools the bitcoins of several users into a single transaction, where each output has identical amounts, which makes it possible to break the links between the inputs and the outputs. The Coinmux protocol ensures that users keep control of their funds throughout the process, by having the transactions signed only when the inputs and outputs correspond exactly to what was agreed. Today, this protocol is no longer used.

07d60d9d-2478-4362-9bb6-919f11c0489f.title: BIP-0349
07d60d9d-2478-4362-9bb6-919f11c0489f.body:
Proposal by Brandon Black and Jeremy Rubin introducing the opcode `OP_INTERNALKEY` in Tapscript. This opcode replaces `OP_SUCCESS203` (`0xcb`) and places the 32-byte *x-only* representation of the Taproot internal key (*internal key*) directly on the stack when a script is executed. Currently, a tapscript that needs to reference the internal key must include it explicitly in its data, which consumes an extra 8 vBytes on-chain. `OP_INTERNALKEY` eliminates this redundancy.

Beyond this space saving, the opcode opens up an important use case: “*re-keying*” while preserving the Merkle tree. When the internal key of a Taproot output is changed (for example, to add or remove a participant), the scripts in the tree's leaves that hardcode a reference to this key become inconsistent. With `OP_INTERNALKEY`, the leaves re-key automatically, because the opcode always returns the current internal key.

07f6f728-ea7c-4b2b-aec7-f98c199177ef.title: ARK
07f6f728-ea7c-4b2b-aec7-f98c199177ef.body:
A joinpool-type upper-layer protocol on Bitcoin, proposed by Burak Keceli in May 2023 and implemented from 2024 by Ark Labs. Ark makes it possible to share on-chain UTXOs between multiple users via *Virtual Transaction Outputs* (VTXOs) in order to improve Bitcoin's scalability.

The protocol is built around *Ark Service Providers* (ASPs), operators who periodically organize “rounds” during which users' VTXOs are consolidated and anchored in new on-chain Bitcoin transactions. This mechanism prevents any fractional reserve. Transfers between users of the same ASP are fast, inexpensive and offer privacy comparable to that of a coinjoin. “Out-of-round” payments are also possible for immediate settlement, at the cost of temporary trust in the ASP and the sender.

The protocol is non-custodial, but VTXOs expire after a defined period. If the user does not show up before expiry, the ASP can recover the liquidity. The user retains the ability to perform a unilateral on-chain exit at any time.

The version implemented without covenants, called *clArk*, emulates spending conditions through n-of-n multisignatures between the participants of a round, at the cost of overhead in bandwidth and storage. Adding covenants to Bitcoin would improve scalability and reduce the required interactivity. Ark is complementary to the Lightning Network and interoperable via gateways.

080efa61-7f74-4d60-9ee4-4fa10920b967.title: DERIVATION PATH

084d8c57-0a1a-4ad0-bb70-923445573908.title: ARBITRAGE
084d8c57-0a1a-4ad0-bb70-923445573908.body: The practice of exploiting differences in the price of BTC (or any other asset) between different exchange platforms to make a profit. Arbitrage involves buying bitcoin on a platform where the price is relatively low and simultaneously selling it on another platform where the price is higher. Price gaps can arise because of differences in liquidity, demand, trading volumes and transfer times between exchange platforms. Arbitrage helps to balance prices across different platforms.

085a9c2f-9791-4030-89fb-418018e89ca6.title: BIP-0374
085a9c2f-9791-4030-89fb-418018e89ca6.body: Defines a discrete logarithm equality proof protocol (*DLEQ proof*) for the secp256k1 curve. This cryptographic mechanism would make it possible to prove that two points on the elliptic curve share the same secret scalar, without revealing the value of that scalar.

0898f8b0-6783-4fc2-be76-08570006d0b5.title: CISA
0898f8b0-6783-4fc2-be76-08570006d0b5.body:
Acronym for "*Cross-Input Signature Aggregation*". It is a technical proposal that aims to optimize the size of Bitcoin transactions by reducing the number of signatures required to validate them.

Currently, on Bitcoin, each input of a transaction must have an individual signature in order to be spent. This proves that the owner of the UTXO in question authorizes the transaction. With CISA, the goal is to combine the signatures of all the inputs of a single transaction into one signature that covers all the inputs. This would reduce the size of transactions that have many inputs, and therefore also reduce their fees. It would be particularly useful for people who perform coinjoins or consolidations, while also making it possible to confirm more transactions on Bitcoin without changing the size or interval of blocks. CISA relies on the Schnorr protocol, which allows linear aggregation of signatures. This means that a single signature can prove possession of several independent keys.

However, implementing CISA on Bitcoin is very complex, because it requires deep modifications to the way scripts work. Currently, script verification on Bitcoin is done input by input. Moving to a model where an entire transaction is verified at once, as CISA proposes, is far from a trivial change.

08d35796-e7b3-48e6-b1b0-7dc4e27e55cd.title: BIP-0065
08d35796-e7b3-48e6-b1b0-7dc4e27e55cd.body: Introduces a new opcode named `OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY` that makes it possible to render a UTXO unspendable until a given point in the future. Enforcing this BIP required a soft fork, which took place on December 14, 2015. It also introduced version 4 blocks.

08e502c7-5117-4794-922a-46ac1dd666cb.title: LIBERTY RESERVE
08e502c7-5117-4794-922a-46ac1dd666cb.body:
A digital currency service based in Costa Rica, founded by Arthur Budovsky in 2006. It allowed users to create accounts with minimal identity verification and to transfer funds denominated in “Liberty Reserve Dollars” (LR) or in euros. The service became popular for illicit transactions because of the anonymity it offered. At its peak, Liberty Reserve had more than one million users worldwide and is said to have processed about 55 million transactions.

In May 2013, the US government seized the service and indicted its operators, accused of having laundered more than 6 billion dollars. Together with the earlier shutdown of e-gold, this episode confirmed that centralized digital currency systems remain vulnerable to state intervention. Bitcoin, thanks to its decentralized architecture that spreads risk among its participants, aims to resist this type of shutdown.

0901716f-cacb-4d65-af33-3871e3de8163.title: BIP-0088
0901716f-cacb-4d65-af33-3871e3de8163.body: Proposal defining a template format for BIP-0032 derivation paths. This format makes it possible to specify ranges and wildcards (*wildcards*) within paths, for example `m/49'/0'/0'/{0,1}/*` to indicate that the change level can be 0 or 1, and that the address index is free. These templates allow wallets to formally describe which derivation paths are allowed, thereby facilitating the validation and verification of wallet policies.

09591bbb-0b18-43db-a2b6-70f6742a2be7.title: BIP-0390
09591bbb-0b18-43db-a2b6-70f6742a2be7.body: Proposal defining the key expression `musig()` for output script descriptors. This expression makes it possible to represent a MuSig2 aggregate key within a descriptor, enabling the standardized description of a Taproot key-path spend (*key-path*) involving several signers. Without this expression, there was no standardized way to describe a MuSig2 multisig in descriptors.

09891220-1ce7-4437-849c-1d3fd4f10f88.title: ALBY

09b8f345-bff4-4744-9a01-dc734f29cb7d.title: BIP-0111
09b8f345-bff4-4744-9a01-dc734f29cb7d.body: Proposes the addition of a service bit named `NODE_BLOOM` to allow nodes to explicitly signal their support for Bloom Filters as described in BIP-0037. The introduction of `NODE_BLOOM` allows node operators to disable this service in order to reduce DoS risks. The BIP-0037 option is disabled by default in Bitcoin Core. To enable it, the parameter `peerbloomfilters=1` must be entered in the configuration file.

0a2462ec-28d5-4bc6-8d51-b32a0cd6dc0d.title: JOINSTR
0a2462ec-28d5-4bc6-8d51-b32a0cd6dc0d.body: Decentralized coinjoin protocol that uses Nostr as a communication layer. Proposed in August 2022 by the pseudonymous developer "1440000bytes", it eliminates the need for a central coordinator, which traditionally constitutes a point of failure in coinjoin implementations. Participants register their outputs via Nostr relays, then the system creates a partially signed Bitcoin transaction (PSBT) that each participant signs individually. Once all signatures have been collected, the combined transaction is broadcast on the network.

0a52830a-b5dc-4237-8062-4201cdda11dd.title: BCOIN
0a52830a-b5dc-4237-8062-4201cdda11dd.body: Alternative implementation of the Bitcoin protocol developed in JavaScript for Node.js. Unlike Bitcoin Core, which is the majority implementation of Bitcoin nodes (about 99% of the network), Bcoin is rather geared toward the needs of businesses and developers who seek to integrate certain Bitcoin-related features into their systems. Bcoin includes a set of complete libraries for integrating a full node, an SPV node, an HD wallet, an indexer, and other features.

0ad5325b-2dac-4a85-a118-94957144318a.title: YPRV
0ad5325b-2dac-4a85-a118-94957144318a.body: Extended private key prefix for Nested SegWit accounts on Bitcoin.

0b2de1d7-cabb-419f-ba5c-3c33faa5f37f.title: COMMIT
0b2de1d7-cabb-419f-ba5c-3c33faa5f37f.body: In the context of Git, represents a snapshot of the changes made to the set of files in a repository. Each commit is identified by a unique hash and includes a descriptive message, the identity of the author and the date. It makes it possible to track the evolution of the project and to return to earlier states if necessary.

0b435ec2-9ebf-4110-94ba-bc6cba923aac.title: PAYNYM
0b435ec2-9ebf-4110-94ba-bc6cba923aac.body:
Unique identifier linked to a Bitcoin wallet that implements this option. Paynyms are available on Samourai Wallet and on Sparrow Wallet. Originally, these identifiers are generated from the wallet's payment code, in accordance with BIP-0047. They thus offer the possibility of connecting with another user in order to generate fresh, unique receiving addresses, without requiring direct interaction. The use of Paynyms was later broadened to support various other features of the Samourai ecosystem. They are notably used to enable encrypted exchanges over the Soroban communication protocol, in order to easily carry out collaborative transactions. Paynyms can also be used for authentication on systems compatible with the AUTH47 protocol. Each Paynym is characterized by a unique identifier and is represented by an illustration of a robot.

![Three examples of Paynym robot illustrations, the visual avatar generated from the BIP-0047 payment code.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/p/paynym/assets/image-1.png)

0b539532-6bbf-4727-8007-6d039daf304e.title: COINSHUFFLE
0b539532-6bbf-4727-8007-6d039daf304e.body: Bitcoin mixing protocol proposed in 2014 by Tim Ruffing, Pedro Moreno-Sanchez and Aniket Kate, inspired by the idea formalized by Gregory Maxwell. CoinShuffle makes it possible to cut the history of coins without requiring a trusted third party. The protocol ensures that no participant can link the inputs to the outputs of the other participants. This concept was never widely adopted, as privacy techniques such as the *Chaumian coinjoin* are preferred to it.

0b8822d2-9b7b-490c-b965-075d85b76399.title: BITMAIN
0b8822d2-9b7b-490c-b965-075d85b76399.body:
A Chinese company founded in 2013 by Jihan Wu and Micree Zhan, specializing in the design of ASIC chips dedicated to Bitcoin mining and the production of mining machines. Bitmain sells the Antminer range, which historically dominates the global mining hardware market in terms of market share. The company also founded AntPool in 2014, one of the largest mining pools, before separating from it in 2021 to refocus on chip design.

Bitmain has played a central role in the industrialization of Bitcoin mining by making ASICs accessible on a large scale. The company has nevertheless stirred controversy, notably over the secret use of AsicBoost (Covert AsicBoost) in its machines and its opposition to the SegWit soft fork during the block size conflict in 2017.

0c2203a2-cf73-4328-877d-ec149d48817e.title: OP_CHECKSIGVERIFY - 0XAD
0c2203a2-cf73-4328-877d-ec149d48817e.body: Performs the same operation as `OP_CHECKSIG`, but if the signature verification fails, the script stops immediately with an error and the transaction is therefore invalid. If the verification succeeds, the script continues without pushing a `1` (true) value onto the stack. To sum up, `OP_CHECKSIGVERIFY` performs the `OP_CHECKSIG` operation followed by `OP_VERIFY`. This opcode was modified in Tapscript in order to verify Schnorr signatures.

0c245a43-10da-465f-afd3-4389c5b9a305.title: BITCOIN NETWORK
0c245a43-10da-465f-afd3-4389c5b9a305.body: Refers to the global infrastructure of the Bitcoin system. The network is made up of all the nodes (computers) that run software implementing the Bitcoin protocol and that connect to their peers. Each node communicates peer-to-peer with the other nodes in order to download and verify the blockchain, to verify and relay new blocks, and to verify and relay new transactions.

0c32601c-1d9e-4ed1-ae6b-3118fe887d46.title: BIP-0130
0c32601c-1d9e-4ed1-ae6b-3118fe887d46.body: Proposal adding the P2P message `sendheaders` to Bitcoin's network protocol. This message allows a node to ask its peer to announce new blocks to it directly via `headers` messages, rather than via `inv` messages followed by an explicit request. This mechanism reduces block propagation latency by eliminating an additional network round trip. The receiving node can thus begin validating the block header immediately after the announcement. BIP-0130 has been deployed and active on the Bitcoin network since 2016.

0c47404b-98cd-4de3-a0b5-584195fced1b.title: BIP-0066
0c47404b-98cd-4de3-a0b5-584195fced1b.body: Introduces a standardization of the signature format in transactions. This BIP was proposed in response to a discrepancy in the way OpenSSL handled signature encoding on different systems. This heterogeneity posed a risk of a blockchain split. BIP-0066 made it possible to standardize the signature format for all transactions by using strict DER (*Distinguished Encoding Rules*) encoding. This change required a soft fork. For its activation, BIP-0066 then used the same mechanism as BIP-0034, requiring the `nVersion` field to be raised to version 3, and rejecting all blocks of version 2 or lower once the 95% miner threshold was reached. This threshold was crossed at block #363,725 on July 4, 2015.

0c4e51fb-d95c-40ce-8307-8b989eadbbdc.title: BUCKETING
0c4e51fb-d95c-40ce-8307-8b989eadbbdc.body:
Method of distributing peer addresses across the tables of Bitcoin Core's addrman module. Each address is assigned to a bucket ("bucket") by a hash computation that combines the address itself, the network group it comes from and a 256-bit secret key (`nKey`) specific to each node. This placement, deterministic but unpredictable from the outside, aims to prevent an attacker from predicting or controlling which positions they occupy in the tables.

The "new" and "tried" tables use distinct bucketing schemes. In the "new" table, the bucket depends on the source network group and the network group of the address. In the "tried" table, it depends only on the network group of the address itself. This separation of criteria limits an attacker's ability to monopolize buckets from a single source, which constitutes a defense against eclipse attacks.

0c809ed2-0373-4cd2-b595-46f71e9bc2f6.title: PULL REQUEST
0c809ed2-0373-4cd2-b595-46f71e9bc2f6.body:
In the context of GitHub and other code hosting platforms, a *Pull Request* represents a request made by a contributor to merge their changes from one branch into another. It triggers a code review and a discussion before the changes are potentially merged (*merge*). This process is widely used in the development of Bitcoin node implementations, notably Bitcoin Core.

*The term “Pull Request” is often abbreviated by the acronym “PR”.*

0c8de08d-082a-452a-85e7-0c0a36aeb876.title: BIP-0017
0c8de08d-082a-452a-85e7-0c0a36aeb876.body: Proposal by Luke Dashjr competing with BIP-0012 and BIP-0016. BIP-0017 introduced a new opcode, `OP_CHECKHASHVERIFY`, designed to allow the verification of a script present in the `scriptSig` against its hash present in the `scriptPubKey` before unlocking the funds. BIP-0016 (P2SH) was ultimately preferred over BIP-0017 (CHV) following a period of intense debate.

0cda73d6-8c4a-4d18-bd03-1d56a12154dd.title: BEARER ASSET
0cda73d6-8c4a-4d18-bd03-1d56a12154dd.body:
A good or financial instrument whose ownership is determined solely by physical possession, without requiring a centralized registry, an intermediary, or a registration in a name. Whoever holds the asset is its legitimate owner. Banknotes, gold coins, and bearer bonds are examples of bearer assets.

This type of asset offers the advantage of not depending on any third party to validate or authorize a transfer of ownership. It gives its holder direct sovereignty, but also implies a responsibility: loss or theft results in the permanent loss of the asset.

Bitcoin in *self-custody* is a digital bearer asset. Possession of the private keys that secure bitcoins confers exclusive control over those funds, without any bank, institution, or centralized registry being involved.

0dc50787-f32e-47b4-b632-e248b333e755.title: UPUB
0dc50787-f32e-47b4-b632-e248b333e755.body: Extended public key prefix for Nested SegWit accounts on Bitcoin Testnet.

0dd19b44-03c3-4e8c-a5a6-1d1bb6e37154.title: BIP-0014
0dd19b44-03c3-4e8c-a5a6-1d1bb6e37154.body: BIP proposed by Patrick Strateman and Amir Taaki in 2011 that aims to distinguish client version numbers from protocol version numbers. BIP-0014 specifies how implementations of the Bitcoin protocol must present themselves on the network. It suggests the use of a user-agent format to identify the version and type of the Bitcoin client used. The main objective of BIP-0014 is to facilitate the management of changes and the detection of incompatibilities between the various existing clients. While it was previously logical to consider Satoshi's client as de facto the Bitcoin protocol, the multiplication of software at that time led BIP-0014 to clearly differentiate clients from the protocol itself.

0e4a2e0d-5d28-4334-9f6b-fd017bad2a38.title: BIP-0081
0e4a2e0d-5d28-4334-9f6b-fd017bad2a38.body: Variant of BIP-0080 defining a hierarchical deterministic derivation path (BIP-0032) for voting pools using colored coins with deterministic multisig wallets. BIP-0081 extended the BIP-0080 scheme to tokenized assets by adding five additional derivation levels to encode the color definition (the hash160 of the definition, split into five groups of 4 bytes in little-endian) within the pool. Like BIP-0080, this proposal remained highly specialized and was never adopted by the Bitcoin ecosystem.

0e66d8f8-818a-455f-8996-a2ece13de37f.title: OP_MAX - 0XA4
0e66d8f8-818a-455f-8996-a2ece13de37f.body: Selects the larger of the top two elements of the stack and pushes it onto the stack. This operation keeps only the larger of the two top values.

0e79fcd1-68f1-41eb-8aab-7a4f4d648597.title: BIP-0379
0e79fcd1-68f1-41eb-8aab-7a4f4d648597.body:
Proposal formalizing Miniscript, a structured representation of a subset of Bitcoin Script that allows analysis, composition and generic signing of spending conditions. Miniscript establishes a correspondence between Script opcodes and a system of composable types, in which spending conditions can be combined using logical operators (AND, OR, thresholds) with correctness guarantees.

This approach allows wallets to automatically determine the signature requirements for a given output, to precisely estimate transaction fees by computing the maximum witness size, and to verify that a spending policy is satisfiable. Miniscript was developed by Pieter Wuille, Andrew Poelstra and Sanket Kanjalkar.

0e7a1a88-0380-4058-83a0-efa7d8f3828e.title: LIGHTNING INVOICE
0e7a1a88-0380-4058-83a0-efa7d8f3828e.body:
Lightning payment request generated by the recipient, which contains all the information necessary to carry out the transaction.

A Lightning invoice contains the destination of the payment in the form of the public key of the recipient node, but also a prefix `ln`, the amount, a time before expiry, the hash of the secret used in the context of HTLCs, as well as other metadata, some of it optional, such as options relating to routing. These invoices are defined by the BOLT-11 standard. Once paid, a Lightning invoice can no longer be reused.

0ea95d38-c720-40b8-bc31-36fcbd3ea268.title: OFF-CHAIN
0ea95d38-c720-40b8-bc31-36fcbd3ea268.body: Refers to transactions or activities more or less related to Bitcoin that take place outside the main blockchain, but that have a link or anchor to it. They are not immediately recorded on the blockchain, but require additional mechanisms to ensure their security and finality. These operations are often justified by a desire to get around the technical limitations inherent to Bitcoin, in order to have transactions with fast finality, low fees, and more capacity or functionality.

0efe56fe-c80b-445a-8791-7e6f00db32ca.title: ADDRESS SPOOFING
0efe56fe-c80b-445a-8791-7e6f00db32ca.body:
An attack in which a malicious actor creates an address (or any other payment identifier) that closely resembles the victim's. The goal is to trick the user into copying this wrong address during a transaction, which leads to the bitcoins being sent to the attacker instead of the intended destination. 

The attacker exploits the user's haste, as they may copy the wrong address if they carry out their transaction without precisely verifying its accuracy. In general, to set up this attack, the attacker makes small payments to the victim's wallet in order to insert the fake address into their transaction history. This attack is rather used with altcoins, where it is common to reuse the same receiving addresses, unlike Bitcoin, where using fresh addresses for each transaction is a more widespread practice. However, Bitcoin users are not immune to this attack.

Another method of putting the wrong address in front of the victim is the use of fraudulent wallet management software that imitates legitimate software, or the modification of the address when a machine is compromised, between the moment it is copied and the moment the transaction is built. This is then sometimes called “*address swapping*”.

To protect against these various attack methods, it is important to verify several characters of the address, especially at the level of its *checksum* (at the end), on the screen of the signing device before signing the transaction.

*This attack is also sometimes referred to as Address Poisoning.*

0f0ce23e-bd9b-4552-be40-9547d7fcbdc2.title: BINARY
0f0ce23e-bd9b-4552-be40-9547d7fcbdc2.body: Base-2 numeral system, which uses the `0` and the `1` to represent information. Each digit in this system is called a bit, which is short for “binary digit”. In the computing context, binary is the form in which data is represented in memory. Computers use binary to process all kinds of information, because it corresponds to the two possible states of an electronic circuit: off or on.

0f51deaa-e8ea-4c9c-8a07-df8fa70ae2f5.title: UNIVERSE
0f51deaa-e8ea-4c9c-8a07-df8fa70ae2f5.body: Data repository serving as a registry for Taproot Assets assets. A *universe* stores and distributes the metadata, proofs, and provenance history of assets issued on Bitcoin via the Taproot Assets protocol. Holders and potential acquirers of assets consult a *universe* to verify the authenticity and validity of assets before accepting them. Each asset issuer can maintain its own *universe*, and these repositories can be synchronized with one another to ensure wide dissemination of the information.

0f67dc95-3000-4c0b-8571-f6f3ad9ac08a.title: OP_NOTIF - 0X64
0f67dc95-3000-4c0b-8571-f6f3ad9ac08a.body: Works in the opposite way to `OP_IF`, executing the following portion of the script if the value at the top of the stack is zero (false).

0f7c38e2-f939-4b65-87c8-8b33c25bff0a.title: BIP-0434
0f7c38e2-f939-4b65-87c8-8b33c25bff0a.body: Proposes a generic mechanism for feature negotiation between Bitcoin network peers when a connection is established. Currently, each new P2P protocol feature requires the addition of specific messages exchanged after the version handshake. BIP-0434 replaces this ad hoc approach with a unified system in which nodes announce the features they support through a standardized set of negotiation messages. This simplifies the implementation of new network features and reduces the complexity of the peer connection protocol.

0fcbfac3-9b1a-44e1-8ced-f13d59e8bf5b.title: LIGHTNING NODE
0fcbfac3-9b1a-44e1-8ced-f13d59e8bf5b.body: A computer that runs an implementation of the Lightning Network (Eclair, LND, Core Lightning...). A Lightning node is set up on top of a Bitcoin node, and makes it possible to create and manage bidirectional payment channels between different users. Lightning nodes are connected to one another, which forms a network of payment channels. These channels make it possible to carry out an almost unlimited number of transactions without needing to publish them individually on the Bitcoin blockchain.

0ff5943f-fb59-4b9b-b650-ffca2a5e82fb.title: OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY - 0XB1

10234a66-11f7-40c6-b13a-8c68b10debd9.title: TESTNET RESET
10234a66-11f7-40c6-b13a-8c68b10debd9.body:
An operation consisting of relaunching the Bitcoin test network with a new genesis block, thereby erasing the existing history and balances. This mechanism ensures that test coins remain easy to mine and without market value, which is important for the testnet to fulfill its function: to offer a free experimentation environment where developers can test attacks, bugs or new features without financial consequences.

The testnet has been reset three times in Bitcoin's history. The first testnet was introduced in October 2010. A first reset was carried out in February 2011, in order to create what would retrospectively be called “testnet2.” Gavin Andresen then launched “testnet3” in April 2012. After 13 years of service, testnet3 was finally replaced by testnet4 in 2024, defined in BIP-0094, notably because its coins had begun to acquire a market value.

102553eb-f247-483f-ab1f-c5cd04687d2a.title: P2PKH
102553eb-f247-483f-ab1f-c5cd04687d2a.body:
P2PKH is the acronym for *Pay to Public Key Hash*. It is a standard script template used to set spending conditions on a UTXO. It allows bitcoins to be locked to a hash of a public key, that is, to a receiving address. This script is associated with the Legacy standard, and was introduced in the earliest versions of Bitcoin by Satoshi Nakamoto.

Unlike P2PK, where the public key is explicitly included in the script, P2PKH relies on a cryptographic fingerprint of the public key. This script includes the `RIPEMD160` hash of the `SHA256` of the public key and stipulates that, to access the funds, the recipient must provide a public key matching this hash, as well as a valid digital signature generated from the associated private key. P2PKH addresses are encoded using the `Base58Check` format, which gives them robustness against typographical errors through the use of a checksum. These addresses always begin with the digit `1`.

103cbfe8-53b6-48f7-876d-3e3bb99e2794.title: ASCII
103cbfe8-53b6-48f7-876d-3e3bb99e2794.body: Acronym for “*American Standard Code for Information Interchange*”. It is a character encoding system for computers. The ASCII standard uses 7 bits to represent 128 different characters: uppercase and lowercase letters of the Latin alphabet, digits, punctuation symbols, and control commands, such as the line break or the tab.

10deae59-e31e-4347-b709-cbe6e51136f1.title: SCB - STATIC CHANNEL BACKUP
10deae59-e31e-4347-b709-cbe6e51136f1.body:
Backup mechanism introduced by LND that makes it possible to recover one's funds in the event of data loss on a Lightning node. The SCB is a file (generally named `channel.backup`, not to be confused with the file `channel.db`) that contains static information about open channels: the identity of peers, the means of contacting them and the channel identifiers.

Unlike the `channel.db` database, which changes with every payment, the SCB is only updated when a channel is opened or closed. It does not contain the detailed state of the channels or the transaction history. The SCB therefore does not make it possible to restore a Lightning node as it was: its role is to ask peers to force-close the channels in order to recover the funds *onchain*.

During a restoration, the user provides their aezeed seed (to recreate the *onchain* wallet) and the SCB file. LND then contacts each peer to notify them of the data loss. The peer broadcasts its latest commitment transaction to close the channel, and the funds reappear in the *onchain* wallet. This mechanism depends on the cooperation and availability of peers: if a peer is offline or uncooperative, the funds in the channel concerned may remain locked indefinitely.

110f88cc-321d-4a0d-88db-3f6dc049a366.title: BIP-0131
110f88cc-321d-4a0d-88db-3f6dc049a366.body: Proposal for so-called “coalescing” transactions introducing *wildcard* inputs capable of automatically consuming all the UTXOs associated with the same address in a single operation. BIP-0131 aimed to simplify UTXO consolidation, but was rejected because of security issues and incompatibility with Bitcoin's existing transaction model.

1114e44e-b342-4862-9b78-bc4005583ef9.title: DIFFICULTY
1114e44e-b342-4862-9b78-bc4005583ef9.body: An adjustable parameter that determines the complexity of the proof of work required to add a new block to the blockchain and earn the associated reward. This difficulty is represented by the difficulty target, a 256-bit value that sets the upper limit that the hash of a block header must respect to be considered valid. The goal is for the hash, computed through a double execution of `SHA256` (`SHA256d`), to be less than or equal to this target. To reach this hash, miners manipulate the `nonce` in the block header. The difficulty adjusts every 2016 blocks, or approximately every two weeks, to keep the average block creation time at about 10 minutes.

113922b6-689b-4688-86ca-2c197ad1e7eb.title: OUTBOUND CAPACITY
113922b6-689b-4688-86ca-2c197ad1e7eb.body: Designates the maximum amount of bitcoins that a node can send through a specific channel on the Lightning Network. It depends on the funds the node committed to the channel when opening it, or that it received during a Lightning payment or routing.

116883cb-7e39-460e-b4f8-22f983ec9acb.title: POSTMIX
116883cb-7e39-460e-b4f8-22f983ec9acb.body:
Account that groups the UTXOs that have participated in at least one coinjoin cycle in the Whirlpool protocol. The postmix represents the mixed funds whose link to their origin has been broken thanks to the coinjoin process.

UTXOs in the postmix account benefit from anonsets that increase with each additional coinjoin cycle. The more a UTXO participates in remixes (which are free in Whirlpool), the more its forward-looking and backward-looking anonymity set grows, which strengthens its privacy.

Using postmix UTXOs requires particular care so as not to degrade the privacy gained. Merging postmix UTXOs with each other or with unmixed UTXOs can re-establish traceable links. Spends from the postmix are best made using privacy-preserving techniques, such as Stonewall or Stonewall x2.

11de35b9-e665-44db-808a-6133d55d209f.title: TRANSACTION PATTERN
11de35b9-e665-44db-808a-6133d55d209f.body:
A transaction *pattern* is simply a typical overall model or structure of a transaction, which can be found on the blockchain, and whose likely interpretation is known and will be useful to us in chain analysis. When studying *patterns*, we focus on a single transaction that we analyze at a high level (as opposed to internal and external chain analysis heuristics). In other words, we will only look at the number of UTXOs as inputs and the number of UTXOs as outputs, without dwelling on more specific details or the environment of the transaction. From the observed pattern, we can interpret the nature of the transaction. We then look for characteristics in its structure and deduce a likely interpretation from them.

*In English, these are called “patterns”.*

121bd39a-dfa7-417a-99bf-f3bf120dc01b.title: MINISCRIPT

126d6f7a-6f09-4678-8a6e-fa59f2d890be.title: OPENDIME
126d6f7a-6f09-4678-8a6e-fa59f2d890be.body: A single-use USB device made by Coinkite, designed as a bearer asset for bitcoins. The Opendime generates a private key internally the first time it is used. This key is known to no one. Bitcoins can then be sent to the associated address. To spend the bitcoins secured by this key, the device must be physically unsealed by inserting a pin into a hole provided for that purpose on the circuit board. The private key is then revealed in WIF format and the user can spend the associated funds. As long as the device remains sealed, it can be passed from hand to hand without generating an on-chain transaction. The physical seal makes it possible to verify with certainty, during an exchange, that the private key is not known to the payer, simply by inspecting the device.

12db32b8-fc26-4fb1-b8df-7bc172582b0d.title: DER

12ffc664-30e0-4401-b10c-6d3aba5d24ed.title: BSV - BITCOIN SATOSHI VISION
12ffc664-30e0-4401-b10c-6d3aba5d24ed.body:
Cryptocurrency system resulting from a hard fork of Bitcoin Cash (BCH), itself a fork of Bitcoin (BTC). The Bitcoin SV fork took place on November 15, 2018 at block 556,766 because of disagreements within the Bitcoin Cash community, notably concerning block size and the supposed vision of Satoshi Nakamoto, the creator of Bitcoin. Two camps clashed: 
* The supporters of the "Bitcoin Cash ABC" fork, which became Bitcoin Cash (BCH). This group was notably backed by the well-known entrepreneur Roger Ver;
* The promoters of the "Bitcoin Cash Satoshi Vision" fork, which led to the creation of Bitcoin Satoshi Vision (BSV). This camp was backed, among others, by Craig Wright.

Bitcoin SV differs from Bitcoin Cash, and even more so from Bitcoin, by its considerably high block size limit. This feature aims to align with what its supporters consider to be Satoshi Nakamoto's original vision for Bitcoin.

![Bitcoin SV logo, a fork of Bitcoin Cash that appeared on November 15, 2018 at block 556,766 around Craig Wright.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/b/bsv-bitcoin-satoshi-vision/assets/image-1.png)

1311f432-f526-4003-940d-ed2ff3e0ae82.title: BDK - BITCOIN DEV KIT
1311f432-f526-4003-940d-ed2ff3e0ae82.body:
Software development kit (SDK) for Bitcoin wallets. BDK is a collection of libraries and tools intended for developers, making it possible to simplify the creation of Bitcoin wallet applications. BDK provides modules for essential features such as wallet management, transaction building, transaction signing and key management. Developers can then rely on these modules to design their own software. BDK's components are built with lightness and modularity in mind, so as to make them adjustable to most possible uses. The goal of this tool is to centralize Bitcoin wallet development in order to concentrate efforts.

*BDK was previously called “Magical Bitcoin”.*

131cc280-fddf-48bf-b1c6-3e4a1fefabc2.title: ANCHOR

13a2cf45-2c9f-4aea-8eb4-30740910ec9d.title: LATENCY
13a2cf45-2c9f-4aea-8eb4-30740910ec9d.body: The delay between the sending and the receipt of a piece of information. In computing, it represents the time needed for data to travel between two computers. In the context of Bitcoin, latency can be studied in terms of the delay in propagating blocks across the network. High latency can put isolated miners at a disadvantage, because they keep working on blocks already invalidated by new blocks until they have received those new blocks. Latency therefore naturally pushes miners to pool together. It also reduces the overall security of the system by wasting the search for a valid proof of work. The purpose of setting a 10-minute period between each block is a measure to reduce the impact of latency on the system.

13d16e87-0b6d-4c08-a914-2bcb9207d212.title: DOJO
13d16e87-0b6d-4c08-a914-2bcb9207d212.body: *Open source* *backend* server built on top of Bitcoin Core, oriented toward privacy and autonomy. Initially developed by the Samourai Wallet teams, the Dojo project is now maintained by the community. Dojo serves as a gateway between a Bitcoin wallet (such as Ashigaru) and the Bitcoin network, making it possible to query blockchain data and broadcast transactions through its own infrastructure. It includes Bitcoin Core, the Fulcrum indexer, and the BTC-RPC Explorer.

141e1831-7aec-408c-b405-ee12577163d2.title: BITREFILL
141e1831-7aec-408c-b405-ee12577163d2.body:
A no-KYC online service that allows you to buy gift cards, phone top-ups and subscriptions using bitcoins. Bitrefill is a gateway between the Bitcoin economy and the traditional economy: users can spend their bitcoins at hundreds of retailers (Amazon, Uber, Steam, etc.) without those retailers directly accepting bitcoin payments.

The service supports on-chain and Lightning Network payments, which allows near-instant transactions. Bitrefill is often used by bitcoiners who want to live as much as possible on BTC, while still accessing the goods and services of traditional commerce.

143dddf7-873b-48ef-a4ef-956c150318bb.title: SIGHASH_ALL | SIGHASH_ACP
143dddf7-873b-48ef-a4ef-956c150318bb.body: Type of SigHash Flag (`0x81`) combined with the modifier `SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY` (`SIGHASH_ACP`) used in Bitcoin transaction signatures. This combination specifies that the signature applies to all outputs and only to one specific input of the transaction. `SIGHASH_ALL | SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY` allows other participants to add additional inputs to the transaction after its initial signature. It is particularly useful in collaborative scenarios, such as crowdfunding transactions, where different contributors can add their own inputs while preserving the integrity of the outputs committed to by the initial signer.

146fdc41-242e-48c1-be63-eb310574fae3.title: FULL NODE
146fdc41-242e-48c1-be63-eb310574fae3.body: A computer that runs a client of the Bitcoin protocol, and which downloads, verifies and stores the entire blockchain, i.e. the complete transaction history since the Genesis block. A full node independently verifies all transactions and blocks according to Bitcoin's consensus rules. It is therefore this type of node that provides the highest level of verification for its user, and that makes it possible to reduce to the maximum the need to trust a third party. The full node requires more storage resources, computing power, RAM and bandwidth than a lightweight node (SPV).

1473c4ba-1407-46c8-9431-ef4119cefa8e.title: VOUT
1473c4ba-1407-46c8-9431-ef4119cefa8e.body:
A specific element of a Bitcoin transaction that determines the destination of the funds sent. A transaction can include several outputs, each one distinctly identified by the combination of the transaction identifier (`txid`) and an index called `vout`. This index, which starts at `0`, marks the position of the output in the sequence of the transaction's outputs. Thus, the first output will be designated by `"vout": 0`, the second by `"vout": 1`, and so on.

Each `vout` mainly encapsulates two pieces of information:
* the value, expressed in bitcoins, which represents the amount sent;
* a locking script (`scriptPubKey`) that stipulates the conditions required for the funds to be spent again in a subsequent transaction.

The combination of the `txid` and the `vout` of a specific coin forms what is called an *outpoint*, for example:

* txid:

```
4c160086e39a940c2459f03bb7cfe5b768fc78373c9960dc2cf2fa61b57d0adf
```

* vout:

```
0
```

* outpoint:

```
4c160086e39a940c2459f03bb7cfe5b768fc78373c9960dc2cf2fa61b57d0adf:0
```

14740648-aa8c-4405-81fd-063c44928336.title: HASHCASH

14959673-c92d-4892-8e22-d30e0c3313a9.title: SPV NODE - LIGHTWEIGHT NODE
14959673-c92d-4892-8e22-d30e0c3313a9.body:
An SPV node (*Simplified Payment Verification*), sometimes called a "lightweight node", is a lightweight client of a Bitcoin node that allows users to validate transactions without having to store the entire blockchain. Instead, an SPV node stores only the block headers, and obtains information about specific transactions by querying full nodes when necessary. This verification principle is made possible by the structure of transactions in Bitcoin blocks, which are organized within a cryptographic accumulator (Merkle Tree).

This approach is advantageous for devices with limited resources, such as mobile phones. However, SPV nodes trust full nodes for the availability of information, which implies an additional level of trust and, consequently, lower security compared with full nodes. SPV nodes cannot validate transactions independently, but they can verify whether a transaction is included in a block by consulting Merkle proofs.

14a4ab7c-1d8a-4347-bbdb-db2c42d8ed48.title: BIP-0098
14a4ab7c-1d8a-4347-bbdb-db2c42d8ed48.body: Proposal for an optimized variant of Merkle trees for Bitcoin, offering faster and more compact inclusion proofs. BIP-0098 was initially designed as part of the first MAST (Merkelized Abstract Syntax Trees) proposals, aiming to allow the conditional execution of script branches. This preparatory work influenced later developments that led to Taproot (BIP-0341).

15517b75-d562-4a34-961d-2842fb96a1ff.title: EREBUS
15517b75-d562-4a34-961d-2842fb96a1ff.body: A very sophisticated form of attack against the Bitcoin network that allows a malicious Internet service provider to isolate specific Bitcoin nodes. It is therefore a form of Eclipse attack. The Erebus attack exploits the structure of the Internet, in particular the chokepoints (or "*bottlenecks*") in routing between autonomous systems (AS). An attacker, by controlling an autonomous system, can manipulate network traffic to isolate a Bitcoin node from the rest of the network, and thus make it believe in a false state of the blockchain (blocks or transactions not known by the node). This isolation can lead to double spends or censorship against the isolated node. This attack has been made much more difficult since version 0.20.0 of Bitcoin Core and the introduction of Asmap.

1560fed2-3853-4b56-b17e-542208fa5c2a.title: JOINMARKET
1560fed2-3853-4b56-b17e-542208fa5c2a.body: Coinjoin implementation created in 2015 by Chris Belcher. JoinMarket stands out from other coinjoin implementations through its unique model for matching users. It works as a P2P marketplace where "*makers*" make their bitcoins available for mixing and receive fees, while "*takers*" use this liquidity, in exchange for payment, to carry out coinjoins with them.

1632ada7-dfea-4bfc-9068-fd3ce0683c34.title: OP_2 TO OP_16 - 0X52 TO 0X60
