1632ada7-dfea-4bfc-9068-fd3ce0683c34.body:
The opcodes from `OP_2` through `OP_16` push the respective numeric values from 2 to 16 onto the stack. They are used to simplify scripts by allowing the insertion of small numeric values. This type of opcode is notably used in multisignature scripts. Here is an example of `scriptPubKey` for a 2/3 multisig: 

```text
OP_2
<Clé publique A>
<Clé publique B>
<Clé publique C>
OP_3
OP_CHECKMULTISIG
```

All of these opcodes are sometimes also named `OP_PUSHNUM_N`.

16520a0f-affd-499c-bacc-3badd9ccd00d.title: SPARK TREE
16520a0f-affd-499c-bacc-3badd9ccd00d.body:
An offchain tree structure used in the Spark protocol to expand a single UTXO into several sub-units of value, in order to solve the problem of classic statechains, which required the transfer of an entire UTXO. The tree is made up of branches (*branch transactions*) and leaves (*leaf transactions*).

The root of the tree corresponds to the on-chain UTXO (`Txn0`), whose operator key is permanently destroyed. The branches are intermediate transactions maintained off-chain, without a timelock, which can only be spent through the aggregation of the keys of all the leaves located beneath them. The leaves are the terminal transactions held by individual users, each associated with an exit transaction with a relative timelock.

The splitting of a leaf relies on a key additivity property: the parent key is split into several child keys whose sum equals the original key (`a_0 = a_1 + a_2 + \ldots + a_n`). This property also allows leaves to be re-aggregated.

166973a3-396b-4474-a326-fc272c606615.title: PLAUSIBLE DENIABILITY
166973a3-396b-4474-a326-fc272c606615.body:
A principle according to which a user can credibly deny possessing or controlling certain bitcoins, because there are several plausible interpretations of a given situation. In the context of Bitcoin, plausible deniability is a goal sought by many privacy techniques.

For example, a coinjoin transaction offers plausible deniability because an observer cannot prove with certainty which output belongs to which participant. If a user is asked whether they own a particular UTXO resulting from a coinjoin, they can credibly deny it, since several participants could be its owner.

Similarly, a hidden wallet (*hidden wallet*) protected by a BIP-0039 passphrase offers plausible deniability. A user under duress can reveal their recovery phrase without the passphrase, giving access to a decoy wallet, while denying the existence of the hidden wallet associated with the secret passphrase.

Plausible deniability is a key concept for the protection of privacy and the physical security of bitcoin holders, particularly against state or criminal adversaries.

16b25d54-8880-4f6f-a424-c3792093c26a.title: TRANSACTION PINNING
16b25d54-8880-4f6f-a424-c3792093c26a.body:
Attack that consists of making the replacement of a transaction prohibitively expensive by exploiting nodes' protections against the waste of bandwidth, CPU and memory. The attacker diverts the rules intended to prevent abuse of the relay system and uses them to block legitimate attempts to increase fees in a multiparty context.

Two main vectors are exploited. The first abuses rule 3 of BIP-0125, which requires that the replacement transaction pay higher absolute fees than the original transaction and all of its children. The attacker attaches a large child transaction with a low fee rate, which forces the victim to pay disproportionately high fees to perform a replacement by RBF. The second vector exploits descendant limits: nodes restrict transactions to 101,000 vbytes of descendants or 25 ancestors/descendants in total. An attacker can saturate these limits with their own child transactions, which completely blocks CPFP.

This attack represents a serious threat to the Lightning Network and other multiparty protocols, where fee management is crucial to meeting settlement time windows. Several countermeasures have been developed: the *CPFP carve-out*, *ephemeral anchors*, v3 transactions and *package relay*.

16f24b24-342f-4eb9-a1c4-bd754018e020.title: BIP-0151
16f24b24-342f-4eb9-a1c4-bd754018e020.body: Proposes a protocol for encrypting P2P communications between peers on the Bitcoin network, in order to strengthen security and privacy. Its goal is notably to prevent traffic manipulation and mass surveillance attacks. Ultimately, BIP-0151 was replaced by BIP-0324 (*P2P transport V2*), which is now implemented as an option in Bitcoin Core.

16fd7312-e023-43a4-8f62-40ee56fd938a.title: ECLAIR
16fd7312-e023-43a4-8f62-40ee56fd938a.body:
A major implementation of the Lightning Network protocol written in the Scala language. Eclair is developed by the French company ACINQ.

*Note that "Eclair" was also the name of a Lightning wallet for mobile devices, developed by the same company. Today, this wallet is no longer maintained.*

17015788-45d2-49ef-abca-ff3516162aea.title: LIBWALLY-CORE
17015788-45d2-49ef-abca-ff3516162aea.body:
An *open source* cryptographic and utility library developed by Blockstream, designed to make it easier to integrate Bitcoin functions into applications. It provides low-level primitives for key management, transaction construction, address encoding and PSBT operations.

Libwally-core is written in C to be portable and performant, with *bindings* available for Python, Java, JavaScript and other languages. It relies on `libsecp256k1` for cryptographic operations on the elliptic curve.

It is notably used as a core dependency of Core Lightning (CLN) for all wallet- and transaction-related operations. Other projects such as Blockstream's Green Wallet also use it.

1757fc8e-1179-4ec5-b7be-097d31ddb93f.title: PURPOSE

176da554-3dd4-41c2-bc3e-5b7f7a2bf34a.title: NLOCKTIME
176da554-3dd4-41c2-bc3e-5b7f7a2bf34a.body:
A 4-byte field built into every Bitcoin transaction, which specifies either an absolute block height (if its value is below 500,000,000) or an absolute Unix timestamp (if its value is greater than or equal to 500,000,000). The transaction is considered final (and therefore includable in a block) only once this value is strictly exceeded by the height of the candidate block (for height mode) or by the MTP, the median of the 11 previous blocks (for time mode). It is therefore an absolute timelock, as opposed to the relative timelocks of the `nSequence` field, and it acts at the level of the entire transaction.

The `nLockTime` is enforced only if at least one input of the transaction has a `nSequence` different from the value `0xFFFFFFFF`. If all inputs have `nSequence = 0xFFFFFFFF`, the field is completely ignored. This is why wallets using the `nLockTime` typically set `nSequence = 0xFFFFFFFE`.

`OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY` complements this mechanism by making it possible to impose a timelock from a `scriptPubKey`. The opcode checks 4 conditions:
* the value at the top of the stack and the transaction's `nLockTime` are of the same type (block height or timestamp),
* the value at the top of the stack is not negative,
* the value at the top of the stack is less than or equal to the transaction's `nLockTime`,
* the `nSequence` of the input being evaluated is not `0xFFFFFFFF`.

CLTV therefore never directly checks the time or the height: it delegates this verification by forcing the spending transaction to declare a `nLockTime` less than or equal to the value wanted by the script.

18060e03-d8e2-46d6-82fa-ce7949682cd6.title: BIP-0119
18060e03-d8e2-46d6-82fa-ce7949682cd6.body: Introduces a new opcode named `OP_CHECKTEMPLATEVERIFY` (CTV). CTV would make it possible to create non-recursive covenants in transactions, in order to impose specific conditions on how a given coin can be spent, including in future transactions. More concretely, it would make it possible to define conditions on the `scriptPubKey` of a transaction's outputs from the `scriptPubKey` of the UTXO spent as input. CheckTemplateVerify is designed to be simple and without dynamic state. Its implementation aims to extend Bitcoin's scripting capabilities to facilitate various applications such as transaction congestion control, the creation of non-interactive payment channels, DLCs, payment pools... This new opcode would be introduced as a replacement for `OP_NOP4`. This change would involve a soft fork.

1821c6f4-a45e-4fcd-900e-9486b7f4547f.title: BOLT-08
1821c6f4-a45e-4fcd-900e-9486b7f4547f.body: Specification that defines the encrypted and authenticated transport layer of the Lightning Network. It is based on the Noise protocol, where the initiator must know the responder's public key before connecting. The *handshake* takes place in three acts, at the end of which both peers share session keys.

183c3c79-9219-4261-91b1-1c9e73b62506.title: SPIRAL
183c3c79-9219-4261-91b1-1c9e73b62506.body:
A subsidiary of Block Inc. (formerly Square) dedicated to funding and developing *open source* Bitcoin projects. Created in 2019 under the name "Square Crypto", then renamed "Spiral" in 2021, the organization funds independent developers, designers and contributors working on Bitcoin and its ecosystem.

Spiral has notably supported projects such as Bitcoin Core or BTCPay Server. The organization also develops the Lightning Dev Kit (LDK) and the Bitcoin Dev Kit (BDK), two *open source* libraries that facilitate the integration of Bitcoin and Lightning into third-party applications.

184d6a47-640a-401a-aa03-bbc1f06a0519.title: TIME WARP
184d6a47-640a-401a-aa03-bbc1f06a0519.body:
A theoretical attack on Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment mechanism that exploits a flaw in the way block timestamps are verified at the boundary between two retarget periods. Every 2,016 blocks, the protocol recalculates the difficulty target by comparing the timestamp of the first block of the period with that of the last. The attack consists, for a miner who controls a majority of the computing power, of manipulating these timestamps: they set the timestamps of almost all the blocks of the period to the minimum allowed by the *Median Time Past* (MTP) rule, then assign the last block a timestamp in the future, which respects the NAT + 2 hours rule. The protocol then deduces that the period lasted much longer than it actually did, which results in an artificial and unjustified reduction of the difficulty for the following period.

By repeating this process over several successive periods, an attacker could theoretically lower the difficulty until producing blocks at an extreme rate (up to a maximum of 6 blocks per second). This extreme deceleration followed by acceleration would compromise the security of funds protected by *timelocks*, could saturate the bandwidth of the network's nodes, would facilitate certain types of attacks such as eclipse attacks, and would lead to numerous major reorganizations making transaction confirmations unreliable. For the attacker, the main benefit they can derive is to collect the block subsidies much faster than normal.

The “Consensus Cleanup” soft fork proposal (BIP-0054) aims to fix this vulnerability by requiring that the first block of a new difficulty period carry a timestamp that is not more than 2 hours earlier than that of the last block of the previous period. This constraint prevents the extreme manipulation of the time gaps between two retarget periods and therefore prevents this attack.

Note that this attack is made possible by a historical bug (*off-by-one*) introduced by Satoshi Nakamoto in the calculation of the difficulty adjustment. This calculation takes as a basis a duration of 2 weeks (supposed to correspond to `2016 \times 10` minutes), and compares it with the difference between the first and the last block of the period, in order to determine a deviation. The problem is that between the first and the last block of a period, there are in reality only 2015 intervals, and not 2016. For the calculation to be correct, it would have been necessary to compare with the difference between the last block of the previous period and the last block of the current period that has just ended, which would indeed have given 2016 intervals. Besides the fact that this bug very slightly biases the adjustment calculation by about 0.05%, it is above all what makes time warp attacks possible. Indeed, if the comparison were made on the last block of the previous period rather than on the first block of the period that has just ended, there would be an overlap of the periods, which would prevent this type of manipulation. The problem is that to truly fix this historical bug, a hard fork would be needed.

184f83b4-5047-4eef-863f-552dd94a1302.title: DCA - DOLLAR COST AVERAGING
184f83b4-5047-4eef-863f-552dd94a1302.body: An investment strategy that consists of investing a fixed amount of fiat currency in a specific asset at regular intervals, regardless of the asset's price. This method reduces the impact of volatility on the overall investment by buying more units when prices are low and fewer when they are high. DCA generally aims to build a position in an asset over the long term while minimizing risk. It is a very popular strategy for investing in bitcoin.

187931ca-e37c-4ff8-bc88-689c4b88d574.title: PPLNS - PAY PER LAST N SHARES
187931ca-e37c-4ff8-bc88-689c4b88d574.body: Method for calculating miner compensation in the context of mining pools. PPLNS rewards miners based on their contribution in *shares* over a given period. In PPLNS, payments are made only when the pool finds a block and are based on the number of *shares* submitted by the miner relative to the total *shares* collected during the observed period. This method favors consistent miners who are active over the long term, because it discourages *pool hopping* (frequently switching pools). The compensation varies with the probability of finding a block, which can lead to lower consistency in the miner's income (more variance than pay-per-task).

18a8053d-8091-4185-992e-2eb9d62ac05c.title: TOR
18a8053d-8091-4185-992e-2eb9d62ac05c.body:
Network of relay servers (*nodes*) that makes it possible to anonymize the origin of TCP connections on the internet. It works by encapsulating data in several layers of encryption. Each relay node removes one layer to reveal the address of the next node, until the final destination is reached. The Tor network ensures anonymity by preventing intermediate nodes from knowing both the origin and the destination of the data, which makes it very difficult for an observer to trace the user's activity. The Tor network can be used with Bitcoin to avoid associating one's IP address with a Bitcoin node, and thus avoid leaking some personal information.

*"Tor" stands for "The Onion Router". It is important to distinguish Tor the network from Tor Browser, a web browser based on Firefox that is specifically designed to use the Tor network.*

192ec4e8-26c4-47d6-a157-4a15bd2231b4.title: ELECTRS
192ec4e8-26c4-47d6-a157-4a15bd2231b4.body: An *open-source* implementation of Electrum Server written in Rust. The role of an electrs is therefore to maintain a complete index of Bitcoin addresses and transactions from the blockchain provided by a full node, in order to easily and quickly make queries from wallet software (such as Electrum for example).

1933e339-01fe-47d4-bb17-8fa3945af373.title: GROTH16
1933e339-01fe-47d4-bb17-8fa3945af373.body: SNARK-type zero-knowledge proof system, proposed by the cryptographer Jens Groth in 2016. Groth16 stands out for the minimal size of its proofs (only three elliptic curve elements, or about 200 bytes) and for a constant verification time, which makes it one of the most efficient schemes for on-chain verification. In return, Groth16 requires a trusted setup ceremony (*trusted setup*) specific to each circuit, during which secret parameters are generated and then ideally destroyed. If these parameters were reconstructed, it would be possible to create false proofs. The RISC Zero framework uses Groth16 as a final wrapping layer to compress large STARK proofs into compact SNARK proofs. This is the mechanism exploited by the Citrea rollup to publish validity proofs on the Bitcoin blockchain.

1953c4ab-5d08-480c-9ede-ddc04ad4ab14.title: BOLT-07
1953c4ab-5d08-480c-9ede-ddc04ad4ab14.body:
Specification that defines the peer-to-peer discovery protocol of the Lightning network. It describes the `node_announcement` messages (by which nodes broadcast their identity and connection addresses), `channel_announcement` (which prove the existence of a channel) and `channel_update` (which publish the routing fees and expiry deltas of each channel).

BOLT-07 establishes the rules for staggered broadcasting of announcements (*gossip*), the mechanism for pruning obsolete channels or channels closed on-chain, and the query-based synchronization protocols that allow nodes to maintain a consistent view of the network topology.

19bf3530-6e38-416d-ae7d-72e6092197d9.title: OP_CHECKHASHVERIFY - CHV
19bf3530-6e38-416d-ae7d-72e6092197d9.body: New opcode proposed in 2012 in BIP-0017 by Luke Dashjr, offering the same functionality as `OP_EVAL` or P2SH. It would have made it possible to hash the end of the `scriptSig`, compare the result with the top of the stack and make the transaction invalid if the two hashes did not match. This opcode was never implemented.

1a26f583-e25a-4f4c-bb55-929cf590e79d.title: BIP-0036
1a26f583-e25a-4f4c-bb55-929cf590e79d.body: Proposal for a mechanism allowing Bitcoin nodes to announce and provide custom services via the peer-to-peer protocol. BIP-0036 aimed to extend the network's capabilities by allowing specialized nodes to offer additional features beyond the standard relay of blocks and transactions. This proposal was never adopted.

1a613f45-cf3f-4c76-812e-2890abf77a2a.title: OP_CODESEPARATOR - 0XAB
1a613f45-cf3f-4c76-812e-2890abf77a2a.body: Modifies the current output script, indicating that only the operations that follow this opcode will be taken into account in the verification of the signatures of the corresponding inputs. This makes it possible to segment a complex script into several parts, where each segment can be signed independently.

1b2f11cb-04fd-4d6e-a6e1-f64727f1996b.title: BYZANTINE FAULT
1b2f11cb-04fd-4d6e-a6e1-f64727f1996b.body:
A Byzantine fault, or Byzantine behavior, is any behavior of a system that does not comply with its own specifications, producing non-conforming results.

“Natural Byzantine faults” are commonly distinguished from “deliberate Byzantine faults”: the former generally stem from undetected physical errors (memory, network transmissions, etc.), while the latter mainly result from attacks aimed at making the system fail (sabotage, malicious intent, backdoor).

Authentication, signatures, and consensus by cryptographic means and “Byzantine Fault Tolerant” or “*Byzantine Fault Tolerant* (BFT)” algorithms make it possible to limit the latter.

*The Byzantine fault refers to the Byzantine Generals Problem, a metaphor dealing with the questioning of the reliability of transmissions and the integrity of the parties communicating.*

1b36c549-465f-4c17-8f79-27f9a2bd77e7.title: SECURE ELEMENT
1b36c549-465f-4c17-8f79-27f9a2bd77e7.body:
Electronic chip resistant to physical attacks, designed to store sensitive data and run cryptographic operations in an isolated environment. In general computing, *secure elements* are found in bank cards, biometric passports, SIM cards and the TPM (*Trusted Platform Module*) modules of computers. They are designed to resist side-channel attacks (*side-channel attacks*), fault injection attacks and attempts at physical reverse engineering. *Secure elements* are generally certified under the international Common Criteria (CC) standard, with assurance levels ranging from EAL1 to EAL7.

In the context of Bitcoin, *secure elements* are used in *hardware wallets* to protect private keys against any unauthorized access, including in the event of physical compromise of the device. The private key is generated and stored inside the chip, and signing operations are performed internally without ever exposing the key outside the component. Most *hardware wallet* manufacturers integrate a *secure element* into their devices: Ledger (with ST chips from STMicroelectronics), Coldcard (with ATECC608 chips from Microchip), BitBox02, Trezor Safe (with the TROPIC01 chip) and others. Some devices such as Blockstream's Jade take an alternative approach called a *virtual secure element*, where the key is protected by a distributed encryption scheme rather than by a dedicated physical chip.

1b6687a6-aba7-4f55-aceb-ba44b553ea5d.title: CRYPTO-ASSET
1b6687a6-aba7-4f55-aceb-ba44b553ea5d.body: Term used in a legal and regulatory context to designate the various types of cryptocurrencies, including bitcoin.

1b839746-62da-4c5e-bc75-61ebce207675.title: FOSS
1b839746-62da-4c5e-bc75-61ebce207675.body: Acronym for "*Free and Open Source Software*". It refers to software under a license that allows anyone to run it for any purpose, to study it, to modify it to suit their needs, and to redistribute it freely, modified or not. This definition implies that the software's source code is publicly accessible.

1b8e2ba3-2faa-4e68-9fef-feace1737cc2.title: UTXO SET
1b8e2ba3-2faa-4e68-9fef-feace1737cc2.body:
Refers to the set of all existing UTXOs at a given moment. In other words, it is a big list of all the different pieces of bitcoins waiting to be spent. If you add up the amounts of all the UTXOs in the UTXO set, you get the total money supply of bitcoins in circulation. Each node of the Bitcoin network maintains its own UTXO set in real time. It updates it as new valid blocks are confirmed, with the transactions they include, which consume certain UTXOs from the UTXO set, and create new ones in return.

This UTXO set is kept by each node in order to quickly verify whether the UTXOs spent in transactions are indeed legitimate. This allows them to detect and reject double-spend attempts. The UTXO set is often at the heart of concerns about Bitcoin's decentralization, because its size naturally grows very quickly. Since part of it must be kept in RAM in order to verify transactions in a reasonable time, it is possible that the UTXO set will gradually make running a full node too costly. The UTXO set also has a strong impact on the IBD (*Initial Block Download*). The larger the share of the UTXO set that can be held in RAM, the faster the IBD. On Bitcoin Core, the UTXO set is stored in the folder named `/chainstate`.

1ba63adf-9645-450f-ab15-352b9e291527.title: FULL RBF
1ba63adf-9645-450f-ab15-352b9e291527.body:
Mempool policy that allows the replacement of any unconfirmed transaction by another transaction that spends at least one of the same inputs, but that offers a higher fee, regardless of whether the original transaction signaled its availability for replacement via the RBF *flag* (field `nSequence`). In classic RBF (opt-in RBF), only transactions that have explicitly enabled this signal can be replaced. Full RBF removes this restriction.

This policy was introduced in Bitcoin Core via the configuration option `mempoolfullrbf`, available starting with version 24.0 (November 2022) with a default value of `0` (disabled). Starting with version 28.0 (October 2024), this option was enabled by default (`mempoolfullrbf=1`), which makes Full RBF the standard behavior of Bitcoin Core.

Full RBF has been the subject of intense debate in the community. Its supporters argue that it improves the efficiency of the fee market and strengthens security by eliminating the false impression that transactions not signaling RBF would be irreversible before confirmation. Its opponents pointed out that it complicates use cases that relied on the acceptance of unconfirmed transactions ("zero-conf" transactions), notably in retail.

1ba93ca0-7a7c-44a0-b5bf-12234b37d344.title: MASF
1ba93ca0-7a7c-44a0-b5bf-12234b37d344.body: Acronym for "*Miner-Activated Soft Fork*". Describes a soft fork in Bitcoin when its activation comes from an action by miners. MASFs are a family of soft fork activation methods on Bitcoin. In these approaches, miners signal their agreement and readiness for a protocol update by mining blocks that support the lock-in of the soft fork. If a significant majority of miners votes in favor of the soft fork, the update is considered accepted and is activated later. This process helps avoid splitting the blockchain and maintains the unity of the network. The MASF is preferred for its gentler and more consensual approach, reducing the risk of a blockchain split while ensuring that the majority of computing power supports the new update. The activation methods BIP-0034, BIP-0009, BIP-0008 (if `LOT=false` or if the voting threshold is reached) or Speedy Trial are MASFs.

1bb981e1-3f5a-4919-a581-dbe6f8d83861.title: BIP-0022
1bb981e1-3f5a-4919-a581-dbe6f8d83861.body: BIP proposed in 2012 by Luke Dashjr that introduces a standardized JSON-RPC method for external mining interfaces, called `getblocktemplate`. As mining difficulty increased, the use of external software specialized in producing proofs of work grew. This BIP proposes a common communication standard for the *block template* between full nodes and software specialized in mining. This method involves sending the entire block structure, rather than just the header, in order to leave the miner the possibility of customizing it.

1bdb482e-52c8-48fe-b31c-d542311f0fc6.title: HASH FUNCTION

1bf8af3a-f6f1-4a51-9efb-7f8bfa2372ae.title: FORCED ADDRESS REUSE
1bf8af3a-f6f1-4a51-9efb-7f8bfa2372ae.body:
Attack that consists of sending tiny amounts of bitcoins to a large number of receiving addresses. The attacker's goal is to push the recipients to merge these amounts with other UTXOs. The attacker then tracks the future movements of these small amounts of bitcoins, with the aim of forming *clusters* of addresses, that is, determining whether several addresses belong to the same entity. By cross-referencing the information gathered during the attack with other data and heuristics used in chain analysis, it is possible for the attacker to identify certain entities and the associated addresses. This method represents a threat only to users' privacy, but does not affect the security of their funds.

*The original term for describing this attack is "Dusting Attack", but some bitcoiners suggest using the term "forced address reuse" instead, because they find the term "dust" inappropriate here.*

1c4b7718-449e-438a-90be-bca12f26ddb5.title: OPCODES
1c4b7718-449e-438a-90be-bca12f26ddb5.body: The set of commands used in Bitcoin's Script system. Script is a stack-based programming language used to establish spending conditions, and therefore, indirectly, to secure bitcoins. The instructions used in the Script language are called "opcodes". They are logical operators and commands for manipulating stacks (*stacks*). These specific instructions are executed by the network's nodes when validating a transaction. Script is a non-Turing-complete language. It can be categorized as a mid-level language (almost low-level) inspired by Forth.

1c564a5c-40f2-4f04-84c6-4f96559cc6ad.title: DEMURRAGE
1c564a5c-40f2-4f04-84c6-4f96559cc6ad.body:
A cost associated with holding a currency. By extension, demurrage sometimes refers to a monetary mechanism in which holding a currency for a prolonged period results in a penalty for its owner, for example by gradually decreasing its value. The goal is often to improve the velocity of circulation of the currency by discouraging long-term saving.

This mechanism is sometimes proposed to be implemented on Bitcoin in order to support the transaction fee market and to distribute the costs of the system more fairly. Indeed, the operating cost of Bitcoin will eventually rest solely on those who make transactions, and not on savers who nevertheless benefit from the security of the system. However, demurrage is very widely rejected by the Bitcoin community, because it penalizes long-term holders and is not consistent with the store-of-value characteristic of BTC. Since it imposes a gradual loss of value, it can be perceived as an infringement of the right to own property.

One could argue against demurrage by explaining that the cost of the current system already inevitably rests on savers, given that they had to make a transaction at some point to obtain their bitcoins. Moreover, the security of a given UTXO increases greatly with the first blocks after its creation, but over time, the additional security gained with each block becomes more and more marginal. Thus, it is not necessarily unfair not to make long-term holders bear the cost of mining.

Demurrage has notably been applied on the altcoin Freicoin, a fork of Bitcoin that implemented a system of negative interest rates.

1c5cfca6-88b1-4560-a570-01fe897636a5.title: CONTRACT PARTICIPANT

1ca467c5-a980-49ee-a680-0f21b34e9c2f.title: OP_RETURN - 0X6A
1ca467c5-a980-49ee-a680-0f21b34e9c2f.body: Marks a script as invalid, which makes the output containing it provably unspendable. Nodes on the network can therefore remove this output from their UTXO set. `OP_RETURN` is often used to inscribe arbitrary data in the blockchain.

1ca8a8c5-3108-4571-8070-ed247de77aa6.title: DANDELION
1ca8a8c5-3108-4571-8070-ed247de77aa6.body:
A proposal that aims to improve the privacy of transaction routing in the Bitcoin network in order to counter deanonymization. In the classic operation of Bitcoin, transactions are immediately broadcast to multiple nodes. This can potentially allow observers to link transactions, which are normally anonymous, with IP addresses. The goal of BIP-0156 is to address this problem. To do so, it introduces an additional phase in the broadcast that preserves anonymity before public propagation. Thus, Dandelion first uses a "stem" phase in which the transaction is sent along a random path of nodes, before being broadcast to the entire network in the "fluff" phase. The stem and the fluff are references to the behavior of the transaction's propagation through the network, which resembles the shape of a dandelion ("*a dandelion*" in English). This routing method blurs the trail leading to the source node, making it difficult to trace a transaction through the network back to its origin.

![Dandelion graph: a linear stem from the source node in gray then fluff in a star shape toward the rest of the network.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/d/dandelion/assets/image-1.png)

1cd9efe5-250b-4656-a16e-f62bd65a7353.title: MINING MANAGEMENT SOFTWARE
1cd9efe5-250b-4656-a16e-f62bd65a7353.body: Software dedicated to managing and optimizing mining operations. This type of software makes it possible to monitor in real time the performance of ASICs, energy consumption, temperatures, and hash rates. It also offers features for managing large-scale mining farms, with the automation of settings (such as *overclocking*, for example), fault detection and remote management of devices.

1d00c248-d26d-4e3c-9594-4b2362757d2e.title: BIP-0177
1d00c248-d26d-4e3c-9594-4b2362757d2e.body:
Proposal to redefine Bitcoin's base unit so that "1 bitcoin" corresponds to the current satoshi, eliminating decimals entirely. Under this new system, the current value of 1 BTC would become 100,000,000 of the new base unit. BIP-0177 aims to simplify the user experience by removing the confusion related to decimal fractions, which is particularly problematic for new users.

This change has been adopted by some applications, notably Bitkit, the wallet developed by Synonym, whose CEO, John Carvalho, is also the author of BIP-0177. In practice, however, the vast majority of wallet software for now keeps the standard of 1 bitcoin = 100,000,000 satoshis.

1d240f78-cc42-44ac-8964-c419c1900987.title: FORFEIT TRANSACTION
1d240f78-cc42-44ac-8964-c419c1900987.body:
Transaction by which a user of the Ark protocol cedes ownership of their input VTXO to the *Ark Service Provider* (ASP) during a round. Since the ASP advances the on-chain liquidity to create the new output VTXOs, it recovers in return the users' old VTXOs via these forfeit transactions.

The forfeit transaction exploits the forfeit clause (*forfeit clause*) written into the VTXO's policy, which consists of a multisig between the user and the ASP. Without an additional protection mechanism, signing this transaction would amount to giving up one's VTXO with no guarantee of getting a new VTXO in return. To solve this problem, a *connector output* from the round transaction is added as an additional input in the forfeit transaction. This link makes the transaction invalid as long as the round transaction is not confirmed on-chain, thus guaranteeing atomicity: the user loses their old VTXO only if the round's new VTXOs are actually created.

The forfeit transaction mechanism is also reused in the context of OOR (*out-of-round*) payments, where the forfeit clause is reused to transfer a VTXO directly to another user without going through a round.

1d9db1a5-d054-48ae-ae2f-70c603078957.title: JADE
1d9db1a5-d054-48ae-ae2f-70c603078957.body:
*Hardware wallet* made by Blockstream, designed to secure Bitcoin private keys and compatible with the Liquid network. The Jade stands out for its original security model: instead of using a *secure element* chip, it relies on a "*virtual secure element*" model in which the private key is encrypted and can only be decrypted by combining a secret stored on the device with a secret held by the Blockstream server (or a personal server).

Jade firmwares are fully open source. The devices have a camera for *air-gapped* mode via QR codes, and work with Blockstream Green, Sparrow Wallet or other compatible software. There are 2 hardware wallets in the Jade family: the classic Blockstream Jade, available pre-assembled or as a DIY kit, and the Blockstream Jade Plus, the most recent and more premium model, featuring a large color screen and a polished UX.

1dd0115e-198d-4141-8716-d7753c181d47.title: SATOCHIP
1dd0115e-198d-4141-8716-d7753c181d47.body:
Belgian company specialized in manufacturing hardware wallets (*hardware wallets*) in a smart card format. The main product, the Satochip, is an NFC card equipped with an EAL6+ certified secure element, which allows Bitcoin private keys to be stored securely.

The range also includes the SeedKeeper, a secure storage device for mnemonic phrases, and the Satodime, a physical bearer instrument for bitcoins. All the associated software is open source.

1df02ba6-a00e-468b-8b15-e0319476e639.title: SAMOURAI WALLET
1df02ba6-a00e-468b-8b15-e0319476e639.body:
Bitcoin wallet software for Android mobile devices, focused on privacy. It offers advanced features such as Whirlpool, Stonewall, StonewallX2, Ricochet and Stowaway (payjoin) coinjoins. Samourai also implements numerous protections to help users protect their privacy against chain analysis.

*On April 24, 2024, the two co-founders of Samourai Wallet were unjustly arrested for simply writing code. I want to express my unwavering support for them. Their commitment to privacy and freedom embodies the fundamental values of Bitcoin. These developers committed no crime; they only worked to offer tools allowing everyone to assert their natural rights. To support them in this ordeal, I invite everyone to sign the online petition: https://billandkeonne.org/.*

1e211062-6127-445e-b231-061276411810.title: MULTISIG
1e211062-6127-445e-b231-061276411810.body:
Multisignature wallets, often abbreviated “multisig”, are designed to strengthen the security of bitcoins by requiring several signatures from different private keys to authorize a spend. This method spreads the risk across several keys, which reduces both the risk of loss and that of theft (depending on the multisig configuration). Multisig wallets work according to an “m-of-n” model, where `m` is the minimum number of signatures required to validate a transaction, and `n` the total number of keys involved. For example, a 2-of-3 configuration requires two signatures out of three possible ones to validate a transaction. This approach offers greater security compared to single-key wallets, but it also introduces more complexity in terms of management and backup. Moreover, transactions using the older multisig standards are less private and more expensive in fees than standard *singlesig* transactions. However, recent innovations such as Taproot and the use of *descriptors* will make it possible to minimize, or even eliminate, these drawbacks of multisigs.

*Some bitcoiners distinguish between the terms “Multisig” and “Threshold Multisig”. Indeed, some claim that a multisig is necessarily an n-of-n, whereas a threshold multisig is an m-of-n. However, in everyday language, it is accepted to speak of “Multisig” even for m-of-n.*

1e23e4b1-5602-4e7c-a451-0c72aa304384.title: BLIND ORACLE
1e23e4b1-5602-4e7c-a451-0c72aa304384.body:
A cryptographic protocol in which an oracle performs operations (signing, encryption) on a confidential message transmitted by a user, without being able to know its content. The user can then verify the validity of the result without having exposed the original message to the oracle. This mechanism generally relies on blind cryptography techniques (*blind cryptography*), such as blind signatures or commitment schemes.

In the context of Bitcoin, the concept of *blind oracle* is notably used in Blockstream's Jade *hardware wallet*. The wallet encrypts the recovery phrase locally and uses a remote oracle for PIN protection, without this oracle having access to the private keys or the recovery phrase. This approach constitutes a “virtual secure element” (*virtual secure element*) that aims to protect against physical attacks, without requiring a dedicated secure chip.

1e39c350-c6f2-43b3-a631-71169e38e229.title: SIGOPS

1f0d5de7-0f3b-4fd3-84f0-6e7c24ac0509.title: FORK

1f4ed341-4975-4d30-81a0-23ec8b1cdb82.title: WALLET.DAT
1f4ed341-4975-4d30-81a0-23ec8b1cdb82.body: File in Bitcoin Core that stores information about the user's wallet, such as private keys and completed transactions. The `wallet.dat` file can be encrypted by the user to secure the funds, but it is not encrypted by default. Since version 0.16.0, this file has been moved to the `/wallets` folder.

1fbfa9c8-8175-4922-b1ab-75269df3b7ef.title: OP_IF - 0X63
1fbfa9c8-8175-4922-b1ab-75269df3b7ef.body:
Executes the following portion of the script if the value at the top of the stack is non-zero (true). If the value is zero (false), these operations are skipped, going directly to those after `OP_ELSE`, if present. `OP_IF` makes it possible to start a conditional control structure in a script. It determines the control flow in a script based on a condition provided at the time the transaction is executed. `OP_IF` is used with `OP_ELSE` and `OP_ENDIF` in the following way: 

```text
<condition>
OP_IF
<opérations si la condition est vraie>
OP_ELSE
<opérations si la condition est fausse>
OP_ENDIF
```

1fcc0d0b-d8b1-4f13-a3e3-f67383f704d4.title: BIP-0001

1fe3b85d-d62e-4634-815d-5f2e13874a36.title: BRAIINS POOL
1fe3b85d-d62e-4634-815d-5f2e13874a36.body: Bitcoin mining pool operated by the Czech company Braiins. Created in 2010 by Marek Palatinus (“Slush”), it is the very first Bitcoin mining pool, and it mined its first block on December 16, 2010. Initially known as “Bitcoin.cz Mining Pool”, then “Slush Pool” from 2016, it was renamed “Braiins Pool” in 2022. Braiins is also behind the Stratum V2 protocol, a major update to the communication protocol between miners and pools, which improves security, reduces bandwidth and allows miners to select for themselves the transactions to include in blocks. The company also develops Braiins OS, an open source firmware for ASIC machines.

200b7978-3740-4c66-a5bf-1e7056ba89a7.title: BITCOIN TREASURY COMPANY
200b7978-3740-4c66-a5bf-1e7056ba89a7.body:
A publicly traded company that places bitcoin at the center of its treasury strategy, accumulating bitcoins on its balance sheet rather than holding its reserves in fiat currency or bonds. The goal is to protect against monetary debasement while offering shareholders indirect exposure to bitcoin through traditional shares.

MicroStrategy (now Strategy) popularized this model under the leadership of Michael Saylor starting in August 2020. The company finances its bitcoin acquisitions through the issuance of convertible debt and shares, which creates a leverage effect on the price of bitcoin. Several other companies have since adopted similar strategies, such as Metaplanet in Japan or Semler Scientific in the United States.

This model allows institutional investors who cannot hold bitcoin directly to gain access to it through a conventional stock market vehicle, but it also exposes shareholders to the risks of financial leverage and of the volatility of the underlying asset.

200bf4d0-a53a-4bd0-a984-379851b58e0f.title: BIP-0146
200bf4d0-a53a-4bd0-a984-379851b58e0f.body: Proposal aiming to fix two residual sources of signature malleability in Bitcoin transactions, after the adoption of strict DER encoding by BIP-0066. The first rule, “LOW_S”, requires that the S value of ECDSA signatures be in the lower half of the curve order, thus eliminating the malleability inherent to ECDSA signatures. The second rule, “NULLFAIL”, requires that any signature failing verification via `OP_CHECKSIG` or `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` be an empty byte array, thus preventing the replacement of invalid signatures with other invalid values. BIP-0146 has “closed” status, because these fixes were partially integrated into the standardness rules and into SegWit (BIP-0141), which solved the malleability problem more completely.

200d7209-8a10-4afb-b994-3c6aed39b8f8.title: MINING FARM
200d7209-8a10-4afb-b994-3c6aed39b8f8.body:
Facility where many mining machines (often ASICs) are grouped together to mine bitcoin by taking part in the proof-of-work process. The purpose of this grouping is to make it easier to manage the fleet of machines and to achieve economies of scale, notably for setup, maintenance, cooling, power supply and network connection. The mining farm also makes it possible to improve the proximity of the miners, and thus to reduce the latency that could affect their profitability.

*Note that the mining farm must not be confused with the mining pool.*

200e6da3-a68c-4b58-a926-e0af0520e209.title: TESTNET4
200e6da3-a68c-4b58-a926-e0af0520e209.body:
The fourth iteration of Bitcoin's public test network, launched in 2024 to replace testnet3, which had become dysfunctional after 13 years of service. Testnet4 is a network distinct from *mainnet* where the bitcoins (TBTC) have no value, allowing developers to test their applications without financial risk.

Testnet3 suffered from several problems. A bug in the difficulty reset rule (which brought it back to 1 if no block had been found in 20 minutes) regularly caused block storms, pushing the chain height beyond 2.5 million blocks. The block reward had fallen to ~0.014 TBTC, making mining ineffective for distributing test coins. And above all, in 2024, TBTC had begun to be bought and sold for fraudulent airdrops, breaking the fundamental principle of their lack of value.

Testnet4, defined in BIP-0094, fixes the difficulty mechanism by forbidding the 20-minute exception for the first block of each retargeting period and by basing the adjustment calculation on the difficulty of the first block of the previous period rather than on that of the last. It uses port 48333 and a new genesis block. It is supported by Bitcoin Core starting with version 28.0.

204df0cf-f8e9-49a5-817a-3380953664d1.title: CAHOOTS

2059f3c9-b1ac-465c-9e7c-af54c8308b27.title: SELF-CUSTODY
2059f3c9-b1ac-465c-9e7c-af54c8308b27.body: Refers to the practice whereby a user keeps direct control of their private keys, and therefore of their bitcoins, without depending on an external entity to manage their assets.

2062f223-15aa-4022-b447-677332268d3b.title: BIP-0321
2062f223-15aa-4022-b447-677332268d3b.body: Proposal updating the `bitcoin:` URI scheme defined by BIP-0021 to support SegWit addresses in bech32 and bech32m format. The original BIP-0021 was designed for Base58 addresses, which are case-sensitive. Since bech32 addresses are case-insensitive, BIP-0321 adapts the specification to allow their correct use in URIs, notably in QR codes where uppercase encoding is more efficient. This BIP ensures the compatibility of the Bitcoin URI scheme with modern address formats.

208a2dfd-412e-4fbb-9fcf-809687a01641.title: MIMBLEWIMBLE
208a2dfd-412e-4fbb-9fcf-809687a01641.body:
A protocol that aims to improve the privacy and scalability of transactions. The *white paper* of this protocol was dropped in 2016 on the IRC channel `#bitcoin-wizards` by a user under a pseudonym. Andrew Poelstra then formalized the protocol in a paper published in October 2016. Mimblewimble relies on *Confidential Transactions* and Pedersen commitments to hide amounts, without preventing verification that inputs equal outputs. It uses neither addresses nor a script system: authentication is done solely through the algebraic structure of the transactions. All the transactions in a block are aggregated into a single one, in the manner of a giant *coinjoin*, which makes the links between sender and recipient indistinguishable.

The protocol was implemented in two distinct blockchains launched in January 2019: Grin and Beam. Litecoin integrated an adapted version in the form of extension blocks in May 2022. Mimblewimble has never been integrated into Bitcoin because of its incompatibility with the current script system and UTXO model.

20c0365a-78c7-4e04-a5b7-36d9766a5324.title: OPENTIMESTAMPS
20c0365a-78c7-4e04-a5b7-36d9766a5324.body: A decentralized *open source* timestamping protocol, developed by Peter Todd. OpenTimestamps uses the Bitcoin blockchain to prove the existence of a document or piece of data at a precise point in time. The protocol computes a cryptographic fingerprint (*hash*) of the file to be timestamped, then anchors this fingerprint in a Bitcoin transaction by means of a Merkle tree. The result is a verifiable and tamper-proof proof attesting that the data existed at the moment the corresponding Bitcoin block was mined. This system is useful for intellectual property, contracts, legal evidence or any situation that requires proof of time.

20ddeda5-0bf8-4d08-914f-81299fc47d75.title: SEGWIT2X
20ddeda5-0bf8-4d08-914f-81299fc47d75.body:
Controversial hard fork attempt aimed at doubling the block size limit on Bitcoin, while integrating SegWit. SegWit2x was introduced at the New York Agreement in 2017, a confidential meeting of more than 50 companies from the ecosystem that aimed to find a solution for scaling the system. SegWit2x sought to increase Bitcoin's transaction capacity by raising the maximum size of a block to 2 MB, compared with the original 1 MB. The hard fork was scheduled for block 494,784, that is, during the month of November 2017.

Despite the activation of SegWit in August 2017, the 2X project to double the size failed to obtain a consensus, notably because of the “NO2X” opposition campaign, which led to its cancellation at the beginning of November. This episode was perceived by many users and developers as an attack on Bitcoin, as part of the Blocksize War.

*SegWit2x is sometimes also called “B2X” or “S2X”. Initially, its name was “SegWit2Mb”.*

20f8ab5d-0912-498c-9491-581b873760bc.title: ATTACK SURFACE
20f8ab5d-0912-498c-9491-581b873760bc.body: Refers to the set of all potential entry points that an attacker can exploit to gain access to a system. The attack surface includes all the interfaces, services, ports, protocols, and other communication vectors that may be exposed. A larger attack surface increases vulnerabilities and therefore makes the system more likely to be attacked. Reducing the attack surface is a good security practice that involves disabling unnecessary services. For example, in the context of Bitcoin, *hardware wallets* have a much smaller attack surface than *software wallets*. Indeed, they isolate the keys on a device that is not connected to the Internet and has very few interfaces and services. In contrast, *software wallets* are installed on general-purpose PCs, which have a much larger attack surface because of the many features and network connections they support.

20f92957-d888-40b0-8ad7-868b49e93af7.title: CIRCULAR REBALANCE
20f92957-d888-40b0-8ad7-868b49e93af7.body: A payment that a Lightning node sends to itself along a path going through other nodes of the network. The goal is to move liquidity from one channel to another without opening or closing a channel. For example, if a node has a lot of outbound liquidity on a channel A but lacks outbound liquidity on a channel B, it can send itself a circular payment that goes out through A and comes back through B, thus rebalancing the two channels. This operation has a cost corresponding to the routing fees charged by the intermediate nodes.

2109b28a-da10-4fc1-a5a4-bc034e4f4301.title: LNP/BP
2109b28a-da10-4fc1-a5a4-bc034e4f4301.body: Swiss non-profit association founded in 2019 by Maxim Orlovsky and Giacomo Zucco. The acronym LNP/BP stands for “*Lightning Network Protocol / Bitcoin Protocol*”. The association is responsible for the development and maintenance of the standards of the RGB protocol, a smart contract system that operates with *client-side validation* on Bitcoin and the Lightning Network. RGB allows the issuance and transfer of digital assets and smart contracts directly on Bitcoin, keeping the data off-chain to preserve privacy and scalability. The association publishes and maintains a set of technical standards (LNPBP) that govern the operation of the protocol.

21845d57-8a08-4555-897d-d8db186b4fb6.title: BRAINWALLET
21845d57-8a08-4555-897d-d8db186b4fb6.body:
Bitcoin wallet backup method that consists of not keeping one's mnemonic phrase on any physical or digital medium, and memorizing it only in one's head. By extension, the term sometimes also refers to choosing the words of one's mnemonic phrase oneself (instead of generating it randomly) in order to memorize it more easily. In both cases, the objective is not to depend on any physical medium.

This approach is doubly dangerous. First, human memory is fallible: forgetting, an accident or a death results in a permanent loss of funds, and raises an obvious problem of succession and inheritance. Second, when the user chooses the words of their mnemonic phrase themselves, the entropy of the phrase is dramatically low. Human beings are incapable of producing true randomness: even a phrase that seems random follows predictable patterns (common words, quotes, song lyrics...). Attackers exploit these biases with dictionaries and brute force techniques, and many brainwallets have been emptied within seconds of their creation.

The only scenario where a brainwallet can be justified is that of an urgent escape (crossing a border, checkpoint...), where no physical medium can be carried without risk. But even in this case, less risky alternatives exist: physical concealment of the phrase, steganography, encryption...

2197f80d-8b0b-4478-b1b6-00164a5ee82a.title: BLKINDEX.DAT
2197f80d-8b0b-4478-b1b6-00164a5ee82a.body: Name of the old file used in Bitcoin Core to store various information about the blockchain, replaced since version 0.8.0 by the files in chainstate/, blocks/index/ and blocks/rev*.dat.

22055bb5-6ed8-484e-ac07-192733cbeb91.title: HEADERS-FIRST SYNC
22055bb5-6ed8-484e-ac07-192733cbeb91.body: An initial synchronization method (IBD) introduced in Bitcoin Core 0.10.0, which consists of first downloading the headers of all blocks before downloading the full blocks themselves. This method replaced *blocks-first* synchronization, used by earlier versions of Bitcoin Core, which downloaded blocks sequentially from a single peer.

221156e2-d7d3-4499-905d-6bf433d4c038.title: BIP-0328
221156e2-d7d3-4499-905d-6bf433d4c038.body: Defines how to construct a synthetic BIP-0032 extended public key (xpub) from a MuSig2 aggregated public key (BIP-0327), and how to use it for child key derivation. Rather than requiring each participant to derive their individual keys before aggregating them at each level, BIP-0328 makes it possible to derive non-hardened child keys directly from a single synthetic xpub built on the aggregated key. This xpub uses a fixed, standardized chain code. This mechanism considerably simplifies the generation of receiving addresses in MuSig2 multisig wallets, by reducing the storage and computation required. When signing, participants must compute the corresponding BIP-0032 derivation tweaks and provide them in the MuSig2 session context.

221e82a8-f5ee-422d-9bdb-c714b267f263.title: SEQUENCER
221e82a8-f5ee-422d-9bdb-c714b267f263.body: Specialized node responsible for ordering transactions and producing blocks in a rollup. The sequencer continuously monitors the mempool, selects pending transactions (prioritized by fees), executes them against the rollup's current state and produces a new block at regular intervals. It then issues a signed “soft confirmation” (*soft confirmation*), providing a fast pre-confirmation to the network's full nodes. Periodically, the sequencer publishes commitments (*commitments*) to the base layer (Bitcoin, in the case of Citrea) to permanently anchor the order of the blocks. The sequencer can influence the order of transactions and cause availability delays (*liveness*), but cannot falsify the rollup's state or steal funds, because validity proofs and the on-chain availability of data guarantee the integrity of state transitions. Decentralization of the sequencer is an active research topic in the rollup ecosystem.

2274abfa-fe6c-486b-874c-a21f65735f1c.title: OP_SHA1 - 0XA7
2274abfa-fe6c-486b-874c-a21f65735f1c.body: Takes the element at the top of the stack and replaces it with its hash using the `SHA1` function. The use of this function is nowadays discouraged in a secure setting.

229b0d6c-08cf-4462-9cd1-897517d4228b.title: BITBOX
229b0d6c-08cf-4462-9cd1-897517d4228b.body: Hardware wallet made by the Swiss company Shift Crypto. The current model, the BitBox02, exists in two versions: a multi-crypto edition and a Bitcoin-only edition whose firmware is strictly limited to Bitcoin, thereby reducing the attack surface. The device includes a secure element, open source firmware and a touch interface operated by sliding on the sides of the device.

22fa77ad-309c-4eb1-91ae-d710b9ae9a6d.title: COMPRESSED PUBLIC KEY
22fa77ad-309c-4eb1-91ae-d710b9ae9a6d.body:
A public key is used in scripts (either directly as a public key, or in the form of an address) to receive and secure bitcoins. A raw public key is represented by a point on an elliptic curve, made up of two coordinates (`x, y`) each of 256 bits. In raw format, a public key is therefore 512 bits long, not counting the extra byte that identifies the format. A compressed public key, on the other hand, is a more compact way of representing a public key. It uses only the `x` coordinate and a prefix (`02` or `03`) that indicates the parity of the `y` coordinate (even or odd). 

If we simplify this to the field of real numbers, since the elliptic curve is symmetric about the x-axis, for any point `P` (`x, y`) on the curve, there exists a point `P'` (`x, -y`) that will also be on this same curve. This means that for each `x` there are only two possible values of `y`, one positive and one negative. For example, for a given x-coordinate `x`, there would be two points `P_1` and `P_2` on the elliptic curve, which share the same x-coordinate but have opposite y-coordinates:

![Elliptic curve symmetric about the x-axis: for a given x-coordinate, two points P1 and P2 exist.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/cle-publique-compressee/assets/image-1.png)
To choose between the two potential points on the curve, we add to `x` a prefix specifying which `y` to choose. This method reduces the size of a public key from 520 bits to only 264 bits (8 bits of prefix + 256 bits for `x`). This representation is known as the compressed form of the public key.

However, in elliptic curve cryptography, we do not use the real numbers, but a finite field of order `p` (a prime number). In this context, the “sign” of `y` is determined by its parity, that is, whether `y` is even or odd. The prefix `0x02` then indicates an even `y`, while `0x03` indicates an odd `y`.

Let us consider the following example of a raw public key (a point on the elliptic curve) in hexadecimal:
```plaintext
K=04678afdb0fe5548271967f1a67130b7105cd6a828e03909a67962e0ea1f61deb649f6bc3f4cef38c4f35504e51ec112de5c384df7ba0b8d578a4c702b6bf11d5f
```

We can isolate the prefix, `x`, and `y`:
```plaintext
Préfixe=04

x=678afdb0fe5548271967f1a67130b7105cd6a828e03909a67962e0ea1f61deb6

y=49f6bc3f4cef38c4f35504e51ec112de5c384df7ba0b8d578a4c702b6bf11d5f
```

To determine the parity of `y`, we look at the last hexadecimal character of `y`:
```plaintext
Base 16 (hexadécimal) : f
Base 10 (décimal) : 15
y est impair
```

The prefix for the compressed public key will be `03`. The compressed public key in hexadecimal becomes:
```plaintext
K=03678afdb0fe5548271967f1a67130b7105cd6a828e03909a67962e0ea1f61deb6
```

230bebec-3a8b-4d46-9258-0e61e9674829.title: WASABI WALLET
230bebec-3a8b-4d46-9258-0e61e9674829.body: Privacy-focused Bitcoin wallet offering features such as coinjoin.

232a8659-9aaf-4842-b275-24ebc331a51b.title: COMPACT BLOCK RELAY
232a8659-9aaf-4842-b275-24ebc331a51b.body: Protocol introduced in Bitcoin Core in 2016 via BIP-0152, which offers a bandwidth-saving method for network nodes. *Compact Block Relay* makes it possible to communicate block information in a compact way, based on the assumption that nodes already have a large share of the transactions of a recent block in their mempool. Rather than transmitting every transaction in full, which would be redundant, *Compact Block Relay* proposes sending only short identifiers for the transactions already known to peers, accompanied by a few selected transactions (notably the coinbase transaction and those the node is likely not to know). The node can then ask its peers for any missing transactions. *Compact Block Relay* thus reduces the amount of data exchanged during block propagation, which in turn reduces bandwidth spikes and improves the overall efficiency of the network.

2399d59b-c952-4182-b5e9-1efc2ea61012.title: SPARK SERVICE PROVIDER
2399d59b-c952-4182-b5e9-1efc2ea61012.body:
A service provider within the Spark ecosystem, whose main role is to facilitate deposits and withdrawals between Bitcoin's main layer and Spark. Several SSPs can coexist within the same Spark network.

SSPs also ensure interoperability with the Lightning Network by acting as intermediaries for Lightning payments. When a Spark user wishes to pay a Lightning invoice, the SSP executes an *atomic swap*.

23d37b39-13d4-4f08-93cf-13e2c763537f.title: OP_3DUP - 0X6F
23d37b39-13d4-4f08-93cf-13e2c763537f.body:
Duplicates the three items at the top of the stack, then places them at the top of the stack. For example, if the stack is:

```text
A
B
C
D
```

`OP_3DUP` will produce:

```text
A
B
C
A
B
C
D
```

23fdd744-349a-48e2-9eaf-c1d1c4a9e52c.title: ZKSNACKS
23fdd744-349a-48e2-9eaf-c1d1c4a9e52c.body: Company that publishes Wasabi Wallet, an open source desktop Bitcoin wallet focused on privacy. zkSNACKs developed the WabiSabi protocol, a coinjoin mechanism used in Wasabi Wallet 2.0 to improve the privacy of Bitcoin transactions. In June 2024, zkSNACKs ended its coinjoin coordination service due to regulatory uncertainty. Wasabi Wallet continues to operate as a standard Bitcoin wallet, and other WabiSabi coinjoin coordinators have emerged.

2428e622-5cc7-40da-af61-d9df91119234.title: CLI
2428e622-5cc7-40da-af61-d9df91119234.body: Acronym for “*Command Line Interface*”, or “interface en ligne de commande” in French. It is a method of interacting with software that relies on entering text commands in a terminal or console. The CLI differs from the GUI (graphical user interface), which offers pointing methods of interaction (with the mouse) and interactive visual elements.

245b52d5-5fd8-4099-a122-2b96d76b1297.title: BIP-0347
245b52d5-5fd8-4099-a122-2b96d76b1297.body: Proposal to re-enable the opcode `OP_CAT` in Tapscript only. `OP_CAT` concatenates the top two stack elements into one (that is, it puts them end to end), with a maximum size of 520 bytes for the result. This opcode was originally present in Bitcoin, but was disabled by Satoshi Nakamoto in 2010 as a precaution, because of potential denial-of-service risks related to the exponential growth of data on the stack. Re-enabling it in Tapscript would make it possible to build covenants, Merkle trees verifiable in Script, quantum-resistant Lamport signature schemes, and many other cryptographic primitives. BIP-0347, proposed by Ethan Heilman and Armin Sabouri, is one of the most debated soft fork proposals since the activation of Taproot, because of the power and versatility that this simple opcode could offer.

249af351-9b40-4f62-848a-07d038814acf.title: EDGE NODE
249af351-9b40-4f62-848a-07d038814acf.body:
A specialized routing node serving as an intermediary between Taproot Assets wallets and the classic Lightning network. An *edge node* maintains public Bitcoin channels to the Lightning network and unannounced Taproot Assets channels with its clients. Its main function is to convert Taproot Assets into BTC (and vice versa) when routing payments, via standard HTLCs.

Concretely, a wallet holding a Taproot asset (for example a dollar stablecoin) can pay any BOLT-11/12 Lightning invoice: the *edge node* receives the asset from the client, performs the conversion and routes the payment in BTC over the network. Conversely, an incoming Lightning payment in BTC can be converted into a Taproot Asset before being delivered to the client. The *edge node* provides quotes (*quotes*) for each conversion and collects routing fees. It never takes custody of the client's funds: exchanges are atomic thanks to HTLCs.

25897219-45c0-434f-82f5-98747a565353.title: SCRIPTPUBKEY
25897219-45c0-434f-82f5-98747a565353.body:
Script located in the output part of a Bitcoin transaction that defines the conditions under which the associated UTXO can be spent. This script therefore makes it possible to secure bitcoins. In its most common form, the `scriptPubKey` contains a condition requiring the next transaction to provide proof of possession of the private key corresponding to a specified Bitcoin address. This is often achieved by a script that requires a signature matching the public key associated with the address used to secure those funds. When a transaction attempts to use this UTXO as an input, it must provide a `scriptSig` that, once combined with the `scriptPubKey`, satisfies the conditions set and produces a valid script. 

For example, here is a classic P2PKH `scriptPubKey`:

```text
OP_DUP
OP_HASH160
OP_PUSHBYTES_20
<hash de la clé publique>
OP_EQUALVERIFY
OP_CHECKSIG
```

The corresponding `scriptSig` would be:

```text
<signature> <clé publique>
```

![Bitcoin transaction: the ScriptPubKey locks the output, the ScriptSig in the input provides the proof to unlock it.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/s/scriptpubkey/assets/image-1.png)

*To refer to this script, one sometimes also speaks of a "locking script" or "script de verrouillage" in French.*

2605aeca-de5e-4813-a8b5-dd32a32a62ac.title: JOININBOX
2605aeca-de5e-4813-a8b5-dd32a32a62ac.body: Minimalist Linux environment designed for using JoinMarket. JoininBox has a terminal-based menu, and provides all the basic JoinMarket commands. It makes it possible to use the JoinMarket coinjoin implementation on a machine dedicated to this task, such as a Raspberry Pi for example.

2694e488-f505-4a76-9378-a55767b465ef.title: WALLET OF SATOSHI
2694e488-f505-4a76-9378-a55767b465ef.body:
Mobile wallet specialized in payments via the Lightning Network. Wallet of Satoshi is designed to offer a simplified user experience: the user can send and receive Lightning payments in a few seconds, without any technical configuration.

Historically, Wallet of Satoshi operated on a *custodial* model: the company held the private keys and managed the funds on behalf of the user. This model simplifies use, but involves a trade-off: the user must trust the provider with the custody of their bitcoins. Since 2025, WoS also offers, as an option, an integration of the Spark protocol, thereby making it possible to adopt a *self-custodial* model.

26bba007-5344-486f-aefd-6d1165f0eec0.title: OP_PUSHDATA1 - 0X4C
26bba007-5344-486f-aefd-6d1165f0eec0.body: Pushes a certain amount of data onto the stack. It is followed by one byte that indicates the length of the data to push (up to 255 bytes). This opcode is used to include variable-size data in scripts.

26c554cc-92a8-4686-83d6-4a8e2185a2a0.title: ASMAP
26c554cc-92a8-4686-83d6-4a8e2185a2a0.body: A tool invented by Gleb Naumenko and used by Bitcoin Core to improve the security and topology of the Bitcoin network by diversifying connections between nodes. It is a map from IP addresses to autonomous system numbers (ASNs), allowing a better distribution of outbound connections based on the ASN rather than on IP prefixes. This helps prevent Eclipse attacks (notably the Erebus attack) by making it harder for an attacker to monopolize a target node's connections via IP addresses belonging to the same autonomous system.

2741f23e-1d27-41ee-9947-7820f58abde6.title: OP_TOALTSTACK - 0X6B
2741f23e-1d27-41ee-9947-7820f58abde6.body: Takes the top of the main stack (*main stack*) and moves it to the alternate stack (*alt stack*). This opcode makes it possible to temporarily store data aside for later use in the script. The moved element is therefore removed from the main stack. `OP_FROMALTSTACK` will then be used to put it back on the top of the main stack.

27df859c-9af1-41c5-a9aa-161383ef616a.title: COINJUMBLE
27df859c-9af1-41c5-a9aa-161383ef616a.body: Software developed by Chris Belcher and launched in August 2014, designed to make coinjoins easier to use with a *GUI*. Unlike other coinjoin implementations of the time, which required participants to want to perform a coinjoin simultaneously, CoinJumble made it possible to share transaction parts asynchronously. Users could exchange through external communication channels to share the encoded transaction parts. Today, CoinJumble is no longer used.

27e3dd7a-75c3-40f1-8ce2-4f3c24242155.title: BIG-ENDIAN
27e3dd7a-75c3-40f1-8ce2-4f3c24242155.body: Data storage format in computer systems where the most significant bytes (the “big ends”) are placed first in address order. This means that in a sequence with several bytes, the byte with the greatest weight (for example, the leftmost digits in hexadecimal) is stored first.

27ef6f8d-b26c-43b7-bcc5-45b521dec9ce.title: SECP256K1
27ef6f8d-b26c-43b7-bcc5-45b521dec9ce.body:
Name given to a specific elliptic curve used in the Bitcoin protocol to implement the ECDSA (*Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm*) and Schnorr digital signature algorithms. The `secp256k1` curve was chosen by Bitcoin's inventor, Satoshi Nakamoto. It has certain interesting properties, notably advantages in terms of performance.

The use of `secp256k1` on Bitcoin means that each private key (a random 256-bit number) is mapped to a corresponding public key by point addition and doubling of the private key by the generator point of the `secp256k1` curve. This operation is easy to carry out in one direction, but practically impossible to reverse, which is the basis of the security of digital signatures on Bitcoin.

The `secp256k1` curve is specified by the elliptic curve equation `y^2 = x^3 + 7`, which means that it has coefficients `a` equal to `0` and `b` equal to `7` in the general form of the equation of an elliptic curve `y^2 = x^3 + ax + b`. `secp256k1` is defined over a finite field whose order is a very large prime number, specifically `p = 2^{256} - 2^{32} - 977`. The curve also has a group order, which is the number of distinct points on the curve, a predefined generator point (or `G` point), which is used in cryptographic operations to generate key pairs, and a cofactor that is equal to `1`.

*“SEC” stands for “Standards for Efficient Cryptography”. “P256” indicates that the curve is defined over a field `\mathbb{Z}_p` where `p` is a 256-bit prime number. “K” refers to the name of its inventor, Neal Koblitz. Finally, “1” indicates that it is the first version of this curve.*

27f4f1dd-ca19-4d2b-926e-dcb0aaebda73.title: CASA
27f4f1dd-ca19-4d2b-926e-dcb0aaebda73.body:
An American company offering multisig bitcoin security solutions for individuals. Casa offers a service where private keys are split between the user (on their *hardware wallet* and their phone) and Casa (which holds an emergency recovery key). This 2-of-3 or 3-of-5 model makes it possible to secure one's funds without a single point of failure, while still having a recovery option in case a device is lost.

Casa also offers a built-in inheritance protocol. It is used through a mobile application and the service operates on a subscription basis with different security tiers.

2827263a-63ba-41be-bc0b-57b7d53182e1.title: COINKITE
2827263a-63ba-41be-bc0b-57b7d53182e1.body:
Canadian company founded in 2012, specialized in the manufacture of security hardware for Bitcoin. Coinkite is mainly known for the Coldcard, a *hardware wallet* designed specifically for the secure storage of keys. The Coldcard stands out for its minimalist approach focused exclusively on Bitcoin, its air-gapped operation (disconnected from any network), and its many advanced security features.

Coinkite also develops other products such as the Blockclock, a clock that displays the bitcoin price and the block height, as well as the SatsCard and the TapSigner, NFC cards that can store or sign Bitcoin transactions.

28402114-7ee7-4370-8f92-5758a6143259.title: OP_TRUE - 0X51
28402114-7ee7-4370-8f92-5758a6143259.body: Identical to `OP_1`. It pushes the value `1` onto the stack. It is often used to represent the boolean value true in scripts.

28679598-5868-475b-afe7-9d1013d95b47.title: WALLETS/DB.LOG
28679598-5868-475b-afe7-9d1013d95b47.body: Log file in Bitcoin Core specific to the wallet database. It records the operations and events related to the wallet database for troubleshooting.

29193a69-fe44-4bf3-9236-5d427db370fd.title: BIP-0173

29a3bf4f-d29f-415e-b86f-e5f0e5e1591c.title: CBTC - CITREA BITCOIN
29a3bf4f-d29f-415e-b86f-e5f0e5e1591c.body: The native representation of bitcoin on the Citrea rollup. cBTC (*Citrea Bitcoin*) is the native currency used to pay *gas* fees and carry out transactions on the Citrea network. It is obtained by depositing BTC on the main Bitcoin chain via the Clementine bridge, which locks the funds and issues an equivalent amount of cBTC on the rollup. It can be converted back into BTC at any time via Clementine's *peg-out* mechanism.

2a73aa52-605c-476a-8dbf-088e87608026.title: TLV
2a73aa52-605c-476a-8dbf-088e87608026.body:
Data encoding format *type-length-value* structured in three fields: a type identifying the nature of the information, a length indicating the size of the data, and a value containing the data itself. This format makes it possible to create extensible messages in which new field types can be added without breaking compatibility with existing implementations.

On the Lightning Network, TLV is used to structure the messages of the BOLT protocol, making it possible to include optional information such as payment metadata or routing data. In the Taproot Assets protocol, each leaf of the asset tree contains a TLV blob that encodes the version, the *asset ID*, the amount held, as well as the signatures and data relating to the asset's previous transfers.

2ad92c38-f85f-41c7-bbc8-f6eae56d88b9.title: CHAINCODE LABS
2ad92c38-f85f-41c7-bbc8-f6eae56d88b9.body: A Bitcoin research and development center founded in 2014 by Alex Morcos and Suhas Daftuar in New York. Chaincode Labs funds and employs Bitcoin Core developers, and organizes training programs for open source contributors to the Bitcoin protocol.

2b1186cb-b885-410f-983d-d2040a2f11ce.title: INBOUND CAPACITY
2b1186cb-b885-410f-983d-d2040a2f11ce.body: Refers to the maximum amount of bitcoins that a node can receive through a specific channel on the Lightning Network. It depends on the funds that the peer node committed to the channel when it was opened, or that one has sent during an outgoing Lightning payment or a routing.

2b1e5e86-e989-4b60-85be-6b42c4721c94.title: FOUNDATION DEVICES
2b1e5e86-e989-4b60-85be-6b42c4721c94.body: American company co-founded in 2020 by Zach Herbert, Jacob Johnston, Ken Carpenter and Matt Beach in Boston, specializing in the manufacture of open source hardware for securing bitcoins. Its flagship product, the Passport, is a hardware wallet (*hardware wallet*) operating in an air-gapped manner via QR codes and microSD cards, with no direct network connection. Foundation Devices also develops Envoy, a companion mobile application that serves as an interface for managing the Passport and interacting with the Bitcoin network. All of the hardware is assembled in the United States and the firmware is fully open source.

2b790f49-a9e2-45e8-b4e8-774e751beec5.title: HEXADECIMAL
2b790f49-a9e2-45e8-b4e8-774e751beec5.body: A base-16 numeral system, which therefore uses 16 distinct symbols to represent numbers. The first 10 symbols are the digits 0 to 9, identical to those of the decimal system (base 10), and the next six symbols are represented by the letters A to F. Thus, A represents the number 10, B represents 11, up to F which represents 15. This system is particularly used in computing, because it offers a more concise representation of binary numbers (base 2), and each hexadecimal digit represents exactly 4 bits, which simplifies conversions. This numeral system is very often found to represent information on Bitcoin.

2be92fa8-c7ad-4835-ba7f-2794b0e38765.title: SIGHASH_SINGLE | SIGHASH_ACP
2be92fa8-c7ad-4835-ba7f-2794b0e38765.body: Type of SigHash Flag (`0x83`) combined with the `SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY` modifier (`SIGHASH_ACP`) used in Bitcoin transaction signatures. This combination specifies that the signature applies to a single specific input and only to the output with the same index as that input. The other inputs and outputs can be added or modified by other parties. This configuration is useful for collaborative transactions where participants can add their own inputs to fund a specific output.

2c0377ac-5255-43f8-b437-22280380a4ea.title: MERKLE SUM TREE
2c0377ac-5255-43f8-b437-22280380a4ea.body: A variant of a Merkle tree in which each node carries not only the hash of the nodes or leaves beneath it, but also the sum of their values. The root of the tree thus contains the hash of all the data and the total sum of all the leaf values. This structure makes it possible to verify both the integrity of the data and the consistency of the amounts at the same time. In the Taproot Assets protocol, *Merkle Sum Trees* are used to commit asset balances to the Bitcoin blockchain, ensuring that no asset can be created or destroyed without changing the root of the tree.

2c101ec0-f616-46c2-97e9-fad4e433d857.title: RUNES
2c101ec0-f616-46c2-97e9-fad4e433d857.body: Protocol developed by the same team as Ordinals that allows the use of Bitcoin transactions to etch, mint and transfer fungible digital assets other than BTC. Unlike Ordinals inscriptions, where each unit is unique, each rune is identical to the others, and therefore interchangeable, which makes it possible to create fungible cryptocurrencies distinct from BTC on Bitcoin. Runes protocol messages, called *runestones*, are stored in `OP_RETURN`.

2c81d29e-66ab-4a84-8ecc-69805aa39e85.title: VIN

2c8338d8-1ad6-4912-a4a9-4f40d66b6b0f.title: BIP-0375
2c8338d8-1ad6-4912-a4a9-4f40d66b6b0f.body: Defines the PSBT fields needed to send Silent Payments (BIP-0352). This BIP includes each signer's ECDH *shares* as well as the DLEQ proofs (BIP-0374) attesting to the correctness of the computations. BIP-0375 allows several signers in a multisig context to collaborate to compute the Silent Payments output addresses through the exchange of PSBT files, without each participant needing to reveal their private key to the others.

2c986477-2ded-491c-8c5d-4d2b20a72763.title: F2POOL
2c986477-2ded-491c-8c5d-4d2b20a72763.body: Bitcoin mining pool founded in April 2013 in China by Chun Wang and Mao Shixing ("Discus Fish"). F2Pool is the very first mining pool created in China and one of the oldest still operating in the world. It regularly ranks among the largest pools in terms of hashrate on the Bitcoin network, and caters to individual miners as well as professional mining infrastructures.

2ca91b48-9ed2-484a-b270-36bcf7ad5892.title: ALERT SYSTEM
2ca91b48-9ed2-484a-b270-36bcf7ad5892.body:
A historical Bitcoin mechanism that made it possible to broadcast emergency messages to all the nodes of the network. Introduced by Satoshi Nakamoto in version v0.3.10, shortly after the *value overflow incident* of August 2010, this system was used to warn node operators in the event of a critical bug or a network problem.

Alerts were relayed through Bitcoin's peer-to-peer network, in the same way as transactions and blocks. Only messages signed with a specific ECDSA private key were considered valid. This key was initially held by Satoshi alone, then shared with a few developers such as Gavin Andresen. In the early versions (up to v0.3.20), a valid alert triggered a "*safe mode*" that automatically disabled the RPC commands related to transactions, which gave its holders considerable power over the network.

Because of the risk of centralization and the possibility of abusive uses, the system was gradually abandoned: the code was removed in Bitcoin Core v0.13.0, and a final "Alert Key Compromised" alert was broadcast to permanently invalidate any future message. The private key was then made public in 2018.

2cc2bc2a-2704-49dd-a1a0-31b3e99b7a54.title: ARK ROUND
2cc2bc2a-2704-49dd-a1a0-31b3e99b7a54.body:
Periodic process at the heart of the Ark protocol by which the *Ark Service Provider* (ASP) consolidates users' VTXO transactions and anchors them on the Bitcoin blockchain. Each round produces an on-chain Ark transaction containing a covenant tree in which all the output VTXOs created during that cycle are recorded.

The operation is conceptually similar to a classic Bitcoin transaction: input VTXOs are spent and new output VTXOs are created. However, the on-chain liquidity for the outputs is advanced by the ASP. In return, users hand over their old VTXOs via *forfeit transactions*. The ASP recovers this liquidity later, when the input VTXOs expire. The atomicity between the surrender of the old VTXOs and the creation of the new ones is guaranteed by *connectors*.

Rounds take place at regular intervals, typically every 15 to 60 minutes depending on the ASP's configuration. For payments requiring immediate settlement, users can resort to OOR (*out-of-round*) payments, which bypass this delay at the cost of a different trust model.

2ce064c3-c7eb-4a34-86e1-525b6a6486f8.title: OP_ADD - 0X93
