2ce064c3-c7eb-4a34-86e1-525b6a6486f8.body: Adds the two items at the top of the stack. It takes the two values at the top of the stack, adds them together and replaces them with the result.

2cf3a022-82c4-4a91-b299-269421a13f62.title: BIP-0388
2cf3a022-82c4-4a91-b299-269421a13f62.body: Proposal defining “wallet policies” (*wallet policies*), a restricted subset of output script descriptors optimized for hardware wallets. Full descriptors can be arbitrarily complex and difficult to display on the limited screens of signing devices. BIP-0388 simplifies the format by separating the structure of the descriptor (the “template”) from the list of keys, while remaining expressive enough to cover common configurations: singlesig, multisig and MuSig2. This approach allows the user to visually verify the spending policy on the screen of their hardware wallet before signing a transaction.

2d1389ce-759b-490c-a6df-d0df962193d0.title: NOTIFICATION TRANSACTION
2d1389ce-759b-490c-a6df-d0df962193d0.body:
Specific Bitcoin transaction used within the BIP-0047 protocol (reusable payment codes). The notification transaction is the first step required to establish a payment link between two users via their respective payment codes.

Concretely, when Alice wants to send payments to Bob using his payment code, she must first send him a notification transaction. This transaction contains, in an `OP_RETURN` output, Alice's payment code encrypted using a shared secret computed with ECDH (*Elliptic-Curve Diffie-Hellman*). Bob, by monitoring his notification address, can decrypt this information and discover Alice's payment code. He can then derive the corresponding addresses to identify Alice's future payments.

The notification transaction only needs to be sent once for each pair of users. Subsequent payments between Alice and Bob no longer require this step.

2d179734-48aa-43dc-b7e3-d9f2d5d6e2ea.title: LNP2PBOT
2d179734-48aa-43dc-b7e3-d9f2d5d6e2ea.body: Open source Telegram bot that allows buying and selling bitcoins peer-to-peer (P2P) via the Lightning Network. LNP2PBot works directly within the Telegram messaging application, where users can create buy or sell offers, and exchange bitcoins for local currencies. Transactions are carried out via the Lightning Network. An *escrow* system built into the bot secures the transactions: it temporarily holds the seller's sats until the buyer confirms the fiat payment.

2d27426b-acdf-48a0-a1b8-d0de71eff51a.title: BIP-0145
2d27426b-acdf-48a0-a1b8-d0de71eff51a.body: Updates the JSON-RPC call `getblocktemplate` to integrate SegWit support, in accordance with BIP-0141. This update allows miners to build blocks taking into account the new “weight” measure of transactions and blocks introduced by SegWit, and other parameters such as the calculation of the sigops limit.

2d7148ba-7ace-44ca-97a8-457e32d5174d.title: INPUT
2d7148ba-7ace-44ca-97a8-457e32d5174d.body:
In the context of Bitcoin, an input within a transaction refers to the UTXOs (*Unspent Transaction Outputs*) used as source funds to satisfy the outputs. Each input contains references to previous UTXOs, which will then be consumed by the transaction. These inputs are used to fund new UTXOs that will be created as outputs of the transaction, and that can then be spent in future transactions. 

The role of a Bitcoin transaction is therefore to consume UTXOs as inputs, and to create new UTXOs as outputs. The difference between the two corresponds to the transaction fees, which can be collected by the miner who validates the block. 

From a broader point of view, in computing, the term “input” generally refers to the data provided to a function, an algorithm, or a system as operands or information required to perform an operation or a calculation. In this sense, the term is used more generically to describe anything provided to a process in order to obtain a result or an output. For example, when data is passed into a cryptographic hash function, this information is called an “input”.

2daaa0d0-d00c-4fb0-95df-b895e470a2cc.title: OP_1NEGATE - 0X4F
2daaa0d0-d00c-4fb0-95df-b895e470a2cc.body: Pushes the value `-1` onto the stack. This opcode is used in scripts to represent the negative value `-1`.

2dcb2f84-1583-4bd7-a9de-de3d7e39ddcf.title: FEE BUMPING
2dcb2f84-1583-4bd7-a9de-de3d7e39ddcf.body:
Set of techniques that make it possible to increase the fees of a transaction already broadcast on the Bitcoin network in order to speed up its confirmation. When a transaction remains stuck in the mempools because its fees are too low relative to the demand for block space, fee bumping techniques make it possible to reassess its priority with miners.

The two existing methods are RBF (*Replace-By-Fee*) and CPFP (*Child Pays For Parent*). With RBF, the sender creates a new version of the original transaction with higher fees, which replaces the initial transaction in the mempools. With CPFP, the recipient (or the sender via a change output) creates a child transaction that spends an output of the stuck transaction, with fees high enough to incentivize miners to confirm both transactions together.

2df24da2-a435-459a-8476-b00c90cd8a82.title: CONTAINER
2df24da2-a435-459a-8476-b00c90cd8a82.body: In the context of mining, a container is a modular structure used to house and operate a large number of ASICs. These containers are designed to optimize space, heat management and power supply. They can be equipped with different cooling systems, such as *air cooling*, *hydro cooling* or *immersion cooling*. Their main advantage lies in their mobility and their ability to be deployed quickly, often close to cheap energy sources.

2e555239-c40f-42cc-a30b-9280ad51284a.title: SHARES
2e555239-c40f-42cc-a30b-9280ad51284a.body:
In the context of mining pools, a share is an indicator used to quantify the contribution of an individual miner within the pool. This measure serves as the basis for calculating the reward that the pool redistributes to each miner. Each share corresponds to a hash that satisfies a difficulty target lower than that of the Bitcoin network.

To explain with an analogy, consider a 20-sided die. On Bitcoin, suppose that proof of work requires rolling below 3 to validate a block (that is, getting a result of 1 or 2). Now, imagine that within a mining pool, the difficulty target for a share is set at 10. Thus, for an individual miner in the pool, each die roll that gives a result below 10 counts as a valid share. These shares are then submitted to the pool by the miner, in order to claim their payment, even if they do not correspond to a valid result for a block on Bitcoin.

For each hash computed, an individual miner in a pool can encounter three different scenarios:
* If the hash value is greater than or equal to the difficulty target set by the pool for a share, then this hash is of no use. The miner then modifies their nonce to try a new hash: `hash > share > bloc`.
* If the hash is lower than the share's difficulty target, but greater than or equal to Bitcoin's difficulty target, then this hash constitutes a valid share that is nevertheless not sufficient to validate a block. The miner can send this hash to their pool to claim the reward associated with the share: `share > hash > bloc`.
* If the hash is lower than the Bitcoin network's difficulty target, it is considered both a valid share and a valid block. The miner submits this hash to their pool, which hurries to broadcast it on the Bitcoin network. This hash is also counted as a valid share for the miner: `share > bloc > hash`.

![Three zones of the hash: above the share target nothing is valid, below it a share, below the block target a block.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/s/shares/assets/image-1.png)

This share system is used to estimate the work done by each individual miner within a pool, without having to individually recompute all the hashes generated by a miner, which would be completely inefficient for the pool.

Mining pools adjust share difficulty to balance the verification load and to ensure that each miner, whether small or large, submits shares approximately every few seconds. This makes it possible to accurately calculate each miner's hashrate and to distribute rewards according to the chosen payout calculation method (PPS, PPLNS, TIDES...).

2eb81a61-aa97-446a-a346-ca24d8f9ed94.title: RPOW
2eb81a61-aa97-446a-a346-ca24d8f9ed94.body:
Acronym for "*Reusable Proofs Of Work*". It is an electronic money system based on the transfer of tokens established on proofs of work, developed and implemented by Hal Finney in 2004. RPoW positioned itself as an improvement on the theoretical concepts of b-money and bit gold. 

Unlike the latter, RPoW actually came into being and was launched. RPoW could have taken the place that Bitcoin currently occupies. It was the most advanced electronic money project before Satoshi's invention. However, Bitcoin surpasses RPoW by solving two critical problems. First, Bitcoin introduced an automatic mining difficulty adjustment, a mechanism absent in RPoW, thus avoiding inflation due to the increase in mining capacity and the growing number of miners. Second, unlike RPoW's dependence on central servers, Bitcoin established a distributed consensus mechanism. This mechanism rests on the principle that nodes synchronize on the chain with the most accumulated work, thus eliminating the need for known servers. RPoW never received the support necessary to emerge and be adopted by the general public.

Unlike b-money and bit gold, Satoshi Nakamoto never cited RPoW, even though this system was surely the one that most resembled their invention.

2ed50b73-5f43-4239-931b-dec4f4e8068f.title: LOOP OUT
2ed50b73-5f43-4239-931b-dec4f4e8068f.body: Operation offered by the Lightning Loop service that allows converting Lightning liquidity into on-chain bitcoins. The user makes a Lightning payment and receives the equivalent (minus fees) in their on-chain Bitcoin wallet via a *submarine swap*. *Loop Out* is useful for recovering funds on-chain without closing a channel, or for rebalancing liquidity by moving funds from a channel saturated on the outbound side to the on-chain wallet.

2f06ddac-bff4-4b60-ab9b-108ad771f29c.title: OP_OVER - 0X78
2f06ddac-bff4-4b60-ab9b-108ad771f29c.body: Duplicates the second element from the top of the stack and places it on the top of the stack.

2f0c7362-0127-4575-9b0a-b43f435905b5.title: BIP-0330
2f0c7362-0127-4575-9b0a-b43f435905b5.body: Proposal known as “*Erlay*” which aims to optimize the propagation of unconfirmed transactions in the Bitcoin network. Currently, transactions are broadcast to all of a node's peers, which causes redundancy and excessive bandwidth use. BIP-0330 proposes to limit this broadcast to 8 peers by default, then to use a reconciliation mechanism to efficiently share the missing transactions. Erlay reduces bandwidth consumption by about 40%. It also avoids a linear increase in bandwidth consumption with the number of peers connected to the node.

2f2e8b29-fe87-41c5-bfe5-88b0f255916a.title: CRYPTOCURRENCY
2f2e8b29-fe87-41c5-bfe5-88b0f255916a.body: Generic qualifier given to any form of money, asset, credit, or digital unit within a computer system in which cryptography is used for exchanges and transactions between users.

2f329b85-fc19-43e1-b904-e7644daf3659.title: MERKLE ROOT
2f329b85-fc19-43e1-b904-e7644daf3659.body: Digest or "*top hash*" of a Merkle tree, which represents a summary of all the information present in the tree. A Merkle tree is a cryptographic accumulator structure, sometimes also called a "hash tree". In the context of Bitcoin, Merkle trees are used to organize the transactions in a block and to facilitate quick verification that a specific transaction is included. Thus, in Bitcoin blocks, the Merkle root is obtained by successively hashing the transactions in pairs until only a single hash remains (the Merkle root). The latter is then included in the header of the corresponding block. This hash tree is also found in UTREEXO, a structure that makes it possible to condense the nodes' UTXO set, and in the Taproot MAST.

2f4abca1-b097-46cc-95b5-578f99df8642.title: LNBITS
2f4abca1-b097-46cc-95b5-578f99df8642.body:
Open source application that sits on top of any Lightning funding source (LND, Core Lightning, LNbits itself, etc.) and makes it possible to create isolated virtual wallets, each with its own API key. The main benefit is never exposing the total balance of the underlying node: each wallet only sees and can only spend the funds allocated to it, which makes it possible to delegate access to third-party applications without risk.

LNbits adopts a modular architecture where the core remains minimal and where all additional features are provided by optional extensions developed by the community: point of sale, payment links, *paywalls*, NIP-05 Nostr, *Bolt Cards*, payment terminals, *crowdfunding*, etc. Developers can create and share their own extensions. LNbits natively supports LNURL and Nostr, provides a complete REST API, and is accessible from a web browser.

2f4d359a-10f3-497b-8ae9-1323c82622d6.title: ONION ROUTING
2f4d359a-10f3-497b-8ae9-1323c82622d6.body:
Communication technique that consists of encapsulating a message in several successive layers of encryption, like the layers of an onion. The message travels through a series of intermediate nodes, and each node can decrypt only the layer intended for it, revealing only the identity of the next node. No intermediary knows both the sender and the final recipient of the message.

This principle is the basis of the Tor network, where internet traffic passes through several successive relays to anonymize connections. On the Lightning Network, onion routing is used to route payments: each node on the route knows only the previous node and the next node, without being able to determine the origin or destination of the payment.

2f50323b-b89d-4189-be53-f1b85a5186d2.title: SINGLE-USE SEAL
2f50323b-b89d-4189-be53-f1b85a5186d2.body: Refers to a promise of cryptographic commitment to a message that is still unknown, which will be revealed only once in the future and must be accessible to an entire determined audience. This mechanism aims to prevent the creation of multiple competing commitments for the same seal, which guarantees the uniqueness of each validation. By imposing this single-use constraint, the Single-use Seal is used on RGB to prevent double-spending.

2f74b661-7b6d-4718-9076-697e7984eef3.title: ZAP
2f74b661-7b6d-4718-9076-697e7984eef3.body: Bitcoin micropayment made via the Lightning Network and cryptographically linked to a Nostr event. Defined by NIP-57, the zap mechanism allows a user to directly reward the author of a post by sending satoshis from their Lightning wallet. Zaps are one of the most successful integrations between Bitcoin and Nostr, enabling a direct compensation model, with no intermediary and no possibility of censorship.

2fa9adb1-1aab-44cb-880a-7db9d469e37a.title: ATOMIC SWAP
2fa9adb1-1aab-44cb-880a-7db9d469e37a.body:
A technology enabling an exchange of cryptocurrencies directly between two parties, without the need for trust and without requiring an intermediary. These exchanges are called "atomic" because they can only have two outcomes:
* Either the exchange succeeds and both participants have effectively exchanged their cryptocurrencies;
* Or the exchange fails and both participants walk away with their original cryptocurrencies.

Atomic Swaps can be carried out either with the same cryptocurrency, in which case they are also called "*coinswaps*", or between different cryptocurrencies. Historically, they relied on "*Hash Time-Locked Contracts*" (HTLCs), a time-locking system that guarantees the exchange is either completed or fully cancelled, thus preserving the integrity of the funds of the parties involved. This method required protocols capable of handling both scripts and timelocks. However, in recent years, the trend has moved toward the use of *Adaptor Signatures*. This second approach has the advantage of dispensing with scripts, which thus reduces operational costs. Its other major strength lies in the fact that it does not require the use of an identical hash for both legs of the transaction, which avoids revealing a link between them.

2fc3c573-173e-4fd0-b8b0-7cd32404f44f.title: GAP LIMIT
2fc3c573-173e-4fd0-b8b0-7cd32404f44f.body:
Parameter used in Bitcoin wallet software to determine the maximum number of consecutive unused addresses to generate before ceasing to search for additional transactions. Adjusting this parameter is often necessary when recovering a wallet to ensure that all transactions are found. An insufficient Gap Limit could cause some transactions to be missed if addresses were skipped during the derivation phases. Increasing the Gap Limit allows the wallet to search further in the address sequence, in order to retrieve all associated transactions. 

Indeed, a single `xpub` can theoretically derive more than 4 billion receiving addresses (internal and external addresses). However, wallet software cannot derive all of them and check their usage without incurring an enormous operational cost. They therefore proceed in index order, because this is normally the order in which all wallet software generates addresses. The software records each used address before moving on to the next, and it stops its search when it encounters a number of consecutively empty addresses. This number is what is called the Gap Limit. 

If, for example, the Gap Limit is set to `20`, and address `m/84'/0'/0'/0/15/` is empty, the wallet will derive addresses up to `m/84'/0'/0'/0/34/`. If this range of addresses remains unused, the search stops there. Consequently, a transaction using address `m/84'/0'/0'/0/40/` would not be detected in this example.

2fc3ec2b-e4c3-4ecd-a661-6ebf8411be7a.title: HARDWARE WALLET
2fc3ec2b-e4c3-4ecd-a661-6ebf8411be7a.body:
A hardware wallet is an electronic device dedicated to securing and managing the private keys of a Bitcoin wallet. These devices are designed to provide enhanced security compared to software wallets, which run on general-purpose machines directly connected to the internet. Hardware wallets store the mnemonic phrase offline, on hardware with a tiny attack surface, which isolates it from potentially vulnerable environments. When a transaction is made, the hardware wallet signs the transaction inside the device itself, without exposing the private key to the outside. Once the transaction is signed, it is transmitted to the Bitcoin network to be confirmed and included in the Bitcoin blockchain. Among the most popular hardware wallet models are: Ledger, Trezor, Coldcard, Passport, BitBox, Satochip, Jade or SeedSigner (non-exhaustive list).

*Some bitcoiners prefer the term "signing device" ("périphérique de signature" in French), in order to avoid giving the impression that the bitcoins are physically located inside the wallet.*

2fccd32d-63d2-469b-9f9f-8b220e2bdaa5.title: VIRGIN BITCOIN
2fccd32d-63d2-469b-9f9f-8b220e2bdaa5.body: A unit of bitcoin freshly issued in a coinbase transaction (block reward) and that has never yet been spent in a subsequent transaction. Its transaction history is therefore free of any association with activities identified by chain analysis tools.

2febe88a-f0e1-458c-b275-696486c47d8e.title: HWI
2febe88a-f0e1-458c-b275-696486c47d8e.body: Acronym for “*Hardware Wallet Interface*”. It is a standardized interface allowing integration and interaction between Bitcoin wallet management software and hardware wallets. More precisely, HWI is both a Python library and a command-line tool. It facilitates communication between these components by using PSBTs (partially signed Bitcoin transactions) and possibly Descriptors (output script descriptors). This interface was first developed for Bitcoin Core, then it became a standard used by most wallet software.

3013e901-385b-4e6d-b17a-ef7953fee38d.title: MEMPOOL.DAT
3013e901-385b-4e6d-b17a-ef7953fee38d.body: Name of the data file used by the Bitcoin Core software to store the current state of the mempool, which is the set of unconfirmed transactions waiting to be added to a block.

30177e9a-d323-4956-a8f5-254db510bbea.title: LIQUIDITY - LIGHTNING
30177e9a-d323-4956-a8f5-254db510bbea.body: Refers to the capacity of a Lightning payment channel to pass transactions between two nodes depending on the bitcoins available on each side of the channel. There are two types of liquidity: inbound and outbound. Outbound liquidity represents the funds that the node can send or forward through the channel. Inbound liquidity represents the funds that it can receive or forward in the opposite direction. Liquidity can also refer to the sum of the liquidity available in all of a node's channels.

3045621b-9063-4937-b910-4bd7485d6ad4.title: DEPTH
3045621b-9063-4937-b910-4bd7485d6ad4.body:
In the context of HD (hierarchical deterministic) wallets, depth designates the specific level of a key (public or private), a chain code, an extended key or an address in the wallet's derivation structure from the master key. Each level of this structure can be seen as a floor in a tree of keys, where the master key is at the root (depth 0) and the subsequent levels define various attributes such as:
the purpose (depth 1), the coin type (depth 2), the account (depth 3), the chain type (depth 4), and the index of the specific address (depth 5). 

![BIP-84 tree with its six depths: 0 master key, 1 purpose, 2 coin type, 3 account, 4 chain, 5 address.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/p/profondeur/assets/image-1.png)

To go from one depth to the next, a derivation process is used from a parent key pair to a child key pair.

*One also sometimes speaks of a “derivation level” rather than depth.*

304dac0e-8052-4ce1-9b9f-0a1dba866108.title: BIP-0077
304dac0e-8052-4ce1-9b9f-0a1dba866108.body: Proposal for an asynchronous version of the Payjoin protocol (BIP-0078). BIP-0077 allows the receiver to be offline when the payment is initiated. The payer publishes an encrypted PSBT transaction on a relay server, which the receiver retrieves and co-signs later. This approach considerably improves the usability of the original Payjoin, which required both parties to be online simultaneously to complete the collaborative transaction. The protocol maintains the same advantages in terms of privacy.

305bab3a-2ccb-43f1-9438-908ce0cb3e62.title: MACHANKURA
305bab3a-2ccb-43f1-9438-908ce0cb3e62.body: Machankura is a service that allows sending and receiving bitcoins by phone, without an internet connection, thanks to the USSD protocol. Created in 2022 by Kgothatso Ngako, a South African developer, the service makes Bitcoin accessible to users of basic phones in Africa. To make a transaction, the user dials a USSD code specific to their country (for example `*920*8333#` in Ghana) and interacts with a text menu. Payments go through the Lightning Network, and Lightning addresses take the form `numéro@8333.mobi`. Machankura is available in several African countries, including Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya and South Africa.

311c7cff-9d41-44ec-a272-cd3d6c96eda9.title: EXTRA TRANSACTION PROOF
311c7cff-9d41-44ec-a272-cd3d6c96eda9.body: In the RGB protocol, the ETP is the part of the Anchor that incorporates the additional data essential for validating a Tapret-type commitment (in the context of Taproot). It includes, among other things, the internal public key associated with the Taproot script and the specific information required for the *Script Path Spend*. This component thus ensures the precise verification of the cryptographic commitments.

31274903-119b-405f-ac3e-e10a6d819a9c.title: OP_WITHIN - 0XA5
31274903-119b-405f-ac3e-e10a6d819a9c.body: Checks whether the first element at the top of the stack lies within the range defined by the second and third top elements. In other words, `OP_WITHIN` checks whether the first element is greater than or equal to the second and less than the third. If this condition is true, it pushes `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise, it pushes `0` (false).

31378cec-23f0-47bb-aa54-f58351853ac5.title: SIGHASH_SINGLE - 0X03
31378cec-23f0-47bb-aa54-f58351853ac5.body: Type of SigHash Flag used in Bitcoin transaction signatures to indicate that the signature applies to all the inputs of the transaction and to a single output, corresponding to the index of the same signed input. Thus, each input signed with `SIGHASH_SINGLE` is specifically linked to a particular output. The other outputs are not committed to by the signature and can therefore be modified later. This type of signature is useful in complex transactions, where participants want to link certain inputs to specific outputs, while leaving flexibility for the other outputs of the transaction.

3173c479-5380-4b12-af70-b512a8b7c1b3.title: P2WSH
3173c479-5380-4b12-af70-b512a8b7c1b3.body:
P2WSH is the acronym for *Pay to Witness Script Hash*. It is a standard script template used to set spending conditions on a UTXO. P2WSH was introduced with the implementation of SegWit in August 2017.

This script is similar to P2SH (*Pay to Script Hash*), since it also locks bitcoins based on the hash of a script. The difference lies in the way signatures and scripts are included in the transaction. To spend the bitcoins on this type of script, the beneficiary must provide the original script, called `witnessScript` (equivalent of the `redeemScript`), as well as the required signatures. This mechanism makes it possible to implement more sophisticated spending conditions, such as multisigs.

Under P2WSH, the signature script information (the `scriptWitness`, the equivalent of the `scriptSig`) is moved from the traditional structure of the transaction to a separate section called `Witness` (witness). This move is a feature of the SegWit (*Segregated Witness*) update that makes it possible to prevent signature-related malleability. P2WSH transactions are generally less costly in terms of fees compared to Legacy transactions, because the part in the witness costs less.

P2WSH addresses are written using the `Bech32` encoding with a checksum in the form of a BCH code. These addresses always begin with `bc1q`. P2WSH is a version 0 SegWit output.

31bcfa58-89de-4989-83fa-d4431653fc2d.title: BTC
31bcfa58-89de-4989-83fa-d4431653fc2d.body:
Stock market or monetary symbol (*ticker*) used to represent one unit of bitcoin on exchange platforms. It is used to quickly identify bitcoin among other assets and currencies. One unit of bitcoin (1 BTC) is equal to 100,000,000 satoshis (or "sats").

*"BTC" is the historical symbol of bitcoin, but it does not comply with the ISO 4217 standard, which governs currency codes. Under this standard, "BT" is assigned to Bhutan, and currencies not backed by a state, such as bitcoin, should begin with an "X". This is why some organizations use the symbol "XBT" for bitcoin. Although "XBT" is not yet officially recognized by the ISO 4217 standard, it nonetheless meets its criteria.*

3274070b-2fca-4dbf-8713-8a7651ba336c.title: STATECHAIN
3274070b-2fca-4dbf-8713-8a7651ba336c.body:
A higher-layer mechanism on Bitcoin that makes it possible to transfer ownership of a UTXO off-chain, without broadcasting an on-chain transaction. The concept was initially proposed by Ruben Somsen in 2018. It relies on a key share between the user and an entity (*Statechain Entity*). The UTXO remains locked on-chain in a multisignature address, but effective control changes hands through a renewal of the private key shares: when Alice transfers to Bob, the entity destroys its share associated with Alice and generates a new one with Bob. Alice's old share becomes unusable.

Security relies on the assumption that the entity actually deletes its old key shares. To reduce this trust risk, the entity can be distributed among several operators via a threshold signature protocol: it is enough for a single operator to be honest to guarantee the integrity of the transfer. A unilateral exit mechanism allows the user to recover their funds on-chain. Statechains are used notably by the Spark protocol for instant transfers of bitcoins and other tokens.

32b5ea0f-2dbb-418e-8d55-200b01b26ad8.title: ORPHAN BLOCK
32b5ea0f-2dbb-418e-8d55-200b01b26ad8.body:
Theoretically, an orphan block designates a valid block received by a node that has not yet acquired the parent block, that is to say the previous one in the chain. This block, although valid, remains locally isolated as an orphan.

However, in common usage, the expression "orphan block" often refers to a block without a child: a valid block, but not retained in Bitcoin's main chain. It occurs when two miners find a valid block at the same chain height within a short period of time and broadcast it on the network. The nodes end up choosing a single block to include in the chain, according to the principle of the chain with the most accumulated work, making the other one an "orphan".

![Fork after block 144: 145-B is followed by block 146 and 145-A remains without a child, described as orphaned.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/o/orphelin/assets/image-1.png)

*Personally, I prefer to use the term "orphan block" to speak of a block without a parent and the term "stale block" (stale block) to designate a block that has no child. I find this more logical and understandable, although a majority of bitcoiners do not follow this usage.*

32b6f51a-5dfb-4897-ba70-ede0c158c719.title: MERKLE BLOCK
32b6f51a-5dfb-4897-ba70-ede0c158c719.body: Data structure used within the framework of BIP-0037 (*Transaction Bloom Filtering*) to provide a compact proof of the inclusion of specific transactions in a block. It is notably used for SPV wallets. The Merkle Block contains the block header, the filtered transactions and a partial Merkle tree, allowing light clients to quickly verify whether a transaction belongs to a block without downloading all the transactions.

32cb4dec-348c-487e-93e5-b0cee060d27b.title: LIGHTSPARK
32cb4dec-348c-487e-93e5-b0cee060d27b.body: A company co-founded by David Marcus, formerly head of PayPal and of the Libra/Diem project at Meta, with the mission of building an open payments infrastructure on Bitcoin. Lightspark first developed services and tools to facilitate integration of the Lightning Network, notably the UMA (*Universal Money Address*) protocol enabling interoperable transactions between institutions. The company then created Spark, a higher-layer protocol based on statechains, designed to overcome Lightning's limits regarding the scalability of self-custody wallets and stablecoin support. Lightspark also offers a *Wallet-as-a-Service* and stablecoin issuance platform leveraging Spark's capabilities.

32d6a370-e949-47b2-9797-ad5ef02e5348.title: CRYPTANALYSIS
32d6a370-e949-47b2-9797-ad5ef02e5348.body: Study of mathematical techniques to attempt to break cryptographic techniques. This includes the processes of searching for errors or weaknesses in the implementation of a cryptographic method or in the cryptographic method itself.

3324d1a5-005e-4453-809a-3c4ab2062282.title: MPP - MULTI-PATH PAYMENTS
3324d1a5-005e-4453-809a-3c4ab2062282.body:
Generic term for all payment techniques on Lightning that make it possible to split a transaction into several smaller parts and route them via different paths. In other words, each fraction of the payment takes a different path of nodes. This makes it possible to work around liquidity limitations on a single channel in the route.

Multi-path payments also offer slight privacy advantages, because it becomes harder for an observer to link each fraction of the payment to the whole transaction. However, in its basic version, all the fragments share the same secret for the HTLCs, which can make the transaction traceable if an observer is present on several routes. Moreover, because the secret is the same for all the fractions of the payment, the payment is not atomic. This means that some parts of the payment may be executed successfully, while others may fail. These drawbacks are fixed with “*Atomic Multi-Path Payments*”.

*This same method is also sometimes called “Multi-Part Payment”.*

332631aa-8674-4fae-8766-c0fe4bc27d5a.title: DRIVECHAIN
332631aa-8674-4fae-8766-c0fe4bc27d5a.body: Specific form of sidechain where the miners of the main blockchain (Bitcoin) have a direct role in the governance of the two-way peg and possibly in the sidechain's consensus mechanism. This protocol was invented by Paul Sztorc and could be put in place thanks to the controversial BIP-0300, which would enable the *two-way peg* with miners, and BIP-0301, which would enable the use of blind merged mining (*Blind Merged Mining*).

33468159-8dc6-4748-b87b-f09b37ce447a.title: OP_2SWAP - 0X72
33468159-8dc6-4748-b87b-f09b37ce447a.body:
Swaps the two items at the top of the stack with the two items located just below them. For example, if the stack is:

```text
A
B
C
D
```

`OP_2SWAP` will produce:

```text
C
D
A
B
```

336298fc-bc80-4d8c-834d-567837f795b7.title: BLIP-0011
336298fc-bc80-4d8c-834d-567837f795b7.body:
bLIP that defines *NameDesc*, a standardized format for structuring BOLT-11 invoice descriptions by embedding the recipient's name. The convention consists of prefixing the description with the merchant's or recipient's name, followed by a colon and two spaces (`: `), then the payment description.

Compatible wallets can thus extract and display the recipient's name separately. Non-compatible wallets simply display the full text as a regular description, which guarantees full backward compatibility. This convention solves the problem of transaction histories where only a technical identifier or a product name appears, with no clear identification of the merchant.

33d2fd70-6b5a-4986-9925-ccefffa1045f.title: SMALL BLOCKERS
33d2fd70-6b5a-4986-9925-ccefffa1045f.body: Name given to the supporters of keeping Bitcoin's block size at a low level during the Blocksize War between 2015 and 2017, in order to preserve the decentralization and security of the system. They support solutions like SegWit, believe that scaling should be done on upper layers such as the Lightning Network, and support the implementation of changes via soft forks rather than hard forks.

33d88007-7f1a-448a-b099-a0b8e8adfbe5.title: BITCOIN MAGAZINE
33d88007-7f1a-448a-b099-a0b8e8adfbe5.body: Publication founded in 2012 by Mihai Alisie and Vitalik Buterin (before the latter created Ethereum), dedicated to Bitcoin news and analysis. Bitcoin Magazine is one of the oldest media outlets specialized in the Bitcoin ecosystem. It offers articles, technical analyses, interviews and educational content covering all aspects of Bitcoin: protocol, economics, regulation, mining and development. The magazine exists as a website, a print publication and video content. Bitcoin Magazine also organizes the "Bitcoin Conference", one of the largest annual events of the Bitcoin community, which is held in the United States and brings together developers, entrepreneurs, investors and enthusiasts from around the world.

340d4389-edd6-428f-a3c3-889ec305ad01.title: DOXXIC CHANGE
340d4389-edd6-428f-a3c3-889ec305ad01.body:
Change output resulting from a *Tx0* transaction in the *Whirlpool* protocol, which represents a risk to the user's privacy. The *doxxic change* is the fraction of bitcoins that cannot be integrated into the chosen coinjoin pool and that returns to the wallet as change.

This change is described as “doxxic” (a portmanteau of “*toxic*” and “*doxx*”, that is, to expose someone's identity) because it retains a direct link to the *Tx0*, and therefore potentially to the user's identity or history. If this change is spent carelessly, for example by merging it with *postmix* UTXOs, it can compromise the privacy gained during the coinjoin cycles.

To limit this risk, the *doxxic change* can be spent separately (for example on gift cards, through donations, or on *Lightning*), used in a new *Tx0*, or consolidated via *atomic swaps* on Monero.

34159a1e-3271-4819-9bba-27c44d455bef.title: OP_HASH160 - 0XA9
34159a1e-3271-4819-9bba-27c44d455bef.body: Takes the item at the top of the stack and replaces it with its hash, using the `SHA256` and then `RIPEMD160` functions in succession. This two-step process generates a 160-bit digest.

34624171-2d77-43cf-828a-035874154bd0.title: FPGA
34624171-2d77-43cf-828a-035874154bd0.body:
Acronym for "*Field-Programmable Gate Array*". Integrated circuit that can be reconfigured after its manufacture to perform specific operations. Unlike conventional processors (CPUs), which are designed to be versatile, FPGAs allow the hardware logic to be programmed directly to adapt it to a precise task, which makes them more efficient in terms of energy consumption and performance for that task.

In the history of Bitcoin mining, FPGAs represented an intermediate stage between GPU mining and the arrival of ASICs. Starting in 2011, miners began using FPGAs to compute `SHA256` hashes, because they offered a better performance/power consumption ratio than GPUs, while remaining reprogrammable. The adoption of FPGAs was nevertheless relatively short, because ASICs, circuits entirely dedicated to `SHA256` hashing, quickly surpassed them in terms of computing power and energy efficiency.

347c7ddf-f508-49d9-b773-5ff40eaaf775.title: MNEMONIC PHRASE
347c7ddf-f508-49d9-b773-5ff40eaaf775.body:
A recovery phrase, also sometimes called a mnemonic, *seed phrase*, or secret phrase, is a sequence usually made up of 12 or 24 words, generated pseudo-randomly from a source of entropy. The pseudo-random sequence is always completed with a checksum (*checksum*). The mnemonic phrase, together with an optional passphrase, is used to deterministically derive all the keys associated with an HD (hierarchical deterministic) wallet. This means that from this phrase, it is possible to deterministically generate and recreate all the private and public keys of the Bitcoin wallet, and consequently to access the funds associated with it. The purpose of the recovery phrase is to provide a means of backing up and recovering bitcoins that is both secure and easy to use.

It is important to keep this phrase in a safe place and in a secure manner, because anyone in possession of the mnemonic would have access to the funds of the corresponding wallet. If it is used in a classic wallet, and without an optional passphrase, it is often a *SPOF* (single point of failure). The recovery phrase is therefore an encoding of the pseudo-random sequence and the *checksum* into everyday words in order to make it easier for humans to write down and read. It is built according to the BIP-0039 standard, which defines and orders a list of 2048 words used for this encoding.

*The list of 2048 words of BIP-0039 is available in several languages; however, it is advisable to use only the English version, because it is the version most widely supported by wallet software.*

34ca60d1-2d69-4378-8699-5f75a281ac01.title: STRATEGIC BITCOIN RESERVE
34ca60d1-2d69-4378-8699-5f75a281ac01.body: Stock of bitcoins built up by a state, an institution or a company as protection against economic instability, monetary depreciation or geopolitical risks.

34cb8d84-1112-49d3-85ed-0725b4f0860c.title: ECLIPSE
34cb8d84-1112-49d3-85ed-0725b4f0860c.body: An attack that consists of isolating and controlling a node's communications in a network by creating an artificial environment around it. The goal is to filter or manipulate the information received and sent by this node, thus cutting it off from its legitimate peers. In the context of Bitcoin, this technique can be used to mislead a node, to censor or alter the data it receives or sends, or to carry out double-spend attacks.

34d344e0-ddb8-4e09-828f-f5820377e360.title: WHIRLPOOL
34d344e0-ddb8-4e09-828f-f5820377e360.body: ZeroLink Chaumian coinjoin protocol, developed by the Samourai Wallet team. Whirlpool was available on the Samourai Wallet (Android), Sparrow Wallet (PC) and Bitcoin Keeper (iOS and Android) wallets.

34ece2fc-6213-4f0e-b9cc-abfda06c7504.title: RANGEPROOFS
34ece2fc-6213-4f0e-b9cc-abfda06c7504.body:
A type of zero-knowledge proof (*zero-knowledge proof*) used in *Confidential Transactions* to demonstrate that a committed amount lies within a valid range, without revealing its exact value. *Rangeproofs* prevent a user from creating negative or excessively large amounts that would allow monetary units to be generated fraudulently, while preserving the confidentiality of the transaction.

In the first implementations of *Confidential Transactions* on Liquid, *rangeproofs* relied on Borromean ring signatures (*Borromean ring signatures*). This mechanism is intended to be replaced by *Bulletproofs++*, which produce more compact proofs that are more efficient to verify.

3509bb0a-1f57-4784-905f-e08a03bd2d2a.title: ZEROCONF
3509bb0a-1f57-4784-905f-e08a03bd2d2a.body: Risky practice of considering a Bitcoin transaction as final, and proceeding to carry out the associated counterpart action (such as the sale of a good or service), before the transaction is actually included in a block on the blockchain. Unconfirmed, or zeroconf, transactions are vulnerable to double-spend attacks, because they are not yet irrevocably recorded in the ledger. Zeroconf may possibly be considered in very specific contexts, where speed is the priority, such as in the case of small commercial transactions or in the case of a transaction between relatives or close friends. In these situations, the risk of double spending is often considered acceptable compared to the advantage of a fast transaction. Nevertheless, for large transactions, especially when the sender is unknown, it is crucial to wait for several confirmations before considering the transaction immutable. The generally accepted standard is to wait for 6 confirmations, which means that 5 additional blocks must be mined after the one including the transaction, in order to consider it final.

351fb883-61fe-4f36-ac7b-acfa90675be5.title: BIP-0106
351fb883-61fe-4f36-ac7b-acfa90675be5.body: Proposal for a dynamic control of the maximum block size based on the fill history of previous blocks. BIP-0106 automatically adjusted the limit according to the actual demand for space in blocks. Proposed during the Blocksize War, it was never adopted, the community having ultimately resolved the scalability problem through the activation of SegWit.

357183c2-e0af-4fed-bc3b-957df0849302.title: JIT CHANNEL
357183c2-e0af-4fed-bc3b-957df0849302.body:
Lightning channel opened on the fly by a Lightning service provider (LSP) at the moment an incoming payment arrives for a client that does not yet have a channel. The term "JIT" (*just-in-time*) means that the channel is created only at the precise moment it is needed, and not in advance.

The mechanism relies on the LSPS2 protocol (bLIP-0052). The client asks the LSP for the opening fee parameters, then obtains a temporary SCID that it includes in its Lightning invoice as a routing hint. When a payer sends the payment, the LSP intercepts the HTLC, opens a zero-confirmation channel to the client and forwards the payment, deducting the opening fee from the amount received. The client claims the payment by revealing the preimage.

Two trust models exist:
* in the default model, the LSP broadcasts the funding transaction before receiving the preimage, which leaves the client the possibility of verifying its validity;
* in the alternative model, the client transmits the preimage immediately after the HTLC is committed.

This mechanism should not be confused with *JIT routing*, which consists of rebalancing existing channels.

3589ab59-e372-4fe8-9c56-e9cf9fea85d4.title: BIP-0101
3589ab59-e372-4fe8-9c56-e9cf9fea85d4.body: Proposal presented by Gavin Andresen in 2015 that aimed to increase the maximum block size from 1 MB to 8 MB and to double this limit every two years until reaching a little over 8 GB in 2036. This proposal was integrated into the Bitcoin XT implementation in August 2015, which became in effect a fork of Bitcoin, but was not followed. This proposal was therefore never adopted. Some consider the implementation of BIP-0101 on Bitcoin XT to be the casus belli of the Blocksize War.

359c143a-aa73-4c6f-89ea-a3670e659054.title: OP_SIZE - 0X82
359c143a-aa73-4c6f-89ea-a3670e659054.body: Measures the size in number of bytes of the element at the top of the stack and returns this size to the top of the stack, without modifying the analyzed element itself.

35bc923f-b553-4d79-9192-50d0dbc21d40.title: BIP-0093
35bc923f-b553-4d79-9192-50d0dbc21d40.body: Informational BIP that suggests a standard for backing up and restoring the seed of a hierarchical deterministic wallet (according to BIP-0032) using Shamir's Secret Sharing. This protocol defines the “codex32” format, which is inspired by the bech32 format, introducing a structured string made up of a prefix, a threshold parameter, an identifier, a share index, a payload and a checksum (BCH). The method makes it possible to split the seed into up to 31 shares, of which a defined threshold (between 2 and 9) is required for the full recovery of the seed.

35e24419-afc6-4800-b48c-8233dcee342e.title: CLEARNET
35e24419-afc6-4800-b48c-8233dcee342e.body:
Term designating the conventional internet, as opposed to overlay networks such as Tor or I2P. On the *clearnet*, communications travel with identifiable IP addresses, which makes them observable by internet service providers, network operators or any intermediary.

In the context of Bitcoin and the Lightning Network, using the *clearnet* means that a node's IP address is directly visible to its peers and to network observers. Many node operators prefer to connect exclusively via Tor to protect their identity, even though the *clearnet* offers faster and more stable connections. Some hybrid configurations allow nodes to be reachable on both Tor and the *clearnet*.

35fcb1e3-715a-44b5-843d-a131dcdb6098.title: DIRECTED ACYCLIC GRAPH
35fcb1e3-715a-44b5-843d-a131dcdb6098.body: A DAG is a mathematical structure made up of nodes interconnected by directed edges, without forming a cycle, which allows a rigorous topological ordering. In the RGB protocol, the DAG is used to represent the structure of contract *Shards*, for the management and verification of state transitions. This graph representation makes it possible to ensure the consistency and traceability of modifications in a distributed environment.

364564fd-e6ee-49ea-a965-e05cc68448e5.title: RTL - RIDE THE LIGHTNING
364564fd-e6ee-49ea-a965-e05cc68448e5.body:
*Open source* web interface for managing a Lightning node through a browser. RTL offers a graphical dashboard for common operations: opening and closing channels, sending and receiving payments, managing liquidity, viewing routed payments and monitoring the node.

RTL is compatible with the three main Lightning implementations: LND, Core Lightning (CLN) and Eclair. It connects to the node's API and provides a unified interface regardless of the underlying implementation.

This tool is often deployed on *node-in-a-box* solutions such as Umbrel or Start9, which makes it accessible to users who do not wish to interact via the command line. RTL is developed by Shahana Farooqui and distributed under the MIT license.

3648a82c-8e8e-4ab4-be20-64760dd834a5.title: FEE RATE - LIGHTNING
3648a82c-8e8e-4ab4-be20-64760dd834a5.body: Proportional component of routing fees on the Lightning Network. For each payment forwarded, a node can charge a *fee rate* calculated in proportion to the routed amount, expressed in parts per million (ppm). For example, a *fee rate* of 100 ppm means that the node charges 100 satoshis for every million satoshis routed. The *fee rate* complements the *base fee*, which is a fixed amount per transaction. Adjusting the *fee rate* is an essential lever in managing a routing node: a rate that is too high discourages traffic, while a rate that is too low does not offset the cost of tying up liquidity in the channel.

36e92a2c-0011-4ffe-afc6-804618367807.title: OUTPUT
36e92a2c-0011-4ffe-afc6-804618367807.body:
In the context of Bitcoin, an output within a transaction refers to the _Unspent Transaction Outputs_ (UTXOs) that are created as destination funds for the payment. More precisely, it is a mechanism by which a transaction distributes funds. A transaction takes UTXOs, that is to say pieces of bitcoins, as "inputs" and creates new UTXOs as "outputs". These outputs stipulate a certain amount of bitcoins, often assigned to a specific address, as well as the conditions under which these funds can later be spent.

The role of the Bitcoin transaction is therefore to consume UTXOs as inputs, and to create new UTXOs as outputs. The difference between the two corresponds to the transaction fees, which can be collected by the winning miner of the block. A UTXO is, in essence, the output of a previous transaction that has not yet been spent. Transaction outputs are therefore the creations of new UTXOs which will, in turn, potentially be used as inputs in future transactions.

From a broader perspective, in computer science, the term "output" generally designates the data resulting from a function, an algorithm, or a system. For example, when data is passed into a cryptographic hash function, this information is called "input", and the result is called "output".

36f69474-d71c-4090-9af5-6a2896bf879b.title: BLIP-0039
36f69474-d71c-4090-9af5-6a2896bf879b.body: bLIP that introduces a new tagged field `b` in BOLT-11 invoices to convey blinded payment paths (*blinded paths*). This extension makes it possible to use *route blinding* (originally designed for BOLT-12) directly in existing BOLT-11 invoices, improving the recipient's privacy before the full deployment of BOLT-12 offers.

376ea445-dbe9-4705-90fd-ee999096e9bd.title: ETF
376ea445-dbe9-4705-90fd-ee999096e9bd.body:
An ETF (*Exchange-Traded Fund*) is an exchange-listed investment fund that replicates the performance of an asset or a basket of assets. Unlike a traditional fund, an ETF is bought and sold continuously on stock markets, like an ordinary share.

In the context of Bitcoin, spot Bitcoin ETFs, approved in the United States in January 2024, allow institutional and individual investors to gain exposure to the price of bitcoin without directly holding the asset. The fund buys and holds actual bitcoins on behalf of its unit holders. There are also futures ETFs (*futures*) that are based on derivative contracts rather than physical holding.

Bitcoin ETFs involve a trusted intermediary (the fund manager) and fees, and do not confer the individual sovereignty provided by direct holding in self-custody.

37706f12-239a-4fb7-a1fa-46db62511dd5.title: BITCOIN UNLIMITED
37706f12-239a-4fb7-a1fa-46db62511dd5.body: A Bitcoin protocol update proposal that appeared at the end of summer 2016, aiming to increase the block size flexibly via a hard fork. This fork was supported by the big blockers during the Blocksize War, with, notably, Roger Ver. Unlike Bitcoin Classic, Bitcoin Unlimited did not set an upper limit on block size, but allowed users to define their own parameters. These parameters included the maximum generation size, the excessive block size and the acceptance depth. However, Bitcoin Unlimited was criticized for its technical complexity and its security flaws. This update was ultimately never adopted.

377cdcda-0743-4e70-86b0-1366fa322e77.title: BREEZ
377cdcda-0743-4e70-86b0-1366fa322e77.body:
Non-custodial Lightning Network mobile wallet that lets users send and receive bitcoin payments almost instantly. Breez embeds a Lightning node directly on the user's device, giving them full control of their funds without relying on a trusted third party.

The application stands out for its simplified interface, which hides the technical complexity of the Lightning Network, notably the management of payment channels and liquidity. Breez also includes point-of-sale features, allowing small merchants to accept Lightning payments directly from their phones. The company also offers the Breez SDK, an open-source development kit that lets other applications integrate Lightning payments by building on the Greenlight implementation of Core Lightning. Breez supports the LNURL and Lightning Address protocols to simplify receiving payments.

37a83a88-5744-44df-862a-a68dadb160cf.title: MERKLE TREE
37a83a88-5744-44df-862a-a68dadb160cf.body:
A Merkle Tree is a cryptographic accumulator. It is a method for proving that a given piece of information belongs to a larger set. It is a data structure that makes it easier to verify information in a compact format. In the Bitcoin system, Merkle trees are used to group and condense the transactions of a block into a single hash, called the Merkle root (or “*Root Hash*”). Each transaction is hashed, then adjacent hashes are hashed together hierarchically until the Merkle root is obtained.

![Complete Merkle tree over 8 transactions, from the leaves TX 1 to TX 8 up to the root HASH 1-2-3-4-5-6-7-8.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/a/arbre-de-merkle/assets/image-1.png)

This structure makes it possible to quickly verify whether a specific transaction is included in a given block without having to analyze all of the transactions. For example, if I only have the Merkle root and I want to verify that the `TX 7` is indeed part of the tree, I will only need the following proofs:
* `TX 7`;
* `HASH 8`;
* `HASH 5-6`;
* `HASH 1-2-3-4`.
Thanks to this small amount of information, I am able to calculate the intermediate nodes up to the Merkle root.

![Merkle proof for TX 7, with the necessary nodes HASH 8, HASH 5-6 and HASH 1-2-3-4 highlighted.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/a/arbre-de-merkle/assets/image-2.png)

Merkle trees are notably used for light nodes (known as “SPV”) that only keep block headers, but not transactions. This structure is also found in the UTREEXO protocol, a protocol for condensing the nodes' UTXO set, and in the Taproot MAST.

*The Merkle tree is named after Ralph Merkle, a cryptographer who designed this structure in 1979. A Merkle tree can also be called a “hash tree”. In English, it is called a “Merkle Tree” or “Hash Tree”.*

384202ca-b17d-4b3d-9bb1-1f15225ed598.title: ROBOSATS
384202ca-b17d-4b3d-9bb1-1f15225ed598.body: *Open source* exchange platform that allows buying and selling bitcoins peer-to-peer via the Lightning Network, without identity verification (KYC). RoboSats runs on Tor and uses ephemeral identities (automatically generated robots) to preserve users' anonymity. Trades rely on *hold invoices*, which serve as an escrow mechanism. Fiat currency payments are made via methods chosen between the parties (bank transfer, PayPal, etc.).

38482b8f-a19c-4df6-9484-56dfc943280d.title: SIGHASH_NONE - 0X02
38482b8f-a19c-4df6-9484-56dfc943280d.body: Type of SigHash Flag used in Bitcoin transaction signatures to indicate that the signature applies to all of the transaction's inputs, but to none of its outputs. The use of `SIGHASH_NONE` implies that the signer commits only to the inputs, but allows the outputs to remain undetermined or modifiable after signing. This type of signature is useful in cases where the signer wishes to authorize other parties to decide how the bitcoins will be distributed in this transaction.

3865b4f9-1127-4a8c-ac17-e38ed5b99429.title: BIP-0120
3865b4f9-1127-4a8c-ac17-e38ed5b99429.body: Proposal for a “proof of payment” standard making it possible to prove that a Bitcoin transaction was indeed sent, by signing the inputs of the original transaction with the same keys. BIP-0120 aimed to provide verifiable cryptographic proof that the payer controlled the funds used in a specific transaction. It was never widely adopted.

38af29d4-579c-415c-ad7c-6c94c87496a7.title: DAEMON
38af29d4-579c-415c-ad7c-6c94c87496a7.body: A type of computer program that runs in the background, independently of user control. These programs perform tasks such as managing network services, monitoring systems, and responding to requests without requiring direct intervention. In the context of Bitcoin Core, the daemon is called "`bitcoind`". It is the version of Bitcoin Core without a user interface, which runs exclusively from the command line.

38c18734-0ae2-4645-9992-a6396a631f08.title: MAST
38c18734-0ae2-4645-9992-a6396a631f08.body:
Acronym for "*Merklized Alternative Script Trees*". A technique employing a Merkle tree to summarize an arbitrary number of user-selected spending conditions in a receiving address, one of which must be fulfilled to spend the bitcoins concerned. The Merkle tree allows the user to choose which condition they wish to fulfill without revealing the details of the other conditions on the blockchain. This makes it possible to reduce the fees associated with these scripts, to create much heavier conditions and, over a longer period, to improve user privacy (in addition to the joint use of Schnorr). This concept was the subject of several proposals, but it was finally added to Bitcoin via the Taproot soft fork in 2021.

*Initially, "MAST" was the acronym for "Merklized Abstract Syntax Tree". The use made of it in the context of Taproot no longer has anything to do with an "Abstract Syntax Tree". However, users continued to use the term MAST. Anthony Towns therefore proposed changing the initial meaning while keeping this widely used acronym with: "Merklized Alternative Script Trees".*

38de0e00-1143-4387-8517-e890f7228b17.title: BIP-0329
38de0e00-1143-4387-8517-e890f7228b17.body: Proposal defining a standard JSON Lines format for exporting and importing wallet labels. This format covers labels for transactions, addresses, extended public keys and UTXOs. The goal is to allow users to migrate their labeling data between different wallet software without loss of information. BIP-0329 meets a practical need, since labeling transactions and addresses is essential for accounting and for users' privacy.

39546d48-65eb-484e-8669-f2d715671ceb.title: DISTRIBUTED
39546d48-65eb-484e-8669-f2d715671ceb.body:
Attribute of a computer network in which decision-making power and control are shared equitably among all participants in the network. This distribution guarantees the resilience of the system. It is also called a peer-to-peer network. Unlike a decentralized network, where power is fragmented and dispersed among several entities, but where some central authorities remain endowed with greater power than the users, a distributed network eliminates the central authority by entrusting management and control to the users themselves. Bitcoin is an example of a distributed system. Bitcoin has no hierarchy or central authority. Maintaining consensus, verifying transactions, and issuing new monetary units are carried out by the users. This distributed structure ensures the system's resilience and resistance to censorship, making it very difficult for a single entity to control or manipulate it.

*Some people speak of Bitcoin as a decentralized system. Indeed, it is not uncommon to see these two terms used interchangeably. A more evocative synonym for the adjective “distributed” could be “peer-to-peer”, sometimes abbreviated “P2P”, the acronym of the English “Peer-to-Peer”.*

397a1a79-8d44-4883-b39e-a89ce5f55f4e.title: LOCK
397a1a79-8d44-4883-b39e-a89ce5f55f4e.body: File used in Bitcoin Core for locking the data directory. It is created when bitcoind or Bitcoin-qt starts to prevent several instances of the software from accessing the same data directory simultaneously. The purpose is to prevent conflicts and data corruption. The locking relies on an operating system lock mechanism applied to the file `.lock`. The file itself remains permanently present on the disk, but the lock is automatically released by the operating system when the process terminates, including in the event of an unexpected shutdown.

399884e5-b4c8-4993-a573-a40b1d0b844e.title: REDEEMSCRIPT
399884e5-b4c8-4993-a573-a40b1d0b844e.body: A script that defines the specific conditions that inputs must meet to unlock the funds associated with a P2SH output. In a P2SH UTXO, the `scriptPubKey` contains the hash of the `redeemScript`. When a transaction wishes to spend this UTXO as an input, it must provide the `redeemScript` in plain text that matches the hash contained in the `scriptPubKey`. The `redeemScript` is therefore given in the `scriptSig` of the input, in addition to the other elements necessary to satisfy the script's conditions, such as signatures or public keys. This encapsulated structure ensures that the details of the spending conditions remain hidden until the bitcoins are actually spent. It is notably used for Legacy P2SH multisig wallets.

39b93449-45b4-4aea-818e-19de91e53578.title: RELAY
39b93449-45b4-4aea-818e-19de91e53578.body: In the context of proof of work on the Bitcoin network, refers to a tool whose main function is to relay the new valid blocks that have been found. A distinction is sometimes made between the role of the miner, who is involved in the entire proof-of-work process, from building the candidate block to broadcasting the validated block, and the role of the hasher, which is limited to participating in the hashing of a block without being involved in its selection or broadcast. The relay role, for its part, consists of broadcasting the new blocks found by a hasher. In the case of mining pools, this relay role is performed by the pool itself. It is this role that incidentally gives it a lot of power over individual hashers. The term "relayer" can also refer to the person or entity that operates a relay.

39de4acc-545e-4898-bc99-6caac5ba1912.title: BITCOIN.CONF
39de4acc-545e-4898-bc99-6caac5ba1912.body: A configuration file used to customize the operation of a Bitcoin node running the Bitcoin Core client. Located in the Bitcoin Core data directory, this text file allows node operators to specify various parameters and options that influence the node's behavior. Among the parameters that can be set in `bitcoin.conf` are items such as the size of the Mempool, restrictions on network connections, the minimum relay transaction fees, as well as other security and performance options.

3a14cd4f-59a9-4b45-bb92-5370d7b50480.title: RGB
3a14cd4f-59a9-4b45-bb92-5370d7b50480.body:
A decentralized and confidential smart contract system, designed to work with Bitcoin and the Lightning Network. RGB operates on a client-side validation model and separates the storage of contract state from the blockchain, so as to keep only cryptographic commitments on it. Thus, the full history of states is maintained off the chain, which allows better scalability and confidentiality. RGB thus enables the creation of complex contracts to issue tokens, NFTs, decentralized identities or DeFi solutions, directly on top of Bitcoin.

On RGB, resistance to double spending is ensured by the use of Single-use Seals, a cryptographic mechanism that takes advantage of the fact that UTXOs on Bitcoin can only be spent once. As for the authenticity of the tokens, it is guaranteed by the client-side verification of the history of states, from the creation of the contract up to its most recent state.

3a770c94-9349-4aff-b145-3f4b3a2e6dae.title: BITAXE
3a770c94-9349-4aff-b145-3f4b3a2e6dae.body: Open source project of a miniature Bitcoin miner based on an ASIC chip. The Bitaxe is a small mining device designed to be accessible, inexpensive and entirely transparent in its design, with hardware schematics and firmware published as open source. It uses mining ASIC chips (taken from consumer machines such as Bitmain's Antminer series) soldered onto a compact, standalone printed circuit board, powered by a simple USB-C cable. The Bitaxe is mainly used for educational purposes or for "lottery mining" (solo mining in the hope of finding a block probabilistically), because its computing power remains very low compared to large industrial mining farms.

3aa32828-d935-4d8c-a1a8-19dd32bad5d1.title: P2P TRANSPORT V2
3aa32828-d935-4d8c-a1a8-19dd32bad5d1.body:
New version of the Bitcoin P2P transport protocol integrating opportunistic encryption to improve the privacy and security of communications between nodes. This improvement aims to address several problems of the base version of the P2P protocol, notably by making the exchanged data indistinguishable to a passive observer (such as an internet service provider), thereby reducing the risks of censorship and of attacks based on detecting specific patterns in data packets.

The encryption put in place does not include authentication, so as not to add unnecessary complexity and not to compromise the fact that connecting to the network remains permissionless. This new P2P transport protocol nonetheless offers better security against passive attacks and makes active attacks (notably MITM attacks) significantly more costly and detectable. The introduction of a pseudo-random data stream complicates the task of attackers wishing to censor or manipulate communications.

P2P transport V2 was included as an option (disabled by default) in version 26.0 of Bitcoin Core, released in December 2023. It can be enabled with the option `v2transport=1` in the configuration file.

3aafd4aa-4f21-40fe-a8be-9693a18cd5d7.title: CONCATENATION
3aafd4aa-4f21-40fe-a8be-9693a18cd5d7.body: In the context of cryptography and computer systems, refers to the process of joining two operands end to end, thus forming a new string of characters or data. This operation is generally written with a symbol of two vertical bars `\Vert`, or with the symbol `\circ`. For example, the concatenation of `45` with `87` will be equal to `4587`. We will write: `45 \Vert 87 = 4587`. The two operands have been put end to end.

3ad9e8ae-cf2a-482f-bfa0-0c5d8eff5c4b.title: RECURSIVE - COVENANT
3ad9e8ae-cf2a-482f-bfa0-0c5d8eff5c4b.body:
A recursive covenant on Bitcoin is a type of smart contract that imposes conditions not only on the current transaction, but also on the future transactions that spend the outputs of this transaction. This makes it possible to create chains of transactions where each one must comply with certain rules defined by the first one in the chain. Recursion creates a sequence of transactions where each one inherits the restrictions of its parent transaction. This would make it possible to establish complex, long-term control over how bitcoins can be spent, but it would also introduce risks to spending freedom and fungibility.

To summarize, a non-recursive covenant will be limited solely to the transaction that immediately follows the one that established the rules. Conversely, a recursive covenant will have the ability to impose specific conditions on a bitcoin indefinitely. Transactions can follow one another, but the bitcoin in question will always retain the initial conditions attached to it. Technically, the establishment of a non-recursive covenant occurs when the `scriptPubKey` of a UTXO defines restrictions on the `scriptPubKey` of the outputs of a transaction that spends said UTXO. By contrast, the establishment of a recursive covenant occurs when the `scriptPubKey` of a UTXO defines restrictions on the `scriptPubKey` of the outputs of a transaction that spends said UTXO, and of all the `scriptPubKey` that will follow the spending of this UTXO.

More generally, in computer science, what is called "recursion" is the ability of a function to call itself, which creates a sort of mise en abyme.

3b1dd060-9cee-4c26-8c25-5d8150cf77ab.title: EXTENDED KEY

3b3f43be-02c1-4aa8-8286-6e9b328214fe.title: ISSUANCE LIMIT
3b3f43be-02c1-4aa8-8286-6e9b328214fe.body: The ceiling set for the total money supply of BTC, established at approximately 21 million units. This limit is defined by the inflation policy in the Bitcoin protocol. New BTC are created and distributed to miners via the subsidy for validating each block. This subsidy is cut in half every 210,000 blocks, a process known as the “*halving*”. This method guarantees that monetary creation will gradually decrease until it reaches zero.

3b467f0a-ae1e-4e9e-8869-78574b57ff5e.title: GLOBAL STATE
3b467f0a-ae1e-4e9e-8869-78574b57ff5e.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the *Global State* designates the set of public properties of a contract, established during the *Genesis*. It acts as a public ledger and groups together the state elements that are accessible to everyone and that can be updated by authorized transitions in accordance with the rules defined by the contract's schema. Unlike *Owned States*, which are associated with specific entities, the *Global State* does not belong to any party in particular.

3b58d9e0-bb4d-4a52-902f-484c5ca34353.title: TCP
3b58d9e0-bb4d-4a52-902f-484c5ca34353.body: Acronym for “*Transmission Control Protocol*.” It is a communication protocol designed to ensure reliable data transmission over the Internet. It establishes a connection, guarantees the order of the data sent, handles retransmission in case of packet loss, and controls congestion.

3b5e46d7-4fb2-40a2-875b-86b8975d683e.title: OP_NUMEQUAL - 0X9C
3b5e46d7-4fb2-40a2-875b-86b8975d683e.body: Compares the top two elements of the stack to check whether they are numerically equal. If the values are equal, it pushes `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise, it pushes `0` (false).

3bd6bfc5-85e4-456b-8454-f2e0bc10f683.title: BIP-0124
3bd6bfc5-85e4-456b-8454-f2e0bc10f683.body: Proposal for hierarchical deterministic script templates extending BIP-0032. BIP-0124 aimed to standardize the way HD wallets generate and manage different types of output scripts. Superseded by output script descriptors, which offer a more flexible and expressive approach to describing a wallet's output scripts.

3bded62b-9686-41e8-8f04-b0903f8d9482.title: KNAPSACK SOLVER
3bded62b-9686-41e8-8f04-b0903f8d9482.body: Former method used for coin selection in the Bitcoin Core wallet before version 0.17. The *Knapsack Solver* attempts to solve the coin selection problem by iteratively and randomly choosing UTXOs, and adding them up in subsets, with the aim of minimizing fees and the size of the transaction. This method has since been replaced by *Branch-and-Bound*.

3c2e851b-3e96-4900-a235-9a41cc97adea.title: HD - HIERARCHICAL-DETERMINISTIC
3c2e851b-3e96-4900-a235-9a41cc97adea.body: Said of a Bitcoin wallet that uses a single piece of information (the seed) to generate a multitude of public and private key pairs in a sequential and reproducible manner. This way of managing keys is defined by the BIP-0032 standard. The main advantage of HD wallets is that they allow users to have a multitude of different key pairs, notably in order to avoid address reuse, while being able to regenerate all of them from a single piece of information. This structure is called hierarchical because it makes it possible to create a tree-like organization of multiple keys and addresses from a single seed. And it is deterministic in the sense that each seed always generates the same sequence of keys in any wallet compliant with this system.

3c5029a7-1727-45c9-9017-3d461b7f58c3.title: ZKP - ZERO-KNOWLEDGE PROOF
3c5029a7-1727-45c9-9017-3d461b7f58c3.body: Cryptographic method allowing one party (the prover) to prove to another party (the verifier) that a piece of information is true, without revealing the information or any aspect of it. A ZKP makes it possible to guarantee the accuracy of a statement, while preserving the confidentiality of the underlying data.

3cab2140-98c3-4024-81c9-070fc4bb3940.title: COLD WALLET
3cab2140-98c3-4024-81c9-070fc4bb3940.body:
Synonym of “hardware wallet”. A hardware wallet is an electronic device dedicated to securing and managing the private keys of a Bitcoin wallet. These devices are designed to provide enhanced security compared to software wallets, which reside on general-purpose machines directly connected to the internet. Hardware wallets store the mnemonic phrase offline, on hardware that has a tiny attack surface, which isolates it from potentially vulnerable environments. 

When a transaction is made, the hardware wallet signs the transaction inside the device itself, without exposing the private key to the outside. Once the transaction is signed, it is broadcast to the Bitcoin network to be confirmed and included in the blockchain. Among the most popular hardware wallet models, one can mention: Ledger, Trezor, Coldcard, Passport, BitBox, Satochip, Jade or SeedSigner (non-exhaustive list).

*The hardware wallet can be expressed in different ways in French. Some speak of “portefeuille matériel” (hardware wallet) or “portefeuille froid” (cold wallet). Others prefer that the term “périphérique de signature” be used, or “signing device” in English, in order to avoid giving the impression that the bitcoins are physically located in the wallet.*

3d4aa1bc-8aed-4176-92ab-10874f164f00.title: INTERNAL KEYCHAIN
3d4aa1bc-8aed-4176-92ab-10874f164f00.body:
In the derivation of hierarchical deterministic wallets, the internal keychain is a derivation branch used to generate receiving addresses intended to receive payments coming from the same wallet, that is, only change addresses. Each account as defined at depth 3 has two keychains at depth 4: an external keychain and an internal keychain (also called “change”). The internal keychain is derived with an index of `/1/`.

![BIP-84 tree with an arrow pointing to the Chains level, where the internal chain /1 derives only change addresses.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/chaine-interne/assets/image-1.png)

3d4aaf2c-33d4-40d6-9baa-1a097a72c83c.title: TESTNET
3d4aaf2c-33d4-40d6-9baa-1a097a72c83c.body: An alternative version of Bitcoin used exclusively for testing and development purposes. It is a network separate from the main network (*mainnet*), with its own blocks and transactions, allowing developers to test new features, applications and updates without risk to the main network. The testnet also makes it possible to avoid paying transaction fees during tests. The bitcoins used on the testnet have no real value.

3d544cc7-dac9-4531-b7eb-f30960c0d421.title: PROOF-OF-KEY DAY
3d544cc7-dac9-4531-b7eb-f30960c0d421.body: An annual initiative observed every January 3 (the anniversary of the Genesis block) that encourages bitcoin holders to all withdraw their assets from exchange platforms at the same time and transfer them to *self-custody* solutions. The goal is to test the solvency of exchange platforms, by forcing them to prove that they do hold their users' bitcoins and that they are not engaging in fractional reserve. However, this practice is less and less followed today, which reduces its effectiveness. Ultimately, the best way to protect oneself against the bankruptcy of *exchanges* remains keeping one's bitcoins in *self-custody* all year round.

3d7fbc3d-cd09-44e5-aae3-d9e1a920851a.title: FIBRE
3d7fbc3d-cd09-44e5-aae3-d9e1a920851a.body:
Acronym for "*Fast Internet Bitcoin Relay Engine*". It is a protocol designed by Matt Corallo in 2016 to speed up the propagation of Bitcoin blocks around the world. Its objective was to reduce propagation delays as close as possible to physical limits. FIBRE aimed to guarantee a fairer distribution of mining opportunities, by ensuring that the proportion of blocks mined by a participant faithfully reflects their contribution in terms of computing power, regardless of their position on the network.

Indeed, latency in block transmission can favor large groups of miners, well connected and often close to one another, to the detriment of smaller ones. This phenomenon could, in the long run, increase mining centralization and reduce the overall security of the system. To address this problem, FIBRE introduced error-correcting codes and the sending of additional data to offset packet loss, as well as the use of compact blocks similar to those described in BIP-0152, all operating over UDP to bypass certain limitations of TCP. Nevertheless, FIBRE was abandoned in 2020, mainly because of its dependence on a single maintainer and because the adoption of BIP-0152 made such a system less indispensable.

3d99e8d6-c063-470e-8abc-3e30dfcb1ee5.title: SILENT PAYMENTS
3d99e8d6-c063-470e-8abc-3e30dfcb1ee5.body:
Method for using static Bitcoin addresses to receive payments without producing address reuse, without interaction and without any visible on-chain link between the different payments and the static address. This technique eliminates the need to generate new fresh receiving addresses for each transaction, which avoids the usual interactions in Bitcoin where the recipient must provide a new address to the payer.

With Silent Payments, the payer uses the recipient's public keys (spend public key and scan public key) and the sum of the private keys of their own inputs to generate a fresh address for each payment. Only the recipient, thanks to their private keys, can compute the private key corresponding to this payment address. ECDH (*Elliptic-Curve Diffie-Hellman*), a cryptographic key exchange algorithm, is used to establish a shared secret which is then used to derive the receiving address and the private key (only on the recipient's side). To identify the Silent Payments intended for them, recipients must scan the blockchain and examine each transaction matching the protocol's criteria. Unlike BIP-0047, which uses a notification transaction to establish the payment channel, Silent Payments remove this step, which saves one transaction. However, the trade-off is that the recipient must scan all the potential transactions to determine, by applying ECDH, whether they are addressed to them.

For example, Bob's static address `B` represents the concatenation of his scan public key and his spend public key:
```math
B\ =\ B_{scan}\ \Vert\ B_{spend}
```
These keys are simply derived from the following path:

```text
scan : m / 352' / 0' / 0' / 1' / 0
spend : m / 352' / 0' / 0' / 0' / 0
```

This static address is published by Bob. Alice retrieves it to make a Silent Payment to Bob. She computes the payment address `P_0` belonging to Bob in this way:
```math
P_0\ =\ B_{spend}\ +\ hash(inputHash \cdot a \cdot B_{scan}\ \Vert\ 0) \cdot G
```
Where:
```math
inputHash\ =\ hash(outpoint_L\ \Vert\ A)
```
With:
* `B_{scan}`: Bob's scan public key (static address);
* `B_{spend}`: Bob's spend public key (static address);
* `A`: The sum of the input public keys (tweak);
* `a`: The tweak private key, that is, the sum of all the key pairs used in the `scriptPubKey` of the UTXOs spent as inputs of Alice's transaction;
* `outpoint_L`: The smallest outpoint (lexicographically) used as an input of Alice's transaction;
* `\Vert`: The concatenation (an operation that consists of placing the operands end to end);
* `G`: The generator point of the elliptic curve `secp256k1`;
* `hash`: The SHA256 hash function tagged with `BIP0352/SharedSecret`;
* `P_0`: The first public key / unique address for the payment to Bob;
* `0`: An integer making it possible to generate several unique payment addresses.

Bob scans the blockchain to find his Silent Payment in this way:
