```math
P_0\ =\ B_{spend}\ +\ hash(inputHash \cdot b_{scan} \cdot A\ \Vert\ 0) \cdot G
```
With:
* `b_{scan}`: Bob's scan private key.

If he finds `P_0` as an address that contains a Silent Payment addressed to him, he computes `p_0`, the private key making it possible to spend the funds sent by Alice to `P_0`:
```math
p_0\ =\ (b_{spend}\ +\ hash(inputHash \cdot b_{scan} \cdot A\ \Vert\ 0)) \mod n
```
With:
* `b_{spend}`: Bob's spend private key;
* `n`: the order of the elliptic curve `secp256k1`.

In addition to this basic version, it is also possible to use labels, which make it possible to generate several different static addresses from a single base static address, with the aim of separating several uses, without unreasonably multiplying the work required during scanning.

3dcc6cb1-dc1e-44c7-9662-2754c0158a24.title: GENERATOR POINT
3dcc6cb1-dc1e-44c7-9662-2754c0158a24.body:
Fixed point on an elliptic curve that serves as the basis for all public-key cryptography operations. In Bitcoin, the generator point `G` is a standard parameter of the secp256k1 curve, defined deterministically. All Bitcoin users share the same generator point `G`. It is a public and universal parameter of the secp256k1 curve. Its coordinates are:

```
x=0x79BE667EF9DCBBAC55A06295CE870B07029BFCDB2DCE28D959F2815B16F81798
y=0x483ADA7726A3C4655DA4FBFC0E1108A8FD17B448A68554199C47D08FFB10D4B8
```

The generator point is the basis of public key derivation: a private key `k` (an integer) is associated with a public key `K` by scalar multiplication on the elliptic curve: `K = k * G`. This operation is easy to compute in one direction, but practically impossible to invert (the discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves).

3dd94036-e292-4c62-97e5-f5002b7836ae.title: OP_TXHASH - 0XBD
3dd94036-e292-4c62-97e5-f5002b7836ae.body:
Opcode `0xbd` proposed in BIP-0346 for Tapscript, replacing `OP_SUCCESS189`. It provides a general-purpose transaction introspection mechanism that produces a configurable hash from certain fields of the spending transaction.

The opcode removes from the top of the stack an element called `TxFieldSelector`, a serialized structure that determines which transaction fields must be included in the hash. This selector makes it possible to target, as desired: global fields (version, locktime, current input index), per-input fields (prevouts, sequences, scriptSigs, values and scriptPubkeys of the spent UTXOs, Taproot annexes) and per-output fields (scriptPubkeys, values). It also offers several modes for selecting inputs and outputs: all, only the one at the current index, the first N, or a set of individual indices. After validating the selector, the opcode pushes onto the stack the 32-byte `SHA256` hash computed from the selected fields.

With an empty `TxFieldSelector`, `OP_TXHASH` produces a hash semantically equivalent to that of `OP_CHECKTEMPLATEVERIFY`, which makes it a strict generalization of BIP-0119. Combined with `OP_CHECKSIGFROMSTACK`, it would make it possible to build arbitrary signature hashes and to emulate `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` as well as other signature modes. This proposal is for the moment still a draft.

3e290a3e-846b-464e-bb20-1449e8d8a045.title: OP_CHECKMULTISIG - 0XAE
3e290a3e-846b-464e-bb20-1449e8d8a045.body: Verifies several signatures against several public keys. It takes as input a series of `N` public keys and `M` signatures, where `M` can be less than or equal to `N`. `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` checks whether at least `M` signatures match `M` of the `N` public keys. Note that, because of a historical *off-by-one* bug, an extra item is removed from the stack by `OP_CHECKMULTISIG`. This item is called the “*dummy element*”. To avoid an error in the `scriptSig`, a `OP_0` is therefore included, which is a useless item meant to satisfy the removal and work around the bug. Since BIP-0147 (introduced with SegWit in 2017), the useless item consumed because of the bug must be `OP_0` for the script to be valid, because it was a malleability vector. This opcode was removed in Tapscript.

3e7055ed-3bab-47c1-90d3-cfd551096ee8.title: CONSENSUS
3e7055ed-3bab-47c1-90d3-cfd551096ee8.body:
Mechanism by which all nodes of the Bitcoin network come to agree on the shared state of the blockchain. Consensus allows all users to align on a single history of Bitcoin transactions, notably in order to prevent double spending. Bitcoin's consensus mechanism is sometimes called “Nakamoto Consensus”. It relies on proof of work and specifies that all network nodes accept the chain with the greatest amount of accumulated work.

*By extension, some people use “Consensus” to refer to the tacit rules of the Bitcoin protocol.*

3e772f6a-a484-464d-82a1-d0d808f825fb.title: BGP HIJACKING
3e772f6a-a484-464d-82a1-d0d808f825fb.body:
Attack in which a malicious actor manipulates BGP announcements to redirect Internet traffic to their own network. By pretending to be the legitimate origin of certain IP address ranges, the attacker can intercept, monitor or block traffic destined for those addresses.

BGP (*Border Gateway Protocol*) is the protocol that determines how traffic is routed between the different autonomous systems (AS) that make up the global Internet. It decides the paths that data takes to go from one point to another.

In the context of Bitcoin, BGP Hijacking can be used to divert traffic between nodes of the Bitcoin network in order to isolate some of them. This attack can also be carried out on Stratum servers used by mining pools, in order to redirect hashers' computing power to the attacker's own pool. Since hashers do not often restart their machines, this redirection can persist for a long time. This attack can not only aim at direct financial gain by usurping block rewards, but also seek to temporarily gain more power over the system.

3eaaa599-9e26-4ff8-aab1-3834cdc9b6bc.title: INDEXES/TXINDEX/
3eaaa599-9e26-4ff8-aab1-3834cdc9b6bc.body: Files in Bitcoin Core that are dedicated to indexing all the transactions present in the blockchain. This indexing makes it possible to quickly look up detailed information about a transaction using its identifier (TXID), without having to go through the entire blockchain. Creating these index files is an option that is not enabled by default in Bitcoin Core. If this feature is not enabled, your node will only index the transactions associated with the wallets attached to your node. To enable indexing of all transactions, you must set the `txindex=1` parameter in the `bitcoin.conf` file. This option is particularly useful for applications and services that frequently search the Bitcoin transaction history.

3f1e3903-ed47-4e72-bc65-8fca6e1aa69d.title: BITCOINJ
3f1e3903-ed47-4e72-bc65-8fca6e1aa69d.body: An open-source library that implements the Bitcoin protocol in Java, created by Mike Hearn in 2011. It is designed to operate in SPV (*Simplified Payment Verification*) mode: instead of downloading the entire blockchain, it retrieves only the block headers and uses Bloom filters to identify relevant transactions. This lightweight operation makes it suitable for mobile devices and resource-constrained environments. Bitcoinj has served as the basis for many projects, notably the Bitcoin Wallet app (which no longer exists), Bisq and RSK.

3f3bd5a3-666a-4465-a056-289aa3bfc804.title: BIP-0140
3f3bd5a3-666a-4465-a056-289aa3bfc804.body: Proposal for normalized TXIDs excluding signature data from the calculation of the transaction identifier, in order to solve the malleability problem. BIP-0140 was an alternative approach to SegWit for obtaining stable transaction identifiers. It was closed because SegWit (BIP-0141) solved the malleability problem in a different way, while also bringing other advantages.

3f3da0be-a4e6-4cb7-955e-275213a94908.title: SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUTANYSCRIPT
3f3da0be-a4e6-4cb7-955e-275213a94908.body: Variant of the modifier SigHash Flag `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` in Bitcoin, introduced in BIP-0118. This SigHash works like `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT`, but in addition to not committing to the specific UTXO spent, the signature commits neither to the script (scriptCode/tapscript) nor to the amount of the input. This allows the same signature to be reused to spend any UTXO using the same BIP-0118 public key, regardless of the associated script or amount.

3f4c7a86-378e-4820-9cf1-d5ca118fde99.title: FOUNTAIN
3f4c7a86-378e-4820-9cf1-d5ca118fde99.body: Podcast application integrating Lightning payments according to the *value-for-value* model. Founded in 2021 by Oscar Merry and Nick Malster, Fountain allows listeners to send micropayments in satoshis directly to content creators in real time while listening, via the Lightning Network. The application relies on the Podcasting 2.0 standard initiated by Adam Curry, which natively integrates Bitcoin payments into RSS feeds. Listeners can also earn satoshis by listening to podcasts, recommending content or interacting with the community. Fountain is available on iOS and Android.

3f8e48a5-f710-4f59-8c71-3825d7380f5b.title: OVERT ASICBOOST
3f8e48a5-f710-4f59-8c71-3825d7380f5b.body: The open and transparent version of AsicBoost. AsicBoost is an algorithmic optimization technique used in Bitcoin mining. Miners using the Overt version manipulate the `nVersion` field of the candidate block and use this modification as an additional nonce. This modification of the `nVersion` field makes it possible to change the data of the first SHA256 chunk of the header, and thus to reuse the intermediate result (*midstate*) of this first chunk for all the iterations of the `Nonce`, which reduces the necessary calculations. This version is publicly detectable and does not hide its modifications from the rest of the network, unlike the Covert version of AsicBoost.

3fcc50a7-2d25-4512-bdd0-ed6ab5c964d9.title: SUBMARINE SWAP
3fcc50a7-2d25-4512-bdd0-ed6ab5c964d9.body:
An atomic exchange between on-chain bitcoins and off-chain bitcoins on the Lightning Network, without counterparty risk. Neither party takes *custody* of the other's funds: either the exchange succeeds in full, or it fails and each party recovers their funds.

The mechanism relies on the same HTLCs (*Hash Time-Locked Contracts*) as those used in Lightning routing. The recipient of the Lightning payment generates a secret preimage whose hash is used to build both an on-chain contract and an off-chain payment. The on-chain payer locks their bitcoins in a conditional script: the funds can be claimed by the recipient if they provide the preimage and their signature, or recovered by the payer after the *timelock* expires. When the Lightning payment is made, the preimage is revealed, which allows the recipient to claim the on-chain funds.

40382fe3-b848-4e45-bfaa-1438b187b3ea.title: ACTIVATION METHOD
40382fe3-b848-4e45-bfaa-1438b187b3ea.body:
An activation method is the process by which the user community decides on the implementation of a soft fork on the Bitcoin protocol, seeking to avoid a split of the blockchain. This process consists of soliciting the opinion of miners to approve a soft fork before its activation. If a large majority accepts the soft fork, the risk of a blockchain split is minimized. This consensus is crucial because if a majority of miners refuse to make the change, the soft fork could create two distinct chains: one with the modified rules and the other without. There are 2 main categories of activation methods: 
* UASFs (User-Activated Soft Forks) when it is the nodes that enforce the update;
* MASFs (Miner-Activated Soft Forks) when it is the miners who trigger the activation.

There are many different activation methods that have been tested as Bitcoin has evolved. In Satoshi's time, the activation process was not formally established. Changes were often arbitrary and sometimes even made without informing the community. Later, the *Flag Day* method was adopted. After Satoshi's departure, other methods were used successively, notably BIP-0034, BIP-0009, BIP-0008, and finally, *Speedy Trial*.

404a66ec-fad7-45c6-8b32-58857e09b057.title: ENGRAVING
404a66ec-fad7-45c6-8b32-58857e09b057.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the *engraving* refers to an optional data string that the holders of a contract can successively inscribe in the history of its transitions. Accessible notably via the RGB21 interface, this feature makes it possible to add commemorative or descriptive information without changing the validity of the operations. It enriches the contract's history by integrating additional metadata.

4082393c-2593-40d3-952a-497f836f69cc.title: CBDC
4082393c-2593-40d3-952a-497f836f69cc.body:
Acronym for “*Central Bank Digital Currency*”. It is a digital form of fiat money issued and controlled directly by a central bank, unlike conventional bank deposits, which are created by commercial banks.

CBDC projects are being developed in many countries: the digital euro in Europe, the digital yuan (e-CNY) in China, or the *Sand Dollar* in the Bahamas. They can operate on centralized ledgers or use technologies inspired by blockchains, but remain under the total control of the issuing authority.

Supporters see them as a tool for modernizing payments and for financial inclusion. Critics, notably in the Bitcoin community, raise major privacy risks: a CBDC would potentially allow the state to monitor, block or place conditions on every transaction of citizens, constituting an unprecedented tool of financial control. CBDCs are fundamentally different from Bitcoin, which is decentralized and censorship-resistant.

40b9661a-7c4f-4e83-9fca-d49516a6ebe7.title: BIP-0084
40b9661a-7c4f-4e83-9fca-d49516a6ebe7.body: Defines the derivation standard for SegWit V0 addresses (`bc1q...`) within a hierarchical deterministic wallet. It defines the index `84'` which must now be used at depth `purpose` of the HD wallet for P2WPKH script templates.

40d2f421-ceb0-4747-969a-39cfbf0089f7.title: NBITS
40d2f421-ceb0-4747-969a-39cfbf0089f7.body:
A 4-byte field present in the header of every Bitcoin block, which encodes the difficulty target in a compact form: the first byte indicates the number of bytes of the full target (the exponent), and the following three bytes make up the mantissa (the significant digits of the target). The decoding formula is: `cible = mantisse \times 256^{(exposant - 3)}`.

A block hash must be less than or equal to the target value encoded in `nBits` for the block to be considered valid. This field is recalculated every 2,016 blocks during the difficulty adjustment, in order to maintain an average interval of about 10 minutes between blocks.

40e0e165-917e-4b42-adc3-c3c6a46cdcf5.title: STASH
40e0e165-917e-4b42-adc3-c3c6a46cdcf5.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the Stash refers to the set of data stored client-side by a user for one or more contracts. This data notably includes the history of transitions, the *consignments* as well as the validity proofs, which are indispensable to the client-side validation process (*Client-side Validation*). Each holder keeps only the relevant fragments of the history (*shards*) needed to verify and update their contracts.

40e2afec-6d48-4999-9667-54d17e8f4c44.title: WTXID
40e2afec-6d48-4999-9667-54d17e8f4c44.body: Extension of the traditional TXID, including the witness data (*witness*) introduced with SegWit. Whereas the TXID is a hash of the transaction data excluding the witness, the WTXID is the `SHA256d` of the entirety of the transaction data, witness included. WTXIDs are stored in a second Merkle tree whose root is placed in the coinbase transaction. This separation makes it possible to eliminate the malleability of the transaction's TXID.

4150f009-d0a2-44c1-9e3e-ccf24f9d4f3d.title: LNC - LIGHTNING NODE CONNECT
4150f009-d0a2-44c1-9e3e-ccf24f9d4f3d.body: Protocol developed by Lightning Labs that allows connecting remotely to a Lightning node via a proxy server, without exposing the node directly on the internet. LNC establishes an end-to-end encrypted connection between the client (for example Lightning Terminal in a browser) and the node, authenticating using a *pairing phrase*. This protocol eliminates the need to configure a VPN, open ports or manage TLS certificates, which considerably simplifies remote access to a personal node hosted behind a NAT or a firewall.

4154ba49-41e5-4a8b-9a27-02d3dfa9fdcf.title: ASHIGARU
4154ba49-41e5-4a8b-9a27-02d3dfa9fdcf.body: A privacy-oriented mobile Bitcoin wallet, forked from the Samourai Wallet code after the seizure of its servers by US authorities in April 2024. Ashigaru carries over Samourai's privacy-protection features, notably Whirlpool coinjoins, Stonewall transactions, collaborative transactions (Stowaway, StonewallX2), ricochets and advanced UTXO control. The project is maintained by an open-source community that continues to develop these privacy tools.

4216ed7f-2a31-48a5-9546-142e7dd8d703.title: HOSTED CHANNEL
4216ed7f-2a31-48a5-9546-142e7dd8d703.body:
A Lightning channel that is not anchored in an on-chain transaction, unlike classic channels. A *hosted channel*, also called a “custodial channel” or “virtual channel”, does not rely on any funding transaction on the Bitcoin blockchain: it exists only at the Lightning protocol level, with no on-chain settlement guarantee.

Its operation involves two asymmetric roles: a host, which provides the channel with liquidity on its side, and a client, which uses this channel to access the Lightning network. The funds remain in the host's custody, which makes the model custodial. However, compared to traditional custodial wallets, *hosted channels* offer additional guarantees: the client generates its own invoices and controls the payment preimages, which makes fraud detectable. The host and the client exchange mutually signed state data, which provides cryptographic proof of the balance owed. Opening and closing these channels costs nothing in mining fees, which makes it easier to onboard new users onto the Lightning Network at a lower cost.

4233584f-5a22-48c8-bc9b-498830a5378f.title: SIDECAR CHANNEL
4233584f-5a22-48c8-bc9b-498830a5378f.body:
Lightning channel opened by a third party (party A) for the benefit of another user (party B), toward a routing node (party C). This mechanism, introduced in Lightning Pool by Lightning Labs, makes it possible to onboard new users onto the Lightning Network without them needing to hold bitcoin beforehand to fund a channel.

Concretely, a node operator with a funded Pool account can buy a channel lease (*channel lease*) on behalf of a third party. The selling routing node then opens a channel directly to the beneficiary, who can immediately receive payments through a peer that is well connected to the network. This model creates a source of revenue for intermediary operators, while promoting the decentralization of the network since new users connect through a diversity of peers rather than a single point. *Sidecar channels* also make it possible to create dual-funded channels (*dual-funded*) and can be deployed as *turbo channels*, without waiting for on-chain confirmations.

426e1e5e-a31d-4338-9497-2be2dcc3ed4f.title: OP_1 - 0X51
426e1e5e-a31d-4338-9497-2be2dcc3ed4f.body:
Pushes the value `1` onto the stack. It is often used to represent the boolean value true in scripts.

`OP_1` is identical to `OP_TRUE` (`0X51`) and `OP_PUSHNUM_1`.

426fb65c-f80b-4552-93a7-32367615ba12.title: FRACTIONAL RESERVES
426fb65c-f80b-4552-93a7-32367615ba12.body: A principle of traditional finance whereby banks keep only a fraction of their customers' deposits as available reserves, and use the rest to grant loans and generate profits. In the context of Bitcoin, although the currency itself is not subject to bank credit creation, the concept of fractional reserve applies when an exchange platform keeps only a portion of the BTC deposited by its users, and uses the rest for other purposes. This poses a liquidity and solvency risk if all users decide to withdraw their funds simultaneously. This is notably why it is essential to hold your own bitcoins in *self-custody*.

42910651-6f20-487e-a9c4-5e75433ee369.title: UTXO
42910651-6f20-487e-a9c4-5e75433ee369.body: Acronym for *Unspent Transaction Output*. A UTXO is a transaction output that has not yet been spent, that is, used as an input for a new transaction. UTXOs represent the fraction of bitcoins that a user owns and that are currently available to be spent. Each UTXO is associated with a specific output script (`scriptPubKey`), which defines the conditions required to spend the bitcoins. Transactions in Bitcoin consume these UTXOs as inputs and create new UTXOs as outputs. The UTXO model is fundamental to Bitcoin, because it makes it easy to verify that transactions are not trying to spend bitcoins that do not exist or that have already been spent.

42a61863-fb16-4771-88fa-212a75ea0343.title: GATEWAY NODE
42a61863-fb16-4771-88fa-212a75ea0343.body:
Lightning routing node that operates private (unannounced) channels to create additional routing opportunities. Unlike a classic routing node whose channels are all public and visible in the network graph, a *gateway node* also maintains private channels with other nodes. These channels are not broadcast via the *gossip* protocol, and therefore do not appear in the public topology of the network.

The value of a *gateway node* becomes apparent when other nodes open public channels to it: these connections create payment paths passing through the private channels, thus offering alternative routes invisible to the rest of the network. The *gateway node* then acts as a bridge between the public network and nodes that do not wish to expose their channels.

42b64d1b-30f5-4c96-8e47-cc569368d694.title: BIP-0385
42b64d1b-30f5-4c96-8e47-cc569368d694.body: Introduces the descriptor functions `addr(ADDR)` and `raw(HEX)`. The function `addr(ADDR)` makes it possible to describe an output script using a receiving address, while the function `raw(HEX)` makes it possible to specify an output script using a raw hexadecimal representation of that script. BIP-0385 was implemented along with all the other descriptor-related BIPs (except BIP-0386) in version 0.17 of Bitcoin Core.

42e3bd23-0ba3-4206-9265-c5f73abd9841.title: THE DAO
42e3bd23-0ba3-4206-9265-c5f73abd9841.body: A project launched in 2016 on Ethereum, which aimed to create an autonomous investment fund managed by *smart contracts*. Although mainly linked to Ethereum, The DAO had a significant impact on the evolution of Bitcoin. In June 2016, The DAO fell victim to a massive hack. In response, the Ethereum community carried out a *hard fork*, which turned out to be a resounding failure. This incident consolidated the conservative positions of the *small blockers* during Bitcoin's Blocksize War. They used this event to argue against rapid changes to the Bitcoin protocol, such as those advocated by the *big blockers*, and against the idea of carrying out *hard forks*, as was done on Ethereum following the hack of The DAO.

4316277e-51e7-4466-a0c4-976e2724b318.title: MAGICAL BITCOIN
4316277e-51e7-4466-a0c4-976e2724b318.body: Former name of the BDK collection of tools and libraries for developers.

4354591e-46dd-4b23-87fa-b3803dc1cd7b.title: LOOP IN
4354591e-46dd-4b23-87fa-b3803dc1cd7b.body: Operation offered by the Lightning Loop service that allows converting on-chain bitcoins into outbound liquidity in a Lightning channel. The user sends bitcoins on the blockchain and receives the equivalent (minus fees) in one of their Lightning channels via a *submarine swap*. *Loop In* is useful for increasing one's sending capacity on the Lightning Network, for example when a user has exhausted their outbound liquidity after making many payments and wants to be able to send more.

43712217-e80b-4c66-a512-adaae753612c.title: AIR COOLING
43712217-e80b-4c66-a512-adaae753612c.body: A cooling system used for ASICs in the context of Bitcoin mining. *Air cooling* consists of using fans to dissipate the heat generated by the components. Ambient air is drawn in to cool the chips before being expelled. This cooling method is the most widespread, because the fans are present directly on the machines when purchased. It is generally the least expensive to acquire, but it is less efficient compared to techniques such as *hydro cooling* or *immersion cooling*.

4377d65a-07ec-43d4-b763-227a137f2595.title: BIP-0090
4377d65a-07ec-43d4-b763-227a137f2595.body: Proposal to simplify the handling of the activation of earlier soft forks by replacing the miner signaling mechanism via block version numbers with simple block height checks. This change would eliminate the need to check the previous 1000 blocks for the activation of consensus rules, which would reduce the technical debt associated with implementing these soft forks.

43ba3400-9a5d-4fd1-815d-0f24fa6a045c.title: BITCOIN OPTECH
43ba3400-9a5d-4fd1-815d-0f24fa6a045c.body: Non-profit organization that focuses on sharing technical information for businesses using Bitcoin. Bitcoin Optech offers a wide variety of technical resources on Bitcoin, notably an excellent weekly newsletter. This newsletter summarizes the most important discussions and the latest news concerning the development of Bitcoin and the Lightning Network. To subscribe to the newsletter, go to: [https://bitcoinops.org/en/newsletters/](https://bitcoinops.org/en/newsletters/).

44082609-5a9a-4b30-a140-6296c691406f.title: PREMIX
44082609-5a9a-4b30-a140-6296c691406f.body:
Intermediate account in the Whirlpool protocol that contains the UTXOs resulting from the Tx0 awaiting their first coinjoin cycle. The premix is a transitional state: UTXOs stay there until they are selected to participate in a coinjoin transaction.

Each UTXO in the premix account has exactly the nominal amount of the chosen pool (for example 0.01 BTC for the 0.01 pool), in addition to the mining fees needed for the first coinjoin cycle. These UTXOs are considered unmixed, because they are still directly traceable to the Tx0 that created them. They have not yet benefited from the link-breaking that coinjoin offers.

Once a premix UTXO is selected for a coinjoin cycle and the transaction is confirmed, it moves into the postmix account.

44552511-eb19-4d7a-a3bb-c9d13b3fee50.title: RAW TRANSACTION

4521e4ea-eb0d-4bb6-934f-246e0e330b01.title: SYNONYM
4521e4ea-eb0d-4bb6-934f-246e0e330b01.body: A technology company founded by John Carvalho, focused on developing software and protocols that promote a peer-to-peer economy centered on Bitcoin. Synonym is the originator of the Slashtags protocol, a decentralized web standard that makes it possible to derive additional key pairs from a BIP-0039 seed in order to create profiles, contacts and passwordless authentication. The company also developed Bitkit, a mobile wallet with an embedded Lightning node.

453e3869-5a5c-4c62-a91a-460806590d7a.title: CLN - CORE-LIGHTNING
453e3869-5a5c-4c62-a91a-460806590d7a.body: Major implementation of the Lightning Network protocol written in the C and Rust languages. Developed by Blockstream, Core-Lightning is designed to be lightweight and high-performing. It stands out for its modular architecture, which allows developers to easily add custom features. This implementation was renamed in 2022. Its original name was previously “C-Lightning”.

4553c372-a52e-4da5-85a1-d07f9e27bdfa.title: OP_2DROP - 0XD6
4553c372-a52e-4da5-85a1-d07f9e27bdfa.body: Removes the two elements at the top of the stack. In other words, `OP_2DROP` removes the top of the stack and the second element of the stack. This opcode is the equivalent of chaining two `OP_DROP`.

45afa1a7-e1a1-473e-8324-8fed218de006.title: MAXIMALIST
45afa1a7-e1a1-473e-8324-8fed218de006.body: Term that designates a person convinced that Bitcoin is the only cryptocurrency endowed with fundamental value, and that altcoins are superfluous, even harmful. The word comes from the English *Bitcoin maximalist*, an expression coined by Vitalik Buterin in a blog post published in November 2014. Initially used pejoratively to criticize a view of the cryptocurrency ecosystem judged to be narrow, the label was subsequently claimed by those it designated.

45f431f2-f91e-4986-a2b3-968252720501.title: PAYMENT CHANNEL
45f431f2-f91e-4986-a2b3-968252720501.body: In the context of the Lightning Network, a payment channel is a bidirectional connection between two Lightning nodes that allows bitcoins to be exchanged off-chain. On-chain, a payment channel is represented by a 2/2 multisig address held by the two participants. The payment channel requires one on-chain transaction to open it and another to close it. Between these two events, the channel's users can carry out a very large number of off-chain bitcoin exchanges, on the Lightning Network, without requiring on-chain activity. On Lightning, it is possible to route a payment through several channels and several nodes, in order to send bitcoins without necessarily opening a direct channel with the recipient.

460023ca-a13c-4178-b28c-54547af6c0a0.title: BITCOIN FOUNDATION
460023ca-a13c-4178-b28c-54547af6c0a0.body:
Non-profit organization founded in September 2012. Its founding members are Gavin Andresen, Charlie Shrem, Mark Karpelès, Peter Vessenes, Roger Ver and Patrick Murck. Its objective was to promote the development of Bitcoin, to fund protocol developers and to represent the community before institutions.

In its early years, the foundation funded the work of developers such as Gavin Andresen and contributed to the standardization of the protocol. However, it was quickly confronted with controversies. Several of its founding members were subject to legal proceedings: Charlie Shrem was arrested in 2014 for money laundering linked to the Silk Road marketplace, and Mark Karpelès was indicted in Japan after the bankruptcy of Mt. Gox.

The foundation lost influence over the years, criticized for its governance and its lack of financial transparency. Part of the Bitcoin community reproached it for wanting to centralize the representation of a project designed to be decentralized.

461a77f8-33ab-4e87-a0bb-edb1e50a78be.title: OP_ROT - 0X7B
461a77f8-33ab-4e87-a0bb-edb1e50a78be.body: Moves the third element from the top of the stack to the top of the stack. The two elements that were above it are pushed below it, keeping their relative order.

461d9b9e-2b9e-4367-a0cd-649c6be43c3c.title: OP_CHECKSIGFROMSTACK - 0XCC
461d9b9e-2b9e-4367-a0cd-649c6be43c3c.body:
Opcode `0xcc` proposed in BIP-0348 for Tapscript, as a replacement for `OP_SUCCESS204`. Unlike `OP_CHECKSIG`, which verifies a signature over a hash derived from the current transaction, `OP_CHECKSIGFROMSTACK` makes it possible to verify a Schnorr signature over an arbitrary message provided directly on the stack.

Execution begins by reading three items from the top of the stack: the public key (top), the message (second position) and the signature (third position). These three items are then removed from the stack. If the public key is empty, the script fails immediately. If it is 32 bytes long, it is interpreted as a BIP-0340 key: a non-empty signature is then validated according to the Schnorr scheme against this key and the message, and any invalid signature causes the script to stop. An empty signature pushes an empty vector onto the stack and execution continues normally. A valid signature pushes the value `0x01`. Keys of a length other than 0 and 32 bytes are treated as unknown types, and their verification always succeeds in order to allow for future extensions.

Each verification with a non-empty signature is counted in the sigops budget defined by BIP-0342. This ability to authenticate arbitrary data would open up possibilities such as transaction introspection, delegation of spending rights and the construction of Lightning Symmetry channels. This proposal is for the moment still a draft, and therefore not implemented on Bitcoin.

46983665-e82e-477e-81b4-bbef5a8cd244.title: LARGEST OUTPUT
46983665-e82e-477e-81b4-bbef5a8cd244.body:
An internal chain analysis heuristic. When a sufficiently large gap is spotted between 2 transaction outputs in a simple payment pattern, one can estimate that the largest output is likely the change output. This largest output heuristic is probably the least precise of all. If identified on its own, it is quite weak. However, this characteristic can be combined with other heuristics in order to reduce the uncertainty of our interpretation.

![Largest output: an input of 451,458 sats yields 57,814 and 390,987, the gap suggesting a change output of 390,987.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/s/sortie-la-plus-grande/assets/image-1.png)

46ce4551-eed7-487d-a792-159fe47eb36b.title: OP_ENDIF - 0X68
46ce4551-eed7-487d-a792-159fe47eb36b.body: Marks the end of a conditional control structure initiated by an `OP_IF` or an `OP_NOTIF`, normally followed by one or more `OP_ELSE`. It indicates that script execution must continue beyond the conditional structure, regardless of which branch was executed. In other words, `OP_ENDIF` delimits the end of conditional blocks in scripts.

46d9de8a-69c5-4b21-99d6-e88ae46e3b02.title: LIBSECP256K1

4791d414-b3d0-41cf-8296-3bd3e5bfd9dd.title: OP_EVAL
4791d414-b3d0-41cf-8296-3bd3e5bfd9dd.body: Opcode proposed by Gavin Andresen in 2011. It takes the script located at the top of the stack, executes it as if it were part of the `scriptPubKey`, and places its result on the stack. `OP_EVAL` was abandoned because of concerns about the complexity of this opcode, which would eventually be superseded by P2SH.

479c7e36-dbd1-475b-90e0-a86572629741.title: TAPSIGNER
479c7e36-dbd1-475b-90e0-a86572629741.body: An NFC card for signing Bitcoin transactions manufactured by Coinkite. The TapSigner stores a BIP-0032 master private key and makes it possible to sign transactions by bringing the card close to an NFC-compatible phone, via a wallet such as Nunchuk. Having no screen, this card is an affordable signing device, suited to small amounts or to use in multisig.

47b5ee48-88cf-4653-b9de-17e0afcdd408.title: SCHNORR PROTOCOL
47b5ee48-88cf-4653-b9de-17e0afcdd408.body: The Schnorr protocol is a digital signature algorithm based on elliptic curve cryptography (ECC). It is used on Bitcoin to derive a public key from a private key and to sign a transaction with a private key. On Bitcoin, just like ECDSA, Schnorr is based on the use of the elliptic curve `secp256k1`, characterized by the equation: `y^2 = x^3 + 7`. The Schnorr signature protocol has been implemented in the Bitcoin protocol since November 2021 with the activation of the Taproot upgrade.

47d3dd40-f2cb-43b8-95b0-dff812552ad7.title: TEMPORAL TEMPLATE
47d3dd40-f2cb-43b8-95b0-dff812552ad7.body:
Certain human behaviors are recognizable on-chain. The one that is perhaps the most useful in chain analysis is your sleep rhythm! Yes indeed, when you are asleep, you presumably do not broadcast Bitcoin transactions. And you generally sleep at roughly the same times. It is therefore common to use temporal analysis in chain analysis. It is simply a matter of recording the times at which the transactions of a given entity are broadcast to the Bitcoin network. Analyzing these temporal patterns allows us to deduce a great deal of information. 

First of all, a temporal analysis can sometimes identify the nature of the tracked entity. If we observe that transactions are broadcast steadily over 24 hours, this betrays strong economic activity. The entity behind these transactions is likely a company, potentially international and perhaps with automated internal procedures. On the contrary, if we see that the temporal *pattern* is instead spread over 16 specific hours, then we can estimate that we are dealing with an individual user, or perhaps a local business depending on the volumes exchanged.

Beyond the nature of the observed entity, the temporal *pattern* can also approximately indicate the user's location thanks to time zones. We can then link other transactions, and use their timestamps as an additional heuristic that can be added to a chain analysis.

In a different vein, it is also a temporal analysis of this type that made it possible to formulate the hypothesis that Satoshi Nakamoto was not operating from Japan, but rather from the United States: [_The Time Zones of Satoshi Nakamoto_](https://medium.com/@insearchofsatoshi/the-time-zones-of-satoshi-nakamoto-aa40f035178f).

48037b46-91b9-4330-b884-74e9ad5d8ff1.title: VALENCY
48037b46-91b9-4330-b884-74e9ad5d8ff1.body: In the RGB protocol, a *Valency* designates a public right that does not require the explicit storage of a state, but that can later be redeemed via a *State Extension*. This mechanism is a possibility declared beforehand in the contract logic, accessible to everyone or to specific actors, and it allows a specific extension of the contract state to be triggered when the defined conditions are met. The *Valency* thus offers a flexible and modular solution for anticipating future changes to the contract.

4838d9ab-212e-4945-a46b-1b158bfa42f0.title: RUST-LIGHTNING
4838d9ab-212e-4945-a46b-1b158bfa42f0.body: Lightning library developed in Rust, created by Matt Corallo, then adopted and developed by Square Crypto (now Spiral). Rust-Lightning provides an implementation of Lightning. It serves as the basis for the *Lightning Development Kit* (LDK).

486310e9-83da-48ae-8978-a516346c432b.title: RSMPPS
486310e9-83da-48ae-8978-a516346c432b.body:
Acronym for "*Recent Shared Maximum Pay Per Share*". It is a method for calculating miners' remuneration in the context of mining pools. RSMPPS is similar to SMPPS, but with priority given to miners who have contributed recently.

This method aims to reward current contributions by increasing the value of shares submitted in the most recent mining rounds, in order to favor miners who remain active and loyal.

48b21fa1-a1ab-4c4d-802c-1baeae4c7d41.title: BIP-0340
48b21fa1-a1ab-4c4d-802c-1baeae4c7d41.body: Defines the Schnorr signature scheme for Bitcoin's secp256k1 curve, activated with SegWit v1 (Taproot) in November 2021. Compared to ECDSA, Schnorr signatures offer several advantages: they are mathematically simpler, have a formal security proof, and natively allow key aggregation (MuSig2), batch verification and more compact multi-signatures. BIP-0340 uses 64-byte signatures (without DER encoding) and 32-byte *x-only* public keys, which reduces the size of on-chain data.

48c74d71-fd0e-4ea1-9b9c-118eb45fd875.title: BLIP-0052
48c74d71-fd0e-4ea1-9b9c-118eb45fd875.body: bLIP that defines LSPS2, a protocol for negotiating *just-in-time* (JIT) channels on the Lightning Network. It allows a client without an existing channel to receive an incoming payment: the LSP opens a channel on the fly when a payment arrives, and deducts the opening fees directly from the transferred amount.

48ca705c-705a-46e2-b5a8-237ab7ebda1b.title: XPUB
48ca705c-705a-46e2-b5a8-237ab7ebda1b.body: Extended public key prefix for Legacy and SegWit V1 accounts on Bitcoin.

492fe6cb-52db-4853-8a60-5dd6fd4a0b90.title: OP_ELSE - 0X67
492fe6cb-52db-4853-8a60-5dd6fd4a0b90.body: Modifies the execution flow in a conditional script: it indicates that the operations that follow it must be executed if the previous condition specified by an `OP_IF` or an `OP_NOTIF` is not met.

497c03e0-73d8-4597-ad9e-3431416a3f66.title: BIP-0110
497c03e0-73d8-4597-ad9e-3431416a3f66.body:
Proposal for a temporary (one-year) soft fork aiming to limit, at the consensus level, the size of arbitrary data that can be inscribed in Bitcoin transactions, in order to combat the use of the system as a data storage medium (notably the Ordinals inscriptions that appeared in 2022).

Concretely, BIP-0110 invalidates `scriptPubKey` larger than 34 bytes (except `OP_RETURN` limited to 83 bytes), witness elements and `OP_PUSHDATA` payloads exceeding 256 bytes, spends of undefined witness versions, the Taproot annex, Taproot *control blocks* larger than 257 bytes (limiting the tree to 128 leaves), as well as the opcodes `OP_SUCCESS` and `OP_IF`/`OP_NOTIF` in Tapscript. UTXOs created before activation are exempt.

The deployment uses a modified BIP-0009 with a threshold reduced to 55%, a mandatory activation by block height, and an active duration of 52,416 blocks (about 1 year), after which the rules expire automatically. This BIP is one of the most controversial of the post-Ordinals era, its supporters seeing in it a defense of Bitcoin as money, its detractors denouncing an arbitrary restriction of block space.

498eeb2f-8171-43dc-a934-02eeb8300459.title: IMMERSION COOLING
498eeb2f-8171-43dc-a934-02eeb8300459.body: Cooling technique used in mining, in which the ASICs are immersed in a non-conductive liquid to dissipate the heat they produce. Immersion has several advantages over air cooling. First of all, there is no need to use fans, which reduces energy consumption. Also, the machines are protected from dust, which improves their performance and longevity. Immersion also allows better heat dissipation, because the components are in direct contact with the cooling fluid.

49ae1eb9-83ef-4830-88c5-34476b0974a5.title: VALUE OVERFLOW INCIDENT
49ae1eb9-83ef-4830-88c5-34476b0974a5.body:
A bug exploited on August 15, 2010 on the Bitcoin network, which led to the creation of more than 184 billion bitcoins in a single transaction. The attacker exploited an integer overflow (*integer overflow*) vulnerability in the amount verification: two outputs of 92,233,720,368.54 BTC each, close to the maximum representable by a signed 64-bit integer, caused an overflow during the addition, which produced a positive result below the detection threshold.

The problem was quickly spotted by Jeff Garzik, who alerted the community on the BitcoinTalk forum. Satoshi Nakamoto published a fix within hours. This fix added an explicit check of each output amount as well as of their sum, and rejected any transaction that contained negative or excessive values. Miners then adopted the new version of the software and produced an alternative chain that excluded the invalid transaction.

The corrected chain overtook the chain containing the bug at block 74,691, after about 53 blocks of disruption. This episode, recorded under the identifier CVE-2010-5139, is the first major incident in the history of Bitcoin and led to the implementation of the network alert system.

4ac004e1-30a6-4070-af5b-cdb840d6f39d.title: STABLECOIN
4ac004e1-30a6-4070-af5b-cdb840d6f39d.body: A category of cryptocurrency designed to maintain a stable value relative to a reference asset, often a fiat currency such as the US dollar.

4b20f04c-4087-48fd-9d3d-578065184015.title: OVERCLOCKING
4b20f04c-4087-48fd-9d3d-578065184015.body: A practice that consists of increasing the operating frequency of the ASIC chips used for mining beyond their nominal specifications. This makes it possible to produce more hashrate and to increase the chances of finding a block. However, this practice also increases the machines' electricity consumption, and therefore generates more heat, which can lead to premature wear of the components and require improved cooling systems, such as immersion cooling.

4b2e959b-217f-407a-9a1d-0660999d0cdc.title: OP_VERIFY - 0X69
4b2e959b-217f-407a-9a1d-0660999d0cdc.body: Requires that the value at the top of the stack be non-zero (true). The transaction is invalid if this is not the case. `OP_VERIFY` is used to confirm script conditions.

4b7235b1-f0dc-441d-ad80-bc41f1ebff5f.title: BIP-0381
4b7235b1-f0dc-441d-ad80-bc41f1ebff5f.body: Introduces functions for descriptors, notably `pk(KEY)` (Pay-to-PubKey), `pkh(KEY)` (Pay-to-PubKey-Hash), and `sh(SCRIPT)` (Pay-to-Script-Hash). These functions standardize the way Legacy script types are described in descriptors. BIP-0381 was implemented along with all the other descriptor-related BIPs (except BIP-0386) in version 0.17 of Bitcoin Core.

4b88524d-358c-4a99-916a-698a7deca19d.title: BIP-0114
4b88524d-358c-4a99-916a-698a7deca19d.body: First formal proposal of MAST (*Merkelized Abstract Syntax Tree*) for Bitcoin, presented by Johnson Lau in 2016. BIP-0114 made it possible to structure the spending conditions of a UTXO as a Merkle tree, where each leaf represents an alternative script. When spending, only the executed branch had to be revealed, the others remaining hidden. This improved privacy and reduced the size of complex transactions. This BIP was closed in favor of BIP-0341 (Taproot), which integrates the MAST concept more elegantly through its *script-path*.

4bb65831-8540-4c8d-be14-1f834fe1afd8.title: BOUNTY
4bb65831-8540-4c8d-be14-1f834fe1afd8.body: Reward offered for the completion of a specific task, often related to the improvement or security of a software project. Bounties are often used to encourage the discovery and fixing of vulnerabilities in software, to develop new features, or to solve complex problems. Participants, generally developers or researchers, receive a reward once their contributions have been verified and accepted. This incentive system helps speed up development and strengthen software security by mobilizing a wider community. Bounties are sometimes used by software in the context of Bitcoin.

4bbfdcee-0e35-4762-bbbb-5ed58fb2e7f9.title: BITKIT
4bbfdcee-0e35-4762-bbbb-5ed58fb2e7f9.body: A self-custodial mobile Bitcoin wallet (*self-custody*) developed by Synonym, which combines on-chain and Lightning Network payments in a single application. Bitkit offers two accounts: “Savings” (on-chain) and “Spending” (Lightning), as well as *coin control* and the purchase of gift cards via Bitrefill. The software is open source.

4be89f70-73c7-4a33-a651-69861ca6a93c.title: TXID - TRANSACTION IDENTIFIER
4be89f70-73c7-4a33-a651-69861ca6a93c.body: Unique identifier associated with each Bitcoin transaction. It is generated by calculating the `SHA256d` hash of the transaction data. The TXID serves as a reference to find a specific transaction within the blockchain. It is also used to refer to a UTXO, via an *outpoint* which is essentially the concatenation of the TXID of a previous transaction and the index of the designated output (also called "*vout*"). For post-SegWit transactions, the TXID no longer takes the transaction's witness into account, which makes it possible to eliminate malleability.

4c067582-2915-41f1-87ae-dc5bad8da68e.title: CRYPTER
4c067582-2915-41f1-87ae-dc5bad8da68e.body: This term does not exist. One says "chiffrer".

4ca400a7-412f-4ec2-846b-fb6639a65d09.title: OP_MIN - 0XA3
4ca400a7-412f-4ec2-846b-fb6639a65d09.body: Selects the smaller of the top two elements of the stack and pushes it onto the stack. This operation keeps only the smaller of the two top values.

4d021329-4084-4897-992e-a828d0054c9d.title: PAIRING PHRASE
4d021329-4084-4897-992e-a828d0054c9d.body: Sequence of words used by the Lightning Node Connect (LNC) protocol to authenticate and secure a remote connection to a Lightning node. The *pairing phrase* is generated by the node via *litd* and passed to the user, who enters it in Lightning Terminal or any other compatible application. It establishes an end-to-end encrypted channel through a proxy server, without requiring a VPN, port forwarding, or direct exposure of the node to the internet.

4d035973-1c9b-49f9-8fa7-681dd7b5f07b.title: BROLLUPS
4d035973-1c9b-49f9-8fa7-681dd7b5f07b.body: Concept of a native rollup on Bitcoin proposed by Burak in June 2024. Unlike optimistic rollups or rollups based on zero-knowledge proofs, Brollups form a category of their own. They rely on the concept of VTXO (*Virtual UTXO*), which comes from the Ark protocol, and use them as a peg mechanism (*peg*). The principle consists of exchanging VTXOs for call data (*calldata*), accompanied by new VTXOs, through coinswaps. Brollups are run by an operator or a quorum of operators who provide liquidity to the protocol and advance the rollup's state by chaining Bitcoin transactions at regular intervals. The Bitcoin blockchain serves as the data availability layer, while transactions are executed on a dedicated virtual machine called the *Bitcoin Virtual Machine*. The peg is executable on-chain and can be redeemed unilaterally at any time. Brollups require no modification to the Bitcoin protocol and are not associated with any token.

4daf8f9e-acb0-44a7-91f7-1304b03f65c8.title: LEVELDB
4daf8f9e-acb0-44a7-91f7-1304b03f65c8.body: A lightweight, fast, open-source key-value storage library designed by Google. It is used in Bitcoin to store the UTXO set and the block index. This database system was introduced in 2012 as part of the “*Ultraprune*” Pull Request aimed at replacing BerkeleyDB. This change had significant repercussions, notably an unintentional hard fork with a major reorganization of 24 blocks on March 12, 2013. This incident was detailed in BIP-0050. Subsequently, the temporary rule limiting *locks* introduced in version 0.8.1 expired on May 15, 2013, resulting in a planned hard fork.

4de7f805-d965-4703-a67a-06df5cafc8b9.title: BATCHED SPENDING
4de7f805-d965-4703-a67a-06df5cafc8b9.body:
Spending technique used mainly by entities with a high transaction volume, such as exchange platforms, to optimize and reduce transaction costs. By grouping several payments intended for different recipients into a single Bitcoin transaction, batched spending consumes less space in blocks, which reduces the associated fees. Batched spending is distinguished by a pattern that is easily recognizable during chain analysis. This pattern shows up as the use of a few UTXOs as inputs (often just one) and the creation of multiple UTXOs as outputs. The interpretation of this pattern is that we are looking at batched spending. Faced with this pattern in chain analysis, one can deduce that the input UTXO comes from a company with substantial economic activity and that the output UTXOs will disperse. Some will belong to the company's customers. Others will perhaps go to partner companies. Finally, there will certainly be a change output that returns to the issuing company.

![Example of batched spending: one UTXO of 570,000 sats as input, five outputs of varying sizes totaling the balance.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/b/batched-spending/assets/image-1.png)

4e78aadf-b3e1-45b7-8ea6-7028e10ff548.title: BITCOIND.PID
4e78aadf-b3e1-45b7-8ea6-7028e10ff548.body: A file generated by the bitcoind software (Bitcoin Daemon) while it is running. This file contains the process identifier (PID) of the running bitcoind instance. It is used to track and manage the software's process, allowing other applications or scripts to easily identify it and interact with it if necessary.

4e8f361d-9db1-453f-96de-bb9be5e746b9.title: VARIANCE
4e8f361d-9db1-453f-96de-bb9be5e746b9.body:
In the context of mining, designates the fluctuations in a miner's income due to the probabilistic nature of the search for valid blocks. Even with constant computing power, the time needed to find a block can vary considerably. Consequently, miners can go through long periods without receiving rewards, followed by periods of substantial gains.

Mining pools are designed to reduce this variance. By pooling the computing power of many individual hashers, pools increase the frequency at which blocks are found, which allows a more regular and predictable distribution of rewards. The variance is thus said to be reduced.

Variance is an inherent flaw of Bitcoin's proof-of-work mechanism that pushes toward the grouping of mining.

4ea626f7-7f38-4581-b65a-0390b89fbc6c.title: NODL
4ea626f7-7f38-4581-b65a-0390b89fbc6c.body: A company founded in late 2018 that designs turnkey Bitcoin and Lightning Network nodes, in the form of ready-to-use hardware boxes. Nodl was the first manufacturer to integrate BTCPay Server, to enforce Tor by default on all its devices, and to offer full disk encryption with a physical security switch (*kill switch*). The company also offers nodl Cloud, an infrastructure service hosted in its own data centers (Paris, Geneva, Zurich) for individuals and businesses who want to run nodes without managing the hardware.

4eb80ccd-11e0-45cc-ad72-32065d22601a.title: BITCOINTALK
4eb80ccd-11e0-45cc-ad72-32065d22601a.body: An online forum dedicated to discussions about Bitcoin. Opened in November 2009 by Satoshi Nakamoto, this forum takes over from the Bitcoin discussion space on sourceforge.net. It acquired its name during the migration from bitcoin.org to bitcointalk.org in August 2011. BitcoinTalk serves as a platform for the exchange of information, news, technical debates and analyses.

4edf1356-22ff-4c2a-b7af-a317d5ed11ff.title: BLIP-0004
4edf1356-22ff-4c2a-b7af-a317d5ed11ff.body: A bLIP that proposes an experimental HTLC endorsement signaling mechanism (*endorsement*) to fight *channel jamming* attacks on the Lightning Network. Each HTLC carries a one-byte TLV field indicating whether it is endorsed (value 7) or not (value 0). Originating nodes mark as endorsed the payments they expect to succeed. Intermediate nodes propagate the positive signal if they are compatible, otherwise they forward the default value of zero. This mechanism is purely observational: the collected data is used to test reputation algorithms without affecting the actual routing of payments. The experiment is limited in time by an expiration date, after which nodes stop relaying the signal.

4eeab84e-7cb7-4de4-a3c4-ca35565fed65.title: ENTROPY
4eeab84e-7cb7-4de4-a3c4-ca35565fed65.body:
Entropy, in the context of cryptography and information, is a quantitative measure of the uncertainty or unpredictability associated with a data source or a random process. Entropy plays a crucial role in the security of cryptographic systems, notably in the generation of keys and random numbers. High entropy guarantees that the generated keys are sufficiently unpredictable and resistant to brute-force attacks, where an attacker tries all possible combinations to guess the key. 

In the context of Bitcoin, entropy is used to generate private keys or seeds. When creating a deterministic and hierarchical wallet, the mnemonic phrase is built from a random number, itself derived from an entropy source. The phrase is then used to generate several private keys, in a deterministic and hierarchical manner, in order to create spending conditions on UTXOs. 

It is essential to have a quality entropy source to guarantee the security of cryptographic systems. Entropy sources can be physical processes, such as electronic noise or thermal variations, or software processes, such as pseudo-random number generators.

4efe0522-8f70-4263-abbd-5ad6116c3d46.title: POLAR
4efe0522-8f70-4263-abbd-5ad6116c3d46.body: Local simulation tool for the Lightning Network intended for development and testing. Developed by Jamal James, Polar makes it possible to quickly create a complete Lightning network on your computer, with several interconnected LND, CLN or Eclair nodes, without needing real bitcoins or a connection to the Bitcoin network. The graphical interface makes it possible to visualize channels, send test payments, and simulate different routing scenarios, which makes it a valuable tool for developers of Lightning applications.

4f4c25e7-bf0c-41a2-b8f7-11341d8ba687.title: MINER
4f4c25e7-bf0c-41a2-b8f7-11341d8ba687.body:
In the context of Bitcoin, a miner refers to a person who operates a mine, that is, a computer engaged in the mining process, which consists of participating in the proof-of-work (*Proof-of-Work*). The miner groups the pending transactions in their mempool to form a candidate block. Then, they search for a valid hash, less than or equal to the target, for the header of this block by modifying the various nonces. If they find a valid hash, they broadcast their block to the Bitcoin network and collect the associated monetary reward, made up of the block subsidy (creation of new bitcoins ex nihilo) and transaction fees.

*In the specific context of mining pools, the role of miner is sometimes distinguished from the role of hasher, given that the individual hashers who take part in the pooling only have to hash and do not take part in the complete process of the mine.*

4fa3adb9-bcc7-4060-8651-92087845e167.title: ANCHOR OUTPUTS
4fa3adb9-bcc7-4060-8651-92087845e167.body: A proposal that aims to improve the management of transaction fees in Lightning channels. At each state change in a Lightning channel, the stakeholders create and sign a new commitment transaction that reflects the new distribution of funds within the channel. The problem with this mechanism lies in determining the transaction fees at the time of its creation. Indeed, transaction fees on the Bitcoin network are subject to strong fluctuations, both upward and downward. If the fees set for the last commitment transaction are insufficient at the time of the unilateral closing of the channel, not only will the transaction take a considerable time to confirm, but the time-locking mechanisms (*timelocks*) could also allow funds to be stolen. *Anchor outputs* make it possible to reserve a small portion of the funds in a commitment transaction to cover future fees. In the event of network congestion and rising fees, *anchor outputs* make it possible to modify the transaction fees after the commitment transaction has been created, thus ensuring a sufficiently fast closing of the Lightning channel.

4fb11b8b-b258-49fa-b451-c01ab0bcb9a1.title: OWNED STATE
4fb11b8b-b258-49fa-b451-c01ab0bcb9a1.body: Within the RGB protocol, the Owned State designates the portion of the Contract State encapsulated in an Assignment and explicitly associated with a particular holder by means of a Single-use Seal pointing to a UTXO. This component represents, for example, a digital asset or a specific contractual right assigned to an individual. By isolating the state linked to each holder, the Owned State guarantees precise and secure management of ownership within RGB smart contracts.

500b92ea-4ac3-4baf-9554-3dedcd375448.title: BIRTH DATE
500b92ea-4ac3-4baf-9554-3dedcd375448.body: Refers to the date on which a wallet was created. This information is important when restoring a wallet, because it lets the software know from which block it must start searching for the transactions associated with that wallet. By knowing the birth date, the software can efficiently synchronize and recover the transaction history without having to scan the entire blockchain from the Genesis block.

501e3e0a-3d9d-447b-82be-991828b5f05e.title: KYC - KNOW YOUR CUSTOMER

502bca8f-c772-4aad-b397-4816442dfa1b.title: DDOS
502bca8f-c772-4aad-b397-4816442dfa1b.body: A form of DOS where the attack comes from multiple sources simultaneously, making defense more complex. Attackers often use networks of computers infected with malware (botnets) to launch massive requests against a single target. This strategy multiplies the effectiveness of the attack by overloading the capacities of the targeted system in order to cause service interruptions.

502e0bc6-b7e4-45ff-bb32-9f726b0a0047.title: SPARROW WALLET
502e0bc6-b7e4-45ff-bb32-9f726b0a0047.body: A Bitcoin wallet software for desktop computers (Windows, macOS, Linux), designed for users who want complete control over their Bitcoin transactions. Sparrow supports most of the *hardware wallets* on the market via PSBT, multisig, *coin control*, *labelling*... It allows connection to one's own Bitcoin node (Bitcoin Core or Electrum server) for sovereign verification of transactions, but can also work with a public server. The software is open source.

50cdd548-de34-4977-94b7-72a847943add.title: BOLTZMANN SCORE
50cdd548-de34-4977-94b7-72a847943add.body:
Indicator used to evaluate the level of privacy of a Bitcoin transaction. The Boltzmann score is based on the number of possible interpretations of a transaction, that is, the number of plausible combinations between the *inputs* and the *outputs*.

The principle is inspired by the statistical physics of Ludwig Boltzmann: the more possible combinations (of microstates) a transaction admits, the higher its entropy, and the harder it is to analyze. The score is generally expressed in bits of entropy. A transaction with a score of 0 bits has only one possible interpretation (each *input* is clearly linked to an *output*). Conversely, a well-constructed *coinjoin* can reach a high score, because the multiple *inputs* and *outputs* of identical amounts generate a very large number of possible combinations.

This score allows users to objectively evaluate the effectiveness of a *coinjoin* or of any transaction in terms of privacy.

50da12ce-4191-4b06-ad63-26b5b1196f90.title: BACKDOOR
50da12ce-4191-4b06-ad63-26b5b1196f90.body:
A *backdoor* is a secret mechanism that provides privileged access to a computer system, software, a function, an algorithm or data, without going through the usual authentication or security procedures. Unlike a security flaw, backdoors are intentionally introduced into the source code by malicious developers. They can be used to spy on, manipulate or steal sensitive information.

*The term "porte dérobée" is rarely used in French. The English term "backdoor" is generally preferred.*

51015851-5323-43ca-8d32-c7c1c1d9847f.title: BLIND SIGNATURE
51015851-5323-43ca-8d32-c7c1c1d9847f.body:
Chaum's blind signatures are a form of digital signature in which the issuer of a signature does not know the content of the message they are signing. But the signature can then be verified against the original message. This technique was developed by the cryptographer David Chaum in 1983.

Take the example of a company wishing to have a confidential document, such as a contract, authenticated without revealing its content. The company applies a blinding process that cryptographically transforms the original document in a reversible way. This modified document is sent to a certification authority, which affixes a blind signature without knowing the underlying content. After receiving the signed blinded document, the company unblinds the signature. The result is an original document authenticated by the authority's signature, without the authority ever having seen the original content.

Chaum's blind signatures therefore make it possible to certify the authenticity of a document without knowing its content, which guarantees both the confidentiality of the user's data and the integrity of the signed document.

On Bitcoin, this protocol is found in Chaumian bank systems built as overlays (Cashu, Fedimint...), but above all in Chaumian coinjoin protocols, in order to ensure that the coordinator is not able to link an input to an output.

5108d669-f96f-40dc-815e-5665bdf5848f.title: OP_CHECKSIG - 0XAC
5108d669-f96f-40dc-815e-5665bdf5848f.body: Verifies the validity of a signature against a given public key. It takes the two items at the top of the stack: the signature and the public key, and evaluates whether the signature is correct for the transaction hash and the specified public key. If the verification succeeds, it pushes the value `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise `0` (false). This opcode was modified in Tapscript in order to verify Schnorr signatures.

5118f3a7-1b37-456f-9347-adf42a6e87dd.title: MERGE
5118f3a7-1b37-456f-9347-adf42a6e87dd.body: In the context of Git, represents the action of integrating the changes from one branch into another, typically bringing the developments of a secondary branch back into the main branch. This operation makes it possible to combine the commit histories of the branches concerned and to resolve any conflicts in order to maintain the integrity of the software.

514096e6-7730-4652-aaba-e7523dc3e8e1.title: BLOCK HEIGHT
514096e6-7730-4652-aaba-e7523dc3e8e1.body: Refers to the sequence number of a particular block relative to the first block, known as the "Genesis block", which is indexed at height zero. This indicator gives us the number of blocks that precede the block under study. For example, if a block is at height 650,000, it means that there are 650,000 blocks preceding it. Block height is used to identify a specific block within the blockchain. Contrary to a widespread belief, block height does not determine which chain is valid, because nodes synchronize on the chain that has accumulated the most work, and not on the longest chain.

514bb0cd-4077-47fd-819e-38cee5e5658f.title: BIP-0148
514bb0cd-4077-47fd-819e-38cee5e5658f.body: Proposal introduced in March 2017 by a developer under the pseudonym Shaolin Fry. The goal of BIP-0148 was to force the activation of the SegWit upgrade on the Bitcoin protocol, in the face of stagnating signaling of this soft fork by miners via the BIP-0009 method. BIP-0148 suggested implementing a UASF (*User-Activated Soft Fork*) to forcibly activate SegWit by nodes on November 15, 2017, if miners had not locked in SegWit by August 1, 2017. Had the BIP-0148 UASF been adopted, Bitcoin network nodes would have rejected blocks that did not signal support for SegWit, thereby putting pressure on miners to adopt the upgrade. Although this historical BIP was ultimately not activated, it played a decisive role in the successful adoption of SegWit, by compelling miners to lock in the soft fork via BIP-0091. In the longer term, BIP-0148 set an important precedent, demonstrating the influence that users can exert through their full nodes on Bitcoin protocol governance decisions.

514f838b-ca24-4319-8595-508adb708d7f.title: 51% ATTACK
514f838b-ca24-4319-8595-508adb708d7f.body:
A hypothetical scenario on the Bitcoin system in which a malicious actor controls more than 50% of the total mining computing power (*hashrate*). With such dominance, the attacker can manipulate the consensus process, enabling malicious actions such as double spending, where the same bitcoins are spent a first time on a chain that is ultimately made obsolete, then a second time on the valid chain. Another goal of a 51% attack is transaction censorship. However, carrying out a 51% attack requires considerable financial, human, energy, and technical resources, and makes the malicious actor liable to be discovered before the attack takes place. Although theoretically possible, a 51% attack on Bitcoin is considered very unlikely due to the decentralization of mining and the large amount of computing power currently deployed.

*This attack is also called the "Goldfinger Attack".*

5169d872-cb3e-4bad-a934-6a448abaf1ca.title: SATSCARD
5169d872-cb3e-4bad-a934-6a448abaf1ca.body: Bearer NFC card manufactured by Coinkite. The Satscard makes it possible to physically transfer bitcoins from hand to hand without an on-chain transaction at the time of the exchange. It contains 10 independent *slots*, each associated with a private key and a unique address: the bitcoins are loaded onto a *slot*, then "unsealed" by the recipient using a PIN code and a compatible application such as Nunchuk.

519cf3cf-6899-4f02-91a3-fa7fcde2d76f.title: OUTPUT SCRIPT DESCRIPTORS
519cf3cf-6899-4f02-91a3-fa7fcde2d76f.body:
Output script descriptors, or simply descriptors, are structured expressions that fully describe an output script (`scriptPubKey`) and provide all the information needed to track transactions to or from a particular script. These descriptors make key management easier in HD wallets thanks to a standard description of the structure and the types of addresses used.

The main value of descriptors lies in their ability to encapsulate all the information essential to restoring a wallet in a single string of characters (in addition to the recovery phrase). By backing up a descriptor with the corresponding mnemonic phrases, it is possible to restore not only the private keys, but also the precise structure of the wallet and the associated script parameters. Indeed, recovering a wallet requires not only knowledge of the initial seed, but also the specific indexes for the derivation of the child key pairs, as well as the `xpub` of each factor in the case of a multisig wallet. In the past, it was assumed that this information was implicitly known to everyone. However, with the diversification of scripts and the emergence of more complex configurations, this information could become difficult to extrapolate, thus turning this data into private information that is hard to brute-force. Using descriptors greatly simplifies the process: it is enough to know the recovery phrase or phrases and the corresponding descriptor to restore everything reliably and securely.

A descriptor is made up of several elements:
* Script functions such as `pk` (Pay-to-PubKey), `pkh` (Pay-to-PubKey-Hash), `wpkh` (Pay-to-Witness-PubKey-Hash), `sh` (Pay-to-Script-Hash), `wsh` (Pay-to-Witness-Script-Hash), `tr` (Pay-to-Taproot), `multi` (Multisignature) and `sortedmulti` (Multisignature with sorted keys);
* Derivation paths, for example `[d34db33f/44h/0h/0h]` which indicates a derived path and a specific master key fingerprint;
* Keys in various formats such as public keys in hexadecimal or extended public keys (`xpub`);
* A checksum, preceded by a hash sign, to verify the integrity of the descriptor.

For example, a descriptor for a P2WPKH wallet might look like:

```text
wpkh([cdeab12f/84h/0h/0h]xpub6CUGRUonZSQ4TWtTMmzXdrXDtyPWKiKbERr4d5qkSmh5h17C1TjvMt7DJ9Qve4dRxm91CDv6cNfKsq2mK1rMsJKhtRUPZz7MQtp3y6atC1U/<0;1>/*)#jy0l7nr4
```

In this descriptor, the derivation function `wpkh` indicates a Pay-to-Witness-Public-Key-Hash script type. It is followed by the derivation path which contains:
* `cdeab12f`: the master key fingerprint;
* `84h`: which means the use of a BIP-0084 purpose, intended for SegWit v0 addresses;
* `0h`: which indicates that it is a BTC currency on the mainnet;
* `0h`: which refers to the specific account number used in the wallet.

The descriptor also includes the extended public key used on this wallet: 

```text
xpub6CUGRUonZSQ4TWtTMmzXdrXDtyPWKiKbERr4d5qkSmh5h17C1TjvMt7DJ9Qve4dRxm91CDv6cNfKsq2mK1rMsJKhtRUPZz7MQtp3y6atC1U
```

Next, the notation `/<0;1>/*` specifies that the descriptor can generate addresses from the external chain (`0`) and internal chain (`1`), with a wildcard (`*`) allowing the sequential derivation of several addresses in a configurable manner, similar to the management of a "gap limit" on conventional wallet software.

Finally, `#jy0l7nr4` represents the checksum used to verify the integrity of the descriptor.

51cb62fd-2d57-4f64-8d3e-6b8c6bb85dbe.title: BIP-0152
51cb62fd-2d57-4f64-8d3e-6b8c6bb85dbe.body: "*Compact Block Relay*" proposal aimed at reducing the bandwidth required for transmitting blocks on the Bitcoin network. Adopted in November 2016 in version 0.13.0 of Bitcoin Core, this protocol makes it possible to communicate block information in a compact manner, based on the assumption that nodes already have a large part of the transactions of a recent block in their mempool. Rather than transmitting each transaction in full, which would be redundant, BIP-0152 proposes sending only short identifiers for the transactions already known to peers, accompanied by a few selected transactions (notably the coinbase transaction and those that the node is likely not to know). The node can then ask its peers for any missing transactions. Compact Block Relay thus reduces the amount of data exchanged during block propagation, which in turn reduces bandwidth spikes and improves the overall efficiency of the network.

520d62da-058e-4370-828d-721044c82254.title: PACKAGE RELAY
520d62da-058e-4370-828d-721044c82254.body:
Improvement to Bitcoin's relay protocol that allows nodes to transmit and evaluate groups of interdependent transactions collectively, rather than processing them individually. Without this mechanism, a parent transaction whose fee rate is too low to be accepted into the mempool is rejected, which prevents any child transaction from being used for CPFP (*Child Pays For Parent*), since the parent is needed for its validation.

This problem is particularly critical for time-constrained protocols such as the Lightning Network, where transactions are signed well before they are broadcast. The minimum fee rate accepted by a node depends on the content of its mempool at a given moment; a parent transaction that was previously eligible for CPFP may therefore no longer be so at the time of its broadcast.

*Package relay* solves this problem by evaluating the combined fee rate of a parent-child set. The current implementation in Bitcoin Core focuses on a variant limited to one parent and one child (1p1c), which does not require a modification of the P2P protocol. BIP-0331 formalizes the more general specification of ancestor package relay. The main development challenge lies in preventing denial-of-service vulnerabilities.

This mechanism is complementary to *anchor outputs* and constitutes an important countermeasure against transaction pinning (*transaction pinning*) attacks.

52153b66-22fb-4e2f-8176-5532f4335ab3.title: LNURL
52153b66-22fb-4e2f-8176-5532f4335ab3.body:
Communication protocol that specifies a set of features designed to simplify interactions between Lightning nodes and clients, as well as third-party applications. This protocol is based on HTTP and allows creating links for various operations, such as a payment request, a withdrawal request, or other features that improve the user experience. Each LNURL is a URL encoded in bech32 with the prefix `lnurl`, which, once scanned, triggers a series of automatic actions on the Lightning wallet.

For example, the LNURL-withdraw feature (LUD-03) allows withdrawing funds from a service by scanning a QR code, without needing to manually generate an *invoice*. Or again, LNURL-auth (LUD-04) allows logging in to online services by using a private key on one's Lightning wallet instead of a password.

521cec31-764c-4aba-8aea-0b71b1615a42.title: BIP-0371
521cec31-764c-4aba-8aea-0b71b1615a42.body: Adds Taproot-specific fields to the PSBT format (BIP-0174). These fields include the internal key (*internal key*), the Merkle path (*Merkle path*) of the scripts, Schnorr signatures, and the Taproot script leaves (*tap leaf scripts*). This extension is necessary so that hardware wallets and multisig coordinators can properly construct, verify and sign Taproot transactions via the PSBT format.

522111d1-498f-428c-a329-c9470e0d70e8.title: NYA - NEW YORK AGREEMENT
522111d1-498f-428c-a329-c9470e0d70e8.body:
Private meeting held in 2017, bringing together more than 50 companies from the Bitcoin ecosystem, following the Consensus 2017 conference. The goal of this meeting was to end the long-standing debate on Bitcoin scaling by reaching an agreement. From this meeting came the SegWit2x proposal, drawing on the earlier SegWit2Mb proposal. It provided for two major changes to the Bitcoin protocol: 
* The adoption of SegWit with an activation threshold set at 80 percent of signaling;
* A hard fork intended to increase the maximum block size from 1 MB to 2 MB.

Despite positive signaling from more than 80% of miners, the project failed to rally sufficient consensus, leading to its abandonment. This event was interpreted by many users and developers as an attempt to attack Bitcoin.

52579519-4ed4-4e4b-addf-40ef24b17943.title: MIT DCI
52579519-4ed4-4e4b-addf-40ef24b17943.body: A research program of the MIT Media Lab devoted to digital currencies and distributed ledger technologies. Founded in April 2015, this initiative was the first academic group exclusively dedicated to Bitcoin. Its creation came at a time when the Bitcoin Foundation, until then the main source of funding for development, was facing financial difficulties. The DCI funds developers and researchers who work on Bitcoin Core and on the security of the protocol. It thus joins other organizations such as Chaincode Labs, Blockstream or Spiral in supporting the open source development of Bitcoin.

529b3c87-6334-44b1-9869-6c8a90c76926.title: PHOENIXD
529b3c87-6334-44b1-9869-6c8a90c76926.body: Specialized implementation of a Lightning node, designed to send and receive payments from a server. Phoenixd uses the same software as the Phoenix mobile wallet/node, but unlike the latter, which is exclusively intended for smartphones, phoenixd is able to run on a server as a *daemon*. Instead of having a graphical user interface (GUI), it is equipped with an HTTP API interface and handles automatic management of channels and liquidity. Phoenixd is a project developed and maintained by the French company ACINQ.

529f418f-23c0-45ff-b320-abb8588e558d.title: GRIEFING ATTACK
529f418f-23c0-45ff-b320-abb8588e558d.body:
Attack on the Lightning Network in which a malicious actor saturates one or more payment channels with HTLCs that never resolve, by refusing to reveal the payment preimage. The victims' funds end up frozen for the entire duration of the timelock, without the attacker stealing anything.

Each channel can only hold 483 pending HTLCs per direction. An attacker can therefore completely block a channel with a relatively small number of fake payments. The victim's only option is to force close the channel, which incurs high on-chain fees since each pending HTLC generates an additional transaction on the chain.

Although the attacker obtains no direct monetary gain, they can derive an indirect benefit by paralyzing competing routes to capture more routing fees, or by demanding a ransom to stop the attack. This vulnerability remains an open problem. The proposed countermeasures include the HTLC-GP protocol, which requires each participant to lock a financial penalty that victims can recover in the event of griefing, as well as upfront payment mechanisms.

52a526bf-bdc8-4abf-b48e-17398368f6a9.title: SO - SPARK OPERATOR
52a526bf-bdc8-4abf-b48e-17398368f6a9.body:
An individual node within the *Spark Entity* (SE), participating in the threshold signing protocol that secures *off-chain* transfers in Spark. Each SO holds a fragment of the SE's key share, without ever possessing the complete key on its own. The set of SOs (or a threshold of them) cooperate via the FROST protocol to co-sign transactions and to refresh key shares during ownership transfers.

SOs also play a *watchtower* role: they monitor the Bitcoin blockchain to detect any fraudulent exit attempts by former owners.

If an SO is unavailable, transfers may be temporarily blocked, but users retain the ability to exit unilaterally to the main layer. At the launch of Spark, two operators (Lightspark and Flashnet) make up the SE, with the aim of widening the number of operators across various jurisdictions in order to spread the risk.

52a7059d-34ea-4cf4-a848-77b56952d004.title: GUISETTINGS.INI.BAK
52a7059d-34ea-4cf4-a848-77b56952d004.body: File in Bitcoin Core used to store a backup of the graphical user interface (GUI) settings. This backup is created when using the `-resetguisettings` option, which resets the GUI settings to their default values. This file allows the user to retroactively inspect their old configurations in order to diagnose any problems related to the GUI settings.

5319c967-bf2e-4045-9e80-4370247365e2.title: BMM - BLIND MERGED MINING
5319c967-bf2e-4045-9e80-4370247365e2.body: A sidechain consensus technique allowing Bitcoin miners to work simultaneously on the main chain and on one or more sidechains, without having to provide more computational work. Unlike classic merged mining, this method does not require setting up a new node for each sidechain being mined. Within the framework of *Blind Merged Mining* (BMM), each sidechain is managed by independent node operators, responsible for creating blocks and collecting the associated rewards on the sidechain.
