In return, these operators must buy Proof-of-Work from the miners of the main blockchain in order to validate their blocks on the sidechain. Thus, Bitcoin miners receive their merged mining rewards from the sidechains in BTC, directly on the main chain. This method, developed by Paul Sztorc for drivechains, requires the implementation of BIP-0301 to be operational on the Bitcoin network.

5345a3e9-f01f-44f4-abb5-a692f9c25f9f.title: SIMPLE PAYMENT
5345a3e9-f01f-44f4-abb5-a692f9c25f9f.body:
Transaction *pattern* (or model) used in chain analysis, characterized by the consumption of one or more UTXOs as inputs and the production of 2 UTXOs as outputs. This model will therefore look like this:

![Simple payment: an input of 50,000 sats produces two outputs, one to the recipient and the other returning as change.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/p/paiement-simple/assets/image-1.png)

This simple payment model indicates that we are likely in the presence of a sending or payment transaction. The user has consumed their own UTXO as inputs to satisfy, as outputs, a payment UTXO and a change UTXO (change returning to the same user). We therefore know that the observed user is likely no longer in possession of one of the two UTXOs in outputs (the payment one), but that they are still in possession of the other UTXO (the change one).

535f78ca-4343-4d55-81f8-e4a0f19a36a1.title: BITCOIN CLASSIC
535f78ca-4343-4d55-81f8-e4a0f19a36a1.body: Protocol fork proposal launched in January 2016 following the abandonment of Bitcoin XT. It aimed to increase the block size limit from 1 MB to 2 MB with BIP-0109, an approach considered more moderate compared to Bitcoin XT, which proposed a much larger increase (8 MB + doubling every 2 years). This initiative was led by developers Gavin Andresen and Jeff Garzik, and had the backing of major companies in the ecosystem such as Coinbase. Bitcoin Classic appeared in a context of sharp intensification of the Blocksize War and was classed in the big blockers camp. Although Bitcoin Classic attracted the attention and support of many players in the sector, its activation mechanism, which required the support of 75% of miners, was controversial and ultimately contributed to its failure.

538faf8a-9d12-4cb7-ae82-979e654005ce.title: SOFT FORK
538faf8a-9d12-4cb7-ae82-979e654005ce.body: A modification of the protocol rules in a backward-compatible way. Unlike a hard fork, a soft fork does not result in the Bitcoin node network splitting into two distinct groups, provided that a majority of the computing power is on the updated chain. If all goes well, nodes with the update and nodes without the update therefore remain on the same blockchain. A modification is backward-compatible when it adds certain protocol rules or makes them more restrictive.

54025d93-966c-474f-b652-cb8c5d13e2fc.title: CHAIN CODE
54025d93-966c-474f-b652-cb8c5d13e2fc.body:
In the context of hierarchical deterministic (HD) derivation of Bitcoin wallets, the chain code is a 256-bit cryptographic salt value used to generate child keys from a parent key, according to the BIP-0032 standard. The chain code is used in combination with the parent key and the index of the child to deterministically generate a new key pair (private key and public key) without revealing the parent key or the other derived child keys. 

There is therefore a unique chain code for each key pair. The chain code is obtained either by hashing the wallet seed, and taking the right half of the bits. In this case, we speak of a master chain code, associated with the master private key. Or, it can be obtained by hashing a parent key with its parent chain code and an index, then keeping the right bits. We then speak of a child chain code. 

It is impossible to derive keys without knowing the chain code associated with each parent pair. It makes it possible to introduce pseudo-random data into the derivation process to ensure that the generation of cryptographic keys remains unpredictable for attackers while being deterministic for the holder of the wallet.

541e12ba-975f-4c95-a040-2fc8b8a3b636.title: GREEN ADDRESSES
541e12ba-975f-4c95-a040-2fc8b8a3b636.body: Old Bitcoin address proposal in which the transactions issued from the address are pre-approved by a trusted third party. This concept allows parties receiving funds via this address to consider them immediately reliable, without waiting for them to be included in a block. It relies on the trust placed in the service that controls the *green address*, as it guarantees that the funds sent have not been and will not be double spent. This type of service was once used to speed up transactions (zero-conf), but it is no longer used today.

54290c9a-e310-4935-88b4-e9db8f100845.title: WHALE
54290c9a-e310-4935-88b4-e9db8f100845.body: Refers to an individual or entity that owns a very large quantity of bitcoins.

544bf8c2-a00d-44ca-8723-12f035bd8434.title: MINING
544bf8c2-a00d-44ca-8723-12f035bd8434.body:
The act of participating in the proof-of-work (*Proof-of-Work*) of the Bitcoin system. Proof-of-work is a mechanism for resisting Sybil attacks. It is the basis of the Nakamoto consensus mechanism, which is the principle used to establish agreement on a single version of the distributed ledger among the different nodes of the network. 

Concretely, mining is the search for a value that, once passed through a random mathematical function, gives a result below a target number. This proof-of-work target is adjusted every 2016 blocks by the nodes. This is what is called the difficulty adjustment. The target number is lowered to increase the mining difficulty, or raised to decrease the difficulty, depending on the change in the computing power deployed by miners during the previous period. 

![Search for the nonce that produces, via SHA256d on the header, a hash below the target adjusted every 2016 blocks.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/m/minage/assets/image-1.png)

This work done by miners is rewarded with each valid block found. The winning miner collects a monetary reward, made up of the block subsidy (creation of new bitcoins ex nihilo) and transaction fees. Today, the difficulty of proof-of-work on Bitcoin is such that mining requires a great deal of computing power to manage to win blocks. As a result, it is often necessary to have electronic chips specialized in executing `SHA256d`, called ASICs, and to participate in mining pools.

545965f5-6f8f-425c-a7a6-3af64e4ee35a.title: OPENNODE
545965f5-6f8f-425c-a7a6-3af64e4ee35a.body: A bitcoin payment processing platform. OpenNode provides an API that allows merchants and developers to accept bitcoin payments, both on the main chain and via the Lightning Network. The platform offers checkout pages, billing links and integration tools. Merchants using this service can choose to receive their funds in bitcoin or directly in fiat currency in their bank account. Note that OpenNode is not a *self-custody* payment terminal, unlike BTCPayServer for example.

545f74d5-7598-45a0-92db-364c50fd576a.title: ON-CHAIN
545f74d5-7598-45a0-92db-364c50fd576a.body: Refers to transactions recorded directly on the Bitcoin blockchain. This term is the opposite of “*off-chain*”, which refers to operations that are more or less linked with the Bitcoin blockchain, but that take place outside the main blockchain.

54e333a5-0593-4f6e-96e0-9a1cf3aa0344.title: GCS - GOLOMB-CODED SET
54e333a5-0593-4f6e-96e0-9a1cf3aa0344.body:
Probabilistic data structure used in BIP-0158 to build *compact block filters* on Bitcoin. A GCS makes it possible to test whether an element belongs to a set, with the guarantee of finding any element that is present, but with a false positive probability of `1/M`.

The construction of a GCS takes place in several steps: the raw elements are first hashed with SipHash into 64-bit integers uniformly distributed over the range `[0, N \times M)`. The resulting values are sorted, then the differences between consecutive values are encoded using Golomb-Rice coding. This coding exploits the natural geometric distribution of the gaps to achieve near-optimal compression: each difference is decomposed into a quotient (encoded in unary) and a remainder (encoded on `P` bits).

Compared to the Bloom filters used in BIP-0037, the GCS produces more compact filters for the same false positive rate. In exchange, the membership test requires sequentially decompressing the filter, which prevents constant-time queries. This structure was chosen for *compact block filters* with the parameters `P = 19` and `M = 784\,931`.

54fa63b4-37b6-4c42-a565-67457e66f08f.title: ANCESTOR MINING
54fa63b4-37b6-4c42-a565-67457e66f08f.body: Another name sometimes given to CPFP (*Child-Pay-For-Parent*). Ancestor mining is the principle whereby a miner does not choose a transaction solely on the basis of its own transaction fees, but also takes into account the fees of the ancestor transactions.

54ffa6e6-72b7-4b49-b7f4-33cce80986f2.title: ONION SERVICE
54ffa6e6-72b7-4b49-b7f4-33cce80986f2.body:
A service hosted on the Tor network, accessible only via an `.onion` address, without exposing the server's IP address. Formerly called “*hidden service*”, the official term was renamed “*onion service*” by the Tor project. The server and the client communicate through Tor circuits, so that neither knows the IP address of its counterpart.

An onion service works by publishing introduction points (*introduction points*) in the Tor network's distributed hash table. The client then chooses a rendezvous point (*rendezvous point*) and communicates it to the service via an introduction point. The client and the server each build a Tor circuit to this rendezvous point, in order to establish a mutual connection without any data passing in the clear over the internet.

In the context of Bitcoin, many Bitcoin Core and Lightning nodes expose an onion service to accept incoming connections anonymously. This allows a node operator to participate in the P2P network without revealing their IP address or their location, which strengthens the censorship resistance and privacy of the infrastructure.

554c8c88-3d2a-4b99-8595-c28eed7045e4.title: STATE EXTENSION
554c8c88-3d2a-4b99-8595-c28eed7045e4.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, a *State Extension* refers to a contractual operation that makes it possible to initiate an update of a contract's state through the redemption of previously declared *Valencies*. This procedure exploits a public right written into the contract to trigger a modification, which only becomes effective after being closed by a *State Transition*. The latter incorporates the definitive update of the contract's state.

55c580b4-a44c-42fa-9416-7675911ef15f.title: ROUND PAYMENT
55c580b4-a44c-42fa-9416-7675911ef15f.body:
Internal chain analysis heuristic on Bitcoin that makes it possible to form a hypothesis about the nature of a transaction's outputs based on round amounts. In general, when faced with a simple payment *pattern* (1 or more inputs and 2 outputs), if one of the outputs spends a round amount, then it represents the payment. By elimination, if one output represents the payment, the other represents the change. It can therefore be inferred that it is likely that the user on the input side is still in possession of the output identified as the change.

It should be emphasized that this heuristic is not always applicable, since the majority of payments are still made in fiat units of account. Indeed, when a merchant in France accepts bitcoin, in general, they do not display stable prices in sats. They will rather opt for a conversion between the price in euros and the amount in bitcoins to be paid through their POS (such as BTCPay Server for example). There should therefore be no round number in the output of the transaction. Nevertheless, an analyst could attempt to perform this conversion by taking into account the exchange rate in effect when the transaction was broadcast on the network. If one day bitcoin becomes the preferred unit of account in our exchanges, this heuristic could become even more useful for analyses.

![Round payment: an input of 451,458 sats yields two outputs, including a round 200,000 sats (payment) and 248,607 (change).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/p/paiement-rond/assets/image-1.png)

56b10e68-7763-4835-b45d-6d993cc5bdfe.title: SCALABILITY
56b10e68-7763-4835-b45d-6d993cc5bdfe.body:
Refers to Bitcoin's ability to handle an increase in transaction volume while maintaining acceptable performance. Bitcoin faces inherent technical limitations, such as block size, the time interval between each block, and the fact that a transaction is only considered immutable after several confirmations. These constraints prevent Bitcoin from processing an unlimited number of transactions efficiently. When demand for block space intensifies, users are forced to increase the fees they offer so that their transactions are processed. Scalability, that is, Bitcoin's ability to handle the increase in transaction volume, can be improved either by direct changes to the protocol or by external solutions such as the Lightning Network. The question of scalability has always been at the heart of heated debates within the community. The first attempt to increase the block size dates back to October 2010 with [a patch proposed by Jeff Garzik](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=1347.0). It is this subject of scalability that notably led to the block size war between 2015 and 2017.

*The French term "scalabilité" is an anglicism. The proper French translation of the English term "scalability" is "évolutivité" or else "passage à l'échelle". However, it is generally accepted within the community to use the term "scalabilité" directly.*

571d6247-8fb4-4439-b39b-c79f06ca93b1.title: ESMPPS
571d6247-8fb4-4439-b39b-c79f06ca93b1.body: Acronym for "*Equalized Shared Maximum Pay Per Share*". It is a method of calculating miner compensation in the context of mining pools. ESMPPS aims to distribute the reward fairly among all submitted shares, regardless of when they were submitted or the pool's luck. It works essentially like SMPPS, but with an added notion of equality for the submitted shares.

57d578b1-202e-4f63-96e4-ba3819713b33.title: BIP-0352
57d578b1-202e-4f63-96e4-ba3819713b33.body:
Improvement proposal by Josibake and Ruben Somsen that introduces Silent Payments, a method for using static Bitcoin addresses to receive payments without producing address reuse, without interaction and without any visible on-chain link between the different payments. This technique eliminates the need to generate a new fresh receiving address for each transaction, which avoids the usual interactions in Bitcoin where the recipient must provide a new address to the payer.

In this system, the payer uses the recipient's public key and their own private key to generate a fresh address for each payment. Only the recipient, thanks to their private key, can compute the private key corresponding to this address. ECDH (*Elliptic-Curve Diffie-Hellman*), a cryptographic key exchange algorithm, is used to establish a shared secret that is then used to derive the receiving address and the private key (on the recipient's side only). To identify the Silent Payments intended for them, recipients must scan the blockchain and examine every transaction that matches the Silent Payments criteria. Unlike BIP-0047, which uses a notification transaction to establish the payment channel, Silent Payments remove this step, which saves one transaction. However, the tradeoff is that the recipient must scan all potential transactions to determine, by applying ECDH, whether they are addressed to them.

57e051f1-5374-4016-ac85-0b73780a4af2.title: ENDIANNESS
57e051f1-5374-4016-ac85-0b73780a4af2.body: Refers to the order in which a sequence of bytes is arranged and interpreted in computing. There are two types: "*big-endian*", where the most significant byte (the one with the highest weight) is stored first, and "*little-endian*", where the least significant byte (the one with the lowest weight) is stored first.

58295725-9bd8-4bb3-84ff-db983061c164.title: BIP-0008

58573377-41ea-451d-9ec7-910868b4cf12.title: BIP-0175
58573377-41ea-451d-9ec7-910868b4cf12.body: Description of the Pay-to-Contract (P2C) protocol allowing a contract to be committed into a public key via a cryptographic tweak. The payer modifies the recipient's public key by incorporating the hash of a contract into it, creating a new key that can only be spent by the recipient. This mechanism makes it possible to prove that a payment is linked to a specific contract without revealing the contract on the blockchain.

589b71e6-7efb-41db-9186-5ad56e686a08.title: LABELING
589b71e6-7efb-41db-9186-5ad56e686a08.body:
Practice of assigning an annotation or a label to a specific UTXO in a Bitcoin wallet. For example, if I own a UTXO coming from a P2P purchase on Bisq with Charles, I could assign it the label "`Non-KYC Bisq Charles`".

Labeling is a good practice that helps to remember the origin or the intended destination of a UTXO, thus making it easier to manage funds and optimize privacy. Labeling is all the more important when it is used with *coin control*. Indeed, by allowing users to differentiate and precisely select UTXOs for their transactions, this practice helps avoid merging UTXOs from different sources. This limits the risks associated with the CIOH (*Common Input Ownership Heuristic*) chain analysis heuristic, which can reveal the common ownership of a transaction's inputs.

58b60099-6608-4874-b8d1-32cf018233d1.title: THUNDERHUB
58b60099-6608-4874-b8d1-32cf018233d1.body: An open source web interface for managing and monitoring Lightning Network nodes based on LND. The tool makes it possible to manage payment channels, send and receive on-chain and Lightning payments, rebalance liquidity and consult detailed reports on the node's activity.

58ea6784-71a5-4c24-a2b1-0ace80de605b.title: BITCOIN - CAPITAL B

5943e2ea-e9c7-40ac-9682-25b86b66e4fb.title: BIP-0071
5943e2ea-e9c7-40ac-9682-25b86b66e4fb.body: Defines a MIME (*Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions*) media type, in accordance with the RFC 2046 standard, for the bitcoin payment request messages in BIP-0070. MIME is an Internet standard that extends the format of electronic messages to allow various types of data to be sent in a structured way. In BIP-0071, the adoption of a specific MIME type for payment messages ensures that wallet software, when sending payment protocol messages by e-mail or HTTP, complies with Internet standards for proper message encapsulation. Since this improvement is bundled with BIP-0070, it was never widely adopted.

5944742e-7018-406c-b3d5-4634f5a86320.title: BLIP-0025
5944742e-7018-406c-b3d5-4634f5a86320.body: bLIP that allows the second-to-last hop of a Lightning route to forward an HTLC of a lower amount than the one encoded in the onion packet. The relay node declares the additional fees it has deducted via a new TLV field called `extra_fee`. This mechanism is mainly designed for Lightning service providers (LSPs) that open *just-in-time* channels for new users. By deducting additional fees from the first payment received, the LSP can offset the on-chain cost of opening the channel. The recipient explicitly verifies the amount of fees deducted, which prevents any abuse by the intermediate node.

59b94728-ff35-4079-bb16-7c56441469c3.title: BIP-0045
59b94728-ff35-4079-bb16-7c56441469c3.body: Proposal defining a specific BIP-0032 derivation path for deterministic P2SH multisignature wallets. The path used is `m/45'/cosigner_index/change/address_index`, where each cosigner is assigned a distinct index. This structure allows all participants to deterministically generate the same multisig addresses, without requiring additional communication after the initial exchange of extended public keys. BIP-0045 was largely superseded by BIP-0048 and BIP-0087, which offer better support for different script types.

5a7fbfe3-ae1e-4275-83b6-dc07e0c8d2fe.title: NSEQUENCE
5a7fbfe3-ae1e-4275-83b6-dc07e0c8d2fe.body: The `nSequence` field in a Bitcoin transaction input is used to indicate how that input is locked in time. Originally, it was intended to allow the dynamic replacement of transactions in mempools in order to enable an overlay payment system similar to Lightning. However, its use evolved with the introduction of the relative timelock via BIP-0068. The `nSequence` field can now specify a relative delay before a transaction is included in a block. This delay can be defined in terms of a number of blocks, or as a multiple of 512 seconds (that is, real time). Note that this new interpretation of the `nSequence` field is only valid if the `nVersion` field is greater than or equal to `2`. This interpretation of the `nSequence` field is done at the level of Bitcoin's consensus rules. Moreover, at the level of standardness rules, this field is also used for RBF signaling. If a transaction includes a `nSequence` lower than `0xfffffffe`, then it can be replaced via RBF on nodes that follow this policy.

5a9ad692-ef80-4ce8-955f-228bfb74cbf2.title: BIP-0158
5a9ad692-ef80-4ce8-955f-228bfb74cbf2.body:
Proposal that defines the structure and construction of the *compact block filters* used by the BIP-0157 protocol. The chosen format is based on *Golomb-Coded Sets* (GCS), a probabilistic structure more compact than the Bloom filters of BIP-0037.

The filter of type `basic` (`0x00`) contains, for each transaction in a block, the output scripts spent as inputs (except the coinbase) and the `scriptPubKey` of each output (except the `OP_RETURN`). The elements are hashed with SipHash (parameters `c = 2`, `d = 4`), the key being the first 16 bytes of the block hash. The hashed values are mapped into the range `[0, N \times M)`, sorted, then the successive differences are compressed by Golomb-Rice coding.

The chosen parameters are `P = 19` and `M = 784\,931`, optimized to minimize overall bandwidth by taking into account both the size of the filters and the number of blocks downloaded because of false positives. This BIP also introduces the service bit `NODE_COMPACT_FILTERS` (`1 << 6`). It was written by Olaoluwa Osuntokun and Alex Akselrod.

5aa92039-7e65-4b9b-bae6-c0a28e894208.title: CENSORSHIP RESISTANCE
5aa92039-7e65-4b9b-bae6-c0a28e894208.body:
A property of a system that makes it capable of operating without any entity being able to prevent legitimate participants from using it. In the context of Bitcoin, censorship resistance means that no government, company or individual can block a valid transaction or prohibit a user from accessing the network.

This property rests on several fundamental characteristics of Bitcoin: the decentralization of the network (thousands of nodes spread around the world), the absence of a central authority able to filter transactions, and the proof-of-work operation, which makes the inclusion of transactions depend solely on the fees offered by the sender.

Censorship resistance is considered one of Bitcoin's most important value propositions, particularly in authoritarian regimes where citizens may have their bank accounts frozen or their transactions blocked. It fundamentally distinguishes Bitcoin from centralized payment systems and CBDC projects, where an authority can decide at any time to exclude users.

5b17757c-5d22-4f59-8807-ba0dca73f3ed.title: STARK
5b17757c-5d22-4f59-8807-ba0dca73f3ed.body: A cryptographic proof system whose acronym stands for *Scalable Transparent ARgument of Knowledge*. STARKs allow a prover to demonstrate the validity of a computation to a verifier, without revealing the underlying data and without requiring an initial trust setup (*trusted setup*). This "transparency" property distinguishes them from SNARKs, which generally require a prior setup ceremony. STARKs rely on hash functions and on the FRI protocol (*Fast Reed-Solomon Interactive Oracle Proof of Proximity*), which makes them resistant to quantum attacks. In return, STARK proofs are significantly larger than SNARK proofs (on the order of several tens of kilobytes), which makes them less suited to direct on-chain verification. To work around this limitation, it is common to wrap a STARK proof inside a more compact SNARK proof before publication. This is the approach adopted by the Citrea rollup on Bitcoin, via the RISC Zero framework.

5b688ef0-b5ba-4910-a954-8eda9e3d282d.title: TRANSITION BUNDLE
5b688ef0-b5ba-4910-a954-8eda9e3d282d.body: In the RGB protocol, a *Transition Bundle* refers to a grouping of *State Transitions* belonging to the same contract, all committed simultaneously in a single Bitcoin *witness transaction*. This mechanism makes it possible to consolidate several updates or transfers into a single *on-chain* anchor point, in order to optimize the use of block space.

5baa2c1f-e52a-413e-b6fd-a07adac8e1e1.title: OP_DROP - 0X75
5baa2c1f-e52a-413e-b6fd-a07adac8e1e1.body: Removes the item at the top of the stack. `OP_DROP` makes it possible to discard data that has become useless during the execution of the script.

5bad3ca9-a431-4f76-84be-9d42413f8672.title: CHANGE AVOIDANCE
5bad3ca9-a431-4f76-84be-9d42413f8672.body:
A UTXO management strategy that consists of selecting a transaction's inputs in such a way as to eliminate or minimize the need to create a change output. The goal is to match the sum of the inputs as closely as possible to the payment amount plus the transaction fees.

The main benefit of this approach is privacy. A change output is often identifiable by chain analysis tools and provides information for tracing funds over time. By eliminating it, the information available to an outside observer is reduced, you avoid revealing information in the future via the CIOH, and you can also mislead chain analysis.

Some wallets implement this strategy automatically in their coin selection algorithm.

5bfcb45e-7a25-4a11-98b6-8bd51b1f75b5.title: BOLT-11
5bfcb45e-7a25-4a11-98b6-8bd51b1f75b5.body: Specification that defines the encoding format of Lightning payment invoices (*payment requests*), designed to be compatible with QR codes. A BOLT-11 invoice is encoded in Bech32 and consists of three parts: a human-readable prefix indicating the network and an optional amount (with multipliers `m`, `u`, `n`, `p`), a data section containing a timestamp and tagged fields (*tagged fields*), and an ECDSA signature. The tagged fields carry the payment hash, the payment secret, the description, the expiry delay, routing hints for private channels and feature flags. BOLT-11 is gradually being complemented by BOLT-12, which brings reusable invoices and better privacy.

5c147279-c4ca-4abf-9fb5-3c1b0105d7bf.title: BIP-0343
5c147279-c4ca-4abf-9fb5-3c1b0105d7bf.body: Specifies an alternative activation mechanism for the Taproot soft fork, based on BIP-0008 with the `LOT=true` parameter (mandatory activation). This BIP, proposed by Shinobius and Michael Folkson, was designed in parallel with the “Speedy Trial” deployed in Bitcoin Core, to ensure that miners could not block indefinitely the activation of a soft fork with overwhelming community consensus. The signaling period began at block 681,408 with a 90% threshold, and provided for mandatory signaling before block 760,032 if lock-in had not been reached. In practice, Taproot was locked in via Bitcoin Core's Speedy Trial at block 687,285 in June 2021 and activated in November, making BIP-0343 obsolete before its mandatory signaling phase became necessary.

5c25c54e-4f92-4a24-8091-3200624a84da.title: IOU
5c25c54e-4f92-4a24-8091-3200624a84da.body: Acronym of the English _I Owe You_ (in French “Je te dois”) used in the context of Bitcoin to refer to digital assets that are backed by underlying assets to which they should normally be pegged. This term applies in particular to *stablecoins* or to representations of BTC on systems external to Bitcoin, such as *sidechains*, *drivechains*, exchange platforms, or even ETFs. These digital assets represent a promise of value equivalent to that of the underlying asset.

5c3693c8-b0de-42d5-adb6-73850405f996.title: TAPROOT CHANNEL
5c3693c8-b0de-42d5-adb6-73850405f996.body:
A Lightning channel anchored in a Taproot output (P2TR), rather than in a classic SegWit output (P2WSH). *Taproot channels* take advantage of the improvements brought by the Taproot soft fork activated in November 2021 on Bitcoin.

In the case of a cooperative closure, a *Taproot channel* is more efficient and more private than a traditional SegWit channel: the closing transaction looks like an ordinary Taproot spend via the *key path spend*, indistinguishable from a simple on-chain payment. This property strengthens the privacy of Lightning Network users.

5c4ce78f-f055-4816-8fcd-ed6d4f0f73fe.title: CONFIDENTIAL TRANSACTIONS
5c4ce78f-f055-4816-8fcd-ed6d4f0f73fe.body:
Cryptographic protocol implemented on the Liquid network that makes it possible to hide the amounts and asset types transferred in a transaction, while still allowing network nodes to verify its validity. *Confidential Transactions* rely on Pedersen commitments (Pedersen *commitments*) to conceal the values, and on range proofs (*rangeproofs*) to guarantee that the committed amounts are positive and do not lead to illegitimate money creation.

This mechanism was proposed by Adam Back in 2013, then formalized and implemented by Gregory Maxwell. CTs have been deployed on Liquid since its launch in 2018. The first versions used Borromean ring signatures (Borromean *ring signatures*) for the range proofs, before adopting more efficient proofs such as Bulletproofs.

5c5a6b9f-4e5d-477a-9611-65883113e709.title: BIP-0121
5c5a6b9f-4e5d-477a-9611-65883113e709.body: Definition of a URI scheme complementary to BIP-0120 for proofs of payment, making it possible to trigger the generation and verification of proofs via a standardized link. The URI contained the parameters needed to identify the original transaction and initiate the proof protocol. BIP-0121 was closed at the same time as BIP-0120, these two complementary proposals never having been adopted by the ecosystem, the use cases being covered by other mechanisms.

5c9c4404-1e4c-47d7-993b-0e64dcdf7947.title: DUAL FUNDING
5c9c4404-1e4c-47d7-993b-0e64dcdf7947.body:
When opening a Lightning channel, *dual funding* allows both participants to lock bitcoins in it. Unlike the traditional model where a single node funds the channel, this method allows both parties to fund it, which makes it possible to balance its liquidity immediately.

*Dual funding* is included in version 2 of the channel construction protocol, which uses a negotiation phase. The two parties collaborate to create the funding transaction by exchanging messages to add or remove bitcoins until the transaction is finalized.

5cb70b76-85fd-4db6-b48f-fcd610e7fef8.title: NIP
5cb70b76-85fd-4db6-b48f-fcd610e7fef8.body: A technical specification that defines a feature, format or expected behavior in the Nostr protocol. NIPs play a role analogous to Bitcoin's BIPs: they are community documents that formally describe how clients and relays must implement a given feature. Each NIP has a number and covers a specific aspect of the protocol. With the exception of NIP-01, which describes the base protocol that everyone should implement, NIPs are optional and backward-compatible. A NIP can be marked as `unrecommended` when it is deprecated or replaced by a more recent specification. The official NIPs repository is maintained on GitHub and open to contributions.

5cc2000b-7d32-4e65-acd4-98087ea90a0b.title: STALE SHARE
5cc2000b-7d32-4e65-acd4-98087ea90a0b.body:
In the context of a mining pool, a stale share is a share (a portion of work) submitted by a miner after a new block has already been found, rendering the work done on the old block obsolete. This generally occurs because of network latency between the miner and the pool server: the miner keeps computing hashes on a block that is no longer current, because it has not yet received the notification of the new block.

Stale shares are rejected by the pool and are not counted in the calculation of the miner's payout. A stale share rate of around 1% is considered normal. A higher rate may indicate network connection problems, excessive latency between the miner and the pool server, or a very high hashrate that generates shares faster than the network can transmit them. To reduce the stale share rate, miners can prefer an Ethernet connection over Wi-Fi, choose a pool geographically close to their equipment, or use a mining proxy.

5cdf5d24-69b0-47c1-a25e-c929dccdcbb2.title: POW - PROOF OF WORK
5cdf5d24-69b0-47c1-a25e-c929dccdcbb2.body:
A protection mechanism against Sybil attacks, which are characterized by the multiplication of fake identities in order to gain an illegitimate advantage. Proof of work thus establishes a significant marginal cost for multiplying votes on Bitcoin. Proof of work is the foundation of Nakamoto consensus, which is the principle used to establish agreement on a single version of the ledger distributed among the various nodes of the network. Concretely, proof of work is the search for a value that, once passed through a random mathematical function, gives a result less than or equal to a target number. This proof-of-work target is adjusted every 2016 blocks by the nodes. This is what is called the difficulty adjustment. The target number is lowered to increase the mining difficulty, or raised to decrease the difficulty, depending on how the computing power deployed by miners changed over the previous period. 

![Proof of work: hashing the header with SHA256d until obtaining a hash that falls below the difficulty target.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/p/preuve-de-travail/assets/image-1.png)

This work performed by miners is rewarded for each valid block found. The winning miner collects a monetary reward, made up of the block subsidy (the creation of new bitcoins ex nihilo) and transaction fees. Today, the difficulty of proof of work on Bitcoin is such that mining requires a great deal of computing power to succeed in winning blocks. As a result, it is often necessary to have electronic chips specialized in running `SHA256d`, called ASICs, and to take part in mining pools.

5d104744-fb6a-4763-b02a-082e54874359.title: BIP-0346
5d104744-fb6a-4763-b02a-082e54874359.body: Proposes adding the opcode `OP_TXHASH` for Tapscript, which places on the stack the hash of certain selected fields of the current transaction. The choice of fields to include in the hash is determined by a *TxFieldSelector* parameter which makes it possible to specify precisely which parts of the transaction (inputs, outputs, amounts, sequences...) must be covered. Combined with `OP_CHECKSIGFROMSTACK` (BIP-0348), `OP_TXHASH` would allow a flexible form of transaction introspection and covenants, without requiring a dedicated opcode for each use case. Proposed by Steven Roose.

5d356cd7-ea19-4208-bf3c-4bfc85b8de59.title: JAM
5d356cd7-ea19-4208-bf3c-4bfc85b8de59.body: JAM is a web interface for JoinMarket focused on ease of use. JoinMarket is a coinjoin implementation on Bitcoin, but using it from the command line can intimidate beginner users. JAM was created precisely to make JoinMarket's advanced features accessible to beginners.

5d5fc17a-4b71-46a4-81d0-58a6025fcb58.title: PROOF OF STAKE
5d5fc17a-4b71-46a4-81d0-58a6025fcb58.body:
A consensus mechanism that is an alternative to proof of work, in which validators are selected to propose and confirm blocks based on the quantity of tokens they lock up (“*stake*”) in the protocol. The more tokens a participant holds and locks up, the greater their probability of being chosen as a validator.

This mechanism is used by several cryptocurrency systems, notably Ethereum since its transition on September 15, 2022. Its proponents put forward a much lower energy consumption than that of proof of work. Its critics point out that it tends to concentrate validation power in the hands of the largest holders, reproducing a dynamic similar to that of traditional financial systems where wealth begets control in a fundamentally closed system, because it does not rely on a natural resource external to the protocol.

Bitcoin does not use proof of stake. Its protocol relies exclusively on proof of work, which ties the publication of a block to a real and verifiable energy expenditure, independent of the wealth accumulated by participants.

5d7357b4-5a04-43c0-abc8-79842c48f0ce.title: BIP-0176
5d7357b4-5a04-43c0-abc8-79842c48f0ce.body: Proposal to use the "bit" (100 satoshis, or one millionth of a bitcoin) as a standard denomination in user interfaces. BIP-0176 argues that the bit offers a good compromise between precision and readability for common amounts. This proposal competes with the movement toward the satoshi as the main reference unit, the latter gaining more traction in the ecosystem.

5d9a18dd-68d3-484b-a1c0-1b001ab16d80.title: WHITE PAPER
5d9a18dd-68d3-484b-a1c0-1b001ab16d80.body:
Report or guide that informs readers concisely about a complex issue. In the case of Bitcoin, it is the name given to the scientific document titled "*Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System*" published by Satoshi Nakamoto for the first time on October 31, 2008. This document describes the fundamental principles of Bitcoin. The White Paper presented nowadays is a second version published on March 24, 2009.

*To download the Bitcoin White Paper: https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.*

5debf0c7-5568-46ca-9408-66de11d5d36c.title: BIP-0054
5debf0c7-5568-46ca-9408-66de11d5d36c.body:
Proposal, currently in draft, for a set of fixes to vulnerabilities in Bitcoin's consensus rules, known as "Consensus Cleanup". BIP-0054 fixes:
* the *time warp* attack by imposing constraints on block timestamps at the boundaries of difficulty adjustment periods,
* limits block validation time by capping the number of signature operations per transaction,
* invalidates 64-byte transactions to fix the weaknesses of the Merkle tree,
* and requires use of the `nLockTime` field in coinbase transactions to eliminate the need for BIP-0030 validation.

This soft fork aims to reduce the protocol's attack surface by cleanly fixing known and documented historical bugs, without changing its basic operation.

5e35134d-82a5-4a01-ace4-3e875507a054.title: BIP-0341
5e35134d-82a5-4a01-ace4-3e875507a054.body:
Defines the spending rules of SegWit version 1, commonly called “Taproot”. This BIP introduces two distinct spending paths: the *key-path*, which allows spending with a simple Schnorr signature, and the *script-path*, which allows revealing and executing a script from a Merkle tree (MAST). Taproot outputs use “tweaked” public keys that combine an internal key with the root of the MAST tree.

The advantage of this structure is that all Taproot outputs look identical on-chain (a simple 32-byte public key), which considerably improves user privacy. BIP-0341 was activated at block 709,632 in November 2021 via the Speedy Trial method.

5e3b25dd-9d7a-4442-9458-dbc6a8b6da3d.title: FORK - GIT
5e3b25dd-9d7a-4442-9458-dbc6a8b6da3d.body: In the context of Git, represents the creation of a copy of an existing repository on a new account, thus allowing the user to modify, test or develop the project independently of the original repository. Forks enable open source collaboration and contribution to projects without affecting the source repository.

5e8e92ec-5848-47bb-b47e-92f655ee1c7f.title: BLOCKSIZE WAR
5e8e92ec-5848-47bb-b47e-92f655ee1c7f.body:
Refers to a period of intense debate and conflict within the Bitcoin community between 2015 and 2017. This conflict was about whether the block size, limited to 1 megabyte since 2010 by Satoshi Nakamoto, should be increased to allow Bitcoin to process more transactions per block, and thus to scale (scalability).

The supporters of increasing the block size (known as the “*big blockers*”), led by early developers such as Jeff Garzik, Gavin Andresen and Mike Hearn, influential figures of the ecosystem such as Roger Ver, as well as a good share of the large mining companies, argued that this increase was necessary to reduce transaction fees and improve Bitcoin's scalability. They believed that this change could be made without consequences for the security of the system. On the other hand, the opponents of increasing the block size (known as the “*small blockers*”), mainly Bitcoin Core developers (Pieter Wuille, Peter Todd, Gregory Maxwell, Wladimir van der Laan, Luke Dashjr...) and part of the technical community, argued that this change would centralize the system because of the increased operational load on nodes. They put forward so-called second-layer scalability solutions, such as the Lightning Network, which would make it possible to handle a large quantity of transactions without having to modify the base protocol.

The debate over Bitcoin's approach to scalability has lasted since at least 2010, with the first attempt to increase the block size in October of that year via [a patch proposed by Jeff Garzik](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=1347.0). But it was during the period of the Blocksize War between 2015 and 2017 that the conflicts were most virulent, with several fork attempts being set up (Bitcoin XT, Bitcoin Classic, Bitcoin Unlimited, SegWit, SegWit2X and Bitcoin Cash), along with propaganda and influence strategies, as well as personal attacks. The abandonment of the SegWit2X hard fork on November 8, 2017, following the massive opposition of the community (“NO2X”), is often seen as the event marking the end of the Blocksize War, while the casus belli is sometimes considered to be the 0.11A update of the Bitcoin XT client, which implemented BIP-0101 on August 15, 2015. One could also consider that the end of the Blocksize War took place on August 24, 2017, the date on which the SegWit soft fork was activated following the campaign in favor of the “UASF”.

*In French, the “Blocksize War” is generally referred to as a proper noun. Some sometimes translate this term as “guerre des blocs” or “guerre de la taille des blocs”.*

5ec445aa-30a7-434e-af7b-43b63cded76c.title: BIP-0126
5ec445aa-30a7-434e-af7b-43b63cded76c.body: Recommendations for transactions using inputs of different script types (P2PKH, P2SH, SegWit...). BIP-0126 aims to reduce identifiable wallet fingerprints when building heterogeneous transactions that are unavoidable or intentional. Transactions mixing script types reveal information about the wallet used, which harms privacy. This document proposes best practices to minimize these information leaks when building heterogeneous transactions.

5fc25ff3-922c-45b4-b717-cba463da9db1.title: NAT - NETWORK-ADJUSTED TIME
5fc25ff3-922c-45b4-b717-cba463da9db1.body:
An estimate of universal time based on the clocks of the network's nodes. Each node calculates its NAT by taking the median of the time differences between its local clock (UTC) and those of the nodes it is connected to, then adding its local clock to the median of these differences, up to a maximum of 70 minutes. The *network-adjusted time* is therefore a median of the nodes' time, calculated locally by each node. This reference is then used to verify the validity of block timestamps. Indeed, for a block to be accepted by a node, its timestamp must lie between the MTP (median time of the last 11 mined blocks) and the NAT plus 2 hours:

```text
MTP < Horodatage valide < (NAT + 2h)
```

5fca9d55-5f6d-4cfa-a93c-c19130cb9826.title: BIP-0069
5fca9d55-5f6d-4cfa-a93c-c19130cb9826.body: Proposal suggesting a lexicographic sorting of the inputs and outputs of a Bitcoin transaction in order to reduce the possibilities of identification by fingerprinting (*fingerprinting*). Inputs are sorted by `txid` then by output index (`vout`), and outputs by amount then by `scriptPubKey`. The goal is to improve privacy by making transactions produced by different software more uniform, which complicates identification of the wallet used. However, this BIP is today considered insufficient in terms of privacy, because a deterministic sort can itself become an identifiable fingerprint.

600be69c-5a75-4f1d-88b2-e5b836e15d00.title: AIR-GAPPED
600be69c-5a75-4f1d-88b2-e5b836e15d00.body:
Describes a computing device that is physically isolated from any network, including the Internet, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or any other wired or wireless connection. In the context of Bitcoin, an air-gapped device is used to secure private keys by keeping them away from any online attack vector.

The principle is simple: if a device is never connected to a network, it becomes extremely difficult for an attacker to access it remotely to extract sensitive information. An air-gapped *hardware wallet* signs transactions offline. Data is exchanged with the Internet-connected computer by a physical means, typically via a microSD card or a QR code, without ever establishing a direct connection.

This approach represents one of the highest levels of security for storing bitcoins. Devices such as the Coldcard, Foundation Devices' Passport, or Blockstream's Jade offer this mode of operation.

603601a4-8661-4162-95e6-0bbfc3d40ce1.title: REVOKEANDACK
603601a4-8661-4162-95e6-0bbfc3d40ce1.body: A Lightning protocol message exchanged between two peers when updating the state of a channel. When a new payment is routed or an HTLC is resolved, both parties build a new commitment transaction. The `revoke_and_ack` message fulfills two simultaneous functions: it revokes the old commitment transaction by transmitting the corresponding revocation key, and it acknowledges receipt of the new state. This mechanism guarantees that at any moment, only the latest state of the channel is valid. If a peer tried to publish a revoked state, the revocation key would allow the counterparty to recover all of the funds.

608f3e1b-edd0-4834-ac9c-22cf6afe032d.title: GENESIS BLOCK
608f3e1b-edd0-4834-ac9c-22cf6afe032d.body:
The Genesis block is the first block of the Bitcoin system. It embodies the concrete launch of Bitcoin. The Genesis block was created by Bitcoin's anonymous founder, Satoshi Nakamoto, on January 3, 2009. Its hash is:

```text
000000000019d6689c085ae165831e934ff763ae46a2a6c172b3f1b60a8ce26f
```

This block contains only one coinbase transaction, which generates 50 bitcoins as a reward for the miner (in this case, Satoshi Nakamoto himself). This block includes a message embedded in the coinbase transaction:

```text
The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks
```

This quote is a reference to an article in the newspaper *The Times*. The message is interpreted as a criticism of the traditional financial system and its excesses, which partly motivated the creation of Bitcoin as a monetary alternative.

Since it embodies the very first block of the Bitcoin blockchain, the Genesis block has a field containing the hash of the previous block, but it is filled with zeros, because there is no previous block. Moreover, the 50 bitcoins generated as a reward in this block are not spendable at the protocol level.

60ce42fd-759e-4281-9cd2-e7d5b148365f.title: API
60ce42fd-759e-4281-9cd2-e7d5b148365f.body: Acronym for "*Application Programming Interface*". In the general context of computer science, an API is a set of rules and specifications that software can follow to communicate with each other. They allow developers to access features or data of an application, an operating system, or another service for their own software.

60f0a3c9-56fc-4fc8-bb54-d542d0434b8a.title: BIP-0032
60f0a3c9-56fc-4fc8-bb54-d542d0434b8a.body: BIP-0032 introduced the concept of the hierarchical deterministic wallet (HD wallet). This proposal makes it possible to generate a hierarchy of key pairs from a common seed, the *master seed*, using one-way derivation functions. Each generated key pair can itself be the parent of other child keys, thus forming a tree (hierarchical) structure. The advantage of BIP-0032 is that it makes it possible to manage multiple different key pairs while needing to keep only a single seed to regenerate them. This innovation notably helped fight the phenomenon of address reuse, which is serious for users' privacy. BIP-0032 also allows the creation of sub-branches within a single wallet in order to facilitate its management.

61102e30-eafb-4279-8213-b3208f6b2126.title: MACAROON
61102e30-eafb-4279-8213-b3208f6b2126.body: Authentication mechanism designed to secure access to services on distributed systems. Macaroons are notably used on Lightning to authenticate users when they access delegated services. For example, with a Lightning node, it is possible to generate a macaroon that authorizes transactions to be made from your smartphone via your remote node. Unlike *cookies*, macaroons have the advantage of being cryptographically verifiable by the issuer or of being delegated for verification.

613c49c8-e479-412d-a5cf-786433ce2689.title: CONTROL BOARD
613c49c8-e479-412d-a5cf-786433ce2689.body: Component in a mining machine that manages and coordinates the device's operations. The control board handles communication between the software and the ASIC chips. It also makes it possible to monitor the hardware's performance and control its temperature.

61425f35-72b4-4ce5-85c1-5d3551e733e6.title: BLK*.DAT
61425f35-72b4-4ce5-85c1-5d3551e733e6.body: Name of the files in Bitcoin Core that store the raw data of the blockchain's blocks. Each file is identified by a unique number in its name. Thus, blocks are recorded in chronological order, starting with the file blk00000.dat. When this file reaches its maximum capacity, the following blocks are recorded in blk00001.dat, then blk00002.dat, and so on. Each blk file has a maximum capacity of 128 mebibytes (MiB), which is equivalent to a little over 134 megabytes (MB). These files have been moved to the `/blocks` folder since version 0.8.0.

61d08245-d158-41d5-a122-aff73bb866d5.title: NULL DATA
61d08245-d158-41d5-a122-aff73bb866d5.body: Type of Bitcoin transaction that allows a small amount of arbitrary data to be inserted using a `OP_RETURN`. Any bitcoins associated with this type of output are provably unspendable, because the `OP_RETURN` signals an invalid script.

61d4b3da-e6df-4938-9f56-65806d086e18.title: OP_CHECKSIGADD - 0XBA
61d4b3da-e6df-4938-9f56-65806d086e18.body:
Pops the three values at the top of the stack: a `clé publique`, a `CScriptNum` `n` and a `signature`. If the signature is not the empty vector and is not valid, the script terminates with an error. If the signature is valid or is the empty vector (`OP_0`), two cases arise:
* If the signature is the empty vector: a `CScriptNum` with the value of `n` is pushed onto the stack and execution continues;
* If the signature is not the empty vector and remains valid: a `CScriptNum` with the value of `n + 1` is pushed onto the stack and execution continues.
In simple terms, `OP_CHECKSIGADD` performs an operation similar to `OP_CHECKSIG`, but instead of pushing true or false onto the stack, it adds `1` to the second value from the top of the stack if the signature is valid, or leaves that value unchanged if the signature is the empty vector. `OP_CHECKSIGADD` makes it possible to create the same multisig policies in Tapscript as with `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` and `OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY` but in a batch-verifiable way, that is, it removes the search process in the verification of a traditional multisig and therefore speeds up verification while reducing the operational load on nodes' CPUs. This opcode was added in Tapscript solely for the needs of Taproot.

61fed473-5d33-4ccd-b002-211472e796e7.title: NFT
61fed473-5d33-4ccd-b002-211472e796e7.body:
Acronym for *Non-Fungible Token*. An NFT represents a unit of bitcoin that, by users of a protocol external to Bitcoin, is interpreted as non-fungible and associated with the ownership of an asset external to Bitcoin, such as an image or any other type of data.

On Bitcoin, protocols such as Ordinals and Stamps allow the creation and management of these NFTs. These protocols are often controversial, because their activity clutters the blockchain with non-financial data. This can have negative consequences for the system, notably by inducing an increased operational load for full nodes or by raising transaction fees through the influence of external economic factors.

621356ed-02e1-48bd-aa8b-3774001d445d.title: DIFFIE-HELLMAN
621356ed-02e1-48bd-aa8b-3774001d445d.body: A cryptographic method allowing two parties to generate a shared secret over an insecure communication channel. This secret can then be used to encrypt the communication between the two parties. Diffie-Hellman uses modular arithmetic so that, even if an attacker can observe the exchanges, they cannot deduce the shared secret without solving a hard mathematical problem: the discrete logarithm. On Bitcoin, a variant of DH using an elliptic curve named ECDH is sometimes used, notably for static address protocols such as *Silent Payments* or BIP-0047.

626b8bf7-467a-496d-ba81-63cdc8d5f058.title: UNCONFIRMED TRANSACTION
626b8bf7-467a-496d-ba81-63cdc8d5f058.body: Bitcoin transaction that has been broadcast on the network, but has not yet been included in a block by a miner. It remains in the nodes' mempools, waiting to get confirmations. Confirmation occurs when the transaction is included in a valid block added to the blockchain. The time needed for a transaction to be confirmed depends on the transaction fees paid and on system congestion.

627ea50a-a23d-4ad8-91dd-55a90a3b13b3.title: RACE ATTACK
627ea50a-a23d-4ad8-91dd-55a90a3b13b3.body: A form of double spend that exploits the propagation delay of transactions across the Bitcoin network. The attacker simultaneously sends two transactions that spend the same UTXOs: one to a merchant to pay for a good or service, and the other to an address they control. If the merchant accepts the transaction without waiting for a confirmation in a block, they risk delivering the good while it is the second transaction that ends up being confirmed by the miners. This attack therefore exclusively targets payments accepted with "zero confirmations" (*zero-conf*). To protect against it, a merchant can wait for at least one confirmation before considering the payment valid, or use double-spend detection techniques by actively monitoring the network.

628f7a20-c45a-42c6-831d-a498ca2e7a10.title: MARKET CAP
628f7a20-c45a-42c6-831d-a498ca2e7a10.body: Represents the total value of an asset in circulation, such as bitcoin. It is calculated by multiplying the total number of coins in circulation by the current price of each unit. This figure gives an indication of the overall size and market value of Bitcoin.

62bb6e93-35b0-49da-ab17-0b84b073c8b5.title: BIP-0112
62bb6e93-35b0-49da-ab17-0b84b073c8b5.body: Introduces the opcode `OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY` (CSV) into Bitcoin's Script language. This operation makes it possible to create transactions whose validity only becomes effective after a certain delay relative to an earlier transaction, defined either as a number of blocks or as a length of time. `OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY` compares the value at the top of the stack with the value of the `nSequence` field of the input. If it is greater and all the other conditions are met, the script is valid. Thus, `OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY` restricts the possible values for the `nSequence` field of the input that spends it, and this `nSequence` field itself restricts the moment when the transaction that includes this input can be included in a block. BIP-0112 was introduced via a soft fork on July 4, 2016 at the same time as BIP-0068 and BIP-0113, activated for the first time using the BIP-0009 method.

62d42032-9afd-4fba-b7e0-bd6e5527ef86.title: MUSIG-DN
62d42032-9afd-4fba-b7e0-bd6e5527ef86.body:
A variant of MuSig proposed in 2020 by Jonas Nick, Tim Ruffing, Yannick Seurin and Pieter Wuille. The acronym “DN” stands for “Deterministic Nonces”. The protocol eliminates the nonce commitment round by requiring each signer to derive their nonces deterministically from their private key and the message, then to provide a zero-knowledge proof attesting to the correctness of the computation. This mechanism reduces the signature to two rounds of communication while preventing nonce manipulation.

Despite its theoretical elegance, generating the proofs turns out to be too resource-intensive for practical use, particularly on *hardware wallets*. MuSig-DN remained an intermediate research step and was superseded by MuSig2, which achieves the same two-round goal with a lighter approach based on multiple random nonces.

637c9440-ef72-484f-bc48-370832be9294.title: AUTOLOOP
637c9440-ef72-484f-bc48-370832be9294.body: A feature of Lightning Loop that automates *Loop In* and *Loop Out* operations based on predefined thresholds. The operator of a Lightning node configures inbound and outbound liquidity limits for their channels, and Autoloop automatically triggers *submarine swaps* when these thresholds are exceeded. This makes it possible to maintain a liquidity balance without manual intervention, which is particularly useful for routing nodes that must constantly adjust the distribution of their funds between channels in order to maximize routing revenue.

63822cc4-3355-4437-bdbe-605fe81d5720.title: BIP-0122
63822cc4-3355-4437-bdbe-605fe81d5720.body: Proposal for a URI scheme to reference specific elements of the blockchain (blocks, transactions) in a standardized way. BIP-0122 would facilitate interoperability between block explorers and applications by defining a uniform format to identify a particular blockchain and point to its data. Each blockchain is identified by the hash of its genesis block. This BIP has remained in draft status since 2015.

638e0ded-9bbc-4291-b5d3-bec7703e465c.title: BOLT-05
638e0ded-9bbc-4291-b5d3-bec7703e465c.body: Specification that defines the behavior of Lightning nodes when a channel is closed on-chain. It covers three scenarios: cooperative closing, unilateral closing (publication of a commitment transaction) and revocation closing (fraud attempt). BOLT-05 details the resolution of each type of output (local, remote, anchor and HTLC outputs), the rules for monitoring the blockchain until all funds are irrevocably resolved (100 blocks deep), and the penalty transactions that make it possible to seize all of the channel's funds when an old revoked state is published. The specification also describes the fee bumping (*fee bumping*) mechanisms via anchor outputs.

639ab934-b26f-4520-b282-5f310ec93859.title: STALE / OBSOLETE - BLOCK

63d59b18-492d-4503-9ea8-5d17be756ab1.title: FINNEY ATTACK
63d59b18-492d-4503-9ea8-5d17be756ab1.body:
A type of double spend that targets zero-confirmation transactions. The attacker, who must be a miner, pre-mines a block containing a transaction from their address A to another address B that they also control. Instead of broadcasting this block, they make a payment from that same address A to a merchant's address C. The merchant sees the transaction in the mempool, detects no conflict, and delivers the goods. The attacker then broadcasts their pre-mined block: the transaction to B is confirmed, while the payment to C is invalidated.

Hal Finney described this attack in 2011 on the BitcoinTalk forum. It differs from the 51% attack because it does not require a majority of computing power: it is enough for the attacker to find a block, even with a modest hashrate. In return, its execution window is narrow and it only works against merchants who accept payments without waiting for a confirmation.

63d911ff-f184-46c1-a1fc-d05864330bd1.title: DOS - DENIAL OF SERVICE
63d911ff-f184-46c1-a1fc-d05864330bd1.body: Cyberattack that aims to make a resource (website, node, online service...) unavailable to its legitimate users. Attackers overload the target with an excessively high volume of data or requests, which exhausts the victim's system and network resources, causing slowdowns or a complete shutdown. DoS methods can vary, but the objective remains the same: to prevent access to services or data. In the specific context of Bitcoin, a DoS attack can aim to saturate the network or nodes with an excessive volume of requests in order to hinder their normal operation. The objective is often to harm a node operator or the availability of the network for honest users.

63f88ad6-90d1-4d06-a5f0-5a18f656b394.title: RENDEZ-VOUS ROUTING
63f88ad6-90d1-4d06-a5f0-5a18f656b394.body:
A Lightning routing technique designed to protect the identity of the recipient of a payment. In classic routing, the sender builds the entire route and therefore knows the final node. With *rendez-vous routing*, the recipient pre-builds an encrypted route segment from an intermediate node (the *rendez-vous point*) to themselves, and passes this segment to the sender via the invoice. The sender completes the route on their end up to the *rendez-vous point*, without ever knowing the nodes beyond it.

This approach does, however, have limitations: the sender cannot insert their own data into the portion encrypted by the recipient, and the amounts must be set in advance in the partial onion, which complicates multi-part payments. For these reasons, *rendez-vous routing* has been superseded by *blinded paths*, a more flexible technique that allows the sender to freely choose the data inserted at each hop and that is reusable with onion messages.

64166554-de15-41dd-a7df-92d84817ca68.title: BTRUST
64166554-de15-41dd-a7df-92d84817ca68.body: Non-profit organization founded in February 2021 by Jack Dorsey and Jay-Z with an initial endowment of 500 bitcoins. Btrust's mission is to decentralize the development of Bitcoin software by encouraging and funding developers in countries of the Global South, notably in Africa and India. The organization offers training programs, development fellowships and grants to strengthen the contribution of these regions to Bitcoin's open-source code and its technical ecosystem.

6425380f-3375-4de1-9230-1415d23131b0.title: GITLAB
6425380f-3375-4de1-9230-1415d23131b0.body: Source code management and hosting platform that facilitates collaboration between developers. GitLab is the main alternative to GitHub. The platform is quite similar, but it also offers the possibility of being self-hosted. As its name indicates, GitLab is built on the Git version control system. This platform therefore makes it possible to track code changes, manage versions and encourage collaboration through tools such as merge requests and issues. Some Bitcoin-related projects such as Samourai Wallet, Whirlpool or RoninDojo use GitLab.

643a18d6-6e51-4812-8aaa-e0c6e35f421b.title: DNS SEEDS

6450c114-13eb-43fc-9ebe-e84e319ca61e.title: BEAR MARKET
6450c114-13eb-43fc-9ebe-e84e319ca61e.body: Prolonged period during which the price of an asset, such as bitcoin, falls relative to a fiat currency, typically the US dollar. Since its introduction in 2009, the cycle of BTC bear markets seems to be influenced by halvings, scheduled events that cut the miners' reward in half and that occur approximately every four years.

6515e629-fbd5-4a80-9a14-35b0c59ed8c3.title: URI
6515e629-fbd5-4a80-9a14-35b0c59ed8c3.body:
Acronym for "*Uniform Resource Identifier*". It is a standardized character string format used to identify a resource on the Internet. A URI can be either a URL (*Uniform Resource Locator*), which provides a means of accessing a resource by indicating its location on a computer network, or a URN (*Uniform Resource Name*), which names the resource without indicating how to locate it. URIs are important in the operation of the *World Wide Web*, as they allow access to resources such as web pages, documents, and services.

In the context of Bitcoin, a URI is used specifically to facilitate transactions. It allows encoding a receiving address, as well as other transaction parameters such as the amount, in a standardized format according to BIP-0021. This simplifies the payment process by allowing users to click on a link or scan a QR code, which automatically feeds the necessary information into their Bitcoin wallet application.

653e2413-a720-41ad-ae91-c82f36d8891f.title: BITCOIN-CLI
653e2413-a720-41ad-ae91-c82f36d8891f.body: `Bitcoin-cli`, an acronym for “*Bitcoin Command Line Interface*”, is a command-line interface designed to interact with a running instance of Bitcoin Core, in particular the daemon, `bitcoind`. It is a standalone program that gives the user a way to communicate and execute commands to control and query the state of the `bitcoind` instance. In addition to network management capabilities, such as monitoring transactions and blocks, `bitcoin-cli` also offers wallet functionality, allowing users to make Bitcoin transactions by sending and receiving funds.

659fc26a-10e7-4d5f-8664-847d02e72ef7.title: IP REPORT
659fc26a-10e7-4d5f-8664-847d02e72ef7.body: Button found on ASICs that makes it possible to quickly find the IP address of the machine on the local network. To use this feature, you must press the ASIC's *IP Report* button for a few seconds. Then, using specialized software on a computer connected to the same network, the miner's IP address will be displayed on the screen. This button notably makes it easy to locate a machine on the local network when you have several machines.

65ba9f36-79c1-4f38-b205-ada896dad7df.title: BLIP-0017
65ba9f36-79c1-4f38-b205-ada896dad7df.body: bLIP that specifies *hosted channels*, Lightning payment channels based on the client's trust in a host, with no on-chain anchoring. Unlike classic Lightning channels, which lock bitcoins in a funding transaction, hosted channels operate without a UTXO or any interaction with the blockchain. The channel state is signed by both parties via encrypted messages exchanged over the Lightning protocol, which prevents the host from unilaterally falsifying balances. The advantages include immediate receiving capacity and the absence of on-chain fees, but the client bears a counterparty risk because they cannot force the channel to close on the blockchain. This model sits between a classic custodial wallet and a classic Lightning channel.

65cf30e1-6c77-48cc-aec7-871d101024ae.title: SHITCOIN
65cf30e1-6c77-48cc-aec7-871d101024ae.body: Pejorative expression frequently used in the cryptocurrency world to describe altcoins deemed worthless or without a future. This term is used in two distinct contexts: in the general cryptocurrency community, it designates a project that lacks technological innovation, that presents no concrete use case, or that is mainly the product of excessive speculation. For maximalist bitcoiners, the term encompasses all cryptocurrencies other than bitcoin (BTC), making “shitcoin” a synonym for “altcoin”. The word is a combination of “shit” and “coin”. The initial use of the term goes back to a message posted by the user Ribuck on November 8, 2010 on the Bitcoin Talk forum.

65eb2e17-8dac-41f6-acf7-30d01d085760.title: BIP-0102
65eb2e17-8dac-41f6-acf7-30d01d085760.body: Proposal presented by Jeff Garzik in June 2015 as part of the Blocksize War. It aimed to increase the maximum block size from 1 MB to 2 MB through a hard fork. It is this proposal that subsequently inspired BIP-0109 and the creation of Bitcoin Classic. This proposal was never adopted.

663689c9-c7df-4dc9-9a82-6abb0bf9b0eb.title: BISQ
663689c9-c7df-4dc9-9a82-6abb0bf9b0eb.body: Open source decentralized exchange (DEX) platform software that allows buying and selling bitcoins peer-to-peer, without a centralized intermediary or identity verification (KYC). Bisq works as a desktop application that connects to a P2P network over Tor. Each trade is secured by a security deposit system in bitcoins (2-of-2 multisig) and an arbitration process in case of dispute. Trades are made against fiat currencies (bank transfer, Revolut, etc.) or other cryptocurrencies. Bisq never holds users' funds and collects no personal data. The software is funded by an integrated DAO (decentralized autonomous organization) that uses the BSQ token for its governance.

66678830-dfda-4c6e-92f7-abba944b766a.title: FEDERATION
66678830-dfda-4c6e-92f7-abba944b766a.body:
Group of participants who collaborate to administer a network or a system, striking a compromise between centralization and decentralization. In a federation, responsibility is distributed among several independent entities rather than concentrated in a single one, which eliminates single points of failure and strengthens the system's resilience.

In the Bitcoin ecosystem, the federated model is used notably by the Liquid network, where a set of functionaries collectively sign blocks and manage the pegging operations (*peg-in* and *peg-out*) between the main chain and the sidechain. The Fedimint protocol also relies on a federated model to manage *Chaumian mints*. The concept of *Strong Federations*, formalized by Blockstream, describes a system in which functionaries operate under strict consensus rules, without requiring individual trust in each member.

666c23e2-51a8-473d-b244-e6c5f37aef4d.title: COMPACTSIZE

66ddbe8b-5fc3-4ea4-8865-98cc2acf1472.title: ANCHORS.DAT
66ddbe8b-5fc3-4ea4-8865-98cc2acf1472.body: A file used in the Bitcoin Core client to store the IP addresses of the outbound *block-relay-only* nodes to which a client was connected before being shut down. `anchors.dat` is therefore created each time the node is stopped and deleted when it is restarted. The nodes whose IP addresses are contained in this file are used to help quickly establish connections when the node restarts.

66f29c78-3f0c-4f55-90da-07b7a2c35503.title: WUMBO CHANNEL
66f29c78-3f0c-4f55-90da-07b7a2c35503.body:
High-capacity Lightning channel, exceeding the historical limit of 16,777,215 satoshis (approximately 0.168 BTC) imposed by default on the first nodes. This limit, encoded on 24 bits, had been introduced as a precaution during the early years of the Lightning Network to limit potential losses in the event of a bug in the implementations.

Subsequently, implementations introduced an option allowing channels of up to 10 BTC to be accepted. These high-capacity channels are nicknamed "Wumbo channels", in reference to an episode of *SpongeBob SquarePants*.

6737cdad-66f5-4848-bba0-834affd3b6b2.title: SPHINX
6737cdad-66f5-4848-bba0-834affd3b6b2.body: A cryptographic packet format used by the Lightning Network to route payments privately via onion routing. Originally designed by George Danezis and Ian Goldberg in 2009 for mix networks, it encapsulates routing instructions in successive layers of encryption. Each intermediate node can only decrypt the layer intended for it, revealing only the next hop without knowing the sender or the final recipient.

6777195e-5552-46de-a654-cc5ddac3c146.title: SEEDXOR
6777195e-5552-46de-a654-cc5ddac3c146.body:
Method of splitting a Bitcoin recovery phrase into several parts using the XOR operation, introduced by Coinkite for Coldcard hardware wallets. The principle consists of dividing a mnemonic phrase of 12 or 24 words into two or more fragments that are themselves valid BIP-0039 phrases. To reconstruct the original phrase, all the parts must be recombined by XOR (an N-of-N scheme, not M-of-N).

Since each fragment is a functional mnemonic phrase, it can serve as a decoy wallet loaded with a small amount, thus offering a form of plausible deniability: an attacker cannot distinguish a SeedXOR fragment from an ordinary recovery phrase. The calculation can be done manually using printable worksheets, or directly on a Coldcard.

67af30fd-2325-4ade-8db2-99bdc0370c0c.title: PROOF OF RESERVES
67af30fd-2325-4ade-8db2-99bdc0370c0c.body:
Mechanism used by bitcoin exchange platforms to demonstrate that they do hold their customers' assets. The goal is to prove the company's solvency by verifying that its bitcoins are equal to or greater than the user balances that they are supposed to hold.

Platforms often use Merkle trees that include all of their users' balances. Each user can then verify that their balance is part of the total set, without revealing information about the other accounts. In parallel, the platform publicly signs the addresses that secure the bitcoins to prove that it controls them.

However, these methods have significant limitations, because proof of possession of the funds does not in itself prove the company's solvency. The exchange could, for example, secretly take on debts by contracting Lombard loans secured by the same bitcoins used in the proof of reserves. It could also display a balance of borrowed bitcoins while remaining insolvent. The problem with proof of reserves is that it focuses solely on verifying the platform's assets, without taking liabilities into account. 

Traditionally on Bitcoin, to celebrate the anniversary of the publication of the Genesis block, every January 3 is "*Proof-of-Keys Day*". Bitcoin holders are invited to all withdraw their funds from exchanges and store them in self-custody wallets, in order to test the solvency of these platforms.

But ultimately, if you truly want to protect yourself against the risk of exchange platforms going bankrupt, the only solution is to keep your bitcoins in self-custody.

67ddd100-665f-4463-98f5-7ba6e2b937bf.title: MEMPOOL.SPACE
67ddd100-665f-4463-98f5-7ba6e2b937bf.body: Open source block explorer and mempool visualizer for Bitcoin, accessible at mempool.space. This tool makes it possible to consult in real time the state of the mempool (the transactions awaiting confirmation), to estimate optimal transaction fees, to explore blocks, transactions and addresses, and to visualize the state of mining. Mempool.space can also be self-hosted on your own node for sovereign and private use.

67ea3695-fe94-476e-abf2-4ee091a2bcf4.title: COUNTERPARTY
67ea3695-fe94-476e-abf2-4ee091a2bcf4.body: Open source meta-protocol launched in January 2014 that made it possible to create and exchange digital assets directly on the Bitcoin blockchain. Counterparty encodes token metadata in Bitcoin transactions, mainly via multisig outputs or `OP_RETURN`, without modifying the base protocol.

680073ad-602a-4263-a6ec-3eaf05098e31.title: TWENTYTWO DEVICES
680073ad-602a-4263-a6ec-3eaf05098e31.body: Company founded by Alekos Filini that develops the Portal, a flat-format *hardware wallet* that communicates with *smartphones* exclusively via NFC, with no cable or battery. The Portal's *firmware* is written entirely in Rust and relies on BDK. Both the hardware and the software are fully *open source*.

6838b8ea-8faf-439f-a3ae-d379dcab9c63.title: MERCHANT
6838b8ea-8faf-439f-a3ae-d379dcab9c63.body: Any natural or legal person who agrees to exchange a good or a service for bitcoins. It is these merchants who give the bitcoin currency its usefulness. The more widely a currency is accepted by a broad range of merchants, the more useful it becomes for individuals. Since merchants have the ability to determine the usefulness of a currency by agreeing to exchange it for goods and services, in the case of Bitcoin they also have considerable weight in the choice of consensus rules. Each has a certain power proportional to the economic activity they are able to bring to a fork. Among merchants, there are obviously businesses, but also exchange platforms, miners and users.

684e2c16-bab8-402c-9c29-2fd6d214c92e.title: GIT
684e2c16-bab8-402c-9c29-2fd6d214c92e.body: Distributed version control system designed to efficiently manage any type of software project. It allows developers to track changes made to a project's source code over time, revert to earlier states, manage branches and merge changes. Git facilitates collaboration between developers by allowing several people to work on the same project simultaneously, with tools to manage any conflicts in files. Each developer works locally and can then synchronize their changes with the central repository. Created in 2005 by Linus Torvalds, Git has become the de facto standard for version control in the software industry. The development of Bitcoin node implementations, including Bitcoin Core, is managed with Git.

6863cade-c97d-4b01-907b-af682e54726c.title: ELECTRUM
6863cade-c97d-4b01-907b-af682e54726c.body: A Bitcoin wallet founded in November 2011 by Thomas Voegtlin, which allows users to manage their funds without downloading the entire blockchain thanks to an SPV (*Simplified Payment Verification*) system. Because it has existed since the very beginning of the 2010s and because of its involvement in the development of Bitcoin, Electrum holds a historic place as wallet software.

6888a2d8-205c-47e6-a68a-98b1219e6f85.title: XBT
6888a2d8-205c-47e6-a68a-98b1219e6f85.body: Stock market and currency symbol (*ticker*) used to represent bitcoin, in accordance with the ISO 4217 standard that governs currency codes. Unlike "BTC", which is the historical symbol, "XBT" follows the convention that currencies not backed by a state begin with an "X". Thus, although not officially recognized by the ISO, "XBT" is used by some organizations to represent units of bitcoin.

68c4d22f-20d6-4075-a8ba-c9459ef062bc.title: HSM
68c4d22f-20d6-4075-a8ba-c9459ef062bc.body:
Acronym for “Hardware Security Module”. It is a physical device dedicated to the secure management of cryptographic keys. An HSM performs key generation, signing and encryption operations in a tamper-resistant hardware environment, designed to withstand attempts at physical or logical extraction of the secrets it contains.

In the context of Bitcoin, HSMs are mainly used by companies and exchange platforms that manage large volumes of funds. They make it possible to sign Bitcoin transactions securely without the private keys ever leaving the protected perimeter of the module. Unlike *hardware wallets* intended for individuals, HSMs are industrial-grade equipment, often compliant with security certifications such as FIPS 140-2, and they are designed to operate in server environments or data centers.

An HSM is therefore distinguished from a *hardware wallet* by its use: it is designed for server environments and high-frequency automated operations, whereas a *hardware wallet* is intended for individual, interactive use. This difference in use also implies a difference in deployment: the HSM is integrated into a network infrastructure, whereas the *hardware wallet* is a personal device connected occasionally.

68dd1d4c-9771-416c-a1d4-eca870680620.title: BIP-0086
68dd1d4c-9771-416c-a1d4-eca870680620.body: Defines the derivation standard for SegWit V1 or Taproot addresses (`bc1p...`) within a hierarchical deterministic wallet. It defines the index `86'` which must now be used at depth `purpose` of the HD wallet for P2TR script templates.

690901c5-0904-4da8-a5bd-4fea08588609.title: BIP-0348
690901c5-0904-4da8-a5bd-4fea08588609.body: Proposes adding the opcode `OP_CHECKSIGFROMSTACK` for Tapscript, replacing `OP_SUCCESS204`. Unlike `OP_CHECKSIG`, which verifies a signature against the hash of the current transaction, this opcode makes it possible to verify a Schnorr signature (BIP-0340) on an arbitrary message supplied on the stack. It consumes three elements: a 32-byte public key, a message and a signature. The BIP deliberately does not define a VERIFY variant, for the sake of simplicity.
