The V2 P2P transport of BIP-0324 was included as an option (disabled by default) in version 26.0 of Bitcoin Core, released in December 2023. It can be enabled with the `v2transport=1` option in the configuration file. This improvement replaces BIP-0151.

7ac21226-1cd2-402a-b7e9-2136bb80d1f5.title: JOINPOOL
7ac21226-1cd2-402a-b7e9-2136bb80d1f5.body:
Type of layer-2 payment system based on the shared ownership of one or more UTXOs, without the need for trust. When funds are withdrawn from a pool in this type of system, it must be impossible to determine on-chain which user made the spend.

The fundamental principle of a joinpool-type system is therefore UTXO sharing to improve Bitcoin's scalability: rather than each participant owning one or more individual UTXOs, a single UTXO represents the funds of the entire group. Each member retains the ability to unilaterally withdraw their funds at any time, either via pre-signed transactions, or through mechanisms proposed at the protocol level such as covenants. Without covenants, the interactivity required between participants increases significantly, because any change to the state of the pool requires the signature of all members.

The Ark protocol can be considered a concrete implementation of the joinpool concept, where an *Ark Service Provider* acts as coordinator and liquidity provider for the participants of the pool.

This type of system is sometimes also referred to as a "*coinpool*" or "*payment pool*".

7b17d15d-8387-48c8-b040-f5a80da9bebf.title: WALLET FINGERPRINT
7b17d15d-8387-48c8-b040-f5a80da9bebf.body:
A set of distinctive characteristics observable in the transactions made by a single Bitcoin wallet. These characteristics can include similarities in the use of script types, address reuse, the ordering of UTXOs, the position of change outputs, RBF (*Replace-by-Fee*) signaling, the version number, the `nSequence` field and the `nLockTime` field. 

Wallet fingerprints are used by analysts to trace the activities of a particular entity on the blockchain by identifying recurring patterns in its transactions. For example, a user who systematically sends their change to P2TR addresses (`bc1p…`) creates a characteristic fingerprint that can be used to track their future transactions. 

As LaurentMT explains in Space Kek #19 (a French-language podcast), the usefulness of wallet fingerprints in chain analysis increases significantly over time. Indeed, the growing number of script types and the increasingly gradual rollout of these new features by wallet software accentuate the differences. It is even sometimes possible to identify exactly the software used by the traced entity. It must therefore be understood that studying a wallet's fingerprint proves particularly relevant for recent transactions, more so than for those initiated in the early 2010s.

7b4c45cc-e0ea-4806-a4a7-0bcb50322c99.title: ADDRESS REUSE
7b4c45cc-e0ea-4806-a4a7-0bcb50322c99.body:
Address reuse refers to the practice of using the same receiving address to lock several UTXOs, sometimes within several different transactions. Bitcoins are generally locked using a cryptographic key pair that corresponds to a unique address. Since the blockchain is public, it is easy to check which addresses are associated with how many bitcoins. When the same address is reused for several payments, one can reasonably assume that all the associated UTXOs belong to the same entity. Address reuse therefore poses a problem for the user's privacy. It makes it possible to draw deterministic links between several transactions and several UTXOs, as well as to perpetuate on-chain tracing of funds. Satoshi Nakamoto already mentioned this problem in his White Paper:

> “*As an additional firewall, a new key pair could be used for each transaction to keep them unlinked to a common owner.*” - Nakamoto, S. (2008). “Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System”. Retrieved from https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

To preserve a minimum of privacy, it is strongly advised to use each receiving address only once. For each new payment, a new address should be generated. For change outputs, a fresh address must also be used. Fortunately, thanks to deterministic and hierarchical wallets, it has become very easy to use a multitude of addresses. All the key pairs associated with a wallet can easily be regenerated from the seed. This is, incidentally, why wallet software always generates a new, different address for you when you click the “Receive” button.

7b64d41e-ef8b-4c4f-9b9e-60ab6bb8a089.title: ADDR.DAT
7b64d41e-ef8b-4c4f-9b9e-60ab6bb8a089.body: Name of the old file used in Bitcoin Core to store information about the network's peers (that is, nodes) with which the user's node has interacted or could potentially interact. This file has been replaced by the `peers.dat` file since version 0.7.0.

7b7cffc9-5562-449d-98fc-2877449883fe.title: PAYMENT HASH
7b7cffc9-5562-449d-98fc-2877449883fe.body: Cryptographic fingerprint of the *preimage* used to secure a payment on the Lightning Network. When a recipient creates an *invoice*, they generate a random secret (the *preimage*), compute its hash, and embed it in the *invoice*. The sender then builds a chain of HTLCs locked by this hash along the payment route. The payment is finalized only when the recipient reveals the corresponding *preimage*, allowing each intermediate node to unlock its funds in turn.

7b8faa3c-6623-4553-b276-f99f9ad92ebb.title: BITCOIN KEEPER
7b8faa3c-6623-4553-b276-f99f9ad92ebb.body: Open source Bitcoin wallet developed by BitHyve, specialized in multisig. The application allows creating multisignature vaults (*vaults*) by combining different hardware wallets and software keys. Bitcoin Keeper supports BIP-0085 for derivation of sub-wallets, purchasing bitcoins directly into cold storage, and automatic transfer to multisig vaults. It is available on mobile (iOS, Android) and on desktop.

7c040dbd-e3a1-4890-b3fb-7e447bafb51f.title: BIP-0300
7c040dbd-e3a1-4890-b3fb-7e447bafb51f.body:
Proposal by Paul Sztorc and CryptAxe defining the “*Hashrate Escrows*” mechanism (escrow by hashrate), which is the first technical building block of drivechains.

This BIP makes it possible to create sidechains whose two-way peg with Bitcoin is managed directly by miners, without relying on a federation of signers. The bitcoins sent to a sidechain are locked in a special output using `OP_DRIVECHAIN` (a redefinition of `OP_NOP5`). To withdraw funds to the main chain, a “*withdrawal bundle*” is proposed and then submitted to a miner vote spanning 26,300 blocks (about 6 months). Each miner can, block by block, vote in favor of a bundle, abstain, or trigger an alarm that reduces the score of all bundles. The withdrawal is executed only if the bundle reaches 13,150 votes in favor, which is about 50% of the hashrate over the period. This slowness is deliberate: it makes any theft attempt publicly visible for months, giving the community time to react.

BIP-0300 defines six consensus messages (M1 to M6) covering the proposal and activation of new sidechains, deposits and withdrawals.

This BIP has been the subject of significant debate: its supporters see it as a way to add features (privacy, smart contracts, scalability) on sidechains without modifying the base layer; its critics raise questions about the security model, since a 51% attack sustained for long enough could allow the theft of all of a sidechain's funds, and about a risk of mining centralization. BIP-0300 is therefore still in draft.

7d07c133-6a37-4f05-a218-b8225bf8eafe.title: M-OF-N
7d07c133-6a37-4f05-a218-b8225bf8eafe.body: Refers to a threshold multisig wallet or script. To strengthen the security of bitcoins, a threshold multisig security system can be used that requires `m` out of `n` signatures to be made in order to spend the funds. In an m-of-n, the letter `m` designates the required signature threshold and the letter `n` designates the total number of existing keys that can sign. For example, in a 2-of-3 configuration, two signatures out of the three possible are required to execute a transaction.

7d38b478-63c6-4c0d-b616-c42e7897158e.title: BIP-0351
7d38b478-63c6-4c0d-b616-c42e7897158e.body: Proposal for a private payment protocol using a payment code published by the recipient on the network. The payer derives a unique address for the recipient without prior interaction, using an encrypted notification transaction. BIP-0351 is an alternative approach to *silent payments* (BIP-0352), with different tradeoffs: it requires an *on-chain* notification transaction, but offers broader compatibility with existing wallets. Both proposals aim to eliminate address reuse while preserving the recipient's privacy.

7d7ea0c6-ff89-4f9f-9b31-c0f264739516.title: WHIRLPOOL STAT TOOL
7d7ea0c6-ff89-4f9f-9b31-c0f264739516.body: Command-line software developed by Samourai Wallet that provides the prospective and retrospective anonsets of a mixed coin within Whirlpool, as well as its diffusion rate in the pool. WST uses the HyperLogLogPlusPlus algorithm, which makes it possible to estimate the number of distinct values in a very large data set.

7dc4ec0f-1939-47c2-aa93-30ea0b716734.title: PREMIUM
7dc4ec0f-1939-47c2-aa93-30ea0b716734.body:
Additional amount paid above the standard or nominal price of an asset. In the context of Bitcoin, a premium can be observed in purchases, notably on exchange platforms, which can sometimes use this technique to make their margins on the brokerage service.

This notion of premium can also be found in peer-to-peer BTC purchases. Indeed, buying non-KYC bitcoins often comes with a premium over the standard market price, which can vary from 1% up to sometimes more than 10%. Several reasons explain this price difference. First, it is a common practice among P2P sellers that has become established over time. Second, sellers have fees associated with the transaction to send the funds to the buyer. There is also an increased risk of theft in P2P sales compared with transactions on regulated platforms, which justifies compensation for the risk taken. Finally, the extra cost may be linked to demand and to the quality of the exchange in terms of privacy. As a buyer, the privacy gain has a price that is reflected in the markup applied by the seller. Some bitcoiners also believe that the marked-up price of BTC bought P2P reflects its true price, and put forward the argument that the lower prices on regulated platforms are the result of a compromise on the privacy of your personal data.

7de0cee4-55d8-460c-98dc-d3fde5623e45.title: JIT ROUTING
7de0cee4-55d8-460c-98dc-d3fde5623e45.body:
Technique proposed by René Pickhardt in 2019 that allows a Lightning routing node to rebalance its channels on the fly in order to forward a payment that would otherwise have been rejected for lack of sufficient liquidity on the outgoing channel. The term "JIT" (*just-in-time*) indicates that the rebalancing is triggered at the precise moment the incoming HTLC arrives, and not preventively.

Concretely, when an intermediate node receives an HTLC to forward but lacks funds on the outgoing channel, it briefly suspends the relay and performs a circular payment through its other channels to move the necessary liquidity. The node exploits its local knowledge of the network to quickly compute low-cost rebalancing cycles. If the rebalancing succeeds and the fees incurred are lower than the routing fees collected, the operation is profitable.

*JIT routing* requires no protocol change: it is a local behavior that each routing node can adopt independently.

This mechanism should not be confused with *JIT channels*, which refer to the on-the-fly opening of a channel by an LSP.

7e06f113-180b-4d77-abda-2a5be7fa9a25.title: TAPROOT ASSETS PROTOCOL
7e06f113-180b-4d77-abda-2a5be7fa9a25.body:
A protocol developed by Lightning Labs that makes it possible to issue assets on the main Bitcoin blockchain, taking advantage of the Taproot update. Taproot Assets allows the creation of fungible assets such as stablecoins and non-fungible assets such as NFTs. Taproot Assets can be transferred via regular Bitcoin transactions or via the Lightning Network. This protocol uses *Merkle-Sum Sparse Merkle Trees* (MS-SMT), a sort of combination of MSTs and SMTs, to ensure the validity and auditability of the assets.

*Taproot Assets Protocol was previously called “TARO.”*

7e28ef78-21c7-4b7e-894e-ba67271d00dd.title: STANDARD TRANSACTION
7e28ef78-21c7-4b7e-894e-ba67271d00dd.body:
Bitcoin transaction that, in addition to complying with the consensus rules, also falls within the standardization rules configured by default on Bitcoin Core nodes. These standardization rules are enforced individually by each Bitcoin node, in addition to the consensus rules, to define the structure of the unconfirmed transactions it accepts into its mempool and broadcasts to its peers.

These rules are therefore configured and executed locally by each node and can vary from one node to another. They apply exclusively to unconfirmed transactions. Thus, a node will only accept a transaction it would judge non-standard if that transaction is already included in a valid block. 

Note that the majority of nodes leave the default configurations as pre-established in Bitcoin Core, which in effect creates a homogeneity of standardization rules across the network. A transaction that, although compliant with the consensus rules, does not comply with these standardization rules will have difficulty propagating on the network. It can nevertheless be included in a valid block if it ever reaches a miner. In practice, these transactions, described as non-standard, are often transmitted directly to a miner through channels external to Bitcoin's peer-to-peer network. This is often the only way to confirm this type of transaction. For example, a transaction that allocates no fees is both valid under the consensus rules and non-standard, because Bitcoin Core's default policy for the `minRelayTxFee` parameter is `0.000001` (in BTC/kvB).

7e465e8d-14c6-4cf8-845c-2b5b8793b29a.title: BIP-0038
7e465e8d-14c6-4cf8-845c-2b5b8793b29a.body:
Bitcoin improvement proposal that introduces an encryption mechanism to add extra protection to private keys through a passphrase. BIP-0038 ensures that even if a third party physically obtains the encrypted private key, they will not be able to use it without knowing its passphrase. This adds an additional layer of security to protect bitcoins against theft, notably for the security of old *paper wallets*.

*Although this proposal is referred to by the term “passphrase”, it is important not to confuse it with the passphrase presented in BIP-0039, the latter being, moreover, much more commonly used. The underlying concept nevertheless remains similar: whereas BIP-0038 aims to secure an individual private key, BIP-0039 provides protection for an entire HD wallet.*

7ebfb5c1-042b-4923-8247-0173ce946bb0.title: SEGWIT V0
7ebfb5c1-042b-4923-8247-0173ce946bb0.body: Post-SegWit script version 0. SegWit V0 scripts represent the first family of scripts introduced with the SegWit update of 2017. P2WPKH and P2WSH scripts embody the SegWit V0 version. The corresponding addresses always begin with `bc1q` and are encoded in `Bech32` format.

7edc3b23-3938-4f16-be67-06463d09a0ab.title: BITCOIN KNOTS
7edc3b23-3938-4f16-be67-06463d09a0ab.body:
Minority implementation of the Bitcoin protocol. Bitcoin Knots is an alternative to the reference software Bitcoin Core, offering a few different rules and features, while remaining compatible with other nodes. Knots is developed and maintained by Luke Dashjr.

![Bitcoin Knots logo, a minority implementation alternative to Bitcoin Core, maintained by Luke Dashjr.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/b/bitcoin-knots/assets/image-1.png)

7f0d503e-7a9e-4041-b270-825c014768cc.title: LIGHTNING LABS
7f0d503e-7a9e-4041-b270-825c014768cc.body: A company founded in 2016 by Elizabeth Stark and Olaoluwa Osuntokun, specializing in developing infrastructure for the Lightning Network. Lightning Labs is the main maintainer of LND, one of the most widespread implementations of the Lightning protocol. The company also develops an ecosystem of complementary tools: Lightning Loop for *submarine swaps*, Lightning Pool for liquidity, Faraday for node analysis, Lightning Terminal for the graphical interface, and the Taproot Assets protocol for issuing assets on Bitcoin.

7f453fdc-0ba2-473c-a590-28ffea271328.title: DIGITAL ARTIFACTS
7f453fdc-0ba2-473c-a590-28ffea271328.body: In the context of the Ordinals protocol, this is a sat that has been inscribed with specific data through the inscription mechanism. These artifacts can include images, texts, or any other type of digital content and are inseparably linked to the corresponding satoshi.

7f52a3da-6184-438d-9a2a-46101a4184ce.title: BIP-0113
7f52a3da-6184-438d-9a2a-46101a4184ce.body: Introduced a change in the computation of timelock operations based on `nLockTime` and `OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY`. It specifies that to evaluate the validity of these timelocks, they must now be compared with the MTP (*Median Time Past*), that is, the median of the timestamps of the last 11 blocks. Previously, only the timestamp of the current block was used. This method makes the system more predictable and prevents miners from manipulating the time reference. BIP-0113 was introduced via a soft fork on July 4, 2016 at the same time as BIP-0068 and BIP-0112, activated for the first time using the BIP-0009 method.

7f6464e3-87fa-402c-a686-bd2c14390b02.title: CANTILLON EFFECT
7f6464e3-87fa-402c-a686-bd2c14390b02.body:
An economic phenomenon described by the Irish-French economist Richard Cantillon in the 18th century, according to which the injection of new money into an economy does not spread uniformly. The first recipients of this newly created money (banks, financial institutions, states) can use it before prices rise, while the last to receive it (wage earners, savers, populations furthest from the banking system) suffer the price increase without having benefited from early access to this liquidity. This creates a hidden redistribution of wealth in favor of those who are close to the source of monetary issuance.

Bitcoin is sometimes presented as a response to this effect: its monetary issuance is programmed, predictable and governed by the protocol. The block subsidy, which decreases over the course of the halvings, is distributed to miners in return for work, without any central authority being able to decide to arbitrarily create new units. There is therefore no privileged intermediary able to capture the value of money creation before the rest of the network.

7f92f5dd-c22e-4ea9-a2fd-fa42a897e11b.title: BOLT-12
7f92f5dd-c22e-4ea9-a2fd-fa42a897e11b.body:
Specification that defines a Lightning payment negotiation protocol that is more flexible than BOLT-11. It introduces three concepts: *offers* (reusable payment templates that can be published via QR codes), *invoice requests* (invoice requests sent over the Lightning network in response to an offer), and the invoices themselves.

Unlike single-use BOLT-11 invoices, BOLT-12 *offers* can be reused indefinitely and remain stateless on the merchant side. The format replaces the *tagged fields* of BOLT-11 with a more extensible TLV (*Type-Length-Value*) encoding, while retaining a bech32-style encoding, supports selective disclosure of fields, allows cross-currency payments and improves privacy via *blinded paths* that hide the recipient's identity.

7fa80378-46ba-480a-b371-9d8a94c5bdfb.title: BLIP-0032
7fa80378-46ba-480a-b371-9d8a94c5bdfb.body:
bLIP that defines a private DNS resolution protocol via Lightning Network onion messages. It allows a node to resolve domain names into TXT records with DNSSEC proofs, without going through a public DNS server. The protocol introduces two onion message types: `dnssec_query` (resolution request) and `dnssec_proof` (response with cryptographic proof).

The main use case is resolving human-readable identifiers in the `utilisateur@domaine` format into payment instructions, integrating with BOLT-12 offers. The recipient publishes their payment instructions in a DNS TXT record, and the payer retrieves them via the Lightning network without exposing their request to the public DNS infrastructure, thus preserving their privacy.

7fadb20f-961a-468c-a1c2-c6b7194bfe37.title: RSK
7fadb20f-961a-468c-a1c2-c6b7194bfe37.body:
Bitcoin *sidechain* designed for the execution of *smart contracts* compatible with Ethereum. Initially known as Rootstock, this *sidechain* was renamed RSK before gradually reverting to the name Rootstock.

Launched in January 2018, RSK operates as a sidechain attached to Bitcoin through a *two-way peg* mechanism, which makes it possible to transfer bitcoins to the *sidechain* in the form of RBTC, tokens pegged 1:1 to bitcoin.

RSK uses *merged mining*: Bitcoin miners can simultaneously secure the RSK *sidechain* without requiring additional computing power. The objective is to extend Bitcoin's functionality through a Turing-complete programmable layer, while taking advantage of the security of Bitcoin's proof of work.

7fb1a439-d6ec-4999-8bb6-5c7e17b1b142.title: HRP - HUMAN READABLE PART
7fb1a439-d6ec-4999-8bb6-5c7e17b1b142.body:
The HRP, for “*Human Readable Part*”, is a component of bech32 and bech32m receiving addresses (SegWit v0 and SegWit v1). The HRP refers to the portion of the address that is specifically formatted to be easily read and interpreted by humans. Let's take the example of a bech32 Bitcoin address:

```text
bc1qar0srrr7xfkvy5l643lydnw9re59gtzzwf5mdq
```

In this address, the initial `bc` represents the HRP. This prefix makes it possible to identify at a glance that this string of characters presented to us is a Bitcoin address and nothing else.

7ff8a419-1f3b-47b1-9175-32be6fe2ad55.title: BLOCK SUBSIDY
7ff8a419-1f3b-47b1-9175-32be6fe2ad55.body: The quantity of new units that can be created by the miner who solves a block. This subsidy is part of the block reward, along with transaction fees. It is distributed within a specific transaction called the “coinbase.” Initially set at 50 bitcoins per block in 2009, this subsidy is halved every 210,000 blocks (roughly every four years) through a process known as the “halving.” When the subsidy falls below the amount of 1 sat, it will no longer be possible to collect it, and the block reward will rely solely on transaction fees. Unless the protocol is modified, the circulating money supply will then no longer be able to increase.

802d53d9-cc5b-4908-9d07-9d6fc4450db6.title: STAMPS
802d53d9-cc5b-4908-9d07-9d6fc4450db6.body: A protocol that makes it possible to embed formatted image data directly on the Bitcoin blockchain via raw multisignature transactions (P2MS). Stamps encodes the binary content of an image in base64 and adds it into the keys of a 1-of-3 P2MS. One key is real and is used to spend the funds, while the other two are fake keys (the associated private key is not known) that store the data. By encoding the data directly as public keys rather than using `OP_RETURN` outputs, images stored with the Stamps protocol are particularly intensive in terms of workload for nodes. This method notably creates multiple UTXOs, which increases the size of the UTXO set and poses problems for full nodes.

80877cba-3fa6-452f-8dfc-c78e6bcd6e51.title: ORDINALS THEORY
80877cba-3fa6-452f-8dfc-c78e6bcd6e51.body: A protocol external to Bitcoin that assigns serial numbers to sats (the smallest unit of bitcoin), which makes it possible to trace them individually and transfer them via Bitcoin transactions. According to Ordinals theory, each sat is numbered according to the order in which it was mined and is transferred on a FIFO (*First-In-First-Out*) basis. The goal of this theory is to make sats non-fungible according to their interpretation within the Ordinals protocol, in order to associate information with them such as images (NFTs) called "inscriptions".

80966d30-7cf6-4c23-94c3-b88b4e5b72b2.title: HTLC ENDORSEMENT
80966d30-7cf6-4c23-94c3-b88b4e5b72b2.body:
A local reputation mechanism on the Lightning Network designed to mitigate channel jamming attacks (*channel jamming*). Its principle consists of letting each routing node mark an incoming HTLC as “endorsed” or not, depending on the profitability history of the peer forwarding it.

When a node receives an HTLC from a peer that has proven reliable and profitable in the past, it can pass this endorsement on to the next hop. Endorsed HTLCs then benefit from priority access to two limited resources of each channel: HTLC *slots* (the maximum number of pending payments) and available liquidity. A share of these resources is reserved exclusively for endorsed HTLCs, while the rest remains accessible to all.

This mechanism creates an economic deterrent against attackers. A peer that carries out a *jamming* attack reduces its perceived profitability to its neighbors, which prevents its future HTLCs from obtaining endorsement and therefore access to the protected resources. Honest nodes, whose payments resolve normally, on the other hand keep their endorsement status. The approach is purely local: each node independently evaluates its peers, with no global reputation registry.

80d9e25b-b521-40cc-8884-c340734a8b2e.title: BIP-0067
80d9e25b-b521-40cc-8884-c340734a8b2e.body: Proposal specifying that the public keys within a P2SH multisignature `redeemScript` must be sorted in lexicographic order. This sorting guarantees that all cosigners generate the same multisig address, regardless of the order in which the keys are inserted when the script is created. Without this standard, different key orders would produce different `redeemScript` and therefore distinct addresses, preventing interoperability between wallet software.

80de0c03-0968-4e81-b248-3dee12138654.title: MEMPOOL PURGE
80de0c03-0968-4e81-b248-3dee12138654.body:
An event during which a Bitcoin node removes some of the pending transactions from its mempool. Each node maintains in memory a set of unconfirmed transactions, but this space is limited by resource constraints and by local policy rules. When certain conditions are met, the node performs a purge to free up space.

The most common cause is exceeding the maximum size allowed for the mempool. In Bitcoin Core, this limit is set by default to 300 MB via the parameter `maxmempool`. When this threshold is reached, the transactions that offer the lowest fee rate are evicted first in order to keep only those most likely to be included in an upcoming block. A transaction can also be purged if it remains pending too long without being confirmed. By default, this expiration period is 336 hours, or 14 days, via the parameter `mempoolexpiry`.

A purged transaction is not permanently canceled. It can be rebroadcast on the network by its sender or by another node that still holds it in its own mempool. The purge is a local resource management mechanism, and not a definitive rejection by the protocol.

81029dcb-7d82-4887-82d1-7d18e1c60515.title: TWEAK
81029dcb-7d82-4887-82d1-7d18e1c60515.body:
In the field of cryptography, "tweaking" a public key consists of modifying that key using an additive value called the "tweak" such that it remains usable with knowledge of the original private key and of the tweak. Technically, a tweak is a scalar value that is added to the initial public key. If `P` is the public key and `t` is the tweak, the tweaked public key becomes:
```math
P' = P + tG
```
Where `G` is the generator of the elliptic curve used. This operation makes it possible to obtain a new public key derived from the original key while retaining certain cryptographic properties that allow it to be used. For example, this method is used for Taproot (P2TR) addresses in order to be able to spend either by presenting a Schnorr signature in the traditional way, or by fulfilling one of the conditions set out in a Merkle tree, also called "MAST".

![Tweaked public key combining the key P and the root M of a MAST grouping four Taproot spending conditions A, B, C, D.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/t/tweak/assets/image-1.png)

814369ec-51cd-4bb2-a2ed-f4295ccd5760.title: TO MAP
814369ec-51cd-4bb2-a2ed-f4295ccd5760.body: In the context of computing, to map refers to the process of associating elements of one dataset with elements of another dataset in a systematic way. This association allows the data of the first set to be substituted for those of the second set or to transition from one to the other. This technique is often used in data transformation operations.

8166f422-ece4-415d-8b40-c1c3f7038c3a.title: CRYPTOLOGY
8166f422-ece4-415d-8b40-c1c3f7038c3a.body: Mathematical science that deals with cryptanalysis and cryptography.

82155f64-a605-4dd8-856b-0a7bc3dcef3c.title: BIP-0016
82155f64-a605-4dd8-856b-0a7bc3dcef3c.body: BIP-0016 introduced the concept of *Pay-to-Script-Hash* P2SH (“pay to the hash of the script”). Initially proposed in January 2012 then activated in April 2012, BIP-0016 aimed to simplify the use of transactions requiring complex scripts, such as multisignature transactions, by allowing users to pay to a *hash* of the script required to spend those bitcoins rather than to the script itself. This innovation made it possible to reduce the amount of data needed in the initial transaction, shifting the burden of providing the full script to the party spending the bitcoins. It also made it possible to reveal the script only when spending the bitcoins committed to the script, rather than upon receipt. BIP-0016 is of historical importance since it symbolizes one of the first major modifications of the Bitcoin protocol after Nakamoto's withdrawal in 2011. This BIP was the center of very tense debates that even led Gavin Andresen, Satoshi's successor as lead maintainer, to take a period of withdrawal. Many other proposals existed and some almost came to be activated instead of BIP-0016.

821a3106-3e96-4496-971e-53088dd91d81.title: PHOENIX
821a3106-3e96-4496-971e-53088dd91d81.body: *Self-custodial* mobile wallet software designed to simplify transactions on the Lightning protocol and make them more accessible. It allows users to manage their funds directly from their mobile devices without needing to connect to a separate Lightning node. Phoenix in fact works as a genuine standalone Lightning node on the phone (*lightning-kmp* implementation). It supports Bitcoin and Lightning transactions, and offers features to ease node management, such as automatic channel management with Acinq's node. Unlike other Lightning wallet applications, which are mostly custodial, Phoenix offers an interesting compromise by combining the use of a Lightning node with the convenience of a smartphone application. It is one of the best solutions that is simple to get started with for a beginner who wants to use Lightning while keeping full possession of their bitcoins (*self-custody*). Phoenix is a project developed and maintained by the French company Acinq.

823330ef-0599-47fa-b4b9-dc7206206888.title: POOL - LIGHTNING
823330ef-0599-47fa-b4b9-dc7206206888.body: Service developed by Lightning Labs. It is a kind of marketplace for liquidity in Lightning channels. Pool connects users who need access to liquidity on LN with those who have capital to deploy on the network​​. Participants can earn satoshis by opening new channels for those looking to receive funds on Lightning for a set period of time​​. Pool also makes it possible to rent a channel in order to instantly accept Bitcoin payments.

82a7f942-2049-4e83-8841-e88807cf61f4.title: REPLACEMENT CYCLING
82a7f942-2049-4e83-8841-e88807cf61f4.body:
An attack that exploits transaction replacement rules (RBF) to remove an unconfirmed transaction from the mempools of full nodes, without any alternative transaction taking its place. It mainly affects multi-party protocols that rely on CPFP to increase fees, such as the Lightning Network. This vulnerability was publicly disclosed in October 2023 by Antoine Riard (CVE-2023-40231 to CVE-2023-40234).

The attack unfolds in several cyclical steps. Bob broadcasts his unilateral exit transaction along with a child transaction for *fee bumping* via CPFP. Mallory responds by broadcasting her own competing exit transaction, which conflicts with Bob's since they spend the same inputs, along with a child transaction paying higher fees. Bob's transaction is replaced in the mempools. Mallory then replaces her own child transaction with a transaction unrelated to the channel, which causes her exit transaction to be evicted. The mempool then no longer contains any settlement transaction. Bob can rebroadcast, but Mallory repeats the cycle at each attempt, each iteration costing her a new UTXO or a higher fee rate.

This attack is particularly dangerous for Lightning Network HTLCs, which must be resolved within a defined time window. If the attacker prevents the victim from confirming their transaction before the deadline expires, they can appropriate the funds. Lightning Network implementations have deployed several mitigations: aggressive and frequent rebroadcasting of transactions, monitoring the local mempool to detect preimages before they are evicted, and increasing the CLTV expiry deltas (`cltv_expiry_delta`).

82ad621f-1e3f-4524-83a2-6a3cf4c873dd.title: ORANGE PILL
82ad621f-1e3f-4524-83a2-6a3cf4c873dd.body:
Inspired by the film *Matrix*, this imaginary pill awakens one to the awareness of Bitcoin. 

*Also used as a verb. To orange-pill someone = to enlist them into Bitcoin.*

82e67460-1685-4adb-bd93-982dfde2d6d1.title: SPY MINING
82e67460-1685-4adb-bd93-982dfde2d6d1.body:
A practice in which a miner or a mining pool connects to a competing pool in order to receive the block header hash as soon as a new block is discovered by that pool. By obtaining this information before it is broadcast on the network, the spy miner can immediately start mining on the new block, without waiting for the network to receive and fully validate it.

This technique provides an advantage of a few seconds over miners who wait for the normal propagation of the block. *Spy mining* is a common practice in the mining industry, which contributes to a competitive environment where pools compete not only with the rest of the network, but also with each other. It is often associated with *validationless mining*, because the spy miner starts working on a new block without having verified all of its transactions.

82f12ac3-08a9-4dcf-8c95-9bdd8350f7f8.title: BIT - UNIT
82f12ac3-08a9-4dcf-8c95-9bdd8350f7f8.body: In the context of Bitcoin, the term "bit" is also used to designate a monetary subdivision of bitcoin. One bit equals 100 satoshis, which represent the smallest indivisible unit of bitcoin. Thus, one bitcoin equals 1,000,000 bits or 100,000,000 satoshis. However, the use of this term as a monetary subdivision is controversial. The majority of bitcoiners use either "sats" or "btc", but not "bit".

831efe16-f1a1-444a-b6bf-00f3dc0945a1.title: ALTCOIN
831efe16-f1a1-444a-b6bf-00f3dc0945a1.body: Refers to any cryptocurrency other than bitcoin (BTC). The term "altcoin" is the contraction of "alternative" and "coin" (alternative coin). Some maximalist bitcoiners also use the term "shitcoins" to refer to altcoins.

83b0060e-baa1-4096-9c79-f9c84f33268a.title: MASTER KEY
83b0060e-baa1-4096-9c79-f9c84f33268a.body:
In the context of HD (hierarchical deterministic) wallets, the master private key is a unique private key derived from the wallet's seed. To obtain the master key, the `HMAC-SHA512` function is applied to the seed, literally using the words "*Bitcoin seed*" as the key. The result of this operation gives a 512-bit output, of which the first 256 bits constitute the master key, and the remaining 256 bits form the master chain code. The master key and the master chain code serve as the starting point for deriving all the child private and public keys in the tree structure of the HD wallet. The master private key is therefore at derivation depth 0.

![BIP-84 tree with an arrow pointing to the master key m, the single starting point of the entire HD derivation.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/cle-maitresse/assets/image-1.png)

8459c610-f4ef-49e8-8d2e-ba70c1eb8082.title: CRYPTOGRAPHY
8459c610-f4ef-49e8-8d2e-ba70c1eb8082.body: Discipline embodying the principles, means, and methods for transforming information, notably with mathematical techniques, in order to hide its semantic content, prevent its unauthorized use, ensure its authenticity, or prevent its undetected modification. Cryptography encompasses the use of hash functions, digital signatures, and encryption algorithms.

84c26c89-abcb-447e-a562-1823e94658af.title: GEOMETRIC METHOD
84c26c89-abcb-447e-a562-1823e94658af.body: A method of calculating miner compensation in the context of mining pools. This payment system is based on a score, designed to counter the *pool hopping* phenomenon. It ensures that the payment per submitted share remains constant, regardless of the time of submission. Miners accumulate scores, calculated with a decay factor, and payments are calculated at the end of the cycle. They are proportional to their score. This method involves variable and fixed fees for the miner and reduces the variance of payments per share.

84e637ac-b1a3-45c3-ab91-8960fe5f9b50.title: OP_VAULT - 0XBB
84e637ac-b1a3-45c3-ab91-8960fe5f9b50.body:
Opcode `0xbb` proposed in BIP-0345 for Tapscript, replacing `OP_SUCCESS187`. It constitutes the mechanism of a specialized covenant vault system, which makes it possible to impose a configurable delay before any spend, with the possibility of recovery in case of compromise.

The opcode consumes several elements from the stack (from the top down): a `<leaf-update-script-body>` that contains the body of the replacement script, a `<push-count>` that indicates the number of additional data elements, the corresponding data elements, a `<trigger-vout-idx>` that designates the index of the trigger output, a `<revault-vout-idx>` that designates the index of an optional “revault” output (`-1` if absent), and a `<revault-amount>` that specifies the amount in satoshis to place back into the vault. From these elements, the opcode builds a replacement script by prefixing the `<leaf-update-script-body>` with the provided data, then verifies that the trigger output has a taptree identical to that of the current input, except for the leaf being executed, which is replaced by this new script. This Taproot leaf substitution preserves all the other leaves, including the recovery path via `OP_VAULT_RECOVER` (`0xbc`).

The opcode records deferred checks to ensure that the value of the input is fully carried over between the trigger output and the possible “revault” output. This mechanism makes it possible to group several vault inputs in a single transaction. On success, the value `0x01` is pushed onto the stack. BIP-0345 has been closed and replaced by BIP-0443 (`OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY`), which is more general-purpose.

84f9a282-e3bd-413a-a47c-97bc74df01ba.title: RIOT PLATFORMS
84f9a282-e3bd-413a-a47c-97bc74df01ba.body: An American Bitcoin mining company listed on the NASDAQ under the symbol RIOT. Founded in 2000 in the biotechnology sector, it pivoted to Bitcoin mining in 2017 under the name Riot Blockchain, before being renamed Riot Platforms in 2023. The company owns and operates mining facilities in Texas and Kentucky, and is among the largest Bitcoin mining companies in the world in terms of hashrate. Riot also has engineering and manufacturing capabilities for electrical infrastructure through its subsidiary ESS Metron. The company is diversifying its activities toward hosting high-performance data centers for third-party customers.

853da785-8ace-4349-9a4e-8b8c5dcba606.title: CLIENT-SIDE VALIDATION
853da785-8ace-4349-9a4e-8b8c5dcba606.body: Process by which each party (client) verifies a set of privately exchanged data, according to the rules of a protocol. In the case of the RGB protocol, this exchanged data is grouped together in what are called consignments. Unlike the Bitcoin protocol, which requires all transactions to be published on-chain, RGB makes it possible to store publicly only commitments (anchored in Bitcoin), while the bulk of the contract information (transitions, attestations, proofs) remains off-chain, shared only between the users concerned.

85658840-7748-4054-980e-79474af562ed.title: OP_PUSHDATA2 - 0X4D
85658840-7748-4054-980e-79474af562ed.body: Makes it possible to push a large amount of data onto the stack. It is followed by two bytes (little-endian) that specify the length of the data to push (up to 65,535 bytes). It is used to insert larger data into scripts.

856af579-2bef-4d2a-97be-22e4f5b96762.title: SEEDSIGNER
856af579-2bef-4d2a-97be-22e4f5b96762.body:
*Open source* DIY (do-it-yourself) hardware wallet project based on a Raspberry Pi Zero, a screen and a camera. SeedSigner is designed to generate and handle Bitcoin private keys in an *air-gapped* manner and communicates exclusively via QR codes.

Its main characteristic is its “*stateless*” nature: the device keeps no data in memory between uses, which means that the mnemonic phrase must be entered each time it is used, by scanning a QR code. This approach eliminates the risk of keys being extracted from the device in the event of physical access.

The software is entirely *open source* and the cost of building it is fairly low, which makes it an accessible solution for signing transactions or managing a multisig. Since it can be assembled from general-purpose computer hardware, it is also an accessible solution for people living under an authoritarian regime.

858d0831-1f1e-4336-acb4-022fa80f3da9.title: ALUVM
858d0831-1f1e-4336-acb4-022fa80f3da9.body: Acronym for "*Algorithmic Logic Unit Virtual Machine*". A register-based virtual machine specifically designed for the deterministic execution of distributed computing tasks and the validation of *smart contracts*, notably within the framework of RGB contracts. AluVM was initially developed by Dr Maxim Orlovsky and is currently maintained by the LNP/BP Standards association.

85970e71-e724-4f30-96ef-d9c47c97d604.title: GRESHAM'S LAW
85970e71-e724-4f30-96ef-d9c47c97d604.body:
Economic principle according to which “bad money drives out good”. When two currencies circulate simultaneously with an imposed legal tender status, economic agents tend to hoard the one that retains its value and to spend first the one that is depreciating. The lower-quality currency then dominates exchanges, while the superior currency disappears from circulation.

This phenomenon was formulated by the English financier Thomas Gresham in 1558, in a letter to Queen Elizabeth I, to describe the state of degradation of English silver coins resulting from the Great Debasement carried out under Henry VIII and Edward VI (1544–1551). It has historically been observed whenever a state imposes an artificial parity between two forms of money: coins with a high precious metal content are melted down, exported or hoarded, while the debased coins continue to circulate.

In the context of Bitcoin, some invoke Gresham's law to explain why bitcoiners prefer to spend fiat currencies, perceived as depreciating, rather than their bitcoins, perceived as appreciating. According to this reading, bitcoin plays the role of the hoarded “good money”, and fiat currencies are spent first, which reinforces bitcoin's role as a store of value at the expense of its use as a means of payment.

However, this application is disputed. Strictly speaking, Gresham's law assumes an imposed legal tender status or a fixed exchange rate between the two currencies, a condition absent between bitcoin and fiat currencies, which trade freely on the markets. Moreover, other, more prosaic factors explain why bitcoin is little spent: in many jurisdictions, every spending of bitcoin constitutes a taxable event subject to capital gains tax, which discourages its everyday use; furthermore, the number of merchants accepting bitcoin remains very limited, making its use as payment simply impractical.

85c1539c-1704-4fcc-9cbb-51a322916743.title: CET
85c1539c-1704-4fcc-9cbb-51a322916743.body: Acronym for “*Contract Execution Transaction*”. It is a transaction specific to a DLC that allows the final settlement between the parties based on the outcome of a future event. When the oracle publishes a signature corresponding to the outcome of the event, the parties use this signature to complete and unlock the CET that sends the funds to the winning party. The signed CET is then broadcast on the network, and the winner receives the bitcoins owed to them according to the terms of the smart contract. All the other potential CETs, which would have been executed in the case of different outcomes, become obsolete and are abandoned.

85ce43a4-0206-4d90-9410-cc164fb1f8d1.title: RAPID GOSSIP SYNC
85ce43a4-0206-4d90-9410-cc164fb1f8d1.body:
A synchronization protocol for the Lightning channel graph that allows a node to catch up with the state of the network by downloading a compact snapshot from a server, rather than collecting *gossip* messages one by one through the peer-to-peer network.

An RGS server records channel announcements and updates, then computes a delta relative to the client's last synchronization. The format omits signatures and encodes data incrementally, which considerably reduces the volume transferred: a full snapshot of the graph takes up about 3.3 MB (1.5 MB compressed), a weekly synchronization about 566 KB, and a daily synchronization only 99 KB compressed.

Developed as part of LDK, this protocol targets mobile clients where bandwidth and synchronization time are limited. Route calculation remains on the client side, which preserves the user's privacy.

8624cbc4-668f-4497-99f2-f0e9e176e959.title: BIP-0132
8624cbc4-668f-4497-99f2-f0e9e176e959.body: Proposal to create a committee in charge of accepting or rejecting BIPs according to a structured voting process with appointed members. BIP-0132 was firmly rejected by the Bitcoin community, as it was judged incompatible with the project's decentralized governance. This BIP was closed.

868a3dc9-9013-43e9-b79a-0264681c2689.title: METADATA
868a3dc9-9013-43e9-b79a-0264681c2689.body: In the general field of computing, this refers to data that provides information about other data. It describes the characteristics, content, quality, format and structure of the data it accompanies. A distinction is thus made between the payload, which represents the core of the information, and the metadata. For example, for a document, the metadata may include the author, the creation date, the file size and the associated keywords. On Bitcoin, metadata can be found in many elements. It is used in receiving addresses, extended keys, blocks...

869781d6-ab34-4d30-b49e-d3a1bbe6b9a8.title: UNIX
869781d6-ab34-4d30-b49e-d3a1bbe6b9a8.body: Family of multitasking operating systems developed starting in 1969 by Bell Labs. Designed to be simple, flexible, and portable, UNIX has influenced many modern systems. Its fundamental principles include a hierarchical file structure, the use of shell scripts, and modular utilities. UNIX is the origin of many variants, including Linux, and remains a reference in terms of stability and performance.

869f42ba-ee24-4f5a-83cd-1c9b1f467004.title: OP_GREATERTHAN - 0XA0
869f42ba-ee24-4f5a-83cd-1c9b1f467004.body: Compares the two items at the top of the stack and checks whether the first item is greater than the second. If the first item is greater than the second, it pushes `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise, it pushes `0` (false).

86bd9870-a392-4090-8d80-818ac0f1265a.title: COINOS
86bd9870-a392-4090-8d80-818ac0f1265a.body: Web application (PWA) that allows sending, receiving and accepting bitcoin payments via on-chain, Lightning Network, Liquid and Ecash, directly from a browser. Coinos is aimed at individuals and merchants, with point-of-sale features and a Nostr integration. The platform is custodial.

872161af-ef17-48cb-949c-05b8a04b5c39.title: BIP-0049
872161af-ef17-48cb-949c-05b8a04b5c39.body: Specification BIP that introduces the derivation method used to generate Nested SegWit addresses in an HD wallet. The proposed derivation path follows the standards of BIP-0043 and BIP-0044, with the index `49'` (hardened derivation) at the purpose depth. For example, the first address of a P2SH-P2WPKH account would come from the path: `m/49'/0'/0'/0/0`. Nested SegWit scripts were invented at the launch of SegWit to facilitate its adoption. They make it possible to use this new standard, even on *wallets* that are not yet natively compatible with SegWit.

87e5d463-4b85-4278-9585-17b3dd3b1c2d.title: CAKE WALLET
87e5d463-4b85-4278-9585-17b3dd3b1c2d.body: An open source wallet available on iOS, Android, macOS, Linux and Windows, initially designed for Monero and later extended to Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies. CakeWallet stands out in the Bitcoin ecosystem for its integration of privacy features, notably support for *Silent Payments* and *Payjoin v2*. The wallet is non-custodial and allows the user to keep control of their private keys. It offers a built-in exchange service to convert between different cryptocurrencies, as well as native Tor integration to strengthen privacy at the network level.

8807d4ed-b2c0-4799-a461-fa0d16bb3fd2.title: SEIGNIORAGE
8807d4ed-b2c0-4799-a461-fa0d16bb3fd2.body:
Revenue that a currency issuer derives from the difference between the face value of the money produced and its cost of production. Historically, seigniorage referred to the profit made by the lord or sovereign when minting metal coins: the cost of the metal and of the minting was lower than the nominal value of the coin put into circulation.

In the modern fiat monetary system, seigniorage takes on considerable scale. Central banks create money at almost zero cost (by a simple accounting entry or by printing), while this money circulates at its nominal value. This mechanism constitutes a form of implicit taxation on holders of existing money, whose purchasing power is diluted by each new issuance.

In Bitcoin, there is no seigniorage in the traditional sense. The issuance of new bitcoins through the block subsidy does not benefit a central authority, but pays miners in return for a real cost: the energy and hardware needed for mining. Eventually, the block subsidy will be zero.

88128b2b-eec6-48aa-88da-f8469e794901.title: DB.LOG
88128b2b-eec6-48aa-88da-f8469e794901.body: A former BDB (*BerkeleyDB*) error file of the Bitcoin Core wallet, moved into the `wallets/` folder since version 0.16.

88591ac4-3272-439c-b5f7-68dc0d00a9c2.title: BIP-0171
88591ac4-3272-439c-b5f7-68dc0d00a9c2.body: Definition of a standard API format for Bitcoin exchange rate data, allowing applications to query different price providers in a uniform and interoperable way. BIP-0171 specified the REST *endpoints*, the JSON response formats and the supported currency pairs, aiming to standardize access to market data. This proposal was closed, as data providers developed their own APIs without adopting a common standard.

88aede57-688d-497e-a78c-64189019c9c8.title: BYZANTINE GENERALS PROBLEM
88aede57-688d-497e-a78c-64189019c9c8.body:
A problem first formulated by Leslie Lamport, Robert Shostak and Marshall Pease in the specialized journal *ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems, vol 4, no. 3* [“The Byzantine Generals Problem”](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/byz.pdf) in July 1982. It is used today to illustrate the challenges of decision-making when a distributed system cannot trust any actor.

In this metaphor, a group of Byzantine generals and their respective armies are camped around a city that they wish to attack or besiege. The generals are geographically separated from one another and must communicate by messenger to coordinate their strategy. Whether they attack or retreat does not matter, as long as all the generals reach a consensus. 

We can therefore consider the following requirements:
* Each general must make a decision: attack or retreat (yes or no);
* Once the decision is made, it can no longer be changed;
* All generals must agree on the same decision and carry it out in a synchronized manner.

Furthermore, a general can communicate with another only through messages carried by a courier, which may be delayed, destroyed, altered or lost. And even if a message manages to be delivered, one or more generals may choose (for whatever reason) to betray the established trust, send a fraudulent message, and sow chaos.

If we apply the dilemma to the context of the Bitcoin blockchain, each general represents a node of the network, which must reach a consensus on the state of the system. In other words, the majority of the participants in a distributed network must agree and carry out the same action in order to avoid a total failure. The only way to reach a consensus in this type of distributed system is to have more than 2/3 of the network nodes be reliable and honest. Therefore, if the majority of the network decides to act maliciously, the system is vulnerable.

*This dilemma is sometimes also called the “Consistent Broadcast Problem”.*

88d2ab79-5097-4421-99bb-d3e764b7fa1e.title: BIP-0327
88d2ab79-5097-4421-99bb-d3e764b7fa1e.body: Defines MuSig2, a multi-signature scheme in which *n* participants jointly produce a single Schnorr signature, indistinguishable *on-chain* from a classic individual signature. The protocol works in two rounds: an exchange of public *nonces*, then the generation of partial signatures which are combined into a final signature. Key aggregation is non-interactive: the aggregated public key can be computed by anyone from the individual public keys. MuSig2 thus enables an *n-of-n* *multisig* that appears as a single-key spend on the blockchain, which improves privacy and reduces transaction fees.

88f94710-2b5f-4f14-ad8a-7fd43565366a.title: BIP-0353
88f94710-2b5f-4f14-ad8a-7fd43565366a.body:
Bitcoin improvement proposal that defines a DNS-based resolution system for human-readable payment addresses. BIP-0353 makes it possible to associate an identifier in the format `utilisateur@domaine.com` with Bitcoin payment instructions, by storing this information in DNS TXT records, secured by DNSSEC.

Concretely, when a wallet receives an address such as `satoshi@example.com`, it makes a DNS query to:

```
satoshi.user._bitcoin-payment.example.com
```

This allows it to retrieve a payment URI in BIP-0021 format. This URI can contain an *on-chain* address, a BOLT-12 *offer* or instructions for *silent payments*, which makes the mechanism compatible with different payment protocols.

The main advantage is the user experience: addresses become memorable and reusable, without sacrificing privacy since the underlying protocols (BOLT-12, *silent payments*...) generate unique addresses/*invoices* for each payment. BIP-0353 was proposed by Matt Corallo and Bastien Teinturier in 2024.

8963c5d3-5902-46d0-b7a0-5e0d9c5a3872.title: BIP-0142
8963c5d3-5902-46d0-b7a0-5e0d9c5a3872.body: Proposal for an address format for SegWit based on the existing Base58Check encoding. BIP-0142 was superseded by Bech32 (BIP-0173), which offers better error detection, case insensitivity and optimized compatibility with QR codes. This address format was therefore never deployed on the Bitcoin network.

8963cdcc-4b1f-42d9-ad98-3009486408e2.title: BLOCKS/REV*.DAT
8963cdcc-4b1f-42d9-ad98-3009486408e2.body: Name of the files in Bitcoin Core that store the information needed to possibly undo the changes made to the UTXO set by previously added blocks. Each file is identified by a unique number that is the same as that of the blk*.dat file it corresponds to. The rev*.dat files contain the undo data corresponding to the blocks stored in the blk*.dat files. This data is essentially a list of all the UTXOs spent as inputs in a block. These undo files allow the node to return to an earlier state in the event of a blockchain reorganization causing previously valid blocks to be abandoned.

89e818b8-a68c-47b8-9d22-6e80cdae3f80.title: MINING POOL
89e818b8-a68c-47b8-9d22-6e80cdae3f80.body:
Refers to a group of miners who collaborate by combining their computing power to take part in the search for valid Proof-of-Work on Bitcoin. This pooling into a single organization is a solution to the growing difficulty of extracting bitcoins, which makes it too unlikely for an individual miner to compete and win rewards in a stable manner. Miners within a mining pool contribute with their machine to the search for valid shares. When a block is mined by the pool, the reward, which includes the newly created bitcoins as well as the transaction fees included in the block, is distributed among the members of the pool according to the chosen payout method. This distribution is proportional to the computing power that each miner has contributed.

By joining forces, miners within a pool increase their chances of finding blocks and thus reduce their variance. This makes it possible to ensure a more regular and predictable source of income compared to solo mining, where a miner may not win a reward for long periods. They can thus smooth their earnings, and therefore have better visibility on their activity, notably to cope with the various costs it entails.

*Note that the mining pool must not be confused with the mining farm.*

89f252be-530d-4502-ac02-552058abdc1c.title: OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY - 0XB2

8a115a8e-7017-49e3-b3fa-e8b98ef0f27f.title: ASSUME UTXO
8a115a8e-7017-49e3-b3fa-e8b98ef0f27f.body:
A feature of the main Bitcoin Core client that allows a newly initialized node (which has not yet done the IBD) to defer verification of the transactions and of the UTXO set before a given snapshot. The concept relies on the use of a UTXO set (list of all UTXOs existing at a given moment) loaded by the user via the RPC command `loadtxoutset` and presumed accurate after verification of its cryptographic fingerprint against a hash hardcoded in Core, which allows the node to be synchronized very quickly on the chain with the most accumulated work. Since the node skips the long IBD step, it is very quickly functional for its user. Assume UTXO splits synchronization (IBD) into two parts:
* First, the node performs the *Header First Sync* (verification of headers only) and it considers valid the UTXO set whose fingerprint matches the hash hardcoded in Core;
* Then, once it is functional, the node will verify the complete block history in the background, updating a new UTXO set that it will have verified itself. If the latter does not match the initially loaded UTXO set, it will provide an error message.

Assume UTXO therefore speeds up the preparation of a new Bitcoin node by deferring the verification process of the transactions and of the UTXO set thanks to a snapshot whose hash is hardcoded in Core.

8a746586-6b6c-4e67-9721-44abfae97ddd.title: TRANSACTION WITNESS
8a746586-6b6c-4e67-9721-44abfae97ddd.body:
Refers to a component of Bitcoin transactions that was moved with the SegWit soft fork in order to solve the problem of transaction malleability. The witness contains the signatures and public keys necessary to unlock the bitcoins spent in a transaction. In Legacy transactions, the witness was the sum of the `scriptSig` of all the inputs. In SegWit transactions, the witness is the sum of the `scriptWitness` of each input, and this part of the transaction is now moved into a separate Merkle tree within the block.

Before SegWit, signatures could be slightly modified without being invalidated before a transaction was confirmed, which changed the transaction identifier. This made it difficult to build various protocols, because an unconfirmed transaction could have its identifier changed. By separating the witnesses, SegWit makes transactions non-malleable, because any change in the signatures no longer affects the transaction identifier (TXID), but only the witness identifier (WTXID). In addition to solving the malleability problem, this separation makes it possible to increase the capacity of each block.

8a892c0f-ae57-4660-8503-6b2de283a801.title: REORGANIZATION
8a892c0f-ae57-4660-8503-6b2de283a801.body:
Refers to a phenomenon in which the blockchain undergoes a change in its structure because of the existence of competing blocks at the same height. This occurs when a portion of the chain of blocks is replaced by another chain with a greater amount of accumulated work.

These reorganizations are part of the natural functioning of Bitcoin, where different miners can find new blocks almost simultaneously, thus splitting the Bitcoin network in two. In such cases, the network can temporarily divide into competing chains. Eventually, when one of these chains accumulates more work, the other chains are abandoned by the nodes, and their blocks become what are called “stale blocks” or “orphan blocks”. This process of replacing one chain with another is the reorganization.

![Resynchronization at height 145: the 145-A chain is abandoned in favor of the 145-B branch that continues to 146.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/r/resynchronisation/assets/image-1.png)

Reorganizations can have various consequences. First, if a user had a transaction confirmed in a block that turns out to be abandoned, but that transaction is not found in the chain that ultimately prevails, then their transaction becomes unconfirmed again. This is why you are advised to always wait for at least 6 confirmations before considering a transaction truly immutable. Past a depth of 6 blocks, reorganizations are so improbable that the chance of one occurring can be considered nil.

Next, at the level of the overall system, reorganizations imply a waste of miners' computing power. Indeed, when a split occurs, some of the miners will be on chain `A`, and another part on chain `B`. If chain `B` is ultimately abandoned during a reorganization, then all the computing power deployed by miners on that chain is by definition wasted. If there are too many reorganizations on the Bitcoin network, its overall security is therefore reduced. This is notably, in part, the reason why increasing the block size or reducing the interval between each block (10 minutes) can be dangerous.

*Some bitcoiners prefer to speak of an “orphan block” to refer to a stale block. Also, even though it is an anglicism, people sometimes prefer in everyday language to speak of a “reorganization” or a “reorg” rather than a “resynchronization”.*

8b418ff2-484f-4f9f-934f-1377161f39aa.title: PASSPORT
8b418ff2-484f-4f9f-934f-1377161f39aa.body: *Hardware wallet* made by the American company Foundation Devices, designed exclusively for Bitcoin. The Passport is a fully *air-gapped* device that communicates with wallet software via a camera and QR codes, with no wired connection for signing transactions. It incorporates a *secure element* and its *firmware* is *open source*. The device has a color screen and a directional pad, and is powered by a removable lithium-ion battery in the Nokia BL-5C format. The Passport works with the Envoy companion app, as well as with third-party software such as Sparrow Wallet.

8b832db5-72b6-4d19-b8e9-4063b696bfac.title: BIP-0074
8b832db5-72b6-4d19-b8e9-4063b696bfac.body: Extension of the BIP-0070 payment protocol making it possible to include zero-value `OP_RETURN` outputs in payment requests. BIP-0074 aimed to allow the embedding of arbitrary data (metadata, order identifiers, proofs) in the transactions generated by the payment protocol, without destroying funds in these outputs. It was unanimously rejected by the community (*Unanimously Discourage for implementation*), its official status being *Rejected*.

8b83d40b-642e-41b1-b4ef-df25dc93d1c3.title: ELTOO
8b83d40b-642e-41b1-b4ef-df25dc93d1c3.body:
A general-purpose protocol for Bitcoin second layers that makes it possible to define how to jointly manage the ownership of a UTXO. Eltoo was designed by Christian Decker, Rusty Russell and Olaoluwa Osuntokun, notably to solve the problems associated with the mechanisms for negotiating the state of Lightning channels, that is, between opening and closing. The Eltoo architecture simplifies the negotiation process by introducing a linear state management system, replacing the penalty-based approach with a more flexible and less punitive update method. This protocol requires the use of a new type of SigHash that makes it possible to take no input into account in the signature of a transaction. This SigHash was first called `SIGHASH_NOINPUT`, then `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` (*Any Previous Output*). Its implementation is planned in BIP-0118.

*Eltoo is sometimes also called "LN-Symmetry".*

8b8e6740-6ec6-46e1-a2cf-5c29706a4d57.title: OP_NOP - 0X61
8b8e6740-6ec6-46e1-a2cf-5c29706a4d57.body:
Has no effect on the stack or the script state. It performs no movement, no verification, and no modification. It simply does nothing, unless it has been decided otherwise through a soft fork. Indeed, since their modification by Satoshi Nakamoto in 2010, the `OP_NOP` (`OP_NOP1` (`0XB0`) through `OP_NOP10` (`0XB9`)) commands have been used to add new opcodes as soft forks. 

Thus, `OP_NOP2` (`0XB1`) and `OP_NOP3` (`0XB2`) have already been used to implement `OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY` and `OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY` respectively. They are used in combination with `OP_DROP` in order to remove the associated time values from the stack, and thus be able to continue script execution, whether the node is up to date or not. The `OP_NOP` therefore make it possible to insert a breakpoint in a script to check additional conditions that already exist or that could be added with future soft forks. Since Tapscript, the use of `OP_NOP` has been replaced by the use of `OP_SUCCESS`, which is more efficient.

8bb02eb3-92a6-4720-8b52-782bfe0517f2.title: HALVING

8bc4de15-c622-4d25-8fd2-7347d43f5f80.title: FPPS - FULL PAY PER SHARE
8bc4de15-c622-4d25-8fd2-7347d43f5f80.body: Method of calculating miner remuneration in the context of mining pools. It is an evolution of the PPS (*Pay Per Share*) method. It pays miners not only for each valid share they submit, but also includes a portion of the transaction fees. The remuneration is calculated on the basis of the previous average transaction fees and the pool's hashrate. Thus, miners receive payment for the shares submitted, whether or not a block is found, but this method also pays for the expected value. It offers stable and predictable remuneration for miners, because it eliminates the variance linked to the probability of finding a block, while exposing them to fluctuations in the fee market. However, it is riskier for pool operators, because they must pay the miners even when no block is found, thus absorbing the variance risk.

8bca8bc5-c1b7-4c8c-9fa1-913ce3c086c3.title: CHACHA20-POLY1305
8bca8bc5-c1b7-4c8c-9fa1-913ce3c086c3.body:
An authenticated encryption algorithm with associated data that combines the ChaCha20 stream cipher and the Poly1305 message authentication code. It takes as input a 256-bit key and a 96-bit nonce, and produces a ciphertext accompanied by a 128-bit authentication tag that guarantees both the integrity and the authenticity of the data.

In the Bitcoin ecosystem, ChaCha20-Poly1305 is used in the P2P v2 transport protocol (BIP-0324) to encrypt communications between nodes of the network. It is also used in the transport layer of the Lightning Network (BOLT-08), where the Noise framework uses it to encrypt and authenticate the messages exchanged between peers after the initial *handshake*.

8bf549d4-8a74-4e5d-b8f5-d9a463ff8609.title: LEGAL TENDER
8bf549d4-8a74-4e5d-b8f5-d9a463ff8609.body:
Legal status assigned to a currency by a state, which obliges any creditor to accept it as payment of a debt. A currency that is legal tender cannot be refused for the settlement of an obligation denominated in the national currency.

In September 2021, El Salvador became the first country to grant legal tender status to bitcoin alongside the US dollar. This decision provoked mixed reactions: some bitcoiners see it as a precedent for Bitcoin adoption, while others criticized the obligation imposed on merchants to accept it, which has since been abandoned.

8c16730a-03a0-43ea-b175-5000922bb022.title: STATE TRANSITION
8c16730a-03a0-43ea-b175-5000922bb022.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the *State Transition* refers to the operation that makes it possible to evolve a contract's state toward a new configuration. It can modify both the data of the *Global State* and that of the *Owned States*. Each transition is strictly verified according to the rules defined in the contract's *Schema*, which guarantees that the modifications comply with the constraints established during the *Genesis*. This operation is anchored in the Bitcoin blockchain via a *commitment*.

8c84c99c-fc27-4a7f-bdf7-b731df6adb01.title: NOSTR EVENT
8c84c99c-fc27-4a7f-bdf7-b731df6adb01.body:
Fundamental unit of data in the Nostr protocol. Any information transmitted on the Nostr network (text post, profile update, reaction, encrypted message, zap receipt...) takes the form of an event. An event is a JSON object containing seven fields:
* `id`: a unique identifier obtained by SHA-256 hashing of the serialized content,
* `pubkey`: the author's public key,
* `created_at`: the Unix timestamp,
* `kind`: the event type identified by an integer,
* `tags`: the structured metadata used to mention users, reference other events or add hashtags,
* `content`: the text content,
* `sig`: the Schnorr signature on secp256k1.

The `kind` field determines the nature of the event: kind 0 for profile metadata, kind 1 for text notes, kind 4 for encrypted direct messages, kind 7 for reactions or kind 9735 for zap receipts. Relays verify the signature before accepting an event, which guarantees the authenticity and integrity of the data.

8cc61c1e-719f-47a5-b4b3-e88aaa2b231c.title: BIP-0155
8cc61c1e-719f-47a5-b4b3-e88aaa2b231c.body: Bitcoin improvement proposal introducing a new format for messages that relay addresses of nodes that accept incoming connections. This proposal makes it possible to support larger addresses, notably to facilitate the integration of network protocols such as Tor V3 or I2P, whose addresses are longer than those supported by the old `addr` message. This improvement is also known as `addrv2`.

8d3a239d-77dd-4ceb-bc98-09590984cb2e.title: BIP-0019
8d3a239d-77dd-4ceb-bc98-09590984cb2e.body: Proposal for a variant of M-of-N *multisig* transactions with a reduced cost in signature verification operations (*sigops*). BIP-0019 was superseded by P2SH (BIP-0016), which offers a more general and more flexible solution for encapsulating complex scripts, including *multisig*, in a script hash address.

8d72bfe8-0405-45a9-a071-9599d05295e6.title: TAGGED HASH FUNCTION
8d72bfe8-0405-45a9-a071-9599d05295e6.body:
Variant of a hash function used in the Bitcoin protocol (notably in Taproot) to ensure domain separation. A tagged hash function takes a tag (a UTF-8 character string) and data as input, and computes the hash as follows:
```math
TaggedHash(tag,\ data) = SHA256(SHA256(tag)\ \Vert\ SHA256(tag)\ \Vert\ data)
```
Prefixing the data with the double hash of the tag ensures that hashes computed in different contexts cannot collide. For example, a hash computed with the tag `TapLeaf` can never be identical to a hash computed with the tag `TapBranch`, even if the data is the same.

This mechanism was introduced by BIP-0340 and is used across all the BIPs related to Taproot (BIP-0341 and BIP-0342). Each step in the construction and spending of a P2TR output uses a distinct tag: `TapLeaf` for the leaves of the script tree, `TapBranch` for the branches, `TapTweak` for the tweak calculation, and `TapSighash` for the creation of the signature hash. BIP-0340 also uses tags for Schnorr signatures: `BIP0340/challenge`, `BIP0340/aux` and `BIP0340/nonce`.

8db351d3-5051-4884-8205-07d2a0cc178c.title: WIF - WALLET IMPORT FORMAT
8db351d3-5051-4884-8205-07d2a0cc178c.body: Method for encoding a Bitcoin private key so that it can be imported or exported more easily between different wallets. WIF is built on a `Base58Check` encoding, which includes information about the version, the compression of the corresponding public key and a checksum for detecting input errors. A WIF private key begins with the characters `5` for uncompressed keys, or `K` and `L` for compressed keys, and contains all the characters needed to reconstruct the original private key. The WIF format provides a standardized way to transfer a private key between different wallet software.

8e0e1e56-256c-40d8-a7b0-6502a8e92c51.title: BIP-0389
8e0e1e56-256c-40d8-a7b0-6502a8e92c51.body: Proposal extending output script descriptors with multipath key expressions (*multipath key expressions*) using the syntax `<M;N>`. For example, `<0;1>` in a derivation path makes it possible to represent both receiving addresses (index 0) and change addresses (index 1) within a single descriptor. Without this extension, two separate descriptors would be needed for the same wallet. BIP-0389 thus simplifies wallet backup by reducing it to a single string containing all the information needed to reconstruct the addresses.

8e6281fa-a934-4a2d-b8d2-8025e1574479.title: BTG - BITCOIN GOLD
8e6281fa-a934-4a2d-b8d2-8025e1574479.body:
Cryptocurrency system created from a *hard fork* of Bitcoin (BTC), which took place on October 24, 2017 at block 491,407. The fork was initiated by a group of developers and investors dissatisfied with the direction Bitcoin had taken, in particular regarding the growing concentration of mining power in the hands of a few large farms using ASICs. Bitcoin Gold wanted to democratize the mining process by using a new proof-of-work algorithm, named *Equihash*, which is ASIC-resistant and therefore favors mining with graphics cards (GPUs). The goal was to make participation in mining accessible to more people in order to decentralize it and reduce the risks linked to centralization. BTG initially used the same mining algorithm as Zcash (ZEC), namely Equihash with the parameters (200,9). In June 2018, they modified it to adopt Equihash-BTG, a variant with the parameters (144,5), in order to strengthen ASIC resistance.

*Note that the altcoin Bitcoin Gold (BTG) should not be confused with bit gold, Nick Szabo's concept.*

8e7c4f45-7a02-4291-aa1f-8d8fee4530b6.title: LIGHTNING CHANNEL CAPACITY
8e7c4f45-7a02-4291-aa1f-8d8fee4530b6.body: The quantity of bitcoins locked in a multisig address that represents a payment channel on the Lightning Network. A channel's capacity is therefore the maximum quantity of sats that can be transmitted through that specific channel. It is defined at the time the channel is created by the sum of the funds the parties commit to the channel. The “*inbound capacity*”, or “incoming capacity”, refers to the maximum quantity of bitcoins a node can receive through a channel. The “*outbound capacity*”, or “outgoing capacity”, represents the maximum quantity of bitcoins a node can send through a specific channel.

8e8ab79e-dd0d-4087-8a88-78e9363f1f9e.title: SCRIPTWITNESS
8e8ab79e-dd0d-4087-8a88-78e9363f1f9e.body:
Element in the inputs of SegWit transactions that contains the signatures and public keys necessary to unlock the bitcoins sent in the transaction. Similar to the `scriptSig` of Legacy transactions, the `scriptWitness` is however not placed in the same location. Indeed, it is this part, called the "witness" ("*witness*" in English), that is moved into a separate data structure in order to solve the problem of transaction malleability. Each SegWit input has its own `scriptWitness`, and all the `scriptWitness` together form the `Witness` field of the transaction.

*Be careful not to confuse the `scriptWitness` with the `witnessScript`. While the `scriptWitness` contains the witness data of any SegWit input, the `witnessScript` defines the spending conditions of a P2WSH or P2SH-P2WSH UTXO and constitutes a script in its own right, in the manner of the `redeemScript` for a P2SH output.*

8e8c8156-ba4a-44c5-8f56-ffe6f72f28fd.title: REUSABLE PAYMENT CODE

8eb4d5df-2d8e-48ff-80f8-680a6a110d5d.title: NODE
8eb4d5df-2d8e-48ff-80f8-680a6a110d5d.body:
In the Bitcoin network, a node is a computer that runs a client of the Bitcoin protocol (such as Bitcoin Core, for example). It participates in the network by maintaining a copy of the blockchain, by relaying and verifying transactions and new blocks and, optionally, by taking part in the mining process. The sum of all Bitcoin nodes represents the Bitcoin network itself.

There are several types of nodes on Bitcoin, including full nodes and lightweight nodes. Full nodes keep a complete copy of the blockchain, verify all transactions and blocks according to the consensus rules, and actively participate in the broadcasting of transactions and blocks on the network. By contrast, lightweight nodes, or SPV nodes (*Simple Payment Verification*), keep only the block headers and rely on full nodes to obtain information about transactions. 

*Some people also distinguish so-called "pruned" nodes ("*pruned node*" in English). These are full nodes, which download and verify all blocks since the Genesis block, but which keep only the most recent blocks in memory.*

8ecc8eda-eea3-486e-9e51-63171fe73ef3.title: PRAXEOLOGY
8ecc8eda-eea3-486e-9e51-63171fe73ef3.body:
General science of human action, developed by Ludwig von Mises within the framework of the Austrian School of economics. Praxeology studies intentional, goal-directed behavior. It rests on a fundamental axiom: the individual acts deliberately to move from a state they judge less satisfactory to a state they perceive as better. This axiom is considered irrefutable, because any attempt to contradict it is itself an action, which validates it. Economics, as catallactics, is a branch of praxeology.

The praxeological method is axiomatic and deductive: it starts from propositions considered true a priori in order to logically deduce economic laws from them, without resorting to empirical experimentation or econometrics. This approach is radically distinct from the positivism of other economic schools of thought. It implies, in particular, that prices, money and economic cycles are analyzed as phenomena emerging from individual action, and not as statistical aggregates.

In the Bitcoin ecosystem, praxeology is often invoked to analyze bitcoin as an emergent money, whose adoption and value stem from the voluntary choices of individuals acting in their own interest, without central planning.

8ed8e9c4-aab0-427d-8a83-3f36e3a320e6.title: PASSPHRASE - BIP-0039
8ed8e9c4-aab0-427d-8a83-3f36e3a320e6.body:
Optional password that, combined with the recovery phrase, provides an additional layer of security for deterministic and hierarchical Bitcoin wallets. HD wallets are generally generated from a recovery phrase made up of 12 or 24 words. This recovery phrase is very important, because it makes it possible to restore all of a wallet's keys in case of loss. However, it is a single point of failure (SPOF).
