If it is compromised, the bitcoins are at risk. This is where the passphrase comes in. It is an optional password, chosen by the user, that is added to the recovery phrase to strengthen the wallet's security. Not to be confused with a PIN code or an ordinary password, the passphrase plays a role in the derivation of the cryptographic keys. 

It works in tandem with the recovery phrase, modifying the seed from which the keys are generated. Thus, even if someone obtains your recovery phrase, without the passphrase they cannot access your funds. Using a passphrase essentially creates a new wallet with distinct keys. Changing the passphrase (even slightly) will generate a different wallet.

The passphrase is arbitrary and can be any combination of characters chosen by the user. Using a passphrase offers several advantages. First, it reduces the risks linked to the compromise of the recovery phrase by requiring a second factor to access the funds. Second, it can be used strategically to create decoy wallets containing small amounts of bitcoins, in the event of physical coercion to steal your funds. Finally, its use is valuable when you want to control the randomness of the generation of the HD wallet's seed. The passphrase must be complex enough to resist brute-force attacks and must be backed up reliably. Losing the passphrase can result in the inability to access the funds, just like losing the recovery phrase.

*The passphrase is sometimes also called: “two-factor seed phrase”, “password”, “seed extension”, “extension word”, or even “13th or 25th word”. Note that there are two types of passphrases on Bitcoin. The best known is the one described above, which depends on BIP-0039, and which makes it possible to secure an entire HD wallet. However, BIP-0038 had also specified a way to secure a single private key using a passphrase. This second type of passphrase is almost no longer used today.*

8edc2ca4-ee02-42e0-bb0e-1685ca749da2.title: AGORISM
8edc2ca4-ee02-42e0-bb0e-1685ca749da2.body: A political philosophy founded by Samuel Edward Konkin III in the 1970s. It is an extension of libertarianism, emphasizing direct action to break free from the yoke of state authority through counter-economics, an economic practice that takes place outside the frameworks regulated by the government. Agorist ideology rests on natural law theory, which asserts that individuals' natural rights are superior to laws imposed by the State. This includes the primacy of private property, respect for physical integrity, and the freedom to contract. Agorists reject any form of traditional political participation such as voting, which they consider a validation of the State's coercive authority. They aspire to a society where economic and social exchanges take place freely in an open market, called the Agora, thus aiming at a peaceful revolution to gradually erode the power of the State. Their emblem is, moreover, “A3”, for “Agora, Anarchy, Action”. The principle of agorism is described in the *New Libertarian Manifesto* published in 1980. This paper is built upon Murray Rothbard's *Libertarian Manifesto*, but it goes even further. Many bitcoiners claim to be agorists and think that Bitcoin is the perfect tool for it.

8f17833c-f095-4d3a-a900-6a8479209a45.title: BIP-0047
8f17833c-f095-4d3a-a900-6a8479209a45.body: Proposed by Justus Ranvier in 2015, this protocol aims to solve the critical problem of Bitcoin address reuse, a practice that seriously compromises users' privacy on the system. Satoshi Nakamoto, in the Bitcoin White Paper, had already emphasized the importance of using a distinct key pair for each transaction in order to maintain segregation between users' different actions. BIP-0047 introduces the concept of reusable payment codes, allowing a user to receive multiple payments without having to manually generate a new Bitcoin address for each transaction. These codes act as virtual identifiers, derived from the user's wallet seed and located at the account level in the derivation structure of an HD wallet. From the combination of the payment codes of the 2 parties, each can derive a large number of unique addresses belonging to the other party, without needing to communicate with them again. The core of this protocol relies on the ECDH (*Elliptic-Curve Diffie-Hellman*) algorithm, a variant of the Diffie-Hellman key exchange built on elliptic curves, which allows both parties to establish a shared secret for generating unique receiving addresses. Although BIP-0047 was not added to Bitcoin Core and received a mixed reception from the community, implementations such as PayNym on Samourai Wallet and Sparrow Wallet adopted it and fully integrated it into their ecosystem of privacy tools.

8f650347-c872-4bcd-a960-d2aafeeb68f7.title: PARTITION TOLERANCE
8f650347-c872-4bcd-a960-d2aafeeb68f7.body: The ability of the Bitcoin network to remain unified and to maintain consensus among users, by maintaining connections and avoiding the separation of certain nodes from the rest of the network, despite attempts to fragment it. For a node to remain in consensus with the network, it must maintain at least one active connection with a set of peers sharing the same consensus rules.

8fa9cf51-8a65-4a4f-a7c2-f33708cc678d.title: ELEMENTS
8fa9cf51-8a65-4a4f-a7c2-f33708cc678d.body:
An open source blockchain platform for deploying federated sidechains pegged to Bitcoin or standalone blockchains. Launched in June 2015, Elements is built on the Bitcoin Core code and extends it with advanced features: *Confidential Transactions* (hidden amounts and asset types), *Issued Assets* (issuance of several types of assets on the same chain), additional opcodes and *Federated Peg* (two-way peg with Bitcoin via a federation of signers).

Consensus relies on blocks signed by a federation of participants with aligned interests, which eliminates the risk of multi-block reorganizations and speeds up transaction finality compared to proof-of-work mining. Liquid Network, the most widely used sidechain in the Bitcoin ecosystem, is the main production implementation of Elements.

9002599e-b839-48e6-9520-a06828c03420.title: CHANNEL RESERVE
9002599e-b839-48e6-9520-a06828c03420.body:
The minimum amount that each party of a Lightning channel must keep on their side and cannot spend. This reserve guarantees that each participant always has something to lose in the event of an attempted fraud, which makes penalty transactions economically dissuasive.

When a channel is opened, each node imposes a *channel reserve* on its peer, generally set at 1% of the channel capacity (with a floor of 546 satoshis, corresponding to the *dust limit*). For example, in a channel of 1,000,000 sats, each party must maintain at least 10,000 sats on their side. This threshold is defined in the `channel_reserve_satoshis` field during channel negotiation (BOLT-02).

The *channel reserve* slightly reduces the effectively usable capacity of a channel. In the v1 protocol, it can be asymmetric, with each side able to impose a different amount. In the case of *dual funding* (v2), the reserve is set at 1% of the channel's total balance for both parties and is no longer negotiable.

90303bd0-3bc8-4a0f-b0c9-e90206f5af07.title: BCH CODE
90303bd0-3bc8-4a0f-b0c9-e90206f5af07.body:
Class of error-correcting codes used to detect and correct errors in a data sequence. In other words, BCH error-correcting codes make it possible to find and correct random errors in transmitted information, in order to ensure that it arrives intact at its destination. The acronym “BCH” stands for the initials of the names of the inventors of these codes: Bose, Ray-Chaudhuri, and Hocquenghem.

This tool is used in many areas of computing, notably in SSDs, DVDs and QR codes. For example, thanks to these error-correcting codes, even if a QR code is partially covered, it is still possible to recover the information it encodes.

In the context of Bitcoin, BCH codes are used for the checksum in the Bech32 and Bech32m address formats (native SegWit). They represent a better compromise between size and error-detection capability for the checksum compared with the simple hash functions previously used on Legacy addresses. In the context of Bitcoin, BCH codes are used only for error detection, not for error correction. Thus, Bitcoin wallet software will identify and report to the user any error in a receiving address, but will not modify the incorrect address automatically. This choice is motivated by the fact that integrating error correction inevitably affects the algorithm's error-detection capabilities.

90d2262c-24cb-4e14-9de2-321548de7541.title: STEGANOGRAPHY
90d2262c-24cb-4e14-9de2-321548de7541.body: Steganography is a technique consisting of concealing sensitive information within a seemingly innocuous cover object or medium (typically a signal such as text, sound, image, video, Bitcoin transaction, etc.), which will not arouse suspicion even if it is in plain sight; only a legitimate recipient will know that there is information there for them and where to look for it.

911e17ef-1a6f-4838-b798-28cb96e56674.title: COINJOIN COORDINATOR
911e17ef-1a6f-4838-b798-28cb96e56674.body: Central server that connects users wishing to do coinjoins and coordinates the construction of collaborative transactions, without being able to link the inputs to each user's specific outputs. This is possible through the use of Chaum blind signatures and the Tor network. Unlike a traditional bitcoin mixer, the coinjoin coordinator never takes possession of the participants' bitcoins and is not able to link the inputs and the outputs.

9134ec46-cc0f-429f-ae9f-71524d8aa4af.title: BITCOIN CORE
9134ec46-cc0f-429f-ae9f-71524d8aa4af.body:
Bitcoin Core is the reference *open-source* software for the Bitcoin system, and is the main implementation of the Bitcoin protocol to date. It is developed and maintained by a large group of volunteer contributors. Initially named "Bitcoin Qt", it is the third client in Bitcoin's history after Bitcoin, by Satoshi Nakamoto, and Bitcoind. It was developed from Satoshi's original code and introduced a graphical user interface. Moreover, even today, the graphical interface of Bitcoin Core is called `bitcoin-qt`. It has been shipped with `bitcoind` since version 0.5. The Bitcoin Core software serves several purposes. First, it acts as a full node client. Bitcoin Core also includes a wallet (*wallet*) for users who wish to store, manage and make transactions directly with Bitcoin Core.

![Official Bitcoin Core logo, the reference implementation of the Bitcoin protocol maintained by volunteer contributors.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/b/bitcoin-core/assets/image-1.png)

9177a343-e1d2-4f83-8170-7f2cd91c6e23.title: OP_DEPTH - 0X74
9177a343-e1d2-4f83-8170-7f2cd91c6e23.body: Pushes the number of items in the stack onto the stack itself. If the stack contains `N` items, `OP_DEPTH` will add the number `N` as a new item at the top of the stack.

91889163-76d1-4635-a75e-dd12c7805961.title: ON-GRID
91889163-76d1-4635-a75e-dd12c7805961.body:
Refers to a Bitcoin mining operation that is connected to the general electrical grid. *On-grid* miners plug into the conventional electrical grid, also used by residential consumers, to power their ASICs. This method offers a stable energy source, but is often more expensive compared to *off-grid* mining, due to more limited negotiating margins.

Sometimes, *on-grid* mining farms participate in demand management programs. They adjust their energy consumption according to fluctuations in electricity production and consumption on the grid, in order to maintain balance and avoid waste or *blackouts*.

918d7fba-2ff7-4e63-8f57-19cfc7c35825.title: SECP256R1
918d7fba-2ff7-4e63-8f57-19cfc7c35825.body:
Name given to an elliptic curve defined by the NIST standard for public-key cryptography. It uses a 256-bit prime field and an elliptic curve equation `y^2 = x^3 + ax + b` with the constants:

```text
a=-3
```

and 

```text
b=41058363725152142129326129780047268409114441015993725554835256314039467401291
```

The `secp256r1` curve is widely used in many protocols, but it is not used in Bitcoin. Indeed, Satoshi Nakamoto opted for the `secp256k1` curve, which was little known in 2009. The precise reason for this choice is unknown, but it may have been in order to minimize the risk of backdoors. The parameters of the `k1` curve are, in fact, significantly simpler than those of the `r1` curve, in particular the constant `b`.

*This curve is sometimes also called “P-256”.*

923ba2d7-6da1-452c-aaa2-bd4fd7ec0cae.title: TIDES
923ba2d7-6da1-452c-aaa2-bd4fd7ec0cae.body: Acronym for “*Transparent Index Of Distinct Extended Shares*.” It is a method of calculating miner compensation in the context of mining pools, introduced by the Ocean pool in 2023. This method distributes rewards according to a weighted percentage of the work devoted to the most recently found shares. Each proof is rewarded several times, with a reward calculation that includes transaction fees. This system ensures great precision in miners' payouts, without requiring a custodial intermediary to process payments, unlike other methods such as FPPS. TIDES is designed for transparent compensation.

923d1e41-9a38-4ba1-a744-91806f722d80.title: BOLT-00
923d1e41-9a38-4ba1-a744-91806f722d80.body: Introductory document and index of the BOLT (*Basis of Lightning Technology*) specifications. It presents an overview of how the Lightning Network works, as well as each BOLT.

92434b37-76da-4265-9f13-0d66c6e7eaa3.title: BIP-0103
92434b37-76da-4265-9f13-0d66c6e7eaa3.body: Proposal by Pieter Wuille during the Blocksize War providing for a gradual increase of the maximum block size of 17.7% per year, following the empirically observed growth of bandwidth. A conservative approach compared with the other proposals of the time, it aimed to maintain the decentralization of the network. BIP-0103 was never deployed, SegWit having been preferred as the solution to the scalability problem.

9276123d-4b4b-4d8b-9689-3cc562636220.title: BRANCH - GIT
9276123d-4b4b-4d8b-9689-3cc562636220.body: In the context of Git, represents a split from the main workflow, allowing parallel development without affecting the main branch (generally named `master` or `main`). Branches allow modifications, testing and experimentation in an isolated environment, before their possible integration into the main project via a *merge*.

927b5e3d-e290-41e1-b6c0-ec86da69de6f.title: CONTRACT OPERATION

9283480e-e51d-4a3d-afb8-60f1179bd9a8.title: LIBBITCOIN
9283480e-e51d-4a3d-afb8-60f1179bd9a8.body:
A set of libraries written in C++ designed to build Bitcoin-related applications. Libbitcoin offers independent foundations for developing mobile applications, software and other systems around Bitcoin. Libbitcoin therefore has a modular architecture. All of the project's libraries are distributed under the free AGPL license.

Launched in 2011 by a team of developers led by Amir Taaki, Libbitcoin was then the second complete implementation of Bitcoin, after Satoshi's original client. Today, Eric Voskuil is the main maintainer and the most active contributor to the project.

92add8cd-72b6-4c34-a509-7276f202da78.title: PUBLIC POOL
92add8cd-72b6-4c34-a509-7276f202da78.body:
An *open source* solo mining pool for Bitcoin, created by Benjamin Wilson. Unlike conventional pools that pool computing power and share rewards, Public Pool operates on the principle of *solo mining*: each miner individually attempts to find a block and, if successful, keeps the entire reward.

The platform charges no fees on its hosted instance. It provides a block *template* to miners, which saves them from having to run their own full node.

Public Pool is part of the *Open Source Miners United* ecosystem and integrates natively with projects such as the NerdMiner and the Bitaxe.

92b35e63-4cc7-4d78-be58-02d655c89a10.title: ANALYSIS HEURISTIC
92b35e63-4cc7-4d78-be58-02d655c89a10.body:
A chain analysis heuristic on Bitcoin is a family of empirical methods used to trace the flows of bitcoins on the blockchain based on characteristics observed in transactions. A heuristic is a practical approach to solving problems, often through approximate methods, but which represents a solution that is good enough to reach a given goal. These heuristics make it possible to obtain fairly reliable results, but never with absolute precision. In other words, chain analysis always involves a dimension of likelihood in the conclusions drawn. For example, one can estimate with more or less certainty that two addresses belong to the same entity, but total certainty will always be out of reach. The whole objective of chain analysis lies precisely in the aggregation of various heuristics in order to minimize the risk of error. It is in a way an accumulation of evidence that allows us to get closer to reality. In this framework, a distinction is made between internal heuristics and external heuristics.

Internal heuristics focus on characteristics specific to the inside of an individual transaction. Their analysis includes elements such as UTXO amounts, the scripts used, versions, or *locktimes*. For example, the round payment heuristic makes it possible to identify a transaction output as likely being a payment if its amount is a round number. These heuristics often make it possible to identify the change (the money that returns to the same user) and thus to continue tracing.

External heuristics, for their part, analyze similarities and characteristics beyond the transaction itself. They encompass the entire environment of the transaction. For example, address reuse across several transactions is an external heuristic. The CIOH is another one.

92c25dc6-2c0b-4d27-9d37-deb45498f761.title: SIMPLIFIED PAYMENT VERIFICATION
92c25dc6-2c0b-4d27-9d37-deb45498f761.body:
Method allowing light clients to verify Bitcoin transactions without downloading the entire blockchain. A node that uses SPV downloads only the block headers, which are much lighter than full blocks. When it needs to verify a transaction, the SPV node requests a Merkle proof from full nodes to confirm that the transaction is included in a specific block. This approach is efficient for devices with limited resources, such as smartphones, but implies a dependence on full nodes, which can reduce security and increase the trust required.

*The acronym "SPV" is often used to refer to this method.*

92ca392b-d5b7-4ddc-b592-d0d740571d68.title: OP_0 - 0X00
92ca392b-d5b7-4ddc-b592-d0d740571d68.body:
Pushes the value 0 onto the stack. It is often used to represent the boolean value false in scripts. `OP_0` is also used to initialize scripts.

`OP_0` is identical to `OP_FALSE` (`0X00`) and `OP_PUSHNUM_0`.

92d2e0f8-9f00-473b-8e39-279eed39973e.title: BORROMEAN RING SIGNATURES
92d2e0f8-9f00-473b-8e39-279eed39973e.body:
Cryptographic ring signature protocol that allows a signer to prove that they hold a private key among a set of public keys, without revealing which one. The name refers to Borromean rings, a topological structure in which three rings are linked in such a way that removing any one of them frees the other two. This scheme was formalized by Gregory Maxwell and Andrew Poelstra in 2015.

In the context of Bitcoin, *Borromean ring signatures* were used on the Liquid network as the initial *rangeproofs* mechanism within *Confidential Transactions*. They made it possible to prove that a committed amount was within a valid range, without revealing its value. This role was subsequently taken over by *Bulletproofs*, which offer more compact proofs.

9303f5b7-85b7-43f6-8fd0-7a1517db7dea.title: BIP-0020
9303f5b7-85b7-43f6-8fd0-7a1517db7dea.body: First version of the `bitcoin:` URI scheme to facilitate payments through clickable links. BIP-0020 notably proposed a system of amounts with exponents (for example `50X8` for `50 \times 10^8` satoshis). It was replaced by BIP-0021, written by Nils Schneider and Matt Corallo based on the work of Luke Dashjr, which removed these alternative amounts and extended the specification with additional parameters.

9312e260-64de-4ca1-99a5-853f3b932aea.title: BLIP-0050
9312e260-64de-4ca1-99a5-853f3b932aea.body: bLIP that defines LSPS0, the standardized transport layer for communication between Lightning service providers (LSPs) and their clients. The protocol reuses existing BOLT-08 peer-to-peer connections and carries JSON-RPC 2.0 messages over them via a unique message identifier (`37913`). The LSP acts as the JSON-RPC server and the client as the client, with named parameters and potentially out-of-order responses. LSPS0 also defines the common encoding schemas for amounts, fees, signatures and addresses used by all the higher-level LSPS specifications (LSPS1 to LSPS5). This architectural choice avoids introducing external dependencies such as HTTP or gRPC.

9332a9d1-9c1e-4278-a0a7-7e12ecdfaf57.title: BLUE WALLET
9332a9d1-9c1e-4278-a0a7-7e12ecdfaf57.body: *Open source* mobile Bitcoin wallet available on iOS and Android. The application makes it possible to create several wallets within the same interface, to manage PSBTs for use with *hardware wallets* and to import wallets as *watch-only*. BlueWallet can be connected to your own Bitcoin node and your own Electrum server for sovereign use. It also offers advanced features such as *coin control*, transaction replacement via RBF and fee customization.

936e543d-59a0-4821-a5f2-711f873484e2.title: OXT
936e543d-59a0-4821-a5f2-711f873484e2.body:
An exploratory analysis tool for the Bitcoin blockchain, created by LaurentMT and then acquired by Samourai Wallet. OXT offered advanced chain exploration and visualization features, with a particular focus on the study of transaction privacy.

The platform made it possible to visualize transaction graphs, to compute privacy metrics such as the Boltzmann score and to identify usage *patterns* (*coinjoins*, consolidations, etc.). It thus served to understand and audit the level of privacy offered by a transaction or a set of transactions.

The service, formerly accessible for free at oxt.me, has been offline since April 2024, following the legal proceedings brought against the founders of Samourai Wallet.

937d8f64-c3f4-4ca3-879b-3ef56b543fe8.title: ERLAY
937d8f64-c3f4-4ca3-879b-3ef56b543fe8.body:
Network protocol proposal whose objective is to improve the efficiency of relaying unconfirmed transactions between Bitcoin nodes.

Currently, each transaction is propagated through a system in which each node broadcasts the transaction it learns of to all of its peers. The problem is that this leads to a great deal of redundancy and bandwidth use for duplicates. Many transaction broadcasts turn out to be useless, because the recipient already knows about these transactions, and each node only needs to know each transaction once. Erlay proposes to limit by default to 8 the number of peers to which a node directly sends the transactions it learns of, and then to use a reconciliation process based on the *minisketch* library to share the missing transactions more efficiently.

Erlay would reduce bandwidth consumption by about 40%, which would make running a full node more accessible to users with limited Internet connections, and would therefore promote better decentralization of the network. This protocol would also maintain a nearly constant bandwidth consumption as the number of connections increases. This means it would be much simpler for node operators to accept a very large number of connections from their peers, which would strengthen the security of the Bitcoin network by reducing the risks of partitioning, whether intentional or accidental. In addition, Erlay would make it harder to determine the origin node of a transaction, which would thus increase privacy for users of nodes that do not operate over Tor.

Erlay is proposed in BIP-0330.

93b4c50a-c7f1-4a8e-9f8f-2c0ef06492b5.title: DLC - DISCREET LOG CONTRACT
93b4c50a-c7f1-4a8e-9f8f-2c0ef06492b5.body: Type of smart contract on Bitcoin that allows contractual conditions to be executed based on the outcome of external events, validated by one or more oracles, without the latter knowing the details of the contract. DLCs were invented by Tadge Dryja in 2017. These smart contracts are mainly useful in financial applications, making it possible, for example, to create financial instruments or conditional bets, while reducing counterparty risk. To build a DLC, several parties lock bitcoins on a multisig address. These bitcoins can only be unlocked when the oracle publishes the specified information at a given time.

93cc6a17-c784-4674-b714-fe31d94db987.title: DUSTING ATTACK
93cc6a17-c784-4674-b714-fe31d94db987.body:
Attack that consists of sending tiny amounts of bitcoin to a large number of receiving addresses. The attacker's objective is to push the recipients to pool these amounts with other UTXOs. The attacker then tracks the future movements of these small amounts of bitcoin, with the aim of forming address *clusters*, that is, determining whether several addresses belong to the same entity. By cross-referencing the information gathered during a dusting attack with other data and heuristics used in chain analysis, it is possible for the attacker to identify certain entities and their associated addresses. This method represents a threat only to users' privacy, but does not affect the security of their funds.

*Some bitcoiners suggest no longer using the term “dusting attack” because it would be misleading. Indeed, the term “dust” describes something quite specific in Bitcoin Core. If the dusting attack actually used dust as described in Core, the attack would be ineffective. Some therefore suggest using the term “forced address reuse” to describe this attack more precisely.*

93d3646f-a39f-4626-8569-3f1dbb06c7a9.title: AUSTRIAN SCHOOL OF ECONOMICS
93d3646f-a39f-4626-8569-3f1dbb06c7a9.body: A school of economic thought that theorizes the market as a set of voluntary individual interactions, emphasizes the spontaneity of economic order, and criticizes state interventions. The Austrian School defends the role of private property, freedom of contract, and free trade, while criticizing the disruptive effects of money creation on the economy. Its contributors, such as Carl Menger, Ludwig von Mises or Friedrich Hayek, worked on concepts such as price formation, the function of money, the dynamics of capital, or the subjective theory of value. The Austrian School criticizes socialism for its inability to carry out efficient economic calculation, and favors a liberal approach. It values the free market and sees state interventionism as a source of economic imbalances. Many bitcoiners adhere to these ideas and consider that Bitcoin is a tool in harmony with this philosophy because of its distributed nature, the limitation of its money creation, and its ability to operate independently of state intervention.

93e25bd9-ac9c-4137-bfff-cb2d7656d527.title: VLS
93e25bd9-ac9c-4137-bfff-cb2d7656d527.body:
Acronym for "Validating Lightning Signer". An open source library in Rust that separates the private keys of a Lightning node from the node software itself, moving them to a dedicated signing device. Before each cryptographic operation, VLS applies a set of more than fifty validation rules to verify that the proposed transaction is safe.

If the node is compromised or attempts a malicious action, such as signing a revoked *commitment transaction* or closing a channel to an unauthorized address, VLS refuses the signature. This mechanism protects the funds even in the event of total compromise of the node software.

VLS offers reference integrations for CLN and LDK. The project is still in active development and has not reached the stage of a stable production release.

9415129d-01e2-4e94-9bbd-49bb7b13e3ee.title: RECOVERY PATH
9415129d-01e2-4e94-9bbd-49bb7b13e3ee.body: In a wallet software using Miniscript, such as Liana for example, the recovery path(s) refer to sets of keys that only become operational after a period of inactivity defined in the script that locks the bitcoins (*timelock*). Recovery paths can only be used once the *timelocks* have passed, and thus offer a method of recovering funds when the primary path is not available. Let's take the example of a script that includes 2 distinct keys: key A, which authorizes the immediate spending of the bitcoins, and key B, which allows them to be spent after a delay defined by a *timelock* of 52,560 blocks. In this example, key A comes from the primary path, while key B comes from the recovery path.

9494a393-bae7-40a7-8497-422f2e542616.title: OP_LESSTHAN - 0X9F
9494a393-bae7-40a7-8497-422f2e542616.body: Compares the top two elements of the stack and checks whether the second element is less than the first. If the second element is less than the first, it pushes `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise, it pushes `0` (false).

94bad1f1-3f70-444b-ab12-e783c9a7aafa.title: BIP-0091
94bad1f1-3f70-444b-ab12-e783c9a7aafa.body: Proposal by James Hilliard to facilitate the activation of the SegWit soft fork, defined in BIP-0141, BIP-0143 and BIP-0147, via a MASF without directly reaching the required threshold of 95% of the computing power signaling support via bit 1. BIP-0091 allows miners to indirectly signal their support for SegWit by using bit 4 in mined blocks. Once 269 blocks out of a window of 336 blocks have included bit 4 (i.e. 80% of the computing power), BIP-0091 locks in, then requiring all compatible nodes to reject blocks that do not include bit 1. This method aimed to make BIP-0148 (UASF) obsolete and to avoid a potential split of the blockchain on August 1, 2017. BIP-0091 was ultimately activated on July 23, 2017 (at block 477,120), just before the fateful August 1 date imposed in BIP-0148. This made it possible to force miners to signal SegWit, which would ultimately lock in on August 9 at block 479,808, then activate on August 24 at block 481,824. To summarize, BIP-0148 (UASF) was created in reaction to miners not signaling SegWit sufficiently, but was ultimately never implemented. BIP-0091 (MASF) was created in reaction to BIP-0148 in order to force miners' hand, without risking the UASF of BIP-0148. BIP-0091 is itself a soft fork, which would ultimately force miners to lock in the SegWit soft fork via the baseline method (MASF BIP-0009).

94d4732f-279a-4473-b0a1-c2620b16394c.title: SHA512
94d4732f-279a-4473-b0a1-c2620b16394c.body: Acronym for “*Secure Hash Algorithm 512 bits*”. It is a cryptographic hash function producing a 512-bit digest. It was designed by the *National Security Agency* (NSA) in the early 2000s. For Bitcoin, the `SHA512` function is not used directly within the protocol, but it is used in child key derivations at the application level, according to BIP-0032 and BIP-0039. In these processes, it is used several times in the `HMAC` algorithm, as well as in the `PBKDF2` key derivation function. The `SHA512` function belongs to the SHA 2 family, like `SHA256`. Its operation is, moreover, very similar to the latter.

94f17f89-70e7-411a-bf2b-0f10da5518d6.title: BIP-0373
94f17f89-70e7-411a-bf2b-0f10da5518d6.body: Adds MuSig2-specific fields (BIP-0327) to the PSBT format to enable collaborative signing via *hardware wallets* and coordinators. These fields include the participants' public keys, the public *nonces* and the partial signatures. BIP-0373 thus makes it possible to coordinate the two-round MuSig2 protocol through the exchange of PSBT files, without the different signers needing to interact directly with each other.

951960ee-7969-48b2-bde6-30ff3079ebc3.title: NPUB
951960ee-7969-48b2-bde6-30ff3079ebc3.body: The encoding format of the Nostr public key in Bech32, defined by NIP-19. The `npub` prefix identifies a Nostr public key. The raw public key is a 32-byte number on the secp256k1 curve, derived from its private key. The npub encoding adds a human-readable prefix (`npub1...`), a checksum to detect input errors, and uses an alphabet excluding ambiguous characters. The npub is the public identifier of a Nostr user: it can be shared freely and allows anyone to find the associated profile and posts. Unlike the nsec, it does not compromise the security of the account if it is disclosed.

955f7c51-91c5-4ae6-a2b2-1ba5496e4c5b.title: BIP-0199
955f7c51-91c5-4ae6-a2b2-1ba5496e4c5b.body: Formalization of the construction of HTLCs (*Hashed Time-Locked Contracts*) in on-chain Bitcoin transactions. BIP-0199 describes the standard mechanism used for *atomic swaps* and Lightning payment channels: a *hashlock* combined with a *timelock* allowing conditional refunds. The recipient must reveal a secret (the hash preimage) before the deadline expires to claim the funds; otherwise, the sender can recover them.

9563078b-c14b-47ca-bdaf-ba5044355f5e.title: POT - PAY ON TARGET
9563078b-c14b-47ca-bdaf-ba5044355f5e.body: Method for calculating miner compensation in the context of mining pools. POT is a compensation system that varies according to the difficulty of the work sent to the pool rather than that of the work provided by the pool. In this approach, the reward for each share submitted by a miner is based on the difficulty of that specific share. This means that more difficult shares are better rewarded than less difficult ones. It is a variant of PPS, but by adjusting the reward according to the actual complexity of the work accomplished, POT involves much more variance for the miner.

95eb53fd-c47e-4e3f-85d2-2be9f35b2b16.title: DUMMY ELEMENT
95eb53fd-c47e-4e3f-85d2-2be9f35b2b16.body: Refers to an additional, useless element consumed by the opcodes `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` and `OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY` when verifying signatures in a transaction. Because of a historical *off-by-one* bug (unit offset error), these 2 opcodes remove an extra element from the stack in addition to their basic function. To avoid an error, it is therefore mandatory to include a dummy value at the beginning of the `scriptSig` in order to satisfy the removal and bypass the bug. This useless value is what is called the “*dummy element*”. BIP-0011, which introduced the P2MS standard, advised putting a `OP_0` as the useless value. But this standard was not enforced at the consensus rule level, which means that any value could be placed there without invalidating the transaction. The dummy element was therefore a vector of transaction malleability. BIP-0147, introduced with the SegWit soft fork, required this dummy element to be strictly an empty byte array (`OP_0`), thus eliminating the malleability associated with this element by making any non-compliant transaction invalid under the consensus rules. This rule, named `NULLDUMMY`, applies to both SegWit and pre-SegWit transactions.

961adcb1-1e9b-424d-96b5-74f4df767da5.title: BOS - BALANCE OF SATOSHIS
961adcb1-1e9b-424d-96b5-74f4df767da5.body:
Command-line tool developed by Alex Bosworth to manage and optimize a Lightning node running LND. It is installed via npm (`npm install -g balanceofsatoshis`) and offers a set of commands accessible through the `bos` prefix to view balances, adjust routing fees, rebalance liquidity between channels, open or close channels, and monitor node activity.

Among its main features, `bos rebalance` makes it possible to move liquidity between channels via circular payments, `bos fees` to dynamically adjust outgoing fees with conditional formulas, and `bos accounting` to produce an accounting statement of transactions. The tool also offers a Telegram integration to receive notifications and interact with one's node remotely.

96af136a-1a80-43b7-9754-767d5189f077.title: CPPSRB
96af136a-1a80-43b7-9754-767d5189f077.body: Acronym for "*Capped Pay Per Share with Recent Backpay*". It is a method of calculating miner remuneration in the context of mining pools. In this system, the pool pays as many shares as it can each time a block is found, giving priority to the most recent shares. This method makes it possible to guarantee the financial stability of the mining pool, while offering per-task remuneration and encouraging miners to stay connected to the pool to avoid *pool hopping*.

96df9ad2-69b1-4cbe-bf22-0b6ae39a6e8f.title: BASE FEE
96df9ad2-69b1-4cbe-bf22-0b6ae39a6e8f.body: Fixed component of routing fees on the Lightning Network. When a node forwards a payment on behalf of another, it can charge a fee made up of two parts: the *base fee*, a constant amount charged for each routed payment regardless of its amount, and the *fee rate*, a proportional share of the amount transferred. The *base fee* is expressed in millisatoshis and is typically 1,000 msat (i.e. 1 satoshi). It is configurable by the node operator for each channel.

9796a556-9f66-4a90-9295-d11042814c50.title: KEYSTORE
9796a556-9f66-4a90-9295-d11042814c50.body: In the context of Bitcoin wallet software, a keystore is a structure that groups together the information needed to track and use a set of keys. It generally contains a label, a master key fingerprint (*master fingerprint*), a derivation path, and an extended public key (`xpub`). These elements allow the wallet to generate receiving addresses and monitor the transactions associated with them.

97ce2180-f932-40fe-a6a8-d78ac73807b4.title: BIP-0105
97ce2180-f932-40fe-a6a8-d78ac73807b4.body: Proposal for a maximum block size retargeting algorithm based on miner consensus. BIP-0105 included a growth cap to avoid an excessive increase in block size. Proposed during the Blocksize War, it is one of the many attempts at dynamic adjustment of the block size limit that were never deployed on Bitcoin.

98218fd1-053e-45ac-8152-41e92e5ffb2b.title: BULLETPROOFS
98218fd1-053e-45ac-8152-41e92e5ffb2b.body:
Zero-knowledge proof system (*zero-knowledge proofs*) used notably in *Confidential Transactions* to verify that an amount committed in a transaction lies within a valid range, without revealing its value. Bulletproofs were introduced in 2017 by Bünz, Bootle, Boneh, Poelstra, Wuille and Maxwell. They replace earlier range proofs (*Borromean ring signatures*) by producing significantly more compact proofs, whose size grows logarithmically (`O(\log n)`) with respect to the number of bits representing the value.

An evolution named Bulletproofs++, proposed by Liam Eagen, Sanket Kanjalkar, Tim Ruffing and Jonas Nick, further improves efficiency in terms of generation and verification. On Liquid, the adoption of Bulletproofs made it possible to reduce the size of confidential transactions, thereby lowering fees and slowing the growth of the chain.

98867f3a-1a80-46ce-ba15-614544a7164b.title: DATABASE/
98867f3a-1a80-46ce-ba15-614544a7164b.body: A former folder containing databases for the Bitcoin Core wallet. Since version 0.16, this database has been moved into the `wallets/` folder.

9895ea98-7345-45d8-b96a-ac61ebd334e9.title: CHAUMIAN COINJOIN
9895ea98-7345-45d8-b96a-ac61ebd334e9.body:
A coinjoin protocol that uses David Chaum's blind signatures and Tor for communications between the participants and the coordinator's server. The goal of a Chaumian coinjoin is to guarantee to participants that the coordinator can neither steal the bitcoins nor link the inputs and the outputs. 

To do this, users submit their input and a cryptographically blinded receiving address to the coordinator. This address, once unblinded, will be intended to receive the bitcoins as a coinjoin output. The coordinator signs these tokens and sends them back to the users. The users then reconnect anonymously to the coordinator's server with a new Tor identity and then reveal their output addresses in clear text for the construction of the transaction. The coordinator can verify that all these receiving addresses do come from legitimate users, since it previously signed their blinded version with its private key. However, it cannot associate a specific output address with a given input user. There is therefore no link between the inputs and the outputs, even from the coordinator's point of view. Once the transaction is built by the coordinator, it sends it back to the participants, who sign it in order to unlock their input, after having verified that their output is indeed in this transaction. The participants send the signature to the coordinator. Once all the signatures have been collected, the coordinator can broadcast the coinjoin transaction on the Bitcoin network.

![Sequence of a Chaumian coinjoin: sending the input and a blinded output, blind signature, anonymous unblinding via Tor.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/chaumian-coinjoin/assets/image-1.png)

This method guarantees that the coordinator can neither compromise the participants' anonymity nor steal the bitcoins throughout the coinjoin process.

It is difficult to determine with certainty who first introduced the idea of coinjoin on Bitcoin, and who came up with the idea of using David Chaum's blind signatures in this context. It is often thought that Gregory Maxwell was the first to mention it in [a message on BitcoinTalk in 2013](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=279249.0):

> *“Using chaum blind signatures: The users connect and provide inputs (and change addresses) and a cryptographically-blinded version of the address they want their private coins to go to; the server signs the tokens and returns them. The users anonymously reconnect, unblind their output addresses, and return them to the server. The server can see that all the outputs were signed by it and so all the outputs had to come from valid participants. Later people reconnect and sign.”*

Maxwell, G. (2013, August 22). *CoinJoin: Bitcoin privacy for the real world*. BitcoinTalk Forum. https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=279249.0

However, there are other earlier mentions, both of Chaum's signatures in the context of mixing, and of coinjoins. [In June 2011, Duncan Townsend presents on BitcoinTalk](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=12751.0) a mixer that uses Chaum's signatures in a way quite similar to modern Chaumian coinjoins. In the same thread, one can find [a message from hashcoin in response to Duncan Townsend](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=12751.msg315793#msg315793) to improve his mixer. This message presents what most closely resembles coinjoins. A mention of a similar system can also be found in [a message from Alex Mizrahi in 2012](https://gist.github.com/killerstorm/6f843e1d3ffc38191aebca67d483bd88#file-laundry), when he was advising the creators of Tenebrix. The term “coinjoin” itself would not have been invented by Greg Maxwell, but would come from an idea of Peter Todd.

9947b93a-25b5-4f2d-b353-fefe5a5b4719.title: CONFIRMATION
9947b93a-25b5-4f2d-b353-fefe5a5b4719.body: Corresponds to the number of blocks whose security a transaction benefits from. When a transaction is broadcast to the Bitcoin network, it is first pending in the nodes' mempools. It is then included in a valid block by a miner. At this stage, the transaction has just been added to the blockchain, so it has one confirmation. When a new block is found on top of the block containing the transaction in question, it will have a second confirmation, and so on. Each new block mined on top of the block containing the transaction constitutes a new confirmation. By counting the number of confirmations of a transaction, one can estimate the risk that it might ultimately be reversed because of a reorganization. The number of confirmations lets us judge the level of immutability of a transaction on the blockchain.

9958fcb9-2554-4663-8d0c-d8927fb4a8a5.title: BIP-0031
9958fcb9-2554-4663-8d0c-d8927fb4a8a5.body: Proposal aimed at improving the network management mechanisms of Bitcoin nodes. Before BIP-0031, Bitcoin nodes had no direct way of knowing whether their peers were still connected, functional and not overloaded. BIP-0031 introduced the use of a `pong` message, in response to the `ping` message, which allows active verification of connectivity between nodes.

99894503-f02b-4426-9501-f5937bed0094.title: MIXER
99894503-f02b-4426-9501-f5937bed0094.body:
Centralized service that makes it possible to break the history of Bitcoin coins by mixing the funds of several users. Unlike coinjoin, where users retain control of their funds throughout the mixing process, a mixer temporarily takes possession of users' bitcoins, mixes them with those of other users, then sends the funds back to new addresses.

Nowadays, the use of bitcoin mixers is fading in favor of Chaumian coinjoins, which offer more security by eliminating the need for trust. Unlike mixers, where users must entrust their bitcoins to an operator who could steal them or keep data about the mixing process, coinjoins do not present these risks.

9991eb82-08e7-4151-8582-d382fb30a31c.title: MYSTERY SHOPPER PAYMENTS
9991eb82-08e7-4151-8582-d382fb30a31c.body: An attack in which an attacker sends a small legitimate bitcoin payment to their target in order to obtain information and attempt to compromise their privacy. This technique is often used against merchants. Take the example of Alice, who owns a bakery that accepts bitcoin payments. Eve, the attacker, could buy a croissant to obtain a receiving address from Alice. Eve could then follow the movements of this UTXO to try to deduce additional information about Alice using tracing heuristics.

99c4221b-0b2d-47e5-b608-1d5610c85e9b.title: RIPEMD160
99c4221b-0b2d-47e5-b608-1d5610c85e9b.body: Acronym of *RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest 160*, where “RACE” stands for *Research and development in Advanced Communications technologies in Europe*. It is a cryptographic hash function that generates a 160-bit digest from an arbitrary input. It is used on Bitcoin to transform a public key into a receiving address for the Legacy and SegWit v0 standards (for SegWit v1, the public key is not hashed). The process first involves applying the hash function `SHA256` to the public key, followed by applying `RIPEMD160` to the result. This combination of two distinct hash functions is known as `HASH160` in the context of Bitcoin. `RIPEMD160` is also used in deterministic and hierarchical wallets to compute key fingerprints. In particular, `HASH160` is used to compute the fingerprint of a parent key, which is then included in the metadata of an extended key (xpub, xprv...).

99c58522-4fba-43ee-a67c-3f69cf3b8663.title: BIP-0035
99c58522-4fba-43ee-a67c-3f69cf3b8663.body: Proposal allowing a Bitcoin node to open up information about its mempool, that is, the transactions awaiting confirmation. Thanks to this, other actors can receive real-time data on unconfirmed transactions by sending a specific message to a node. Before the adoption of BIP-0035, nodes could only access information about transactions that were already confirmed. This improvement gives SPV wallets the ability to receive information about unconfirmed transactions, allows a miner not to omit transactions with high fees after a restart, and facilitates the analysis of mempool information by external services.

99cbf6f7-86dd-4e05-bbe3-c3985005f1b9.title: BIP-0172
99cbf6f7-86dd-4e05-bbe3-c3985005f1b9.body: Proposal to officially define the satoshi (sat) as the standard subunit of Bitcoin and to promote its use in user interfaces. BIP-0172 aims to clarify the denomination by establishing that 1 bitcoin = 100,000,000 satoshis, and recommends displaying amounts in satoshis for small values, in order to avoid confusion related to decimal numbers.

9a727a0a-46fe-4b42-8e52-21e2712b7d13.title: BIP-0034
9a727a0a-46fe-4b42-8e52-21e2712b7d13.body: Soft fork applied in March 2013, which introduced version 2 for Bitcoin blocks. The last block in version 1 is block 227,835. This new version requires each block to include, in the `scriptSig` of the coinbase transaction, the height of the block being created. On the one hand, this modification clarifies the way the network agrees to modify the block structure and the consensus rules. On the other hand, it forces the uniqueness of each block and of each coinbase transaction.

9aaf4d4e-a573-4126-91b5-81b99162de3e.title: EPHEMERAL ANCHORS
9aaf4d4e-a573-4126-91b5-81b99162de3e.body:
Relay policy proposal that allows zero-fee transactions to be broadcast on the network, provided they are accompanied by a child transaction that pays sufficient fees for both. The parent transaction contains a zero-value output with an *anyone-can-spend* script, which allows any participant in the network to create a child transaction that spends this ephemeral output, attaching the appropriate fees to it at the time of broadcast.

This mechanism solves a fundamental problem of contract protocols such as the Lightning Network: transactions are signed by the participants well before they are broadcast, which makes it impossible to determine in advance a fee rate suited to network conditions. *Ephemeral anchors* make it possible to defer the choice of fees to the time of publication, offering a form of "fee sponsorship" (*fee sponsorship*) accessible to any party, whether or not they are a beneficiary of the transaction's other outputs.

This proposal builds on the v3 transaction relay rules and on *package relay*. It is an evolution of the traditional Lightning Network *anchor outputs*, themselves based on the *CPFP carve-out* rule. Bitcoin Core introduced the standardized *Pay-To-Anchor* (P2A) output type to implement this mechanism. *Ephemeral anchors* are also an effective countermeasure against transaction pinning attacks.

9ab60958-f206-42d9-8ad1-c902aeef62c3.title: PRIVATE CHANNEL
9ab60958-f206-42d9-8ad1-c902aeef62c3.body:
A Lightning channel that is not announced to the network and is therefore absent from the public node graph. Unlike a standard public channel, a private channel does not broadcast an announcement message (*channel announcement*) to other peers. It is invisible to third-party nodes and cannot be used to route payments for other users.

Private channels are the recommended channel type for nodes that do not route, such as nodes embedded in mobile devices. To receive a payment through a private channel, the existence of the channel and its parameters are revealed to the payer through *routing hints* embedded in the Lightning invoice.

The term “private” is somewhat misleading here: it simply means “unannounced”. On-chain heuristics, such as analysis of funding transactions or force closures, can allow an observer to infer the existence of these channels, as can analysis of payments to that node. It is in fact because of these channels that it is impossible to know the real size of the Lightning Network, since only public channels can be counted with certainty.

9ae4a06d-01b3-484a-b7f3-c9502776d6af.title: GUI
9ae4a06d-01b3-484a-b7f3-c9502776d6af.body: Acronym for "*Graphical User Interface*", or "interface graphique utilisateur" in French. It is a form of user interface that allows interaction with software through interactive visual elements (buttons, icons, images, windows...) and that favors the use of pointing devices (the mouse) rather than text commands as with the CLI.

9afe1eb4-b554-4c6e-97ec-ebc4cdb7eb83.title: SHAMIR SECRET SHARING - SSS
9afe1eb4-b554-4c6e-97ec-ebc4cdb7eb83.body:
Cryptographic secret sharing scheme designed by Adi Shamir in 1979. It makes it possible to divide a secret into n distinct shares, such that a minimum of t shares is needed to reconstruct the original secret, while t-1 shares or fewer reveal no information about it. The (t, n) parameters are defined when the shares are created.

In the Bitcoin ecosystem, Shamir's secret sharing is used in several contexts. The Codex32 protocol, formalized in BIP-0093, relies on this scheme to allow the backup and manual reconstruction of seeds. It is also an option offered on Trezor *hardware wallets*. Threshold signature protocols such as FROST also rely on this mechanism during the distributed key generation phase.

9b169cba-1d42-496a-a622-6162e25c8b82.title: WITNESS TRANSACTION
9b169cba-1d42-496a-a622-6162e25c8b82.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the Witness Transaction designates the Bitcoin transaction that closes the Single-use Seal around a message incorporating a Multi Protocol Commitment (MPC). This operation consists of spending an existing UTXO, thereby closing the previous seal, while creating a new output containing a commitment to a new seal definition, in order to lock in the contractual commitment recorded in the protocol. The Witness Transaction thus constitutes on-chain proof that the state of the RGB contract was fixed at a specific moment.

9b22b406-2cf6-4ff0-9bad-d1ab5a0c8f38.title: TRANSACTION MALLEABILITY
9b22b406-2cf6-4ff0-9bad-d1ab5a0c8f38.body:
Refers to the possibility of slightly modifying the structure of a Bitcoin transaction, without altering its effect, but while changing the transaction identifier (*TXID*). This property can be exploited maliciously to mislead stakeholders about the status of a transaction, thus causing problems such as double spending. Malleability was made possible by the flexibility of the digital signature used. Malleability notably made an implementation of the Lightning Network complicated. The SegWit soft fork was introduced to solve this problem, by excluding the malleable data of the transaction from the TXID calculation.

*Although it is rare, the term "mutability" is sometimes found to refer to the same concept.*

9b250f78-2063-4c30-a742-affe781e4368.title: BLIP-0051
9b250f78-2063-4c30-a742-affe781e4368.body:
bLIP that defines LSPS1, a standardized API allowing Lightning wallets to buy payment channels from Lightning service providers (LSPs). The process takes place in three steps:
* the client queries the LSP's available options via `lsps1.get_info`,
* it creates an order with the desired parameters (capacity, duration, balance distribution) via `lsps1.create_order`,
* then it pays via a BOLT-11 invoice, a BOLT-12 offer or an on-chain payment.

The LSP then opens the requested channel. The specification supports public and private channels, zero-confirmation channels, and provides for an automatic refund if the opening fails. LSPS1 relies on the LSPS0 transport layer of bLIP-0050.

9b32ed34-45aa-4742-8f3e-ca2443d7fd7d.title: BRUTE FORCE ATTACK
9b32ed34-45aa-4742-8f3e-ca2443d7fd7d.body: Cryptanalysis method for finding a password or a key, which consists of trying, by trial and error, all possible combinations of keys or passwords until finding the one that grants access to a privilege or to protected information. This technique relies on intensive computation and can be extremely long, especially against large keys. To deal with this type of attack, longer password and key sequences must be used in order to multiply the number of operations required for the attacker. In theory, the complexity of such an attack is exponential in the length of the target.

9b3445ea-b0d0-4558-9c77-5701429b352f.title: SELFISH MINING
9b3445ea-b0d0-4558-9c77-5701429b352f.body:
Strategy (or attack) in mining, where a miner or a group of miners intentionally withholds blocks with valid proof of work without immediately broadcasting them to the network. The goal is to keep a lead over the other miners in terms of proof of work, which potentially allows them to mine several blocks in a row and publish them all at once, thus maximizing their gains. In other words, the group of attacking miners does not mine on the last block validated by the whole network, but rather on a block they created themselves, which differs from the one validated by the network.

This process generates a kind of secret branch of the blockchain, which remains unknown to the whole network until this alternative chain potentially surpasses the honest blockchain. Once the attacking miners' secret chain becomes longer (that is, it contains more accumulated work) than the honest, public chain, it is then broadcast across the whole network. At that moment, the network's nodes, which follow the chain with the most accumulated work, will synchronize on this new chain. There is therefore a reorganization.

*Selfish mining* is annoying for users, because it reduces the security of the system by wasting part of the network's computing power. If successful, it also leads to blockchain reorganizations, thus affecting the reliability of transaction confirmations for users. This practice nonetheless remains risky for the group of attacking miners, because it is often more profitable to mine normally on top of the last publicly known block rather than allocate computing power to a secret branch that will probably never surpass the honest blockchain. The greater the number of blocks in the reorganization, the lower the probability that the attack succeeds.

*Note that a selfish mining attack must not be confused with a block withholding attack.*

9b5e1149-7abc-41f2-a38e-29757ffcc4ce.title: PEERS.DAT
9b5e1149-7abc-41f2-a38e-29757ffcc4ce.body:
File in which Bitcoin Core serializes the tables of the `addrman` module: the "new" table (addresses that have been discovered but not yet tested) and the "tried" table (addresses to which the node has already connected successfully). It contains the IP addresses of the other nodes, port numbers, last-connection timestamps, and the bucketing key (`nKey`) that determines the placement of addresses in the buckets.

On first launch, the file does not exist and the tables are empty: the node queries the DNS seeds to obtain an initial list of peers. As connections are made, addresses are inserted into the tables and `peers.dat` is periodically updated. It is also possible to add addresses manually via the `-addnode` option or the `addnode` RPC command.

This file replaced `addr.dat` starting with Bitcoin Core 0.7.0 (2012), when Pieter Wuille introduced `addrman` with its deterministic bucketing system.

9b71f725-e52e-42fe-a115-98bf0e4f9e66.title: LIGHTNING SERVICE PROVIDER
9b71f725-e52e-42fe-a115-98bf0e4f9e66.body:
A company operating on Lightning whose business is to provide liquidity services to users. 

On Lightning, payments are made off-chain via bidirectional channels, whose capacity is limited by the funds locked in the on-chain 2/2 *multisig*. The main role of an LSP is to facilitate the management of this liquidity, either by helping to convert on-chain funds to Lightning, or by opening new channels to increase users' inbound capacity.

These services are often used by *non-custodial* wallets, so that the user can immediately receive Lightning payments without having to handle opening and managing channels themselves. In exchange, the LSP charges fees.

9b846f85-74f9-4d8f-ba5a-b668de49187e.title: BIP-0179
9b846f85-74f9-4d8f-ba5a-b668de49187e.body: Informational document proposing to replace the term "address" with "invoice" (or "*Bitcoin Invoice Address*") to designate payment reception identifiers in Bitcoin. BIP-0179 starts from the observation that the word "address" suggests permanent information (like a postal or email address), whereas Bitcoin addresses are designed for single use. The term "invoice" is proposed to better reflect this ephemeral nature and the link to a specific transaction. The permitted variants are "*Bitcoin Invoice Address*", "*Bitcoin Invoice*", "*Invoice Address*" and "*Invoice*", the suffix "*Address*" being tolerated as a transitional measure.

9b8a7e80-7dde-48a6-9133-66a083db2dca.title: BIP-0073
9b8a7e80-7dde-48a6-9133-66a083db2dca.body: Extension of the BIP-0070 payment protocol using the HTTP header `Accept` for negotiating the response format between the client and the merchant server. BIP-0073 allowed the wallet to specify the accepted content types. Deployed jointly with BIP-0070, it became obsolete with the general abandonment of the payment protocol.

9ba3165a-b72c-41be-96b2-221a576821d2.title: BIP-0326
9ba3165a-b72c-41be-96b2-221a576821d2.body: Improvement proposal aimed at developers of Bitcoin wallet software supporting Taproot transactions. Its main goal is to strengthen the privacy of second-layer protocols that might use PTLCs (*Point Time Locked Contracts*), such as CoinSwap, the Lightning Network or DLCs (*Discreet Log Contracts*). To do this, this proposal aims to create plausible deniability by automatically setting the `nSequence` field of Taproot transactions in the same way the `nLocktime` field was set in other types of transactions in order to discourage *fee sniping* attacks. In other words, BIP-0326 asks wallet software to use the `nSequence` field rather than the `nLocktime` field to prevent *fee sniping* attacks, in order to offer increased privacy for all *off-chain* protocols using this field in a similar way. Thus, a Taproot transaction with a specific value in the `nSequence` field could be either an ordinary wallet spend, all things considered, or a settlement transaction of a second-layer protocol with a timelock, making these two cases indistinguishable. If this improvement proposal were widely applied by Bitcoin wallet software developers, it would greatly improve the privacy and fungibility of Bitcoin as a whole.

9bb36b3d-8ba5-4ff0-bd58-b0c33384d5da.title: PRUNED NODE
9bb36b3d-8ba5-4ff0-bd58-b0c33384d5da.body:
A full node that performs pruning of the blockchain. This consists of progressively deleting the oldest blocks, after having duly verified them, in order to keep only the most recent blocks. The retention limit is set in the `bitcoin.conf` file via the `prune=n` parameter, where `n` is the maximum size taken up by the blocks in megabytes (MB). If `0` is written after this parameter, then pruning is disabled, and the node keeps the blockchain in its entirety.

Pruned nodes are sometimes considered as types of nodes different from full nodes. Using a pruned node can be particularly useful for users facing constraints in terms of storage capacity. Currently, a full node must have more than 800 GB just for storing the blockchain. A pruned node can limit the required storage to as little as 550 MB. Although it uses less disk space, a pruned node maintains a level of verification and validation similar to that of a full node. Pruned nodes therefore offer more trust to their users compared with lightweight nodes (SPV).

9bb7d1e4-4a71-43a0-bee9-b218229b62f6.title: PENALTY TRANSACTION
9bb7d1e4-4a71-43a0-bee9-b218229b62f6.body:
Bitcoin transaction used on the Lightning Network to punish a peer who has published an old, revoked commitment transaction on the blockchain. It allows the wronged party to recover all of the channel's funds, including the attacker's share.

The mechanism relies on revocation keys. When a channel state is updated, each party gives the other a key that makes it possible to spend all of the funds if the old state were to be published. If a node tries to cheat by broadcasting an old commitment, its peer has a time window in which to detect the fraud and build the penalty transaction using this revocation key. This time window is guaranteed by a timelock `OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY` on the cheater's output.

*Watchtowers* are third-party services that monitor the blockchain continuously to detect such frauds and broadcast penalty transactions on behalf of offline nodes.

9befe482-55b3-44c3-9727-c19a1aebabc1.title: MTGOX
9befe482-55b3-44c3-9727-c19a1aebabc1.body: Bitcoin exchange platform founded in 2010 by Jed McCaleb in Tokyo, Japan, then acquired by Mark Karpelès in 2011. At its peak, Mt. Gox handled about 70% of bitcoin transactions worldwide, making it by far the largest exchange platform. In February 2014, Mt. Gox suspended withdrawals and then declared bankruptcy after revealing the loss of about 850,000 bitcoins, 750,000 of which belonged to its customers. The name “Mt. Gox” is an acronym for “Magic: The Gathering Online eXchange”, because the site had originally been designed as a marketplace for cards from that game. This collapse remains one of the most significant events in Bitcoin's history and highlighted the risks of keeping one's bitcoins on a centralized platform.

9bffcb2f-983a-4d16-ac75-7e0e4c6097b6.title: L402
9bffcb2f-983a-4d16-ac75-7e0e4c6097b6.body:
L402, formerly known as LSAT (*Lightning Service Authentication Token*), is an authentication and payment standard for distributed services. It takes its name from the HTTP status code 402 (*Payment Required*). L402 combines two mechanisms: macaroons, which are bearer authentication tokens that can be verified with simple cryptography and no centralized database, and the Lightning Network, which provides an instant payment system.

L402 works by associating a macaroon with the hash of a Lightning payment. When a user wants to access a protected service, the service hands them a macaroon along with a Lightning invoice. Once the payment is made, the user obtains the preimage which, combined with the macaroon, forms a valid L402 credential. The service does not need to directly check whether the invoice has been paid: simply presenting a preimage that matches the payment hash is enough to prove settlement.

L402 is implemented in Aperture, a reverse proxy developed by Lightning Labs, which handles the issuance of macaroons and invoices, then forwards authenticated requests to the protected APIs.

9c53157d-f8c1-4db3-a71e-1e94331197cf.title: P2WPKH
9c53157d-f8c1-4db3-a71e-1e94331197cf.body:
P2WPKH is the acronym for *Pay to Witness Public Key Hash*. It is a standard script template used to set spending conditions on a UTXO. P2WPKH was introduced with the implementation of SegWit in August 2017.

This script is similar to P2PKH (*Pay to Public Key Hash*), since it also locks bitcoins based on the hash of a public key, that is, of a receiving address. The difference lies in the way signatures and scripts are included in the transaction. Under P2WPKH, the signature script information (`scriptSig`) is moved from the traditional structure of the transaction to a separate section called `Witness` (witness). This move is a feature of the SegWit (*Segregated Witness*) update that makes it possible to prevent signature-related malleability. P2WPKH transactions are generally less costly in terms of fees compared to Legacy transactions, because the part in the witness costs less.

P2WPKH addresses are written using the `Bech32` encoding with a checksum in the form of a BCH code. These addresses always begin with `bc1q`. P2WPKH is a version 0 SegWit output.

9c675486-f054-45d7-9a81-6a847eee9e12.title: CURTAILMENT
9c675486-f054-45d7-9a81-6a847eee9e12.body: Refers to the voluntary reduction of a mining farm's electricity consumption by shutting down machines. This reduction is part of certain contracts made with electricity producers. When there is an overproduction of energy relative to market demand, miners use this surplus. When there are demand peaks relative to production, miners can reduce their consumption in order to stabilize the grid.

9ca445f5-27fc-40ce-9af2-dd172571f50f.title: HUMAN RIGHTS FOUNDATION
9ca445f5-27fc-40ce-9af2-dd172571f50f.body: A nonpartisan nonprofit organization founded in 2005 by Thor Halvorssen, dedicated to promoting human rights around the world, with a particular focus on authoritarian societies. Since 2020, the foundation has managed a *Bitcoin Development Fund* that finances open source projects aimed at improving Bitcoin's privacy, decentralization and accessibility. The HRF considers Bitcoin a tool of financial emancipation for populations living under authoritarian regimes, where access to the traditional banking system is restricted or monitored. The foundation also organizes educational events around Bitcoin and individual freedoms.

9cec86a0-2874-4fc7-83a8-9ad1bb984360.title: TARO
9cec86a0-2874-4fc7-83a8-9ad1bb984360.body: Former name of the Taproot Assets Protocol.

9d2edbfc-eeb0-4310-9072-3500451301fc.title: FINNEY HAL
9d2edbfc-eeb0-4310-9072-3500451301fc.body:
Harold T. Finney II, known as Hal Finney, was a cryptographer and developer famous for his crucial role in the early days of Bitcoin and his contributions to cryptography. As soon as the Bitcoin White Paper was published in 2008, he was one of the first to interact with Satoshi Nakamoto. He gave feedback, reported bugs and proposed improvements after the software's launch in January 2009. He was the recipient of the first Bitcoin transaction (apart from coinbases), receiving 10 BTC from Satoshi in block no. 170:

```text
f4184fc596403b9d638783cf57adfe4c75c605f6356fbc91338530e9831e9e16
```

Hal Finney is also probably the first person, after Satoshi, to have mined a block: block no. 78. More than that, Hal Finney was the first promoter of Bitcoin during a period when the project was still little known.

Outside of Bitcoin, he is also recognized for his invention of RPoW (*Reusable Proofs of Work*), an electronic money system launched in 2004. Although RPoW did not meet with the expected success, it remains one of Bitcoin's most accomplished precursors. As a committed cypherpunk, Hal Finney also played a decisive role in the development and improvement of PGP (*Pretty Good Privacy*). Hal Finney left us on August 28, 2014, taken by amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Lou Gehrig's disease). He was cryopreserved by the Alcor foundation. He will remain a major figure in the history of cryptography and of Bitcoin.

9d371d4f-f1ea-407b-839a-a3c698fbbe2d.title: OUTBOUND PEER / OUTGOING CONNECTION
9d371d4f-f1ea-407b-839a-a3c698fbbe2d.body: Node to which your own Bitcoin node actively establishes a connection. By default, a node attempts to connect to 8 outbound peers. These connections are preferred and considered more reliable than inbound peers, because they are chosen by the node. Inbound and outbound peers share the same type of information. The main difference between inbound and outbound peers lies not in the type of information exchanged, but in the way these connections are established.

9d4987a5-460b-4f47-8d63-4669f8928f9d.title: SHARDS - RGB
9d4987a5-460b-4f47-8d63-4669f8928f9d.body: In the RGB protocol, a *Shard* represents a distinct branch within the directed acyclic graph (DAG) that traces the history of a contract's *State Transitions*. It constitutes a coherent subset of the set of transitions, corresponding for example to the sequence of operations needed to attest to the validity of a particular asset since the *Genesis*. This mechanism makes it possible to isolate specific segments of the overall history, in order to facilitate client-side validation.

9d578cea-a756-4aff-b436-fc8a5e90a98c.title: NAKAMOTO SATOSHI
9d578cea-a756-4aff-b436-fc8a5e90a98c.body: Pseudonym of the person or group who created Bitcoin and wrote its original white paper in 2008 (White Paper). Nakamoto, who communicated only online, eventually disappeared from the public scene in 2011.

9d6e2699-4d86-46aa-bf18-064d21ee35ff.title: ORACLE
9d6e2699-4d86-46aa-bf18-064d21ee35ff.body: A third-party source of information that provides real-world data that can be interpreted on Bitcoin. Oracles allow smart contracts, such as DLCs, to execute contractual conditions based on external events. In general, they provide a specific signature that corresponds to the outcome of an event. This signature is then used to complete and make valid an execution transaction that sends the bitcoins to the party that is supposed to receive them according to the terms of the smart contract.

9d7ce4f7-c1a7-4b42-8031-d2d7b7f2a240.title: LEAD MAINTAINER
9d7ce4f7-c1a7-4b42-8031-d2d7b7f2a240.body: The lead maintainer was a role within the hierarchy of Bitcoin Core. This role has not existed since February 2023. This person was in charge of leading the project and therefore had more power than the maintainers. The role of lead maintainer was naturally taken on by Satoshi Nakamoto until their departure in early 2011. Subsequently, Gavin Andresen, who had already contributed alongside Satoshi, took over at the head of the software until early 2014. From that date, Wladimir J. van der Laan took on this role until February 2023. Since then, there has been no lead maintainer for the project.

9d840de1-c93e-4ab0-90e8-6239692dc691.title: BERKELEYDB
9d840de1-c93e-4ab0-90e8-6239692dc691.body: Embeddable database management system with a key-value storage architecture. It was used in the early versions of Bitcoin and was replaced by LevelDB in 2013.

9db2402c-6ea6-4b27-b3a5-6d3dcb61abc0.title: BIP-0061
9db2402c-6ea6-4b27-b3a5-6d3dcb61abc0.body: Introduces a reject message in the communication protocol between nodes. The goal of BIP-0061 is to add a feedback mechanism when a node receives, from another node, a transaction or a block that it considers invalid. This reject message would allow a node to tell the sender the reason why it was rejected. This type of communication was meant to help improve interoperability between the different clients and communications between full nodes and SPV clients. The features brought by BIP-0061 were eventually abandoned starting with version 0.20.0 of Bitcoin Core, because they were considered unnecessary while implying increased bandwidth requirements.

9db79d23-8470-4075-af0f-94f54372a6e6.title: THE EYE OF SATOSHI
9db79d23-8470-4075-af0f-94f54372a6e6.body: An open source watchtower implementation for the Lightning Network. A watchtower continuously monitors the Bitcoin blockchain on behalf of a user and automatically intervenes by broadcasting a penalty transaction if a counterparty attempts to cheat by publishing an old channel state.

9db9bb41-4162-4e9b-b7b2-ee74099a61a8.title: OP_FROMALTSTACK - 0X6C
9db9bb41-4162-4e9b-b7b2-ee74099a61a8.body: Removes the top of the alternate stack (*alt stack*) and places it on top of the main stack (*main stack*). This opcode is used to retrieve data temporarily stored on the alternate stack. To put it simply, it is the inverse operation of `OP_TOALTSTACK`.

9de74bf0-e9c5-4597-9abd-3889c7f4bc1d.title: VALIDATIONLESS MINING
9de74bf0-e9c5-4597-9abd-3889c7f4bc1d.body: A mining practice that consists of starting work on a new candidate block as soon as the hash of the previous block's header is received, without having downloaded or verified all of its transactions. Also called *SPV mining*, this method lets the miner gain a few seconds over those who wait for full validation of the block before starting their own work.

9e049074-4a73-4567-8fc3-0678aecdbcf7.title: BIP-0109
9e049074-4a73-4567-8fc3-0678aecdbcf7.body: Proposal presented by Gavin Andresen in January 2016 as part of the Blocksize War. It aimed to increase the maximum block size from 1 MB to 2 MB through a hard fork, while adding certain limits on the number of sigops and sighashes (unlike BIP-0102). The activation of BIP-0109 required support from 75% of the hash power over a window of 1,000 blocks, followed by a grace period of 28 days. This proposal was an integral part of the Bitcoin Classic fork, which sought to offer a solution for scaling Bitcoin. This proposal was never adopted.

9e25f457-ebb3-4e15-90d2-bea9130eeec5.title: UNECONOMICAL OUTPUT
9e25f457-ebb3-4e15-90d2-bea9130eeec5.body:
Refers to extremely small amounts of bitcoin coins that are too tiny to be sent in a transaction, because the fees needed to include them in a block would be proportionally higher than their value. The precise definition of "dust" may vary depending on the context, but it is generally any transaction output that requires more fees to be spent than the value it embodies. For the Bitcoin user, it is important to manage their UTXOs, and to practice consolidating them, so that they do not become dust.

*In English, the term "uneconomical outputs" is sometimes encountered to refer to dust.*

9e510056-14ea-470c-94b8-9e58f133980a.title: PEELING CHAIN
9e510056-14ea-470c-94b8-9e58f133980a.body:
Transaction pattern on the blockchain in which a large amount of bitcoins is gradually distributed through a long series of successive transactions. At each step, a fraction is sent to a recipient, while the remainder goes back to a new change address. The residual balance thus decreases from transaction to transaction: each amount is “peeled” (*peeled*) from the remaining total. The chain can extend over hundreds, even thousands of transactions.

This pattern is characteristic of automated withdrawals from exchange platforms, mining pools, or payment services, but it is also used for money laundering, because the small individual amounts attract less attention from compliance systems.

In chain analysis, the *peeling chain* is an easy pattern to identify, because each transaction generally has only one input and two outputs with very asymmetric amounts. Identifying it makes it possible to follow the thread of payments and reconstruct the flows of funds from a single source.

9e5b89ab-5444-4efb-9d6c-76b3a51b79b9.title: HONG KONG ROUNDTABLE
9e5b89ab-5444-4efb-9d6c-76b3a51b79b9.body:
A historic event of the Blocksize War that took place on February 20, 2016, in Hong Kong. It was an important meeting between Bitcoin Core developers and miners to discuss the scalability of the system and the strategy to adopt in order to scale it. Tensions were high before the meeting, notably because of the rise of Bitcoin Classic, a *hard fork* proposal backed by Gavin Andresen that aimed to increase the block size to 2 MB. At this meeting, influential figures in the ecosystem took part in the discussions, including Jihan Wu and Micree Zhan, the co-founders of Bitmain, Adam Back, the president of Blockstream, as well as Luke Dashjr, Matt Corallo and Peter Todd.

The miners, frustrated by the lack of progress, threatened to support Bitcoin Classic if a 2 MB *hard fork* was not implemented. The developers defended SegWit as a viable solution. After hours of tense negotiations, an agreement was reached, stipulating that the Bitcoin Core developers would work on a *hard fork* after the implementation of SegWit. This agreement was supposed to ease tensions, but it ultimately created more mistrust and confusion. Each side interpreted the agreement differently, which exacerbated the divisions within the community. Although this agreement temporarily slowed the momentum of Bitcoin Classic, it was seen by many as an unsatisfying and clumsy solution.

9e63fb0e-b53a-4bf1-9a34-a373d2f0d422.title: INSCRIPTIONS
9e63fb0e-b53a-4bf1-9a34-a373d2f0d422.body:
In the context of Ordinal theory, inscriptions are arbitrary content engraved on sats, turning them into digital artifacts native to Bitcoin. Inscriptions are made through transactions that expose the content of the information in the script of a Taproot input in this way:

```text
OP_FALSE
OP_IF
  OP_PUSH "ord"
  OP_PUSH 1
  OP_PUSH "<content type>"
  OP_PUSH 0
  OP_PUSH "<la data ici>"
OP_ENDIF
```

These digital artifacts, like NFTs, can be traded and kept.

9e8ddc27-219c-4bc1-9db5-5826aa530a3d.title: RASPIBLITZ
9e8ddc27-219c-4bc1-9db5-5826aa530a3d.body: An *open source* project that allows you to deploy a full Bitcoin and Lightning node on a Raspberry Pi. RaspiBlitz provides a preconfigured system that includes Bitcoin Core, a Lightning implementation, and a suite of complementary tools such as a block explorer, an Electrum server, or node management interfaces.

9f1cad71-54ab-4199-b5fd-a13bee7865b6.title: VPUB
9f1cad71-54ab-4199-b5fd-a13bee7865b6.body: Extended public key prefix for SegWit V0 accounts on Bitcoin Testnet.

9f43fce7-aa0b-4b65-86e0-44b56c0c2135.title: NERDMINER
9f43fce7-aa0b-4b65-86e0-44b56c0c2135.body: An *open source* solo Bitcoin mining project that runs on ESP32 microcontrollers.
