Created by BitMaker in 2022, it lets you assemble a small, very low-power miner to discover concretely how mining works. The device can be connected to a solo mining pool such as Public Pool. With a *hashrate* of about 78 kH/s, the chances of finding a block are astronomically low, but the project is above all educational and playful. NerdMiner displays real-time statistics about hashing and the Bitcoin network on its built-in screen.

9f81fba7-3785-41b9-aa10-347de13feb23.title: LNCLI
9f81fba7-3785-41b9-aa10-347de13feb23.body: Command-line interface provided with LND to administer a Lightning node. LNCLI (*Lightning Network Command Line Interface*) allows executing RPC calls to the LND daemon to manage channels, send and receive payments, check balances, adjust routing fees and perform all the common operations of a node. Each command corresponds to an underlying gRPC call.

9fa0c2d1-1763-4c3b-a8c7-a6cb7db1fda0.title: ZEROSYNC
9fa0c2d1-1763-4c3b-a8c7-a6cb7db1fda0.body: Project developed to take advantage of ZKPs (zero-knowledge proofs) in the Bitcoin ecosystem, in order to improve the scalability and privacy of the system. Their main protocol (also named *ZeroSync*) makes it possible to compress the history of the Bitcoin blockchain, in order to speed up the initial synchronization of nodes with the network through the use of a compact proof, without compromising verification.

9fa13088-9635-45e6-b7be-aae56aa7d448.title: BLOCK HEADER
9fa13088-9635-45e6-b7be-aae56aa7d448.body:
The block header is a data structure serving as the main component in the construction of a Bitcoin block. Each block is composed of a header and a list of transactions. The block header contains the crucial information that ensures the integrity and validity of a block within the blockchain. The block header contains 80 bytes of metadata and consists of the following elements:
* The block version;
* The hash of the previous block;
* The Merkle root of the transactions;
* The block timestamp;
* The difficulty target;
* The nonce.

For example, here is the header of block no. 785,530 in hexadecimal format, mined by Foundry USA on April 15, 2023:

```text
00e0ff3f5ffe3b0d9247dc437e18edc19252e4517cee941752d501000000000000000000206bde3a10826e2acb2f28fba70463601c789293d0c9c4348d7a0d06711e97c0bcb13a64b2e0051743f09a40
```

If we break down this header, we can recognize:
* The version: 

```text
00e0ff3f
```

* The previous hash:

```text
5ffe3b0d9247dc437e18edc19252e4517cee941752d501000000000000000000
```

* The Merkle root:

```text
206bde3a10826e2acb2f28fba70463601c789293d0c9c4348d7a0d06711e97c0
```

* The timestamp:

```text
bcb13a64
```

* The target:

```text
b2e00517
```

* The nonce: 

```text
43f09a40
```

To be valid, a block must have a header that, once hashed with `SHA256d`, produces a hash less than or equal to the difficulty target.

9ffee778-2e40-4552-a0e4-e4b47629711f.title: CASHU
9ffee778-2e40-4552-a0e4-e4b47629711f.body: An open-source Chaumian electronic money protocol, similar to David Chaum's eCash system, but which works on Bitcoin and the Lightning Network. More precisely, Cashu is inspired by a variant of eCash proposed in 1996 by David Wagner called “*Chaumian ecash without RSA*”. Cashu can be used on custodial wallets so that the server can identify neither the owners of the funds nor the details of the transactions, thus offering an improvement in privacy. Users can generate Cashu tokens in exchange for bitcoins, which are signed by the server without knowing the user. The tokens can then be transferred between users instantly, privately and without fees.

a03f35ba-155e-4798-b3c6-0ca0f1c585ae.title: SBI CRYPTO
a03f35ba-155e-4798-b3c6-0ca0f1c585ae.body: Bitcoin mining pool based in Tokyo, operated by SBI Crypto, a subsidiary of the Japanese financial group SBI Holdings. SBI Holdings has been mining on its own account since 2017, before opening its pool to the public in 2021. It is aimed at individual miners as well as professional operators.

a0570a67-2fb2-4cf7-8311-9e940fa93414.title: NVERSION
a0570a67-2fb2-4cf7-8311-9e940fa93414.body: The `nVersion` field in a Bitcoin transaction is used to indicate the version of the transaction format being used. It allows the network to distinguish the different evolutions of the transaction format over time, and to apply the corresponding rules. This field has an impact at the level of consensus rules: when `nVersion >= 2`, the interpretation of the `nSequence` field as a relative timelock is activated, in accordance with BIP-0068. However, no value assigned to this field causes the transaction to be invalidated. On the other hand, the `nVersion` field has standardness rules that currently accept only the values `1`, `2` and `3`. Version `3` was introduced with Bitcoin Core 28.0 for TRUC (*Topologically Restricted Until Confirmation*) transactions, as defined in BIP-0431. For the moment, this field is mainly useful for activating the `nSequence` field and for signaling TRUC transactions.

a066159b-a5a7-4e63-8e7e-fcf4c18611f1.title: COVENANT
a066159b-a5a7-4e63-8e7e-fcf4c18611f1.body:
Mechanism that makes it possible to impose specific conditions on how a given coin can be spent, including in future transactions. Beyond the conditions usually allowed by the script language on a UTXO, the covenant enforces additional constraints on how to spend that bitcoin coin in subsequent transactions. Technically, a covenant is established when the `scriptPubKey` of a UTXO defines restrictions on the `scriptPubKey` of the outputs of a transaction that spends said UTXO. By broadening the scope of script, covenants would enable many developments on Bitcoin such as the two-way peg of drivechains, the implementation of vaults, or the improvement of overlay systems like Lightning. Covenant proposals are differentiated according to three criteria:
* Their scope;
* Their implementation;
* Their recursiveness.

There are a great many proposals that would allow the use of covenants on Bitcoin. The most advanced in the implementation process are: `OP_CHECKTEMPLATEVERIFY` (CTV), `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` (APO) and `OP_VAULT`. Among the other proposals are: `OP_TX`, `OP_TAPLEAFUPDATEVERIFY` (TLUV), `OP_EVICT`, `OP_CHECKSIGFROMSTACK` (CSFS), `OP_CAT`, etc.

To properly understand the concept of covenant, I suggest an analogy: imagine a safe containing €500 in small bills. If you manage to unlock this safe with the right key, then you are free to use this money as you see fit. That is Bitcoin's normal situation. Now, imagine that this same safe does not contain €500 in banknotes, but rather meal vouchers of equivalent value. If you succeed in opening this safe, you can make use of that sum. However, your freedom to spend is restricted, because you can only use these vouchers to pay in certain restaurants. Thus, there is a first condition for spending this money, which is to manage to open the safe with the appropriate key. But there is also an additional condition regarding the future use of this sum: it must be spent exclusively in partner restaurants, and not with complete freedom. This system of constraints on future transactions is what we call a covenant.

*In French, there is no term that precisely captures the meaning of the word "covenant". One could speak of a "clause", a "pact", or a "commitment", but this would not correspond exactly to the term "covenant". The latter is in fact borrowed from a legal terminology used to describe a contractual clause imposing persistent obligations on a property.*

a073c884-0f6a-49f4-bdc9-fa5b8cc37133.title: BIP-0141
a073c884-0f6a-49f4-bdc9-fa5b8cc37133.body: Introduces the concept of segregated witness (*Segregated Witness*) which gives its name to the SegWit soft fork. BIP-0141 introduces into the Bitcoin protocol a major modification aiming to solve the transaction malleability problem. SegWit separates the witnesses (signature data) from the rest of the transaction data. This separation is achieved by inserting the witnesses into a distinct data structure, committed in a new Merkle tree, which is itself referenced in the block via the coinbase transaction, which makes SegWit compatible with older versions of the protocol.

a08d80c6-798e-477e-9347-18e18b40fd03.title: BLOCKS INDEX
a08d80c6-798e-477e-9347-18e18b40fd03.body: LevelDB data structure in Bitcoin Core that catalogs metadata about all the blocks. Each entry in this index provides details such as the block identifier, its height in the blockchain, the pointer to the block in the database, and other metadata. This indexing makes it possible to quickly find a block stored in memory.

a0ba6bcd-7eca-4953-afc3-ba737aefa644.title: COINBASE
a0ba6bcd-7eca-4953-afc3-ba737aefa644.body:
The coinbase transaction is a special and unique transaction included in every block of the Bitcoin blockchain. It is the first transaction of a block and is created by the miner who successfully found a header that validates the Proof-of-Work (*Proof-of-Work*), that is, one that is less than or equal to the target.

The coinbase transaction mainly serves two purposes: allocating the block reward to the miner and adding new units of bitcoin to the circulating money supply. The block reward, which is the economic incentive for miners to contribute to carrying out the proof of work, comprises the fees accumulated for the transactions included in the block and a determined amount of newly created ex-nihilo bitcoins (block subsidy). This amount, initially set at 50 bitcoins per block in 2009, is halved every 210,000 blocks (approximately every 4 years) during an event called the “halving”.

The coinbase transaction differs from regular transactions in several ways. First, it has no input, which means that no existing transaction output (UTXO) is consumed in it. Second, the signature script (`scriptSig`) for the coinbase transaction generally contains an arbitrary field allowing additional data to be incorporated, such as custom messages or mining software version information. Finally, the bitcoins generated by the coinbase transaction are subject to a maturity period of 100 blocks (101 confirmations) before they can be spent, in order to prevent the potential spending of non-existent bitcoins in the event of a chain reorganization.

*There is no French translation of “Coinbase”. It is therefore accepted to use this term directly.*

a0d2bc7c-633f-4e3e-8c96-34d609cd37a0.title: MINIBITS
a0d2bc7c-633f-4e3e-8c96-34d609cd37a0.body: A mobile wallet dedicated to eCash, which uses the Cashu protocol to issue digital tokens backed by bitcoin via the Lightning Network. The application allows payments to be sent and received almost instantly, with a high level of privacy, since eCash transactions are hard to trace.

a0e11b68-19b7-4bb8-bb85-338f08726ca7.title: OPENSATS
a0e11b68-19b7-4bb8-bb85-338f08726ca7.body: A non-profit organization founded in 2021, dedicated to funding free and *open source* projects related to Bitcoin. Structured as a charitable association in the United States, OpenSats distributes grants to developers and projects that contribute to the Bitcoin ecosystem and its adjacent technologies.

a0f6ef6f-f758-4978-9e95-e11a605d3507.title: LIGHTNING TERMINAL
a0f6ef6f-f758-4978-9e95-e11a605d3507.body:
A web graphical interface developed by Lightning Labs to administer a Lightning node. Lightning Terminal offers a visual dashboard for viewing the state of channels, liquidity, routed payments and node performance. It integrates the Loop, Pool and Faraday tools into a unified interface.

Lightning Terminal runs via the *litd* daemon and can be accessed remotely through the *Lightning Node Connect* (LNC) protocol, without requiring a VPN or complex network configuration. It is designed to simplify the day-to-day management of an LND node, by making accessible operations that usually require the command line.

a0fc55d0-9a76-44c0-8669-fb4062bec4ec.title: DLP - DISCRETE LOGARITHM PROBLEM
a0fc55d0-9a76-44c0-8669-fb4062bec4ec.body: The discrete logarithm problem (DLP) is a mathematical problem on which the security of public-key cryptographic algorithms relies, notably those used on Bitcoin. In a cyclic group of order `q`, with a generator `g`, if we have an equation of the form `g^x = h`, then `x` is called the discrete logarithm of `h` with respect to the base `g`, modulo `q`. In simple terms, it consists of determining the exponent `x` when `g`, `h`, and `q` are known. The discrete logarithm is therefore the inverse of exponentiation in a finite cyclic group. However, for large values of `q`, solving the discrete logarithm problem is considered algorithmically hard. This property is exploited to ensure the security of many cryptographic protocols, such as the Diffie-Hellman protocol for key exchange. The discrete logarithm is also used in elliptic curve cryptography (ECC), among others in the ECDSA algorithm (*Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm*). In the context of elliptic curves, the discrete logarithm problem extends to finding a scalar `k` such that `k \cdot G = K`, where `G` and `K` are points on the curve, and `\cdot` represents the point multiplication operation. In the context of Bitcoin, standard transactions use either ECDSA or the Schnorr protocol in order to lock UTXOs. Both rely on the impossibility of computing the discrete logarithm.

a11565d1-daa1-41d2-9bf7-ae34cdc7ed5e.title: LUD
a11565d1-daa1-41d2-9bf7-ae34cdc7ed5e.body: Acronym for "*LNURL Document*". LUDs are documents that define standardized protocols used within LNURL. Each LUD specifies a feature, such as payments (LUD-06), withdrawals (LUD-03) or authentication (LUD-04). They therefore allow good interoperability between the different Lightning services and clients using LNURL.

a13b0a65-be0d-4c07-9994-30b62851240f.title: P2TR
a13b0a65-be0d-4c07-9994-30b62851240f.body:
P2TR is the acronym for *Pay to Taproot*. It is a standard script template used to set spending conditions on a UTXO. It was introduced with the implementation of Taproot in November 2021. P2TR uses the Schnorr protocol to aggregate cryptographic keys, as well as Merkle trees for alternative scripts, known as MAST (*Merkelized Alternative Script Tree*). Unlike traditional transactions where the spending conditions are publicly exposed (sometimes at receipt, sometimes at spending), P2TR makes it possible to hide complex scripts behind a single apparent public key.

Technically, a P2TR script locks bitcoins to a single Schnorr public key, called `K`. However, this `K` key is actually an aggregate of a public key `P` and a public key `M`, the latter being computed from the Merkle root of a list of `scriptPubKey`. Bitcoins locked with a P2TR script can be spent in two distinct ways: either by publishing a signature for the public key `P`, or by satisfying one of the scripts contained in the Merkle tree. The first option is called the “*key path*” and the second the “*script path*”.

Thus, P2TR allows users to send bitcoins either to a public key, or to several scripts of their choice. Another advantage of this script is that, although there are multiple ways to spend a P2TR output, only the one that is used must be revealed at spending, allowing the unused alternatives to remain private. P2TR is a version 1 SegWit output, which means that the signatures for P2TR inputs are stored in the witness of a transaction, and not in the `scriptSig`. P2TR addresses use a `Bech32m` encoding and begin with `bc1p`.

a157dfd3-86e2-4c6d-aeee-7f04a9c95758.title: CHANNEL BREACH
a157dfd3-86e2-4c6d-aeee-7f04a9c95758.body:
An attempt at cheating on the Lightning Network, in which a peer publishes an old commitment transaction (*commitment transaction*) to try to recover a balance that no longer belongs to them. When such a revoked state is broadcast on the blockchain, the counterparty has a period defined by the *timelock* to detect this fraud and publish a justice transaction that allows them to recover all of the channel's funds.

The detection of a channel breach can be handled directly by the node if it is online, or delegated to a *watchtower* that monitors the blockchain continuously. If the breach is not contested before the *timelock* expires, the cheater keeps the funds unduly recovered.

a184573c-7acd-4bd3-9618-25a1eb44d4aa.title: TRANSACTION RELAY POLICY
a184573c-7acd-4bd3-9618-25a1eb44d4aa.body:
Subset of relay policy that groups together all the rules applied by a Bitcoin node specifically for processing and relaying transactions on the peer-to-peer network. Transaction relay policy notably encompasses mempool policy and, by extension, standardness rules.

These rules determine whether a transaction received from a peer will be accepted, stored in the mempool, and then relayed to the other nodes on the network. They go beyond the mere format of individual transactions (covered by standardness rules) and also include considerations related to network management.

Like all policy rules, transaction relay policy is configured locally by each node and may vary from one node to another. It is distinct from relay policy in the broader sense, which also covers aspects not related to transactions, such as block handling or the management of connections with peers.

a1cbf11c-d87e-4866-a1cd-61a653d8a853.title: BIT
a1cbf11c-d87e-4866-a1cd-61a653d8a853.body: The word "bit" is the contraction of the terms "binary" and "digit". In the context of computing and cryptology, a bit is the fundamental unit of digital information and represents the smallest possible quantity of information. A bit can only take two distinct values: `0` or `1`. These values are also called binary states and can represent various things, such as the answers `yes` or `no`, `true` or `false`, and `on` or `off`. Bits are the foundation of digital systems and are used to store and transmit information in computers and networks. The name "Bitcoin" probably comes from the concatenation of the term "Bit", to evoke the electronic nature of the payment system, and the term "Coin", to evoke its monetary purpose.

a1e6ab88-6b66-46a1-9846-d59fa9072a89.title: CHECKPOINTS
a1e6ab88-6b66-46a1-9846-d59fa9072a89.body:
Hashes of specific blocks that were hard-coded in Bitcoin Core. Each checkpoint associated a block height with an expected hash, and any fork below an already synchronized checkpoint was rejected.

Introduced by Satoshi Nakamoto on July 17, 2010 (version 0.3.2), this mechanism aimed to prevent any rewriting of the historical chain, even by an attacker with a majority of the computing power. In practice, checkpoints mainly served as an anti-DoS protection during the IBD: without them, an attacker could exploit the *time warp* bug to overwhelm a new node's memory with millions of minimum-difficulty headers. But these checkpoints did not add any real security to consensus: if checkpoints had to influence the choice of the chain, the system would already be compromised. The last one was added at block 295,000, in April 2014.

Checkpoints were removed in Bitcoin Core 30.0 (October 2025), replaced by the *headers presync* mechanism (August 2022), which verifies a chain's proof of work before storing its headers, eliminating any data hard-coded by the developers.

a2401850-c268-4b41-b2a7-32101186bcf9.title: BANLIST.DAT
a2401850-c268-4b41-b2a7-32101186bcf9.body: Name of the former file used by the Bitcoin Core software to record the IP addresses of nodes that have been banned by the user. Since version 22.0, the file `banlist.json` is used instead.

a2e10cda-5549-48a2-8b05-010a04b6ed0a.title: MASTER CHAIN CODE
a2e10cda-5549-48a2-8b05-010a04b6ed0a.body: Designates the chain code associated with the wallet's master key, at the base of the derivation tree of all keys.

a3188665-9f51-4672-a5da-302ac7ba2692.title: SINGLE-SIG
a3188665-9f51-4672-a5da-302ac7ba2692.body: Bitcoin wallet configuration in which a single private key is enough to sign a transaction and authorize the spending of funds. This mode of operation, also called "single signature", is the simplest and most widespread form of securing a wallet. Unlike multisig, which requires several signatures coming from different keys to validate a transaction, single-sig relies only on the possession of a single seed.

a3559e0e-4bda-402c-8e4e-754d35e2eb1f.title: SIGN-TO-CONTRACT
a3559e0e-4bda-402c-8e4e-754d35e2eb1f.body:
Cryptographic protocol that makes it possible to commit arbitrary data into the nonce of a digital signature, without this commitment being visible from the outside. This technique is the analogue of Pay-to-Contract, but applied to the nonce (the random value `k`) rather than to the public key. The principle relies on "tweaking" the nonce: from an original nonce `k` and a commitment `c`, a new nonce `k' = k + H(R \| c)` is computed, where `R = k \cdot G` is the public point of the original nonce and `H` a hash function. The resulting public nonce `R' = k' \cdot G` appears as an arbitrary point on the curve, but it encodes a verifiable commitment to `c`. To prove the commitment, it is enough to reveal `R` and `c`.

This construction has several applications in Bitcoin. In particular, it makes it possible to timestamp documents: the fingerprint of a file is inserted into the nonce of an ordinary transaction. It is also the underlying mechanism of the anti-exfiltration protocol (anti-exfil), where a host software injects its own entropy into the nonce of a *hardware wallet* to prevent the leakage of the private key through a covert channel.

a360db79-5809-44e6-9520-9b28bbc74f9c.title: OP_IFDUP - 0X73
a360db79-5809-44e6-9520-9b28bbc74f9c.body: Duplicates the top of the stack if it is non-zero. If the value at the top of the stack is true (that is, non-zero), this value is duplicated on the stack; otherwise, the stack remains unchanged.

a38975e1-4280-49a2-9aef-10c506618aa9.title: BTCD - BTC SUITE
a38975e1-4280-49a2-9aef-10c506618aa9.body: Minority implementation of the Bitcoin protocol. BTCD is an alternative to the majority software Bitcoin Core (notably Bitcoind). Unlike Bitcoin Core, which is developed in C++, BTCD is written in Go (golang). Its goal is to follow the consensus rules established by Bitcoin Core to ensure compatibility with the other nodes of the network. BTCD is developed as part of the BTC Suite project.

a3913f01-8ccd-4b0e-9e5d-bb5d3acc1289.title: CLEMENTINE
a3913f01-8ccd-4b0e-9e5d-bb5d3acc1289.body: Trust-minimized two-way bridge developed by Chainway Labs for the Citrea rollup. Clementine makes it possible to transfer BTC between the main Bitcoin chain and Citrea (BTC ↔ cBTC) without relying on a conventional trusted multisig. The protocol is based on BitVM2 and operates with a 1-of-N trust assumption: it is enough for a single participant in the group of verifiers to be honest for the funds to be protected against theft. For a deposit (*peg-in*), the user sends BTC to a Taproot address encoding two spending paths: one path allows the signers to move the funds to a vault (*vault*), the other allows an automatic refund after a *timelock* if the bridge does not respond. For a withdrawal (*peg-out*), the user burns their cBTC on Citrea, then an operator advances the funds in BTC on Bitcoin and is subsequently reimbursed from the vault, provided that no challenger proves fraudulent behavior through a challenge mechanism using BitVM2. Clementine is open source.

a3ad6a6c-2765-41fe-b1d5-38c7b7e4a34a.title: TRANSACTION FEES
a3ad6a6c-2765-41fe-b1d5-38c7b7e4a34a.body:
Transaction fees represent an amount intended to compensate miners for their participation in the proof-of-work mechanism. These fees incentivize miners to include transactions in the blocks they create. They are the result of the difference between the total amount of the inputs and the total amount of the outputs of a transaction:

```text
frais = inputs - outputs
```

They are expressed in `sats/vBytes`, which means that the fees do not depend on the amount of bitcoins sent, but on the weight of the transaction. They are freely chosen by the sender of a transaction and determine its speed of inclusion in a block through an auction mechanism. For example, imagine that I make a transaction with an input of `100 000 sats`, an output of `40 000 sats` and an output of `58 500 sats`. The total of the outputs is `98 500 sats`. The fees allocated to this transaction are `1 500 sats`. The miner who includes my transaction will be able to create `1 500 sats` in their coinbase transaction in exchange for the `1 500 sats` that I did not recover in my outputs. 

Transactions with higher fees, relative to their size, are processed with priority by miners, which can speed up the confirmation process. Conversely, transactions with lower fees may be delayed during periods of heavy congestion. It should be noted that Bitcoin transaction fees are distinct from the block subsidy, which is an additional incentive for miners. The block reward is composed of the new bitcoins created with each mined block (block subsidy), as well as the collected transaction fees. While the block subsidy decreases over time due to the limitation of the total supply of bitcoins, transaction fees will continue to play a crucial role in encouraging miners to participate. 

At the protocol level, nothing prevents users from including transactions with no fees in a block. In reality, this type of fee-free transaction is an exception. By default, Bitcoin nodes do not relay transactions with fees below `1 sat/vBytes`. If some fee-free transactions have gotten through, it is because they were included directly by the winning miner, without traveling across the network of nodes. For example, the following transaction includes no fees:

```text
fd456524104a6674693c29946543f8a0befccce5a352bda55ec8559fc630f5f3
```

In this specific example, it was a transaction initiated by the director of the F2Pool mining pool. As a normal user, the lower limit is therefore currently `1 sat/vBytes`.

The purge limits must also be taken into account. During periods of heavy congestion, nodes' mempools purge their pending transactions below a certain threshold, in order to respect their allocated RAM limit. This limit is freely chosen by the user, but many leave the default Bitcoin Core value of 300 MB. It can be modified in the `bitcoin.conf` file with the `maxmempool` parameter.

a3d71f9e-2c84-4b6a-9e15-8f4d1c7a3b92.title: LIQUIDITY SWAP
a3d71f9e-2c84-4b6a-9e15-8f4d1c7a3b92.body:
Mechanism for coordinated opening of Lightning channels in which several node operators mutually commit to opening channels toward one another in a circular arrangement. Each participant opens a channel toward the next one in the circle, which guarantees that everyone obtains both inbound and outbound liquidity. This concept is also known as a “*ring of fire*”.

The LN+ platform is the most widely used service for organizing these exchanges. On this platform, the participants, generally between three and five, agree on an identical channel capacity. Once all the channels are open, the circle forms a loop in which each node has improved connectivity to the network. A circular rebalancing can then be performed to distribute the liquidity evenly across the channels.

a3e9c07b-1076-4ab9-9695-c27cb52fe42f.title: WATCH-ONLY WALLET
a3e9c07b-1076-4ab9-9695-c27cb52fe42f.body: A watch-only wallet is a type of software that allows a user to view the transactions associated with a specific Bitcoin key or set of keys, without owning the corresponding private keys. It provides visibility into the balance and transaction history, without however allowing the wallet's funds to be spent. For example, the Sentinel application is a watch-only wallet.

a3f8386d-0c3b-49ab-8252-2008448eedc6.title: P2SH-P2WSH
a3f8386d-0c3b-49ab-8252-2008448eedc6.body:
P2SH-P2WSH is the acronym for *Pay to Script Hash - Pay to Witness Script Hash*. It is a standard script template used to set spending conditions on a UTXO, also known as “*Nested SegWit*”.

P2SH-P2WSH was introduced with the implementation of SegWit in August 2017. This script describes a P2WSH wrapped within a P2SH. It locks bitcoins based on the hash of a script. The difference from the standard P2WSH is that the script is wrapped in the `redeemScript` of a standard P2SH.

This script was created at the launch of SegWit to facilitate its adoption. It makes it possible to use this new standard, even with services or *wallets* not yet natively compatible with SegWit. Today, it is therefore no longer very relevant to use this type of *wrapped* SegWit scripts, since most *wallets* have implemented native SegWit. P2SH-P2WSH addresses are written using the `Base58Check` encoding and always begin with `3`, like any P2SH address.

a4423e2f-7a1e-485b-9bbb-6460d2654e3c.title: ZPRV
a4423e2f-7a1e-485b-9bbb-6460d2654e3c.body: Extended private key prefix for SegWit V0 accounts on Bitcoin.

a449f71c-1648-4028-bb90-852289e803b3.title: PPS+
a449f71c-1648-4028-bb90-852289e803b3.body:
Acronym for "*Pay Per Share Plus*". Method for calculating miner compensation in the context of mining pools, which combines the PPS and PPLNS approaches. For the portion related to the block subsidy, miners receive fixed compensation for each valid *share* submitted, calculated according to the classic PPS method, regardless of whether the pool found a block or not. For the portion related to transaction fees, the compensation is distributed according to the PPLNS method, only when a block is actually found by the pool.

PPS+ thus offers miners a stable income base thanks to the PPS component, while allowing them to benefit from transaction fees when the pool finds a block. This method is less risky for the pool operator than FPPS, because the operator does not advance the transaction fees.

a4857ce4-9b8e-4e26-9310-14acd52d1851.title: MTP - MEDIAN TIME PAST
a4857ce4-9b8e-4e26-9310-14acd52d1851.body: Concept used in the Bitcoin protocol to determine a margin on the network's consensus timestamp. The MTP is defined as the median of the timestamps of the last 11 mined blocks. Using this indicator avoids disagreements between nodes about the exact time in case of clock offset. The MTP was initially used to verify the validity of block timestamps relative to the past. Since BIP-0113, it is also used as the network's time reference to verify the validity of timelock operations (`nLockTime`, `OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY`, `nSequence` and `OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY`).

a4902301-5664-4d64-bdcd-0a1027408fdc.title: ECDSA
a4902301-5664-4d64-bdcd-0a1027408fdc.body:
Acronym for "*Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm*". It is a digital signature algorithm built on elliptic curve cryptography (ECC). It is a variant of the DSA (*Digital Signature Algorithm*) algorithm. ECDSA uses the properties of elliptic curves to provide security levels comparable to those of traditional public-key algorithms, such as RSA, while using significantly smaller keys. ECDSA allows the generation of key pairs (public key and private key) as well as the creation and verification of digital signatures.

In the context of Bitcoin, ECDSA is used to derive public keys from private keys. It is also used to sign transactions, in order to satisfy a script to unlock bitcoins and spend them. The elliptic curve used on Bitcoin within ECDSA is `secp256k1`, defined by the equation `y^2 = x^3 + 7`. This algorithm has been used since the early days of Bitcoin in 2009. Today, it shares its place with the Schnorr protocol, another digital signature algorithm introduced with Taproot in 2021.

a4a63857-0bd2-4651-ac7b-1a455fd3eab0.title: BIP-0078
a4a63857-0bd2-4651-ac7b-1a455fd3eab0.body: Introduces a protocol for using Payjoin on Bitcoin, a transaction structure that improves payment privacy by having the recipient join the payer in the inputs. This BIP draws inspiration from BIP-0079, which had already presented a similar concept. However, these two BIPs do not mark the origin of the Payjoin concept. Indeed, the Stowaway implementation of Samourai Wallet already existed beforehand and this transaction structure had first been mentioned by LaurentMT in 2015, under the name "*steganographic transaction*".

a4ea1500-8e79-464a-ae74-de72b98169b3.title: BBQR
a4ea1500-8e79-464a-ae74-de72b98169b3.body:
Acronym for “Better Bitcoin QR”. Protocol that makes it possible to encode files too large for a single QR code into a series of successive QR codes (animated QR). The target data types are PSBTs (BIP-0174) and signed transactions, but the format also supports CBOR, JSON and text data.

The protocol is adopted by several software applications and *signing devices*, notably COLDCARD Q, Sparrow Wallet and Nunchuk. The specification is published by Coinkite as an open standard.

a523b34d-5c65-4d56-9c60-e0117e659efc.title: SCRIPT TEMPLATE
a523b34d-5c65-4d56-9c60-e0117e659efc.body: *Template* allowing the use of standard scripts. A script template is essentially a small list of *opcodes* put together to form a standard that specifies a way of setting spending conditions on bitcoins. Here are some examples of script templates: P2PK, P2PKH, P2WPKH, P2SH...

a5382091-2a05-46c8-8499-39853ddcdc94.title: ATOMIC MULTI-PATH PAYMENTS
a5382091-2a05-46c8-8499-39853ddcdc94.body:
An improved version of MPPs (*Multi-Path Payments*) in which each payment fragment has a distinct partial secret, which ensures that the transaction is settled atomically, that is, in full or not at all. 

MPPs are payment techniques on Lightning that make it possible to split a transaction into several smaller parts in order to route them through different paths. In other words, each fraction of the payment takes a different path of nodes. This makes it possible to work around the liquidity limitations of a single channel in the route. In basic MPPs, each payment fraction shares the same secret, and therefore the same hash in the HTLCs. This can make the transaction traceable if an observer is present on several routes, because they can link all these identical secrets together. Moreover, because the secret is the same for all fractions of the payment, the payment is not atomic. This means that some parts of the payment can be executed successfully, while others can fail.

In AMPs, unique partial secrets are used for each fraction. Once all the fragments are received, they allow the recipient to reconstruct the original overall secret and claim the entire payment. This method makes partial settlement of the payment impossible, because possession of all the partial secrets is necessary to unlock the complete payment. This ensures that the payment either fully succeeds or fully fails (that is, it is atomic). AMPs also improve privacy, because there are no longer any visible links between the different routes.

An advantage of AMPs is that they work even if only the receiver and the sender have implemented this method. Intermediate nodes process these payments as regular transactions using HTLCs, without being aware that they are processing fractions of a larger payment.

*"Atomic Multi-Part Payment" is also sometimes used to refer to this same method.*

a5e43413-b88c-4269-bd96-513fac09e873.title: BOLT-10
a5e43413-b88c-4269-bd96-513fac09e873.body: Specification that defines a DNS-based Lightning node discovery mechanism. It allows a node starting up with no known contacts to find initial peers (*bootstrap*) by querying authoritative DNS servers (*seed nodes*). Queries support filters by address type (IPv4, IPv6), by specific node identifier and by desired number of results. The DNS servers return a random sample of healthy nodes, with IP addresses via `A`/`AAAA` records (standard port `9735`) and `SRV` records for non-standard ports.

a5f05ecc-5a81-4f97-aa00-f79484ebc76e.title: FUNGIBILITY
a5f05ecc-5a81-4f97-aa00-f79484ebc76e.body: Property of a currency that ensures that each unit is interchangeable and indistinguishable from another similar unit. Bitcoin, as a unit of account, is in principle fungible, because one bitcoin is always worth another bitcoin: 1 BTC = 1 BTC. However, the traceability of UTXOs (the medium of the units) on the blockchain can sometimes compromise this fungibility. Indeed, each satoshi can be distinguished by its history, which thus gives it a specific identity. The perception of the history of each UTXO can influence the parties' judgment on the fungibility of the bitcoins used. Thus, although fungibility is an intrinsic characteristic of monetary units, it can be altered by the specificities of the medium used for these units, as is the case with Bitcoin.

a5ff44d9-c519-4f2b-954b-fac294667025.title: SCRIPTSIG
a5ff44d9-c519-4f2b-954b-fac294667025.body:
Element in a Bitcoin transaction located in the inputs. The `scriptSig` provides the data necessary to satisfy the conditions set by the `scriptPubKey` of the previous transaction whose funds are being spent. It therefore plays a complementary role to the `scriptPubKey`. Typically, the `scriptSig` contains a digital signature and a public key. The signature is generated by the owner of the bitcoins using their private key and proves that they have the authorization to spend the UTXO. In this case, the `scriptSig` demonstrates that the holder of the input possesses the private key corresponding to the public key associated with the address specified in the `scriptPubKey` of the previous outgoing transaction.

When the transaction is verified, the data of the `scriptSig` is executed in the corresponding `scriptPubKey`. If the result is valid, this means that the conditions for spending the funds have been fulfilled. If all the inputs of the transaction provide a `scriptSig` that validates their `scriptPubKey`, the transaction is valid and can be added to a block for its execution.

For example, here is a classic P2PKH `scriptSig`:

```text
<signature> <clé publique>
```

The corresponding `scriptPubKey` would be:

```text
OP_DUP
OP_HASH160
OP_PUSHBYTES_20
<hash de la clé publique>
OP_EQUALVERIFY
OP_CHECKSIG
```

![ScriptSig in the input with an open padlock and ScriptPubKey locking the output: the pair validates the spending of a UTXO.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/s/scriptsig/assets/image-1.png)

*The `scriptSig` is also sometimes called "unlocking script" or "script de déverrouillage" in French.*

a61b5d3a-da3c-4bc8-bac2-24265a18e981.title: ANONSETS - ANONYMITY SETS
a61b5d3a-da3c-4bc8-bac2-24265a18e981.body:
Anonsets serve as indicators for evaluating the degree of privacy of a particular UTXO. More specifically, they measure the number of indistinguishable UTXOs within the set that includes the coin under study. Since a group of identical UTXOs is needed, anonsets are generally calculated within a cycle of coinjoins. They make it possible, where relevant, to judge the quality of coinjoins. A large anonset means an increased level of anonymity, because it becomes difficult to distinguish a specific UTXO within the set. Two types of anonsets exist:
* The forward anonymity set;
* The backward anonymity set.

The first indicates the size of the group among which the UTXO under study is hidden at the output, given the input UTXO. This indicator makes it possible to measure the resistance of the coin's privacy against an analysis going from past to present (input to output). In English, the name of this indicator is "*forward anonset*", or "*forward-looking metrics*".

![Diagram of the forward anonset calculation over three successive coinjoin mixes, totaling 13 indistinguishable UTXOs.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/a/anonsets-anonymity-sets/assets/image-1.png)

The second indicates the number of possible sources for a given coin, given the output UTXO. This indicator makes it possible to measure the resistance of the coin's privacy against an analysis going from present to past (output to input). In English, the name of this indicator is "*backward anonset*", or "*backward-looking metrics*".

![Backward anonset, which traces back from a coinjoin to its ancestor inputs stage by stage up to the genesis coinjoin.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/a/anonsets-anonymity-sets/assets/image-2.png)

*In French, it is generally accepted to use the term "anonset". However, it could be translated as "ensemble d'anonymat" or "potentiel d'anonymat". In both English and French, one also sometimes speaks of a "score" to refer to anonsets (forward score and backward score).*

a629be3a-115c-4c34-9c8a-cc67f611b0ff.title: MUSIG2
a629be3a-115c-4c34-9c8a-cc67f611b0ff.body:
An evolution of MuSig that reduces from three to two the number of rounds needed to produce an aggregated Schnorr multisignature. Proposed in 2020 by Jonas Nick, Tim Ruffing and Yannick Seurin, the protocol eliminates the nonce commitment round through the use of several random nonces per signer: each participant sends their nonces in the first round, even before knowing the message to sign, then the partial signatures are exchanged in the second round.

Like MuSig, the resulting signature is indistinguishable from an individual signature on the blockchain. However, reusing nonces across signing sessions irreparably compromises the security of the scheme. MuSig2 was formalized in BIP-0327.

a63da214-1470-4dd7-aa04-8009088924d1.title: CONTRACT RIGHTS

a64c6263-b1aa-423a-a1b4-3faeefb3decf.title: GENESIS
a64c6263-b1aa-423a-a1b4-3faeefb3decf.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the Genesis designates the set of initial data, governed by a specific schema, that establishes the starting state of any contract. This information constitutes the anchor point from which the evolution of smart contracts and the management of RGB tokens take place. It can be compared to the concept of the *Genesis Block* on Bitcoin, or to the concept of a Coinbase transaction, but here at the *client-side* level and for RGB tokens.

a7440e2a-a951-4a73-9350-2321d8cb900c.title: MINITAPSCRIPT
a7440e2a-a951-4a73-9350-2321d8cb900c.body:
A version of Miniscript for Tapscript. Tapscript has a few notable differences from Script in its original version. MiniTapscript thus provides support for Tapscript in Miniscript.

*This term is sometimes disputed. Indeed, some bitcoiners prefer to speak of “TapMiniscript”.*

a749f19c-ac51-4565-a219-feaabe89eb56.title: PAYJOIN
a749f19c-ac51-4565-a219-feaabe89eb56.body:
Specific Bitcoin transaction structure that improves users' privacy when spending by collaborating with the payment recipient. The distinctive feature of Payjoin is its ability to generate a transaction that looks ordinary at first glance, but is in reality a mini coinjoin between two people. To do this, the transaction structure involves the payment recipient in the inputs alongside the actual sender. The recipient therefore includes a payment to themselves in the middle of the transaction that itself serves to pay them. For example, if you buy a baguette for `6 000 sats` using a UTXO of `10 000 sats`, and you opt for a Payjoin, your baker will add a UTXO of `15 000 sats` belonging to them as an input, which they will recover in full as an output, in addition to your `6 000 sats`.

The Payjoin transaction fulfills two purposes. First, it aims to mislead an outside observer by creating a decoy in chain analysis based on the CIOH heuristic (*Common Input Ownership Heuristic*). Usually, when a transaction on the blockchain has several inputs, it is assumed that all these inputs likely belong to a single entity. Thus, when an analyst examines a Payjoin transaction, they are led to believe that all the inputs come from one person. However, this perception is wrong, because the payment recipient also contributes inputs alongside the actual payer. Second, Payjoin also makes it possible to deceive an outside observer about the actual amount of the payment that was made. By examining the structure of the transaction, the analyst might believe that the payment is equivalent to the amount of one of the outputs. In reality, the payment amount does not match any of the outputs. It is in fact the difference between the recipient's UTXO as an output and the recipient's UTXO as an input. In this respect, the Payjoin transaction falls within the domain of steganography. It makes it possible to hide the actual amount of a transaction within a fake transaction that acts as a decoy.

![Payjoin between a buyer and a baker: 2 inputs and 2 outputs mixed together, the actual payment of 6,000 sats remains hidden.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/p/payjoin/assets/image-1.png)

*Payjoin is also sometimes called “P2EP (Pay-to-End-Point)”, “Stowaway”, or “steganographic transaction”.*

a78b1bd4-6e09-491e-830b-75a3841bd08c.title: BSMS
a78b1bd4-6e09-491e-830b-75a3841bd08c.body:
Acronym for "*Bitcoin Secure Multisig Setup*". BSMS is a protocol standardized by BIP-0129 that makes it possible to create a multisignature wallet securely among several signers (*hardware wallets*, software), ensuring that all of them agree on the same configuration before using it.

The protocol works in two rounds of exchanges between a Coordinator and the Signers. In the first round, the Coordinator defines the multisig parameters (M-of-N threshold, script type) and optionally distributes an encryption token (`TOKEN`) to each signer. Each signer then provides their extended public key, accompanied by their derivation path and a signature proving that they control the corresponding private key. In the second round, the Coordinator gathers all the keys, generates a wallet descriptor (*output descriptor*) and redistributes it to each signer. Each signer verifies that their own key is indeed included and that the wallet's first address is correct, which serves as a checksum over the whole configuration.

Three encryption modes are possible for the exchanges: no encryption, standard encryption with a shared 64-bit token, or extended encryption with a unique 128-bit token per signer. The encryption uses AES-256-CTR with a key derived via PBKDF2. The BSMS protocol is notably implemented in Nunchuk, Sparrow and ColdCard.

a7c3e1f2-8d4b-4a6e-9f01-3c5d7e8b2a49.title: FLOOD AND LOOT
a7c3e1f2-8d4b-4a6e-9f01-3c5d7e8b2a49.body: Attack on the Lightning Network that exploits the HTLC mechanism to steal funds. It was described in 2020 by Jona Harris and Aviv Zohar. The attacker controls two nodes and opens channels with many intermediate victims. They route a large number of HTLCs from their source node to their target node through the victims, then refuse to reveal the preimage. As the *timelocks* approach expiry, all the victims are forced to unilaterally close their channels at the same time, which causes massive congestion of the blockchain. This congestion prevents some closing transactions from being confirmed in time. HTLCs not claimed before expiry revert to the attacker, who can bid up the fees thanks to RBF. Unlike *griefing*, which temporarily freezes funds without stealing them, *flood-and-loot* allows actual theft. The researchers estimated that about 85 channels attacked simultaneously are enough to guarantee a gain. The attack has never been observed in real-world conditions. The proposed countermeasures include reducing the maximum number of HTLCs per channel, adopting *anchor outputs* to dynamically adjust fees during a forced closure, and shortening expiry delays.

a8036f6b-9bc1-4715-906e-46b7363d041d.title: ONION ADDRESS
a8036f6b-9bc1-4715-906e-46b7363d041d.body:
A special address used to access an *onion service* on the Tor network. It ends with the suffix `.onion` and is not resolved by conventional DNS: only a client connected to the Tor network can reach it. A v3 onion address (the current format) is a string of 56 alphanumeric characters derived from the service's public key `Ed25519`, which allows the client to cryptographically verify that it is communicating with the right server.

In the Bitcoin ecosystem, onion addresses allow Bitcoin and Lightning nodes to expose their services without revealing their real IP address. A node configured with an address `.onion` remains reachable by its peers on the P2P network, while concealing its geographic location and the identity of its operator. This strengthens censorship resistance and privacy, at the cost of slightly higher latency than *clearnet*.

a83623aa-d839-4a46-92aa-cdb6cc6ed4db.title: FUNDING TRANSACTION
a83623aa-d839-4a46-92aa-cdb6cc6ed4db.body:
On-chain Bitcoin transaction that marks the opening of a payment channel on the Lightning Network. It sends funds to a 2/2 multisignature address jointly controlled by the two parties of the channel. These funds make up the total capacity of the channel and can only be spent if both participants sign together.

Before publishing the funding transaction on the blockchain, the channel initiator first builds a commitment transaction (*commitment transaction*) signed by both parties. This precaution guarantees that the initiator will be able to recover their funds even if their peer becomes uncooperative. The channel is considered open once the funding transaction is confirmed. Its output identifier (`txid:output_index`) constitutes the *channel point*, which serves as a unique reference to identify the channel throughout its lifetime.

a8484022-ce46-47ef-ad43-7b896394da2c.title: BIP-0431
a8484022-ce46-47ef-ad43-7b896394da2c.body:
Informational BIP that describes “*transaction pinning*” attacks, and proposes topological restrictions on transaction packages in the mempool in order to mitigate this type of attack. Pinning is a technique in which an attacker exploits the limitations of mempool policies to prevent the confirmation of a legitimate transaction, which is particularly problematic for upper-layer protocols such as Lightning.

BIP-0431 proposes limiting the structure of transaction packages: no multiple unconfirmed parents, restricted package size, and prohibition of certain complex topologies. These constraints make transaction replacement more predictable and reliable, thereby facilitating the operation of protocols that depend on the rapid confirmation of transactions.

a84a3e6f-ebc7-44fd-a4f5-607e1269851f.title: OP_NUMEQUALVERIFY - 0X9D
a84a3e6f-ebc7-44fd-a4f5-607e1269851f.body: Combines the `OP_NUMEQUAL` and `OP_VERIFY` operations. It numerically compares the top two elements of the stack. If the values are equal, `OP_NUMEQUALVERIFY` removes the true result from the stack and script execution continues. If the values are not equal, the result is false and the script fails immediately.

a84ae094-d3ee-4c73-8fa6-87ddd4e50b34.title: BETTERHASH
a84ae094-d3ee-4c73-8fa6-87ddd4e50b34.body:
Mining protocol developed by Matt Corallo in 2018 to try to counter the growing centralization of mining in pools. It differs from Stratum, which was then the standard, by giving hashers more control over the selection of transactions to include in *block templates*. The main idea behind BetterHash is to give hashers back the ability to manage the construction of the *block template* themselves, while keeping the advantages of mining pools such as reduced income variance.

In the Stratum protocol, mining pools control the creation of *block templates*, meaning that they choose which transactions are included in blocks and also determine the chain on which to mine. This centralization weakens Bitcoin, because it makes the transaction confirmation process vulnerable to censorship.

BetterHash allows hashers to take back control over these operations, while leaving the pool to manage the distribution of rewards. It is therefore in a way one of the forerunners of Stratum V2.

a9574625-3857-4ab8-b865-d10cb56ffab1.title: NOSTR RELAY
a9574625-3857-4ab8-b865-d10cb56ffab1.body: A server that constitutes the distribution infrastructure of the Nostr protocol. A relay accepts events published by clients via WebSocket connections, stores them (temporarily or permanently) and retransmits them to subscribed clients according to query filters. Unlike a classic centralized server, a relay cannot modify the content of the events it transmits, because these are cryptographically signed by their authors. Each relay applies its own moderation, storage and access policies. There are several types of relays: public (open to all), private (restricted access), paid (requiring a subscription) and specialized (dedicated to certain types of content). A Nostr user generally connects to several relays simultaneously to guarantee redundancy and resistance to censorship.

a98db427-c5fc-42bb-b745-dd343576d6ae.title: TIME-DILATION ATTACK
a98db427-c5fc-42bb-b745-dd343576d6ae.body:
An attack on the Lightning Network that combines an eclipse attack with a deliberate slowing of block delivery to the victim. The attacker takes control of all the connections of the victim's Bitcoin node, then transmits new blocks to it with a calculated delay (typically just under Bitcoin Core's 30-minute detection threshold). The victim gradually accumulates a lag relative to the real chain. This time offset is exploited to bypass the security mechanisms of the Lightning Network that rely on *timelocks*. For example, the attacker can broadcast an old, revoked commitment transaction on the real network. The victim, whose view of the blockchain is behind, does not detect this attempted fraud in time to publish a penalty transaction before the expiration of the contest delay. The attack requires no mining power.

This concept was formalized in 2020 by Antoine Riard and Gleb Naumenko. Three variants have been identified, the most effective of which (the packet finalization attack) requires only a few hours of eclipse and a single channel with the victim. The countermeasures rely on the use of *watchtowers* on independent infrastructure, the reception of blocks through alternative channels and the strengthening of anti-eclipse protections.

a9ac33b3-8ef6-4cbe-afdc-31ea80b61dc6.title: BIP-0360
a9ac33b3-8ef6-4cbe-afdc-31ea80b61dc6.body: Proposes a new output type called “Pay-to-Merkle-Root” (P2MR), via a soft fork. P2MR works similarly to P2TR (Taproot, BIP-0341), but removes the key-path spend (*key-path spend*). This change is mainly intended to protect funds against long-term attacks by quantum computers, which could use Shor's algorithm (or another, still unknown algorithm) to derive private keys from public keys exposed on the blockchain. By removing the internal public key from the output, P2MR prevents this exposure and allows Tapscript scripts to be used in a way that is resistant to long-term quantum attacks.

a9c74e21-3f8b-4d5a-b1e6-7c2d9f0a5b83.title: MURCH-ZAWY VULNERABILITY
a9c74e21-3f8b-4d5a-b1e6-7c2d9f0a5b83.body:
A theoretical attack on Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment mechanism, described by Zawy and formalized by Murch (Mark Erhardt) in August 2024. Unlike the classic *time warp* attack, this vulnerability does not exploit the *off-by-one* error in the calculation of the duration of retarget periods, but relies on the strategic alternation of timestamps at the last block of each difficulty period.

The attacker, who controls a majority of the computing power, keeps timestamps at the minimum allowed by the *Median Time Past* (MTP) rule during each period, then sets the timestamp of the last block far in the future to reduce the difficulty by a factor of 4. By then alternating between a minimal timestamp and a future timestamp for the last blocks of each period, they make the difficulty oscillate between a quarter and a sixteenth of the initial value. Some periods then show a negative calculated duration, but the protocol treats it as half a week, which raises the difficulty only by a factor of 4.

In practice, the attack requires about 16 weeks of selfish mining. At the end of this period, the attacker publishes their secret chain, reorganizes about 8,064 blocks and collects the rewards of about 39,816 blocks. Murch proposed a variant that reduces the difficulty exponentially by increasing the future timestamp in steps.

BIP-0054 (Consensus Cleanup) fixes this vulnerability by requiring that the timestamp of the last block of a difficulty period be greater than or equal to that of the first block of the same period.

a9e4c058-f48b-469d-880f-6f4fdfede65f.title: AQUA
a9e4c058-f48b-469d-880f-6f4fdfede65f.body: A mobile wallet developed by JAN3, available on iOS and Android, designed to simplify the use of Bitcoin, the Lightning Network, and the Liquid network in a single application. Aqua allows you to send and receive bitcoins on-chain or on the Liquid sidechain. For Lightning payments, Aqua uses atomic swaps, which allows it to do without an embedded Lightning node while keeping custody of the funds at all times.

aa0260de-cecb-4560-bb58-fce7d2c394fc.title: SPLICING
aa0260de-cecb-4560-bb58-fce7d2c394fc.body:
A Lightning Network mechanism that allows a payment channel to be resized without closing it, either by adding funds to it (*splice-in*) or by withdrawing funds to an on-chain output (*splice-out*). The channel remains fully operational throughout the operation.

Splicing creates a new 2-of-2 multisignature transaction that spends the existing funding UTXO into a new UTXO with the adjusted capacity. The channel first enters "*quiescence*" mode (STFU) to freeze its state, then the two parties negotiate the transaction via the interactive-tx protocol, where each can add inputs and outputs. Third parties can also join their own operations to this same transaction, which makes it possible to share the on-chain fees. During confirmation, the old and the new channel state coexist, which makes it possible to continue routing payments without interruption.

Splicing reduces from two to just one the number of on-chain transactions needed to adjust a channel's capacity. It also makes possible single-balance wallets that unify on-chain and Lightning funds into a single balance for the user.

aa1fee82-5009-41ce-9821-614fb59dfef3.title: PUBLIC KEY
aa1fee82-5009-41ce-9821-614fb59dfef3.body:
The public key is an element used in asymmetric cryptography. It is generated from a private key using an irreversible mathematical function. On Bitcoin, public keys are derived from their associated private key using the ECDSA or Schnorr elliptic curve digital signature algorithms. The public key, unlike the private key, can be shared freely without compromising the security of funds. Within the Bitcoin protocol, the public key serves as the basis for creating a Bitcoin address, which is then used to create spending conditions on a UTXO using a `scriptPubKey`. Public keys are frequently confused with the master key or with extended keys (`xpub`...). Yet these elements are quite different.

*In French, a public key is called “clé publique”. This term is sometimes abbreviated as “pubkey”, or “PK”.*

aa3c50f9-1f4f-4c1b-87b8-de1777bcb707.title: HASH256
aa3c50f9-1f4f-4c1b-87b8-de1777bcb707.body:
A cryptographic function used for various applications on Bitcoin. It consists of applying the SHA256 function twice to the input data. The message is passed through SHA256 a first time, and the result of this operation is used as the input to pass through SHA256 a second time. The output of this function is therefore 256 bits.
```math
HASH256(x)\ =\ SHA256(SHA256(x))
```

aa8d186e-25bc-4e88-be07-82d3477e1bca.title: NUNCHUK
aa8d186e-25bc-4e88-be07-82d3477e1bca.body: Bitcoin wallet software specialized in multisig, available on desktop and mobile (iOS, Android). Nunchuk makes it easier to create and manage multisignature wallets by offering an accessible interface, even for non-technical users. The application supports most *hardware wallets* on the market and uses PSBTs to coordinate signatures between multiple devices. Nunchuk also offers collaborative features that allow several people to cosign transactions asynchronously. The software includes assisted recovery and inheritance options. It exists in a free version with the basic features and in a paid version with additional services such as assisted multisig.

aaaac5c5-d29d-4cb6-86ec-413e06934b10.title: SWAP-IN POTENTIAM
aaaac5c5-d29d-4cb6-86ec-413e06934b10.body:
A protocol that makes it possible to transfer on-chain bitcoins to the Lightning Network almost instantly, without relying on 0-conf channels. Proposed by Jesse Posner and ZmnSCPxj in 2023, it relies on an on-chain address shared between the user (Alice) and an LSP (Bob).

This address encodes two spending paths: a cooperative path, where Alice and Bob jointly sign to move the funds, and a unilateral recovery path, where Alice can take back her bitcoins after a *timelock* expires. When funds are received and confirmed at this address, Alice can, with the help of the LSP, immediately move them into an existing or new Lightning channel, via the cooperative path. If the LSP is unavailable, Alice retains the ability to recover her funds on-chain after the specified delay.

The main advantage of *Swap-in Potentiam* is that it reduces trust requirements compared with other methods of instantly opening channels. The temporary co-ownership of the funds and the security *timelock* ensure that neither Alice nor the LSP can steal the funds. The Phoenix wallet from the company ACINQ uses a variant of this protocol called “Swaproot,” adapted to the constraints of mobile devices with intermittent connectivity.

aab65e71-7454-4b5d-af76-bc038f9bd44c.title: FORCE CLOSE
aab65e71-7454-4b5d-af76-bc038f9bd44c.body:
Mechanism for the non-cooperative closure of a Lightning channel. When two users open a channel with a 2/2 multisig, each of them can unilaterally close the channel by broadcasting the latest commitment transaction, which is already signed, in order to recover their bitcoins *onchain*. In this case, we speak of a "*force close*".

This method is generally used if one of the participants no longer responds or if a cooperative closure of the channel is impossible. If a *force close* can be avoided, that is better, because it requires more time to recover one's funds *onchain* and can cost much more in fees.

During a *force close*, one of the two users broadcasts the commitment transaction that reflects the last known state of the Lightning channel. There is then a safety delay (*timelock*) before the bitcoins can be recovered *onchain*, which gives the other party time to verify that the transaction does correspond to the latest state of the channel. If a user attempts to cheat by publishing an outdated commitment transaction, the other party can use the revocation secret to punish the cheater and recover all of the channel's funds.

aac36f3f-0012-4809-9dd4-bafb1a9febae.title: OUTPUT LINKING
aac36f3f-0012-4809-9dd4-bafb1a9febae.body: A synonym sometimes used to refer to address reuse. *Output linking* refers to the practice of using the same receiving address to lock several UTXOs, sometimes within several different transactions. Bitcoins are generally locked using a cryptographic key pair that corresponds to a unique address. Since the blockchain is public, it is easy to see which addresses are associated with how many bitcoins. In the case of reuse of the same address for several payments, one can imagine that all the associated UTXOs belong to the same entity. Address reuse therefore poses a problem for the user's privacy. It makes it possible to make deterministic links between several transactions and several UTXOs, as well as to perpetuate *on-chain* fund tracing.

aac84938-1871-40fb-86b8-335badf87019.title: INBOUND PEER / INCOMING CONNECTION
aac84938-1871-40fb-86b8-335badf87019.body: Node on the Bitcoin network that initiates a connection to your node without any action on your part. Bitcoin Core allows a maximum of 114 inbound peers by default (out of a total of 125 connections), in order to facilitate connectivity within the network. Inbound peers are treated with caution, because there is no way to be sure they are honest, since they are initiated by third parties. Inbound and outbound peers share the same type of information. The main difference between inbound and outbound peers lies not in the type of information exchanged, but in the way these connections are established.

ab0ee3fe-8543-4ff3-afd6-1e5d79c3765e.title: PROBING
ab0ee3fe-8543-4ff3-afd6-1e5d79c3765e.body: A technique consisting of sending payments over the Lightning Network with no intention of completing them, in order to discover information about the network, notably the available routes and channel balances.

ab464d7e-8423-4d1b-a481-b4c982ace69c.title: BIP-0127
ab464d7e-8423-4d1b-a481-b4c982ace69c.body: Definition of a standard proof-of-reserves format based on intentionally invalid Bitcoin transactions. Currently at draft status, BIP-0127 allows custodians to prove cryptographically that they control certain UTXOs without having to move them. The proof transaction includes a first so-called “commitment” input (*commitment input*) whose `txid` is replaced by the SHA-256 hash of a proof message. It is this fictitious input that makes the transaction invalid and impossible to confirm on the blockchain. The other inputs are signed normally and correspond to the funds held. The transaction has a single output whose amount is equal to the sum of all the inputs, with no mining fees. BIP-0127 relies on the PSBT format of BIP-0174 to facilitate the construction of proofs with existing wallet infrastructure, and also defines a file format based on Protocol Buffers to group several proofs together with their associated metadata.

ab4e00c3-f6bb-4973-a5fe-66ee75f3bb50.title: BIP-0322
ab4e00c3-f6bb-4973-a5fe-66ee75f3bb50.body: Proposes a new standard to replace BIP-0137 for signing messages with Bitcoin private keys and their associated addresses, in order to prove ownership of an address. These signatures are useful for various applications such as proof of funds, auditing, and other uses requiring authentication of an address via its private key. Compared to BIP-0137, BIP-0322 extends the message signing standard beyond classic addresses, using a script-based approach. It allows wallet software to sign a message for any script they could unlock in order to spend bitcoins. To do this, the method consists of signing a text by producing a signature for a virtual Bitcoin transaction. For traditional P2PKH addresses, BIP-0322 remains compatible with the traditional signature format.

ab51af7f-85b2-4ac9-ac88-3b2217ff73cc.title: SEED
ab51af7f-85b2-4ac9-ac88-3b2217ff73cc.body:
In the specific context of a Bitcoin hierarchical deterministic wallet, a seed is a 512-bit piece of information derived from randomness. It makes it possible to generate, in a deterministic and hierarchical manner, a set of private keys, and their corresponding public keys, for a Bitcoin wallet. The seed is often confused with the recovery phrase itself. Yet it is a different piece of information. The seed is obtained by applying the `PBKDF2` function to the mnemonic phrase and to the optional passphrase.

![Generation of the seed via PBKDF2 (mnemonic + passphrase) then derivation of the master key via HMAC-SHA512.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/g/graine/assets/image-1.png)

The seed was invented with BIP-0032, which defines the foundations of the hierarchical deterministic wallet. In this standard, the seed can be between 128 and 512 bits long (256 bits being recommended). This makes it possible to derive all the keys of a wallet from a single piece of information, unlike JBOK (*Just a Bunch Of Keys*) wallets, which require making new backups for every key generated. BIP-0039 subsequently came to propose an encoding of this seed, in order to make it easier for humans to read. This encoding takes the form of a phrase, generally called a mnemonic phrase or recovery phrase. This standard helps avoid errors when backing up the seed, notably thanks to the use of a checksum.

Outside the context of Bitcoin, in the field of cryptography in general, a seed is an initial value used to generate cryptographic keys, or more broadly, any type of data produced by a pseudo-random number generator. This initial value must be random and unpredictable to guarantee the security of the cryptographic system. Indeed, the seed introduces entropy into the system, but the generation process that follows is deterministic.

*In everyday language, the majority of bitcoiners refer to the mnemonic phrase when they talk about the “seed”, and not to the intermediate derivation state that sits between the mnemonic phrase and the master key.*

ab9cf26b-816e-4718-b839-75bf7b9c132e.title: WIZARDSARDINE
ab9cf26b-816e-4718-b839-75bf7b9c132e.body:
Company specialized in the security and custody of bitcoins, founded in 2020 by Kevin Loaec and Antoine Poinsot, and incorporated in the Azores (Portugal). Wizardsardine develops open source Bitcoin wallet management solutions, with an emphasis on advanced security mechanisms such as *vaults* and configurable spending policies.

The company is behind the Revault protocol, an institutional custody system using pre-signed transactions and *watchtowers* to secure organizations' funds. Wizardsardine also develops Liana, a Bitcoin wallet that leverages Miniscript to offer recovery and inheritance configurations based on *timelocks*.

abac8bae-cc00-4335-9f65-a85a4db349d6.title: SOROBAN
abac8bae-cc00-4335-9f65-a85a4db349d6.body: An encrypted communication protocol established on Tor that allows collaboration with other users in the context of a Cahoots transaction. Soroban was developed by the Samourai Wallet teams to facilitate the exchange of partially signed transactions (PSBT) between users who wish to carry out collaborative transactions (*Stowaway*, *Stonewall x2*...). This protocol is used in the Samourai Wallet application and in the Sparrow Wallet software.

abbab2ae-f361-48f2-a376-e596da4a41cb.title: BCH - BITCOIN CASH
abbab2ae-f361-48f2-a376-e596da4a41cb.body:
Cryptocurrency system resulting from a *hard fork* of Bitcoin (BTC) carried out on August 1, 2017 at block 478,558. This fork occurred following disagreements within the Bitcoin community over the solutions to adopt to solve the protocol's scaling problems (Blocksize War). While Bitcoin implemented SegWit (*soft fork*), which includes an indirect, slight increase in block capacity, Bitcoin Cash opted for a direct increase in block size (*hard fork*), going from 1 MB to 8 MB, with the aim of reducing transaction fees and improving confirmation times.

![Official Bitcoin Cash logo, created after the hard fork of August 1, 2017 separating the BCH chain from Bitcoin.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/b/bch-bitcoin-cash/assets/image-1.png)

abcafb03-d107-46eb-92af-dcc66a28cd36.title: VBYTES
abcafb03-d107-46eb-92af-dcc66a28cd36.body:
A unit of measurement used to evaluate the size of a Bitcoin transaction while taking into account the weighting introduced by SegWit. A vByte (virtual byte) represents a normalized weight unit: 4 weight units (WU) correspond to 1 vByte. This measurement makes it possible to fairly compare SegWit transactions and *legacy* transactions.

Before SegWit, the size of a transaction was measured in raw bytes. With SegWit, witness data (*witness*) benefit from a discount: each witness byte counts for 1 WU, versus 4 WU for other data. Calculating in vBytes smooths out this difference. For example, a transaction whose total weight is 600 WU is 150 vBytes.

Transaction fees are calculated in satoshis per vByte (sat/vB). Using vBytes allows wallets to correctly estimate fees regardless of the structure of the transaction. A Bitcoin block can contain a maximum of 4 million WU, equivalent to 1 million vBytes.

abecb775-62a8-43f1-8230-bacceb878150.title: AVERAGE ROUND DURATION
abecb775-62a8-43f1-8230-bacceb878150.body:
The average round duration is an indicator used to estimate the time a mining pool needs to find a block, based on the network difficulty and the pool's hashrate. It is calculated by taking the number of shares expected to find a block and dividing it by the pool's hashrate. For example, if a mining pool has 200 miners, and each generates an average of 4 shares per second, the pool's total computing power is 800 shares per second:

```text
200 * 4 = 800
```

Assuming that, on average, 1 million shares must be produced to find a valid block, the pool's *Avg. Round Duration* will be 1,250 seconds, or about 21 minutes:

```text
1 000 000 / 800 = 1 250
```

In practical terms, this means that on average, the mining pool should find a block roughly every 21 minutes. This indicator fluctuates with variations in the pool's hashrate: an increase in hashrate reduces the *Avg. Round Duration*, while a decrease lengthens it. It will also fluctuate with each periodic change in Bitcoin's difficulty target (every 2016 blocks). This measure does not take into account blocks found by other pools and focuses solely on the internal performance of the pool under study.

ac395c89-7ab1-4fdd-94b0-3a6da84fc28a.title: SETTINGS.JSON
ac395c89-7ab1-4fdd-94b0-3a6da84fc28a.body: File used in Bitcoin Core to store dynamic settings defined via the graphical interface (GUI) or via RPCs. It keeps information about the user's configurations, such as the wallets that are open, for example. When Bitcoin Core is restarted, this file makes it possible to automatically reopen the wallets that were active before the application was closed. If a wallet is closed via the GUI, it is also removed from this file, and it will therefore not be automatically reopened at the next startup.

ac5be5f7-85b3-4dba-b006-14b9bf55a40c.title: BIP

ac60e08d-4d7b-4f43-8837-5f93f80d2369.title: STACK
ac60e08d-4d7b-4f43-8837-5f93f80d2369.body:
In the context of the scripting language used to attach spending conditions to Bitcoin UTXOs, the stack is a "LIFO" (*Last In, First Out*) data structure used to store temporary elements during the execution of a script. Each operation in the script manipulates these stacks, where elements can be added (*push*) or removed (*pop*). Scripts use stacks to evaluate expressions, store temporary variables, and handle conditions.

In the execution of a Bitcoin script, 2 stacks can be used: the main stack and the alt (alternative) stack. The main stack is used for the majority of a script's operations. It is on this stack that script operations add, remove, or manipulate data. The alternative stack, for its part, is used to temporarily store data during the execution of the script. Certain specific opcodes, such as `OP_TOALTSTACK` and `OP_FROMALTSTACK`, make it possible to transfer elements from the main stack to the alternative stack and vice versa.

For example, when validating a transaction, the signatures and public keys are pushed onto the main stack and processed by successive opcodes to verify that the signatures match the keys and the transaction data.

ac6fe449-7feb-42a7-9956-647c4797b14c.title: CLARK - COVENANTLESS ARK
ac6fe449-7feb-42a7-9956-647c4797b14c.body:
A version of the Ark protocol that can be implemented without requiring covenants to be added to Bitcoin via a soft fork. The name "clArk" is the contraction of "*covenantless Ark*". When Ark was initially proposed in May 2023 by Burak Keceli, the protocol required covenants, which were not yet available on Bitcoin. The clArk version, developed starting in 2024, works around this limitation.

In the absence of covenants, clArk emulates the spending conditions by asking all the participants of a round to sign n-of-n multisig transactions. Each participant must sign the entire VTXO tree making up the round, whereas covenants would allow signing only the clauses concerning their own funds. This approach results in a significant overhead in bandwidth, storage and interactivity: all participants must be online simultaneously during the round.

The possible addition of covenants to Bitcoin would substantially improve the protocol: users would no longer need to be connected permanently, the liquidity management of ASPs would be optimized, and the protocol could better handle certain scenarios. ClArk therefore represents a compromise that makes it possible to deploy Ark on Bitcoin as it exists today, without needing to do a soft fork.

ac77bc32-6233-4cd1-99de-85bfc3705063.title: WABISABI
ac77bc32-6233-4cd1-99de-85bfc3705063.body: Central-coordinator coinjoin protocol used on the Wasabi 2.0 wallet. This model was designed by Ádám Ficsór (nopara73), Yuval Kogman, Lucas Ontivero and István András Seres in 2021, and was integrated into the Wasabi 2.0 software the following year.

acd325f2-b54d-465f-9747-c0c9c63bcf67.title: QR CODE
acd325f2-b54d-465f-9747-c0c9c63bcf67.body:
A type of two-dimensional barcode that can be quickly scanned by mobile devices. The QR code stores information as black and white pixels arranged in a square on a white background. An important characteristic of QR codes is that they embed Reed-Solomon error correction codes, which make it possible to restore the data even if the QR code is partially obscured.

The QR code is widely used on Bitcoin to facilitate the transmission of information between two devices. It is mainly used to share receiving addresses, encoded in URI format in accordance with BIP-0021. But its use also extends to extended keys, PSBTs, Lightning invoices, etc.

*QR code stands for "Quick Response Code".*

acd9c2e0-892d-47ee-b9cf-086ba4509aa8.title: NSEC
acd9c2e0-892d-47ee-b9cf-086ba4509aa8.body: Bech32 encoding (NIP-19) of a Nostr secret (private) key, with the prefix `nsec`. The key corresponds to a 32-byte value used as a secret on secp256k1; it makes it possible to produce the Schnorr signatures of Nostr events and thus to prove control of the identity (via the `npub`). Losing the nsec means losing control of that identity. The nsec must never be shared or entered into an untrusted web client; to reduce exposure, NIP-07 standardizes `window.nostr`, through which an extension can sign events without disclosing the key to the application.

acdcbd6a-29fe-42b8-a01d-3dd55b6a21c9.title: LAYER
acdcbd6a-29fe-42b8-a01d-3dd55b6a21c9.body:
A protocol or network built on top of the main Bitcoin network, stacked above it. It uses the Bitcoin network as a foundation and is therefore dependent on its protocol. However, the Bitcoin network is not dependent on its layers. An example of such a layer is the Lightning Network.

These layers are designed to extend the capabilities of the Bitcoin network by adding additional features or capabilities, such as faster transactions, tokens or micropayments. They are often created to address certain limitations of the Bitcoin network, while benefiting from its security and decentralization. It is important to note that although these layers are built on the Bitcoin network, they have their own protocols and mechanisms, distinct from those of the Bitcoin network itself.

ad162151-8d99-4bf3-85d6-69587d90f21f.title: SEGWIT V1
ad162151-8d99-4bf3-85d6-69587d90f21f.body: Post-SegWit script version 1. SegWit V1 scripts represent the second family of scripts introduced after the SegWit update of 2017. Specifically, SegWit V1 scripts were introduced with the Taproot update in 2021. The P2TR script is of the SegWit V1 version. The corresponding addresses always begin with `bc1p` and are encoded in `Bech32m` format.
