ad37f532-bb0f-41a9-aa7a-f0982828377d.title: HYPERINFLATION
ad37f532-bb0f-41a9-aa7a-f0982828377d.body:
An economic phenomenon characterized by an extremely rapid and uncontrollable rise in prices. Hyperinflation occurs when a government or a central bank issues money in excessive quantities, often to finance budget deficits, leading to a total loss of confidence in the national currency.

The most striking historical examples are the Weimar Republic in Germany (1923), Zimbabwe in the 2000s, or Venezuela starting in 2016. In these cases, the currency lost its function as a store of value and a medium of exchange, pushing populations toward alternative currencies or barter.

The risk of hyperinflation is a central argument for bitcoiners, who highlight the supply limited to 21 million units of BTC as protection against this kind of monetary excess. Unlike fiat currencies, no authority can arbitrarily increase the quantity of bitcoins in circulation.

ad44c071-92b1-475f-ba58-9eaab6a23263.title: BIP-0015
ad44c071-92b1-475f-ba58-9eaab6a23263.body: Proposal for an alias system making it possible to associate human-readable names with Bitcoin addresses, via different resolution mechanisms. BIP-0015 aimed to simplify the user experience by replacing long alphanumeric addresses with memorable identifiers of the type `alias@domaine.com`. Four mechanisms were proposed: FirstBits (using the blockchain as a directory), DNS TXT records, resolution via an HTTPS request, and Namecoin (via a decentralized naming system). This BIP is a conceptual precursor of BIP-0353, which takes up the idea of human-readable addresses via DNS. It was never implemented and was closed.

adf5dcb7-c068-487e-971a-fb6da9266717.title: FIDELITY BOND
adf5dcb7-c068-487e-971a-fb6da9266717.body:
Mechanism by which a user deliberately sacrifices bitcoin value to make a cryptographic identity costly to obtain, which deters Sybil attacks. The concept, initially proposed by Peter Todd in 2013, found its main application in JoinMarket, where it strengthens the privacy of coinjoins.

In JoinMarket, a *maker* who publishes a high-value *fidelity bond* has a greater probability of being selected by *takers* to participate in coinjoins, and therefore of earning fees. The most common way to create a *fidelity bond* is to send bitcoins to an address time-locked via a `OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY`. What is sacrificed is not the capital itself, but its time value: the bitcoins remain the property of the *maker*, but are immobilized until the lock expires. A long-term holder can thus build a *fidelity bond* at almost zero cost, since they did not plan to spend their bitcoins before the deadline.

An alternative consists of destroying bitcoins by sending them to a `OP_RETURN` output, making the sacrifice permanent and the proof trivial to verify.

adfcbbf5-695d-4a7b-b4ad-319d22528630.title: SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT
adfcbbf5-695d-4a7b-b4ad-319d22528630.body:
Proposal to implement a new modifier SigHash Flag in Bitcoin, introduced with BIP-0118. `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` allows greater flexibility in transaction management, particularly for advanced applications such as payment channels on the Lightning Network and the Eltoo update. The `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` makes it possible to bind the signature to no specific prior UTXO (*Any Previous Output*). Used in combination with `SIGHASH_ALL`, it would allow signing all inputs and all outputs of a transaction, but without committing to the specific UTXO spent by each input. This would allow the signature to be reused for different transactions, as long as certain specified conditions are met.

*This modifier SigHash `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` is inherited from the idea of `SIGHASH_NOINPUT` initially proposed by Joseph Poon in 2016 to improve his idea of the Lightning Network.*

ae093994-512c-4bf4-8aa9-1b6e11dc6950.title: CHANNEL JAMMING
ae093994-512c-4bf4-8aa9-1b6e11dc6950.body:
A denial-of-service attack on the Lightning Network that consists of blocking the routing capacity of one or more payment channels for a prolonged period, preventing honest nodes from routing payments. The attacker sends a fictitious payment to themselves through a series of intermediate channels, then refuses to finalize or cancel the HTLC, which immobilizes the routing nodes' funds at no cost to the attacker.

The attack comes in two variants:
* *Liquidity jamming* (described as early as 2015 under the name “loop attack”) exploits the leverage effect of multi-hop routing: with `x` bitcoins, an attacker can lock up to `20x` bitcoins on a path of 20 channels.
* *Slot jamming* exploits the limit of 483 simultaneous HTLCs per channel: by sending 483 micro-payments, an attacker saturates the available slots with minimal capital.

Several mitigation approaches are being explored: fees paid in advance (*upfront fees*) by the sender, a local reputation system between peers, proof-of-funds certificates (*stake certificates*), and reputation tokens. bLIP-0004 proposes an HTLC approval mechanism (*HTLC endorsement*) as a first concrete measure. No definitive solution has yet reached consensus.

ae239b0e-5722-4280-a3fa-7e41c73d6331.title: EXIT TRANSACTION
ae239b0e-5722-4280-a3fa-7e41c73d6331.body:
Pre-signed Bitcoin transaction allowing a user to unilaterally withdraw their funds from Spark (or a statechain) to the main layer, without requiring the cooperation of the *Spark Entity*.

The exit transaction is created and co-signed by the user and the SE at the time the user receives funds on Spark. Each new owner obtains an exit transaction with a shorter relative *timelock* than that of the previous owner. This decreasing hierarchy of timelocks ensures that the current owner can always publish their transaction on-chain before the previous owners, thus preventing double-spend attempts. To exit, the user broadcasts the exit transaction along with its parent transactions on the Bitcoin network.

ae28517c-ba16-432e-bd2d-73de74b29fbf.title: ASIC RESISTANCE
ae28517c-ba16-432e-bd2d-73de74b29fbf.body:
A property of a mining algorithm that aims to limit the advantage of application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) over consumer hardware, such as processors (CPUs) or graphics cards (GPUs). The goal is to maintain decentralization of mining by preventing a situation where only actors with expensive, specialized hardware can participate effectively in block validation.

To achieve this resistance, some alternative cryptocurrencies use hash functions that require a lot of random-access memory (*memory-hard*), such as Scrypt or Ethash, which makes ASIC manufacturing harder or less advantageous. The idea is that if the algorithm demands varied resources (memory, bandwidth, computation), an ASIC does not offer as clear a performance gain as for a simple algorithm like SHA-256.

In the case of Bitcoin, ASIC resistance has never been a goal. Bitcoin uses SHA-256, a function that lends itself very well to hardware optimization. The Bitcoin network therefore saw ASICs appear as early as 2013, which gradually made CPU and GPU mining unprofitable. ASIC resistance remains a subject of debate: its supporters see it as a guarantee of decentralization, while its critics point out that it merely delays hardware specialization without ever durably preventing it.

ae55205d-dad4-4151-91b7-699b195366ca.title: LIQUID NETWORK
ae55205d-dad4-4151-91b7-699b195366ca.body: Bitcoin sidechain designed by Blockstream to provide fast and confidential transactions. Unlike the main Bitcoin blockchain, Liquid uses a consensus mechanism based on a federation (a selected group of node operators, generally Bitcoin-related companies), thereby replacing the Nakamoto consensus mechanism. This approach considerably speeds up transactions and reduces costs, while offering more advanced features. Liquid also allows the issuance of digital assets, including tokens representing other cryptocurrencies. The bitcoins on Liquid, called L-BTC, are tied to BTC through a two-way peg system relying on part of the federation. The participants in this federation are called “functionaries”, and they can take on both the role of “watchman” (*watchmen*) and of “block signer” (*blocksigner*).

ae7b6935-6659-43ae-8484-7f23c58f7436.title: GALOY
ae7b6935-6659-43ae-8484-7f23c58f7436.body: Company founded in 2019 by Nicolas Burtey and Chris Hunter, developing open source Bitcoin banking infrastructure. Galoy is the origin of the Blink wallet (formerly “Bitcoin Beach Wallet”), the application that served as the foundation of the Bitcoin circular economy in El Zonte, El Salvador, before the country adopted bitcoin as legal tender in 2021. The Galoy platform allows organizations to deploy their own Bitcoin and Lightning banking infrastructure, either self-hosted or as a managed service (*Banking-as-a-Service*). The company also develops bitcoin-backed lending solutions.

ae814cae-4ded-4a0f-9132-49e6ab7346d2.title: START9
ae814cae-4ded-4a0f-9132-49e6ab7346d2.body:
An American company (Start9 Labs, Inc.) developing StartOS, a free operating system for personal servers. Like Umbrel, Start9 aims to democratize self-hosting by allowing non-technical users to install and manage *open source* applications on their own hardware, without depending on third-party *cloud* services.

Start9 sells preconfigured servers and offers a *marketplace* of self-hosted applications including Bitcoin Core, Lightning implementations, storage and communication solutions, etc.

ae922c94-0926-40a0-af0f-817dd7b4f88e.title: CLUSTER MEMPOOL
ae922c94-0926-40a0-af0f-817dd7b4f88e.body:
Proposal to overhaul mempool management in Bitcoin Core. The cluster mempool organizes unconfirmed transactions into “clusters” (*clusters*): sets of transactions linked by parent-child relationships. Within each cluster, a linearization algorithm pre-computes the optimal mining order and groups the transactions into “chunks” (*chunks*) sorted by decreasing fee rate.

This overhaul fixes an inconsistency in how the mempool currently works. Transaction selection for mining uses the highest ancestor fee rate, whereas eviction uses the lowest descendant fee rate. Since these two heuristics are not symmetrical, it can happen that the best transaction in the mempool is evicted first. With the cluster mempool, block building and eviction become exactly inverse operations: chunks are included from most profitable to least profitable, and evicted in the reverse order.

This approach is viable thanks to the limit on cluster size, which replaces the former ancestor and descendant limits. Since optimal chunks never cross the boundaries between clusters, adding a transaction only requires recomputing its own cluster. The fee rate of each chunk then serves as a unified score for all mempool operations: block building, eviction, RBF evaluation, transaction relay and fee estimation.

aeee9bab-050e-405c-8062-76ccf67f1ae5.title: KRUX
aeee9bab-050e-405c-8062-76ccf67f1ae5.body: Open source firmware that turns Kendryte K210 microcontroller devices, such as the Maix Amigo or the M5StickV, into Bitcoin transaction signing devices. Krux makes it possible to generate and manage private keys, sign transactions offline, and interact with coordinator wallets (Sparrow, Specter...) via QR codes or microSD cards. The project is aimed at users who want to build a low-cost *hardware wallet* from generic off-the-shelf hardware, while retaining full control over the source code.

af8e0007-4649-4416-861b-3824e29b2cbc.title: TRIMMED HTLC
af8e0007-4649-4416-861b-3824e29b2cbc.body:
On the Lightning Network, an HTLC is said to be "*trimmed*" when its value is too low to justify the creation of a dedicated output in the commitment transaction. Concretely, if the HTLC amount is below the channel's *dust limit*, it would be uneconomical to resolve it *on-chain*. Instead of creating a separate output, the value of these HTLCs is absorbed into the transaction fees of the commitment transaction.

This mechanism is essential to allow Lightning channels to relay very small payments, potentially of a single satoshi, without being limited by the dust threshold imposed by the Bitcoin protocol. From an operational standpoint, *trimmed HTLCs* are built and resolved exactly like ordinary HTLCs: they transit normally between nodes and are honored or canceled according to the same rules. The difference only appears if the commitment transaction has to be published *on-chain*, in which case their value is lost to fees instead of being recoverable.

This design nevertheless poses security problems. A malicious actor can create many *trimmed HTLCs* with no intention of resolving them, which forces their counterparty to pay higher transaction fees, or destroys part of the channel's value. Several improvements have been proposed, such as redirecting the value of *trimmed HTLCs* to ephemeral *anchor outputs* or using probabilistic payments.

af9d1791-ec90-4784-b67e-78d37d264660.title: BIP-0087
af9d1791-ec90-4784-b67e-78d37d264660.body: Proposal defining the derivation path `m/87'/coin_type'/account'` specifically for multisignature wallets using *output script descriptors*. Unlike BIP-0048, which encodes the script type in the derivation path, BIP-0087 takes a simpler approach by delegating the specification of the script type to the descriptor itself. This design is better suited to the modern wallet ecosystem, which relies on descriptors to precisely describe spending conditions.

b0216b99-853f-44a7-99d4-13ea5a1f8296.title: SPARKSCAN
b0216b99-853f-44a7-99d4-13ea5a1f8296.body: A public explorer and analytics suite dedicated to the Spark protocol. Sparkscan makes it possible to look up addresses, transactions, tokens (BTKN) and real-time activity on the Spark network.

b03b485c-02b0-49b7-8dfa-748d9168c996.title: PEG-OUT
b03b485c-02b0-49b7-8dfa-748d9168c996.body: The reverse mechanism of the peg-in, by which tokens circulating on a sidechain are destroyed in order to release the corresponding bitcoins on the main blockchain. The user initiates the process by sending their tokens to a burn address on the sidechain, which triggers the unlocking of the BTC previously locked on the main chain. The peg-out is the second step of the two-way peg (*two-way peg*) and makes it possible to return to the Bitcoin blockchain at any time. Depending on the implementation, this process may be handled by a federation of signers, as is the case on Liquid, or in an automated way via cryptographic proofs.

b0c41084-126c-4966-b40c-d1800cda9e4e.title: WATCHMEN
b0c41084-126c-4966-b40c-d1800cda9e4e.body: In the context of Liquid (a Bitcoin sidechain), these are entities responsible for maintaining the peg of L-BTC, Liquid's native token, by managing and securing the underlying BTC. They ensure that the assets transferred between the main Bitcoin blockchain and the Liquid sidechain are correctly locked and unlocked. The goal of their actions is to maintain the same value between the L-BTC circulating on Liquid and the BTC circulating on Bitcoin. In Liquid, the watchmen are among the functionaries, alongside the *blocksigners*.

b0e0c7c8-0e77-4434-b376-b40fcde70959.title: ONION_PRIVATE_KEY
b0e0c7c8-0e77-4434-b376-b40fcde70959.body: A file formerly used in Bitcoin Core to store a private key associated with a Tor V2 hidden service for the `-listenonion` option. This file has no longer been used since version 0.21.0, in favor of Tor V3.

b110d035-735f-49d3-917d-d5d1d5c9edfd.title: FARADAY
b110d035-735f-49d3-917d-d5d1d5c9edfd.body: Tool developed by Lightning Labs, designed to extract data from an LND node and analyze it to assist its operator. It offers recommendations for closing underperforming channels and provides detailed information on the node's routing behavior. Faraday helps identify low-volume channels and those with availability (*uptime*) problems. This tool aims to assist node operators in allocating their capital across their channels.

b133b70c-2f9a-4d80-a41d-a39e898618d7.title: BIP-0370
b133b70c-2f9a-4d80-a41d-a39e898618d7.body: Defines the second version of the PSBT format (BIP-0174). Unlike version 0, where the unsigned transaction was fixed from creation, PSBT v2 allows interactive modification of the transaction before signing: participants can add or remove inputs and outputs collaboratively.

b14e99c8-2007-4a3e-b6ab-3c079549c446.title: SPIDERPOOL
b14e99c8-2007-4a3e-b6ab-3c079549c446.body: A Bitcoin mining pool founded in China. SpiderPool is among the main mining pools in the world in terms of hashrate. It offers FPPS and PPLNS payout methods, and caters to both individual miners and professional mining farms.

b184d003-b753-49f9-8538-c3725bd4f0ea.title: PPS - PAY PER SHARE
b184d003-b753-49f9-8538-c3725bd4f0ea.body:
Method for calculating miner compensation in the context of mining pools. PPS is a system in which miners are paid for each valid share submitted, regardless of whether or not the pool finds a block. They are therefore paid on the expected value. It is a pay-per-task compensation method. 

Each submitted share is considered a contribution to the mining process and has a predetermined fixed value. This method offers stable and predictable compensation for miners, because it eliminates the variance linked to the probability of finding a block. However, it is riskier for pool operators, because they must pay miners even when no block is found, thereby absorbing the variance risk. Unlike the FPPS method, PPS does not include transaction fees in the calculation of compensation.

b1e0449c-31dd-4705-a235-d7ff86dceb8b.title: BIP-0085
b1e0449c-31dd-4705-a235-d7ff86dceb8b.body: Solution for unifying the derivation of different Bitcoin wallets by using a single master seed for all of them. This proposal makes it possible to derive entropy from root information in order to generate several mnemonic phrases for several wallets, without compromising security. The goal of BIP-0085 is to make it easier to manage and back up multiple Bitcoin wallets. Instead of having to secure several phrases, a single piece of information is enough for all the others.

b2388d11-0acc-41fe-8d54-6ebf172e6511.title: BIP-0021
b2388d11-0acc-41fe-8d54-6ebf172e6511.body:
Proposal written by Nils Schneider and Matt Corallo, based on BIP-0020 written by Luke Dashjr, which itself came from another document written by Nils Schneider. BIP-0021 defines how receiving addresses should be encoded in URIs (*Uniform Resource Identifier*) to facilitate payments. For example, a Bitcoin URI following BIP-0021 in which I would ask, under the label “*Pandul*”, to be sent 0.1 BTC would look like this:

```text
bitcoin:bc1qmp7emyf7un49eaz0nrxk9mdfrtn67v5y866fvs?amount=0.1&label=Pandul
``` 

This standardization improves the user experience of Bitcoin transactions by making it possible to click on a link or scan a QR code to launch their parameters. The BIP-0021 standard is now widely adopted in Bitcoin wallet software.

b24f7ccf-965a-4b03-b046-c3d74a0dca31.title: DIGITAL SIGNATURE
b24f7ccf-965a-4b03-b046-c3d74a0dca31.body: Cryptographic proof that demonstrates possession of a specific private key, associated with a unique public key, without having to disclose it. On Bitcoin, it is built using the private key and the hash of a transaction. It attests to ownership of the bitcoins concerned and makes it possible to satisfy a script that unlocks a UTXO. It is generated by means of an elliptic curve digital signature algorithm such as ECDSA or the Schnorr protocol.

b2903d20-e580-4fa2-aab7-460751f021c4.title: BIP-0147
b2903d20-e580-4fa2-aab7-460751f021c4.body: Proposal included in the SegWit soft fork aimed at resolving a malleability vector related to the dummy element ("*dummy element*") consumed by the `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` and `OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY` operations. Because of a historical *off-by-one* bug (a unit offset error), these 2 opcodes remove one extra element from the stack in addition to their basic function. To avoid an error, it is therefore mandatory to include a dummy value at the start of the `scriptSig` in order to satisfy the removal and work around the bug. This value is useless, but it must be there for the script to be valid. BIP-0011, which introduced the P2MS standard, advised using a `OP_0` as the useless value. But this standard was not enforced at the consensus rule level, which means that any value could be placed there without invalidating the transaction. This is why `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` and `OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY` contained a malleability vector. BIP-0147 introduces a new consensus rule, known as `NULLDUMMY`, requiring that this dummy element be an empty byte array (`OP_0`). Any other value causes the script evaluation to fail immediately. This change applies to pre-SegWit scripts as well as P2WSH scripts and required a soft fork.

b296db91-93b2-4232-b9a6-7fb893838d7a.title: LOCALBITCOINS
b296db91-93b2-4232-b9a6-7fb893838d7a.body:
Peer-to-peer bitcoin exchange platform, founded in June 2012 by Jeremias Kangas in Finland. The service connected bitcoin buyers and sellers around the world, facilitating P2P transactions. Users posted ads specifying the amounts, prices and accepted payment methods (bank transfers, cash, online payment services...). An escrow system (*escrow*) protected both parties during the transaction. This model made it possible to exchange bitcoins for local currency in practically every country, including those lacking conventional exchange platforms.

LocalBitcoins shut down in February 2023, due to unfavorable market conditions and increasing regulation.

b2b62776-d7fd-45a4-903d-e6e853e1aefe.title: TREZOR
b2b62776-d7fd-45a4-903d-e6e853e1aefe.body: Brand of *hardware wallets* made by the Czech company SatoshiLabs, launched in 2014 with the Trezor One, considered the first commercially sold Bitcoin hardware wallet. Trezor offers devices that make it possible to secure private keys offline. The devices run *open source* *firmware*, which allows independent verification of the code by the community. Interaction with the wallet is done through the Trezor Suite application or compatible software such as Sparrow Wallet.

b2c534fc-1d7d-4e21-bfa1-0457f46dafcf.title: P2PK
b2c534fc-1d7d-4e21-bfa1-0457f46dafcf.body:
P2PK is the acronym for *Pay to Public Key*. It is a standard script template used on Bitcoin to set spending conditions on a UTXO. It allows bitcoins to be locked directly to a public key, rather than to an address.
Technically, the P2PK script contains a public key and an instruction that requires a matching digital signature to unlock the funds. When the owner wishes to spend the bitcoins, they must provide a signature produced with the associated private key. This signature is verified with the ECDSA algorithm (*Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm*). P2PK was often used in the early versions of Bitcoin, notably by Satoshi Nakamoto. It is almost no longer used today.

b30dfb76-5daa-464f-9db9-7e436e45f4b4.title: TERMINAL CONSIGNMENT
b30dfb76-5daa-464f-9db9-7e436e45f4b4.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the *Terminal Consignment* designates the *transfer consignment* incorporating the final state of a contract, obtained through the *State Transition* generated from the recipient's *Invoice* (*payee*). This mechanism represents the end point of a transfer, gathering all the data necessary to attest that the ownership or the state of the contract has been duly transmitted and validated.

b330d0a9-f375-4d8e-a2d6-e2d9f237f0dd.title: P2P - PEER-TO-PEER
b330d0a9-f375-4d8e-a2d6-e2d9f237f0dd.body:
Refers to a model of communication and data distribution in which participants, often called nodes or peers, share their resources (such as files, processing power, bandwidth, assets…) directly with each other, without requiring a centralized intermediary. In a P2P system, each participant acts simultaneously as a client (consumer of resources) and as a server (provider of resources).

The Bitcoin system operates according to a P2P model, where nodes are responsible for validating transactions and storing the blockchain. This means that, unlike traditional banking systems which depend on centralized entities, Bitcoin operates on a distributed structure where no single entity holds control. The nodes of the Bitcoin network communicate with each other to broadcast transactions and blocks, and to reach consensus on the state of the ledger.

b356cf75-a40c-4869-b2bb-f30885832e02.title: MILLISATOSHI
b356cf75-a40c-4869-b2bb-f30885832e02.body: A subunit of the satoshi equal to one thousandth of a satoshi, that is one hundred-billionth of a bitcoin (`10^{-11}` BTC). The millisatoshi does not exist on the Bitcoin blockchain, where the satoshi is the minimum indivisible unit. The Lightning Network, however, uses the millisatoshi as an internal unit of account for payments and the calculation of routing fees, allowing finer granularity.

b365a328-efd9-4bf5-861c-4cab3cfbf9af.title: BLOOM FILTER
b365a328-efd9-4bf5-861c-4cab3cfbf9af.body:
Probabilistic data structure used to test whether an element is part of a set. Bloom Filters make it possible to quickly check membership without testing the entire data set. They are particularly useful in contexts where space and speed are critical, but where a low, controlled error rate is acceptable. Indeed, Bloom Filters do not produce false negatives, but they do produce a certain quantity of false positives. When an element is added to the filter, several hash functions generate positions in a bit array. To check membership, the same hash functions are used. If all the corresponding bits are set, the element is probably in the set, but with a risk of false positives. Bloom filters are widely used in the field of databases and networks. Google is notably known to use them for its distributed storage system for structured data *BigTable*. In the Bitcoin protocol, they are notably used for SPV wallets according to BIP-0037.

*When speaking specifically of the use of Bloom Filters in the context of Bitcoin transactions, the term “Transaction Bloom Filtering” is sometimes found.*

b36f431e-8a5f-4d46-83f5-c2aee91b70b7.title: TAIL EMISSION
b36f431e-8a5f-4d46-83f5-c2aee91b70b7.body:
A monetary policy mechanism that consists of maintaining a fixed block reward indefinitely after the initial issuance schedule of a cryptocurrency has been exhausted. Unlike Bitcoin's model, where the block subsidy gradually decreases through *halvings* until it reaches zero, a *tail emission* guarantees a constant flow of newly created units with each block. Although highly controversial, it is a proposal that occasionally resurfaces in debates around Bitcoin.

Monero is the most notable example of this approach: since June 2022, each block has produced a fixed reward of 0.6 XMR, after the main issuance of approximately 18.1 million units was exhausted.

Supporters of *tail emission* argue that it solves the problem of funding network security in the long term by guaranteeing a permanent incentive for miners, without depending exclusively on transaction fees. They also maintain that the inevitable loss of coins (forgotten keys, deaths of holders) would naturally offset the monetary creation, causing the circulating supply to converge toward a stable equilibrium. Opponents consider that it contradicts the principle of a fixed and deterministic maximum supply, a fundamental characteristic of Bitcoin. They also argue that permanent inflation dilutes the value of existing units and that a sufficiently developed transaction fee market can secure the network on its own in the long term.

In the context of Bitcoin, adding a *tail emission* would require a *hard fork* and is a highly controversial proposal. Bitcoin's fixed monetary policy, with a cap of 21 million bitcoins, is considered by a large part of the community to be a fundamental attribute of the protocol.

b3a6e8eb-b4bb-4e94-9c46-225973b2fc48.title: ECASH - DAVID CHAUM
b3a6e8eb-b4bb-4e94-9c46-225973b2fc48.body: A protocol proposed by David Chaum in 1982, which is one of the first digital currency systems designed to preserve users' anonymity. It relies on public-key cryptography principles to create a digital currency that can be exchanged securely and anonymously. eCash works by creating digital tokens signed by a bank. It is therefore an evolution of deposit banks, without being decentralized. During transactions, these tokens are transferred between the parties without revealing the users' identity, thus preserving their privacy. eCash is considered a precursor of cryptocurrencies. It also frequently comes up in discussions around Bitcoin, some wanting to use eCash-like systems as an overlay. Today, the trend is rather toward so-called "federated Chaumian" systems such as Fedimint.

b3abe24a-5382-4787-b997-0fc4534d3d9e.title: GNU
b3abe24a-5382-4787-b997-0fc4534d3d9e.body:
Project initiated in 1983 by Richard Stallman to create a free operating system compatible with Unix. The project has developed many free software programs that can be used as an operating system or as a complement to another operating system. GNU is the foundation of the free software movement, which has been widely adopted in the Bitcoin community. Combined with the Linux kernel, it forms the GNU/Linux operating systems.

*The name “GNU” is a recursive acronym meaning “GNU's Not Unix”.*

b3ba4c6f-b86e-48d7-b990-80f6a70dcea8.title: BOLT-04
b3ba4c6f-b86e-48d7-b990-80f6a70dcea8.body:
Specification that defines the onion routing protocol of the Lightning Network. It describes the construction and processing of 1,366-byte encrypted packets containing an ephemeral key, nested routing instructions and an integrity HMAC. Each intermediate node sees only the next hop, without knowing the sender or the final recipient.

BOLT-04 also covers *route blinding*, which hides the identity of downstream nodes to protect the recipient's privacy, and the encrypted error return mechanism that allows the sender to identify which node failed.

b3f59e7b-5f94-46d6-92fe-77d76176e816.title: BITCOIND
b3f59e7b-5f94-46d6-92fe-77d76176e816.body: Acronym for “*Bitcoin Daemon*”. It is software that implements the Bitcoin protocol and allows users to run a node for remote procedure calls known as RPC (“*Remote Procedure Call*”). It is a command-line program (without a GUI) that serves as a communication interface with Bitcoin. In other words, it is a program that runs in the background with which the user can interact (daemon). `Bitcoind` was part of Satoshi Nakamoto's original client. Some consider it the second client in the history of Bitcoin, after Satoshi's first one, since version 0.2.6 of the software allows this execution as a daemon without a graphical interface. It was subsequently merged with Bitcoin QT in 2011, a client later renamed “Bitcoin Core”, in 2014. Today, `bitcoind` is therefore fully integrated into the Bitcoin Core client.

b3ffca6f-478c-4cb2-bbd7-bc5d47a7a6d6.title: FROST
b3ffca6f-478c-4cb2-bbd7-bc5d47a7a6d6.body:
Schnorr threshold signature protocol proposed by Chelsea Komlo and Ian Goldberg in 2020, whose acronym stands for *Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold Signatures*. FROST optimizes the collaborative signing process by reducing it to two rounds of communication between participants, or even a single round when nonce preprocessing is performed.

The protocol relies on a (t, n) threshold scheme: among n participants who each hold a fragment of the private key, at least t of them must cooperate to produce a valid signature. The resulting signature is a standard Schnorr signature compliant with BIP-0340, indistinguishable from a signature issued by a regular payment. This property is particularly interesting in the context of Taproot, because it makes it possible to carry out multisignature operations on-chain without revealing the underlying threshold structure, which improves privacy and reduces transaction fees.

b41b2435-727a-42b8-a0c3-16d49a7a6d9f.title: BPM - BITCOIN POOLED MINING
b41b2435-727a-42b8-a0c3-16d49a7a6d9f.body:
Another name given to the “SCORE BASED METHOD” for calculating miners' remuneration in the context of mining pools. It is a proportional reward method, but weighted by the time at which the share is submitted. BPM values shares according to the time elapsed since the start of the mining cycle. The later a share is submitted in the cycle, the higher its value. This method encourages miners to stay, because each time a miner stops mining, their score stagnates while that of the others increases ever more quickly.

“*Bitcoin Pooled Mining*” was also the name of Slush's mining pool in 2010, which is the origin of the remuneration calculation method of the same name.

b44914a9-4221-4af0-966a-698abfcb104d.title: HODL
b44914a9-4221-4af0-966a-698abfcb104d.body: A popular term in the Bitcoin community that refers to keeping one's bitcoins for the long term, despite market volatility, and not selling them. The term originated from a typo in [a message posted in 2013 on the BitcoinTalk forum](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=375643.msg4022997#msg4022997) by the user *GameKyuubi*, who seemed to be intoxicated, in which they wrote "I AM HODLING" instead of "I AM HOLDING", which means "to keep" in English. This word quickly became a meme and a slogan.

b45aaf58-7966-498d-aa66-37cbe79ef4ce.title: NAMECOIN
b45aaf58-7966-498d-aa66-37cbe79ef4ce.body: The first altcoin in Bitcoin's history, launched in April 2011. Namecoin is a fork of the Bitcoin source code that aims to provide a decentralized system for registering and managing domain names, as an alternative to the traditional DNS (*Domain Name System*). Its main use case is the `.bit` extension, which allows censorship-resistant domain names to be registered directly on the blockchain.

b4821e84-0b30-4b18-b694-5b2c78c9262d.title: GRPC
b4821e84-0b30-4b18-b694-5b2c78c9262d.body:
Remote procedure call framework (*Remote Procedure Call*) developed by Google. gRPC uses the Protocol Buffers format to serialize data and the HTTP/2 protocol for transport, offering performant and typed communications between a client and a server.

In the Lightning ecosystem, gRPC is the main interface used by LND to expose its functionality. Tools like LNCLI interact with the Lightning node through gRPC calls to manage channels, send payments, check balances or configure routing.

b4d089e8-2c52-4ad4-84e3-7cc0372d753f.title: VOLATILITY
b4d089e8-2c52-4ad4-84e3-7cc0372d753f.body: A measure of the amplitude of an asset's price variations over a given period. In the context of Bitcoin, volatility designates the sometimes significant fluctuations of the BTC price relative to fiat currencies such as the dollar or the euro. High volatility means that the price can experience sharp rises or falls in a short time.

b5652785-3799-4e95-aca5-27cfc8ac53bc.title: SEEDQR
b5652785-3799-4e95-aca5-27cfc8ac53bc.body:
Format for representing a recovery phrase as a QR code. Developed by the SeedSigner project, SeedQR encodes each word of the BIP-0039 mnemonic phrase by its index in the word list (four-digit position, padded with zeros), then concatenates these indices into a single numeric string. The numeric mode of QR codes makes it possible to obtain a compact result.

A variant called Compact SeedQR directly encodes the binary entropy of the phrase (128 bits for 12 words, 256 bits for 24 words), which reduces the size of the QR code by 35 to 40%. The format is adopted by several signing devices such as SeedSigner, Coldcard Q and Blockstream Jade.

SeedQR offers an alternative to the classic transcription in words: the phrase can be backed up on a physical medium (metal, paper) in the form of a QR code, then scanned directly by the signing device to import the *seed* without manual entry.

b6168446-91ea-4bb3-b01b-18bc52285bfd.title: BLINDED PATHS
b6168446-91ea-4bb3-b01b-18bc52285bfd.body:
A Lightning routing technique that hides part of the payment path in order to protect the recipient's identity. In classic routing (SPHINX), the sender builds the entire route and therefore knows the recipient's public key. With *blinded paths*, the recipient encrypts the last hops of the route through an ECDH key exchange: it derives a shared secret with each node of the hidden segment, generates blinded node identifiers and produces encrypted data allowing each relay to discover only the next hop. The sender sees the route only up to an *introduction point*, without knowing the nodes beyond it or the final recipient.

*Blinded paths* are specified in BOLT-04 and are an important element of BOLT-12 offers, where each invoice includes one or more blinded paths. They can also be used in BOLT-11 invoices via bLIP-0039. *Blinded paths* also make it possible to route payments through private channels without revealing them. The recipient can add dummy hops (*dummy hops*) to strengthen anonymity, because the sender cannot distinguish the real relays from the decoys.

b64a302d-cfea-4808-8ad2-68cf4ba5313f.title: PRIMARY PATH
b64a302d-cfea-4808-8ad2-68cf4ba5313f.body: In a wallet software using Miniscript, such as Liana for example, the primary path refers to the set of keys allowing immediate spending of funds, without any time condition. This path is always accessible and is used for the day-to-day management of bitcoins, without requiring any waiting (*timelock*), unlike recovery paths. Let's take the example of a script that includes 2 distinct keys: key A, which authorizes the immediate spending of the bitcoins, and key B, which allows them to be spent after a delay defined by a *timelock* of 52,560 blocks. In this example, key A comes from the primary path, while key B comes from the recovery path.

b668d29d-190c-4e82-be53-d8c37a9c54e7.title: BITCOIN JESUS
b668d29d-190c-4e82-be53-d8c37a9c54e7.body: Nickname given to entrepreneur and investor Roger Ver, who was a promoter of Bitcoin from the early 2010s. This nickname was given to him because of his influential role in popularizing Bitcoin at its launch. He is also known for his support of the Bitcoin Cash (BCH) *hard fork*, which he considers more faithful to Bitcoin's original vision.

b69bc93d-53fd-4b21-ac3c-21ae63f283d9.title: BIP-0159
b69bc93d-53fd-4b21-ac3c-21ae63f283d9.body: Proposal defining the service bit `NODE_NETWORK_LIMITED` (bit 10) for pruned nodes of the Bitcoin network. This bit indicates that a node is able to serve at least the last 288 blocks of the blockchain (about 2 days), even without having the full history. Before this BIP, pruned nodes could not signal their partial serving capability, which excluded them from block relay. BIP-0159 thus allows pruned nodes to actively participate in the propagation of recent blocks, improving the decentralization of the network without requiring storage of the entire chain.

b6aacf9a-f4ca-4ee2-b806-f2541ca4c7fa.title: BLIP-0055
b6aacf9a-f4ca-4ee2-b806-f2541ca4c7fa.body: bLIP that defines LSPS5, a *webhook* registration protocol allowing Lightning service providers (LSPs) to notify mobile clients when an event requires their attention. Mobile applications, suspended by the operating system when they are not active, lose their network connections and cannot receive payments or process expiring HTLCs. With LSPS5, the client registers a *webhook* URL with the LSP via three APIs: `lsps5.set_webhook`, `lsps5.list_webhooks` and `lsps5.remove_webhook`. The LSP contacts this *webhook* when an incoming payment arrives, when an HTLC is about to expire, when liquidity changes, or when an onion message needs to be delivered. Notifications are cryptographically signed by the LSP node's identity key.

b6b8fd4d-6b87-4f43-8b42-5f641a841d06.title: OSINT
b6b8fd4d-6b87-4f43-8b42-5f641a841d06.body:
Acronym for "*Open Source Intelligence*". OSINT refers to the collection and analysis of publicly available information from sources accessible to everyone. These sources can include websites, forums, social networks, public databases, academic publications, government documents, etc. The main goal of OSINT is to transform raw data into actionable information, by identifying trends, correlations and investigative leads.

In the context of Bitcoin, OSINT can be used to support a chain analysis in order to trace funds, notably to identify an entry point, that is to say a link between on-chain activity and a form of identity belonging to a real entity. For example, if you publish your receiving address on Twitter under your name, an analyst could find it and associate it with your identity.

![OSINT link: a tweet by Loïc Morel publishing their address bc1q...acd makes it possible to link this address cluster to their identity.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/o/osint/assets/image-1.png)

b6dd4e18-1c00-47ae-8b06-9950372a9c84.title: OP_INTERNALKEY - 0XCB
b6dd4e18-1c00-47ae-8b06-9950372a9c84.body: Opcode proposed in BIP-0349 to be added to Tapscript (`0xcb`), which pushes the Taproot internal key (*internal key*) onto the stack. In practice, when a script in a Taproot leaf needs to know the public key that was used to construct the output, it can call `OP_INTERNALKEY` instead of having to hardcode this key in the script. The result is the 32-byte *x-only* representation of the internal key.

b6e373f4-f327-4951-99a2-739c01e6efa8.title: BIP-0331
b6e373f4-f327-4951-99a2-739c01e6efa8.body: Proposal (draft) describing a P2P protocol for relaying packages of related transactions (*ancestor packages*). This BIP makes it possible to relay a low-fee parent transaction together with its higher-fee child transaction, thus making the CPFP (*Child Pays For Parent*) mechanism effective at the network relay level. Without this protocol, a parent transaction whose fees are below the mempool minimum cannot be propagated, even if a child transaction is ready to compensate. BIP-0331 solves this problem by allowing nodes to evaluate the fee rate of the whole package rather than of each transaction individually.

b72a1cc0-9029-4bd8-b5ea-853e5c445b6d.title: DIGICASH
b72a1cc0-9029-4bd8-b5ea-853e5c445b6d.body: Company founded in 1989 by the cryptographer David Chaum, which was a pioneer in the field of anonymous electronic payments. DigiCash developed the eCash system, a digital money protocol based on the blind signatures invented by Chaum. This mechanism allowed a bank to issue digital tokens without being able to trace the transactions made by users, thus guaranteeing anonymity comparable to that of cash. Despite trials with several banks, notably Mark Twain Bank in the United States and Deutsche Bank, the system failed to achieve sufficient adoption. DigiCash went bankrupt in 1998. The eCash concept is considered an important precursor to Bitcoin, notably for its approach to privacy in digital payments.

b7c3e8a1-5d42-4f9b-a1e6-3c8d7f2b9e04.title: ADDRMAN
b7c3e8a1-5d42-4f9b-a1e6-3c8d7f2b9e04.body:
A Bitcoin Core module that manages the addresses of known peers on the network. It maintains two in-memory tables: the “new” table, which contains addresses that have been discovered but not yet tested (1024 buckets of 64 entries), and the “tried” table, which contains addresses to which the node has already successfully connected (256 buckets of 64 entries). These tables are serialized in the `peers.dat` file.

The module was introduced by Pieter Wuille in 2012, replacing the previous system that stored addresses in `addr.dat` without any bucketing structure. Its operation was strengthened by the addition of *feeler connections* and the *test-before-evict* mechanism, which make it possible to verify the reachability of addresses before promoting or evicting them.

b7ccc482-2d03-403a-8c45-77f71579bdcd.title: BITKEY
b7ccc482-2d03-403a-8c45-77f71579bdcd.body: A hardware wallet (*hardware wallet*) developed by Block, Inc. (formerly Square), the company founded by Jack Dorsey. Launched in December 2023, Bitkey relies on a 2-of-3 multisignature architecture that distributes the keys between the physical device, a mobile application and an encrypted recovery server managed by Block. This design aims to simplify *self-custody* for non-technical users by eliminating the need to manage a recovery phrase oneself. The device comes in a compact form that includes a fingerprint sensor and communicates with the application via NFC.

b7d0c86b-a0d1-4863-b72e-fb257b66d962.title: STANDARDNESS RULES
b7d0c86b-a0d1-4863-b72e-fb257b66d962.body:
A subset of the mempool policy, made up of the rules adopted individually by each Bitcoin node, in addition to the consensus rules, to define the accepted format of unconfirmed transactions taken individually. More precisely, standardness rules dictate the structure of a transaction evaluated in isolation, independently of its context in the mempool. These rules are configured and executed locally by each node and can vary from one node to another. They apply exclusively to unconfirmed transactions. Thus, a node will only accept a transaction it would judge non-standard if it is already included in a valid block.

Standardness rules exist primarily for three reasons:
* Protection against DoS attacks: some transactions are more costly than others for the node to verify, and the asymmetry between the low cost of sending an unconfirmed transaction and the high cost of processing it creates a denial-of-service attack vector;
* Soft fork preparation mechanism: making a type of transaction non-standard before making it invalid by consensus via a soft fork guarantees that a non-updated miner will not include a newly invalid transaction in a block, which makes soft forks safer to deploy;
* Behavioral incentive: standardness rules can steer users toward practices that are less harmful to the network, or slightly discourage certain activities, such as the excessive storage of arbitrary data in the blockchain.

Note that the majority of nodes leave the default configurations as pre-established in Bitcoin Core, in effect producing a homogeneity of standardness rules across the network. A transaction that, although compliant with the consensus rules, does not comply with these standardness rules will have difficulty being broadcast on the network. It may nevertheless be included in a valid block if it ever reaches a miner. In practice, these transactions, described as "non-standard", are often transmitted directly to a miner through channels external to Bitcoin's peer-to-peer network. This is often the only way to confirm this type of transaction.

For example, a transaction that allocates no fee is both valid according to the consensus rules and non-standard, because Bitcoin Core's default policy for the `minRelayTxFee` parameter is `0.000001` (in BTC/kvB).

*Standardness rules are a subset of the mempool policy, which is itself a subset of the transaction relay policy, which is part of the relay policy in the broad sense. Standardness rules should therefore not be confused with the mempool policy, which is a more encompassing concept.*

b80ec0d7-d56f-46c4-a0b3-45a3144de0e5.title: BOLT
b80ec0d7-d56f-46c4-a0b3-45a3144de0e5.body: Acronym for “*Basis of Lightning Technology*”. It is a series of specifications intended to enable Lightning interoperability between the different implementations of this second-layer protocol (*LND*, *Core Lightning*, *Eclair*...). These specifications detail the rules and standards to be followed so that Lightning nodes form one and the same network.

b81be87d-05d5-49ce-b61c-bc5af4e0e0de.title: BINARY PREFIXES
b81be87d-05d5-49ce-b61c-bc5af4e0e0de.body: Units used in computing to quantify multiples of data sizes based on powers of 2. Unlike metric system prefixes, which use a base of 10, binary prefixes, such as kibi (Ki), mebi (Mi), gibi (Gi), and tebi (Ti), multiply by powers of 2 (`2^{10}`, `2^{20}`, `2^{30}`, `2^{40}` respectively). These prefixes are inherited from the earliest ways of measuring the size of information on computers. They are sometimes found in Bitcoin, for example to designate the size limit of the `BLOCKS/BLK*.DAT` files that store the raw blockchain data in the Bitcoin Core software. These files thus have a maximum capacity of 128 mebibytes (MiB), which is equivalent to a little over 134 megabytes (MB).

b888e875-627e-46ee-aa19-6df6f7c419a9.title: CHAMPION - BIP
b888e875-627e-46ee-aa19-6df6f7c419a9.body:
In the context of Bitcoin Core development (the majority implementation of Bitcoin), the champion is the person who writes and takes charge of managing a BIP (Bitcoin Improvement Proposal). The champion is responsible for writing the BIP following the formal process, defending it before the community, answering questions and guiding discussions to refine the proposal. They also work to obtain the consensus necessary for the BIP to be accepted and implemented. They can

*The champion is also sometimes called the “author”. Their name can in fact be found noted after the “Author” header in BIPs. There can sometimes be several champions for the same BIP.*

b89d1435-f776-4305-a743-c2d95ebcdf91.title: PRIVATE KEY
b89d1435-f776-4305-a743-c2d95ebcdf91.body:
A private key is a fundamental element of asymmetric cryptography. It is a number (256 bits in the case of Bitcoin) that represents a cryptographic secret. This key is used to digitally sign transactions and to prove possession of a Bitcoin public key (and by extension, of a receiving address) by satisfying a `scriptPubKey`. Private keys therefore make it possible to spend bitcoins by unlocking the UTXOs associated with the corresponding public key. Private keys must be kept strictly confidential, because their disclosure could allow malicious third parties to take control of the associated funds. 

In the Bitcoin system, the private key is linked to a public key through an elliptic curve digital signature algorithm (ECDSA or Schnorr). The public key is derived from the private key, but the reverse is practically impossible to achieve because of the computational difficulty inherent in solving the underlying mathematical problem (the discrete logarithm problem). The public key is generally used to generate a Bitcoin address, which serves to lock bitcoins using a script. In cryptography, private keys are often random or pseudo-random numbers. In the specific context of Bitcoin hierarchical deterministic wallets, private keys are derived deterministically from the seed. Private keys are frequently confused with the seed or with the recovery phrase (mnemonic). However, these elements are quite different.

*In French, a private key is called "clé privée". This term is sometimes abbreviated as "privkey", or "PV".*

b8c46a73-5966-43a4-b013-e992ea5dd5c2.title: WRENCH ATTACK
b8c46a73-5966-43a4-b013-e992ea5dd5c2.body:
Physical attack that aims to force a bitcoin holder to hand over their funds under threat or through violence. The name refers to a cheap wrench (with a symbolic value of 5 dollars) used as a tool of coercion, and illustrates the idea that the most robust cryptography can be bypassed by a simple physical assault.

Several countermeasures exist to limit the risks related to this attack. The use of a BIP-0039 passphrase makes it possible to create a hidden wallet, which offers a form of plausible deniability. The use of multisig with a geographic distribution of keys prevents an attacker from obtaining all the necessary signatures in a single place. Timelocks can also be employed to make funds temporarily inaccessible. Finally, discretion about one's bitcoin holdings remains the most basic preventive measure.

This notion is a reminder that security in the Bitcoin ecosystem is a global issue that goes beyond the computing dimension alone. It also involves operational security (OPSEC) considerations and physical protection.

b8d328dd-a9bc-4aaf-b87e-32f736585c20.title: CHAIN ANALYSIS

b910ddcb-1d74-440d-83a0-b9f1adbf19e3.title: PEACH
b910ddcb-1d74-440d-83a0-b9f1adbf19e3.body:
Peer-to-peer (P2P) bitcoin exchange mobile application, founded in 2022 in Switzerland. Peach Bitcoin, often simply called “Peach”, allows users to buy and sell bitcoins directly between themselves without going through a centralized exchange platform.

The application works with an *escrow* system to secure transactions and supports many payment methods in Europe, such as SEPA transfers, Revolut, PayPal, or cash payments at in-person meetings.

b9596734-9906-48ab-87c9-93abea4f23c6.title: ADDRV2
b9596734-9906-48ab-87c9-93abea4f23c6.body: An evolution of the `addr` message on the Bitcoin network, proposed with BIP-0155. The `addr` message was used to broadcast the addresses of nodes that accept incoming connections, but it was limited to 128-bit addresses. This size was adequate for IPv6, IPv4, and Tor V2 addresses, but insufficient for other protocols. The updated version `addrv2` is designed to support longer addresses, notably 256-bit Tor V3 hidden services, as well as other network protocols such as I2P or future protocols.

b9ad0af8-136f-437c-b183-e9d6c27ee924.title: NATURAL BRANCHING / CHAINSPLIT
b9ad0af8-136f-437c-b183-e9d6c27ee924.body: A temporary split of the blockchain resulting from the near-simultaneous broadcast of several blocks by different miners at the same height. This situation occurs when two blocks, designated as `A` and `B`, are found almost simultaneously, causing a temporary division of the network. Since each node considers the first block it received as valid, but not everyone received the same block first, some of the nodes follow the chain containing block `A`, while the others follow the one with block `B`. This branching is resolved when one of the two competing chains overtakes the other in terms of accumulated work. At that moment, all the nodes of the network automatically agree on the longest chain (with the most accumulated work), a process called reorganization or resynchronization. These natural branchings are inherent to the distributed operation of Bitcoin. They are perfectly normal and resolve spontaneously after a few blocks (generally just one). If there are too many of them, these branchings can nevertheless be harmful, because they cause a waste of computing power on a branch that will eventually become obsolete.

b9b74b6e-c356-4b3f-8929-244088c0d7dd.title: LND
b9b74b6e-c356-4b3f-8929-244088c0d7dd.body: Acronym for “*Lightning Network Daemon*”. It is a major implementation of the Lightning Network protocol written in the Go language. Developed by Lightning Labs, LND allows the creation and management of payment channels and nodes on the Lightning network.

b9d5ad29-532b-4219-9f1c-a3e48703caa3.title: DERIVATION

b9d8cc0c-4207-4ade-884f-aeddf43a9a86.title: BOLT-01
b9d8cc0c-4207-4ade-884f-aeddf43a9a86.body: Specification that defines the base messaging protocol between Lightning nodes. It establishes the message format, their classification into five categories (setup, channel, commitment, routing and custom messages) and the fundamental data types. BOLT-01 introduces the TLV (*Type-Length-Value*) format, an extensible encoding that allows implementations to ignore unknown fields while maintaining compatibility. It also specifies the `init` message exchanged on connection between two peers to declare their features, the `error` and `warning` messages for error handling, and the `ping`/`pong` mechanism for keeping connections alive.

b9f40806-acfa-44c8-8a37-6994954101be.title: SIMPLICITY
b9f40806-acfa-44c8-8a37-6994954101be.body: Low-level programming language designed by Russell O'Connor at Blockstream to express contracts on blockchains that rely on the UTXO model. Presented in a white paper in 2017, Simplicity differs from languages like Solidity (Ethereum) in that it is not Turing-complete: it can express any finite function, but prohibits unbounded loops and global state. This restriction makes it possible to guarantee that every execution terminates, and that the resource cost of a program is known before its execution. The language was deployed on Liquid in July 2025, where it gives asset issuers the ability to create verifiable contracts. Unlike Miniscript, which is limited to signatures, timelocks and hash preimages within Script, Simplicity can express arbitrary functions, but requires a consensus environment distinct from that of Bitcoin.

b9f5ce0a-baa4-4e12-8f4c-08c77ce82099.title: TIMELOCK
b9f5ce0a-baa4-4e12-8f4c-08c77ce82099.body:
A smart contract primitive that makes it possible to define a time condition to be met before a transaction can be added to a block. There are two types of timelocks on Bitcoin: 
* The absolute timelock, which specifies a precise moment before which the transaction cannot be included in a block; 
* The relative timelock, which defines a delay starting from the acceptance of a prior transaction. 

The timelock can be defined either as a date expressed in Unix time, or as a block number. Finally, the timelock can apply either to a transaction output through the use of a specific opcode in the locking script (`OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY` or `OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY`), or to an entire transaction through the use of the `nLockTime` field, or to a specific input through the use of the `nSequence` field.

*One also sometimes speaks of a “locktime” to refer to a timelock.*

ba1ad375-829d-436a-bd13-570d31abe544.title: LIGHTNING NETWORK
ba1ad375-829d-436a-bd13-570d31abe544.body: A higher-layer protocol, built on top of the Bitcoin protocol, aimed at enabling fast, low-cost transactions. It allows the creation of payment channels between participants, within which transactions can be made almost instantly and with minimal fees, without having to record each individual transaction on the blockchain. Channels can remain open almost indefinitely, and only require on-chain transactions when they are opened and closed. The Lightning Network aims to improve Bitcoin's scalability and to make it possible to use it for low-value payments.

ba286b8c-fd05-42c6-9709-a48ba8e527ef.title: BIP-0143
ba286b8c-fd05-42c6-9709-a48ba8e527ef.body:
Introduces a new way of hashing the transaction for signature verification in post-SegWit scripts. The objective is to minimize redundant operations during verification and to include the value of the input UTXOs in the signature. This solves two major problems of the original transaction hashing algorithm: 
* The quadratic growth of data hashing with the number of signatures; 
* The lack of inclusion of the input value in the signature, which posed a risk for *hardware wallet*s, particularly regarding knowing the fees committed in the transaction.
Since the SegWit update, explained in BIP-0141, introduces a new form of transactions whose script will not be verified by old nodes, BIP-0143 takes the opportunity to solve this problem without requiring a *hard fork*. BIP-0143 is therefore part of the SegWit *soft fork*.

ba33538f-40a4-41a6-8335-d13dec0df50a.title: AMBOSS
ba33538f-40a4-41a6-8335-d13dec0df50a.body: Amboss is a Lightning Network analytics and monitoring platform, founded in 2021 by Jesse Shrader and Anthony Potdevin. It provides detailed data on the network topology, nodes, channels, and liquidity flows, allowing node operators to optimize their management. Amboss also offers Magma, a marketplace dedicated to Lightning liquidity, where operators can buy and sell channel capacity.

bacc85e4-5f65-4d37-a12e-f8707e046b6c.title: PUBLIC CHANNEL
bacc85e4-5f65-4d37-a12e-f8707e046b6c.body: A Lightning channel announced to the network via a *channel announcement* message broadcast to peers. Unlike a private channel, a public channel is included in the Lightning network graph: other nodes know of its existence, its capacity and its fee policies, which allows them to use it to route payments.

bafda9f7-e466-465b-93fe-e0d2d521b0e5.title: OP_2DUP - 0X6E
bafda9f7-e466-465b-93fe-e0d2d521b0e5.body:
Duplicates the two elements at the top of the stack, then places them at the top of the stack. For example, if the stack is:

```text
A
B
C
D
```

`OP_2DUP` will produce: 

```text
A
B
A
B
C
D
```

bb16f43f-ff58-4861-b57c-d51aa51ddaa1.title: BIP-0197
bb16f43f-ff58-4861-b57c-d51aa51ddaa1.body: Proposal of HTLCCs (*Hashed Time-Locked Collateral Contracts*), an extension of HTLCs (*Hashed Time-Locked Contracts*) adding a collateral mechanism. BIP-0197 is designed to create debt agreements between two parties (a borrower and a lender), where bitcoin collateral is locked in a P2SH to guarantee a loan whose principal is denominated on another blockchain. In case of non-repayment, the collateral can be liquidated via an atomic swap or seized according to predefined conditions.

bb475b31-99b7-4ea4-b936-0da174037ae6.title: SHARES DIFFICULTY
bb475b31-99b7-4ea4-b936-0da174037ae6.body: Difficulty target higher than Bitcoin's (thus less difficult), defined by a mining pool to qualify a hash as a share and to evaluate the contribution of each individual miner in the pool. To efficiently manage the verification load and ensure that each miner, regardless of their computing power, submits shares regularly, pools adjust share difficulty. The difficulty assigned to each miner determines the number of shares they accumulate: for example, if a miner has an assigned difficulty of 10 and submits 5 valid proofs of work at this difficulty, they obtain 50 shares. A more powerful miner with a difficulty of 100 who submits 7 valid proofs of work will receive 700 shares. This system makes it possible to precisely quantify each miner's hashrate and to distribute rewards according to the chosen payout calculation method (PPS, PPLNS, TIDES...).

bb71c4d4-8957-48d0-aa64-d5adbb821617.title: DGM
bb71c4d4-8957-48d0-aa64-d5adbb821617.body: Acronym for "*Double Geometric Method*". It is a method for calculating miner rewards in the context of mining pools. DGM is a hybrid method, meant to combine the advantages of PPLNS and of the so-called "geometric" method. It has low variance on shares, in the manner of PPLNS, and then allows the pool operator to absorb part of the variance risk in a second step. DGM is resistant to *pool hopping* by ensuring that the expected payout per share remains constant. The method is based on scores, making payouts independent of the pool's history and almost entirely independent of future difficulty changes.

bb75812c-bfec-4229-8314-5e0b52607f35.title: C++
bb75812c-bfec-4229-8314-5e0b52607f35.body:
A general-purpose programming language, evolved from C, known for its power and flexibility. Used for complex software development, it supports object-oriented programming and offers rich features for managing memory and system resources. 

Bitcoin Core, the majority implementation of the Bitcoin protocol, is written in C++. This is a legacy of Satoshi's very first client, which was also written in this programming language. To guarantee strictly consistent node behavior across the network, notably to avoid *forks*, it was decided not to change languages since 2009.

bbb44c74-279f-4379-9160-c4304fcb87f8.title: LOOP
bbb44c74-279f-4379-9160-c4304fcb87f8.body: Service developed by Lightning Labs designed to facilitate liquidity balancing in Lightning channels. Loop allows users to move funds between Bitcoin and the Lightning Network, without having to close or open a channel. Loop thus helps optimize one's liquidity and reduce the costs of managing one's channels.

bbf5f967-9d73-448b-8e56-dedd8b89afe3.title: RUST BITCOIN
bbf5f967-9d73-448b-8e56-dedd8b89afe3.body:
*Open source* library written in Rust for manipulating Bitcoin protocol data structures and messages. It makes it possible to serialize and deserialize transactions, blocks and network messages, to manage private keys, addresses and BIP-0032 derivation, or to work with PSBTs.

Rust Bitcoin is not designed for consensus validation: discrepancies, both known and unknown, exist with the Bitcoin Core reference implementation, which makes it unsuitable for a full node. It instead targets developers building wallets, explorers, analysis tools or any software that interacts with the Bitcoin network without fully validating it.

The project, released under the CC0 license (public domain), is accompanied by companion *crates* such as `bitcoin_hashes`, `secp256k1` or `miniscript`, and works in a `no-std` environment for embedded systems.

bc063b54-5a9c-4e63-a7ad-09dd21916273.title: BIP-0129
bc063b54-5a9c-4e63-a7ad-09dd21916273.body: Proposal defining the BSMS (*Bitcoin Secure Multisig Setup*) protocol, a standard for the secure setup of multisignature wallets between different hardware and software signers. The protocol uses an encryption scheme and token-based (*token*) coordination for the exchange of extended public keys and of the wallet configuration. It ensures that all cosigners agree on the same parameters (signature threshold, descriptor, derivation paths) before finalizing the creation of the wallet. BIP-0129 is adopted by several software products such as Nunchuk and Sparrow.

bc1f0a29-0f6c-465b-8d51-f08ba911491d.title: SNAPSHOT
bc1f0a29-0f6c-465b-8d51-f08ba911491d.body:
An instantaneous capture of the state of Bitcoin's UTXO set at a given block. A snapshot records all the UTXOs existing at that block height, forming a complete picture of all the unspent coins on the network.

The main use of the snapshot in Bitcoin is through the Assume UTXO mechanism, built into the Bitcoin Core client. When a new node is initialized, it can load a snapshot of the UTXO set that has been pre-computed and whose cryptographic fingerprint is verified. This approach allows the node to be functional almost immediately, without having to validate the entire blockchain history from the genesis block. Full verification of the chain is then carried out in the background.

bca5dfc1-10e0-4d8b-bbe3-a15d91f0ae0b.title: FEE SNIPING
bca5dfc1-10e0-4d8b-bbe3-a15d91f0ae0b.body:
Attack scenario in which miners seek to rewrite a recently confirmed block in order to recover the transaction fees it contains, while also adding to it high-fee transactions that have arrived in the meantime in the mempool. The ultimate goal of this attack for the miner is to increase their profitability. *Fee sniping* can become increasingly profitable as the block reward decreases and transaction fees represent a larger share of miners' revenues. It can also be advantageous when the fees contained in the previous block are significantly higher than those of the next best candidate block. To simplify, the miner faces this choice in terms of incentives:
* Mine normally on top of the last block, with a high probability of winning a low reward;
* Attempt to mine an earlier block (*fee sniping*), with a low probability of winning a high reward.

This attack constitutes a risk for the Bitcoin system, because the more miners adopt it, the more the other miners, initially honest, are incentivized to do the same. Indeed, each time a new miner joins those attempting *fee sniping*, the probability that one of the attacking miners succeeds increases, and the probability that one of the honest miners extends the chain decreases correspondingly. If this attack is carried out on a massive scale and sustained over time, block confirmations would no longer be a reliable indicator of the immutability of a Bitcoin transaction. This could potentially render the system unusable. 

To counter this risk, most wallet software automatically fills in the `nLocktime` field so that it makes the validity of the transaction conditional on its inclusion at the next block height. Thus, it becomes impossible to include the transaction in a rewrite of the previous block. If widespread use of the `nLocktime` is adopted by Bitcoin users, this considerably reduces the incentives for *fee sniping*. Indeed, it encourages the progression of the blockchain rather than its rewriting by reducing the potential benefits of the latter. For Taproot transactions, BIP-0326 proposes using the `nSequence` field in a similar way to achieve the same effect as the `nLocktime` field for the other transaction types. This use would kill two birds with one stone by also improving the privacy of second-layer protocols that use this same field.

bcaa0b20-9dcd-4ea2-a64d-e35e1a97eb78.title: ASSET PROOF
bcaa0b20-9dcd-4ea2-a64d-e35e1a97eb78.body: A cryptographic proof that makes it possible to verify the existence, ownership and provenance of an asset issued via the Taproot Assets protocol. An *asset proof* contains the asset script as well as the path in the *Sparse Merkle Sum Tree* leading to the leaf of the relevant holder. The recipient can partially reconstruct the tree, tweak the issuer's public key and verify that the genesis transaction does exist on the Bitcoin blockchain.

bccb87c2-3cf6-4552-afd6-870130b962f9.title: PBKDF2
bccb87c2-3cf6-4552-afd6-870130b962f9.body:
`PBKDF2` is the acronym for *Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2*. It is a method for creating cryptographic keys from a password using a derivation function. It takes as input a password and a cryptographic salt, and iteratively applies a predetermined function (often a hash function such as `SHA256` or a `HMAC`) to this data. This process is repeated many times in order to generate a cryptographic key. 

In the context of Bitcoin, `PBKDF2` is used in conjunction with the `HMAC-SHA512` function to create the seed of a deterministic and hierarchical wallet (seed) from a recovery phrase of 12 or 24 words. The cryptographic salt used in this case is the string `"mnemonic"` concatenated with the optional BIP-0039 passphrase, and the number of iterations is `2048`.

bcda76f1-8daf-4d1e-bab2-431fe6991f83.title: FLAG DAY
bcda76f1-8daf-4d1e-bab2-431fe6991f83.body:
Soft fork activation method used in the early years of Bitcoin. This process simply defines a deadline date, known as the "*Flag Day*", before which the protocol upgrade must be adopted by the whole network. This approach is simple and direct: after this date, nodes and miners must have updated their software to comply with the new rules, failing which they risk finding themselves on an incompatible chain.

However, this method is very risky nowadays, because it requires significant coordination and consensus within the community, failing which the network may suffer a split, and the updated chain may not be the longest (with the most accumulated work). The *Flag Day* method can nevertheless be used for uncontroversial changes or urgent technical corrections.

bcddfad0-4e8d-48da-80e2-a02557bcc1f9.title: BINOHASH
bcddfad0-4e8d-48da-80e2-a02557bcc1f9.body:
Collision-resistant hash function for Bitcoin transactions, proposed by Robin Linus (ZeroSync) in 2026, which enables a limited form of transaction introspection in Bitcoin Script without modifying consensus. The name comes from the binomial coefficient `\binom{n}{t}` that makes its construction possible.

The problem solved by Binohash is that Bitcoin Script cannot natively read a transaction's data (inputs, outputs, amounts). This limitation prevents the *trustless* verification of transaction properties in Script, which is necessary for protocols like BitVM bridges.

Binohash exploits the *FindAndDelete* behavior of legacy `OP_CHECKMULTISIG`, a historical artifact that removes signatures from the *scriptCode* before the *sighash* is computed. By embedding a pool of signatures in the *locking script* and selecting subsets via `OP_ROLL`, each selection produces a different *sighash*. The spender performs proof-of-work *grinding* (ECDSA signature puzzles verifiable by `OP_SIZE`) until finding a subset that satisfies a size constraint. The indices of the winning subset constitute the Binohash, directly readable in the *unlocking script*.

bcfce645-505b-494b-afd5-03ec043ecad3.title: BIP-0135
bcfce645-505b-494b-afd5-03ec043ecad3.body: Proposal generalizing the *version bits* signaling mechanism defined in BIP-0009, with more flexibility in the soft fork activation parameters. BIP-0135 made it possible to configure the activation thresholds, signaling periods and expiration deadlines independently for each proposal. It was never deployed on Bitcoin.

bd0e5f62-271d-4c02-9728-6b0791c44cf7.title: EXTRA-NONCE
bd0e5f62-271d-4c02-9728-6b0791c44cf7.body:
Field used in the `scriptSig` of a block's coinbase transaction, which allows a greater number of possibilities to be tested to obtain a hash lower than or equal to the difficulty target, in addition to the classic nonce which is located directly in the header of each block.

Modifying the extra-nonce in the coinbase transaction changes the identifier of this transaction, and therefore the Merkle root of all the transactions in the block, which also modifies the block header. This allows the miner to keep searching for hashes when the range of the classic nonce is already exhausted, without changing the structure of their candidate block.

In the context of mining pools, the extra-nonce is often divided into two parts: one generated by the pool to identify each hasher, and another modified by the hasher in the search for a valid *share*. This allows the different hashers in the pool to work simultaneously on the same candidate block with the entire range of nonces, without duplicating the same work at the pool level.

bd2933e9-ee46-4cb5-925a-69f18c0f8eb7.title: BLOCK EXPLORER
bd2933e9-ee46-4cb5-925a-69f18c0f8eb7.body: Online or local tool that transforms the raw data of the Bitcoin blockchain into a structured, easily human-readable format. The explorer generally includes a search engine to easily locate a specific block, transaction or address.

bd2b27e0-5c81-486a-b102-b226c4f985cb.title: MONETARY DARWINISM
bd2b27e0-5c81-486a-b102-b226c4f985cb.body:
A concept that applies Darwin's theory of natural selection to the monetary domain. It postulates that the different forms of money compete with one another and that the currencies with the best-suited properties (scarcity, durability, divisibility, portability, fungibility, verifiability) eventually supplant those that perform less well.

From this perspective, proponents of this concept see Bitcoin as a superior currency likely to prevail over fiat currencies through the sheer strength of its intrinsic properties. Its strictly limited supply, its censorship resistance and its decentralized nature would constitute decisive competitive advantages in this monetary selection.

This concept is closely linked to that of hyperbitcoinization and follows in the tradition of Thiers' law (good money drives out bad), in opposition to Gresham's law (bad money drives out good).

bdaa23dd-6db5-4b61-8124-47d0a6347470.title: ESCROW
bdaa23dd-6db5-4b61-8124-47d0a6347470.body:
Mechanism by which funds are entrusted to a trusted third party who holds them until the conditions agreed between the parties are met. In French, it is called a "séquestre". Escrow is commonly used in commercial transactions to protect both the buyer and the seller.

In the context of Bitcoin, escrow can be implemented in different ways. The most common method uses multisig addresses (2-of-3), where three keys are distributed among the buyer, the seller and an arbitrator. The funds can only be released if at least two of the three parties sign the transaction, which allows dispute resolution without any single party controlling the funds.

Timelocks can also be built in to ensure that the funds do not remain locked indefinitely. On-chain escrow is notably used by peer-to-peer exchange platforms such as Bisq or HodlHodl to secure transactions without a centralized third party.

bdb50a85-22c0-426c-9cb0-2083abb80255.title: PORTAL
bdb50a85-22c0-426c-9cb0-2083abb80255.body: *Open source* Bitcoin *hardware wallet* developed by TwentyTwo Devices, which works entirely via NFC, with no cable or battery. The device is powered directly by the *smartphone*'s NFC field. Its *firmware* is written in Rust with BDK (*Bitcoin Dev Kit*) and it is compatible with mobile wallets such as Nunchuk or Bitcoin Keeper for signing transactions.

bddd07b1-ae8d-4a3c-af27-d325bec2ca14.title: ONION MESSAGE
bddd07b1-ae8d-4a3c-af27-d325bec2ca14.body:
Lightweight and flexible messages transmitted between peers on the Lightning Network using onion routing, without requiring the sending of funds or the locking of liquidity. Unlike Lightning payments that go through HTLCs, onion messages are simply relayed from peer to peer along existing connections, which makes them free for the sender.

Onion messages are the communication building block of the BOLT-12 protocol (*offers*). They allow a payer to contact a recipient to request an invoice, even without a direct channel between them. Thanks to *blinded paths*, the recipient can receive these messages without revealing their identity or their position in the network: they build an encrypted route to themselves from a popular node, which dilutes their identity among many possible candidates.

Beyond *offers*, onion messages pave the way for asynchronous payments: an LSP can hold a payment and use an onion message to signal that the recipient is online, thus eliminating the requirement for the receiver to be connected permanently.

be0e6dd6-cc83-4f02-9fb6-8b1a1d4d4006.title: CHAINSPLIT
be0e6dd6-cc83-4f02-9fb6-8b1a1d4d4006.body: A name sometimes given to a natural fork, that is, a temporary split of the blockchain resulting from the near-simultaneous broadcast of several blocks by different miners at the same height.

be6acfa8-f0d5-466e-9ecd-f5be269006f0.title: REDEEM
be6acfa8-f0d5-466e-9ecd-f5be269006f0.body: In the RGB protocol, within a *State Extension*, the term *Redeem* refers to the action of recovering or exercising a previously declared *Valency*. The *Valency*, as a public right recorded in the contract state, gives an authorized participant the ability to claim a specific extension of that state. This mechanism thus makes it possible to formalize the exercise of specific rights defined in the contract schema, ensuring that only the legitimately authorized party can initiate the corresponding transition and make use of the associated resources.

be8b9420-2573-4ed1-8805-e0974dd80707.title: FEELER CONNECTION
be8b9420-2573-4ed1-8805-e0974dd80707.body:
Ephemeral outbound connection that Bitcoin Core establishes every two minutes, once the 10 permanent outbound connections are filled (8 regular and 2 block-relay-only). It is limited to the `VERSION`/`VERACK` handshake to verify that an address does correspond to a reachable Bitcoin node, then closes.

The feeler connection alternates between two behaviors. If the eviction buffer contains addresses (the case of a collision during insertion into the "tried" table), it tests one of them: if the existing address responds, the new one is discarded; otherwise, the old one is replaced. This mechanism is called *test-before-evict*. If the buffer is empty, the feeler draws a random address from the "new" table and attempts to connect to it: if successful, the address is promoted to "tried".

This mechanism was introduced by Ethan Heilman as a countermeasure to certain types of eclipse attack. By populating the "tried" table with recently verified addresses, it reduces the proportion of obsolete addresses and makes it harder to eclipse a node. When no new block has been received for 30 minutes, Bitcoin Core detects a possible *stale tip* and establishes an additional outbound connection to a new peer, in order to check whether it has a more recent block and to bypass a possible network partition. This mechanism is distinct from feeler connections.

be9a5c03-7500-42b4-bf1d-6a8e96a6a4ea.title: OP_ABS - 0X90
