be9a5c03-7500-42b4-bf1d-6a8e96a6a4ea.body: Replaces the top item of the stack with its absolute value. This operation removes the sign of the item, turning any negative value into a positive one, without changing positive values.

bee5e035-ae75-4556-a773-919454964c2d.title: SILK ROAD
bee5e035-ae75-4556-a773-919454964c2d.body:
Silk Road was a *dark web* platform founded by Ross Ulbricht, also known by the pseudonym *Dread Pirate Roberts*. Launched in 2011, this online marketplace allowed users to buy and sell products and services, both licit and illicit, while preserving their anonymity through the use of Tor and bitcoin payments. Silk Road offered a varied range of items, mainly drugs and normally prescription-only medicines, but excluded activities deemed contrary to natural-law principles, such as the sale of hitman services or child sexual abuse material.

The platform reflected Ross Ulbricht's agorist convictions, by promoting a free and unregulated market, thus escaping government control and taxation. Silk Road played a significant role in the initial adoption of Bitcoin in the early 2010s, by contributing to its notoriety and its use beyond *cypherpunk* circles.

Silk Road was shut down in 2013. Ross Ulbricht was arrested the same year and sentenced to two life sentences plus 40 years, without the possibility of parole, along with restitution of 183 million dollars. This sentence raises questions about the proportionality of the penalties imposed for non-violent online crimes. Ross Ulbricht was finally pardoned by President Donald Trump on January 21, 2025, after spending more than 11 years in prison.

bf33fc73-d6fc-4b8f-b213-2bd18481bca7.title: BIP-0002
bf33fc73-d6fc-4b8f-b213-2bd18481bca7.body: Document written by Luke Dashjr in 2016 that revises the BIP (*Bitcoin Improvement Proposals*) process defined by BIP-0001. BIP-0002 clarifies the possible statuses of proposals (“*Draft*”, “*Proposed*”, “*Final*”, “*Deferred*”, “*Withdrawn*”, “*Rejected*”, “*Replaced*”, “*Obsolete*”, “*Active*”) and specifies the objective criteria for moving from one status to another. In particular, it introduces concrete rules for a BIP to reach “*Final*” status: for example, a soft fork requires a clear majority of miners, whereas an application-layer BIP must be implemented by at least two independent software projects. BIP-0002 also adds a public comment system, a classification by layer (*layer*) taken from BIP-0123, and licensing requirements for new proposals. This process has since been replaced by that of BIP-0003. Its status is “*Closed*”.

bf5fb26d-f603-43e0-b1af-234d3a7721e2.title: ASSET SPLIT
bf5fb26d-f603-43e0-b1af-234d3a7721e2.body: An operation that consists of dividing a Taproot Assets asset into two parts distributed across distinct Taproot outputs. The sender updates the *Merkle-Sum Sparse Merkle Tree* of their own output by reducing their balance, then the recipient builds a second tree committed in a new Taproot output containing the received assets. Each transfer of assets between holders relies on this splitting mechanism. Asset proofs (*asset proofs*) must trace back to the genesis transaction to attest to the provenance of the assets after each *split*. It is the inverse operation of an *asset merge*.

bf6376b1-3988-46ff-844f-a7bf79fc3179.title: VIABTC
bf6376b1-3988-46ff-844f-a7bf79fc3179.body: A Bitcoin mining pool founded in 2016 in China. ViaBTC is among the main mining pools in the world in terms of hashrate. It stands out for the diversity of its payout methods: PPS+, PPLNS and *solo mining*, allowing miners to choose the model best suited to their risk profile.

bf751a57-9c20-4e51-b956-69ee342ec64c.title: SENTINEL
bf751a57-9c20-4e51-b956-69ee342ec64c.body: *Watch-only* wallet Android application, originally developed by the Samourai Wallet team and now maintained by the community. Sentinel makes it possible to monitor the balances and transaction history of a Bitcoin wallet by importing its extended public keys (`xpub`, `ypub`, `zpub`), without ever exposing the private keys. The application supports PSBTs, connection via Tor and attachment to a personal Dojo node.

bf96e1ea-f4a3-4f68-b585-653a603b31f7.title: P2SH
bf96e1ea-f4a3-4f68-b585-653a603b31f7.body:
P2SH is the acronym for *Pay to Script Hash*. It is a standard script template used to set spending conditions on a UTXO. Unlike the P2PK and P2PKH scripts, where the spending conditions are predefined, P2SH allows the integration of arbitrary spending conditions and additional functionality within a transaction script.

Technically, in a P2SH transaction, the `scriptPubKey` contains the cryptographic fingerprint of a `redeemScript`, rather than explicit spending conditions. This fingerprint is obtained using a `HASH160` hash, that is, a `SHA256` followed by a `RIPEMD160`. When sending bitcoins to a P2SH address, the underlying `redeemScript` is not revealed. Only its fingerprint is included in the transaction. P2SH addresses are encoded in `Base58Check` and begin with the digit `3`. When the recipient wishes to spend the bitcoins received, they must provide a `redeemScript` matching the fingerprint present in the `scriptPubKey`, as well as the data needed to satisfy the conditions of this `redeemScript`. For example, in a multisignature P2SH, the script could require signatures from several private keys.

Using P2SH gives more flexibility, as it allows the construction of arbitrary scripts without the sender knowing their details. P2SH was introduced in 2012 with BIP-0016.

bfaa4ed3-b33c-461f-b444-695d9fa2d63d.title: SRC-20
bfaa4ed3-b33c-461f-b444-695d9fa2d63d.body: A fungible token standard on Bitcoin that relies on the STAMPS protocol to inscribe metadata directly into UTXOs. Unlike the BRC-20 standard, which stores its data in the *witness* part of transactions (which can be pruned by nodes), SRC-20 data is inscribed in unspent outputs, which makes it permanent and non-deletable.

bfddd138-88b4-42bc-81fb-bbbc0e0097d3.title: BRC-20
bfddd138-88b4-42bc-81fb-bbbc0e0097d3.body: Standard enabling interaction with non-native tokens on Bitcoin, based on inscriptions of the Ordinals protocol. Created by Domo in March 2023, this experimental standard sparked strong speculative enthusiasm, leading to a historic rise in transaction fees in April and May 2023. BRC-20 tokens use Bitcoin to store and timestamp JSON functions managing these assets. The functions are `deploy` (token creation), `mint` (token minting) and `transfer` (token transfer). To run this protocol, people must maintain servers that keep track of all the functions. The BRC-20 standard is thus a very poorly optimized use of Bitcoin compared to other token creation protocols such as RGB.

bffaadfd-53ad-4ac6-b6df-8d7dd31bcee8.title: BRANCH-AND-BOUND
bffaadfd-53ad-4ac6-b6df-8d7dd31bcee8.body:
Method used for coin selection in the Bitcoin Core wallet since version 0.17 and invented by Murch. BnB is a search to find a set of UTXOs that matches the exact amount of the outputs to be satisfied in a transaction, in order to minimize the change output and the associated fees. Its goal is to reduce a waste metric that takes into account both the immediate cost and the expected future costs for the change output. This method is more precise in terms of fees compared to earlier heuristics such as the *Knapsack Solver*. *Branch-and-Bound* is inspired by the problem-solving method of the same name, invented in 1960 by Ailsa Land and Alison Harcourt.

*This method is also sometimes called “Murch's Algorithm” in reference to its inventor.*

bffbeb5c-437c-4a34-9a81-4b7664332b5a.title: BITCOIN XT
bffbeb5c-437c-4a34-9a81-4b7664332b5a.body: A Bitcoin fork launched in 2015 by the well-known developer Mike Hearn and supported by Gavin Andresen (former lead maintainer of Bitcoin following Satoshi's departure). Bitcoin XT was originally an implementation of the Bitcoin protocol compatible with Bitcoin Core. However, in August 2015, version 0.11A of Bitcoin XT adopted BIP-0101: a hard fork proposed to increase the block size limit from 1 MB to 8 MB, with a planned increase to double this size every two years until reaching a little over 8 GB per block in 2036. This proposal was one of the casus belli of the Blocksize War that took place between 2015 and 2017. It was supported by a large share of miners, and by influential companies such as BitPay, Blockchain.info and Circle. Ultimately, Bitcoin XT would not manage to obtain enough support from the community, and Mike Hearn would end up announcing his departure from the community and the sale of his bitcoins. He would express his disappointment in a blog post in which he would notably declare that Bitcoin had failed.

c00d630f-37bc-4f81-96b4-0badfa230d0b.title: OP_PUSHDATA4 - 0X4E
c00d630f-37bc-4f81-96b4-0badfa230d0b.body: Makes it possible to push a very large amount of data onto the stack. It is followed by four bytes (little-endian) that indicate the length of the data to push (up to approximately 4.3 GB). This opcode is used to insert very large data into scripts, although its use is extremely rare because of the practical limitations on transaction size.

c0342cb7-6e78-4c9b-8399-45743c6a4428.title: SOLO MINING
c0342cb7-6e78-4c9b-8399-45743c6a4428.body:
A mining practice in which a miner uses their own equipment to search for valid proofs of work autonomously, without joining a mining pool. The solo miner operates their own full node to retrieve pending transactions, build their candidate blocks and attempt to find a hash satisfying the network's difficulty target.

In *solo mining*, the miner keeps the entire block reward when they manage to find a valid block, with no pool fees to pay, and retains full control over the selection of transactions included in their blocks. On the other hand, the probability of finding a block is directly proportional to the miner's hashrate relative to the total hashrate of the network. For an individual miner with a modest hashrate, this probability is extremely low, which makes income very irregular and unpredictable. It is this high variance that motivated the emergence of mining pools, where miners pool their computing power to obtain more frequent and regular payouts.

c0633ecc-f3c1-4de1-9bd8-a92a203a9fba.title: STACKER
c0633ecc-f3c1-4de1-9bd8-a92a203a9fba.body: A term used in the Bitcoin community to describe the act of regularly accumulating sats. It is a long-term savings strategy that consists of buying bitcoin on a recurring basis, regardless of the market price, often through the DCA (*Dollar-Cost Averaging*) method.

c06ceef4-51bf-4777-98c6-180fc4f17790.title: COMMITMENT TRANSACTION
c06ceef4-51bf-4777-98c6-180fc4f17790.body: In the context of a bidirectional channel within Lightning, the commitment transaction is a transaction that both parties create and sign, without however publishing it on the main chain. It represents the current state of the distribution of funds between the parties of a channel, each Lightning payment resulting in a new commitment transaction. These transactions are valid, but are only broadcast when the channel is closed unilaterally. They contain outputs for each party, reflecting the distribution of funds according to the Lightning payments made since the channel was opened. Penalty mechanisms are associated to deter the parties from broadcasting obsolete states of the channel, that is, old commitment transactions that reflect an incorrect distribution of funds.

c0854b23-f72a-4b47-96a1-ea3efc0e2fec.title: SDK - SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT KIT
c0854b23-f72a-4b47-96a1-ea3efc0e2fec.body:
Set of software tools providing the resources developers need to create applications on a specific platform. An SDK includes libraries, development guides, code examples or even build processes. SDKs make development easier and faster by offering reusable modules. On Bitcoin, there are the BDK (*Bitcoin Dev Kit*) and the LDK (*Lightning Dev Kit*).

*In English, SDKs are also sometimes called "devkit".*

c0ae585c-1a11-451c-9324-b4e45792fbb8.title: BULL MARKET
c0ae585c-1a11-451c-9324-b4e45792fbb8.body: Prolonged period during which the price of an asset, such as bitcoin, rises relative to a fiat currency, typically the US dollar. The expression "Bull Run", in a more colloquial register, is often used to refer to this same phenomenon.

c0ce95d5-0641-4b1a-b495-e67d6cc0320f.title: BOLT-03
c0ce95d5-0641-4b1a-b495-e67d6cc0320f.body: Specification that defines the exact formats of the Bitcoin transactions and scripts used in Lightning channels. It details the structure of the funding transaction (2-of-2 multisig P2WSH output), of the commitment transactions (*commitment transactions*) that represent the current state of the channel with their `to_local` and `to_remote` outputs, and of HTLC transactions. BOLT-03 also specifies fee calculation, dust (*dust*) limits, key derivation procedures and the expected transaction weights for a correct fee estimation.

c0e07ffd-6c2a-47e2-9090-265435f2b7bf.title: BIP-0133
c0e07ffd-6c2a-47e2-9090-265435f2b7bf.body: Proposal adding the P2P message `feefilter` to Bitcoin's network protocol. This message allows a node to inform its peers of the minimum fee rate it accepts for transaction relay. When a node receives a `feefilter`, it refrains from sending transactions whose fees are below the indicated threshold. This mechanism reduces bandwidth consumption by avoiding the transmission of transactions that would be rejected anyway by the peer's mempool. BIP-0133 has been deployed and active on the Bitcoin network since version 0.13.0 of Bitcoin Core.

c118d464-1899-4023-b515-8cfd2fa5ec35.title: COLLATERAL
c118d464-1899-4023-b515-8cfd2fa5ec35.body:
Asset given as a guarantee by a borrower to a lender to secure a loan or a financial obligation. In the event of the borrower's default, the lender can seize the collateral to cover their loss. This mechanism reduces counterparty risk and makes it possible to access more favorable borrowing conditions.

In the context of Bitcoin, this term can appear in different situations. Most of the time, it is used in the context of Lombard loans. Entities can thus deposit their bitcoins as collateral to obtain loans in *fiat* currency, which allows them to keep their exposure to bitcoin without having to sell it. It can also make it possible to live off one's bitcoins without selling them, and therefore without triggering a taxable event on capital gains. This type of bitcoin-backed Lombard loan is offered by various platforms.

c12424c1-47db-4e4e-a180-86773ce902d5.title: ZOMBIE CHANNEL
c12424c1-47db-4e4e-a180-86773ce902d5.body: Lightning channel considered inactive, generally because the remote peer has suffered a failure or has not been online for a prolonged period. A *zombie channel* ties up capital without being usable to route payments, which reduces the node operator's available liquidity. This type of channel can also be problematic when attempting to recover a Lightning node via an SCB (*Static Channel Backup*). It is recommended to close these channels when it becomes unlikely that the peer will come back online.

c13d850f-1c37-463c-bcdf-10582aa5b442.title: STEALTH ADDRESS
c13d850f-1c37-463c-bcdf-10582aa5b442.body: A privacy technique that allows a recipient to receive payments on single-use addresses, derived on the fly by the sender, without these addresses being publicly linkable to the recipient's identity. The principle relies on elliptic curve cryptography: the recipient publishes a static public key (the *stealth address*), and each sender generates an ephemeral receiving address by combining this public key with a shared secret derived by ECDH (*Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman*). Only the recipient, thanks to their private key, can identify and spend the funds received on these ephemeral addresses. This approach avoids address reuse. The *stealth address* concept was initially proposed by a BitcoinTalk forum user under the pseudonym "ByteCoin" in 2011, then formalized by Peter Todd in January 2014, and served as a foundation for the creation of the BIP-0047 and *Silent Payments* protocols.

c1417266-bb82-4aec-9d71-84a9020a4384.title: PIZZA DAY
c1417266-bb82-4aec-9d71-84a9020a4384.body: Event celebrated every May 22 by the Bitcoin community that commemorates the first transaction of bitcoins for a physical good. In 2010, Laszlo Hanyecz, a Bitcoin developer, [proposed on the BitcoinTalk forum](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=137.msg1141#msg1141) to buy two large pizzas for 10,000 BTC, then equivalent to about 40 dollars. On May 22, he confirmed that the offer had been accepted by a 19-year-old Californian student, Jeremy Sturdivant, known under the pseudonym Jercos. He ordered the pizzas from Papa John's and had them delivered to Laszlo in Florida. This day marks an important moment for Bitcoin since it demonstrates its potential as a medium of exchange. Every year, the community celebrates this event by eating pizzas paid for in bitcoins.

c154c1f0-dcb8-4c68-9091-9afad9726283.title: BOLTZ
c154c1f0-dcb8-4c68-9091-9afad9726283.body: *Open source* service for performing *submarine swaps* and *atomic swaps* in a *non-custodial* manner between on-chain Bitcoin, the Lightning Network and the Liquid network. Launched in 2019, Boltz uses HTLCs to ensure that exchanges take place in a *trustless* manner, without either party having to trust the other. The service is sometimes integrated directly into wallet applications, in order to make it possible to use Lightning without having a node, while remaining in *self-custody*.

c1574db6-f193-4f77-beb4-cbb3c54b28eb.title: COIN TYPE

c1660c81-b409-4ab8-b7ea-55192d748cf5.title: BIP-0350
c1660c81-b409-4ab8-b7ea-55192d748cf5.body: Introduces Bech32m, a variant of the Bech32 address format (BIP-0173) that fixes a weakness in error detection for SegWit v1 and higher addresses. The original Bech32 format had a flaw: the insertion or deletion of “q” characters just before a final “p” character was not always detected by the checksum. Bech32m solves this problem by modifying the final constant of the *checksum*. SegWit v0 addresses (starting with `bc1q`) keep the original Bech32 format, while v1 and higher addresses (such as `bc1p` for Taproot) use Bech32m.

c177db11-5c60-4f7b-b22a-2f5e644b0572.title: MITM - MAN-IN-THE-MIDDLE
c177db11-5c60-4f7b-b22a-2f5e644b0572.body: An attack in which a malicious actor covertly positions themselves between two communicating parties, in order to intercept and potentially modify the messages exchanged, without the two parties noticing their presence.

c1c5f2b7-28cc-4c95-a858-c0ce3ef4d31d.title: DECENTRALIZATION
c1c5f2b7-28cc-4c95-a858-c0ce3ef4d31d.body:
A principle of organization of a system in which no single entity holds control or authority over its overall operation. A decentralized system relies on a set of independent participants who collaborate according to common rules, with no single point of failure and no need to trust a central third party.

In Bitcoin, decentralization manifests itself at several levels. The network is composed of thousands of nodes spread across the world, each independently verifying transactions and blocks according to the protocol rules. Mining is carried out by many competing actors, and no miner can impose changes on its own. The development of the software is open and collaborative, with no single decision-making authority.

c2040734-7f83-4c0b-92b0-36d5304211ab.title: FOUNDRY USA
c2040734-7f83-4c0b-92b0-36d5304211ab.body: Bitcoin mining pool based in the United States, operated by Foundry Digital, a subsidiary of Digital Currency Group (DCG). Launched in 2020, Foundry USA Pool has become one of the largest mining pools in the world in terms of hashrate, regularly occupying first place. It provides mining services to institutional operators and to large North American mining farms. Foundry also offers financing, hardware purchasing and consulting services for professional miners. Foundry USA's predominance in the distribution of Bitcoin's hashrate raises questions about the geographic centralization of mining, with the majority of its computing power being concentrated in the United States.

c206f0b9-0399-43e7-8b1e-6b9d6897648e.title: YPUB
c206f0b9-0399-43e7-8b1e-6b9d6897648e.body: Extended public key prefix for Nested SegWit accounts on Bitcoin.

c209440f-1f9e-4044-ab66-87ebb3804617.title: ADDR
c209440f-1f9e-4044-ab66-87ebb3804617.body: A network message formerly used on Bitcoin to communicate the addresses of nodes that accept incoming connections. This old format, limited to 128 bits per address, was only suited to IPv6, IPv4, and Tor version 2 addresses. In the face of the arrival of new protocols such as Tor V3 and the need for better extensibility for future network protocols, the `addr` format was superseded by `addrv2`, introduced in BIP-0155.

c247829f-ddfa-40a9-bc50-88a5701d4628.title: BIP-0013
c247829f-ddfa-40a9-bc50-88a5701d4628.body: Presents a standardized method for creating P2SH addresses. BIP-0013 specifies the P2SH address format, which begins with the prefix `3`, and which includes the hash of a script rather than the hash of a public key. This type of address would remain the preferred standard for multisig wallets for a long time.

c2643951-dea0-4c8b-8e49-40cf36218630.title: ACINQ
c2643951-dea0-4c8b-8e49-40cf36218630.body: French company specializing in the development of solutions for the Lightning Network. ACINQ is the originator of Eclair, a major implementation of the Lightning protocol written in Scala. The company also develops Phoenix, a *self-custodial* mobile wallet that integrates a Lightning node directly on the user's phone. ACINQ also operates one of the largest Lightning nodes on the network.

c2692ce0-d5b4-493b-a63d-9b6f104acf01.title: COINJOIN POOL
c2692ce0-d5b4-493b-a63d-9b6f104acf01.body: In the context of coinjoins, a pool is a group of users who agree to mix their UTXOs uniformly in order to break their histories. A coinjoin pool imposes a fixed amount for the participating UTXOs, which guarantees that the inputs and outputs of the coinjoin transactions are identical, and thus prevents a link from being made between them. The more participants there are in a pool, the larger the anonsets the coins can gain there by going through several remix cycles.

c27548c5-dba5-4019-bd64-a30d53b6ae4a.title: BIP-0042
c27548c5-dba5-4019-bd64-a30d53b6ae4a.body: Bitcoin Core improvement proposal that addresses a minor bug in the block reward reduction schedule. This anomaly, if it had not been corrected, would have led to a total creation of bitcoins greater than the intended limit of 21 million. More precisely, after the end of the *halvings*, a new cycle of bitcoin creation could theoretically have been triggered around the year 2214. The Core code in question used a binary right shift operation on the value of the miner's reward. The bug came from using this shift operation in a context where the behavior was undefined according to the C++ language standards. Right-shifting a 64-bit integer (`int64_t`) by more than 63 bits falls into this category of undefined behavior. In the Bitcoin Core code, this could have happened after 64 *halvings*, at block height 13,440,000. Beyond this limit, the behavior of the bit shift was undefined, which means that different compilations could interpret the code differently. This could have led to unpredictable results, including the possibility of creating infinite inflation of bitcoins. BIP-0042 fixed this problem by requiring that the block reward be set to zero after 64 *halvings*, thus avoiding the use of a right shift operation in an undefined-behavior context. This modification, which was a *soft fork*, thus made it possible to clarify the behavior of the Bitcoin Core code. Although entirely serious, this bug fixed by BIP-0042 was not immediately critical, since it would only have manifested around the year 2214. Published on April 1, 2014 by Pieter Wuille, BIP-0042 is thus distinguished by its humorous tone.

c2901a6f-397f-4b80-b7f9-1d25e4eeb4fe.title: BYTE
c2901a6f-397f-4b80-b7f9-1d25e4eeb4fe.body: A unit of computer data measurement equivalent to 8 bits. Each bit is a binary digit (`0` or `1`), which means that a byte can represent 256 (`2^8`) unique combinations.

c2be7598-8cad-4b94-afe4-6bec52482c2e.title: BLOCKCHAIN
c2be7598-8cad-4b94-afe4-6bec52482c2e.body:
The blockchain is the name commonly given to the distributed timestamp server of the Bitcoin system. It is a chain of blocks. Each block is linked to the next by its cryptographic hash. To prevent double spending on Bitcoin without resorting to a central authority, each user must verify the non-existence of a transaction in the system. The only way to ensure the absence of a transaction is to be aware of all past Bitcoin transactions. To this end, transactions are timestamped within blocks, and each user has the entire blockchain.

*Following the many abusive marketing uses of the term “Blockchain”, notably in the late 2010s, many bitcoiners refuse to use this word. Some prefer to speak of “TimeChain” to refer to this concept. Others, referring to Satoshi Nakamoto's White Paper, speak of a “Proof-of-Work Chain”. In French, the English term “Blockchain” is generally accepted. One can also use the translation “chaîne de blocs”.*

c2f2c7b3-50e1-4d83-a9c6-dc87fb35c761.title: BIP-0339
c2f2c7b3-50e1-4d83-a9c6-dc87fb35c761.body: Proposal modifying transaction relay to use the `wtxid` (*witness transaction identifier*) instead of the classic `txid` when announcing and requesting transactions between peers. Before this BIP, a malicious peer could send invalid witnesses (*witnesses*) for a valid `txid`, thus wasting the receiving node's bandwidth. By using the `wtxid`, which incorporates SegWit witness data in its computation, each witness variant has a unique identifier, which prevents this class of denial-of-service attacks. Nodes signal their support via the `wtxidrelay` message exchanged during the version handshake.

c3489abe-3dba-45df-8cc4-36a0d8b2762e.title: TURBO CHANNEL
c3489abe-3dba-45df-8cc4-36a0d8b2762e.body:
Lightning channel usable immediately, without waiting for the usual on-chain confirmations. Normally, a Lightning channel is only considered operational after several confirmations of its funding transaction, which generally means several tens of minutes. A *turbo channel*, also called a *zero-conf* channel, removes this wait: both ends of the channel consider it active as soon as the funding transaction is broadcast in the mempools.

This mechanism involves a trust trade-off: as long as the funding transaction is not confirmed, the party that opened the channel could theoretically carry out a double spend by publishing a competing transaction. In practice, this trust is accepted in a setting where the channel opener is a liquidity service provider (LSP) whose reputation would be destroyed by such fraud. Some implementations strengthen security by requiring that the opening transaction come from a multisignature address with a trusted cosigner.

*Turbo channels* are widely used by mobile embedded nodes such as Phoenix, because they allow new users to send and receive payments as soon as the channel is opened, with an experience closer to that of custodial solutions.

c36d7bef-5012-418c-bc76-073c554c1e5f.title: COMPACT BLOCK FILTERS
c36d7bef-5012-418c-bc76-073c554c1e5f.body:
Mechanism allowing light clients to check whether a block contains transactions concerning them, without downloading the entire blockchain and without revealing their addresses to a third-party node. Unlike the Bloom filters of BIP-0037, where the client sends a filter to a full node (thereby exposing its data), here it is the full nodes that generate deterministic filters for each block. The client downloads them, tests them locally, then retrieves the full blocks only in the event of a match.

The filters are built according to BIP-0158 using *Golomb-Coded Sets* (GCS), a probabilistic structure more compact than Bloom filters. The peer-to-peer distribution protocol is defined in BIP-0157, which introduces dedicated messages (`getcfilters`, `cfilter`, `getcfheaders`...) as well as a system of chained headers making it possible to verify the authenticity of the filters received. A client with at least one honest peer can thus detect any invalid filter.

This mechanism offers better privacy, since blocks can be downloaded from any source, and reduces the computational load imposed on full nodes. In return, the bandwidth consumed in normal operation is higher than that of BIP-0037.

c3c84489-2a3c-4173-96eb-3f6fb9451030.title: NORMAL DERIVATION
c3c84489-2a3c-4173-96eb-3f6fb9451030.body: A process for generating child keys in HD wallets. Normal derivation uses the parent public key as input to the `HMAC-SHA512` function, which makes it possible to generate child public keys from the parent public key and the parent chain code. The process involves concatenating the parent public key and an index lower than `2^{31}`, followed by applying `HMAC-SHA512` with the parent chain code. The result is split into two parts: the first 256 bits are added to the parent private key to obtain the child private key, while the remaining 256 bits form the child chain code. This method ensures that the extended public key can be used to derive the child public keys. In a standard derivation, normal derivation is used at all derivation levels from the account depth onward. In derivation path notations, a normal derivation is identified when there is just the index without any apostrophe `'`.

c41af2fa-d961-4781-9a63-5e1261ecfe5d.title: JAN3
c41af2fa-d961-4781-9a63-5e1261ecfe5d.body: Company founded in 2022 by Samson Mow, former chief strategy officer of Blockstream. The name "JAN3" refers to January 3, 2009, the date on which Satoshi Nakamoto created Bitcoin's genesis block. Jan3 is dedicated to accelerating Bitcoin adoption at the nation-state level, by developing infrastructure based on layers such as the Lightning Network and sidechains such as the Liquid network. The company works in particular with El Salvador and the autonomous region of Madeira to integrate Bitcoin into their financial systems. Jan3 is also active in software development, notably with the Aqua wallet.

c41c8a9d-0141-4559-ac23-7295e954f3e1.title: POLICY - MINISCRIPT
c41c8a9d-0141-4559-ac23-7295e954f3e1.body:
High-level, user-oriented language for simply specifying conditions under which a UTXO can be unlocked within the framework of Miniscript. The *policy* is an abstract description of the spending rules. It can then be compiled into miniscript, which is one-to-one equivalent to operations of Bitcoin's native script language. 

![Miniscript pipeline: the readable policy compiles into miniscript, which is then translated into native Bitcoin script.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/p/policy-miniscript/assets/image-1.png)

The *policy* language is slightly different from the miniscript language. For example, imagine a security system with key A on the primary path, and key B on the recovery path, but under a one-year *timelock* (about 52,560 blocks). In *policy*, this would give:

```plaintext
or(pk(A),and(pk(B),older(52560)))
```

Once compiled into miniscript, it would give: 

```plaintext
andor(pk(B),older(52560),pk(A))
```

And once converted into native script, it would give:

```plaintext
<B>
OP_CHECKSIG
OP_NOTIF
<A>
OP_CHECKSIG
OP_ELSE
<50cd00>
OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY
OP_ENDIF
```

c42a4dc7-6cf2-4464-8898-ec512b10f4e2.title: WEIGHT UNIT - WU
c42a4dc7-6cf2-4464-8898-ec512b10f4e2.body:
Unit of measurement introduced by SegWit (BIP-0141) to quantify the space that a transaction or a block occupies relative to the maximum authorized limit. Each *weight unit* (WU) represents 1/4,000,000th of the maximum capacity of a block. This unit replaces the raw byte measurement that was used before SegWit, and makes it possible to apply a differentiated weighting depending on the nature of the data in a transaction.

The calculation of a transaction's weight rests on a distinction between *non-witness* data (version, inputs, outputs, *locktime*) and *witness* data (signatures, public keys and other proof elements added by SegWit). The formula is as follows:
```math
poids\ =\ taille\ sans\ witness \times 4\ +\ taille\ du\ witness \times 1
```
In other words, each byte of *non-witness* data counts for 4 WU, whereas each byte of *witness* data counts for only 1 WU. For a *legacy* transaction (without SegWit), there is no *witness* data, so the weight is simply 4 times the size in bytes. For example, a standard *legacy* P2PKH transaction of 226 bytes weighs `226 \times 4 = 904` WU.

For an equivalent SegWit transaction (P2WPKH, 1 input, 2 outputs), the total size is approximately 222 bytes, including approximately 110 bytes of *witness* (signature and public key). The weight is then:
```math
112 \times 4 + 110 \times 1 = 448 + 110 = 558\ WU
```
This represents a reduction of approximately 38% compared to the equivalent *legacy* transaction, which makes it possible to include more transactions in a block.

The block limit is set at 4,000,000 WU. If a block contains only *legacy* transactions, this limit is equivalent to the former limit of 1,000,000 bytes (`1\,000\,000 \times 4 = 4\,000\,000`), which ensures backward compatibility with nodes that have not been updated. In practice, with a majority of SegWit transactions, blocks reach approximately 2 to 3 MB in actual size. The theoretical maximum approaches 4 MB, but only in the pathological case of a block filled almost exclusively with *witness* data.

To convert a weight into virtual bytes (*vbytes*), simply divide by 4: `vbytes\ =\ poids\ /\ 4`. Transaction fees are generally expressed in sat/vB (satoshis per *vbyte*).

c45d222b-92e2-4a01-9fef-c7751816da26.title: BITCOIN INQUISITION
c45d222b-92e2-4a01-9fef-c7751816da26.body: Software fork of Bitcoin Core that aims to test the integration of new Bitcoin improvement proposals in a controlled environment on test networks such as a Signet. It includes, for example, support for BIP-0118 (ANYPREVOUT) and BIP-0119 (CHECKTEMPLATEVERIFY). The goal of Bitcoin Inquisition is to experiment, in order to gain a better understanding of the applications, advantages, risks and trade-offs associated with these changes. Bitcoin Inquisition is maintained by Anthony Towns.

c47a5a69-25e3-4600-b1ee-99e7c8ae53d1.title: BURN ADDRESS
c47a5a69-25e3-4600-b1ee-99e7c8ae53d1.body:
Bitcoin address to which funds are sent irreversibly, with no possibility of spending them afterward. No one possesses the corresponding private key: sending bitcoins to such an address amounts to destroying them permanently, unless it one day becomes possible to break the underlying cryptography.

These addresses are generally constructed arbitrarily, without being derived from a private key, so that one can prove one does not know it. The probability that a valid private key corresponds to a randomly chosen address is astronomically low, which makes the funds effectively unrecoverable. For example, there is the address: `1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE`.

Burning bitcoins can serve various purposes. The Counterparty protocol used it in 2014 during its *proof of burn* phase to distribute its own tokens in exchange for destroyed bitcoins. It can also be proof of irreversible commitment in certain cryptographic mechanisms, or simply a playful action.

c4b669f1-0d6c-4206-9537-82282ca1ca24.title: BITVM
c4b669f1-0d6c-4206-9537-82282ca1ca24.body: A protocol introduced by Robin Linus in 2023, which aims to extend Bitcoin's application development capabilities. BitVM makes it possible to perform any computation in an arbitrary way and to use that computation to direct the committed bitcoins. The protocol consists of moving all computation off-chain while allowing the computation to be challenged on-chain if the other party claims a fraudulent result. BitVM thus gives Bitcoin a quasi Turing-complete computing capability, without requiring any change at the consensus level. BitVM reproduces the behavior of a `NAND` logic gate through the joint use of the opcodes `OP_BOOLAND` (which itself reproduces the behavior of a `AND` logic gate) and `OP_NOT` (which reproduces the behavior of a `NOT` logic gate). Indeed, this `NAND` logic gate can be chained to reproduce the behavior of all the other existing logic gates. This is what is called a “universal gate”. By extension, a series of `NAND` logic gates can therefore reproduce any computation circuit. The idea with BitVM is to store these series of `NAND` computations as leaves in the MAST of a Taproot transaction.

c514d1b9-8b58-47d2-a493-18d6e1e90a68.title: BOLT-02
c514d1b9-8b58-47d2-a493-18d6e1e90a68.body: Specification that defines the peer-to-peer protocol for managing Lightning channels. It covers the entire lifecycle of a channel: establishment (in the classic version with a single funder, and in version 2 with dual funding via interactive transaction construction), normal operation (adding and resolving HTLCs, updating commitment transactions) and cooperative closing. BOLT-02 also specifies the mechanisms for increasing fees via RBF, the quiescence (*quiescence*) of the channel for protocol updates, and the message retransmission protocol upon reconnection between peers.

c5465ec6-2f26-45f5-910b-a9dee66a2bd3.title: MEASURE AT THE WALL
c5465ec6-2f26-45f5-910b-a9dee66a2bd3.body: In the mining industry, refers to measuring the actual electrical consumption of an ASIC directly at its connection point, that is, at the wall power outlet. Unlike theoretical specifications, this measurement makes it possible to precisely quantify the energy consumed by the machine, including all losses during actual operation.

c54b2883-1aab-41b8-be01-f87deb67f3a8.title: PREIMAGE
c54b2883-1aab-41b8-be01-f87deb67f3a8.body:
In mathematics, the preimage of an element `y` under a function `f` is the set of all `x` such that `f(x) = y`. It is the operation of inverting the function: going back from the output to the input.

In cryptography, this concept underlies the security of hash functions: preimage resistance requires that, given a hash `h`, it be computationally infeasible to find `m` such that `H(m) = h`. The function `H` acts as a one-way function: easy to compute, nearly impossible to invert.

On Bitcoin, this term comes up whenever hash functions are discussed, but it takes on a more specific meaning on Lightning, where the preimage designates the random secret value whose hash serves as a lock for payments. When a recipient issues an invoice, they generate a 32-byte *preimage*, compute its SHA-256 hash (the *payment hash*) and include it in the invoice. The HTLCs established along the payment route are locked by this hash. The payment is finalized only when the recipient reveals the *preimage* to the node preceding them on the route. That node can then unlock the corresponding HTLC, and the *preimage* propagates in the opposite direction, allowing each intermediate node to claim its funds. The revelation of the *preimage* thus constitutes the cryptographic proof that the payment was indeed received.

c55c028b-acb4-47d1-b9a8-4032bef3ce83.title: LITECOIN
c55c028b-acb4-47d1-b9a8-4032bef3ce83.body: Altcoin created in 2011 by Charlie Lee, a former Google engineer. Litecoin (LTC) is a fork of the Bitcoin source code with a few parameter modifications: a block time reduced to 2.5 minutes instead of 10, a total number of units capped at 84 million (versus 21 million for Bitcoin), and the use of the Scrypt hashing algorithm instead of SHA-256 for proof of work. It has sometimes served as a testing ground for features later adopted by Bitcoin, such as SegWit, which was activated on Litecoin in May 2017, before being activated on Bitcoin in August of the same year.

c59e150d-b83a-4079-b1ab-a721ba56ef13.title: BITCOIN ATM
c59e150d-b83a-4079-b1ab-a721ba56ef13.body: Physical kiosk that allows buying or, in some cases, selling bitcoins in exchange for fiat currency (cash or bank card). Also called BTM (*Bitcoin Teller Machine*), this type of machine offers a direct access point to Bitcoin without going through an online exchange platform.

c59e5503-270d-4ab1-ad72-fe495364d576.title: COINJOIN
c59e5503-270d-4ab1-ad72-fe495364d576.body:
Coinjoin is a technique for breaking the traceability of bitcoins. It relies on a collaborative transaction with a specific structure of the same name: the coinjoin transaction. Coinjoin transactions improve the privacy of Bitcoin users by making transaction analysis more difficult for outside observers. This structure makes it possible to mix several coins into a single transaction, making it difficult to determine the links between input and output addresses.

The general operation of coinjoin is as follows: several users who want to mix each deposit an amount as an input of a transaction. These inputs will come out as several outputs of the same amount. At the exit of the transaction, it is therefore impossible to determine which output belongs to which user. Technically, there is no link between the inputs and the outputs of the coinjoin transaction. The link between each user and each UTXO is broken, in the same way as the history of each coin.

![Coinjoin with five participants: the UTXOs of Alice through Emma form five outputs of 100,000 sats indistinguishable from one another.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/coinjoin/assets/image-1.png)

To allow coinjoin without any user losing control of their funds at any time, the transaction is first built by a coordinator and then passed on to each user. Each of them then signs the transaction on their own side, checking that it suits them, and then all the signatures are added to the transaction. If a user or the coordinator tries to steal the funds of the others by modifying the outputs of the coinjoin transaction, then the signatures will be invalid and the transaction will be rejected by the nodes. When the registration of the participants' outputs is done using Chaum blind signatures to avoid the link with the input, it is called a “*Chaumian coinjoin*”.

This mechanism increases transaction privacy without requiring any changes to the Bitcoin protocol. Specific coinjoin implementations, such as Whirlpool, JoinMarket or Wabisabi, offer solutions to facilitate the coordination process between participants and strengthen the efficiency of the coinjoin transaction. Here is a coinjoin transaction as an example: 

```text
323df21f0b0756f98336437aa3d2fb87e02b59f1946b714a7b09df04d429dec2
```

It is difficult to determine with certainty who first introduced the idea of coinjoin on Bitcoin, and who had the idea of using David Chaum's blind signatures in this context. It is often thought that Gregory Maxwell was the first to mention it in [a message on BitcoinTalk in 2013](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=279249.0):

> *“Using chaum blind signatures: The users connect and provide inputs (and change addresses) and a cryptographically-blinded version of the address they want their private coins to go to; the server signs the tokens and returns them. The users anonymously reconnect, unblind their output addresses, and return them to the server. The server can see that all the outputs were signed by it and so all the outputs had to come from valid participants. Later people reconnect and sign.”*

Maxwell, G. (2013, August 22). *CoinJoin: Bitcoin privacy for the real world*. BitcoinTalk Forum. https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=279249.0

However, there are other earlier mentions, both of Chaum signatures in the context of mixing, and of coinjoins. [In June 2011, Duncan Townsend presents on BitcoinTalk](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=12751.0) a mixer that uses Chaum signatures in a way quite similar to modern Chaumian coinjoins. In the same thread, one can find [a message from hashcoin in response to Duncan Townsend](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=12751.msg315793#msg315793) to improve his mixer. This message presents precisely what most resembles coinjoins. A mention of a similar system can also be found in [a message from Alex Mizrahi in 2012](https://gist.github.com/killerstorm/6f843e1d3ffc38191aebca67d483bd88#file-laundry), when they were advising the creators of Tenebrix. The term “coinjoin” itself was reportedly not invented by Greg Maxwell, but would come from an idea of Peter Todd.

*The term “coinjoin” has no French translation. Some bitcoiners also use the terms “mix”, “mixing” or even “mixage” to refer to the coinjoin transaction. Mixing is rather the process used at the heart of coinjoin. Also, one must not confuse mixing through coinjoins with mixing through a central actor who takes possession of the bitcoins during the process. That has nothing to do with coinjoin, where the user never loses control of their bitcoins during the process.*

c5ad62f5-34ac-4692-aca9-f414370c3f48.title: MOSTRO
c5ad62f5-34ac-4692-aca9-f414370c3f48.body: Peer-to-peer bitcoin exchange protocol without KYC, built on Nostr. Mostro makes it possible to buy and sell bitcoins for fiat currencies via the Lightning Network. The protocol uses Lightning *hold invoices* as an escrow mechanism: the seller's bitcoins are locked in a pending invoice and are only released to the buyer after confirmation that the fiat payment has been received. The use of Nostr as a communication layer makes the system censorship-resistant, unlike centralized solutions. Mostro is written in Rust and is open source.

c5ade0e3-62ac-43d3-85b4-aecc3a8daac5.title: BIP-0080
c5ade0e3-62ac-43d3-85b4-aecc3a8daac5.body: Closed proposal defining a hierarchical deterministic derivation path (BIP-0032) for deterministic multisig wallets used in “*voting pools*” without *colored coins*. A “*voting pool*” is a FIFO-type mechanism for collaboratively managing funds in *cold storage*, where several participants share control of multisig wallets. BIP-0080, a specific application of BIP-0043 based on BIP-0044, defines the path `m / purpose' / coin_type' / series' / address_index` allowing each participant to derive keys in a coordinated manner in order to build the multisig deposit scripts. This highly specialized proposal was never widely adopted by the Bitcoin ecosystem.

c5cae2fe-f24f-4bd2-b9b2-3ae826d7e838.title: OP_BOOLOR - 0X9B
c5cae2fe-f24f-4bd2-b9b2-3ae826d7e838.body: Reproduces the behavior of a logical `OR` gate. It takes two values at the top of the stack and returns `1` if either one of the items or both are non-zero. Otherwise, it returns `0`.

c5e6d0e7-7546-4f70-829b-c3618a56e9b0.title: DKG
c5e6d0e7-7546-4f70-829b-c3618a56e9b0.body: Type of protocol that allows a set of n participants to collectively generate a cryptographic key pair, without relying on a trusted third party and without any participant knowing the complete private key. Each participant obtains a share of the private key, while the common public key is accessible to everyone. The acronym “DKG” stands for *Distributed Key Generation*.

c6064c2d-d424-416c-969d-41f2f64f08a6.title: BIP-0134
c6064c2d-d424-416c-969d-41f2f64f08a6.body: Proposal by Tom Zander (Bitcoin Classic) introducing a new flexible transaction format (“Flexible Transactions”) aiming to solve the transaction malleability problem. BIP-0134 was a direct competitor to SegWit, proposing a different approach based on tag encoding. It was never adopted, the network having activated SegWit (BIP-0141) instead.

c666359c-91f4-40a4-a073-efd7378df6ef.title: BIP-0342
c666359c-91f4-40a4-a073-efd7378df6ef.body: Defines Tapscript, the script language used for spends by script path (*script-path*) in Taproot (BIP-0341). Tapscript brings several changes compared to traditional Bitcoin Script. It replaces `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` and `OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY` with `OP_CHECKSIGADD`, a new opcode that facilitates batch verification of Schnorr signatures. BIP-0342 also introduces the `OP_SUCCESS` opcodes, which reserve ranges of opcodes for future protocol extensions without requiring a complex soft fork. Signature validation relies on the Schnorr scheme defined in BIP-0340. In addition, Tapscript removes the 10,000-byte per-script limit and the limit of 201 non-push opcodes that applied to Legacy scripts, thus offering more flexibility to developers.

c6772aaa-b0b3-4c35-9658-a3ca15b06e85.title: ECDH
c6772aaa-b0b3-4c35-9658-a3ca15b06e85.body: A cryptographic key exchange method built on the principles of the Diffie-Hellman key exchange, but which uses elliptic curves to provide a high level of security with smaller key sizes. This protocol allows two parties to generate a shared secret using their public and private key pairs, without ever having to exchange the private keys themselves. The shared secret can then be used to encrypt subsequent communication. This algorithm is sometimes found in Bitcoin improvement proposals, notably BIP-0047 or BIP-0352 for deriving fresh receiving addresses from a static identifier.

c6775cf9-b4bd-404e-bd93-71dda95b0358.title: DIFFICULTY TARGET
c6775cf9-b4bd-404e-bd93-71dda95b0358.body:
The difficulty factor, also known as the difficulty target, is a parameter used in the proof of work (*Proof of Work*, PoW) consensus mechanism on Bitcoin. The target represents a numerical value that determines how difficult it is for miners to solve a specific cryptographic problem, called proof of work, when creating a new block on the blockchain. 

The difficulty target is an adjustable 256-bit (32-byte) number that sets an acceptability limit for the hash of the block header. In other words, for a block to be valid, the hash of its header with `SHA256d` (double `SHA256`) must be numerically less than or equal to the difficulty target. Proof of work consists of modifying the `nonce` field of the block header or of the coinbase transaction until the resulting hash is lower than the target value. 

This target is adjusted every 2016 blocks (approximately every two weeks), during an event called an "adjustment". The difficulty factor is recalculated based on the time it took to mine the previous 2016 blocks. If the total time is less than two weeks, the difficulty increases by adjusting the target downward. If the total time is greater than two weeks, the difficulty decreases by adjusting the target upward. The goal is to keep the average mining time per block at 10 minutes. This time between each block helps avoid splits in the Bitcoin network, which result in a waste of computing power. The difficulty target is found in each block header, within the `nBits` field. Since this field is reduced to 32 bits and the target is actually 256 bits, the target is compacted into a less precise scientific format.

![Candidate block hashed with SHA256d: the hash is valid if it falls below the target adjusted every 2016 blocks.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/cible-de-difficulte/assets/image-1.png)

*The difficulty target is sometimes also called the "difficulty factor". By extension, it can be referred to through its encoding in block headers with the term "nBits".*

c68550e1-12d0-4d7b-933e-8dfb979a7bd2.title: SATOSHIDICE
c68550e1-12d0-4d7b-933e-8dfb979a7bd2.body:
Bitcoin gambling website, launched in April 2012 by Erik Voorhees. The service operated as a probabilistic dice game: players sent bitcoins to addresses corresponding to different levels of winning probability, and automatically received a payment back according to the result. The site quickly dominated transaction activity on the Bitcoin blockchain. At its peak in 2012 and early 2013, it accounted for nearly half of the transactions recorded on the network.

In July 2013, Erik Voorhees sold the service for 126,315 BTC (approximately 12.4 million dollars at the time). In June 2014, the *Securities and Exchange Commission* (SEC) brought charges against Voorhees for the sale of unregistered securities, related to offerings of shares in SatoshiDice and FeedZeBirds to investors in 2012 and 2013. It is considered one of the first large-scale commercial services on Bitcoin.

c6ddec7a-1524-4409-8156-3de4f0a85887.title: ATLC
c6ddec7a-1524-4409-8156-3de4f0a85887.body: Acronym for "*Anchor Timelock Contracts*". It is a conditional payment used within the Ark protocol to provide an atomic payment schedule to a hub, by means of connectors that make it possible to form what is called a "txlock". The purpose of an ATLC is substantially the same as that of an HTLC on Lightning.

c6e10840-f387-47bf-8d49-24838f141054.title: ORDINAL NUMBER
c6e10840-f387-47bf-8d49-24838f141054.body: Within the Ordinals protocol, it is a unique identifier assigned to each sat according to its mining order. These numbers make these sats non-fungible under the Ordinals protocol, and therefore make it possible to track and transfer these specific sats.

c6e3085c-e793-4dd3-aef6-7357dba80a34.title: DOUBLE SPENDING ATTACK
c6e3085c-e793-4dd3-aef6-7357dba80a34.body:
Attack in which a malicious user attempts to use the same UTXO (*Unspent Transaction Output*) more than once in order to enrich themselves at the expense of the counterparties of the transactions involved. In principle, once a transaction is confirmed in a block and added to the blockchain, the use of those bitcoins is permanently recorded, preventing any later spending of those same bitcoins. Preventing double spending is even the primary purpose of the blockchain. 

In a double spending attack, the attacker first makes a legitimate transaction to a merchant, then creates a second, competing transaction that spends the same coins, either by sending them back to themselves to recover the amount, or by using them to buy another good or service from another merchant. 

Two main scenarios can enable this attack. The first, and the simplest for the attacker, consists of executing the fraudulent transaction before the legitimate transaction is included in a block. To get their fraudulent transaction confirmed first, the attacker attaches to it significantly higher transaction fees than the legitimate transaction. It is a sort of fraudulent RBF. This scenario is only possible if the merchant agrees to finalize the sale with “zeroconf”, that is, with no confirmation at all for the payment transaction. This is why it is strongly recommended to wait for several confirmations before considering a transaction as immutable. The second scenario, much more complex, is that of a 51% attack. If the attacker controls a significant share of the network's computing power, they can mine a chain competing with the one containing the legitimate transaction, but including their fraudulent transaction. Once the merchant has accepted the sale and the attacker has managed to create a longer chain (with more accumulated work) than the legitimate chain, they can then broadcast their fraudulent chain, which will be recognized by the network's nodes as the valid one.

c714d557-16a0-4126-9cc1-6e67b5168c2f.title: OUTPOINT
c714d557-16a0-4126-9cc1-6e67b5168c2f.body:
A unique reference to a transaction output (*output*). It consists of two elements:
* `txid`: the identifier of the transaction that created the output;
* `vout`: the index of the output in the transaction.

The combination of these two elements makes it possible to precisely identify a transaction output. For example, if a transaction has a `txid` of `abc...123` and the output index is `0`, the outpoint will be written:

```text
abc...123:0
```

The outpoint is used in the inputs (`vin`) of a new transaction to indicate which UTXO is being spent.

*The term "outpoint" is often used as a synonym for "UTXO".*

c74d5b45-8034-4cd3-92d9-a57d9c849c30.title: MATURITY PERIOD
c74d5b45-8034-4cd3-92d9-a57d9c849c30.body: The waiting period required before a block reward becomes spendable by the miner who received it. This period is set at 100 blocks following the mined block, i.e. 101 confirmations for the coinbase transaction. During this time, the bitcoins newly created in the block reward are not spendable. The purpose of this rule is to avoid the complications linked to the use of bitcoins coming from a chain that could later be made obsolete. Indeed, valid blocks sometimes end up being invalidated if another block, at the same height, is integrated into a chain benefiting from more work. This phenomenon, called a reorganization, results in the creation of an "orphan block" or "stale block," thus depriving the miner of the bitcoins contained in the coinbase of the abandoned block. If newly created bitcoins were immediately spendable, any transaction involving them could be cancelled after the fact, causing losses for the holders of those bitcoins. Such a scenario could lead to serial cancellations of otherwise valid transactions, thus affecting all users involved in this chain of transactions. The maturity period is therefore a mechanism to prevent this risk. By imposing a delay of 100 blocks before newly issued bitcoins can be used, we prevent coins from blocks that are ultimately invalidated from disrupting the system by circulating and affecting other transactions. The probability of a 101-block reorganization occurring is so low that it is considered nil.

c7eb659d-8283-44ba-aea9-bbb99c0e0f41.title: BIP-0137
c7eb659d-8283-44ba-aea9-bbb99c0e0f41.body: Proposes a standardized format for signing messages with Bitcoin private keys and their associated addresses, in order to prove possession of an address. This BIP aims to resolve the ambiguity related to the different types of Bitcoin addresses (P2PKH, P2SH-P2WPKH, P2WPKH...) when signing a message. It introduces a method making it possible to explicitly distinguish these address formats through the signatures. These signatures are useful for various applications such as proof of funds, auditing, and other uses requiring authentication of an address via its private key. BIP-0322 has since introduced a new signature format that makes it possible to extend this standard and generalize it to any type of script.

c83d2e94-2a77-4fef-b1ce-e9c563d62a79.title: BLIXT WALLET
c83d2e94-2a77-4fef-b1ce-e9c563d62a79.body: *Open source* and *non-custodial* Lightning wallet for Android and iOS. Blixt embeds an LND node directly on the user's phone, thanks to Neutrino.

c83d8215-fff1-4940-8aa6-26993cf494de.title: SIDECAR TICKET
c83d8215-fff1-4940-8aa6-26993cf494de.body: Token allowing the beneficiary of a *sidecar channel* purchased on Lightning Pool to claim the opening of the channel. When a participant in a Pool auction buys a channel for a third party (for example a mobile wallet), they generate a *sidecar ticket* containing the information needed for the opening. The beneficiary presents this ticket so that the seller opens the channel directly to them. This mechanism allows users who do not directly participate in Pool auctions to benefit from inbound liquidity.

c84e350d-9afb-4716-b0c5-800f42070fb3.title: UTREEXO

c896b0a5-6317-4187-8603-56d65d02feea.title: BIP-0100
c896b0a5-6317-4187-8603-56d65d02feea.body: Proposal by Jeff Garzik during the Blocksize War allowing miners to vote to dynamically adjust the maximum block size between 1 and 32 MB. The mechanism relied on a vote per block, where miners expressed their preference for an increase or a decrease of the limit. This BIP-0100 was rejected, the community having ultimately opted for SegWit rather than a direct increase in block size.

c89cc132-125a-4dce-88f7-265ac5e50021.title: VERSIONING
c89cc132-125a-4dce-88f7-265ac5e50021.body: In the context of Bitcoin, designates the process of assigning specific versions to various elements of the protocol, in order to facilitate their tracking, management and updating. Versions are numbered sequentially, making it possible to identify the changes made, new features or bug fixes. For example, each block of the blockchain contains a version number, indicating the consensus rules and data structures applied when it was created. Versioning exists for script types, for transactions, for blocks, for the Bitcoin Core software, for network communications...

c8ba8e24-016c-430f-a4ac-903603a45551.title: REPOSITORY / REPO
c8ba8e24-016c-430f-a4ac-903603a45551.body: A central data structure used in Git where a project's versioning information is stored. A repository contains the complete history of all changes, branches and tags. Each repository is an independent collection of files and folders, accompanied by a history of commits, enabling collaboration and tracking of changes over time. For example, the Bitcoin Core repository is stored on GitHub here: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin.

c8d36eaa-8bcb-46b7-aa75-25c89d84eefc.title: CONNECTOR
c8d36eaa-8bcb-46b7-aa75-25c89d84eefc.body:
Special output created in the round transaction of the Ark protocol to guarantee atomicity between the surrender of the old VTXOs (via the *forfeit transactions*) and the creation of the new ones. Without this mechanism, a user signing a forfeit transaction would hand over control of their VTXO to the ASP with no assurance that the round will succeed and that new VTXOs will be created.

Concretely, the round transaction generates, in addition to the tree containing the output VTXOs, a second covenant tree with one leaf per input VTXO. These leaves are the *connector outputs*. They carry no significant economic value, but serve as a cryptographic link: by including a connector output as an input in a forfeit transaction, the latter becomes valid only if the round transaction is confirmed on-chain. If the round fails, the forfeit transaction is invalid and the user keeps their original VTXO. This mechanism ensures that the two operations (forfeit and creation) are inseparable.

c8dfd10b-05df-415f-8348-30264dfd867b.title: SPREAD - WST
c8dfd10b-05df-415f-8348-30264dfd867b.body:
In the Whirlpool Stat Tool software, the spread is an indicator for measuring the homogeneity of the mixing process from the point of view of a given coin. Two spreads are distinguished: the prospective one and the retrospective one.

The prospective spread is calculated as the ratio between the prospective anonset of your coin and the total number of coins created after your Tx0. For example, if there are 100 coins in your pool and your coin has an anonset of 70, the prospective spread of your coin is then 70%. 

The retrospective spread, for its part, is the ratio between the retrospective anonset of your coin and the total number of Tx0s created before the last mix of your coin. Thus, if the retrospective anonset of your coin is 95 and there were 100 Tx0s before your last mix, then the retrospective spread of your coin is 95%.

These two indicators make it possible to evaluate the effectiveness of your coin's mixing relative to the potential offered by the pool. A low prospective spread, such as 5% for example, indicates a large margin for possible improvement through additional mixes. Conversely, a high prospective spread, such as 97% for example, means that little additional anonset can be gained with additional coinjoins.

c9108dfb-a248-42dc-9f46-80e97c0592f4.title: PROTON WALLET
c9108dfb-a248-42dc-9f46-80e97c0592f4.body: An open source Bitcoin wallet in *self-custody* developed by Proton, the Swiss company known for its privacy-focused services. Available as a web and mobile application, it is linked to a Proton account. Its distinctive feature is sending bitcoins via the recipient's email address: Proton automatically generates a fresh Bitcoin address associated with the recipient's wallet.

c92c41f2-7db3-43e3-aa2c-61a440716a3e.title: CHANNEL LEASE
c92c41f2-7db3-43e3-aa2c-61a440716a3e.body: A contract to open a Lightning channel for a fixed duration, negotiated via the Lightning Pool platform. A liquidity buyer (*taker*) pays a premium to a seller (*maker*) so that the latter opens a channel of a defined capacity and duration, expressed in number of blocks. The seller commits to keeping the channel open for the entire duration of the lease.

c9753626-0b70-474e-800e-e503b9e1c6ff.title: BIP-0011
c9753626-0b70-474e-800e-e503b9e1c6ff.body:
BIP introduced by Gavin Andresen in 2011 that proposes a standard method for creating multisignature transactions on Bitcoin. This proposal improves the security of bitcoins by requiring multiple signatures to validate a transaction. BIP-0011 introduces a new script type, named “M-of-N multisig”, where `M` represents the minimum number of signatures required among `N` potential public keys. This standard exploits the opcode `OP_CHECKMULTISIG`, already existing in Bitcoin, but which previously did not comply with the nodes' standardness rules. Although this type of script is no longer commonly used for real multisig wallets, in favor of P2SH or P2WSH, its use remains possible. It is notably used in meta-protocols such as Stamps. Nodes can however choose not to relay these P2MS transactions with the parameter `permitbaremultisig=0`.

*Nowadays, this standard is known under the name “bare-multisig” or “P2MS”.*

c98e67ee-23c9-4768-8e48-8194aa20c541.title: DEPEG
c98e67ee-23c9-4768-8e48-8194aa20c541.body: Refers to the situation where the value of a digital asset, typically an IOU, becomes detached from the underlying asset to which it is normally pegged, thus causing price fluctuations relative to that asset. This phenomenon is particularly observed with *stablecoins*, designed to maintain a strict parity with fiat currencies or other reference assets. A *depeg* can also occur in the case of representations of bitcoins on *sidechains* or ETFs, where, in the event of a problem, the nominal value can diverge from that of bitcoin.

c9ba79fa-2634-47a2-bb36-62fa930975bf.title: RISC ZERO
c9ba79fa-2634-47a2-bb36-62fa930975bf.body: A company and open source framework specializing in the creation of general-purpose zero-knowledge proofs. RISC Zero provides a zkVM (*zero-knowledge virtual machine*) based on the RISC-V instruction set architecture, making it possible to execute arbitrary code written in common languages (Rust, C, C++) and to cryptographically prove the validity of its execution. The prover generates STARK proofs, which are then wrapped in SNARK proofs via a Groth16 circuit to reduce their size and make on-chain verification easier. Citrea uses RISC Zero's infrastructure to build its Type 2 zkEVM, which allows it to prove the validity of each batch of transactions executed on the rollup. RISC Zero also offers Boundless, a decentralized network of provers that makes it possible to outsource proof generation.

c9bbca4b-b417-4c78-82db-62b9ffff043b.title: BIP-0044

c9c750bc-7a5a-4ea4-998d-90462fda54ca.title: CHAINALYSIS
c9c750bc-7a5a-4ea4-998d-90462fda54ca.body: An American company founded in 2014, specializing in blockchain analysis and the tracing of cryptocurrency transactions. Chainalysis provides software and services to governments, law enforcement, financial institutions and exchange platforms to detect and track the flow of funds on public blockchains, notably Bitcoin's. Its tools make it possible to track funds and to identify links between transactions and real-world entities. To do so, Chainalysis exploits chain analysis heuristics.

c9cf3f68-6ddc-49f2-998d-0b11219e5b5b.title: OP_CAT - 0X7E

c9eea020-0114-4689-a5a4-9b27d3cfb006.title: LIQUIDITY ADS
c9eea020-0114-4689-a5a4-9b27d3cfb006.body: Mechanism of the Lightning Network protocol that allows node operators to advertise their willingness to provide inbound liquidity in exchange for compensation. A node that has funds can publish an offer on the network, specifying the amount of liquidity it is willing to allocate, the duration of the commitment, and the fee requested. When another node needs inbound capacity to receive payments, it can accept this offer and open a channel funded by the liquidity provider. This system creates an open and decentralized market for liquidity on Lightning, which solves a recurring problem for new nodes that cannot receive payments without inbound capacity. *Liquidity ads* have been formalized in the Lightning protocol specification, notably through the message `node_announcement` which allows nodes to advertise their offers, and the *dual funding* protocol (`open_channel2`) which allows the channel opening to be negotiated. This system makes it possible to automate the negotiation between the parties without a trusted intermediary.

ca4afe58-72e3-43ca-b4a1-8e2da3ca2f6d.title: BITCOIN CORE GUI-QML
ca4afe58-72e3-43ca-b4a1-8e2da3ca2f6d.body:
Project underway to create a Bitcoin wallet and node application built on Bitcoin Core, but with an intuitive graphical interface developed using QML (*Qt Modeling Language*). The goal of Bitcoin Core GUI-QML is to modernize the Bitcoin Core user interface to offer a simpler, smoother and more dynamic experience. 

The traditional Bitcoin Core interface is mainly developed in C++ with Qt Widgets, which is a system that produces very classic user interfaces. This new project now relies on QML, which is a declarative language used to design GUIs with animations, transitions and a more responsive and stylized interface. This will allow Core to move closer to modern application interfaces with rich interactions. The goal is for this software to be available on both PC and mobile.

ca4db974-f81c-4549-9ffb-4a97bd2832a2.title: CHAINWAY LABS
ca4db974-f81c-4549-9ffb-4a97bd2832a2.body: The company behind the development of Citrea, the first ZK rollup deployed on Bitcoin. Founded with the goal of building infrastructure solutions for Bitcoin, Chainway Labs specializes in zero-knowledge proof technologies applied to the Bitcoin ecosystem. The team notably develops Citrea and its bidirectional bridge Clementine, based on BitVM. All the code produced by Chainway Labs is open source, published under the GitHub account `chainwayxyz`.

ca5ac0f5-9195-41ba-b6dc-bfc0fc6f4f00.title: ZEROLINK
ca5ac0f5-9195-41ba-b6dc-bfc0fc6f4f00.body: Chaumian coinjoin protocol that aims to break all links between sets of separate coins through advanced mixing techniques. The ZeroLink protocol stands out for its ability to protect users' anonymity against various forms of chain analysis at the transaction and network level. ZeroLink introduces a framework for coinjoin wallets, with the use of segregated pre-mix and post-mix accounts, as well as a mixing technique of its own: the Chaumian coinjoin. The two main implementations of ZeroLink have been Wasabi Wallet (version 1.0) and Whirlpool, available on Samourai Wallet and Sparrow Wallet. This protocol [was introduced by nopara73 and TDevD in 2017](https://github.com/nopara73/ZeroLink/blob/master/README.md).

ca7ad011-0bf8-4b20-ad10-a94cf422d118.title: BIP-0123

cb1d6f65-174e-4427-8af6-b9d0dc839512.title: VPRV
cb1d6f65-174e-4427-8af6-b9d0dc839512.body: Extended private key prefix for SegWit V0 accounts on Bitcoin Testnet.

cb7935a4-0ffd-4f11-b754-36de6cfbd9ae.title: OP_GREATERTHANOREQUAL - 0XA2
cb7935a4-0ffd-4f11-b754-36de6cfbd9ae.body: Compares the two items at the top of the stack and checks whether the second item is greater than or equal to the first. If the second item is greater than or equal to the first, it pushes `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise, it pushes `0` (false).

cbace699-79b8-4a87-a2ec-ee8552ff143e.title: BIP-0048
cbace699-79b8-4a87-a2ec-ee8552ff143e.body:
Proposal defining the derivation path for multisignature wallets supporting several script types:

```
m/48'/coin_type'/account'/script_type'
```

The `script_type'` level makes it possible to distinguish the address format used: `1'` for P2SH-P2WSH and `2'` for native P2WSH. This structure allows a single hardware wallet to manage several multisig configurations with different script formats, while maintaining a clear separation between each of them. BIP-0048 is widely adopted in the software and hardware ecosystem. It is currently the de facto standard for key derivation in multisignature wallets.

cbd4c934-50ef-4b9f-ae93-8a5a7afe14f9.title: BLINK
cbd4c934-50ef-4b9f-ae93-8a5a7afe14f9.body: A custodial mobile Bitcoin wallet, formerly known as “Bitcoin Beach Wallet”. Developed by Galoy, it was originally created for the Bitcoin Beach community of El Zonte in El Salvador. It allows you to manage balances in BTC and USD (via Stablesats), and to send or receive Lightning and on-chain payments.

cbe0ba52-1ef9-431d-95c6-0ad9525ab1fa.title: ESPLORA
cbe0ba52-1ef9-431d-95c6-0ad9525ab1fa.body: *Open source* block explorer developed by Blockstream and publicly accessible at `blockstream.info`. The interface takes the form of a single-page web application (*SPA*) that consumes the HTTP API provided by *esplora-electrs*, a modified version of *Electrs* in Rust that indexes the blockchain from a Bitcoin Core node. The tool also supports Liquid and Elements-based chains, with handling of confidential transactions and *peg-in/peg-out* operations.

cc1092b3-394e-43c4-a299-a982d3304062.title: MEMPOOL POLICY
cc1092b3-394e-43c4-a299-a982d3304062.body:
Subset of transaction relay policy that groups together the set of rules applied by a Bitcoin node to determine which unconfirmed transactions it accepts into its mempool. Mempool policy encompasses the standardness rules, but extends beyond them by including rules that take into account the context of the mempool as a whole, and not only the format of individual transactions.

For example, the rules relating to the minimum relay fee rate (`minRelayTxFee`), the maximum size of the mempool (`maxmempool`), or the transaction replacement rules (RBF) fall under mempool policy. These rules are configured locally by each node and may vary from one node to another.

Mempool policy is distinguished from standardness rules in that the latter concern only the format of a transaction taken in isolation, whereas mempool policy takes into account contextual factors such as mempool congestion, relationships between transactions, or the fee thresholds configured by the node operator.

cc35e0dc-b3e8-4f01-a1e8-33fbe2f44c7a.title: OP_1ADD - 0X8B
cc35e0dc-b3e8-4f01-a1e8-33fbe2f44c7a.body: Adds `1` to the value at the top of the stack.

cc5153da-5757-46a2-84d3-2923bca407fb.title: OCEAN
cc5153da-5757-46a2-84d3-2923bca407fb.body: A Bitcoin mining pool launched in November 2023 by Luke Dashjr, a long-time developer of Bitcoin Core and Bitcoin Knots. Ocean stands out for its approach focused on decentralizing mining: miners can select or build their own block *templates*, which reduces dependence on centralized pool operators. The pool uses the TIDES payout system (*Transparent Index of Distinct Extended Shares*), which rewards miners directly through the outputs of *coinbase* transactions. The project continues the work of Eligius, the mining pool that Luke Dashjr had launched in 2011.

cc674cd1-8220-4080-9107-fd92c305394c.title: BASE58CHECK
cc674cd1-8220-4080-9107-fd92c305394c.body:
The `Base58Check` is an encoding used in the Bitcoin system to represent Legacy receiving addresses and certain other data, such as extended keys, as human-readable strings of characters. It is a variant of the `Base58` system, a base 58 positional representation designed to minimize human transcription errors. It uses a set of 58 alphanumeric characters, made up of the digits from `1` to `9`, the uppercase letters from `A` to `Z` (except the letters `I` and `O` to avoid confusion with the digits `1` and `0`) and the lowercase letters from `a` to `z` (except the letter `l` to avoid confusion with the digit `1`). The `Base58Check` differs from the `Base58` by the addition of a checksum (*checksum*). It is represented by a shortened version of a double hash `SHA256` of the original data (`SHA256d` or `HASH256`), of which only the first 4 bytes are kept. This checksum is concatenated to the end of that same data, still in binary format, and the resulting whole is then encoded in `Base58`. During verification, the checksum is recalculated and compared with the one that was added during encoding. If the two fingerprints match, the data is considered valid; otherwise, a corruption or transcription error is reported. 

Using `Base58Check` in Bitcoin addresses and keys provides several advantages. First, it reduces human errors during transcription and reading by avoiding ambiguous characters. Second, it protects against input errors by detecting and reporting them thanks to the *checksum*. Third, the compact representation of data in `Base58Check` reduces the space required to store and share addresses and keys. The most recent receiving addresses (post-SegWit) have abandoned this `Base58Check` encoding in favor of `Bech32` and `Bech32m` encodings, which have a more advanced checksum (with BCH codes).

cc78de7f-4a95-405e-9f8e-09a352ce3ac7.title: BIP-0012
cc78de7f-4a95-405e-9f8e-09a352ce3ac7.body: Proposal by Gavin Andresen to improve the flexibility and privacy of Bitcoin transaction scripts. This BIP proposes to implement a new script opcode, named `OP_EVAL`, which makes it possible to evaluate a script contained in the data of a `scriptSig` during the transaction validation process. The main modification of BIP-0012 is to allow the inclusion of a script inside another script. This technique allows the creation of more complex conditions that can be verified at spending time, without needing to reveal them to the users who send bitcoins to the address used. BIP-0012 was later replaced by other, safer proposals, notably BIP-0016 (P2SH), which offers a different method to achieve the same objectives as `OP_EVAL`.

ccd2e351-a6c8-4af7-a928-5ea70af064eb.title: MINISKETCH
ccd2e351-a6c8-4af7-a928-5ea70af064eb.body:
A set reconciliation library (*set reconciliation*) developed mainly by Pieter Wuille (sipa). Minisketch implements an algorithm that allows two peers in a peer-to-peer network to efficiently determine which elements one has that the other does not, without each having to transmit the complete list of its elements.

The principle relies on sketches (*sketches*): each peer computes a compact representation of its set of elements, whose size depends on the number of expected differences and not on the total size of the sets. By exchanging these sketches, the two peers can identify the missing elements on each side and transmit only those. This mechanism considerably reduces the bandwidth consumed by broadcast protocols (*gossip*).

Minisketch is the fundamental technical building block of Erlay, a proposal to improve transaction relay on the Bitcoin network. Currently, each node announces each transaction to all its peers, which generates significant redundancy. With Erlay, nodes would only announce transactions to a small number of peers, then use reconciliation via Minisketch to synchronize their mempools with the others. This approach could reduce the bandwidth used for transaction announcement by about 84%, and overall bandwidth consumption by about 40%.

cd0c8e19-e3ea-4e07-b42a-34de86984dfa.title: BLOCKSTREAM
cd0c8e19-e3ea-4e07-b42a-34de86984dfa.body: Company specializing in the development of solutions around Bitcoin. Blockstream is behind the Liquid sidechain, the Core Lightning implementation of the Lightning Network, and the Jade and Green wallets. It is also known for employing Bitcoin Core developers. The company Blockstream is currently led by the cypherpunk and cryptographer Adam Back, the inventor of Hashcash, the protocol that inspired the proof of work on Bitcoin.

cd227863-8cee-47e4-bb0b-a48d2e5f596c.title: FIAT
