cd227863-8cee-47e4-bb0b-a48d2e5f596c.body:
Currency, often state-issued, whose exchange value is imposed by public force.

*The term "fiat" is sometimes translated as "fiduciaire" although the latter term does not capture the dimension of legitimate violence that the term "fiat" embodies. In French, it is often accepted to use the English term "fiat" directly.*

cd275407-be3f-45c1-85eb-b8c33835a7f2.title: ZBD
cd275407-be3f-45c1-85eb-b8c33835a7f2.body: Company founded in 2019 specializing in integrating Lightning payments into the video game industry. Formerly known as Zebedee, it provides APIs and SDKs that allow game developers to integrate transactions in sats and that give players the ability to earn and spend real bitcoins in virtual worlds. ZBD also offers a mobile application that acts as a Lightning wallet dedicated to gaming, as well as a streaming payments infrastructure.

cd48975a-d743-4215-9225-1f4784bbe0ec.title: NETWORK EFFECT
cd48975a-d743-4215-9225-1f4784bbe0ec.body:
An economic phenomenon in which the value or utility of a product or service increases as the number of its users grows. The more participants a network has, the more attractive it becomes to new users, creating a virtuous circle of adoption. This concept is closely related to Metcalfe's law.

The network effect is fundamental to understanding money: a currency has value only because other people accept it. The greater the number of people who accept a currency, the more useful that currency is as a medium of exchange. This mechanism explains the natural tendency toward a single monetary standard within an economy.

cd889805-d323-4410-a76c-ff88820171ad.title: ZEUS
cd889805-d323-4410-a76c-ff88820171ad.body: Open source mobile application that allows managing a Lightning Network node from a phone. Zeus can operate in two modes: remote connection to an existing Lightning node (LND, Core Lightning or Eclair), or use of a Lightning node integrated directly into the application thanks to an embedded LND implementation. Zeus makes it possible to send and receive Lightning and on-chain payments, manage one's payment channels, view the status of one's node and configure routing fees.

cda5df8c-50b1-4876-9625-9cf8713b1748.title: BIP-0325
cda5df8c-50b1-4876-9625-9cf8713b1748.body: Proposal defining Signets, test networks for Bitcoin in which block production is controlled by a set of authorized signers, in addition to proof of work. Unlike the classic testnet, where anyone can mine and cause unpredictable reorganizations, blocks on Signet must contain a valid signature issued by designated keys. This makes the network stable, predictable and suited to application development and testing. The default signet is maintained by Kalle Alm and AJ Towns. It is possible to create custom signets with your own signing keys.

cdc2973c-3096-4f6e-ad86-584259de56e9.title: OP_NEGATE - 0X8F
cdc2973c-3096-4f6e-ad86-584259de56e9.body: Reverses the sign of the top element of the stack. If the value is positive, it becomes negative, and vice versa.

cdcbdc03-81fa-4f39-a51f-467b6c79cbeb.title: TX0
cdcbdc03-81fa-4f39-a51f-467b6c79cbeb.body:
Preparatory transaction specific to the Whirlpool protocol, which constitutes the first step before the coinjoin cycles. The Tx0 takes one or more UTXOs from the user's wallet and restructures them into several outputs calibrated to match exactly the amounts of the chosen coinjoin pool, in addition to the mining fees for the first cycle.

Concretely, the Tx0 produces several types of outputs: UTXOs of a fixed amount intended to enter the coinjoin cycles (which will go into the premix account), an output for the coordinator's fees, and possibly a change output (the "*doxxic change*") which corresponds to the excess that cannot be integrated into the pool.

cddd7a63-8d9c-4ca1-a782-3ce020275816.title: NESTED SEGWIT
cddd7a63-8d9c-4ca1-a782-3ce020275816.body: A script standard used to wrap native SegWit scripts within a P2SH script. Nested SegWit scripts were invented at the launch of SegWit to facilitate its adoption. They make it possible to use this new standard even with services or *wallets* that are not yet natively compatible with SegWit. It is a sort of transitional script toward the new standard. Today, it is therefore no longer very relevant to use this type of *wrapped* SegWit script, since most *wallets* have implemented native SegWit.

cdfc675f-8e81-4730-9da6-f374df1f46de.title: BEHIND-THE-METER
cdfc675f-8e81-4730-9da6-f374df1f46de.body: In the context of Bitcoin mining, refers to electricity that is produced and distributed directly to a farm, without going through the public grid.

ce1964cb-ef67-49c0-ba06-62a45dd67e91.title: BLIP-0003
ce1964cb-ef67-49c0-ba06-62a45dd67e91.body: A bLIP that formalizes the specification of *keysend*, a spontaneous payment mechanism on the Lightning Network. With *keysend*, the sender generates a random 32-byte preimage, includes it in a TLV record (type `5482373484`) of the onion packet and uses its SHA-256 hash as the payment hash. The recipient verifies the match between the preimage and the hash to validate the payment. *Keysend* should eventually be replaced by more complete mechanisms such as BOLT-12 offers.

ce80ff4c-2ee8-4a97-ba4c-0ef0206be35e.title: PAPER WALLET
ce80ff4c-2ee8-4a97-ba4c-0ef0206be35e.body: Offline storage method that consists of printing or writing down a pair of cryptographic keys giving access to bitcoins on paper (or possibly another physical medium) only. Paper wallets are considered a cold storage method, because they are not connected to the internet, provided they were produced manually and not printed. Their security then relies on the physical protection of the paper against loss, destruction, and theft. They are now often considered obsolete, because they offer a weaker security model than modern solutions. Moreover, their use often involves reusing the same public key, which is very problematic for the user's privacy.

ceba18be-da61-4cdb-ad9a-5affc3bb7c7f.title: BARE-MULTISIG
ceba18be-da61-4cdb-ad9a-5affc3bb7c7f.body: Standard P2MS script template used to set spending conditions on a UTXO. It makes it possible to lock bitcoins with several public keys. To spend these bitcoins, a signature must be provided with a predefined number of the associated private keys. For example, a P2MS `2/3` has `3` public keys with `3` associated secret private keys. To spend the bitcoins locked with this P2MS script, a signature must be made with at least `2` of the `3` private keys. It is a threshold security system (*threshold*). This script was standardized in 2011 by Gavin Andresen, with the publication of BIP-0011, when he had just taken over maintenance of the main Bitcoin client. The opcode `OP_CHECKMULTISIG`, on which it relies, already existed in Bitcoin's original source code, but scripts that used it were not standard before this proposal. Today, P2MS is only marginally used by some applications. The vast majority of modern multisignatures use other script templates such as P2SH, P2WSH or P2TR. Compared with these, P2MS is extremely rudimentary. The public keys that make it up are revealed as soon as the transaction is received. Using a P2MS is also more expensive than using other multisignature scripts.

ceff9344-d739-4eae-ae39-9a47b0a0b35e.title: BITCOIN BEACH
ceff9344-d739-4eae-ae39-9a47b0a0b35e.body:
Community initiative launched in the village of El Zonte, on the Pacific coast of El Salvador, which transformed this small town into the first circular economy running on Bitcoin. The project was born in 2019 thanks to a donation from an anonymous bitcoiner, with the aim of proving that Bitcoin could concretely improve the daily lives of people excluded from the traditional banking system.

Bitcoin Beach allowed residents to pay their bills (water, electricity, phone), their groceries or even the hairdresser directly in bitcoins via the Lightning Network. The wallet developed for the project, initially called "Bitcoin Beach Wallet", was later renamed "Blink".

The El Zonte experiment played an important role in El Salvador's decision to adopt Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021, making the country the first state to take this step. The model has since inspired similar initiatives in other countries, notably Bitcoin Jungle in Costa Rica.

cf3a3c43-ce13-4796-9e3c-86153f727b35.title: CPU - CENTRAL PROCESSING UNIT
cf3a3c43-ce13-4796-9e3c-86153f727b35.body: Main component of a computer responsible for executing the machine instructions of software. In the context of Bitcoin, the CPU was initially used for mining by nodes before being surpassed by mining with GPUs (graphics cards), and then by the use of specialized chips called "ASICs".

cf636265-0f74-495f-b7b6-e59afdec3855.title: BLIP-0001
cf636265-0f74-495f-b7b6-e59afdec3855.body: The first bLIP, which establishes the process for creating and managing bLIPs (*Bitcoin Lightning Improvement Proposals*). It defines the lifecycle of a proposal: submission of a draft, review by the editors for technical soundness and formatting, then progression through the *Draft*, *Proposed* and *Final*/*Active* statuses. bLIP-0001 clarifies the distinction with BOLTs: bLIPs cover application features and non-universal extensions, while BOLTs remain reserved for protocol changes requiring adoption by all implementations.

cf685eea-f224-4ffd-b0e7-e5228e6f1705.title: SATODIME
cf685eea-f224-4ffd-b0e7-e5228e6f1705.body: Bearer NFC card developed by Satochip, a Belgian company. The Satodime supports up to three independent "vaults" for storing bitcoins. The private keys are generated and sealed in an EAL6+ certified secure chip and are only revealed at the moment of unsealing, which means that physical possession of the card is equivalent to ownership of the funds.

cf8665d5-e90a-4ead-b203-50e128b5a85e.title: STRATUM V2
cf8665d5-e90a-4ead-b203-50e128b5a85e.body: An evolution of Stratum, the well-known network protocol layered on top of Bitcoin designed for mining. This type of protocol is designed to optimize communication between individual miners and mining pool servers in order to increase their profitability. Developed by the Braiins pool (formerly "Slush Pool"), Stratum V2 introduces several improvements, notably more efficient communication between miners and mining pools, thereby reducing the bandwidth required. It also reduces infrastructure needs for pools. In terms of security, it adds cryptographic authentication in order to prevent various man-in-the-middle attacks, notably eavesdropping and malicious hashrate redirection. An important aspect of Stratum V2 is that it includes sub-protocols allowing individual miners to choose their own sets of transactions to include in the blocks they work on. This feature gives more power to individual miners, unlike the original protocol where pools had full control over the *block template*. This method would thus strengthen the decentralization of the mining process by pools.

cf93019b-5e0a-4887-9021-13f56abce4cf.title: MIT X11
cf93019b-5e0a-4887-9021-13f56abce4cf.body: A very permissive free software license that allows users to copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell the software. It only requires that the original license and copyright notices be retained in all copies or substantial distributions of the software. Unlike the GPL license, the MIT license does not require that adaptations or derivative versions of the software be distributed under the same license. This flexibility makes the MIT X11 license a popular choice for many *open source* projects, including in the Bitcoin environment. Satoshi Nakamoto, moreover, chose this license for the first version of Bitcoin published in 2009, and it remains in use for the Bitcoin Core project today.

cf9dd495-1b21-4a15-9a09-e030c1dd1705.title: P2MS
cf9dd495-1b21-4a15-9a09-e030c1dd1705.body:
P2MS is the acronym for *Pay to Multisig* (meaning “pay to multiple signatures”). It is a standard script template used to set spending conditions on a UTXO. It allows bitcoins to be locked using several public keys. To spend these bitcoins, a signature must be provided with a predefined number of the associated private keys. For example, a `P2MS 2/3` has `3` public keys with `3` associated secret private keys. To spend the bitcoins locked with this P2MS script, a signature must be made with at least `2` of the `3` private keys. It is a threshold (*threshold*) security system.

This script was standardized in 2011 by Gavin Andresen, with the publication of BIP-0011, when he had just taken over maintenance of Bitcoin's main client. The opcode `OP_CHECKMULTISIG`, on which it relies, already existed in Bitcoin's original source code, but scripts that used it were not standard before this proposal. Today, P2MS is only marginally used by some applications. The vast majority of modern multisignatures use other scripts such as P2SH, P2WSH or P2TR. Compared to these, P2MS is extremely trivial. The public keys that make it up are revealed as soon as the transaction is received. Using a P2MS is also more expensive than the other multisignature scripts.

*P2MS scripts are often called “bare-multisig”, which can be translated as “naked multisignatures”, or “raw multisignatures”. In early 2023, P2MS scripts were at the center of a controversy because of their misuse within the Stamps protocol. Their impact on the UTXO set was notably singled out.*

cfa14188-eafb-4413-9e39-0d4aa83e1896.title: OBOE - OFF-BY-ONE ERROR
cfa14188-eafb-4413-9e39-0d4aa83e1896.body:
A logic error where a loop iterates one time too many or one too few, often due to incorrect use of comparison operators or wrong indices when handling data structures. Two notable instances of this bug exist in Bitcoin.

The more consequential one is found in the difficulty adjustment calculation. The algorithm measures the time elapsed during a period of 2016 blocks by comparing the timestamp of the first block of the period with that of the last, then compares this duration with the target time of `1\,209\,600` seconds (`2016 \times 600`). The problem is that the difference between the first and the last block of a period covers only 2015 block intervals, not 2016:
```math
T = t_{2015} - t_0
```
The intervals counted are:
```math
\underbrace{[t_0 \to t_1]}_{1},\ \underbrace{[t_1 \to t_2]}_{2},\ \ldots,\ \underbrace{[t_{2014} \to t_{2015}]}_{2015}
```
That is 2015 intervals. To obtain 2016, the last block of the previous period would have had to be used as the starting point:
```math
T_{correct}\ =\ t_{2015}\ -\ t_{-1}
```
Where `t_{-1}` denotes the timestamp of the last block of the previous period (block `n - 1` for a period that begins at block `n`). The algorithm therefore compares 2015 actual intervals with the theoretical time of 2016 intervals. This offset introduces a bias of approximately `\frac{1}{2016} \approx 0{,}05\,\%` toward a slightly overestimated difficulty.

The main consequence of this bug is that retarget periods do not overlap: the timestamp of the last block of one period does not enter into the calculation of the next period. This discontinuity makes the *time warp* attack possible, in which a majority attacker manipulates the timestamp of the last block of a period without it affecting the calculation of the following period. Truly fixing this bug would require a hard fork, but *time warp* attacks can be prevented through a simple soft fork by adding constraints on timestamps.

The second instance of an *off-by-one* bug in Bitcoin is the *dummy element* in `OP_CHECKMULTISIG`, where the opcode consumes an extra stack element by mistake. This bug was effectively fixed by BIP-0147 (*NULLDUMMY*), which requires this element to be a null value.

d007d392-ba8d-431c-8efb-0d2049a1a122.title: DYNAFED - DYNAMIC FEDERATIONS
d007d392-ba8d-431c-8efb-0d2049a1a122.body: Governance mechanism deployed on the Liquid network that makes it possible to change the composition of the federation of functionaries without interrupting the operation of the network. Before the introduction of Dynamic Federations (DynaFed), any change to the list of block signers or watchmen (*watchmen*) required manual coordination and a network interruption. DynaFed was activated on Liquid in October 2021 through a *hard fork*.

d008b909-b41b-4a5e-8131-7f5a099dfe09.title: SIGNET
d008b909-b41b-4a5e-8131-7f5a099dfe09.body: Specific versions of the Bitcoin network designed for development and testing. Signets simulate the behavior of the main network (*mainnet*) but with the ability to control various parameters. They thus provide an environment to test new features or modifications without risking disrupting the main network and without incurring its fees. Compared to *testnet*, signets offer more structured control over block generation, often managed by one or more trusted entities or by a custom consensus mechanism. This makes it possible to create more predictable test scenarios, compared to *testnet*, which is subject to the vagaries of mining, in the same way as *mainnet*.

d01a0cf2-c1c3-4ff1-bcba-0b43a140d3d2.title: LUCK
d01a0cf2-c1c3-4ff1-bcba-0b43a140d3d2.body:
Metric used in mining pools to measure a pool's performance relative to its theoretical expectations. As its name indicates, it evaluates how lucky the pool is at finding a block. Luck is calculated by comparing the number of shares theoretically required to find a valid block, based on Bitcoin's current difficulty, with the actual number of shares produced to find that block. A number of shares lower than expected indicates good luck, whereas a higher number indicates bad luck.

By relating Bitcoin's difficulty to the number of shares it produces each second and the difficulty of each share, the pool can calculate the number of shares that are theoretically required to find a valid block. For example, suppose that theoretically, 100,000 shares are needed for a pool to find a block. If the pool actually produces 200,000 before finding a block, its luck is 50%:

```text
100 000 / 200 000 = 0.5 = 50 %
```

Conversely, if this pool found a valid block after producing only 50,000 shares, then its luck is 200%:

```text
100 000 / 50 000 = 2 = 200 %
```

Luck is a metric that can only be updated after the pool discovers a block, which makes it a static metric that is updated periodically.

d03605f7-1bac-401b-9a8e-1c4609bda158.title: BIP-0089
d03605f7-1bac-401b-9a8e-1c4609bda158.body: Proposal (draft) describing *Chain Code Delegation* (CCD), a mechanism for multisignature wallets in which a privileged participant (the “delegatee”) holds back the BIP-0032 chain codes of one or more unprivileged participants (the “delegators”), and provides them with per-input scalar adjustments (*tweaks*) at signing time. Delegators hold only a simple key pair (no extended key) and therefore can neither derive other addresses of the wallet, nor observe the balance or spending activity of the other combinations of co-signers. This BIP is particularly useful in collaborative custody setups where the wallet owner wishes to keep their balance private from their co-signer or *custodian*. BIP-0089 supports two signing modes: a non-blinded mode, where the delegator sees the transaction they are signing, and a blinded mode (*blinded*), where they see neither the message nor the child public key used.

d04a1f81-d497-4094-ad4c-4e28dc28cba7.title: THIERS' LAW
d04a1f81-d497-4094-ad4c-4e28dc28cba7.body:
Economic principle that is the inverse of Gresham's law, according to which “good money drives out bad”. Formalized in 1989 by the economist Peter Bernholz in reference to the writings of the French historian Adolphe Thiers on the hyperinflation of the revolutionary assignats, this law describes a spontaneous market mechanism. When a currency deteriorates to the point of losing the confidence of economic agents, they end up refusing it in favor of a currency perceived as more reliable, despite legal constraints.

Thiers' law is mainly observed in situations of hyperinflation. When a national currency collapses, the laws imposing its legal tender status become ineffective: merchants demand to be paid in foreign currencies or in tangible goods. Historical examples include Zimbabwe, where the US dollar replaced the Zimbabwean dollar during its dollarization in 2009, or Weimar Germany, where the mark collapsed in 1923 to the point that trade was conducted in foreign currencies or by barter.

Some bitcoiners invoke Thiers' law to argue that Bitcoin could gradually establish itself as a medium of exchange in economies where the national currency is heavily depreciated, thus going beyond its sole role as a store of value.

d0d66201-bbc4-4539-9205-3ddc98768810.title: TUMBLEBIT
d0d66201-bbc4-4539-9205-3ddc98768810.body: Concept of an anonymous payment hub compatible with Bitcoin proposed in 2016 by Ethan Heilman, Leen AlShenibr, Foteini Baldimtsi, Alessandra Scafuro and Sharon Goldberg. TumbleBit is a bitcoin mixing system that does not require trust in an intermediary. It allows users to make fast, anonymous, off-chain payments via a coordinator called the *Tumbler*. TumbleBit guarantees anonymity by ensuring that even the *Tumbler* cannot link a payer's payment to its recipient. The TumbleBit protocol ensures that the *Tumbler* can neither steal bitcoins nor print fake bitcoins by issuing payments to itself. The anonymity offered by TumbleBit is comparable to that of a Chaum *eCash* system. However, this concept was never widely adopted, as privacy techniques such as the Chaumian coinjoin were preferred to it.

d0eb74f6-c28b-400e-865c-8e205c2425c7.title: CYPHERPUNKS
d0eb74f6-c28b-400e-865c-8e205c2425c7.body:
Informal, international community of people promoting the use of cryptography as a means of ensuring individual freedoms on the Internet. Cypherpunks defend the fundamental right of the individual to protect their privacy, particularly in a context of increasing state surveillance and data exploitation by private entities. Their name comes from the English words *cypher*, "cipher" (in the sense of secret code), and *punk*. It is a calque of the term *cyberpunk*, which designates a literary genre describing a dystopian future where cutting-edge technology is married to the vice and crime of a decaying society.

The cypherpunk movement dates back to the early 1990s, when groups of cryptographers, programmers, and libertarians began discussing the political implications of cryptography during their first meetings in Silicon Valley. The main figure in the community was Tim May, who had written the *Crypto Anarchist Manifesto* in 1988, a founding text of the movement. Among the key moments in cypherpunk history is the founding, in 1992, of the "Cypherpunks mailing list", an email distribution list that served for these discussions. The publication by Eric Hughes in 1993 of *A Cypherpunk's Manifesto*, a document setting out the goals and actions of cypherpunks, was also an important moment.

The idea of an electronic currency that is not based on a central entity, like Bitcoin, is rooted in the philosophy of the cypherpunks. The creation of Bitcoin is often considered a major achievement of this vision, alongside PGP, Tor, and WikiLeaks.

d100a604-1b22-446d-872f-2dd642d6c81f.title: BULL RUN
d100a604-1b22-446d-872f-2dd642d6c81f.body: Prolonged period during which the price of an asset, such as bitcoin, increases relative to a fiat currency, most often the US dollar. The expression "Bull Run" refers to the same phenomenon as "Bull Market", but in a more colloquial register.

d14a7db6-3a49-4c0d-8300-a0b917e5833a.title: CONSENSUS CLEANUP
d14a7db6-3a49-4c0d-8300-a0b917e5833a.body:
Soft fork proposal (BIP-0054) grouping together several fixes for old vulnerabilities in Bitcoin's consensus rules. Rather than deploying one soft fork per bug, the “Consensus Cleanup” bundles them to share the fixed cost of a consensus change. The proposal, led by Antoine Poinsot and Matt Corallo, targets four distinct problems.

First, the *time warp* attack: by manipulating timestamps at the boundaries of difficulty adjustment periods, a majority attacker can artificially and unfairly reduce the difficulty to its minimum in a few periods. The fix requires that the first block of a period have a timestamp at most 2 hours before that of the previous block, and that the last block have a timestamp at least equal to that of the first (no negative period in time).

Second, block validation time: specifically crafted blocks can take more than an hour to validate on modest hardware. A limit of 2,500 potentially executed signature operations per transaction reduces the worst case by a factor of 40.

Third, the weakness of the Merkle tree: a 64-byte transaction can be confused with an intermediate node of the tree, making it possible to forge inclusion proofs. These transactions are now invalid.

Fourth, the duplication of coinbase transactions: some blocks prior to BIP-0034 contain a valid height commitment for a future block, which could create duplicates starting from block 1,983,702. Requiring a `nLockTime` equal to the height minus one in coinbases permanently eliminates the need for BIP-0030 validation. This BIP currently has “Draft” status.

d1af921f-2a71-4f7a-a6ae-ee425e64b289.title: CONSOLIDATION
d1af921f-2a71-4f7a-a6ae-ee425e64b289.body:
Specific transaction in which several small UTXOs are merged as inputs to form a single, larger UTXO as output. This operation is a transaction made to one's own wallet. The goal of consolidation is to take advantage of periods when fees on the Bitcoin network are low to merge several small UTXOs into a single one that is larger in value. In this way, one anticipates mandatory spending in case fees rise, which saves on future transaction fees. 

Indeed, transactions with many inputs are heavier and, consequently, more expensive. Besides the savings that can be made on transaction fees, consolidation is also a form of long-term planning. If your wallet contains very small UTXOs, these can become unusable if the Bitcoin network enters a prolonged period of high fees. For example, if you need to spend a 10,000 sats UTXO but the minimum mining fees amount to 15,000 sats, spending it would exceed the value of the UTXO itself. These small UTXOs then become economically irrational to use and remain unusable as long as fees do not fall. These UTXOs are commonly called “*dust*”. By regularly consolidating your small UTXOs, you reduce this risk associated with fee increases.

However, it is important to note that consolidation transactions are recognizable in chain analysis. Such a transaction indicates a CIOH (*Common Input Ownership Heuristic*), meaning that the inputs of the consolidation transaction are owned by a single entity. This may have privacy implications for the user.

![Consolidation transaction: five small UTXOs merged as inputs to form a single UTXO of 550,000 sats as output.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/consolidation/assets/image-1.png)

d1db2a05-5a20-431e-b425-3c06b6b578f6.title: OP_TUCK - 0X7D
d1db2a05-5a20-431e-b425-3c06b6b578f6.body:
Copies the element at the top of the stack and inserts it between the second element and the third element of the stack. For example, if the stack is:

```text
A
B
C
D
```

`OP_TUCK` will duplicate the top `A` and place it in third position. The resulting stack will be:

```text
A
B
A
C
D
```

d1f05b25-df3d-4075-afcc-7cc4699b1c5c.title: OP_SUCCESS
d1f05b25-df3d-4075-afcc-7cc4699b1c5c.body:
The `OP_SUCCESS` represent a series of opcodes that were disabled in the past and are now reserved for future use in Tapscript. Their ultimate purpose is to facilitate upgrades and extensions of the script language, by allowing the introduction of new features via soft forks. When one of these opcodes is encountered in a script, it causes the immediate and unconditional success of the entire script, regardless of the data or conditions present. Execution does not continue: the script is directly considered valid. 

Thus, when a new opcode is added to an `OP_SUCCESS`, this necessarily represents the addition of a rule that is more restrictive than the previous rule. Up-to-date nodes can then verify compliance with this rule, and nodes that are not up to date will not reject the associated transactions and the blocks that include them, because the `OP_SUCCESS` validates this part of the script. There is therefore no hard fork. 

In comparison, the `OP_NOP` (*No Operation*) also serve as placeholders in the script, but they have no effect on script execution. When a `OP_NOP` is encountered, the script simply continues without modifying the state of the stack or the course of the script. The key difference therefore lies in their impact on execution: `OP_SUCCESS` causes the immediate success of the entire script, whereas `OP_NOP` is neutral, and affects neither the stack nor the flow of the script. These opcodes are designated by `OP_SUCCESSN` where `N` is a number that makes it possible to differentiate the `OP_SUCCESS`.

d1fc8770-ba12-45e5-98f7-f2514c2ca0d9.title: HYDRO COOLING
d1fc8770-ba12-45e5-98f7-f2514c2ca0d9.body: A cooling system for ASICs that uses a closed loop in which water circulates through cooling blocks, pipes, then a radiator. The goal is to extract heat from the components and maintain a good temperature for their operation.

d244b4a8-ac64-4124-9c84-7bd154909ad9.title: MULTI PROTOCOL COMMITMENT
d244b4a8-ac64-4124-9c84-7bd154909ad9.body: In the RGB protocol, the MPC refers to the Merkle tree structure designed to embed, within a single Bitcoin transaction, several *Transition Bundles* from distinct contracts. This mechanism makes it possible to group various commitments, which correspond to different contracts or assets, into a single anchor point. By consolidating these transitions in a hierarchical structure, the MPC optimizes block space usage, in order to reduce transaction fees and improve the efficiency of blockchain use.

d2535c2b-6dee-4052-b5d7-f32bedbfde9d.title: FROSTSNAP
d2535c2b-6dee-4052-b5d7-f32bedbfde9d.body: Frostsnap is a security system for bitcoins based on the FROST protocol (*Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold Signatures*). Unlike classic multisig using Bitcoin script, FROST produces a single *on-chain* Schnorr signature, indistinguishable from a single-signature transaction, which improves privacy and reduces transaction fees. The Frostsnap team, made up notably of Nick Farrow and Lloyd Fournier, is developing dedicated hardware devices that connect in a chain via USB-C. The system makes it possible to add or remove signers after key generation, without changing the public address. The hardware and software are entirely *open source* under the MIT license.

d26600df-84f3-4dbf-8b3d-5822dd19f949.title: ENCRYPT - ENCRYPTION
d26600df-84f3-4dbf-8b3d-5822dd19f949.body: A cryptographic method for converting raw information into encrypted information. Encrypted information hides the original meaning of the data to prevent it from being known. Encryption consists of a series of transformations performed on the original information using a key. If these transformations are reversible, the corresponding inverse process is called "decryption", and it makes it possible to restore the information to its raw state.

d26d38ab-3eab-422d-b8dd-e3ff7fbc1521.title: ECASH - XEC
d26d38ab-3eab-422d-b8dd-e3ff7fbc1521.body: A cryptocurrency system, previously known as Bitcoin Cash ABC (BCHA), resulting from a hard fork of Bitcoin Cash (BCH). The eCash fork occurred on November 15, 2020 at block 661,648, resulting from a conflict within the Bitcoin Cash community.

d2d99060-3757-428b-ac6d-a18cd5e800bd.title: BITCOIN-DEV
d2d99060-3757-428b-ac6d-a18cd5e800bd.body:
An email mailing list dedicated to the development of the Bitcoin protocol. Bitcoin-dev was created by Jeff Garzik in 2011 and initially hosted on Sourceforge.net. The mailing list was later moved to the Linux Foundation, then to Open Source Lab, and finally, since February 2024, it has been hosted on Google Groups: https://groups.google.com/g/bitcoindev

This mailing list is a meeting point for developers and researchers involved in the evolution of Bitcoin. Discussions there are strictly technical or academic. It is notably here that drafts of BIPs (Bitcoin Improvement Proposals) must be sent, before possibly being integrated into the BIPs GitHub repository. Its moderators are currently Ruben Somsen, Bryan Bishop and Warren Togami.

Participation in this list is open to all contributors, but it is mainly aimed at those with technical expertise in the field of Bitcoin. If you wish to receive these exchanges by email, you can subscribe to this mailing list. If you would rather have a summary of these discussions, you can also subscribe to the Bitcoin Optech newsletter: https://bitcoinops.org/en/newsletters/

d2fb1930-f9b3-47f3-867b-527ba1a24d33.title: ALBY HUB
d2fb1930-f9b3-47f3-867b-527ba1a24d33.body: Open-source application that lets you run a personal Lightning Network node and connect it to various applications via the Nostr Wallet Connect (NWC) protocol. Alby Hub is installed on a personal server, a computer, or in the cloud, and serves as a control center for the user's Lightning payments. Alby Hub is non-custodial: the user keeps their private keys and full control of their funds. It uses an LDK (*Lightning Development Kit*) implementation to manage the Lightning node.

d3155ae4-d8fb-40fa-94d0-c6eada07659f.title: BIP-0337
d3155ae4-d8fb-40fa-94d0-c6eada07659f.body: Proposal of a compression format for Bitcoin transactions, significantly reducing their size by omitting data that is redundant or deducible from context.

d3247e42-55d4-49a1-83d6-86f39be83163.title: BLOCK-RELAY-ONLY
d3247e42-55d4-49a1-83d6-86f39be83163.body:
Type of outbound connection in Bitcoin Core that only relays blocks, without exchanging transactions or node addresses. Since version 0.19.0 (November 2019), each node establishes 2 *block-relay-only* connections by default in addition to its 8 regular outbound connections.

These connections strengthen resistance to network partitioning and protection against eclipse attacks, because they increase the node's connectivity without revealing information about the network topology. Indeed, transactions and addresses are the main vectors through which an adversary can map the links between nodes. The absence of these exchanges makes *block-relay-only* connections invisible to a spy analyzing transaction propagation. They thus guarantee the node access to the legitimate blockchain even if all of its regular connections are compromised.

d3291108-dd07-4932-843b-d2ae65a4e34f.title: SE - SPARK ENTITY
d3291108-dd07-4932-843b-d2ae65a4e34f.body:
Group of operators responsible for managing shared keys and signing operations within the Spark protocol. The SE collectively holds one half of the spending key associated with the UTXOs locked in Spark, the other half being held by the user. During a transfer on Spark, the SE participates in the renewal of the key shares: it destroys its share associated with the previous owner and generates a new one with the recipient, which makes the old share cryptographically unusable.

The SE is not a single entity but a set of independent *Spark Operators* (SO) that cooperate via a threshold signature protocol, based on Schnorr signatures. No individual operator possesses the complete key. The security model relies on a 1-of-n assumption: it is enough for a single SO to be honest to prevent any collusion with a previous owner. Trust is only required at the time of the transfer: once the old keys are destroyed, the operators can no longer affect the funds, even if they are compromised later.

d332c8d7-5475-45ca-89d4-cf750ce2385b.title: TAPSCRIPT
d332c8d7-5475-45ca-89d4-cf750ce2385b.body:
An update whose purpose is to modify certain opcodes of Bitcoin's classic scripting language, in order to define the new scripting language used for P2TR spends via the script path (*script path*). Tapscript was introduced by BIP-0342, implemented with the Taproot soft fork.

In order to implement the various changes associated with Taproot, it proved necessary to revisit the scripting language. That is the purpose of Tapscript, which disables or modifies certain opcodes, and adds new ones.

d34497aa-4b7c-4af1-85a5-cbf2a932818d.title: PEG-IN
d34497aa-4b7c-4af1-85a5-cbf2a932818d.body:
Mechanism by which the value of bitcoins is transferred from the main blockchain to a sidechain. The process consists of locking BTC on the main chain by sending them to a special address managed by a trusted third party or a group, or to a script that makes them temporarily unusable, and then issuing an equivalent quantity of tokens on the sidechain. This locking guarantees that the bitcoins cannot be spent simultaneously on both chains. Once the peg-in is done, the user can make use of the features specific to the sidechain. The peg-in is the first step of the two-way peg (*two-way peg*) that links the main chain to the sidechain.

As an individual, it is generally not necessary to use a peg-in, since there are *atomic swap* systems that make it possible to exchange *onchain* bitcoins for bitcoins on Liquid (or on another sidechain, as applicable).

d3575fcd-307e-4fe0-b10c-e1c791700ca7.title: VANITY ADDRESS
d3575fcd-307e-4fe0-b10c-e1c791700ca7.body: A custom receiving address that contains a specific sequence of characters chosen by the user, generally for aesthetic reasons. These addresses are generated by running a computational process, in which many private keys are created until one of them corresponds to a receiving address containing the desired sequence. This process does not compromise the security of the address, but it can require considerable computing time and resources, especially for longer or more specific sequences. It is a kind of *brute force* process.

d39ccdd1-24d3-4516-a077-bde3508aa1c7.title: SIGHASH FLAG

d3b546c8-0c98-413f-bf30-8bc3fb91e573.title: VAULT
d3b546c8-0c98-413f-bf30-8bc3fb91e573.body:
An advanced security mechanism for holding bitcoins, based on a two-step spending process that imposes a delay between the announcement of a withdrawal and its actual execution. In the first transaction, the user signals their intention to move the funds. A waiting period then elapses, during which the legitimate owner can detect any theft attempt and redirect the funds to a secure recovery address ("*clawback*"). If no intervention takes place, a second transaction finalizes the transfer.

Several technical approaches have been proposed to implement vaults. The first relies on presigned transactions: the spending transactions are signed in advance, then the signing keys are destroyed in order to guarantee that only the predefined paths remain usable. This method requires no modification of the protocol, but it demands rigorous management of key destruction. The second approach, more elegant, relies on covenants, that is, constraints applied directly in scripts to limit the way a UTXO can be spent. The proposal `OP_VAULT`, formalized in BIP-0345, introduces dedicated opcodes (`OP_VAULT` and `OP_VAULT_RECOVER`) that considerably simplify the construction of vaults at the consensus level, but this proposal was abandoned in favor of `OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY`, which is more general-purpose.

Vaults are particularly suited to institutional cold storage, where security takes precedence over speed of access to the funds.

d3caf2d7-84cc-479b-b829-02c32d22ddf8.title: BIP-0443
d3caf2d7-84cc-479b-b829-02c32d22ddf8.body: BIP written by Salvatore Ingala that proposes the addition of `OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY` (CCV), a general-purpose opcode for implementing covenants on Bitcoin. CCV makes it possible to verify that a transaction output respects a contract defined by a combination of a hash and data embedded in the Taproot public key through the *tweaking* mechanism. Unlike previous proposals targeting a specific use case, CCV offers a flexible framework that can serve multiple constructions: vaults with a recovery mechanism, improved Lightning channels, payment pools, and other protocols requiring introspection of transaction outputs.

d3d501f0-d106-42b6-8024-14a5468e9681.title: SMART CONTRACT
d3d501f0-d106-42b6-8024-14a5468e9681.body:
Program that executes automatically when certain predefined conditions are met. A smart contract is thus a set of clauses between several parties that can be fulfilled without requiring the intervention of a trusted third party. These contracts generally trigger specific actions such as a transfer of bitcoins.

*In French, the term “contrat autonome” is also sometimes used.*

d3fc35ff-180c-41a8-839c-381a57a2f174.title: RBF - REPLACE-BY-FEE
d3fc35ff-180c-41a8-839c-381a57a2f174.body:
A transactional mechanism that allows the sender to replace a transaction with another one with a higher fee, in order to speed up its confirmation. If a transaction with a fee that is too low remains stuck, the sender can use *Replace-By-Fee* to increase the fee and prioritize their replacement transaction in the mempools. 

RBF is applicable as long as the transaction is in the mempools; once it is in a block, it can no longer be replaced. When initially sending, the transaction must specify that it is available to be replaced by setting the value of `nSequence` to a value lower than `0xfffffffe`. This is what is called an RBF "flag". This parameter signals the possibility of updating the transaction after it has been broadcast, which subsequently makes it possible to perform an RBF. However, it is sometimes possible to replace a transaction that has not signaled RBF. Nodes using the configuration parameter `mempoolfullrbf=1` accept this replacement even if RBF was not initially signaled.

Unlike CPFP (*Child Pays For Parent*), where it is the recipient who can act to speed up the transaction, RBF (*Replace-By-Fee*) allows the sender to take the initiative to speed up their own transaction by increasing the fee.

d4100bb7-ead9-4d95-8ddb-2412719325f3.title: COIN CONTROL
d4100bb7-ead9-4d95-8ddb-2412719325f3.body:
Feature found in some Bitcoin wallet software, which gives users the ability to manually select the specific UTXOs to use as inputs to make a transaction. In other words, coin control offers the possibility of choosing precisely which pieces of bitcoins will be spent. This feature is similar to the action of choosing a specific coin from your wallet to pay for your baguette. 

Coin control is particularly useful for managing your transaction fees and for improving your privacy. Indeed, by specifically selecting the UTXOs to consume, users can avoid merging UTXOs from different sources, which could reveal information about all of their funds (CIOH). This feature often goes hand in hand with the ability to label transaction outputs.

d4195790-4784-4e8c-9649-064f20766d9d.title: DISCRETE LOGARITHM
d4195790-4784-4e8c-9649-064f20766d9d.body:
The discrete logarithm is a mathematical problem that is used in certain public-key cryptographic algorithms. In a cyclic group of order `q`, with a generator `g`, if we have an equation of the form `g^x = h`, then `x` is called the discrete logarithm of `h` with respect to the base `g`, modulo `q`. In simple terms, it involves determining the exponent `x` when `g`, `h`, and `q` are known. The discrete logarithm is therefore the inverse of exponentiation in a finite cyclic group. However, for large values of `q`, solving the discrete logarithm problem is considered algorithmically hard. This property is exploited to ensure the security of many cryptographic protocols, such as the Diffie-Hellman protocol for key exchange. 

The discrete logarithm is also used in elliptic curve cryptography (ECC), among others in the ECDSA algorithm (*Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm*). In the context of elliptic curves, the discrete logarithm problem extends to finding a scalar `k` such that `k \cdot G = K`, where `G` and `K` are points on the curve, and `\cdot` represents the point multiplication operation. In the context of Bitcoin, scripts can use either ECDSA or the Schnorr protocol in order to lock UTXOs. They both rely on the infeasibility of computing the discrete logarithm.

d4432b81-1d4b-443e-ad2f-30b7c7aa515e.title: GREEN WALLET
d4432b81-1d4b-443e-ad2f-30b7c7aa515e.body: Bitcoin wallet software available on PC, Android and iOS, developed by Blockstream since the acquisition of the GreenAddress software in 2016. It includes several features such as multisig protection with two-factor authentication. It is also compatible with most hardware wallets. It is simple software to get to grips with and can be used by beginners.

d44e149a-79f9-4ae1-9b88-133798b7a380.title: FEE RATE - BITCOIN
d44e149a-79f9-4ae1-9b88-133798b7a380.body:
Measure of the unit cost of the fees of a Bitcoin transaction, expressed in satoshis per virtual byte (sat/vB). The *fee rate* determines the priority of a transaction in the mempool: the higher the rate, the more miners are incentivized to include it quickly in a block. The absolute amount of fees corresponds to the difference between the total of the inputs and the total of the outputs of a transaction. The *fee rate* is obtained by dividing this amount by the weight of the transaction:
```math
fee\ rate\ (sats/vB) = \frac{frais\ (sats)}{poids\ (vB)}
```
This rate is freely chosen by the issuer of the transaction and works as an auction mechanism. During periods of congestion, the minimum *fee rate* for a transaction to be included in a block increases.

d46c6972-591f-4b70-95d8-fa7e9584fd0e.title: KEYNESIANISM
d46c6972-591f-4b70-95d8-fa7e9584fd0e.body:
School of economic thought based on the work of the British economist John Maynard Keynes. Keynesianism advocates active state intervention in the economy to stabilize economic cycles. Keynesian policies rely on the ability of central banks to adjust the money supply and interest rates, as well as on the ability of governments to borrow and spend. This theoretical framework largely dominates contemporary economic policy.

In the Bitcoin community, Keynesianism is often criticized. Bitcoiners, who are generally close to the Austrian school, criticize it for encouraging monetary expansion, distorting price signals through the manipulation of interest rates, promoting malinvestment, and generating growing public debt. Bitcoin, with its fixed supply and the impossibility of manipulating it monetarily, is fundamentally incompatible with Keynesian monetary policy tools.

d4857dab-1e59-424a-8e4d-8053d34b85ae.title: CONTRACT STATE

d491965e-9cd1-4bd5-9c97-3c6a5e04b142.title: OP_SWAP - 0X7C
d491965e-9cd1-4bd5-9c97-3c6a5e04b142.body: Swaps the top two elements of the stack. The element that was at the top is moved to second position, and the element that was in second position is placed at the top of the stack.

d4e1458f-9eac-462c-926a-fa98fea825b0.title: TRANSACTION FINALITY
d4e1458f-9eac-462c-926a-fa98fea825b0.body: Concept that designates the moment from which a transaction is considered irreversible and permanently recorded in the blockchain. On Bitcoin, finality is probabilistic rather than absolute: each new block added on top of the block containing the transaction makes reversing it exponentially more difficult and costly. By convention, a transaction is generally considered final after 6 confirmations, or about one hour, because the probability that an attacker could reorganize the chain, or that a natural fork would reach such a depth, is extremely low. However, for modest amounts, one or two confirmations may be deemed sufficient.

d4f54026-f93e-4a4c-9fc9-4aa546a1dbd3.title: DARKWALLET
d4f54026-f93e-4a4c-9fc9-4aa546a1dbd3.body: A privacy-focused Bitcoin wallet software launched by Amir Taaki and Cody Wilson in 2014, running as an extension for the Google Chrome browser. DarkWallet had features to improve the privacy of Bitcoin users, such as stealth payments and *coinjoins*. Its development has been abandoned since January 2015.

d52a8910-78e2-42e2-82d0-3844ce5b202e.title: MS-SMT
d52a8910-78e2-42e2-82d0-3844ce5b202e.body: The *Merkle Sum Sparse Merkle Tree* (MS-SMT) is a data structure combining the properties of a *Sparse Merkle Tree* (SMT) and a *Merkle Sum Tree*. It makes it possible both to produce proofs of inclusion and non-inclusion (thanks to its “sparse” nature, where each leaf has a position determined by the hash of its key), and to verify the conservation of sums (thanks to the propagation of values in each node up to the root). In the Taproot Assets protocol, the MS-SMT is used to commit assets to the Bitcoin blockchain: its root is embedded in a tapscript of a Taproot transaction. This structure guarantees that it is possible to prove that an asset exists, that an asset does not exist, and that the total of issued assets is consistent, preventing any unauthorized inflation.

d535f3a7-5368-47f3-aca2-500ce9decd2b.title: SCID - SHORT CHANNEL ID
d535f3a7-5368-47f3-aca2-500ce9decd2b.body:
Compact identifier used on the Lightning Network to uniquely reference a payment channel. Rather than using the public keys of the two nodes or the full txid of the funding transaction, the SCID encodes the exact position of the channel in the blockchain in a condensed format.

The SCID is made up of three elements concatenated over 8 bytes: the number of the block containing the funding transaction (3 bytes), the index of that transaction in the block (3 bytes), and the index of the output (*output*) corresponding to the channel (2 bytes). For example, an SCID `700000x1x0` means: block no. 700,000, transaction no. 1, output no. 0.

d54e6872-878a-43fa-a7a1-db62d921a606.title: ASSET MERGE
d54e6872-878a-43fa-a7a1-db62d921a606.body: An operation that consists of combining two Taproot Assets assets of the same type into one within a single Taproot output. During an *asset merge*, assets coming from distinct Taproot outputs are grouped into a single *Merkle-Sum Sparse Merkle Tree* committed in a new transaction. The total sum at the root of the tree then reflects all of the merged assets. This operation is the inverse of an *asset split*. It makes it possible to consolidate balances fragmented after several receipts and to simplify the management of a holder's asset tree.

d6599e15-5ee2-4069-9cef-913159ac2b90.title: NO2X
d6599e15-5ee2-4069-9cef-913159ac2b90.body: Name of the campaign launched in August 2017 following the lock-in of the SegWit soft fork, whose goal is to convince users not to implement the doubling of the block size from 1 MB to 2 MB as planned in the SEGWIT2X update.

d65d6315-3cc2-4a3c-9473-3de32166f3cc.title: CLN - C-LIGHTNING
d65d6315-3cc2-4a3c-9473-3de32166f3cc.body: Former name of the Core-Lightning implementation.

d6a97280-ac95-482f-86d7-123aabccd83a.title: PEDERSEN COMMITMENT
d6a97280-ac95-482f-86d7-123aabccd83a.body:
A Pedersen commitment is a type of cryptographic commitment with the property of being homomorphic with respect to the addition operation. This means it is possible to validate the sum of two commitments without revealing the individual values.

Formally, if:
```math
C_1\ =\ commit(m_1,\ r_1) \quad C_2\ =\ commit(m_2,\ r_2)
```
then:
```math
C_3\ =\ C_1 \cdot C_2\ =\ commit(m_1\ +\ m_2,\ r_1\ +\ r_2)
```
This property becomes useful, for example, to conceal the amounts of *tokens* exchanged in cryptocurrency systems, such as RGB, while still being able to verify the totals.

d6a9c6cc-76c8-4245-adef-772710a37473.title: SPEEDY TRIAL
d6a9c6cc-76c8-4245-adef-772710a37473.body:
A soft fork activation method initially conceptualized for Taproot in early 2021 by David A. Harding, based on an idea by Russell O'Connor. Its principle is to use the BIP-0008 method with a `LOT` parameter set to `faux`, while reducing the activation period to only 3 months. This reduction of the voting period allows a quick verification of miner approval. If the required approval threshold is reached during one of the periods, the soft fork is then locked in. It will be activated several months later, thus giving miners the time needed to update their software.

The success of this method for Taproot, which benefited from broad consensus within the Bitcoin community, does not however guarantee its effectiveness for all upgrades. Although the Speedy Trial method allows faster activation, some developers express concerns about its future use. They fear that it could lead to too rapid a succession of soft forks, which could potentially threaten the stability and security of the Bitcoin protocol. Compared to BIP-0008 with the `LOT=true` parameter, the Speedy Trial method is much less threatening for miners. No UASF is automatically planned. This activation method has not yet been formalized in a BIP.

*"Speedy Trial" is borrowed from a legal terminology that indicates an "expedited trial". This evokes the fact that the improvement proposal is quickly sent before the miners' court, so that we are made aware of their intentions. It is generally accepted to use the English term directly in French.*

d6c9951a-94ae-4700-aa31-9a9561b3bfc4.title: BIP-0118
d6c9951a-94ae-4700-aa31-9a9561b3bfc4.body: Bitcoin improvement proposal aiming to introduce two new modifier SigHash Flags: `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` and `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUTANYSCRIPT`. These features extend the capabilities of Bitcoin transactions, particularly with regard to smart contracts and layer-two solutions such as the Lightning Network. BIP-0118 would notably enable the use of Eltoo. The main advantage of `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` is that it allows signatures to be reused across several transactions, which offers more flexibility. Concretely, these SigHashes make it possible to obtain a signature that does not cover any input of the transaction.

d6efa179-e094-4127-940e-50647d887468.title: SCHEMA
d6efa179-e094-4127-940e-50647d887468.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, a Schema refers to a piece of declarative code that defines the set of variables, rules and business logic (*Business Logic*) governing the operation of a contract. It specifies the structure of the state, notably the initial configuration established during the Genesis, and details the types of transitions allowed as well as the strict conditions for their validation. The Schema serves as a normative framework, ensuring that any change to the contract's state conforms to the rules established by the developer of the Schema.

d7456a01-75cc-4680-9e1b-dd26d0f4897d.title: FULCRUM
d7456a01-75cc-4680-9e1b-dd26d0f4897d.body:
Electrum server implementation developed in C++ by Calin Culianu, initially for Bitcoin Cash, and released under the GPLv3 license. Fulcrum indexes all the transactions of the Bitcoin blockchain from a full node and responds to queries from wallets compatible with the Electrum protocol.

Designed as a high-performance replacement for ElectrumX, Fulcrum uses a RocksDB database and takes advantage of the multithreaded and asynchronous programming of C++20 to offer fast response times, even under heavy load. It requires a Bitcoin Core (or Bitcoin Knots) node configured with `txindex=1` and without pruning.

The initial synchronization of the index with the blockchain takes much longer than with Electrs, and its storage currently approaches 200 GB. In return, it is significantly faster in use, whereas Electrs is slower, but stands out for its lightness.

d7abc29f-6a39-4d71-9a36-ca58bf44fed9.title: LITTLE-ENDIAN
d7abc29f-6a39-4d71-9a36-ca58bf44fed9.body: Data storage format in computer systems where the least significant bytes (the “little ends”) are placed first in address order. In a sequence of several bytes, the byte with the lowest weight (for example, the rightmost digits in hexadecimal) is stored first.

d7c3e1a4-5b92-4f8e-a6d1-3e7f9c2b8a05.title: KEY TELEPORT
d7c3e1a4-5b92-4f8e-a6d1-3e7f9c2b8a05.body: Coldcard feature that allows the encrypted transfer of confidential data between two devices. Transferable data includes *seeds* (main *seed* or *Seed Vault*), notes and passwords, full backups, and multisig PSBTs.

d7ce15e2-ae52-437a-af0c-7544420824c4.title: SIGHASH_ALL
d7ce15e2-ae52-437a-af0c-7544420824c4.body: Type of SigHash Flag used in Bitcoin transaction signatures to indicate that the signature applies to all components of the transaction. By using `SIGHASH_ALL`, the signer covers all inputs and all outputs. This means that neither the inputs nor the outputs can be modified after signing without invalidating the signature. This type of SigHash Flag is the most common in Bitcoin transactions, because it ensures complete finality and integrity of the transaction.

d84cffe5-9d68-44a5-846f-95b8aa9a47ea.title: COMMITMENT FEE
d84cffe5-9d68-44a5-846f-95b8aa9a47ea.body:
Fee included in the commitment transaction (*commitment transaction*) of a Lightning channel. This transaction allows each participant to recover their funds in the event of a unilateral closure of the channel. To be confirmed within a reasonable time, it must include sufficient mining fees.

With the introduction of *anchor channels*, the *commitment fee* can be set at a very low amount during channel negotiation. Indeed, *anchor outputs* make it possible to increase the fees at the time the commitment transaction is actually broadcast by attaching an additional UTXO to it via the CPFP (*Child Pays For Parent*) mechanism. This avoids overestimating the fees when the channel is created, while guaranteeing quick confirmation in the event of a forced closure.

d84e3fd5-7c72-4820-b388-261cb1961330.title: ASIC
d84e3fd5-7c72-4820-b388-261cb1961330.body: An ASIC is an electronic component designed to perform a specific function with optimal efficiency. In the context of Bitcoin mining, ASICs are specialized integrated circuits that perform hashing operations at high speed and low power consumption. They specialize in running the `SHA256` hash function used in the proof-of-work mechanism. The ASIC is originally the name of the chip. By extension, the acronym “ASIC” often also refers to the machine that houses this chip. Thus, computers specialized in Bitcoin mining are sometimes called “ASICs”, or “miners”. ASICs have gradually replaced other mining methods, such as the use of processors (CPUs) and graphics cards (GPUs), because of their superior energy efficiency and much higher hashrate.

d8576541-d8ef-4de0-b57e-305db884dc84.title: INFLATION
d8576541-d8ef-4de0-b57e-305db884dc84.body:
Refers to the increase in the money supply in circulation, leading to a decline in the value of each unit of currency and a rise in the prices of goods and services. For state currencies, this phenomenon occurs when central banks issue new monetary units.

In the context of Bitcoin, inflation is controlled by the protocol. New bitcoins are generated with each block validation through the subsidy awarded to the winning miner. This subsidy was initially 50 BTC per block and it is halved every 210,000 blocks in an event known as the “halving”. The total issuance of bitcoins is capped at approximately 21 million units, which means that the monetary inflation of BTC is decreasing and will stop once the maximum number of units is reached.

d86926e9-4093-4911-8101-bf9fcd6b58ab.title: WITNESSSCRIPT
d86926e9-4093-4911-8101-bf9fcd6b58ab.body:
Script that specifies the conditions under which bitcoins can be spent in P2WSH or P2SH-P2WSH UTXOs. Typically, the `witnessScript` determine the conditions of a multisig wallet under the SegWit standard. In these script standards, the `scriptPubKey` of the UTXO (the output) contains a hash of the `witnessScript`. To use this UTXO as an input in a new transaction, the holder must reveal the original `witnessScript`, in order to prove its match with the digest in the `scriptPubKey`. The `witnessScript` must then be included in the `scriptWitness` of the transaction, which also contains the elements needed to validate the script, such as signatures.  The `witnessScript` is thus the SegWit equivalent of the `redeemScript` in a P2SH transaction, with the difference that it is placed in the transaction's witness, and not in the `scriptSig`.

*Note, the `witnessScript` must not be confused with the `scriptWitness`. While the `witnessScript` defines the spending conditions of a P2WSH or P2SH-P2WSH UTXO and is a script in its own right, the `scriptWitness` contains the witness data of any SegWit input.*

d89f336d-bd0b-4d11-bb82-1a4676cd2929.title: BIP-0083
d89f336d-bd0b-4d11-bb82-1a4676cd2929.body: Proposal for an extension of hierarchical deterministic key trees (BIP-0032) allowing the dynamic creation of new derivation levels according to the needs of the application. BIP-0083 was closed, as the standard derivation paths defined by BIP-0044, BIP-0049 and BIP-0084 were deemed sufficient for the majority of use cases.

d8d073ff-cb4c-4159-bf50-9713261290bd.title: OP_NUMNOTEQUAL - 0X9E
d8d073ff-cb4c-4159-bf50-9713261290bd.body: Compares the top two elements of the stack to check whether they are numerically not equal. If the values are not equal, it pushes `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise, it pushes `0` (false). It is the inverse of `OP_NUMEQUAL`.

d8dd8728-f52c-44e0-b9af-078490aa586a.title: COIN SELECTION
d8dd8728-f52c-44e0-b9af-078490aa586a.body: Process by which Bitcoin wallet software chooses which UTXOs to use as inputs to satisfy the outputs of a transaction. The coin selection method is important, because it has consequences for the cost of a transaction and the user's privacy. It often aims to minimize the number of inputs used, in order to reduce the size of the transaction and the associated fees, while trying to preserve privacy by avoiding merging coins from different sources (CIOH). Several methods exist for coin selection, such as the *Knapsack Solver* or *Branch-and-Bound*. When coin selection is done manually by the user, it is called “*Coin Control*”.

d8f778ee-5507-45ea-9065-940561c001af.title: VANITYGEN
d8f778ee-5507-45ea-9065-940561c001af.body: The first open source command-line software used to create custom receiving addresses (*vanity address*). It works by generating and testing key pairs by trial and error until a receiving address matching the criteria specified by the user (such as a certain sequence of specific characters) is found. Vanitygen requires an intensive computational process, particularly for long sequences.

d910cf73-985d-44e0-810f-619230f923ac.title: OP_SHA256 - 0XA8
d910cf73-985d-44e0-810f-619230f923ac.body: Takes the element at the top of the stack and replaces it with its hash using the `SHA256` function.

d9461a0b-ca50-405d-b622-67cf5e63d3ee.title: SEED NODES
d9461a0b-ca50-405d-b622-67cf5e63d3ee.body:
Static list of public Bitcoin nodes, built directly into the source code of Bitcoin Core (`bitcoin/src/chainparamsseeds.h`). This list serves as connection points for new Bitcoin nodes joining the network, but it is only used if the DNS seeds do not provide a response within 60 seconds of being queried. In that case, the new Bitcoin node will connect to these seed nodes to establish a first connection to the network and request IP addresses of other nodes. The ultimate goal is to acquire the information needed to perform the IBD and synchronize with the chain that has the most accumulated work. The list of seed nodes includes several hundred nodes, identified according to the standard established by BIP-0155. Thus, seed nodes are the third method a Bitcoin node uses to connect to the network, after the possible use of the `peers.dat` file, created by the node itself, and querying the DNS seeds.

*Note that seed nodes must not be confused with “DNS seeds”, which are the second way of establishing connections.*

d9966ec1-5cac-479d-a051-bcb75167696c.title: BITCOIN QT
d9966ec1-5cac-479d-a051-bcb75167696c.body:
Bitcoin QT is a Bitcoin client integrating a graphical interface, released in November 2011. It follows in the lineage of Satoshi's own client. In 2014, Bitcoin QT was renamed "Bitcoin Core". Today it is the reference implementation of the Bitcoin protocol. It has been shipped with `bitcoind` since version 0.5. Moreover, even today, the graphical interface of Bitcoin Core is called `bitcoin-qt` in reference to the software's origins.

*"QT" comes from the name of the library used for the graphical interface. The name "QT" is sometimes interpreted as a pun on the sound of the term "cute" ("mignon" in French).*

d9b36e70-8762-42fd-85f9-dcec678261ed.title: GRAFTROOT
d9b36e70-8762-42fd-85f9-dcec678261ed.body:
Bitcoin protocol improvement proposal formulated by Gregory Maxwell in February 2018. Graftroot extends the concept of Taproot by adding a mechanism for delegating spending conditions. With Taproot, a group of participants who share an aggregated key can either spend directly with that key, or reveal an alternative script contained in a Merkle tree. Graftroot additionally allows these participants to delegate their spending capacity to arbitrary scripts by signing those scripts with their aggregated key.

The main usefulness of this protocol lies in the absence of a limit on the number of alternative spending conditions. Each delegation materializes as a simple Schnorr signature over the authorized script, with no overhead proportional to the number of delegated scripts. In Taproot, adding branches to the Merkle tree increases the size of the spending proof, whereas Graftroot maintains a constant cost.

Graftroot was never formalized in the form of a BIP and was not integrated into the Bitcoin protocol.

da174fdd-78cd-4f2d-8232-1eb357c71017.title: OP_CHECKTEMPLATEVERIFY - 0XB3
da174fdd-78cd-4f2d-8232-1eb357c71017.body:
Opcode `0xb3` proposed in BIP-0119, as a replacement for `OP_NOP4`. It requires the spending transaction to match a predefined template exactly, which makes it a non-recursive covenant mechanism.

The opcode reads the item at the top of the stack without removing it. If this item is 32 bytes long, it is compared to the `DefaultCheckTemplateVerifyHash` computed from the current transaction and the index of the input being executed. This hash is the `SHA256` of the serialized concatenation of: the transaction version, the locktime, the hash of the scriptSigs (if they are non-empty), the number of inputs, the hash of the sequences, the number of outputs, the hash of the outputs and the index of the current input. If the two values do not match, the script fails. If the item is not 32 bytes long, the opcode behaves like a `OP_NOP` in order to allow for future extensions.

By constraining almost all of the fields of the spending transaction, CTV makes it possible to specify the exact outputs in advance without resorting to signatures or ephemeral keys. This property opens the way to applications such as payment trees for congestion control, *vaults*, joinpools or improving the efficiency of DLCs. This proposal is for the moment still a draft.

da353952-da58-44e3-9fd5-68061a4d5d60.title: STONEWALL
da353952-da58-44e3-9fd5-68061a4d5d60.body:
A specific form of Bitcoin transaction aimed at increasing users' privacy when spending by imitating a coinjoin between two people, without actually being one. Indeed, this transaction is not collaborative. A user can build it alone, involving only UTXOs belonging to them as inputs. You can therefore create a Stonewall transaction for any occasion, without needing to synchronize with another user.

The Stonewall transaction works as follows: as the transaction's input, the sender uses 2 UTXOs that belong to them. As output, the transaction produces 4 outputs, 2 of which will be of exactly the same amount. The other 2 will be change outputs. Among the 2 outputs of the same amount, only one will actually go to the payment recipient.

There are therefore only 2 roles in a Stonewall transaction:
* The sender, who makes the actual payment;
* The recipient, who may be unaware of the specific nature of the transaction and simply expects a payment from the sender.

![Stonewall: 2 inputs from the same sender and 4 outputs including two identical amounts imitate a coinjoin without a real collaborator.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/s/stonewall/assets/image-1.png)
Stonewall transactions are available on both the Samourai Wallet application and the Sparrow Wallet software.

The Stonewall structure adds a great deal of entropy to the transaction and muddies the trail for chain analysis. Seen from the outside, such a transaction can be interpreted as a small coinjoin between two people. But in reality, just like the Stonewall x2 transaction, it is a payment. This method therefore generates uncertainty in chain analysis, and even points toward false leads. Even if the outside observer manages to identify the pattern of the Stonewall transaction, they will not have all the information. They will not be able to determine which of the two UTXOs of the same amounts corresponds to the payment. Moreover, they will not be able to determine whether the two input UTXOs come from two different people or belong to a single person who merged them. This last point is due to the fact that Stonewall x2 transactions follow exactly the same pattern as Stonewall transactions. Seen from the outside and without additional information about the context, it is impossible to differentiate a Stonewall transaction from a Stonewall x2 transaction. Yet the former are not collaborative transactions, whereas the latter are. This adds even more doubt about this spend.

da3bb49f-15b3-4613-8b1b-6fe164956ab0.title: BIP-0039
da3bb49f-15b3-4613-8b1b-6fe164956ab0.body: BIP-0039 introduces a method for converting a wallet's random seed into a sequence of memorizable, human-readable words, known as a mnemonic phrase. This phrase, generally made up of 12 or 24 words, makes it possible to regenerate all of a wallet's private keys deterministically. Thus, instead of having to memorize or store a complex cryptographic seed, users can back up their bitcoins via a phrase of a few words. BIP-0039 has thereby helped simplify the management of a Bitcoin wallet.

da773fd3-c1e6-43fb-8764-2cca100725d5.title: ELLIPTIC CURVE
da773fd3-c1e6-43fb-8764-2cca100725d5.body: In the context of cryptography, an elliptic curve is an algebraic curve defined by an equation of the form `y^2 = x^3 + ax + b`. These curves are used in elliptic curve cryptography (ECC), which is a public-key cryptography method for creating encryption algorithms, digital signatures, and key exchange. In the context of Bitcoin, the ECDSA (*Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm*) or the Schnorr protocol are used with the `secp256k1` curve. This curve was chosen for its performance and security properties. These algorithms are used to generate public keys from private keys, as well as to sign transactions, and therefore unlock bitcoins.

da78514e-08b0-4741-b2e3-ce0a541eb77f.title: BIP-0043
da78514e-08b0-4741-b2e3-ce0a541eb77f.body: Improvement proposal that introduces the use of a derivation level to describe the purpose (“*purpose field*”) in the structure of HD wallets, previously introduced in BIP-0032. According to BIP-0043, the first derivation level of an HD wallet, right after the master key denoted `m/`, is reserved for the purpose number, which indicates the derivation standard used for the rest of the path. This number is recorded as an index (hardened). For example, if the wallet follows the SegWit standard (BIP-0084), the beginning of its derivation path will be: `m/84'/`. BIP-0043 thus makes it possible to clarify the standards followed by each wallet software in order to have better interoperability between them. The standardization of the rest of the derivation path is described in BIP-0044.

da7b74cf-e772-49ec-a73b-fc31185bb001.title: BTCPAY SERVER
da7b74cf-e772-49ec-a73b-fc31185bb001.body:
Open-source payment processor that allows merchants and users to accept bitcoin payments without depending on a third party to process transactions. Launched in 2017, BTCPay Server offers a bitcoin payment integration solution for e-commerce sites, with advanced features such as *hardware wallet* support, invoicing and accounting tools, as well as compatibility with the Lightning Network. Its development was initiated by Nicolas Dorier, in reaction to the actions of BitPay which, according to him, had misled its users by pushing them toward the adoption of SegWit2x, which the company wrongly considered to be the "real" Bitcoin. This opposition crystallized in a now-famous tweet by Nicolas Dorier in August 2017:

> "_This is lies, my trust in you is broken, I will make you obsolete_".

da88b768-3192-4f9e-a45d-beb88d47fbfc.title: BIP-0115
da88b768-3192-4f9e-a45d-beb88d47fbfc.body: Proposal for a mechanism protecting against transaction replay in the event of a *hard fork*, by committing each transaction to a specific *blockhash*. BIP-0115 added an opcode making it possible to verify that a particular block exists in the active chain, making the transaction invalid on an alternative chain resulting from a fork. This proposal was never deployed.

dadbcc81-325e-4dbb-be52-96817ed8d520.title: EXTERNAL ADDRESS REUSE
dadbcc81-325e-4dbb-be52-96817ed8d520.body:
Address reuse is said to be “external” when it occurs across several different transactions. In this configuration, external address reuse is a chain analysis heuristic that makes it possible to put forward a plausible hypothesis that all these addresses belong to the same entity.

![External reuse: the same address bc1q...xyz appears in three distinct transactions, a sign of a common owner.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/r/reutilisation-d-adresse-ext/assets/image-1.png)

dae3b880-1e67-4718-b472-f0b56b5c6748.title: OP_1SUB - 0X8C
dae3b880-1e67-4718-b472-f0b56b5c6748.body: Subtracts `1` from the value at the top of the stack.

dae51823-888b-4bef-bc16-e58cbb916b29.title: BITCOIN IMPLEMENTATION
dae51823-888b-4bef-bc16-e58cbb916b29.body:
Refers to software that applies and follows the rules defined by the Bitcoin protocol. What is called “Bitcoin” is generally the electronic cash system. It is a protocol that specifies rules. It is represented, concretely, by nodes that form a network. This system does not specifically have code. It is simply a set of major tacit rules imposed by the consensus of users through their nodes. On the other hand, what does have computer code, and can therefore be developed, maintained and modified, is rather the Bitcoin node software. These are independent implementations of the Bitcoin protocol, which can connect to the rest of the network.

Among Bitcoin implementations, Bitcoin Core is by far the most widespread, since it represents the vast majority of the node network. However, there are also minority implementations such as btcd, Bcoin, and Bitcoin Knots. Despite the diversity of software clients available, the predominance of Bitcoin Core on the network gives it an almost exclusive influence over the enforcement of the Bitcoin protocol. It is therefore said that Bitcoin Core in practice represents the Bitcoin protocol itself.

db3c0493-b075-467f-995c-904fa6fb2569.title: IP_ASN.MAP
db3c0493-b075-467f-995c-904fa6fb2569.body: File used in Bitcoin Core to store the ASMAP, which improves the *bucketing* (that is, the grouping) of IP addresses, based on autonomous system numbers (ASNs). Rather than grouping outbound connections by IP network prefixes (`/16`), this file makes it possible to diversify connections by establishing a map from IP addresses to ASNs, which are unique identifiers for each network on the Internet. The idea is to improve the security and topology of the Bitcoin network by diversifying connections to protect against certain attacks (notably the Erebus attack).

db70edee-b5a3-435b-8f3a-760b21383d0f.title: SHA256
db70edee-b5a3-435b-8f3a-760b21383d0f.body: Acronym for “*Secure Hash Algorithm 256 bits*”. It is a cryptographic hash function producing a 256-bit digest. Designed by the *National Security Agency* (NSA) in the early 2000s, it became a federal standard for processing sensitive data. In the Bitcoin protocol, the `SHA256` function is ubiquitous. It is used to hash block headers as part of proof of work. `SHA256` is also used in the process of deriving a receiving address from a public key. It is also used to aggregate transactions and witnesses within Merkle trees in blocks. `SHA256` is also found in key fingerprint calculation, in the calculation of certain checksums and in many other processes around Bitcoin. When it is applied twice in a row, it is called a `HASH256`. This double application is the one mostly used on Bitcoin. When `SHA256` is used together with the `RIPEMD160` function, it is called a `HASH160`. This double hash is used for key fingerprints and for hashing public keys. The `SHA256` function belongs to the SHA 2 family.

dbf8b5dc-6bc5-48cd-9f20-fced1421eab5.title: SMT - SPARSE MERKLE TREE
dbf8b5dc-6bc5-48cd-9f20-fced1421eab5.body: A data structure that extends the properties of a classic Merkle tree by making it possible to produce proofs of non-inclusion in addition to proofs of inclusion. In an SMT, each element is placed at a position in the tree determined by the SHA-256 hash of its data: each bit of the hash indicates a left or right path through the binary tree. Because the majority of leaves remain empty, the tree is said to be "sparse" (*sparse*), which allows efficient generation and updating thanks to the pruning of empty branches. SMTs are used in the Taproot Assets protocol to manage asset transfers and to prove that a given asset has not been spent twice.

dcc11d31-0350-4831-b2c9-d2ac081bf468.title: ASYNC PAYMENTS
dcc11d31-0350-4831-b2c9-d2ac081bf468.body:
A mechanism that makes it possible to send a Lightning payment to a recipient who is not online at the time of sending. On the classic Bitcoin network, transactions are naturally asynchronous since the recipient does not need to be connected to receive funds. By contrast, the Lightning protocol normally requires the receiver to be online to reveal the secret (the preimage) that finalizes the payment via an HTLC.

This constraint poses a significant problem for mobile wallets, which are not permanently connected. Several approaches have been proposed to solve this limitation. The most promising relies on the use of PTLCs (*Point Time-Locked Contracts*) combined with static BOLT-12 invoices, which allow the payer to build a valid payment without prior interaction with the recipient. Another approach uses trampoline relay nodes: a trusted intermediate node holds the payment until the recipient reconnects, then forwards it to them.

Concrete implementations have emerged, notably in LDK and Eclair. LDK has integrated asynchronous payment logic on the client side and the server side, while Eclair makes it possible to wake up a disconnected mobile peer to forward a pending payment to it. These advances are essential to make Lightning truly usable on mobile devices, where permanent connectivity cannot be guaranteed.

dcc5ee68-382d-48d9-aa3b-51773f4efb18.title: TAPD
dcc5ee68-382d-48d9-aa3b-51773f4efb18.body: Daemon software that is the reference implementation of the Taproot Assets protocol, developed by Lightning Labs. `tapd` makes it possible to create (*mint*), send and receive digital assets encoded in Taproot outputs on the Bitcoin blockchain.

dd0fc5ee-1e46-46a2-bc27-484463840e58.title: SHOR'S ALGORITHM
