ed1cda46-11ad-481b-9b9d-81673eca37fc.body: A file used in Bitcoin Core to store a private key associated with a Tor hidden service for the `-listenonion` option. When this option is enabled, `bitcoind` automatically creates a Tor hidden service, allowing the node to communicate on the Tor network.

ed4d09d5-7e70-4d10-9d73-991293824b63.title: BIP-0117
ed4d09d5-7e70-4d10-9d73-991293824b63.body: Proposes introducing tail call (*tail call*) execution semantics into Bitcoin's Script system. This mechanism would allow a script to transfer execution to another script without increasing the stack depth, analogously to *tail call* optimization in programming languages. Combined with BIP-0116 (`OP_MERKLEBRANCHVERIFY`), it would provide general MAST capabilities, making it possible to dynamically select and execute a sub-script from a set structured as a Merkle tree. This BIP, proposed by Mark Friedenbach in 2017, was superseded by Taproot (BIP-0341).

edf8e78d-6943-458f-a266-2b9a3c0c1593.title: LIGHTNING NETWORK+
edf8e78d-6943-458f-a266-2b9a3c0c1593.body:
Lightning Network+ is an online service that facilitates the creation of *liquidity swaps* on the Lightning Network. Several node operators coordinate to simultaneously open payment channels among themselves in a circular fashion, which guarantees that each of them receives as much inbound capacity as they offer. For example, 3 users A, B and C agree on the LN+ site on a *liquidity swap* of 1M sats: A opens a 1M sats channel to B, B does the same to C, and C in turn opens a channel to A.

This system thus makes it possible to improve the connectivity of one's Lightning node, while obtaining as much inbound liquidity as the outbound liquidity committed.

ee10d374-8a94-48ec-8dfd-d58317fd146b.title: PATOSHI
ee10d374-8a94-48ec-8dfd-d58317fd146b.body: Refers to a distinct pattern of nonces and timestamps observed in blocks mined during the first months of Bitcoin's existence. This pattern is suspected to be attributable to a single entity or individual, most likely Satoshi Nakamoto himself, the inventor of Bitcoin. The term “Patoshi” is a portmanteau combining “*pattern*” and “Satoshi”. Several analyses of Bitcoin's first blocks revealed patterns in the way nonces and extra-nonces were chosen, and in how timestamps were set. These patterns were distinct enough to suggest that a particular miner or group of miners was responsible for a large proportion of the blocks mined during this period, while using a modified client. Sergio Demian Lerner, a computer science researcher, is credited with discovering this pattern in 2013. Lerner estimated that the Patoshi miner had mined about 1.1 million bitcoins. This led to widespread speculation about the motivations, identity, and current intentions of the Patoshi miner. Some believe that Patoshi was Satoshi himself, mining bitcoins to support and secure the nascent network. It is important to note that, although the Patoshi pattern is widely accepted as evidence of concentrated early mining activity, there is no definitive confirmation of the identity behind Patoshi or of their intentions.

ee3d1438-cf99-4908-b1c1-9bdea5a3d2f8.title: TEN31
ee3d1438-cf99-4908-b1c1-9bdea5a3d2f8.body: A venture capital fund specialized in investing in companies of the Bitcoin ecosystem. Founded in 2020, Ten31 takes its name from October 31 (10/31 in the American format), the date the White Paper was published by Satoshi Nakamoto in 2008.

eeced097-5ca4-4e4b-9d6b-71809a504616.title: OP_SUB - 0X94
eeced097-5ca4-4e4b-9d6b-71809a504616.body: Subtracts the top two elements of the stack. It takes the two values at the top of the stack, subtracts them, and replaces them with the result.

eefc35f8-7b36-4cf0-a095-a4e353b6342f.title: BLOCKSIGNERS
eefc35f8-7b36-4cf0-a095-a4e353b6342f.body: In the context of Liquid (a Bitcoin sidechain), these are the entities responsible for building and validating blocks within this chain. Liquid uses a federation model where the *blocksigners*, selected from among the federation members, operate jointly to confirm transactions and create new blocks in order to form the sidechain's consensus. The *blocksigner* role is part of the functionaries in Liquid. The latter fulfill both this role and that of *watchmen* (guardians).

ef52e4c2-bdd0-4d1b-bcd8-d2770bccf4f6.title: PPA
ef52e4c2-bdd0-4d1b-bcd8-d2770bccf4f6.body: Acronym for "*Power Purchase Agreement*". It is a long-term contract between a large bitcoin mining farm and an energy provider, for the direct purchase of electricity at a fixed rate. This type of contract allows mining farms to secure stable and competitive energy costs over several years, which reduces the impact of fluctuations in the electricity market.

ef70aa4a-7364-4b70-8d04-f628c67b1404.title: PAYLOAD

ef719414-3941-4713-913f-316af4858c8d.title: BIP-0104
ef719414-3941-4713-913f-316af4858c8d.body: Proposal nicknamed “Block75” that provided for an automatic adjustment of the maximum block size aiming for a fill rate of 75%. The mechanism was similar to difficulty retargeting: if blocks were too full, the limit increased; if they were too empty, it decreased. This BIP-0104, proposed during the Blocksize War, was never adopted.

ef87c27d-fcbc-4108-bba1-fb5776a17257.title: LUXOR
ef87c27d-fcbc-4108-bba1-fb5776a17257.body: American company founded in 2017 by Nick Hansen, specializing in infrastructure services for Bitcoin mining. Luxor operates a pool, a custom firmware for ASICs (LuxOS), an analytics data platform (Hashrate Index), a hashrate derivatives desk and a marketplace for ASIC machines. The company primarily targets professional and institutional North American miners.

ef9e627f-c813-4684-9945-4cb59cf28b96.title: QUBIT
ef9e627f-c813-4684-9945-4cb59cf28b96.body: The basic unit of information on a quantum computer. These qubits can take the value 0, the value 1, or a superposition of 0 and 1. By using this superposition of states together with other quantum phenomena such as entanglement and quantum interference, a quantum computer can parallelize computational processes, and thus solve certain specific problems much faster.

efd226d6-a5c5-4bad-a0c6-0d24f4763dc9.title: OP_LESSTHANOREQUAL - 0XA1
efd226d6-a5c5-4bad-a0c6-0d24f4763dc9.body: Compares the top two elements of the stack and checks whether the second element is less than or equal to the first. If the second element is less than or equal to the first, it pushes `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise, it pushes `0` (false).

f01a2f8d-4120-4323-af5f-b26dbd4b8bf5.title: CANAAN
f01a2f8d-4120-4323-af5f-b26dbd4b8bf5.body: A company founded in 2013 by Nangeng Zhang, specializing in the manufacture of bitcoin mining machines. Canaan is the originator of the AvalonMiner, the very first ASIC designed specifically for Bitcoin mining. Based in Singapore, Canaan became in 2019 the first company in the mining ASIC sector to be listed on the NASDAQ.

f02bd4a9-468b-4b70-9d76-c3f93e87533e.title: BIP-0072
f02bd4a9-468b-4b70-9d76-c3f93e87533e.body: Complements BIP-0070 and BIP-0071 by defining the extension of Bitcoin URIs (BIP-0021) with an additional parameter `r`. This parameter makes it possible to include a link to a secure payment request signed by the merchant's SSL certificate. When a customer clicks on this extended URI, their wallet contacts the merchant's server to request the payment details. These details are automatically filled into the wallet's transaction interface and the customer can be informed that they are paying the owner of the domain corresponding to the signing certificate (for example, "pandul.fr"). Since this improvement is bundled with BIP-0070, it was never widely adopted.

f089771a-9aeb-4dc8-a587-a66e222f657a.title: VOLTAGE
f089771a-9aeb-4dc8-a587-a66e222f657a.body:
A cloud infrastructure platform dedicated to the Lightning Network. Voltage allows businesses and developers to deploy and manage Lightning nodes (LND, Core Lightning) without having to administer the underlying infrastructure.

The platform offers node hosting, monitoring tools and liquidity management services. These features make it easier to integrate the Lightning Network into commercial applications.

Voltage's model is non-custodial: the node operator retains control of their keys and funds.

f0a265ae-0cf6-423a-8002-a245422fcf6e.title: P2POOL
f0a265ae-0cf6-423a-8002-a245422fcf6e.body:
Decentralized mining pool protocol for Bitcoin, designed to eliminate the need for a central operator. P2Pool works by creating a secondary blockchain called the “share chain”, whose difficulty is adjusted to produce a block approximately every 30 seconds. The blocks of this *share chain* are structurally identical to those of the Bitcoin blockchain, but with a lower difficulty target. Each miner runs their own P2Pool node connected to a Bitcoin full node and contributes to the peer-to-peer network of the *share chain*.

When one of the blocks of the *share chain* also satisfies the difficulty required by the Bitcoin network, it is broadcast on the Bitcoin network. The block reward is then distributed among the miners who contributed the most recent shares in the *share chain*. This mechanism ensures that the distribution of rewards is proportional to each miner's contribution, without a central operator controlling the funds or the selection of transactions.

P2Pool was created in 2011 by Forrest Voight. It saw significant adoption in the early years of Bitcoin, but its use declined in the face of the growth of centralized pools, which offered simpler interfaces and lower variance for individual miners. The last block mined by P2Pool dates from 2019.

f0ac80de-658b-4cfc-ac53-f4d1e9553cb1.title: ROAST
f0ac80de-658b-4cfc-ac53-f4d1e9553cb1.body:
Asynchronous Schnorr threshold signature protocol, whose acronym stands for *Robust Asynchronous Schnorr Threshold signatures*. ROAST was proposed in 2022 by Tim Ruffing, Viktoria Ronge, Elliott Jin, Jonas Schneider-Bensch and Dominique Schröder. It works as a wrapper around an existing threshold signature scheme, such as FROST, to make it resistant to uncooperative participants or high network latency.

In a classic threshold scheme, a subset of signers must coordinate their responses to produce a valid signature. If some participants do not respond or attempt to disrupt the process, the signing session can be blocked. ROAST solves this problem by automatically restarting parallel signing sessions until a functioning quorum is obtained. This protocol is particularly useful for federations, such as the Liquid network federation, where it could make it possible to considerably increase the number of signers while maintaining the reliability of the signing process.

f0affa56-0c9f-4271-9f50-518f84496f47.title: MUSIG
f0affa56-0c9f-4271-9f50-518f84496f47.body:
An n-of-n Schnorr multisignature protocol proposed in 2018 by Gregory Maxwell, Andrew Poelstra, Yannick Seurin and Pieter Wuille. It aggregates the public keys of several signers into a single key and produces a single valid signature, indistinguishable from an individual signature on the blockchain. To counter the rogue key attack (“*rogue key attack*”), in which a participant manipulates their public key to alone control the aggregated key, the protocol multiplies each key by a coefficient derived from the set of keys.

The signing process takes place in three rounds of communication: exchange of cryptographic commitments to the nonces, revelation of the nonces, then exchange of the partial signatures. This three-round structure protects against nonce manipulation attacks, but imposes a constraining interactivity. MuSig has been superseded by MuSig2, which reduces the process to two rounds.

f103ee23-7a82-495c-a348-cd457a104a86.title: ALGORITHM
f103ee23-7a82-495c-a348-cd457a104a86.body: A finite and unambiguous sequence of instructions for carrying out a task. In the context of computer science, it is a process written in a programming language that tells a computer how to carry out a mission.

f1764fe0-499b-42fa-8a51-aa8f7391178a.title: NULLDUMMY
f1764fe0-499b-42fa-8a51-aa8f7391178a.body: Consensus rule introduced with BIP-0147 in the SegWit soft fork that requires the dummy element ("*dummy element*") used in the `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` and `OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY` opcodes to be an empty byte array (`OP_0`). This measure was put in place to eliminate a malleability vector by prohibiting any value other than `OP_0` for this element.

f17ce504-d668-4c73-a24c-885acfa0b86c.title: PTLC
f17ce504-d668-4c73-a24c-885acfa0b86c.body:
Conditional contracts intended to replace HTLCs (*Hash Time Locked Contracts*) for routing payments on the Lightning Network. A PTLC (*Point Time Locked Contract*) works on the same principle as an HTLC (locking funds that are released only if a cryptographic condition is satisfied) but uses elliptic curve points and signatures instead of hashes and preimages.

In an HTLC, all the hops of the same payment share the same hash. A spy node present on several hops can correlate the payments and identify that they belong to the same transaction. PTLCs eliminate this problem: each hop uses a different public key/signature pair, which makes payments untraceable from one hop to another.

The mechanism relies on *adaptor signatures*, a construction made practical by Schnorr signatures. The receiver provides a point (public key) to the payer. At each hop, a new secret is added through key aggregation, so that the revelation of the final signature compromises only the local secret, not the relationship between hops. If a PTLC is published on-chain, it appears as an ordinary Taproot spend, indistinguishable from a standard payment.

Beyond privacy, PTLCs reduce the block space used and open the way to new constructions such as *stuckless payments*, which make it possible to retry a stuck payment without risk of double payment. Their deployment requires changes to the Lightning protocol and relied on the availability of Schnorr signatures, activated with Taproot in 2021.

f1f4e2a7-8080-4da8-8480-4f2962d21f3c.title: HMAC-SHA512
f1f4e2a7-8080-4da8-8480-4f2962d21f3c.body:
`HMAC-SHA512` is the acronym for "*Hash-based Message Authentication Code - Secure Hash Algorithm 512*". It is a cryptographic algorithm used to verify the integrity and authenticity of messages exchanged between two parties. It combines the cryptographic hash function `SHA512` with a shared secret key to generate a unique message authentication code (MAC) for each message.

In the context of Bitcoin, the natural use of `HMAC-SHA512` is slightly diverted. This algorithm is used in the deterministic and hierarchical derivation process of a wallet's tree of cryptographic keys. `HMAC-SHA512` is notably used to go from the seed to the master key, then for each derivation from a parent pair to child pairs. This algorithm is also found within another derivation algorithm, named `PBKDF2`, used to go from the recovery phrase and the passphrase to the seed.

f23b26a4-a8fc-4f8a-8b85-8fbf74031361.title: BIP-0387
f23b26a4-a8fc-4f8a-8b85-8fbf74031361.body: Proposal defining the output script descriptors `multi_a()` and `sortedmulti_a()` for multisig in Tapscript using the opcode `OP_CHECKSIGADD`. These descriptors are the equivalent of `multi()` and `sortedmulti()` used in traditional scripts, but adapted to Taproot script-path spending (*script-path spending*). The variant `sortedmulti_a()` sorts the public keys in lexicographic order to guarantee a deterministic result.

f292cddc-9d6d-4fb9-a0ed-f263e94bb270.title: OFFER
f292cddc-9d6d-4fb9-a0ed-f263e94bb270.body: Within the framework of BOLT-12, “*offers*” are static QR codes for making multiple payments on the Lightning Network. Unlike classic invoices, *offers* can be reused. They make it possible to generate multiple invoice requests. When a user scans a QR code containing an *offer*, they send a message to request a new invoice from the associated Lightning node. The node responds with an invoice that the payer can use. *Offers* thus make it possible to have a single identifier to receive many payments from several different users on Lightning.

f2da558b-aaae-476c-af0d-a818270b93c4.title: BLOCK REWARD
f2da558b-aaae-476c-af0d-a818270b93c4.body:
The total bitcoins collected by a miner when they find a valid block on Bitcoin. This reward is made up of two elements: the block subsidy and the transaction fees. The block subsidy is a fixed quantity of bitcoins that the miner can create *ex nihilo*. This quantity gradually decreases over the course of the *halvings*. The transaction fees are the cumulative fees paid by users to carry out the transactions included in the mined block. The fees are also bitcoins created by the miner, but their quantity is limited to the amount of bitcoins destroyed in the transactions. Indeed, the fee of a transaction represents the difference between the total of the *inputs* and the total of the *outputs*.

The block reward is distributed within a specific transaction called the "coinbase". The bitcoins extracted from it are automatically locked for a period of 100 blocks. This is what is called the maturity period.

f30dedc9-de67-4e1a-a03c-d16db2c9a7e4.title: BIP-0174
f30dedc9-de67-4e1a-a03c-d16db2c9a7e4.body:
Defines the PSBT (*Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction*) format, a standard for exchanging unfinalized Bitcoin transactions between different actors such as software wallets, hardware wallets or multisig coordinators. The PSBT makes it possible to separate the steps of creating, updating, signing and finalizing a transaction. The protocol defines six distinct roles: the *Creator* creates the base transaction, the *Updater* adds the necessary information (UTXO, scripts), the *Signer* applies their signature, the *Combiner* merges the partial signatures, the *Finalizer* builds the final unlocking script, and the *Extractor* produces the transaction ready to be broadcast.

This format is essential for multisigs, hardware wallets, coinjoins, and any other workflow where signing is not done on the same device as the construction of the transaction.

f337c682-bedc-4e1d-9f3b-f9a3b2e22d96.title: CONTRIBUTOR
f337c682-bedc-4e1d-9f3b-f9a3b2e22d96.body: A contributor in the context of Bitcoin Core (the majority node implementation on the Bitcoin network) is a person who actively participates in the development of the software by writing code, and by reviewing and testing changes proposed by others. Unlike maintainers, contributors do not have the power to merge changes into the main code; their role is rather to submit *pull requests* (PRs) and to take part in the discussion and validation of these proposals. Any interested individual can become a contributor without needing a nomination or formal approval, which differs from maintainers, who are entrusted with higher administrative and decision-making responsibilities in the project.

f398863e-35ae-4f91-a3e8-0f2c7ee9c6d3.title: BIP-0107
f398863e-35ae-4f91-a3e8-0f2c7ee9c6d3.body: Proposal for a dynamic block size limit in two phases. The first phase provided for scheduled increases: 2 MB in 2016-2017, 4 MB in 2018-2019, then 6 MB in 2020. The second phase introduced an automatic adjustment mechanism: every 4,032 blocks (about 4 weeks), if more than 75% of blocks were filled to at least 60%, the maximum size increased by 10%. This mechanism only allowed increases, never decreases. BIP-0107 has the status “Closed” and was never deployed on Bitcoin.

f3c06327-4716-4dc9-84ea-0113b33ff9ea.title: MYNODE
f3c06327-4716-4dc9-84ea-0113b33ff9ea.body: Open source software that makes it easy to deploy a Bitcoin and Lightning full node. MyNode offers an intuitive web interface to manage Bitcoin Core, LND and a set of complementary applications: block explorer, Electrum server, Mempool.space, BTCPay Server, and other tools. MyNode exists in a free version (Community Edition) and a paid version (Premium) with additional features and dedicated support.

f45a443f-1fa7-40c3-83d0-507da548113e.title: SMPPS
f45a443f-1fa7-40c3-83d0-507da548113e.body: Acronym for "*Shared Maximum Pay Per Share*". It is a method for calculating miner remuneration in the context of mining pools. It is a variant of the PPS method. It limits payouts so that the pool never pays more than what it has earned in block rewards. Thus, even if miners submit valid shares, the total reward distributed cannot exceed the pool's revenue. This method aims to maintain the financial balance of the pool while using a pay-per-task payment system, which reduces the variance for individual miners.

f462ab19-ba86-4f80-9395-3370ea2936ee.title: BIP-0079
f462ab19-ba86-4f80-9395-3370ea2936ee.body: Proposal predating BIP-0078 for a “*pay-to-endpoint*” (P2EP) protocol, also known as Bustapay. The receiver added one of their inputs to the payer's transaction, thereby breaking the chain analysis heuristic that assumes all inputs belong to the same owner. BIP-0079 was superseded by Payjoin (BIP-0078), which formalized and improved this collaborative transaction approach.

f46e0f76-4365-4ac8-a1d3-1cffd5848097.title: OAP - OPEN ASSETS PROTOCOL
f46e0f76-4365-4ac8-a1d3-1cffd5848097.body: The Open Assets Protocol (OAP), designed by Flavien Charlon in 2013, represents the first functional implementation of Colored Coins. This protocol made it possible to store and transfer non-native assets on the Bitcoin blockchain, in the form of tokens called “Colored Coins”. These are specifically marked to symbolize a promise, whether formal or informal, of exchange for real goods or services.

f49ce9b9-7d6a-422f-8e6a-0853aa1aa2e9.title: SATOSHILABS
f49ce9b9-7d6a-422f-8e6a-0853aa1aa2e9.body: Czech company founded in 2013 by Marek Palatinus and Pavol Rusnák, known for having created the Trezor, the very first hardware wallet (*hardware wallet*) in history. Based in Prague, SatoshiLabs has also contributed to the development of important standards for the Bitcoin ecosystem, including BIP-0039, which defines mnemonic phrases.

f4ab9b96-5fb5-47c7-8ff6-5d68da739f7c.title: BIP-0030
f4ab9b96-5fb5-47c7-8ff6-5d68da739f7c.body: Improvement proposal involving a soft fork implemented on March 15, 2012 in order to resolve the problem of duplicate transaction identifiers. Before BIP-0030, it was technically possible to have two different transactions with the same transaction identifier (TXID) in the blockchain. This notably happened twice for coinbase transactions: the one in block 91,880 has the same TXID as the coinbase of block 91,722, and the one in block 91,842 has the same TXID as the coinbase of block 91,812. BIP-0030 resolved this flaw by imposing a simple new rule: no new transaction can have the same TXID as a previously recorded transaction, unless the original transaction has been completely spent (that is, all of its outputs have been used). This soft fork was activated using the *flag day* method. It is therefore one of the first UASFs.

f4f1b663-d2f4-4bb2-b5a4-d6c29a9b080c.title: ELECTRUM SERVER
f4f1b663-d2f4-4bb2-b5a4-d6c29a9b080c.body: An indexer implemented on a Bitcoin full node that allows Electrum wallet software (or any other wallet that supports them) to operate without downloading the entire Bitcoin blockchain. An Electrum Server maintains a complete index of Bitcoin addresses and transactions, which makes it possible to make fast queries from other software. To put it simply, an Electrum Server acts as a kind of bridge between wallet software and a Bitcoin node that has the blockchain.

f50c7c5a-db84-4178-b1b3-7c99a441b746.title: BOLT-09
f50c7c5a-db84-4178-b1b3-7c99a441b746.body: Specification that establishes the centralized registry of *feature bits* used in the Lightning Network to signal the features supported by each node. Features are announced by *flags* in the `init`, `node_announcement` and `channel_announcement` messages. Each feature uses a pair of bits: the even bit indicates mandatory support, the odd bit indicates optional support.

f550b498-51cb-42b9-9c78-0e729e30e696.title: ISSUE
f550b498-51cb-42b9-9c78-0e729e30e696.body: In the context of GitHub and other code hosting platforms, an issue is a report that flags a bug, proposes an improvement or suggests a new feature. It serves as a discussion point for contributors and makes it possible to track tasks to be accomplished or problems to be solved in the project. As a Bitcoin user, you can help the open source software you use by reporting possible bugs through issues on the project's repository.

f5b583c2-19ba-43d0-ac58-8147eb3cdef7.title: BIP-0023
f5b583c2-19ba-43d0-ac58-8147eb3cdef7.body: This BIP is an extension of BIP-0022, aimed at encouraging its adoption by mining *pools*. Proposed by Luke Dashjr, this extension extends the `getblocktemplate` standard of BIP-0022 to cover the full set of features of the *Getwork* protocol, the predecessor of *Stratum*, in order to facilitate the transition of *pools* from *Getwork* to `getblocktemplate`. The main objective of BIP-0023 is to transmit the entire *block template* to miners, thereby allowing them to audit and possibly modify the block structure proposed by the *pool*. This approach aims to mitigate concerns related to mining centralization, by giving individual miners greater control and better transparency over the block creation process.

f5d53aa0-c0e9-42c2-8795-80acdb50ddcb.title: APERTURE
f5d53aa0-c0e9-42c2-8795-80acdb50ddcb.body:
An HTTP 402 reverse proxy developed by Lightning Labs, designed to enable paid access to web services via the Lightning Network. Concretely, Aperture sits in front of a web server or an API and requires a Lightning micropayment before authorizing access to the requested resource.

Aperture relies on the L402 protocol (*Lightning HTTP 402*), which combines the HTTP 402 status code ("Payment Required"), macaroons, and the Lightning Network to create an authentication and payment standard on the web. When a client sends a request to a protected resource, Aperture responds with a 402 code accompanied by a macaroon and a Lightning invoice. Once the payment is made, the client obtains a preimage which, combined with the macaroon, forms a valid L402 token. This token then serves as both authentication and proof of payment for subsequent requests.

Aperture supports proxying of gRPC (HTTP/2) and REST (HTTP/1 and HTTP/2) requests. It also includes a *rate limiting* system per token or per IP address, based on a *token bucket* algorithm. Used in production notably by Lightning Loop, Aperture illustrates a vision of the web where micropayments replace traditional subscription or advertising models to monetize APIs and online services.

f642e13b-424f-415f-9e2f-39a0065a629d.title: CLONE
f642e13b-424f-415f-9e2f-39a0065a629d.body: In the context of Git, consists of creating a local copy of a remote repository. This operation downloads the entire repository, including all branches and the commit history. As a Bitcoin user, you may have to use this command when downloading software.

f67db5a4-538c-4257-b7a9-db221101c879.title: BLKTREE/
f67db5a4-538c-4257-b7a9-db221101c879.body: Name of the old folder used in Bitcoin Core to catalog metadata about all the blocks. This folder was replaced by the `blocks/index/` folder in version `0.8.0`.

f6b44559-b2cd-4ef6-b02f-d3315198122d.title: FAUCET
f6b44559-b2cd-4ef6-b02f-d3315198122d.body:
Website or application that gives away small amounts of bitcoin for free to its visitors, generally in exchange for solving a captcha or a simple task. The term "faucet" refers to the idea of dispensing currency drop by drop.

The first Bitcoin faucet was created by Gavin Andresen in June 2010 and distributed 5 BTC per visitor. In total, about 19,700 BTC were distributed by this site, with the aim of raising awareness of Bitcoin and encouraging its adoption at a time when the cryptocurrency had almost no market value.

Today, faucets exist mainly on test networks (testnet, signet), where they serve to provide test bitcoins to developers. On the main network, faucets have essentially disappeared because of the high value of bitcoin and the proliferation of bots.

f6cf0fb8-84ee-40fb-9e13-6ecf18800468.title: BIP-0033
f6cf0fb8-84ee-40fb-9e13-6ecf18800468.body: Proposal for a system of “stratified” nodes (*stratized nodes*) where light clients delegate validation and blockchain lookups to specialized services (*blockchain services*), rather than performing these operations themselves. BIP-0033 aimed to reduce the validation burden for clients on low-powered or portable devices, by allowing them to rely on several external services and to accept a piece of information only if a common subset of these services confirms it. This approach was never implemented on Bitcoin.

f6d4dd84-764f-4a7d-a144-af263b8b11a6.title: ASSUME VALID
f6d4dd84-764f-4a7d-a144-af263b8b11a6.body:
A configuration parameter in the main Bitcoin Core client that allows a newly initialized node (which has not yet done the IBD) to skip signature verification for all transactions included in blocks prior to a certain given block. This famous block is defined by the fingerprint of its header, that is to say its hash. The chosen block is renewed with each new version of Bitcoin Core. At initialization, since this parameter is enabled by default, the node will therefore verify the chain of block headers to find the branch with the most accumulated work. If the node detects the hash provided by Core in the branch it has retained, it will omit signature verification for the prior blocks. Otherwise, the node will carry out a traditional synchronization (IBD) to verify everything by itself.

The goal of Assume Valid is to speed up the initial synchronization process of a node without compromising security, by assuming that the majority of the network has already validated these transactions in the past. The only real trade-off for the node is that in the event of a prior theft of bitcoins, it will not be warned. However, it can still make sure of the correctness of the quantity of bitcoins issued. Nodes continue to verify the signatures of transactions after the Assume Valid block. This approach rests on the assumption that if a transaction has been accepted by the network for long enough without challenge, it is unlikely to be fraudulent.

f6f1e02f-a08f-4522-9312-02c99ac21fbd.title: EXTENSION BLOCK
f6f1e02f-a08f-4522-9312-02c99ac21fbd.body:
Proposal that aims to increase Bitcoin's transaction capacity by adding a secondary block attached to the main block via a commitment in the coinbase transaction. This concept was initially proposed by Johnson Lau in 2013 under the name "*auxiliary blocks*", then taken up in March 2017 by Christopher Jeffrey, Joseph Poon, Fedor Indutny and Stephen Pair, in the midst of the Blocksize War. In this mechanism, a miner includes in the coinbase an output `OP_RETURN` that contains the Merkle root of an extension block. This secondary block has its own UTXO set and its own consensus rules, while still being validated by the full nodes that support it. Funds move between the main chain and the extension block through "resolution transactions" that consolidate the inputs and outputs between the two sets.

This proposal was never formalized as a BIP and was not activated. It was criticized for its complexity, for its effects similar to those of a hard fork from an economic point of view, and for the absence of real benefits compared to SegWit.

f77a8448-c9f7-42e9-8aad-c98b021d02d1.title: CHECKSUM
f77a8448-c9f7-42e9-8aad-c98b021d02d1.body:
A checksum is a value calculated from a set of data, used to verify the integrity and validity of that data during its transmission or storage. Checksum algorithms are designed to detect accidental errors or unintentional alterations of data, such as transmission errors or file corruption. Different types of checksum algorithms exist, such as parity checks, modular checksums, cryptographic hash functions, or BCH codes (*Bose, Ray-Chaudhuri and Hocquenghem*).

On Bitcoin, checksums are used at the application level to ensure the integrity of receiving addresses. A checksum is calculated from the payload of a user's address, then appended to that address in order to detect possible errors when it is entered. A checksum is also present in recovery phrases (mnemonic).

*It is generally accepted to use the English term "checksum" directly in French.*

f798a1a9-516c-49f9-8e6a-22f3b7e6e017.title: INTERFACE IMPLEMENTATION
f798a1a9-516c-49f9-8e6a-22f3b7e6e017.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the *Interface Implementation* refers to the set of declarations establishing the correspondence between an *Interface* and a *Schema*. It makes it possible to carry out the semantic translation of a contract's binary data, in order to ensure its correct interpretation by the user or by applications, such as *wallets*.

f7c1e8d1-260e-43fd-9496-be8c71cbd211.title: HYPERBITCOINIZATION
f7c1e8d1-260e-43fd-9496-be8c71cbd211.body:
A theoretical concept describing a process of massive and irreversible adoption of Bitcoin as the dominant currency worldwide, gradually replacing fiat currencies. The term was popularized by Daniel Krawisz in 2014, who described it as a voluntary transition from an inferior currency to a superior one, or more precisely as a “Bitcoin-induced currency demonetization” (*Bitcoin-induced currency demonetization*).

Hyperbitcoinization assumes a scenario in which the loss of trust in fiat currencies (due to inflation, financial control or monetary instability) pushes individuals and institutions to adopt Bitcoin massively. Hyperbitcoinization would be a voluntary and decentralized movement, in which each individual freely chooses to migrate to a sounder monetary standard.

This concept is debated within the Bitcoin community itself: some consider it an inevitable long-term goal, while others see it as a theoretical ideal that is unlikely in its absolute form, Bitcoin being able to coexist with other monetary systems, or else simply remaining a currency used at the margins, solely in the counter-economy.

f81bb688-9fed-4884-8477-c93b01e58a89.title: BIP-0068
f81bb688-9fed-4884-8477-c93b01e58a89.body: Introduces the ability to use relative timelocks (*relative lock-time*) through the `nSequence` field. This allows a transaction to specify a relative delay before it can be included in a block. This delay can be defined in terms of a number of blocks, or as a multiple of 512 seconds (that is, real time). Note that this new interpretation of the `nSequence` field is only valid if the `nVersion` field is greater than or equal to `2`. This interpretation of the `nSequence` field is done at the level of Bitcoin's consensus rules. The relative timelock defines a delay starting from the acceptance of a prior transaction, whereas the absolute timelock specifies a precise moment before which the transaction cannot be included in a block. BIP-0068 was introduced via a soft fork on July 4, 2016 together with BIP-0112 and BIP-0113, activated for the first time using the BIP-0009 method.

f83f1367-fa30-4cbd-bc65-6cb6270f5f26.title: RELAY POLICY

f8a21c3e-4d67-4b9a-82e5-1c9d3f6a7b04.title: LOTTERY MINING
f8a21c3e-4d67-4b9a-82e5-1c9d3f6a7b04.body:
Form of *solo mining* in which a miner uses a low-hashrate device to attempt to find a block on their own, without joining a pool. The probability of success is extremely low, but the reward, if a block is found, is collected in full by the miner.

The devices used are generally compact or open-source ASICs such as the Bitaxe, whose hashrate is around 0.5 to 1.2 TH/s depending on the model. At this power, the chances of solving a block are roughly one in several million per ten-minute period. Some miners connect to *solo mining* services such as Solo CKPool or Braiins Solo, which provide them with block *templates* and relay valid blocks to the network, without pooling the rewards.

The approach is more of a hobby than a profitable activity. Its adherents justify it by the contribution to the decentralization of the hashrate and by the appeal of a full reward in case of success.

f8dc865c-9834-4c44-aa1c-700799235c83.title: BULL BITCOIN
f8dc865c-9834-4c44-aa1c-700799235c83.body:
Canadian bitcoin exchange platform founded by Francis Pouliot. Bull Bitcoin stands out for its *non-custodial* model: unlike traditional exchange platforms, it does not take custody of its customers' bitcoins. Purchases are sent directly to the user's personal wallet, and sales are made from that same wallet.

The company adopts a strictly "Bitcoin only" philosophy and offers no other cryptocurrency. Bull Bitcoin supports payments via the Lightning Network for small-amount transactions. The platform is particularly popular in Canada and has expanded to other markets. Its *non-custodial* model reduces counterparty risk for users, since the platform never holds the funds, which brings it closer to the principles of financial sovereignty promoted by Bitcoin.

f8e2a635-08c8-4dfa-a0d8-d7efb162ebd6.title: SLIP
f8e2a635-08c8-4dfa-a0d8-d7efb162ebd6.body: Acronym for "*SatoshiLabs Improvement Proposals*". It is a set of proposals aimed at improving or standardizing the use of Bitcoin, originating from SatoshiLabs, the company behind the Trezor hardware wallets. These proposals are often structured as extensions of BIPs (*Bitcoin Improvement Proposals*), with the aim of enriching existing standards. They set out technical decisions made by SatoshiLabs that do not find their place in the BIPs, but that remain relevant for other wallet software or hardware wallet developers, in particular to help standardize processes.

f8e4e565-f041-45d1-a058-ae9441283d79.title: REVOCATION KEY
f8e4e565-f041-45d1-a058-ae9441283d79.body:
A cryptographic key used in the Lightning Network to allow the punishment of a peer who publishes an old channel state. Each commitment transaction contains a `to_local` output that offers two spending paths:
* one subject to a relative delay (`OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY`) for the owner,
* the other immediately spendable by the counterparty if it holds the corresponding revocation key.

The revocation key is built collaboratively. For a given commitment transaction, Alice provides a commitment point (`C_A`) and Bob provides a revocation base point (`R_B`). The revocation public key is calculated as follows:
```math
Rev\ =\ R_B \cdot SHA256(R_B\ \Vert\ C_A)\ +\ C_A \cdot SHA256(C_A\ \Vert\ R_B)
```
Neither Alice nor Bob can derive the corresponding private key alone. When the channel state is updated, Alice reveals the secret `c_A` associated with her commitment point. Bob can then combine `c_A` with his own secret `r_B` to obtain the revocation private key and, if necessary, build a penalty transaction.

f951d721-85ca-4196-8bb8-75cc81306bb6.title: BIP-0380
f951d721-85ca-4196-8bb8-75cc81306bb6.body: Improvement proposal that introduces a standard language for describing collections of output scripts (*output scripts*) of Bitcoin HD wallets. This language is called “*Output Script Descriptors*”. It aims to standardize the way output scripts are represented and managed, in order to make wallet backup, export and import easier. In addition to private data such as the recovery phrase, the *descriptors* provide all the information needed to recover the key pairs used in an HD wallet. BIP-0380 describes the general operation of *descriptors*, while BIP-0381, BIP-0382, BIP-0383, BIP-0384, BIP-0385 and BIP-0386 specify the expressions used. BIP-0380 was implemented along with all the other BIPs related to *descriptors* (except BIP-0386) in version 0.17 of Bitcoin Core.

f957e3d3-9ba0-435e-96d8-eac6308b9c61.title: TX - TRANSACTION
f957e3d3-9ba0-435e-96d8-eac6308b9c61.body:
In the context of Bitcoin, a transaction (abbreviated "TX") is an operation recorded on the blockchain that transfers ownership of bitcoins from one or more inputs to one or more outputs. Each transaction consumes UTXOs as inputs, which are outputs of previous transactions, and creates new UTXOs as outputs, which can be used as inputs in future transactions.

Each input includes a reference to an existing output as well as a signature script (`scriptSig`) that fulfills the spending conditions (`scriptPubKey`) established by the output it refers to. This is what makes it possible to unlock bitcoins. Outputs define new spending conditions (`scriptPubKey`) for the transferred bitcoins, often in the form of a public key or an address with which the bitcoins are now associated.

f9770873-141e-4717-8698-1da966fe44ca.title: BRAIDPOOL
f9770873-141e-4717-8698-1da966fe44ca.body:
Proposal for a decentralized mining pool for Bitcoin, designed by Bob McElrath. Braidpool aims to solve the centralization problem of traditional mining pools, where the pool operator selects the transactions and controls block construction.

The protocol is based on a DAG (*Directed Acyclic Graph*) mined in parallel to the Bitcoin blockchain. The blocks of the DAG are “weak blocks”: valid Bitcoin blocks that do not satisfy the difficulty target of the main network, but only a reduced target specific to Braidpool. These weak blocks act as shares and make it possible to measure each miner's contribution. Unlike P2Pool, which uses a linear sharechain, the DAG structure better tolerates network latency and reduces the rate of stale (orphan) blocks.

Each miner builds their own block templates and chooses the transactions to include, which preserves the decentralization of Bitcoin's consensus. At the end of each difficulty adjustment period, rewards are distributed to miners via a multisig transaction that uses the FROST protocol. Braidpool is still under development and is not yet deployed in production.

f9bcef6d-f786-4092-a6da-f3370621758c.title: SNARK
f9bcef6d-f786-4092-a6da-f3370621758c.body: A cryptographic proof system whose acronym stands for *Succinct Non-interactive ARgument of Knowledge*. A SNARK allows a prover to convince a verifier that a statement is true, without interaction and without revealing the underlying data, by producing a very small proof (a few hundred bytes) that can be verified in constant time. This succinctness is the main advantage of SNARKs over STARKs. On the other hand, most SNARK constructions, such as Groth16, require a trusted setup ceremony (*trusted setup*) specific to the circuit being proven. If the secret parameters of this ceremony are compromised, it becomes possible to forge false proofs. SNARKs rely on hardness assumptions related to elliptic curves and are therefore not inherently resistant to quantum attacks. In the Bitcoin ecosystem, SNARKs are used notably to compress larger STARK proofs before their on-chain publication, as in the case of the Citrea rollup.

fa141894-01af-4c5e-a973-280389c80816.title: BIP-0018
fa141894-01af-4c5e-a973-280389c80816.body: Proposal by Luke Dashjr titled “*hashScriptCheck*”, which aimed to replace the `scriptSig` and `scriptPubKey` fields of transactions with three new elements: `dataSig` (pure data pushed onto the stack), `scriptCheck` (the validation script) and `hashScriptCheck` (the hash of the expected script placed in the output). Unlike BIP-0017 by the same author, which proposed a new opcode `OP_CHECKHASHVERIFY`, BIP-0018 took a more radical approach by redefining the very structure of transaction inputs and outputs. At the protocol level, the result was identical to BIP-0016 (P2SH), but BIP-0018 formalized the explicit deprecation of `scriptSig` and `scriptPubKey`.

fa2c274c-9fb6-4591-8842-862b8c65c2d1.title: ECONOMIC MAJORITY
fa2c274c-9fb6-4591-8842-862b8c65c2d1.body: Refers to the largest proportion of the economic activity related to the bitcoin currency, generated by merchants. A merchant is any natural or legal person accepting to exchange a good or a service for BTC. These merchants, which include businesses, users, exchange platforms, and miners, vary in size and economic influence. Some are major players, generating substantial economic activity, while others are more modest. The economic majority is therefore defined by those whose combined economic activity represents the preponderant share of this currency. This majority has an influence on the consensus rules, notably in the event of a fork.

fa8d9dad-568c-447e-9c1c-c65b615d46c9.title: BIP-0050
fa8d9dad-568c-447e-9c1c-c65b615d46c9.body: Informational BIP reporting a bug related to the switch from BerkeleyDB to LevelDB that caused a split of the Bitcoin blockchain followed by a major 24-block reorganization on March 12, 2013. This BIP details the incident and the corrective actions implemented.

fab44652-c698-4407-bb2c-9cfeb780a6c8.title: CHAINWORK
fab44652-c698-4407-bb2c-9cfeb780a6c8.body:
A metric that quantifies the total number of hashes expected to produce a given blockchain. Chainwork serves as the criterion for determining the valid chain: nodes always follow the chain that has the greatest chainwork, and not simply the one that contains the most blocks. The calculation relies on the difficulty target of each block. For a given block, the average number of hashes needed to obtain a hash less than or equal to the target is:
```math
\frac{2^{256}}{cible\ +\ 1}
```
The total chainwork of a chain is the sum of these values for each block, from the genesis block up to the block in question. Since difficulty varies over time, two chains of identical lengths can have a very different chainwork: a chain mined under high difficulty will have a higher chainwork than a longer chain built under artificially low difficulty.

In the first version of the software, Satoshi Nakamoto used the number of blocks as the criterion for selecting the valid chain. This approach was vulnerable to manipulation, because an attacker could build a longer chain by keeping the difficulty at a low level. Chainwork replaced this metric to ensure that the valid chain is indeed the one that required the most actual work. The value is accessible via the command `bitcoin-cli getblock` in the field `chainwork`.

fabbc014-067f-4de9-945a-8ef079134902.title: BITCOIN - LOWERCASE B
fabbc014-067f-4de9-945a-8ef079134902.body: The bitcoin (written with a lowercase "b") refers to the monetary unit used for exchanges on the Bitcoin electronic cash system (with a capital "B"). The bitcoin is often abbreviated as "BTC" or "XBT" and serves as a medium of exchange, store of value and unit of account within the network. Each bitcoin is divisible into 100 million smaller units, called "satoshis" or "sats", in honor of its creator, Satoshi Nakamoto. Bitcoins are issued through the proof-of-work process (mining). The total number of bitcoins is limited to approximately 21 million.

fabd96cf-3f56-4f3e-9c1c-5930ae05c34a.title: PSEUDO-RANDOM
fabd96cf-3f56-4f3e-9c1c-5930ae05c34a.body:
This adjective is used to describe a sequence of numbers that, although the result of a deterministic process, displays characteristics approaching those of an ideal, truly random sequence. The notion of ideal randomness implies a total absence of predictability and of correlation between successive elements. A pseudo-random number is generated by a deterministic algorithm and therefore, in theory, it is entirely predictable if one knows the initial state of the generator.

A pseudo-random number generator (“*PRNG*” in English, or “GNPA” in French) is an algorithm used to produce such numbers. It generally starts from an initial value, or “seed”, and then applies a series of mathematical transformations to produce the sequence of numbers. Because of this determinism, it is important for cryptographic security that the initial seed remain secret. Pseudo-random sequences are widely used in various fields, notably cryptography, because they exhibit an apparently random behavior that is sufficient for many applications. Evaluating the quality of a PRNG rests on the extent to which its output approaches true randomness in terms of distribution, correlations and other statistical properties. In the context of Bitcoin, pseudo-random numbers are used to produce private keys, or to produce a seed for hierarchical deterministic wallets.

fb6c88ad-769d-4730-b3bd-e4fe07817fb5.title: FEDIMINT
fb6c88ad-769d-4730-b3bd-e4fe07817fb5.body: Bitcoin payment and management protocol designed to improve privacy and reduce the demands placed on the main chain by pooling the custody of funds. Fedimint was created by Eric Sirion in 2021. It relies on a Chaumian bank system which, instead of being centralized around a single trusted actor, relies on federations. These federations are groups of trusted guardians who collectively hold and manage the bitcoins of the users in their group. Within the group, users can make payments with notes issued in exchange for their deposit of bitcoins. The idea behind Fedimint is to deploy this concept at the level of local communities. It is therefore a sort of evolution of the deposit bank based on bitcoin, with David Chaum's eCash system, and the use of a federation of trusted people in charge of the deposit and the issuance of the underlying asset.

fb886440-f094-4b84-9bc4-54f08f9724e4.title: COLLABORATIVE TRANSACTION
fb886440-f094-4b84-9bc4-54f08f9724e4.body: Bitcoin transaction that involves several different entities as inputs of the transaction. It is therefore also a transaction model that can be used in chain analysis. The typical example of a collaborative transaction is the coinjoin, where several users pool their UTXOs as inputs to recover the sum (minus transaction fees) in outputs of the same amount, in order to prevent tracing by breaking the history of the coins.

fc01ce56-bee1-4c5b-a9fe-acb98cf1c63a.title: COOPERATIVE CLOSE
fc01ce56-bee1-4c5b-a9fe-acb98cf1c63a.body:
Closing of a Lightning channel carried out with the mutual agreement of both parties. It is the most advantageous closing method: both channel partners jointly sign a closing transaction that redistributes the funds to their respective addresses, without a timelock.

Unlike a forced closure (*force close*), where a unilateral commitment transaction is broadcast and imposes a *timelock* before the funds become accessible, a cooperative close produces a simple transaction. Mining fees are therefore reduced (since they can be adjusted to the current fee market), and the funds are available as soon as the transaction is confirmed.

fc559da9-6ece-4c56-89bf-50f511f16307.title: BIP-0052
fc559da9-6ece-4c56-89bf-50f511f16307.body: Proposal for a new proof-of-work paradigm called "Optical Proof of Work" (oPoW), aimed at reducing the energy consumption of Bitcoin mining. BIP-0052 introduces "HeavyHash", a cryptographic construction that combines a Keccak (SHA-3) hash with a matrix-vector multiplication. This multiplication operation is designed to be executed optimally by photonic coprocessors, a new class of chips using light instead of electric currents to perform computations. The goal is to shift the costs of mining from operating expenses (OPEX), mainly electricity, to capital expenditures (CAPEX), that is, hardware. This would make mining profitable regardless of the local cost of electricity, thus promoting greater geographic decentralization. Although the BIP is classified as a hard fork, the authors suggest that it would be possible to implement oPoW via a soft fork in *dual PoW* (SHA-256 and oPoW in parallel). This proposal remains at the draft stage.

fc722a57-45f7-4263-b2a1-6d3bf7b8c060.title: BITCOIN ADDRESS

fcbac257-820e-4ab4-ab39-4ff0eda4f1eb.title: PATHFINDING
fcbac257-820e-4ab4-ab39-4ff0eda4f1eb.body:
Process used by a node to determine the optimal path to route a payment through the network of Lightning channels. *Pathfinding* is performed by the payer's node, which must select the most suitable intermediate nodes to reach the recipient. This choice is based on several criteria such as fees, channel capacity, and *timelocks*.

*Pathfinding* algorithms build a graph of the network topology from *gossip* data and evaluate the different possible routes between the paying node and the receiver. These routes are ranked from best to worst according to various criteria. The node then tries these routes until it succeeds in making the payment on one of them.

fcc6b84e-16b3-4b18-911e-da0abcad2845.title: DUSTRELAYFEE
fcc6b84e-16b3-4b18-911e-da0abcad2845.body:
Standardness rule used by network nodes to determine what they consider the "dust limit". This parameter sets a fee rate in sats per virtual kilobyte (sats/kvB) that serves as a reference for calculating whether the value of a UTXO is lower than the fees needed to include it in a transaction. Indeed, a UTXO is considered "dust" on Bitcoin if it requires more fees to be spent than the value it represents itself. The calculation of this limit is as follows:

```text
limite = (taille entrée + taille sortie) * taux de frais
```

Since the fee rate required for a transaction to be included in a Bitcoin block constantly varies, the `DustRelayFee` parameter makes it possible to define the fee rate used in this calculation by each node. By default, on Bitcoin Core, this value is set to 3,000 sats/kvB. For example, to calculate the dust limit of a P2PKH input and output, which measure 148 and 34 bytes respectively, the calculation would be: 

```text
limite (sats) = (148 + 34) * 3000 / 1000 = 546 sats
```

This means that the node in question will not relay transactions including a UTXO secured with P2PKH whose value is lower than 546 sats.

fcddc21f-8489-4d35-a042-f9b30a6538b5.title: CITREA
fcddc21f-8489-4d35-a042-f9b30a6538b5.body: The first zero-knowledge proof rollup (ZK rollup) deployed on Bitcoin, developed by Chainway Labs. Citrea uses a Type 2 zkEVM, built with RISC Zero, which offers full compatibility with the Ethereum virtual machine and allows Solidity developers to deploy their contracts directly on Bitcoin. The system processes transactions off-chain in batches, generates STARK proofs (then wrapped into SNARK proofs) and publishes these proofs directly on Bitcoin, which serves as both the data availability layer and the settlement layer. Citrea's two-way bridge, named Clementine, relies on BitVM2 and operates with a 1-of-N trust assumption: as long as at least one verifier of the bridge is honest, the funds are safe. The native bitcoin on Citrea is called cBTC. The platform also offers ctUSD, a dollar-pegged stablecoin backed by US Treasury bills, issued in partnership with MoonPay and M0. Citrea requires no modification to Bitcoin's consensus rules. The *mainnet* has been live since January 2026.

fd043cb1-d219-4448-a4c8-ebe1de19a3f8.title: I2P
fd043cb1-d219-4448-a4c8-ebe1de19a3f8.body:
Anonymous communication network designed to ensure the confidentiality of exchanges on the Internet. Like Tor, I2P encrypts network data and uses a routing system called *garlic routing*. This method guarantees the anonymity of communications by passing them through intermediary servers that redirect the information without knowing the identity of the sender or that of the recipient. Just like Tor, I2P can be used on a Bitcoin node, in order to secure its network communications.

*The acronym “I2P” stands for “Invisible Internet Project”.*

fd28eb68-d1b8-4e2b-aa85-500480c7f8d4.title: ENTRY POINT
fd28eb68-d1b8-4e2b-aa85-500480c7f8d4.body:
Information that makes it possible to link an *on-chain* activity (an address, a transaction, a *cluster*...) to a form of identity belonging to a user or an entity. For example, if you publish your receiving address on Twitter under your name, an analyst could find it and associate it with your identity. In this case, the tweet would constitute an entry point for a chain analysis. To identify an entry point, analysts can use OSINT, but the most common method for associating an *on-chain* activity with an identity remains KYC.

![OSINT entry point: a public address on Twitter links Loïc's identity to the observed address cluster.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/p/point-d-entree/assets/image-1.png)

fd394e4b-9289-45f7-8fb2-ce21aec7dc2b.title: SYBIL
fd394e4b-9289-45f7-8fb2-ce21aec7dc2b.body: A computer attack in which an individual or entity creates multiple false identities in a system in order to exert undue influence or gain an unauthorized advantage. In the context of Bitcoin, such an attack aims to gain undue influence over the system, thereby making it possible to manipulate the consensus mechanisms. To counter Sybil attacks, Satoshi Nakamoto devised a proof-of-work system that imposes a non-negligible marginal cost on the creation of multiple votes.

fd644fe9-2c34-46a0-b40c-f9d3f2920661.title: RPC - REMOTE PROCEDURE CALL
fd644fe9-2c34-46a0-b40c-f9d3f2920661.body:
Computer protocol allowing a program to execute a procedure on another remote computer, as if it were executed locally.

Specifically in the context of Bitcoin, it is used to allow applications to interact with `bitcoind`. It can be used to execute commands on a Bitcoin node, such as sending transactions, managing wallets or accessing information about the blockchain. The security of this interaction is ensured by authentication via a `.cookie` file or credentials, so that only authorized clients can make RPC calls on the node.

fd64d3cd-a155-4e51-b56b-8f424c448024.title: RICOCHET
fd64d3cd-a155-4e51-b56b-8f424c448024.body: A technique consisting of making several dummy transactions to oneself in order to simulate a transfer of ownership of the bitcoins. Ricochet makes it possible to blur the specificities that can compromise the fungibility of a Bitcoin coin. For example, if you perform a coinjoin, your coin coming out of the mix will be identified as such. This label of “_coin from a coinjoin_” can affect the fungibility of a UTXO. Regulated entities, such as exchange platforms, may refuse to accept a UTXO that has gone through a coinjoin, or even demand explanations from its owner, with the risk of having one's account blocked or one's funds frozen. In some cases, the platform may even report your behavior to state authorities. This is where the Ricochet method comes into play. To blur the footprint left by a coinjoin, Ricochet executes four successive transactions in which the user transfers their funds to themselves on different addresses. After this chain of transactions, the Ricochet tool finally routes the bitcoins to their final destination, such as an exchange platform. The objective is to create distance between the original coinjoin transaction and the final act of spending. In this way, chain analysis tools will think that there was likely a transfer of ownership after the coinjoin, and that it is therefore pointless to take action against the sender. The most common use case for Ricochet arises when it is necessary to conceal prior participation in a coinjoin on a UTXO, notably to avoid being the target of the AML/CFT policies of regulated platforms or of *blacklists*. The Ricochet tool is available on the Samourai Wallet wallet.

fe21d359-96e4-4ecc-976c-8410360faa1b.title: PROPAGATION / BROADCAST
fe21d359-96e4-4ecc-976c-8410360faa1b.body: Process by which information, such as transactions and blocks, is passed from node to node across the Bitcoin network. When a user makes a transaction, it is first verified by the node they are connected to. After validation, this transaction is relayed to the other nodes connected to that node, which in turn verify it and then propagate it. Quickly, a large share of the nodes on the network will be aware of the transaction. If it offers enough fees, miners will include it in their candidate block. When a block containing this transaction is validated, the transaction is then confirmed.

fe221820-ee07-4e49-a1a7-4a16b188bb33.title: ANTPOOL
fe221820-ee07-4e49-a1a7-4a16b188bb33.body: A Bitcoin mining pool founded in 2014 by Bitmain Technologies, the leading manufacturer of ASIC mining hardware. Based in China, Antpool regularly ranks among the largest mining pools in the world in terms of hashrate. It offers several payout methods and caters to individual miners and professional mining infrastructures alike.

fe3088e7-4183-4b62-8f88-da30dec601e3.title: CLUSTER
fe3088e7-4183-4b62-8f88-da30dec601e3.body: In the context of chain analysis, a cluster is a set of receiving addresses that are associated with the same entity by an analyst. Using various heuristics, it is possible to detect *on-chain* activities that appear to originate from a single person or organization. This grouping of activities forms what is called a *cluster*. The goal of chain analysis is often to identify an entry point into this cluster, thereby making it possible to link all of these activities to some form of real-world identity.

fe5b11fb-800c-485a-9a88-83004eb6fc1a.title: LIANA
fe5b11fb-800c-485a-9a88-83004eb6fc1a.body: *Open source* Bitcoin wallet management software developed by the company Wizardsardine (founded by Kevin Loaec and Antoine Poinsot). Liana stands out for its use of Miniscript to enable advanced, highly customizable security setups, notably recovery mechanisms based on *timelocks*. For example, a user can define a primary key for everyday spending, then one or more recovery keys that only become active after a defined period of inactivity. This model makes it possible to set up inheritance plans or automatic backup mechanisms without a trusted third party. Liana is compatible with *hardware wallets* that support Miniscript.

fe624acb-2d22-4ebb-ba81-1293e16f380c.title: HARDENED DERIVATION
fe624acb-2d22-4ebb-ba81-1293e16f380c.body: A process for generating child keys in HD wallets. Hardened derivation uses the parent private key as input to the `HMAC-SHA512` function, which makes it impossible to generate child public keys from the parent public key and the parent chain code. The process involves concatenating the parent private key and an index greater than or equal to `2^{31}`, followed by applying `HMAC-SHA512` with the parent chain code. The result is split into two parts: the first 256 bits are added to the parent private key to obtain the child private key, while the remaining 256 bits form the child chain code. This method ensures that even if an extended public key is compromised, it cannot be used to derive the child public keys. In a standard derivation, hardened derivation is used at all derivation levels down to the account depth. In derivation path notations, a hardened derivation is identified with an apostrophe `'` or, more rarely, with a `h`.

feb36d7f-0654-4621-b1d8-78a00f0e652b.title: HASHER
feb36d7f-0654-4621-b1d8-78a00f0e652b.body: In the context of mining pools, participants are often referred to as "hashers". The main task of these individual miners is to hash block *templates* provided by the pool's server, searching for hashes that satisfy the difficulty target defined for *shares*, and not Bitcoin's. The rest of the mining process, which includes the actual construction of blocks, the selection of transactions, and the verification and broadcast of the valid proof of work according to Bitcoin's own difficulty, is carried out directly by the pools.

fef1d427-6445-4d2b-a07e-dd52edfb0954.title: EXTERNAL KEYCHAIN
fef1d427-6445-4d2b-a07e-dd52edfb0954.body:
In the derivation of hierarchical deterministic wallets, the external keychain is a derivation branch used to generate receiving addresses intended to receive payments coming from the outside, that is, from another wallet. Each account as defined at depth 3 has two keychains at depth 4: an external keychain and an internal keychain (also called “change”). The external keychain is derived with an index of `/0/`.  The external keychain derives addresses intended to be shared publicly, that is, the addresses we are offered when we click the “receive” button in our wallet software.

![BIP-84 tree with an arrow pointing to the Chains level, where each account splits into an external chain /0 and an internal chain /1.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/c/chaine-externe/assets/image-1.png)

ff62c78d-122a-43d2-a3b4-0fc9c720f75d.title: BIP-0003
ff62c78d-122a-43d2-a3b4-0fc9c720f75d.body:
Major revision of the BIP process made in 2024 and adopted in 2026, replacing BIP-0002, which had been in force since 2016. BIP-0003 simplifies the workflow by reducing the previous nine statuses to four: “*Draft*”, “*Complete*”, “*Deployed*” and “*Closed*”. It redefines the BIP types by replacing “*Standards Track*” with “*Specification*”, thereby clarifying that all BIPs are individual recommendations from their authors and not imposed standards. The role of BIP editors is refocused on administrative and editorial tasks, with less discretionary judgment on the acceptance of proposals.

Among the new features, BIP-0003 introduces a semantic versioning system with a mandatory “*Changelog*” after the “*Complete*” status, the ability to appoint “*Deputies*” to assist authors, and the use of SPDX expressions for licenses. The *Markdown* format is now accepted in addition to *MediaWiki*. The comment system of BIP-0002, judged ineffective for lack of participation, is abolished. “*Process*” BIPs become living documents modifiable indefinitely by rough consensus. BIP-0003 has the “*Deployed*” status.

ffbbd17a-e7f1-4fe4-bc0b-3d9db3cf4a78.title: WATCHTOWER
ffbbd17a-e7f1-4fe4-bc0b-3d9db3cf4a78.body:
External service that monitors the Bitcoin blockchain in place of a Lightning node to detect any attempt to cheat on its channels. If a dishonest peer publishes an old commitment transaction while the node is offline, the watchtower automatically broadcasts the corresponding justice transaction to recover all of the channel's funds before the *timelock* expires.

The mechanism is designed to preserve the node's privacy: with each update of a channel, the node encrypts the pre-signed penalty transaction with the TXID of the relevant commitment transaction, then sends the watchtower this encrypted blob along with a truncated portion of the TXID. The watchtower can only decrypt the transaction if it observes a matching TXID on the blockchain by means of the truncated portion, that is, in the event of actual cheating. It therefore has no visibility into the identity of peers, the balances or the structure of the channels during normal operation. It will learn this information only in the event of cheating.

The watchtower constitutes a minimal trusted third party: it can neither modify nor divert the funds, since the justice transaction is already signed with outputs fixed in favor of the channel's owner. The only risk for the node is to rely on a watchtower that would not fulfill its role at the moment it is actually needed. This is why a node can configure several of them, in order to ensure that at least one of them will act correctly when needed.

There are so-called "altruistic" watchtowers, which are offered publicly and free of charge, and any Lightning node can also play this role for other nodes.

ffc8d20e-2173-4513-a1ec-d278c3720034.title: BOSMINER
ffc8d20e-2173-4513-a1ec-d278c3720034.body: *Open-source* mining software developed in Rust by Braiins as a more modern alternative to CGMiner. BOSminer is specifically designed for ASICs. Integrated into the Braiins OS ecosystem, it allows advanced management of ASICs, with features such as overclocking, detailed performance monitoring and Stratum V2 support.

ffd11420-f7e2-4861-a85c-f23b988938d2.title: BIP-0301
ffd11420-f7e2-4861-a85c-f23b988938d2.body: Proposal by Paul Sztorc and CryptAxe defining “*Blind Merged Mining*” (BMM), a blind merged mining mechanism for drivechains. BMM allows Bitcoin miners to collect sidechain transaction fees in BTC on Bitcoin, without needing to run the software of each sidechain. BIP-0301 complements BIP-0300 to form the complete technical basis of drivechains.

ffe49b3b-d7d7-4859-a54a-4aeef9bb2570.title: CUSTODY
ffe49b3b-d7d7-4859-a54a-4aeef9bb2570.body:
In the context of Bitcoin, refers to the holding and management of the private keys that allow control of bitcoins. BTC *custody* can be provided in two ways: either personally by the user, who keeps the private keys needed to access their bitcoins themselves (what is called "*self-custody*"), or by a third party, such as an exchange platform, where the company holds the private keys and manages the bitcoins on the user's behalf. This second option is riskier than *self-custody*, as it exposes the user's funds to the risks of hacking, bankruptcy, or fraudulent behavior on the part of the custodian.

*In French, the English term "custody" is generally used. It could also be translated as "garde".*
